**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):**

**Surah al-Ma'idah (The Table Spread)**

It is also called Surah al-'Uqud (The Contracts) and al-Munqidhah (The Deliverer). Ibn al-Furs said: "It is so called because it delivers its reciter from the angels of punishment."

It is Medinan (*madaniyyah*, revealed after the Hijrah) according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. Abu Ja'far ibn Bishr and al-Sha'bi said: "It is Medinan, except for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾, which was revealed in Makkah."

Abu 'Ubayd related, from Muhammad al-Qurazi, who said: "Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the Farewell Pilgrimage, between Makkah and Madinah, while he was on his camel. Its shoulder split, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dismounted from it, because of the heaviness of the revelation."

Several narrators related, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: "al-Ma'idah is the last surah to be revealed."

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi related, from Ibn 'Umar: "The last surahs were al-Ma'idah and al-Fath."

It has already been mentioned above, from al-Bara', that the last surah revealed was Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). Probably each one mentioned what he knew. Nothing in this is traced back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Yes, Abu 'Ubayd related, from Damrah ibn Habib and 'Atiyyah ibn Qays, who both said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make lawful what it makes lawful and make unlawful what it makes unlawful." However, this does not fully fit the intended meaning, because of the word *min* (among).

Some people used this report to argue that nothing in this surah has been abrogated (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation). Among those who explicitly stated that there is no abrogation in it were 'Amr ibn Shurahbil and al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with them both), as Abu Dawud related from them. He also related from al-Sha'bi that nothing in it has been abrogated except the words of Allah: ﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) related that he said: "Two verses of this surah have been abrogated: the verse of the garlands, and the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾." Some claimed that it contains nine abrogated verses. The discussion of this will come, Allah willing.

[p. 48]

Its number of verses is one hundred and twenty according to the Kufans, twenty-three according to the Basrans, and twenty-two according to others.

The connection between it and Surah al-Nisa', as mentioned by al-Jalal al-Suyuti (may Allah have mercy on him), is that Surah al-Nisa' included many contracts, both explicit and implicit. The explicit ones are marriage contracts, the contract of dowry, the contract of alliance, and the contract of covenant and safe-conduct. The implicit ones are the contract of bequest, deposit, agency, loan and hire, and others that fall under the general meaning of the words of Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾. So it was fitting that it be followed by a surah that opens with the command to fulfil contracts. It is as if it was said: "O people, fulfil the contracts whose mention was completed in the surah that has ended", even though this surah also contains contracts.

Also, the reason for placing al-Nisa' first and al-Ma'idah after it is that the beginning of the former is "O people" (*ya ayyuha al-nas*), and this address occurs in several places, and it is more similar to the revelation of the Makkan surahs. The beginning of the latter is "O you who believe" (*ya ayyuha alladhina amanu*), and this address occurs in several places, and it is more similar to the address of the Medinan surahs. Placing the general and the Makkan-like before is more fitting.

Furthermore, these two surahs are, in their closeness and unity, like al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran. Those two shared in establishing the fundamentals, such as monotheism and prophethood and the like, while these two establish the branches of the legal rulings.

Al-Ma'idah ends with the attribute of power, just as al-Nisa' began with it. Al-Nisa' began with the beginning of creation, and al-Ma'idah ends with the final end of resurrection and recompense. So it is as if they were one surah that contained the rulings from the beginning to the end. This surah also has a connection with al-Fatihah and the two Zahrawan (al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran), as is clear to the one who reflects.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾. *Al-wafa'* is preserving what the contract requires and carrying out its obligations. It is said: *wafa*, *waffa* and *awfa* have the same meaning, but the intensified form (*waffa*) carries more emphasis than the basic form. The root meaning of *al-'aqd* is tying firmly, and then it was used figuratively for a firmly bound covenant.

Al-Tabarsi distinguished between *al-'aqd* and *al-'ahd* (covenant or pledge). *Al-'aqd* carries the sense of strengthening and tightening, and it cannot be done except between two parties, whereas *al-'ahd* may be made by one party alone.

The scholars differed about what is meant by these contracts, in several views:

First: It means the covenants that Allah, the Exalted, took from His servants to believe in Him and obey Him regarding what He made lawful or unlawful for them. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).

Second: The contracts that people make among themselves, such as the oath of allegiance, the marriage contract, the sale contract, and the like. This is the view of Ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Aslam.

Third: The covenants that were taken in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) for mutual support and assistance against whoever wronged someone. This is related from Mujahid, al-Rabi' and Qatadah, and others.

Fourth: The covenants that Allah, the Exalted, took from the People of the Book to act upon what is in the Torah and the Gospel, which requires believing in the Prophet ﷺ and in what he brought. This is related from Ibn Jurayj and Abu Salih.

According to this view, what is meant by "those who believe" is the believers among the People of the Book, and this goes against the apparent meaning. Some commentators chose that what is meant by it is everything that Allah, the Exalted, obligated on His servants, and all the religious duties and rulings that He bound them to, as well as what they contract among themselves, such as contracts of trust and transactions and the like, which must be fulfilled or which are religiously good. The command is to be understood as general demand, either recommended or obligatory. This includes avoiding what is forbidden and what is disliked, because this is more in accordance with the general wording, since it is a plural definite noun (*jam' muhalla bi-al-lam*), and more comprehensive in its benefit.

Al-Zamakhshari inclined to the view that what is meant is the contracts of Allah, the Exalted, upon them in His religion, namely making lawful what He made lawful and making unlawful what He made unlawful. This is because it contains, as stated in *al-Kashf*, the excellence of the opening and the detail after the general statement. However, it is mentioned in the same work that the preferred view of the one group is better, because it achieves both aims and adds greater generality. It also says that the noble surahs contain the fundamentals of religious duties in both roots and branches, and that even if there were nothing but the words: ﴿Cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾ and ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾, it would suffice. This view was criticized with remarks that are not free from scrutiny.

Some claimed that it implies removing the leather sock before reaching water, but what al-Zamakhshari inclined to is free of that. The matter is minor. Al-Raghib was inclined to the general view, as is apparent. He said: Contracts, in terms of the one contracted and the contractor, are of three kinds:

A contract between Allah, the Exalted, and the servant, a contract between the servant and himself, and a contract between him and another human being. Each of these, in terms of what makes it binding, is of two kinds:

The first is what reason requires, which is what Allah, the Exalted, placed the knowledge of within man. He reaches it either by the immediate understanding of reason or by minimal reflection. This is indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, and the rest of the verse.

The second is what the Shari'ah (sacred law) requires, which is what the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ have shown us. This makes six kinds, and each of them is either imposed initially or imposed by a person's own undertaking.

The second (what a person undertakes) has four kinds:

The first is what must be fulfilled, such as vows related to acts of devotion, for example, saying: "It is upon me to fast if Allah grants me health."

The second is what is recommended to fulfil but it is permissible to leave, such as one who swears to abstain from a permissible act. He may expiate for his oath and do that act.

The third is what it is recommended not to fulfil, and this is what the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you swears to something and sees something better than it, let him do what is better and expiate for his oath."

The fourth is what it is obligatory not to fulfil, such as saying: "It is upon me to kill such-and-such a Muslim."

So multiplying six kinds by four gives twenty-four kinds. The apparent meaning of the verse requires every contract except those whose abandonment is an act of devotion or obligatory. So understand this and do not be heedless.

﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock﴾. This begins the detailed explanation of the rulings that He commanded them to fulfil. Allah, glorified is He, began with this because it relates to the essential needs of livelihood. *Al-bahimah* (beast) refers to animate creatures that have no intellect at all. Al-Zajjaj held this view, and it was called *bahimah* because of its lack of discernment and because matters are obscured to it.

Imam al-Sha'rani related from his shaykh 'Ali al-Khawwas (may his secret be sanctified) that the reason the beasts were called *bahaim* is only that the matter of their speech and conditions is obscured to most creatures, not that the matter is obscured to them. He mentioned what indicates their reason and knowledge, and the explanation of that will come, Allah willing.

Many said: *al-bahimah* is the name for every four-legged creature of land and sea. Its being attached to *al-an'am* (grazing livestock) is for specification, like "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*). That is: lawful for you is the eating of the beasts from among the grazing livestock, which are the eight pairs mentioned in its surah. This is objected to because *bahimah* is a genus noun and *al-an'am* is a species of it, so attaching it to it is like attaching "animal" to "human", and this is considered unpleasant. The answer is that attaching a general term to a specific term, when it comes from an eloquent speaker who intends a benefit by mentioning it, is good, as in "the city of Baghdad". Since the word "Baghdad" was not Arabic and its meaning was not known, the word "city" was attached to it to explain what it names and to clarify it. Similarly, "the tree of the arak (toothbrush tree)": since *arak* is used for its twigs, it is attached to clarify what is meant, and so on. Otherwise it would be superfluous and objectionable verbiage. Here, since *al-an'am* may be specifically applied to camels, because that is its basic meaning, according to what is said, and for this reason it is only said "*al-na'am*" for them, the word *bahimah* was attached to it to indicate what is intended. The word *bahimah* is mentioned and in the singular to mean the genus, and *al-an'am* is in the plural to include its types. The gazelles and wild cattle were added to it. It was also said that these two are what is meant by *bahimah*, and similar animals that resemble grazing livestock in chewing the cud and lacking fangs. This is related from al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.

In that case, its attachment to *al-an'am* is because of the resemblance between them. Some verifiers permitted, in the attachment of the similar to what it resembles, that it means the *lam* (of possession), by making the connection of the similar to what it resembles a specific relation between them. Or it means *min* (of explanation), by making the similar itself the same as what it resembles. The benefit of this attachment here is to signal the shared reason for the ruling between the two items being attached, as if it were said: "Lawful for you are the beasts that resemble grazing livestock, whose lawfulness was previously explained to you, which share with them the ground for the ruling."

It was also said: what is meant by *bahimat al-an'am* is what comes out of their bellies of unborn young after their slaughter, which is dead meat. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, and it is the view related from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them all). In that case the verse explicitly states the lawfulness of eating them, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. He based it on more than one report. From it is understood the lawfulness of livestock.

The placing of the prepositional phrase (*lakum*, for you) before the deputy subject (*uhillat*, was made lawful) is to show concern for what is placed first, because it brings quick pleasure and creates anticipation for what is mentioned later.

[p. 49]

In the verse there is a refutation of the Magians, for they made the slaughter of animals and eating them unlawful. They said: "Because slaughtering them is causing pain, and causing pain is ugly, especially the pain of one who has reached such helplessness that he cannot defend himself, and the ugly is not approved by the Merciful, Wise God."

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on surah 5, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

They claimed, may God curse them, that the suffering of animals proceeds only from the forces of darkness and not from the light. The Tanasukhiyya (adherents of metempsychosis) did not permit the suffering to proceed from Him, exalted is He, initially and in any way, except by way of recompense for crimes previously committed. They held that beasts are morally accountable (mukallafa), aware of the pains inflicted on them, and that these pains are a recompense for their own deeds. Were this not so, their being deterred from returning to the offence by pain, through their transfer to a nobler body, could not be conceived.

Some of them claimed that there is no species of beast without a prophet sent to it from among its own kind. Others went further and claimed that all inanimate things (jamadat) are living, morally accountable beings, and that they are recompensed for the good and evil they commit. Imam al-Sha'rani attributed something of this kind to the Sufi masters. The people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) rejected this utterly. When the Bakriyya, a group among the Muslims, found it difficult to answer this doubt on their own principles, yet believed that the command to slaughter animals had come from God, they claimed that beasts do not feel pain, and likewise children who do not reason. It is not hidden that this contradicts what is self-evident, and it is no less than denying the life, movements, sensation and perception of those mentioned.

The Mu'tazila answered with what the Ahl al-Sunna refuted. They answered that the permission to slaughter animals is a disposal by God, exalted is He, over His pure dominion, so there is no objection to it. The rational notions of good and evil (al-tahsin wa al-taqbih al-'aqliyyan) have been folded away from discussion in the science of kalam (theology), and so too the doctrine of light and darkness.

Some of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: Since man is the noblest of the kinds of animals, and the order of the world is completed by him, it is not rationally repugnant to make something beneath him a food for him, by slaughtering it and inflicting pain on it, out of concern for his welfare, in accordance with the wisdom whose secret the bird of thought cannot soar to.

Some people said: The verse is ambiguous (mujmala), since what is meant may be the permission to benefit from its hide, bone or wool, or all of these. In this there is scrutiny, for the evident implication of the eating is something over which two rams hardly butt heads. Yes, Ibn al-Subki and others mentioned that God's words ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ are ambiguous because its meaning was unknown before the revelation of what explains it, and the ambiguity extends to what precedes it. But that is not the locus of dispute.

The exception is continuous (muttasil) from (بَهِيمَةُ) (beast), with a deleted genitive (mudaf mahdhuf) from (ما يُتْلى), meaning: except the forbidden [ones] (مُحَرَّمٌ) of what is recited to you, and by the forbidden is meant the carrion, and that over which the name of other than God has been invoked, down to the end of what is mentioned in the third verse of the surah. Or it is from the subject of (يُتْلى), meaning: except what the verse of its prohibition recites to you, so that (ما) denotes the forbidden animal, not the recited word. It is also permitted to regard it as a metaphorical attribution (majaz fi al-isnad) without any deletion, and this is not far-fetched.

As for making it a stripped-off (mufarragh) exception in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: except as a thing in the circumstances that are recited, it is very far-fetched, as al-Shihab said. Some held that it is disjunctive (munqati') on the basis of the apparent sense, since what is recited is an utterance, and the excepted-from is not of its kind. Most follow the first view. The place of the exception is accusative (nasb), and the nominative (raf') has been permitted, as established in grammar.

﴿not violating the sanctity of game﴾: (غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي الصَّيْدِ) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (لَكم), according to what most exegetes hold. (الصَّيْدِ) may be a verbal noun (masdar) or an object (maf'ul). His words, exalted is He, (وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ) ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾, is a circumstantial clause from what is concealed in (مُحِلِّي).

(الحُرُمُ) is the plural of (حَرامٌ), meaning the one in the state of ihram. The sense resulting is: these things are made lawful for you, not as those who make hunting or eating game lawful while in ihram.

Al-Zamakhshari explained the non-permission of game in the state of ihram as abstention from it while they are in ihram. He said: It is as if it were said: We have made lawful for you some of the cattle at a time when you are abstaining from hunting, ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾, so that there be no hardship upon you. He did not take the making lawful as the belief in its lawfulness, supposing that restricting the making lawful to the absence of belief in its lawfulness is unsound. It may be said: the matter is so if what is meant is the absolute belief in lawfulness. But if what is meant is the absence of a belief arising from the Law and consequent upon it, then it is not so, for his state, if it is not the very state of abstention, is not foreign to it, as will not be hidden from one who reflects. Shaykh of our shaykhs Jirjis Efendi al-Arbili, may God have mercy on him, pointed to this.

It was objected in al-Bahr, in accordance with what most have held, that it entails restricting the permission of the beast of the cattle to a state in which the lawfulness of game is absent while they are in ihram, although the cattle were made lawful for them absolutely. So no benefit appears in it unless by the beast of the cattle is meant the game that resembles them, such as gazelles, wild oxen and wild asses. It was answered that, even without the consistent application of the understood sense (mafhum), it is known from it by a stronger inference what is other than it; for if they are made lawful when the non-permission of other things is in effect, while they are in ihram, to remove hardship from them, how much more so outside this state? So it is an explanation of God's bounty upon them by what He has permitted them of that, and an explanation that they are in no need of game and of violating the sanctity of the Haram.

The expression of al-Zamakhshari is almost explicit in this. Al-'Allama al-Thani (al-Kafawi?) refuted it by saying that what is meant by the cattle is what is more general than the domestic and the wild, metaphorically, or by generalisation (taghlib), or by implication (dalala), or however you wish; and their being made lawful in their entirety is restricted to the state in which you are not making game lawful while in ihram, for with that some of them become forbidden, namely the wild. It is not hidden that this is a wild interpretation which Hamza (the "Forest of Revelation") should not intend among the targets of his expressions.

Al-Akhfash went to the view that the accusative of (غَيْرَ) is circumstantial from the pronoun in (أوْفُوا). This was judged weak, because it involves separating the circumstantial clause and its owner by a sentence that is not parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), since it is explanatory (mubayyina), and some parts of the explained intervene between parts of what is explained, together with what is necessary in it of restricting the contracts to what is obligatory or recommended in the Pilgrimage. Otherwise there remains no point to the restriction by that state, given that they are commanded with all contracts, absolutely.

Al-'Allama claimed that it is closer to the first in meaning, though further in wording, and he cited evidence for it from what is at the edge of the thyme. Then he said: Some have made it a circumstantial clause from the subject of (أحْلَلْنا), implied by God's words (أُحِلَّتْ لَكم) ﴿made lawful for you﴾. This also makes (وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ) a circumstantial clause from an implied element, meaning: in a state in which we are not making game lawful while you are in your state of ihram. This is not far-fetched, except in that it involves the placing of two interlocking circumstantial clauses without the owner of the circumstance being apparent in the wording.

Abu Hayyan criticised it, saying that it is corrupt, because they have stated explicitly that the deleted subject in such a case becomes forgotten and forsaken (nasyan mansiyyan), so it is not permissible for a circumstantial clause to fall from it. They said: If you say, "The rain was sent down answering their supplication," with (مُجِيبًا) being a circumstantial clause from the subject of the passive verb, it is not permitted, especially according to the view of those who hold that the passive form is an original formation, not transformed from the active. Moreover, there is also debate about the restriction. Some made it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (عَلَيْكم) in the genitive, and it is refuted by saying that what is recited (يُتْلى) is not restricted to a state in which they are not making game lawful while in ihram; rather it is recited to them in this state and in others.

Al-'Allama al-Baydawi transmitted from some that the accusative is by way of exception, and mentioned that in it there is strain (ta'assuf). Our master, Shaykh of All, Sibghat Allah Efendi al-Haydari, may God's mercy be upon him, clarified this by saying: If it were an exception, it would be either from the pronoun in (لَكم) or in (أوْفُوا), since it cannot be excepted from (بَهِيمَةُ الأنْعامِ). On the first view, the beast must be restricted to what is other than the cattle of what resembles them; or it remains general but with the condition that only the like is intended within the scope of the exception; and the phrase (وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ) must be made part of what is excepted, by being a circumstantial clause from what is concealed in (مُحِلِّي), so that the exception is valid, for it has no validity without these two considerations. The flow of the expression requires that one say: "and they are in ihram," because the exception has removed the non-permitters from the company of those addressed. And to regard it as a shift of person (iltifat) here is far-fetched, since that would lift [the connection] within what is like a single word. On the second view, the contracts must be restricted to the obligations stated in the Pilgrimage, and the interpretation of the prescriptive statement (kalam talabi) must be by what it entails of information, together with what it entails of separating the excepted from the excepted-from by a foreign element. All of that is strained, what a strain indeed! End of quotation.

It seems that he, may God have mercy on him, did not mention the possibility that the exception is an exception from an exception, although al-Qurtubi transmitted it from the Basrans. For that is corrupt, as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan said, not merely strained, since it would entail the permission of hunting within the Haram, because what is excepted from the forbidden is lawful. Yes, Abu Hayyan mentioned that it is an exception from (بَهِيمَةُ الأنْعامِ) in a specific aspect, and he found it to involve artifice and strain. He, may God have mercy on him, said: The difficulty arose in the verse, so that people became confused in its derivation, because the orthography of (مُحِلِّي) is with a yā'. They thought it is an active participle from (أحَلَّ), and that it is annexed to (الصَّيْدِ) as the annexation of an active participle transitive to its object, and that it is a plural from which the nūn was deleted for annexation, and its original form is (غَيْرُ مُحِلِّينَ الصَّيْدِ).

What dispels the difficulty and makes the meaning clear is that God's words (غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي الصَّيْدِ) be taken as in the manner of their saying: (حِسانُ النِّساءِ) "the beautiful women", meaning: the beautiful women. Likewise this is originally: (غَيْرُ الصَّيْدِ المُحَلِّ), "other than the game that is made lawful," and (المَحَلُّ) is an attribute of the game, not of the people. Describing the game as (مُحَلٌّ) may be either in the sense of entering into lawfulness, as you say, "The man became lawful (أحَلَّ)," meaning he entered into lawfulness, and "he entered ihram (أحْرَمَ)," meaning he entered the Haram; or in the sense of becoming possessed of lawfulness, meaning lawful by God's making it lawful, exalted is He. The coming of (أفْعَلَ) in both of the mentioned senses is frequent in the language of the Arabs. From the first are (أعْرَقَ) "he became of noble stock," (أشْأمَ) "he became ill-omened," (أيْمَنَ) "he went right," (أنْجَدَ) "he went to the highlands," (أتْهَمَ) "he became suspect." From the second are (أعْشَبَتِ الأرْضُ) "the land became grassy," (وأبْقَلَتْ) "and sprouted herbage," (وأغَدَّ البَعِيرُ) "the camel became well-fed." When it is established that the game is described as being made lawful in accordance with both senses, it becomes clear that it is a second exception. Then, if what is meant by (بَهِيمَةُ الأنْعامِ) is the animals themselves, it is a disjunctive exception; or if it means the gazelles and the like, then it is continuous, on the interpretation of (المُحِلّ) as that which reaches the state of lawfulness while they are in ihram. If you say: What is the benefit of this exception with the qualification of reaching lawfulness, when the game that is in the Haram is also not lawful?

I say: The game that is in the Haram is not lawful to the one in ihram nor to one not in ihram, and the purpose is to explain the prohibition of what is specifically prohibited to the one in ihram.

If you say: What you have mentioned of this strange interpretation is marred by its orthography in the Mushaf with a yā', and by its being pronounced with a pause on it (waqf) with it?

I say: They wrote in the Mushaf things that differ from pronunciation, such as (لَأذْبَحَنَّهُ) with an alif, and in pausing they followed the orthography. End of quotation.

Al-Safaqisi criticised it in the same manner as we have stated before, in respect of the addition of the yā', and in it there is confusion between the singular and the plural, and they flee from any addition or omission in the orthography. How then would they add an addition from which confusion arises? In respect of the annexation of the attribute to the qualified noun, which is not analogical!

Al-Halabi said: In it there is a breach of consensus (ijma'), for they have not parsed (غَيْرَ) except as a circumstantial clause, and they only differed about its owner. Then al-Safaqisi said: Two derivations are possible in it:

One of them is that (غَيْرَ) is a disjunctive exception and (مُحِلِّي) is a sound plural, and what is meant by it is the people who have entered the lawfulness of the game, meaning: but if you enter the lawfulness of the game, then hunting is not permitted to you.

Second, it may be connected to "beast of cattle" (bahimat al-an'am), and the speech contains an elision of a modifier (mudaf), meaning: "Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except the game of those who enter [the sacred precinct] while being in the state of hunting [ihram]" — so it is not lawful [for them]. It is also possible that it retains its original sense of permission (al-tahlil), and the exception is connected, with the modifier elided, meaning: "except the game of those who make hunting lawful (muhillin al-istiyad), while you are in the state of ihram." By "those who make it lawful" is meant those who act as one who believes it to be lawful; so it is not lawful. Its meaning would then be: the game of the sacred precinct is like carrion, its eating is not lawful at all. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "for you" (lakum), and the coordinated term has been elided because of the indication of it, which is common, and its estimated form is: "not those who make hunting lawful, but those who make it lawful," just as the Exalted said: ﴿It protects you from the heat﴾, meaning: "and the cold." This is a fine interpretation.

That said, it is not hidden that the hand of God the Exalted is with the community (al-jama'ah), and that what others have mentioned hardly escapes objection.

﴿Indeed, God decrees what He wills﴾ of the rulings, according to what His will requires, based on profound wisdoms before which thoughts stand still. Thus the permission and prohibition mentioned enter into it at the first level. "Decrees" (yahkumu) has been given the sense of "does" (yaf'alu), so it takes its object directly; otherwise it takes it with the preposition "bi-".

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, made clear the prohibition of violating the Sacred Precinct, which is among the rites of the Hajj, He followed it, exalted is His majesty, with an explanation of the violation of the remaining rites. The word *sha'a'ir* (rites) is the plural of *sha'ira*, which is a noun for what has been marked (*ush'ira*), meaning made a sign and a token of the rite, such as the standing places of Hajj, the places where the pillars are stoned, the *tawaf* and the *sa'y*, and the acts that are the marks by which the pilgrim is recognized: the *ihram*, the *tawaf*, the *sa'y*, the shaving of the head, and the sacrifice. Its attribution to Allah, the Exalted, is for its honour and to magnify the gravity of violating it. The intended meaning is the disregard of its sanctity and that they be prevented from those who would overturn them.

It is narrated from 'Ata' that he interpreted the *sha'a'ir* as the landmarks of Allah's limits, His commands, His prohibitions, and His obligations. It is narrated from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i that what is meant by them is the markers set up to distinguish between the sacred territory (*hill*) and the Sacred Precinct (*haram*), and that violating them, in his view, means passing beyond them into Makkah without *ihram*. It has also been said that they are al-Safa and al-Marwa, and the *hady* (sacrificial animals) from camels and others. This was narrated from Mujahid.

﴿Nor the Sacred Month﴾: that is, do not violate it by fighting your enemies from among the polytheists in it, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Or [it means do not violate it] by *nasi'* (intercalation, postponing the sacred month), as was reported from al-Qutaybi. The first is the more appropriate for the condition of the believers.

It has been disputed what is meant by it. It has been said that it is Rajab. It has been said that it is Dhu al-Qa'da, and this was narrated from 'Ikrima. It has been said that it is the four sacred months, and this was chosen by al-Jubba'i and al-Balkhi. Its being singular is for the intention of the genus.

﴿Nor the sacrificial animals (*hady*)﴾: by harassing them or by preventing them from reaching their place of sacrifice. What is meant by it is what is brought as an offering to the Ka'ba, whether camels, cattle, or sheep. It is the plural of *hadya*, as *jad'* and *jad'ya* (kid goat), and it is what is attached beneath the saddle or the riding gear. It is singled out for mention on the basis that it is included among the rites, because it benefits people, because it is property about which one may be lax, and to glorify it, because it is among the greatest of them.

﴿Nor the garlands (*qala'id*)﴾: the plural of *qila'da*, which is what the *hady* is garlanded with, such as a sandal, bark of a tree, or other things, so that it is known to be a *hady* and is not harassed. The intended meaning is the prohibition of harassing the garlanded animals themselves from among the *hady*, which are the camels, and they are singled out for mention to honour them and show concern for them. Or [it means] the prohibition of harassing the garlands themselves, as an intensification of the prohibition against harassing their essence, as in His saying, ﴿and not to reveal their adornment﴾ (24:31), for when they are forbidden to display adornment such as anklets and bracelets, the prohibition of revealing the place of these is understood even more so.

It is reported from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i that what is meant is the prohibition of making lawful the garlands themselves, and the obligation to give them in charity if they have value. This was narrated from al-Hasan. It is narrated from al-Suddi that what is meant by the garlands are the owners of the *hady*, for the Arabs used to garland themselves with bark from the trees of Makkah. A man would remain in Makkah until the sacred months ended and he wished to return to his family; he would then garland himself and his she-camel with bark from the trees, and thus he would be safe until he reached his family.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Sacred Precinct used to garland themselves with tree bark, and those other than the people of the Sacred Precinct used to garland themselves with wool, hair, and other things. It is narrated from al-Rabi' and 'Ata' that what is meant is the prohibition of the believers from pulling up anything from the trees of the Sacred Precinct with which they garland themselves, as the polytheists used to do in their pre-Islamic ignorance.

﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾: that is, do not make lawful for people who intend the Sacred House, by preventing them from it in any way. It is also permissible that it be by an omitted modifier, meaning the fighting of a people or the harming of a people (*amminin*).

[Page 54]

It is read as ﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾ with the genitive construction, and *al-Bayt* (the House) is then the direct object, not an adverbial of place. The way the active participle governs it is clear. His saying, ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾, is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun concealed in *amminin*. It is also permissible that it be a qualifier, and this was deemed weak on the ground that the active participle that is qualified does not govern, because its resemblance to the verb is weakened, since being qualified removes the resemblance, as qualification is among the distinctive features of nouns. It was answered that the qualifier is only prevented from governing when the object precedes it; if it follows, it is not prevented, since it comes after the completion of what it requires, as stated by the author of *al-Lubb* and others.

The indefiniteness of *fadlan* (bounty) and *ridwanan* (approval) is for magnification. The phrase *min rabbihim* (from their Lord) is related either to the act itself or to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of *fadlan*, which dispenses with describing what is coordinated with it. That is: a bounty that is from their Lord, and an approval likewise. Mentioning the title of Lordship with the attachment to their pronoun is for their honour, and as a hint that their aim is attained. What is meant by them is the Muslims exclusively, and the verse is *muhkam* (not abrogated).

In general there is an indication of the reason for the prohibition and of the reprehensibility of violating it, so it is said, but it has been objected that harassing Muslims is forbidden absolutely, whether they are *amminin* or not, so there is no basis for restricting the prohibition against making them lawful to them alone. For this reason al-Hasan and others said: what is meant by *amminin* are the polytheists exclusively, and what is meant by the bounty then is the profit in their trade, and by the approval what they assume. It is permissible to keep *fadl* on its apparent meaning if what is meant is also what is assumed, but since it is possible to take it as what is in reality, taking it that way is preferable. This view is supported by the report that the verse was revealed, as al-Suddi and others said, "concerning a man from the Banu Rabi'a called al-Hutam ibn Hind. He came to the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, alone, leaving his horses outside Madinah, and said: 'To what do you call the people?' The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: 'To the testimony that there is no god but Allah, establishing the prayer, and giving the zakat.' He said: 'Good, but I have chiefs whom I do not decide any matter without, and perhaps I will embrace Islam and bring them.' The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, had said to his companions: 'A man will enter upon you who speaks with the tongue of a devil.' Then he left from his presence. When he left, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: 'He came in with the face of a disbeliever and went out with the outcome of a treacherous one, and the man is not a Muslim.' He passed by the herd of Madinah and drove it off, and went away with it, reciting verse and saying:

*The night has wrapped it with a driver, fierce and violent,*
*Not a herdsman of camels nor of sheep,*
*Nor a bellowing one on the back of a pack-beast.*
*They spent the night asleep, and the son of Hind did not sleep.*
*He spent the night driving them, a youth like an arrow-shaft,*
*Round-calved, with smoothed-off feet.*

The Muslims pursued him but could not overtake him. When the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, went out in the year of the *qada'* of the *'umra* from which he had been prevented, he heard the *talbiya* of the pilgrims of Yamama, and he said, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him: 'This is al-Hutam and his companions, so seize them.' He had garlanded what he had plundered from the herd and made it a *hady*. When they set out for that, the noble verse was revealed, and they refrained."

It is narrated from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah concerning horsemen from the polytheists who were heading to the House, reciting the *talbiya* for an *'umra*. The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, these polytheists are like these; let us raid them." So Allah, glorified is He, revealed the verse.

Those who held that what is meant by *amminin* are the polytheists differed about whether it is abrogated or not. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that there is no abrogation, because it is possible that the polytheists are attacked with fighting in the sacred months. You know that the verse is not a clear text on fighting, even granting the assumption of what is within the scope of instruction. Abu Muslim said that the verse is abrogated by His saying, ﴿so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ (9:28). It was said that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword (9:5). It was said that it is abrogated by both. It was said that only the garlands were abrogated from this verse, and this was narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid. Some have claimed that what is meant by *amminin* is what includes both Muslims and polytheists, and the specificity of the occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording; the abrogation in that case applies to the polytheists alone.

[Page 55]

Some scholars call such a thing a specification (*takhsis*), as has been verified in the principles of jurisprudence. On this view it is necessary to interpret *fadl* and *ridwan* in a way that suits both groups. Humayd ibn Qays al-A'raj read *tabtaghuna* (you seek) with a *ta'*, addressing the believers, and the clause on that reading is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the addressees in *tuhillu* (you violate), with the aim being to show that their condition is incompatible with the forbidden act, not to restrict the prohibition by it.

It is objected that if the address to the believers were intended, the appropriate phrasing would be *min rabbikum wa rabbihim* (from your Lord and their Lord). It is answered that leaving out the expression mentioned is for intimidation, that their Lord protects them and does not approve of what they did; there is a rhetorical eloquence here that is not hidden, and an indication that Allah, the Exalted, is Lord of the worlds and not the Muslims alone.

Shaykh al-Islam said: the attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of *amminin*, on the reading of address, is to hint at restricting the honour to them and depriving the addressees of it and of attaining what they seek. In this there is, for the reason of the prohibition and its emphasis, and the intensification of the reprehensibility of what is prohibited, what is not hidden.

﴿And when you have come out (*halaltum*)﴾ from the *ihram* indicated by His saying, glorified is He, "while you are in the state of *ihram*" ﴿then hunt﴾: that is, there is no blame upon you for hunting, because the impediment has been removed. So the command is for permissibility after prohibition. A similar example is: "Do not enter this house until you pay its price; when you have paid, enter it," meaning: when you have paid, entering it is permitted for you. Many have held that the command is for permissibility after prohibition.

The author of *al-Qawati'* said: this is the apparent meaning of al-Shafi'i's words in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*, and Ibn Burhan transmitted it from most jurists and theologians, because the preceding prohibition is a diverting indication. This is one of three positions on the matter.

The second is that it is for obligation, because the form requires it, and its coming after a prohibition has no effect. This is the view chosen by Qadi Abu al-Tayyib, Shaykh Abu Ishaq, al-Sam'ani, and the Imam in *al-Mahsul*. Abu Hamid al-Isfara'ini transmitted it in his book from most of the Shafi'is, then said: this is the view of the whole body of jurists and most theologians.

The third is suspension between the two. This is the view of Imam al-Haramayn, although he had rejected suspension in its wording when it occurs without a prior prohibition. According to what al-Zarkashi said, it is not far-fetched to say here that the state returns to what was before, as has been said regarding the matter of a prohibition coming after an obligation.

Whoever holds that the literal meaning of the command in question is obligation says it is an intensification of the validity of the permitted, to the point that it is as if it were obligatory. It has also been said that the command in such a case is for the obligation to believe in the permissibility, so the figurative use is in the root (*madda*), as if it were said: believe in the permissibility of hunting. But this is nothing.

It is read as *ahlaltum* (you have come out of *ihram*), which is a dialect form of *halla*. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he read *fa-istadu* with a *kasra* on the *fa'*, by transferring the vowel of the hamzat al-wasl onto it. This was deemed weak from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, since transferring a vowel onto a vowelled letter is contrary to analogy. It has also been said that he did not read with a pure *kasra*, but inclined it, to incline the *ta'*, although it is among the emphatic letters.

﴿And let not hatred (*yajrimannakum*)﴾: that is, let not provoke you, as al-Qatada explained it, and it is narrated from Tha'lab, al-Kisa'i, and others. They recited for it the verse:

*I had indeed stabbed Abu 'Uyayna with a stab*
*that caused Fazara after it to become angry.*

[p. 56]

Thus *fa-jaramun ʿalā hādhā* (فَجَرَمَ عَلى هَذا) is transitive to one object directly and to the other through *ʿalā*. Al-Farrāʾ (al-Farrāʾ) and Abū ʿUbayda (Abū ʿUbayda) said that the meaning is: *lā yaksibannakum* ("let it not earn you"). *Jaramа* (جَرَمَ) functions like *kasaba* (كَسَبَ) in meaning and in being transitive to one object or to two. It is said: *jarama dhanban* ("he earned a sin"), meaning *kasabahu* ("he acquired it"), and *jaramtuhu dhanban* ("I caused him to earn a sin"), meaning *kasabtuhu iyyāhu*. The difference is that *jarama* is mostly used for earning what has no good in it, and this is the reason it was chosen here over the second form. From it comes *al-jarīma* (الجَرِيمَة, "crime"). Its root basically signifies cutting off, because the earner is cut off by his earning. It may also be said *ajramathu dhanban*, transferring the transitive verb to two objects by means of the *hamza* (the causative form), as one says *aksabtuhu dhanban*. On this reading is the recitation of ʿAbdullāh (ʿAbd Allāh): *lā yujrimannakum* (لا يُجْرِمَنَّكم) with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*, and *shanaʾānu qawmin* (شَنِئانِ قَوْم) with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn*. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim), and Ismāʿīl (on the authority of Nāfiʿ) read the *nūn* with a sukūn.

[p. 57 would follow; the following is the continuation as given]

There are two possibilities for *shanaʾān* and *shanaʾān* (the vowel-pattern):

The first is that both are verbal nouns (maṣdar, مَصْدَر) meaning hatred or intensity of hatred, as an irregular form. This is because *faʿalān* with a *fatḥa* is the verbal noun of verbs indicating motion, like *jawalān* ("roaming"), and it does not come from a transitive verb, as stated. But this verb is transitive, since one says *shaniʾtuhu* ("I hated him"), and there is no indication of motion here except in the sense of distance. *Fiʿlān* with a sukūn is rare among verbal nouns, as in *lawaytuhu liyānan* meaning *maṭaltuhu* ("I postponed him").

The second is that both are adjectives (ṣifāt, صِفَات), since *fiʿlān* is common among adjectives, like *sakrān* ("drunk"). It also occurs rarely with a *fatḥa* in adjectives, like *ḥimārin qaṭawān* ("a donkey slow in its pace") and *taysin ʿadawān* ("a he-goat much given to running"). If it is a verbal noun, the apparent reading is that its genitive construction is with the object, i.e., "that you hate a people." It is also permitted that it be with the subject, i.e., "that a people hate you." The first is more apparent, as in *al-Baḥr* (the exegetical work *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*). If it is an adjective, it means *baghīḍ* ("hateful"), and its genitive construction is explanatory (bayāniyya), and it is not an annexation to its object or subject as with the verbal noun, i.e., "the hateful one among them."

﴿أنْ صَدُّوكُمْ﴾ ("because they barred you") with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, by supposing a *lām* before it, so that it is a reason for the hatred, i.e., "because they barred you in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyya." Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read it with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, so that *in* is conditional (shartiyya), and what precedes it is the indication of the response, or the response is what precedes it according to the less preferred opinion that it may precede. It was objected to this that there was no barring after the conquest of Mecca.

It was answered that it is a rebuke, on the basis that the barring prior to the conquest of Mecca is something whose occurrence can only be validly supposed as a hypothetical case. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ قَوْمًا مُسْرِفِينَ﴾ ("if you are a people who exceed the limits"). It is also permitted that it be by supposing *in kānū qad ṣaddūkum* ("if they had barred you"), and that it be on its apparent meaning, as an indication that it is not fitting that ﴿شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ أنْ صَدُّوكم﴾ ("the hatred of a people because they barred you") should cause you to transgress after the manifestation and strength of Islam. From this is understood the prohibition of that, on account of the earlier barring, by a more fitting way. ﴿عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ ("from the Sacred Mosque") means from visiting it and circumambulating it for the ʿumra. This, as Shaykh al-Islām (Shaykh al-Islām) said, is a clear sign of the generality of *āmmīn* (آمِّين, "those coming to it") to the polytheists with certainty. Some made it an evidence for restricting it to them.

﴿أنْ تَعْتَدُوا﴾ ("that you transgress"), i.e., against them. It is omitted, relying on its clarity, and as an allusion that the primary purpose is to prevent the transgression from being committed by those addressed, in order to preserve the glorification of the rites, not to prevent its occurrence against the people out of consideration for them. And *ʿalā* is elided, i.e., *ʿalā an taʿtadū*. The position after it is either genitive or accusative according to the two schools. That is: "Let not the hatred of a people for their barring you from the Sacred Mosque move you to transgress against them and take revenge on them for the sake of satisfaction." Or there is no elision, and what is formed by *an* and the verb is the second object of *yujrimannakum*, i.e., "let not their transgression against you earn you that." This, on both suppositions, although it is apparently a prohibition of the hatred from what is attributed to it, is in reality a prohibition to them from transgression in the most emphatic and eloquent manner. For the prohibition of the causes of a thing and its beginnings that lead to it is a prohibition of it by demonstrative means, and an annulment of its causality. It is said: "Let me not see you here," and the intended meaning is the prohibition of the addressee from being present.

Al-ʿAllāma al-Ṭībī (al-Ṭībī) directed the objection with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وإذا حَلَلْتُمْ فاصْطادُوا﴾ ("And when you have come out of the state of ihram, then hunt") between what preceded and this prohibition connected with it, so that it is an indication and an incidental inclusion that those intending the sanctuary, as long as they are in ihram and not seeking bounty from their Lord, are like game at the sanctuary, so do not molest them. And when you have left ihram, you and they, then your affair is with them, for they have become like lawful game, which is permitted to you to molest at that time.

Shaykh al-Islām said: Perhaps the delay of this prohibition about that, although its connection to what precedes is evident, is to indicate that the sanctity of transgression does not end with leaving ihram, as the sanctity of hunting ends with it. Rather it remains as long as their connection to the rites is not entirely severed. By this is known the continuation of the sanctity of molesting all the others coming to the sanctuary, by a more fitting way. And perhaps this is the better view.

﴿وتَعاوَنُوا عَلى البِرِّ والتَّقْوى﴾ ("And cooperate in righteousness and piety") is coordinated with ﴿ولا يَجْرِمَنَّكم﴾ ("and let not ... earn you") in meaning, as if it were said: "Do not transgress against those intending the Sacred Mosque because you were barred from it, and cooperate in pardon and overlooking."

Some said: it is a new sentence (istiʾnāf, اسْتِئْناف), and the pause on *an taʿtadū* is obligatory. But more than one chose that by *al-birr* (البِرّ) is meant following the command in general, and by *al-taqwā* (التَّقْوى) is meant avoiding desire, so that the verse becomes one of the comprehensive utterances (jawāmiʿ al-kalim, جَوامِع الكَلِم), and serves as a concluding summary (tadhyīl, تَذْيِيل) of the discourse. Thus there enters into *al-birr* and *al-taqwā* all the rites of the Ḥajj, for He, exalted is He, said: ﴿فَإنَّها مِن تَقْوى القُلُوبِ﴾ ("for indeed it is from the piety of hearts"). Pardon and overlooking also enter, by primary inclusion. And on this generality is also interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ولا تَعاوَنُوا عَلى الإثْمِ والعُدْوانِ﴾ ("and do not cooperate in sin and aggression"), so that the prohibition covers everything belonging to the category of injustice and disobedience, and the prohibition of cooperation in transgression and revenge is included in it.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (Ibn ʿAbbās), may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Abū al-ʿĀliya (Abū al-ʿĀliya) that they interpreted *al-ithm* (الإثْم, "sin") as abandoning what He commanded them and committing what He forbade them, and *al-ʿudwān* (العُدْوان, "aggression") as going beyond the limits that He, glorified is He, set for His servants in their religion and imposed upon them in their own selves. The adornment (taḥliya, التَّحْلِيَة, positive action) was placed before the clearing away (takhliya, التَّخْلِيَة, negative action), in haste toward establishing what is the primary aim in itself.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿واتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("and fear Allah") is a command to be mindful in all matters, among which is opposing what was mentioned of the commands and prohibitions. The obligation of being mindful in them is established by demonstrative means.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ ("Indeed Allah is severe in punishment") for whoever does not fear Him. This is in the position of giving a reason for what precedes. The manifestation of the glorious Name (instead of a pronoun) is for what has passed more than once.

[Page 58 of the source]

﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. This begins the explanation of the prohibited things, which were alluded to in His words, glorified is He: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾. What is meant is the prohibition of eating carrion (maytah), which is that which has died by its own means, without any external cause. ﴿And blood﴾, that is, blood that has been poured forth. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic era of ignorance) used to put it in intestines, roast them and eat them. As for blood that is not poured forth, such as the liver, it is permitted. As for the spleen, most scholars hold it to be permitted, while the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'is) unanimously hold it to be prohibited. Disapproval of it is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾. The mention of "flesh" here is an insertion, for the reason already mentioned. Dāwūd (al-Ẓāhirī) and his companions took its apparent meaning, so they prohibited only the flesh and permitted the rest. The apparent sense of the conjunction is that the swine is prohibited in the same way as the other things (i.e., the prohibition applies to all of it).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported in al-Muṣannaf, from Qatādah, that he said: "Whoever eats the flesh of swine, repentance is offered to him; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed." This is a strange report. Perhaps the reason is that eating it has today become one of the signs of disbelief, like wearing the zunnār (the distinguishing belt of non-Muslims). But there is room for reflection on this.

﴿And that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾, that is, the voice has been raised for other than Allah, the Exalted, at the time of its slaughter. The meaning of "invocation" (ihlāl) here is the mention of that to which the animal is sacrificed, such as al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā. ﴿And the strangled﴾. Al-Suddī said: it is that whose head enters between two branches of a tree, so it is strangled and dies. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah said: it is that which is strangled by the hunter's rope, so it dies.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to strangle the animal and eat it, so this was prohibited for the believers. The better view is that it should be taken to mean that which died by strangling in any manner.

﴿And the beaten to death﴾, that is, that which is beaten until it dies. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and by Qatādah and al-Suddī. It derives from "waqadhtuhu," meaning "I struck him." Its origin is that you strike it until it becomes limp, and from it comes "waqadhahu al-nuʿās," meaning "drowsiness overcame him."

﴿And the fallen﴾, that is, that which falls from a high place or into a well and dies. ﴿And the gored﴾, that is, that which is gored by another and dies. Its ta' (feminine ending) is for transfer from the adjective to the noun (naql), so it is not objected that *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* does not take the ta'. Some of the Kufis said that this applies when the qualified noun is mentioned, as in *kaffun khaḍībun* (a dyed hand) and *ʿaynun kaḥīlun* (a kohl-rimmed eye). But when the noun is omitted, it is permissible for the ta' to enter it, and there is no need to say that it is for transfer. It is also read *al-manṭūḥah*.

﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾, that is, what the beast of prey has eaten from it, so that it died. It was explained this way because if it had eaten the whole animal, no ruling would attach to it. And the exception stated by Allah, the Exalted, cannot properly be made from it: ﴿except what you have slaughtered﴾, that is, except what you have reached while it still has some life left in it, convulsing as a slaughtered animal convulses, and you have slaughtered it.

It is reported from the two noble leaders al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the minimum by which slaughter (dhakāh) is attained is that you reach it while it is moving its ear, its tail or its eyelid. This was also the view of al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Ibrāhīm, Ṭāwūs, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd. Others said that a stable life (al-ḥayāh al-mustaqirrah) is required, which is life on the verge of ceasing. Its sign, as is said, is that it convulses after the slaughter, not at the time of it.

It is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the exception refers to all the prohibited things mentioned earlier, except those that do not accept slaughter: carrion, blood, swine, and what the beast of prey has eaten, if it is kept on its apparent meaning. It was also said that it is an exception from the prohibition itself and not from the prohibited things, and the meaning is: all that has been mentioned is forbidden to you, but what you have slaughtered of what Allah has permitted, by slaughter, is lawful to you.

This was reported from Mālik and a group of the people of Madinah, and al-Jubbāʾī chose it. Slaughter (tadhkiyah) in the Sharīʿah is cutting the windpipe and the gullet with a sharp instrument. The details are in jurisprudence (fiqh). The verse has been cited as evidence that if hunting animals eat from what they have caught, it becomes unlawful (for the hunter).

al-Ḥasan read *al-subʿu* (with a sukun on the ʿayn... ) (as *al-sabʿu*, with the sukun on the ya'), and Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read *wa-akīlu al-subʿi* (what the beast of prey has eaten).

﴿And that which is slaughtered on the nuṣub﴾. *Nuṣub* is the plural of *niṣāb*, like *ḥumur* and *ḥimār*. It was also said that the singular of *anṣāb* is *nuṣub*, like *ṭunub* and *aṭnāb*. It has been disputed what they are. It was said: they are stones that were around the Kaʿbah, numbering three hundred and sixty, and the people of the Jahiliyyah used to slaughter upon them. So *ʿalā* (upon) is in its original sense. Perhaps their slaughtering upon them was a sign that it was for other than Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: they are idols, because they are set up and worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted. *ʿAlā* is either in the sense of *lām* (for), or in its original sense with the implied meaning: "and what is slaughtered, named, upon the idols."

It is objected that in that case it would be a repetition of His words, glorified is He: ﴿and what has been invoked with other than Allah﴾. But the matter is simple. The relative clause is coordinated with the prohibited things.

It is also read *al-nuṣb* with a *ḍammah* on the *nūn* and a sukun on the *ṣād* for lightness, and it is read with two *fatḥahs*, and with a *fatḥah* then a sukun.

﴿And that you seek decision through the arrows﴾. *Azlām* is the plural of *zalam*, like *jamal*, or *zulam*, like *ṣurad*, and it means an arrow-shaft (qadah), that is: it is prohibited for you to seek decision by means of arrow-shafts. That was because, as reported from al-Ḥasan and others, when they intended to do something, they would strike three arrow-shafts. On one was written "My Lord has commanded me," on the second "My Lord has forbidden me," and the third they left blank with nothing written on it. If the one marked "commanded" came out, they went ahead with their need; if the one marked "forbidden" came out, they refrained; if the blank one came out, they shuffled them again. So the meaning of *istiqsām* is seeking knowledge of what has been apportioned to them, rather than what has not been apportioned, by means of the arrows.

The prohibition of this has been questioned, on the grounds that it is part of *tafāʾul* (seeking good omen), and the Prophet ﷺ used to love good omens. It was answered that it was a seeking of counsel from the idols and seeking help from them, as is indicated by what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that when they wanted to do this, they came to the house of their idols and did what they did. That is why it became prohibited. It was also said that it involves fabrication against Allah, the Exalted, if "my Lord" is intended to mean Allah, and ignorance and polytheism if it is intended to mean an idol. It was also said that it is an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen, which Allah, the Exalted, has reserved for Himself.

It was objected: we do not accept that intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen is unlawful. The meaning of Allah's reserving the knowledge of the unseen for Himself is that it cannot be known except from Him. For this reason, seeking knowledge of good and evil from astrologers and soothsayers (kuhhān) has become forbidden and prohibited, unlike *istikhārah* (seeking guidance) from the Qurʾān, which is seeking knowledge from Allah, the Exalted. That is why they agreed on its permissibility. Whoever considers the arrangement of premises, or does spiritual discipline (riyāḍah), seeks nothing but knowledge of the unseen from Him, glorified is He. So if seeking knowledge of the unseen were unlawful, the path of thought and discipline would be closed, and no one holds that.

Al-Imām (al-Rāzī), may Allah have mercy on him, said: If it were not permissible to seek knowledge of the unseen, it would follow that the science of interpreting dreams would be disbelief, since it is a seeking of the unseen, and that those possessed of miracles (karāmāt) who claim inspirations (ilhāmāt) would be disbelievers. It is known that all of this is false.

The view that *istikhārah* by the Qurʾān is permissible was criticised on the grounds that its practice was not transmitted from the earlier generations (salaf). It has been said that Imām Mālik disliked it.

As for what is in the fatwās of the Ṣūfiyyah, quoting al-Zandawastī, that there is no harm in it, and that ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and Muʿādh, may Allah be pleased with him, did it, [Page 59]

and it is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "Whoever wishes to seek good omen from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, let him recite *Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad* seven times, and let him say three times: 'O Allah, by Your Book I seek good omen, and upon You I rely. O Allah, show me in Your Book what is the hidden part of Your secret, stored in Your unseen,' then he seeks good omen from the opening of the page." About this there is something troubling in the soul.

In *Kitāb al-Aḥkām* by al-Jaṣṣāṣ, it is said that the verse indicates the invalidity of drawing lots (qur'ah) in the manumission of slaves, because it has the very same meaning, when it involves establishing what the lot has produced without entitlement. An example is when someone frees one of his slaves on his deathbed, as explained in jurisprudence. It is not objected that drawing lots is permitted in dividing spoils, for example, and in choosing which women go out (on a journey). We say: in those cases it serves to console hearts and to clear one of suspicion of favouring some over others. If they agreed on that by mutual consent, it would be permissible without a lot. As for the freedom that falls upon one of the slaves in the case under discussion, it is not permissible to transfer it from him to another, and using the lot involves such a transfer.

al-Shāfiʿī differed on this and permitted drawing lots in manumission, as he permitted it in other matters, and the apparent evidences are with him. The detailed investigation of this belongs in its proper place.

My own view is that the *istiqsām* practised by the people of the Jahiliyyah is prohibited without doubt, as the explicit text of the Book states. Its prohibition arises from bad belief, and it is not free from pessimism (tashāʾum), and it is not pure optimism (tafāʾul). Such practice is not at all an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen; rather it is an entry into conjecture (ẓann). The seeking of guidance (*istikhārah*) by the Qurʾān is among things for which nothing reliable has been transmitted from the first generation, and leaving it is dearer to me, especially since Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ have sufficed us with the *istikhārah* that has been established as a Sunnah, in reports that are sound. And the believing of astrologers in matters other than eclipses and solar and lunar phenomena, in what they foretell of future events, is forbidden. It is not from the knowledge of the unseen nor an intrusion into it, even if al-Zajjāj claimed it, because it is built on causes.

Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn al-Nawawī, in his commentary on Muslim, quoted from al-Qāḍī: Soothsaying (*kahānah*) among the Arabs was of three kinds:

The first is that a person has a companion (*rī'*) from the jinn who informs him of what he steals by listening from the sky. This kind ceased from the time Allah, the Exalted, sent our Prophet ﷺ.

The second is that he informs him of what happens and occurs in the regions of the earth, and of what is hidden from him, whether near or far. The existence of this is not unlikely. The Muʿtazilah and some theologians denied these two kinds and deemed them impossible. But there is no impossibility in that, nor is its existence far-fetched. However, they are believed and disbelieved, and the prohibition of believing them and listening to them is general.

The third is the astrologers (*munajjimūn*). This kind is that Allah, the Exalted, has given some people a certain power, but lying is more prevalent in it. Among this art is *ʿirāfah* (fortune-telling), and its practitioner is an *ʿarrāf*, who infers matters by causes and premises which he claims to know, such as divination by omens and by casting pebbles. All these kinds are called *kahānah*. The Sharīʿah has declared them liars and forbidden believing them and going to them. End of quotation.

Perhaps the prohibition of this is because lying predominates in their speech, and because believing them opens a door that leads to *Laẓā* (the blazing fire), since it may lead to the abandonment of the Sharīʿah and to finding fault with it, especially among the common people. The exception of what is of the kind of eclipses and solar and lunar phenomena is due to the rarity of their error in it, indeed to its non-occurrence when they can calculate. It is not so with what they foretell of events, since they have built that on the positions of the planets relative to one another, or relative to some of the fixed stars. There is no doubt that this does not suffice for the purpose, nor for comprehending all the positions and what they entail, which is impossible to comprehend for anyone other than the Knower of the unseen. So let this be understood.

It was also said: what is meant by *istiqsām* is dividing the slaughtered camel by arrow-shafts upon the known shares, that is, seeking a portion of the camel, or what Allah, the Exalted, has apportioned to him from it. This is the gambling (*maysir*), whose explanation has already passed. This was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm from the Imams al-Ṣādiqīn, may Allah be pleased with them. It was preferred on the grounds that it fits with its being mentioned alongside the prohibited foods.

It is reported from Mujāhid that he explained *al-azlām* as the dice of the Arabs and the knucklebones of the Persians, with which they gamble.

[Page 60]

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 5, verse 3 (part 2 of 2):

It is related on the authority of Waki' that they are the pieces of chess. ﴿That﴾, i.e., the seeking of decision by arrows (al-istiqsam bi'l-azlam). The sense of distance in the demonstrative refers to the distance of its rank in evil. ﴿Is a transgression﴾, i.e., a great sin and a departure from obedience to God Most High into disobedience, for the reason we have pointed out. It is also related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that ﴿that﴾ is a reference to the consumption of all the prohibited things mentioned earlier, which is understood from the context. ﴿Today﴾, i.e., the present time and the times connected to it that follow. It has also been said: the day the verse was revealed. This is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. It was, as al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related on the authority of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, the afternoon of Friday, the day of 'Arafah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage. It has also been said: the day the Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah, eight days before the end of Ramadan in the year nine; and it has been said: in the year eight. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed by the words of God Most High: ﴿The disbelievers have despaired of your religion﴾. Despair (al-ya's) is the cutting off of hope, and it is the opposite of greed (al-tama').

The meaning is: their hope has been cut off from nullifying your religion and from your returning from it by making these vile things lawful and others, or from their overcoming you in it, since they witnessed that God fulfilled His promise, in that He caused it (the religion) to prevail over all religion.

It is related that when the verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) looked at the gathering and saw none but Muslims. This possibility is preferred because it is the most fitting with His words, glorified be He: ﴿So do not fear them﴾ that they will prevail over you. This is a consequence of despair. ﴿But fear Me﴾, that I may inflict My punishment upon you if you oppose My command and commit My disobedience.

﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ through victory and manifestation, because by that they execute the rulings of the religion without any obstacle, and with it its completion is achieved. This is like saying: "My kingdom is complete when you have been spared what you fear." This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

It is related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi that the meaning is: Today I have perfected for you My limits, My obligations, what is lawful and what is unlawful, by sending down what I have sent down and clarifying what I have clarified for you, so there is no addition to it nor reduction from it by abrogation after this day. This was the Day of 'Arafah in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Jubba'i, al-Balkhi and others chose this view, and they claimed that after that nothing of the obligations was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning either permission or prohibition, and that he, peace be upon him, did not remain after that except eighty-one days, and passed away, may my soul be his ransom, to the Highest Companion (al-Rafiq al-A'la), may God bless him and grant him peace.

When 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, heard the verse, he understood it to announce the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn Abi Shaybah related on the authority of 'Antarah: "When the verse was revealed, 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, wept. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'It makes me weep that we were in increase of our religion, but now that it is complete, nothing has ever been completed without decreasing.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'You have spoken the truth.'" It is not to be cited, according to this view, as evidence against analogy (qiyas), as some have claimed; because the intended meaning is the completion of the religion itself by clarifying what must be clarified, and what is derived from it, and the explicit statement of the foundations of belief and the establishment of the principles of the Sharia and the rules of ijtihad.

It is related on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah that the meaning is: ﴿Today I have perfected for you﴾ your pilgrimage, and confirmed you in the Sacred Land, that you perform it apart from the polytheists. This was chosen by al-Tabari, who said: what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, may God be pleased with them, that God sent down after that the verse of kalalah, which is the last verse revealed, contradicts it. This was objected to by denial. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (lakum) signals from the outset that the completion is for their benefit and welfare; and it also contains an arousal of anticipation for the deferred element, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾. The prepositional phrase there is not connected to "favor" (ni'mati), because a verbal noun (masdar) does not have its complement placed before it. It has been said that it is connected to it, and there is no harm in the fronting of the complement of a verbal noun when it is an adverbial expression.

The completion of the favor upon the addressees is by the conquest of Makkah and entering it secure and victorious, the demolition of the markers and rites of the Jahiliyyah, the prohibition of the pilgrimage of the polytheists, and the circumambulation of the naked. It has been said: by completing guidance and success through completing their causes. It has been said: by the completion of the religion. It has been said: by giving them knowledge and wisdom that was not given to anyone before them. It has been said: the meaning of "My favor has been completed upon you" is that I have fulfilled for you My promise in His words, glorified be He: ﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾.

﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾, i.e., I have chosen it for you from among the religions. It is the religion with God Most High, and nothing else; it is the accepted one, and upon it the matter turns.

Ibn Jubayr related on the authority of Qatadah, who said: "It has been mentioned to us that every people will be shown their religion on the Day of Resurrection. As for faith (al-iman), it will give good news to its companions and its people and promise them good, until Islam comes and says: 'My Lord, You are Peace (al-Salam) and I am Islam.' He says: 'Today I accept only you, and today I reward only through you.'"

The notion of approval (al-ridaa) has been examined in terms of its meaning as choice, and therefore it is construed with (li) [the preposition]. Some have made the prepositional phrase an attribute of "religion," which was fronted upon it, so it became an accusative of state (hal). "Islam" and "religion" are then the two objects of "I approved" if it is taken to imply the meaning of "I made it" (sayyara); or "religion" is in the accusative of state from "Islam," or a specification (tamyiz) from "for you." The sentence, according to what al-Karkhi held, is a new, independent sentence and not conjoined to "I have perfected"; otherwise the implication would be that He had not approved Islam as a religion for them before that day, and this is not so, since Islam has always been a religion approved by God Most High, and by the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may God be pleased with them all, since it was legislated. The majority hold that it is conjoined. The restriction is answered by saying that the intended meaning of His approval, glorified and exalted be He, is His judgment, by His choice, as an eternal ruling that is not abrogated, and this was on that day.

The Shi'ah related on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this verse was revealed after the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning 'Ali, may God honor his face, at Ghadir Khumm: "Whoever I am his mawla, then 'Ali is his mawla." When it was revealed, he, peace be upon him, said: "God is greatest for the completion of the religion, the perfection of the favor, the approval of the Lord of my message, and the walaya of 'Ali, may God honor his face, after me." It is not hidden that this is one of their fabrications, and the weakness of the report is evidence of that from the outset. Yes, it is established with us that he (ﷺ) said concerning the Commander, may God honor his face, there: "Whoever I am his mawla, then 'Ali is his mawla," and he added to that, as in some reports; but there is no indication in all of them for what they claim of the Great Imamate and the Supreme Leadership, as will come, God willing, not far off.

We have expanded the discussion of this in our book (al-Nafahat al-Qudsiyyah fi Radd al-Imamiyyah), which has not been completed until now, and we ask God Most High to complete it.

Their narrations in this section, their wording cries out that they are fabricated, and Yusuf al-Awali has greatly multiplied them; upon him is what is upon him.

﴿So whoever is compelled﴾ is connected to the mention of the prohibited things and what lies between them, and it consists of seven clauses, according to what al-Tibi said. It is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) with what necessitates avoiding them, namely that consuming them is a great transgression, and their prohibition is part of the complete religion, the perfect favor, and the approved Islam.
