Compulsion (al-idtirar) is falling into necessity, i.e., whoever falls into the necessity of consuming any of these prohibited things ﴿in a famine﴾, i.e., a hunger in which the stomachs are emptied, i.e., become thin, in which death is feared or its precursors. ﴿Without inclining to sin﴾, i.e., not inclining or deviating toward it and not choosing it, by eating of them beyond what keeps his life-breath; for that is unlawful, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, may God be pleased with them, and this is the view of the people of Iraq. The people of Madinah said: it is permissible to eat until satiated in a state of necessity. It has been said: the meaning is one who is not disobedient, by being a transgressor, or an aggressor by snatching it from another compelled person, or going out in disobedience; this too was related from Qatadah.

﴿Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾; He does not hold him to account for eating. This is the real answer, and its cause has been placed in its position. It has been said: the answer is implied in the sentence.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 5, verse 4:**

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾. This begins the detailing of the lawful things, some of which were mentioned in summary after the explanation of the unlawful things.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, and others related from Abu Rafi' who said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked permission to enter. He was given permission, but he delayed. So (the Prophet) took his cloak and went out to him, and he (Jibril) was standing at the door. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'We have given you permission.' He said: 'Indeed, but we do not enter a house in which there is a picture or a dog.' Then they looked, and in some of their houses there was a puppy." Abu Rafi' said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) then ordered me to kill every dog in Medina, and I did so. People came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us from this community which you have ordered to be killed?' The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent, and Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿They ask you﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir also related from Ikrimah that the questioners were Asim ibn Adi, Sa'd ibn Khaythamah, and Uwaym ibn Sa'idah.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that the questioners were Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhal al-Ta'i. The question has been given the meaning of saying (*al-qawl*), and therefore the clause is reported (after it) as it would be after saying, and it is not suspended (*mu'allaq*). This is because it, although it is among the verbs of the heart, is a cause of knowledge and a path to it, so it is suspended just as knowledge is suspended. This is contrary to Abu Hayyan. Thereby the objection is dismissed, which said that the question is not something that governs clauses and does not take a preposition, so one does not say "he was asked about such-and-such." Some have claimed, for this reason, that there is an elided noun (*mudaf*), meaning "the answer to what." The first view is preferred by most scholars. The pronoun of absence is used instead of the first person used in their speech, because ﴿they ask﴾ is in the third-person form, just as you say: "Zayd swore that he would strike," and if you said "I will strike" it would be permissible. And the matter asked about, in view of the preceding discourse, is what is lawful of foods and edibles. It has also been said that the matter asked about is what is lawful of game and slaughtered animals.

﴿Say: What is good (*al-tayyibat*) has been made lawful for you﴾. That is, what sound natures do not find repulsive and from which they do not recoil. Al-Balkhi held this view, and it is also reported from Abu Ali al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim. It has also been said that it is what Allah, glorified is He, has permitted to be eaten among edible things, slaughtered animals, and game. It has also been said that it is what no text or analogy (*qiyas*, analogical reasoning) has prohibited, and this includes consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement), since it must rest on a text even if you are not aware of it. According to these two views, "good" (*tayyib*) means "lawful" (*halal*), and according to the first view it means "pleasant." It has come with both meanings.

﴿And what you have taught from the trained hunting animals (*al-jawarih*)﴾. This is coordinated (*'atf*) upon ﴿the good things﴾ with an elided noun, on the basis that *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), and its returning pronoun is elided. That is: "and the game of what you have taught them." It has been said that what is meant is the act of hunting, since that is what is made lawful; its coordination with ﴿the good things﴾ is coordination of the particular upon the general. It has also been said that it is evident that there is no need to make *al-sayd* (the hunting) mean *al-masid* (the game caught), since lawfulness and unlawfulness pertain to the act. It is possible that *ma* is conditional (*shartiyyah*) and the subject (*mubtada'*), with the answer (*jawab*) being ﴿then eat﴾, and the predicate being the answer, and the condition is in accordance with the preferred view. The clause is coordinated upon the clause ﴿it has been made lawful for you﴾ and does not need an elided noun.

It is transmitted from al-Zamakhshari that he said that there is an elision in it, and he said: "Its elision does not invalidate *ma* being conditional, because what is attached to a conditional noun has the status of what is attached to it, as you say: 'The servant of whoever strikes, I will strike,' just as you say: 'Whoever strikes, I will strike.'" It was objected that on that elision the predicate would be devoid of a pronoun referring to the subject, unless one labors to make ﴿what they have held back﴾ a case of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for ﴿what you have taught﴾. So understand.

It is also permitted that it be the subject, on the assumption that it is also a relative pronoun, with the predicate being ﴿eat﴾. The *fa'* (then) entered only in imitation of the relative pronoun with the conditional noun; but this is contrary to the apparent sense. ﴿From the trained hunting animals﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the relative pronoun or of its elided pronoun. *Jawarih* is the plural of *jarihah*, and the *ha'* in it, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is for intensification (*mubalaghah*). It is a predominant attribute, since the qualified noun is hardly ever mentioned with it.

[p. 63]

It has been interpreted as "the predatory ones among wild animals and birds," and it comes from the saying: "So-and-so *jarraha* (gained/earned) for his family good," when he earned for them; and "So-and-so is the *jarihah* of his family," meaning their earner. It has also been said that they were called *jawarih* because they generally wound (*tajrah*) the game.

It is reported from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, and this is what is narrated from the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt according to the claim of the Shi'a, that they are dogs alone.

﴿Trained (*mukallibin*)﴾, that is, teaching them to hunt. The *mukallib* is the trainer of the hunting animals and the one who makes them strike at game. It is derived from *kalb* (dog) for this well-known animal, because training very often occurs with it; or because every predator is called a dog, according to what has been said. Al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* related, and said: "Its chain is sound," from the hadith of Abu Nawfal who said: "Lahab ibn Abi Lahab used to revile the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, set upon him a dog from Your dogs, or Your dog.' So he went out in a caravan wishing to go to Syria. They stopped at a place where there were predators, and he said: 'I fear the supplication of Muhammad (ﷺ).' So they placed his goods around him and sat guarding him. A lion came, snatched him away, and went off with him." It is not hidden that there is some difficulty in including birds of prey in this, and there is no evidence in calling the lion a dog.

It is permitted that it be derived from *kalb*, which means "rapacity," as one says: "He is a *kalb* for such-and-such," if he is rapacious for it. Its accusative (*nasb*) is in the circumstantial sense from the subject of *'allamtum* (you have taught), and its benefit is to emphasize the teaching, because the *mukallib* applies only to one who is expert in his knowledge. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them, that they read *mukbilin* with a light vowelling, from *akyala* (a form of the verb), and *fa'ala* and *af'ala* are sometimes used with one meaning.

﴿You train them﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of *mukallibin*, or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'nafiyyah*) if *ma* is not conditional; otherwise it is an intervening clause (*mu'taridah*). It is permitted that it be a second circumstantial clause from the pronoun of *'allamtum*. Abu al-Baqa' prohibited this, on the ground that one single governing element does not govern two circumstantial clauses, but there is room for discussion in this. It was not considered good to make it a circumstantial clause of *al-jawarih* because of the separation between them.

﴿From what Allah has taught you﴾: from the stratagems and methods of teaching and training. This is either by inspiration from Him, glorified is He, or by the intellect which He created in them, exalted is He. It has been said that what is meant is: from what Allah, glorified is He, made known to you, that you should teach it, from following game, by sending them out at the command of their owner, by their obeying his call, by their turning back at his summons, by holding the game for him, and by not eating from it.

This has been preferred, because it indicates that the trainer should also be a jurist (*faqih*). The *min* here is causal (*ajaliyyah*). It has been said that it is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), meaning: some of what Allah has taught you.

﴿Then eat of what they hold for you﴾. This is a clause consequent upon the explanation of the lawfulness of game caught by trained hunting animals, explaining the elided noun and pointing to the result and effect of the training. Or it is the answer to the condition, or the predicate of the subject. The *min* is partitive, since some of what is held is not eaten, such as the skin, the bone, and other things. It has been said that it is superfluous according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. The exclusion of what has been mentioned is self-evident. *Ma* is relative or descriptive, and the returning pronoun is elided, meaning: "what they held it." The feminine pronoun refers to the trained hunting animals. ﴿For you﴾ is connected to ﴿they held﴾, and the sense of "upon" is figurative. The restriction by this is to exclude what they hold for themselves, and its sign is that they eat from it, so it is not to be eaten. The Prophet (ﷺ) has indicated this. The authors of the *Sunan* related from Adi ibn Hatim who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the game of a trained dog, and he (peace be upon him) said: 'When you send your trained dog and mention the name of Allah, then eat of what it holds for you. If it has eaten from it, then do not eat, for it has held only for itself.'" This is the view of the majority of jurists. It is reported from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Sha'bi, and Ikrimah.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions said: "If the dog has eaten from the game, then it is not trained, and its game is not to be eaten. The game of the falcon and the like is eaten even if it has eaten, because training birds of prey to the point of not eating is impossible."

This is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Abd ibn Humayd related from him

[p. 64]

that he said: "If the dog has eaten, then do not eat. If the falcon has eaten, then eat, because you can strike the dog but you cannot strike the falcon." Imam al-Haramayn among the Shafi'is held this view. Malik and al-Layth said: "It is eaten even if the dog has eaten from it."

It has been related from Salman, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them, that if the dog has eaten two-thirds of it and one-third remains, and you have mentioned the name of Allah over it, then eat.

﴿And mention the name of Allah over it﴾. The pronoun refers to *ma 'allamtum* (what you have trained), as the preceding report indicates. The meaning is: "Say the name over it when you release it." This is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. It has been said that it refers to *ma amsakna* (what they held), meaning: say the name over it if you reach its slaughter. It has been said that it refers to the verbal noun implied by *kulu* (eat), meaning: mention the name of Allah, exalted is He, upon eating. This is far-fetched, even though Abu Hayyan preferred it. The command is for obligation according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and for recommendation according to al-Shafi'i. According to the last view it is for recommendation by consensus.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding His prohibitions, among which is eating the game of trained hunting animals that were not trained.

﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. That is, swift in bringing His reckoning, or swift in completing it when He begins it. It has been reported that He, glorified is He, will reckon all creation in half a day. According to both interpretations, what is meant is that He, majestic is His glory, will hold you accountable for all actions, small and great. The explicit mention of the majestic Name is to instill awe and to give the reason for the ruling. Perhaps the mention of this after the explanation of the ruling on game is to urge those who engage in it toward piety, because it is a place where negligence and heedlessness of obedience to Allah, exalted is He, tend to occur. For we have seen that most who engage in it abandon the prayer and do not care about impurity. Those in need of game who guard their religion are rarer than a white crow, and they are rewarded for it.

Al-Tabarani related from Safwan ibn Umayyah: "That Urfutah ibn Nahik al-Tamimi said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I and the people of my household are provided with sustenance from this game, and for us there is in it a share and blessing. But it is a distraction from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and from the prayer in congregation. We have need of it. Do you permit it or forbid it?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I permit it, because Allah, exalted is He, has permitted it. An excellent occupation! Allah, exalted is He, is more deserving of excuse. Before me there were messengers, all of whom hunted or sought game. It is enough for you regarding the prayer in congregation, when you are absent from it while seeking provision, that you love the congregation and its people, and that you love the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and its people. Seek the lawful of it for yourself and your dependents, for that is struggle in the way of Allah, exalted is He.'"

Know that the help of Allah, exalted is He, is with the righteous merchants. The verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of training animals and striking them for a benefit, since training may require that. It is also used as evidence for the permissibility of keeping a dog for hunting, and guarding has been analogized to it, and that the game of a Magian's dog is not lawful. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, held this view. It is related from him concerning a Muslim who takes a Magian's dog, or his hawk, or his falcon, or his eagle, and sends it, that he said: "Do not eat it, even if you mention the name, because it is from the training of a Magian." Allah, exalted is He, only said: ﴿You train them from what Allah has taught you﴾.

[p. 65]

﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you.﴾ Restating this ruling serves to emphasize it and to prepare for what follows. The reason for mentioning "today" is known from what was mentioned yesterday.

Al-Naysaburi said: The benefit of the repetition is to make known that this ruling remains in place now that the religion has been completed and firmly established. But the first explanation is better.

﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you.﴾ That is, it is permissible (ḥalāl). The relative phrase refers to the Jews and Christians, including the Arab Christians according to us. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that he excepted the Christians of the Banu Taghlib, saying: "They are not Christians in the true sense; they took from Christianity only the drinking of wine." Ibn Jubayr held this view, and al-Rabiʿ related it from al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him. The "food" of the People of the Book means what includes their slaughtered animals and other foods, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-Darda', Ibrahim, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them all. Al-Jubba'i, al-Balkhi, and others also said this.

[p. 65 continues]

In al-Bukhari, it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the term refers to slaughtered animals, because the permissibility of other foods is not disputed. Most commentators hold this view. It has also been said that the verse applies specifically to grains and to things that do not require ritual slaughter (tadhkiya). This is the view narrated by the Imamiyya from Abu ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group of the Zaydiyya also held it. According to them, the slaughter of the People of the Book is not lawful. The ruling on the Sabians, according to the Great Imam (Abu Hanifa), may Allah be pleased with him, is the same as the ruling on the People of the Book. His two companions said: The Sabians are of two kinds. One kind reads the Psalms and worships the angels, and the other kind reads no scripture and worships the stars. The latter are not among the People of the Book.

As for the Magians, the Sunna was established regarding them to treat them like the People of the Book in levying the jizya tax, but not in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women. This is because ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, and al-Bayhaqi related, through al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to the Magians of Hajar, inviting them to Islam. Whoever accepts it will be accepted; whoever persists will have the jizya imposed on them, except for those who marry their women." Although this report is mursal (its chain is missing a companion) and its isnad includes Qays ibn al-Rabiʿ, who is weak, the consensus of most Muslims, as al-Bayhaqi said, supports it.

Scholars differed on the permissibility of the slaughter of a Jew or Christian over which the name of someone other than Allah was invoked, such as ʿUzayr or ʿIsa, peace be upon them both. Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It is not lawful. This is also the view of Rabiʿa. But most scholars held that it is lawful, as did al-Shaʿbi and ʿAta'. They said: Allah has made their slaughtered animals lawful, and He knows what they say.

Al-Hasan said: If a Jew or Christian slaughters and mentions the name of someone other than Allah in your presence, do not eat it. But if it happens out of your sight, eat, for Allah has made it lawful for you.

﴿Your food is lawful for them.﴾ Al-Zajjaj and many later scholars said: This is an address to the believers, meaning: there is no blame on you, O believers, if you feed the People of the Book from your food. Therefore, this verse is not evidence for those who hold that disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Sharia, because permissibility is a ruling, and Allah has linked it to them here just as He linked rulings to believers. The apparent meaning has been objected to on the grounds that it would only work if "feeding" (iṭʿām) were in place of "food" (ṭaʿām). If they claim that "food" stands in place of "feeding" by extension, then separating a verbal noun from its complement by the predicate of the subject is impermissible. Scholars have explicitly stated that it is not allowed to say "Zayd's feeding is good for the poor" or "your striking is severe to Zayd." So how is "Your food is lawful for them" acceptable? Some said: If it is asked what the wisdom is in this clause when they are disbelievers who do not need our explanation, the answer is: the meaning is, look at what has been made lawful for you in your Sharia, and if they feed you that, then eat it; do not look at what was forbidden to them. The flesh of camels and similar animals was forbidden to them, and then it was abrogated (naskh) in our Sharia. So the verse is an explanation for us, not for them. That is, know that what was forbidden to them, but is lawful for you, has also been made lawful for you. For this reason, if they feed us pork or something similar and say, "It is lawful in our Sharia," we would deny them, and say: The food that is lawful for you is the food that is lawful for us, and nothing else.

The summary of the meaning is: their food is lawful for you if it is food that I have made lawful for you. This interpretation is the meaning of al-Suddi's statement and others. Understand it, for it has been confusing to some contemporary scholars.

﴿And the chaste women from among the believers.﴾ This is coordinated with "the good things" (al-ṭayyibāt), or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, because what preceded indicates it. That is: lawful for you too. The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the chaste women," or to the pronoun in it, as Abu al-Baqa' said. By "them" (the chaste women), according to al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, and Ibrahim, is meant the chaste ones. According to Mujahid, it means free women (ḥarāʾir). This was preferred by Abu ʿAli. According to a group, it means both the chaste and the free. Specifying them by mention is to encourage what is better, not to negate what is beyond them. For the marriage of Muslim slave women under the required conditions is valid by consensus, and likewise the marriage of unchaste women among them. As for the Christian and Jewish slave women, they are like Muslim women according to the Great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you.﴾

[p. 66]

Even if they are at war with you, as is the apparent meaning.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Marriage to women at war with you is not permissible, and he restricted the verse to protected (dhimmi) women. He argued with the verse: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.﴾ And marriage requires affection, according to the verse: ﴿He created for you spouses from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy.﴾ Al-Jassas said: This, according to us, only indicates disapproval, and our companions dislike marrying the people of war. The Imamiyya held that it is not permissible to contract a permanent marriage with the women of the Book, based on the verse: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe﴾ and the verse: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage with disbelieving women.﴾ They interpreted this verse to mean that "the chaste women from among those who were given the Book" refers to those among them who have embraced Islam, and "the chaste women from among the believers" refers to those who were believers originally. This is because some people felt scruples about marrying a woman who had converted from disbelief, so Allah made clear that there is no fault in that.

Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, also took "the chaste women" to mean those who embraced Islam. It is not hidden that this goes against the apparent meaning and the structure of the verse rejects it. For this reason, some claimed that the apparent meaning is intended, but that permissibility is restricted to temporary marriage (nikāḥ al-mutʿa) and to ownership by the right hand (milk al-yamin), and that intercourse with them is lawful on both grounds according to the Shiʿa. You know that this is more calamitous and bitter. Therefore, some fled to the claim that the verse was abrogated by the two verses mentioned just before, citing a report transmitted by al-Jarud from Abu Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him, on this matter. But this is not authentic according to the people of the Sunna. Yes, Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade categories of women except for believing emigrant women, and he forbade every woman of a religion other than Islam."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that he was asked about a Muslim marrying a Jewish or Christian woman, and he said: "We married them in the time of the conquest, when we could hardly find Muslim women in abundance. When we returned, we divorced them."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan that he was asked: "Does a man marry a woman from the People of the Book?" He said: "What does he have to do with the People of the Book? Allah has made Muslim women abundant. If he must do it, let him aim for a chaste woman who is not a prostitute." The man said: "And what is a prostitute?" He said: "She is one who, when a man glances at her, follows him."

﴿When you have given them their wages.﴾ That is, their dowries (mahr), which are the exchange for enjoying them, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others said. The restriction of permissibility to giving them their dowries is to emphasize its obligation and to guard against neglect. It is also possible that "giving" means undertaking and committing, metaphorically. This is perhaps closer to the first meaning, though the outcome is the same. "When" (idhā) is a temporal clause relating to the omitted verb "become lawful" (ḥalla). It may also be conditional, with its answer omitted: that is, when you have given them their wages, they become lawful for you.

﴿Being chaste.﴾ That is, guarding yourselves through marriage. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "you have given them." Likewise, his words: ﴿not committing illicit sex﴾. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "chaste," or a descriptive qualifier of "chaste": that is, not openly committing fornication.

﴿Nor taking secret lovers.﴾ That is, nor keeping them secretly. A "lover" (khidn) is a close friend, applied to both male and female. It has been said that the first phrase forbids fornication and the second forbids intimacy with them. The participle "taking" may be in the genitive as a coordinate of "committing illicit sex," with "not" added to emphasize the negation implied by "not." It may also be in the accusative as a coordinate of "not committing illicit sex," according to its three grammatical possibilities.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith.﴾ That is, whoever denies what is to be believed in, which is the laws of Islam, among which are the rulings mentioned here regarding what is lawful and unlawful, and refuses to accept them. ﴿Then his deeds have become void.﴾ That is, the deeds he did, believing them to be a means of drawing near to Allah.

[p. 67]

﴿And in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.﴾ That is, the ruined. The verse is a concluding clause (tadhyil) to the statement: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you,﴾ etc., to glorify the status of what Allah has made lawful and what He has forbidden, and to be severe against whoever opposes that. So interpreting "faith" in its verbal sense, and supposing an omitted genitive, as has been said, meaning "by the requirement of faith," which is Allah the Exalted, is nothing, even though Mujahid's statement seems to suggest it. The pronoun of the nominative is the subject, and "among the losers" is its predicate. The prepositional phrase "in" is connected to what the predicate connects to, namely the absolute settledness. It has also been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by what is mentioned, meaning: losers in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is connected to "the losers," with "al-" being definite and not relative, because what follows it does not govern what precedes it. It has also been said that in a prepositional phrase of time, what is not allowed elsewhere is permitted, as in the poet's line:

I raised him until, when he had grown up strong,
my reward was that I be beaten with a stick.

* * *

This is the allusive (ishara) interpretation of the verses:

﴿O you who believe﴾ by scholarly faith. ﴿Fulfill the contracts.﴾ That is, with the firm resolutions of obligation. Abu al-Hasan al-Farisi said: Allah commanded His servants to guard their intentions in dealings, to exercise discipline in self-accountings, to be vigilant in passing thoughts, and to be watchful in what is witnessed. Some said: "Fulfill the contracts" means the contract of the heart through knowledge, the contract of the tongue through praise, and the contract of the limbs through humility.

It has been said: The first contract made with a person is the contract of responding to Him, the Exalted, with lordship and not disobeying by turning to anything other than Him. The second contract is the contract of bearing the trust and abandoning betrayal.

﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle.﴾ That is, all kinds of enjoyments and pleasures are made lawful for you by sound souls, which are not dominated by predatory and gluttonous tendencies. ﴿Except what is recited to you﴾ of enjoyments that are contrary to virtue and justice. ﴿Not hunting while you are in the state of ihram.﴾ That is, not enjoying pleasures while you are stripped for the journey and intend the Kaʿba of union, turning toward the sanctuary of the attributes of beauty and majesty. ﴿Indeed, Allah decides what He wills.﴾ So let the wayfarer be content with His judgment, so that he may find rest and be guided to the path of right guidance.

(﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾) from among the maqamat (spiritual stations) and ahwal (spiritual states) by which the wayfarer (al-salik) travels to the sanctuary of his Lord, glorified is He: patience, reliance, gratitude, and the like. That is, do not step outside their rulings. (﴿Nor the sacred month﴾), which is the time of the true pilgrimage, the time of journeying toward the King of kings. Violating it means departing from its ruling and busying oneself with what contradicts it. (﴿Nor the sacrificial animal﴾), which is the soul made ready and prepared for approach when it reaches the Presence. Violating it means using it for what diverts it, or burdening it with what causes it weariness. (Nor the garlands), which are the sacred acts the soul has garlanded itself with, without which arrival cannot be completed. Violating them means treating them lightly and not performing them in their complete form. (﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾), who are the wayfarers. Violating their path means repelling them and occupying them with what blocks or enervates them. (﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord﴾) through the manifestations of the Acts, (﴿and approval﴾) through the manifestations of the Attributes. (﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾), that is: when you return to subsistence after annihilation (fana'), there is no blame upon you for enjoyment.

(﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾), that is: let not the hostility of the carnal faculties, because they hinder you from the journey, lead you to (﴿transgress﴾) against them and subdue them entirely, so that they become idle or weakened in their benefits. Or: let not the hatred of a people among your relatives or friends, because they bar you, lead you (﴿to transgress﴾) against them by harboring enmity toward them, harming them, and wishing them evil.

(﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾) by directing those faculties and governing them, or by caring for family and friends and being good to them. (﴿But do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾), for that cuts you off from arrival.

It is related from Sahl that righteousness is faith, piety is the Sunnah, sin is disbelief, and aggression is innovation.

And it is related from al-Sadiq (may Allah be pleased with him): righteousness is faith, piety is sincerity, sin is disbelief, and aggression is acts of disobedience.

It has been said: righteousness is what the scholars agree upon without disagreement, piety is opposing one's desire, sin is seeking dispensations, and aggression is overstepping into doubtful matters.

(﴿And fear Allah﴾) regarding these matters. (﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾), so He will punish you with what He knows best.

(﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾), which is the complete extinguishing of desire, for it is the vice of neglect that contradicts chastity. (﴿And blood﴾), which is indulging in the desires of the soul. (﴿And the flesh of swine﴾), that is, all other forms of indulgence through greed, gluttony, and lack of zeal. (﴿And that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾) from deeds performed for show and reputation. (﴿And the strangled animal﴾), which are good actions in appearance while desire remains hidden within them. (﴿And the one struck to death﴾), which are actions compelled by desire. (﴿And the fallen﴾), which are actions inclined toward neglect and deficiency. (﴿And the one gored﴾), which are actions done out of fear of disgrace or for example to deter the enjoiner of good. (﴿And that which has been eaten by a predator﴾), which are actions suited to the irascible faculty, such as pride and carnal zeal. (﴿Except what you slaughter [in time]﴾) of good actions that proceed from a deliberate intention of the heart, not mixed with anything that defiles them. (﴿And that which is sacrificed on stone altars﴾), which is what the people of customs do, without a rational or legal purpose. (﴿And that you seek decision through arrows﴾), by seeking happiness and perfection through lots and omens, abandoning action and saying: "If it had been decreed for us, we would have acted," for the decree may be contingent upon striving. (﴿That is grave disobedience﴾), a departure from the true religion, because it involves commanding and forbidding and relying on what is decreed, rendering them futile. (﴿This day﴾), which is the time of the attainment of perfection, (﴿those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾), by barring you from the path of truth. (﴿So do not fear them﴾), for they will no longer have dominion over you. (﴿But fear Me﴾), so that you may attain what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. (﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion﴾) by clarifying what I have clarified. (﴿And completed upon you My favor﴾) by that, or by guidance to Me. (﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾), that is, submission to being effaced. (﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger﴾) to consume a pleasure, (﴿in a state of severe hunger﴾), which is intense anguish of the soul, (﴿without intending sin﴾), not inclining toward vice, (﴿then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾), who will conceal that and show mercy through the aid of divine success.

(﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: Lawful for you are the good things﴾) among the realities that come to you through your intellects, hearts, and spirits. (﴿And [the game caught by] what you have taught of the trained hunting animals﴾), which are the senses, outward and inward, and all other bodily faculties and instruments. (﴿Trained to hunt﴾), instructing them to acquire virtues. (﴿You train them in what Allah has taught you﴾), from the sciences of ethics and the laws. (﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾), from what leads to perfection. (﴿And mention the name of Allah upon it﴾), by intending that it is one of the means of reaching Him, exalted is His station, and not merely a carnal pleasure. (﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾), which is the station of distinction and unity. (﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾), so there is no harm in your feeding them from it, by joining unity to the people of distinction and distinction to the people of unity. (﴿And [lawful are] chaste women from among the believers﴾), who are the refined and perfected souls. (﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾), that is: their rights of perfection suited to them, and by bringing them to the level of the chaste women among the believers, (﴿when you have given them their due compensation, being chaste, not unlawful fornicators or secret lovers﴾), but intending their perfection and the benefit of their beneficial effects, not mere companionship, and pouring out the waters of knowledge without fruit. (﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith﴾), by denying the laws and realities and refusing to accept them, (﴿his deeds have become worthless﴾) by his denial of the laws. (﴿And he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers﴾) by his denial of the realities. The apparent meaning is that there is no distribution here, and Allah the Exalted knows best His intent, and He is the Granter of success to what is right.

[Page 68]

[Page 69]

﴿O you who have believed﴾ marks the beginning of the explanation of the rulings related to their religion, after the explanation of what relates to their worldly affairs. The reason for this ordering is evident. ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾ means: when you intend to stand up for it and occupy yourselves with it. The intention to perform the act is expressed by the act that results from it, as a metaphor (majaz). Its purpose is brevity and alerting the listener to the fact that one who intends worship should hasten to it, so that the act is not separated from the intention. It has also been said that the intended meaning may be: when you intend prayer, and one of the two concomitants of a thing is expressed by its other concomitant. The apparent meaning of the verse requires ablution (wudu') for everyone who rises to prayer, even if he is not in a state of minor impurity, based on the generality of ﴿those who have believed﴾, without restriction to those who are in a state of minor impurity. The sentence contains no indication of repeating the act, and that would be contrary to the sound position; but the consensus (ijma') is against that.

Muslim and others have narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the five prayers with one ablution on the day of the Conquest. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Did you do something you did not used to do?" He, peace be upon him, said: "I did it deliberately, ʿUmar," meaning to show that it is permissible. Therefore the majority favoured the view that the verse is restrictive (muqayyidah), and the meaning is: ﴿when you rise to prayer﴾ while in a state of minor impurity, by the indication of the situation (qarinah dalalat al-hal). Also, impurity is a condition for the substitute, which is tayammum (dry ablution); so if it had no role in wudu' while having a role in tayammum, the substitute would not be a substitute.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you find no water﴾ is explicit about its being a substitute. Some later scholars held that there is a conditional clause in the sentence, meaning: ﴿when you rise to prayer, then wash﴾ etc., if you are in a state of minor impurity; because the coordination of ﴿and if you are in a state of major impurity (janabah), then purify yourselves﴾ with it fits it perfectly. It has also been said that the command is recommendatory (nadb), and the obligation for one in a state of minor impurity is known from the Sunnah. This was deemed unlikely, because there is consensus that the obligation of wudu' is derived from this verse, while it requires restriction to those other than those in a state of minor impurity without evidence. Even less likely is that it is recommended for some and obligatory for others. It has also been said that it is obligatory, and that wudu' was obligatory for everyone who stood for prayer at the beginning, and then it was abrogated (nuskh).

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Hakim have narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Hanzalah al-Ghasil that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to perform wudu' for every prayer, whether he was pure or not. When that became difficult for him (ﷺ), he was commanded to use the miswak for every prayer, and wudu' was lifted from him except for minor impurity. This is not contradicted by the report that al-Ma'idah was the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, etc., because it is not of the same strength; so much so that al-Iraqi said: "I have not found it traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)." Yes, the derivation of the obligation for the entire Ummah initially, then the abrogation of the obligation for them at the end, by what indicates the obligation for him, peace be upon him, at the beginning, and its abrogation for him at the end, is not free of difficulty, as is not hidden.

Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and others have narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that the interpretation of the verse, ﴿when you rise﴾ from the beds, meaning sleep, ﴿to prayer﴾, is evident. It is reported from Dawud that he obligated wudu' for every prayer, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the caliphs after him used to perform wudu' in this way. ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, used to perform wudu' in this way and recite this verse. But in this there is that the hadith of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, refutes the continuation of the Prophet, peace be upon him, on what was mentioned. The report from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, is not established. The practice of the caliphs indicates no more than recommendation (nadb) and desirability (istihbab). It has been reported: "Whoever performs wudu' while already in a state of purity, Allah records for him ten good deeds."

﴿So wash your faces﴾, meaning: pour water over them. The limit of pouring is that the water drips, even a single drop, according to Abu Hanifah and Muhammad. According to Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him, dripping is not a condition. As for rubbing (dalk), it is not part of the reality of washing, contrary to Malik. Therefore its reality does not depend on it. It has been said: their evidence for this is the saying of the Arabs, "The rain washed the earth," and there is nothing in that except pouring. This is refuted: the impact of rain from above, especially with its force and repetition, is indeed rubbing of the strongest kind! And they only say it when the earth has been cleaned, and that happens only by rubbing. Also, it is not consistent with the rationale of the legislation of washing, which is beautifying the appearance of the visible limbs for standing before the Lord, glorified and exalted, which is not complete for the rest of the one performing wudu' except by rubbing.

It is reported from him that rubbing is not obligatory in itself, but is obligatory to ensure the arrival of water; so if that is achieved, it is not obligatory, as Ibn al-Hajj said in his commentary on al-Munya. Among the strange points is that he held that rubbing is a condition of washing, but did not require flowing in the case where one passes ice over a limb: he said that this suffices even if the ice does not melt and flow. al-Awzaʿi agreed with him on this, although that is not called washing at all, and it is far-fetched that it substitutes for it.

The limit of the face according to us is, in length, from the beginning of the surface of the forehead to the bottom of the two jaws, and in width, what lies between the two earlobes, because facing (muwajahah) occurs in this state, and the word (wajh, face) is derived from it. The derivation of a triliteral form from a derived form, when the derived form is more common in the meaning they share, is common.

The scholar Akmal al-Din said: What they mention about prohibiting the derivation of a triliteral from a derived form applies only to the minor derivation (al-ishtiqaq al-saghir). As for the major derivation (al-ishtiqaq al-kabir), which is when there is correspondence between two words in form and meaning, it is permissible. The apparent meaning of the limit requires the obligation to include the white area that lies between the sideburn and the ear after it grows, and this is the position of the two disciples (Abu Yusuf and Muhammad) according to them, contrary to Abu Yusuf. It also requires the obligation to pour water over the hair of the beard.

The reports from the Great Imam (Abu Hanifah), may Allah be pleased with him, and others differ on this. From him: it is obligatory to wipe a quarter of it; from him: wiping what touches the skin; from him: nothing is required concerning it, and this is a narration from Abu Yusuf. From Abu Yusuf: it is obligatory to cover all of it. From Muhammad: it is obligatory to wash the whole of it. It has been said, and this is the more correct view, and in al-Fatawa al-Zahiriyyah it says: "On this is the fatwa," because it has taken the place of the skin, so the obligation shifts to it, like the eyebrow.

In al-Bada'i' it says, from Ibn Shuja': "They returned from everything other than this." All of this concerns thick hair. As for thin hair through which the skin is visible, it is obligatory to make the water reach what is beneath it. If one passes water over the hair of the chin and then shaves it, it is not obligatory to wash the chin. In al-Baqqal: if one trims the moustache, it is not obligatory to pass water through it (takhlil); but if it is long, passing water through it is obligatory, as is making water reach the two lips. The likely reason is that trimming it is sunnah, so its presence is not considered in the removal of what is beneath it, unlike the beard, for leaving it grow (i'fa') is the sunnah. Shaykh al-Islam al-Marghinani, in al-Tajnis, counted making water reach the roots of the eyebrow hair and the moustache among the etiquettes, without detailed distinction.

As for the lip, it has been said: it is a follower of the mouth. Abu Jaʿfar said: what is hidden when the lips are closed is a follower of it, and what is visible belongs to the face. This definition has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with them all, and others.

It has also been said: the face is everything below the place of hair growth on the head down to the end of the chin, in length, and from ear to ear, in width: what appears of that to the eye of the observer, and what is inside, such as the interior of the nose and mouth, and likewise what faces the two ears.

It has been narrated from Anas ibn Malik, Umm Salamah, ʿAmmar, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and a group, that they made obligatory the washing of all of that. I have not found a textual basis for them regarding the inside of the eye. The apparent position is that washing it is not obligatory, because of the great hardship and the expectation of harm. For this reason some have stated that washing it is not even sunnah, and some said it is disliked. However, there comes to mind a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he used to make washing the inside of the eye obligatory in a full washing (ghusl) and would do it, and that it was the cause of the preservation of his sight, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And your arms to the elbows﴾. The word (mirfaq, elbow) is the plural of (mirfaq), with a kasrah then fathah, which is more eloquent than the reverse. It is the junction of the forearm with the upper arm. Perhaps the reason for naming it so is that one leans on it (yurtafaq bihi), meaning one rests upon it from the hand. The majority of jurists hold that it is included.

It has been narrated from al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I know of no disagreement that the elbows must be washed." For this reason it was said that (ila) here means (maʿa, with), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He will add strength to your strength﴾ and ﴿who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ It was also said: it only conveys the meaning of a limit (ghayah).

Among the established principles is this: what comes after a limit, if it would have been included in the thing named had the limit not been mentioned, is included; otherwise it is not. There is no doubt that the elbows are included in what is named, so they are included. As for the objection to this principle, that if someone swears not to speak to so-and-so until tomorrow, the one addressed is not included, although he would be included if the limit were omitted, this is not damaging to it; because the discussion here concerns the requirement of the language, while oaths are based on custom, and custom may differ from language.

Some researchers mentioned that (ila) is used both where what follows is included in the ruling concerning what precedes it, and where what follows is not included. Some scholars judged that it is shared (mushtarak); others judged that inclusion is the apparent meaning; others judged that the apparent meaning is non-inclusion. The grammarians hold this last view. The inclusion of the elbows is established by the Sunnah, for it is reported authentically from him, peace be upon him, that he passed the water over them.

Our scholars transmitted the view that they are not included from Zufar, and he argued by the conflict of similar things (taʿarud al-ashbah), and that in including them in what is named there is also doubt, so they are not included in case of doubt. The hadith of passing the water does not necessitate that it is obligatory, since it may be by way of sunnah, like the addition in wiping the head until one covers all of it.

It is answered: there is no conflict with the predominance of usage in the established principle. Also, according to what he said, ambiguity (ijmal) is established regarding their inclusion, so his, peace be upon him, limiting the washing to the elbow occurred as an explanation of what was meant by the hand. Thus the inclusion of what it included is established, as in ("wash your hand for eating"), by the use of the name of the whole for a part, relying on the indication.

The scholar Ibn Hajar said: their inclusion is indicated by the following (ittiba') and consensus (ijma'). Indeed the verse also indicates it, by taking (ila) as a limit for a omitted verb, on the basis that the hand in reality extends to the shoulder, as is the most famous usage in the language. It seems that by consensus he meant the consensus of the people of the first generation, for otherwise there is no doubt that opponents existed later. Dawud and likewise Imam Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, were counted among those. I have doubts about counting the latter, for Ibn Hubayrah transmitted the consensus of the four imams on the obligation of washing both hands with the elbows.

It has been said: This dispute has the following consequence: one who lacks a hand from the elbow is obligated, according to the one who holds that the elbow is included, to pass water over the end of the bone; but it is not obligatory according to the opponent, because the locus of obligation no longer exists at all, just as if one lacked the hand together with what is above the elbow. Yes, it is recommended for him to wash what remains of the upper arm, in order to preserve the whiteness (tahjil).

Furthermore, full washing of the hands that are commanded is an obligation (fard), as the apparent meaning of the verse indicates. So if dry mud or the like sticks to the base of the nail, or a spot the size of a needle's head remains unwashed in the place of washing, it is not valid. It is not obligatory to remove a ring and move it if it is loose. For a tight one, the preferred view is that it is obligatory. In al-Jami' al-Asghar it says: if one has long nails and there is dirt, mud, or dough beneath them, it is permissible, both in rural and urban areas, according to the correct view on which the fatwa is given, as al-Dabbusi said. It has also been said: it is obligatory to make the water reach what is beneath them, except for the dirt, because it is generated from it.

[Page 72]

Al-Saffar said: Washing (of the feet) is obligatory absolutely if the nail is long. Ibn al-Humam (d. 861 AH) approved this view, because washing, although it is restricted to the outer surfaces, becomes like an obstruction when the nail is long, such as a drop of wax. In the *Nawazil* (a collection of legal cases): it is obligatory for the townsman (*al-misri*) but not for the villager (*al-qarawi*), because the grease under the nails of the townsman prevents water from reaching the skin, unlike the villager. If a person's nails grew long until they extended beyond the tips of the fingers, washing them is obligatory by unanimous agreement. If a person was born with two hands on the shoulder, then the complete hand is the original one and must be washed, while the other is an extra. Whatever part of the extra hand corresponds to the place of obligation must be washed, and whatever does not correspond need not be washed. Strangely, some people made it obligatory to begin washing the hands from the elbows, so that if someone washed from the tips of the fingers, his ablution would not be valid.

Al-Tabarsi related this in *Majma' al-Bayan*, and it appears that this group is from the Shi'a, though I find no basis for them in this view.

﴿and wipe your heads﴾. It was said: the *ba'* (preposition "bi") is extra (*za'idah*), to make the verb transitive directly. It was also said that it indicates partialness (*tab'id*). Ibn Malik reported from Abu 'Ali in *al-Tadhkirah* that it comes for this purpose, and he cited:

[Page 73]

They drank from the water of the sea, then they rose up,
when the green deep waters roared for them.

It was also said: custom has shifted it to partialness in transitive verbs.

The obligatory amount in wiping, according to us, is the measure of the forelock (*nasiyah*), which is a quarter of the head from any side above the two ears, based on what Muslim narrated from al-Mughirah: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ablution and wiped over his forelock." The Qur'anic text is general (*mujmal*) regarding the quantity, so this hadith is taken as its explanation. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) rejects this and says: the text is absolute (*mutlaq*), not general (*mujmal*), because it did not intend a specific quantity to be left vague; rather, it intended mere generality. Thus, according to him, wiping the head is fulfilled by the least amount that can be called "wiping the head." Moreover, the hadith of al-Mughirah has two versions: "over his forelock" (*'ala nasiyatihi*) and "with his forelock" (*bi-nasiyatihi*). The first does not require covering the entire forelock, since mentioning it may serve to rule out the assumption that he wiped the side of the head or the back of the head. So it does not prove your claim. If such a construction indicated full coverage, then wiping over the leather socks (*khuffayn*) would also indicate it, yet no one among us or among you holds that there. When we return to the second version, the point of dispute is the *ba'* as in the verse, and partialness returns. For this reason some scholars said: it is better to cite the report of Abu Dawud from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performing ablution, and he had a Qatari turban on him. He put his hand under the turban and wiped the front of his head." Abu Dawud remained silent about it, so it is a proof. Its apparent meaning is covering the entire front part, and the entire front part of the head is the quarter called the forelock. A similar report is what al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Ata': "that he (ﷺ) performed ablution, uncovered the turban, and wiped the front of his head, or he said: his forelock." This is a proof, even if it is a *mursal* report according to us (a report in which a successor omits the companion from the chain). And how not, when it is strengthened by a connected report?

There remains one point: that the act being established in this manner does not necessitate the negation of the permissibility of less. Therefore, one must add the premise: "if less were permissible, he would have done it once to teach its permissibility." This may be rejected on the grounds that when permissibility is derived from something other than the act, there is no need for the act to establish it. Here it is similar, in view of the verse, since the *ba'* in it indicates partialness, and that implies the permissibility of less. So the discussion returns to the indication of the verse. It is then said: the *ba'* here indicates attachment (*ilsaq*), which is the meaning agreed upon for it, unlike partialness. For many of the verifying scholars of the Arabic language deny that partialness is an independent meaning of *ba'*, unlike when it is within attachment, as in our present case. The attachment of the instrument to the head, which is the required thing, does not cover the whole head. So when it is attached and does not cover the whole, one leaves the obligation by that part. Then the quarter is determined, because the hand generally covers only about that amount, so it is necessary.

In some reports it is said that the obligation is the measure of three fingers, and some scholars authenticated this, considering that the requirement is the attachment of the hand, and the fingers are its base. This is why the full blood-money of the hand is due when it is cut off, and three fingers are most of it, and most of something has the ruling of the whole. The problems with this are not hidden, even if it is said to be the apparent narration.

Imam Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) and Imam Ahmad, according to the most apparent of his narrations, held that covering the entire head with wiping is obligatory. The Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'a) hold the view of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him). If rain falls on the required amount, the obligation is fulfilled according to us, and it is not required that it reach the head by the hand, because the instrument is intended only to bring the water to the place. When it reaches, the instrument is no longer needed. If one wipes with moisture on his hand that he did not take from another limb, it is permissible; if he took it from another limb, it is not permissible. If one wipes with one finger, extending it to the required amount, it is not permissible, and likewise with two fingers according to what has been said, in contrast to Zufar. They gave as the reason that the moisture has become used water. Yet this is subject to a problem: water does not become used until it separates, so this would not necessitate that stretching three fingers is impermissible if it is held that less than a quarter is not sufficient. The well-known view is permissibility.

Shams al-A'immah chose that the prohibition regarding extending one finger or two is not based on the moisture becoming used, as evidenced by the fact that wiping with two fingers in *tayammum* (dry ablution) is not permissible even when there is nothing that becomes used, especially if one performs *tayammum* on bare rock. Rather, the correct reasoning for him is that we are commanded to wipe with the hand, and two fingers of it are not called a hand, unlike three, because three is most of what is basically intended. This is good, as Ibn al-Humam said, but it requires that contact must be specifically with the hand, and this is refuted by the case of rain. It may be answered that what is meant is that contact is specifically with the hand, or what takes its place among the instruments, when intentionally bringing it about by action. However, this implies that such an instrument other than the hand must be equal in measure to three fingers of the hand, so that if it were a stick, for example, which does not reach that measure, we would say that wiping with it is not permissible.

It may also be said that the impermissibility with one finger is based on the moisture disappearing and running out before reaching the required measure, unlike two fingers, for the water is held between two joined fingers, an extra amount that can extend to the required measure. This is either observed or presumed, so the ruling must be established based on it. Thus, on the view that the sufficiency of the measure of three fingers is valid, it is permissible to extend two fingers, because the water between them extends the measure of a third finger. On the view that validity depends on a quarter, it is not permissible, because the water between them does not generally reach the extent of a quarter. However, this is in conflict with the impermissibility of *tayammum* with two fingers. If someone puts his head into a vessel of water intending to wipe, it is permissible. Abu Yusuf held that the water is pure, because it is not given the ruling of used water until after separation, and what touched the head of its parts adhered to it and purified it, while what did not touch it is not used.

The jurists agreed that wiping over a turban is not valid, except Ahmad, who permitted it on the condition that some of the turban be under the chin. This is a single narration. Regarding whether it is required that one had put on the turban in a state of ritual purity, there are two narrations. There is also a difference in his narration concerning a woman wiping over her round veil beneath her throat. It is reported from him that wiping is permitted like a man's turban with a chin-strap, and it is also reported from him that it is prohibited. It is reported from al-Awza'i and al-Thawri that wiping over a turban is permitted, but I have not found any report from them about the condition or its absence. The evidence for permissibility has been mentioned to us in the *al-Ajwibah al-'Iraqiyyah* in answer to the *al-As'ilah al-Iraniyyah*.

﴿and your feet up to the two ankles﴾. The two ankles (*al-ka'bayn*) are the two bones protruding from both sides at the joint of the leg and the foot. From this comes *al-ka'ib* (the young woman whose breasts appear for the first time). Hisham reported from Muhammad that the ankle (*ka'b*) is the joint in the middle of the foot at the place where the shoelace crosses, because *ka'b* is a name for a joint, and from it comes *ku'ub al-rumh* (the joints of a spear). The joint in the middle of the foot is a joint below what is on the leg. This is correct for the pilgrim in the state of consecration (*muhrim*) who does not find sandals, for he cuts his leather socks below the two ankles. Perhaps this is what Muhammad meant. As for ritual purification, there is no doubt that it is what we mentioned.

There are three recitations (*qira'at*) regarding "the feet." One is anomalous (*shadhdh*), and two are widely transmitted (*mutawatirah*). As for the anomalous one, it is the nominative (*raf'*), which is the recitation of al-Hasan. As for the two widely transmitted ones: the accusative (*nasb*), which is the recitation of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub; and the genitive (*jarr*), which is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr from him).

From here people differed regarding washing the two feet and wiping them. Imam al-Razi said: al-Qaffal in his *tafsir* reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, 'Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, and Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir (may Allah be pleased with them all) that the obligation regarding them is wiping, and this is the view of the Imamiyyah. The majority of jurists and exegetes said that their obligation is washing. Dawud said: it is obligatory to combine both (wiping and washing). This is the view of al-Nasir li-l-Haqq of the Zaydiyyah. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the one who is obligated is given a choice between wiping and washing. The evidence of those who hold wiping is the genitive recitation, for it requires that the feet be coordinated with (*ma'tufah 'ala*) the heads. So just as wiping is obligatory for them, it is obligatory for the feet.

The claim that it is a genitive by proximity (*jarr bi-l-jiwar*), as in their saying: "this is the hole of a ruined lizard (*dabb*)," and the saying of the poet:

As if Thabir, on the noses of its heavy rain,
is a great man wrapped in a mantle.

is false for several reasons:

The first is that the kasra by proximity is counted among the errors that may be tolerated for the necessity of poetry, whereas the speech of Allah Most High must be exalted above this.

The second is that the kasra is only resorted to where there is no risk of ambiguity, as in the examples they cited, whereas in the verse the absence of ambiguity is not established.

The third is that the genitive by proximity occurs only without the conjunctive particle, whereas with the conjunctive particle the Arabs never spoke that way.

They refuted the recitation of the accusative by the recitation of the genitive, saying: it also requires wiping, because the coordination in that case is with the place of the heads due to its nearness, so they share the ruling. This is a well-known view of the grammarians. Then they said: or it is not permissible to lift this by informing (*ikhbar*), because they are all of the category of solitary reports (*ahad*), and abrogating the Qur'an by a solitary report is not permissible.

Then the Imam said: know that this cannot be answered except in two ways:

The first is that numerous reports were transmitted requiring washing, and washing includes wiping but not vice versa. So washing is closer to caution, and it is necessary to adopt it. On this basis, it must be affirmed that washing the feet takes the place of wiping them.

The second is that the obligation regarding the feet is limited to the two ankles, and the limit was stated in connection with washing, not wiping. The scholars answered this in two ways:

The first is that the ankle refers to the bone beneath the joint of the foot, and on this interpretation wiping over the top of the two feet is required.

The second is that they conceded that the two ankles refer to the two protruding bones on both sides of the leg, but they held that the top of the two feet must be wiped up to these two points, and then this question does not arise. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the discussion of washing and wiping is one in which disputes have multiplied, and many feet have slipped in it. What the Imam (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned indicates that he is a pedestrian in this field and one who is skilled but cannot climb to the summit of a well-versed master, a verification in which minds and hearts rejoice. So let us expand the discussion on verifying this, in defiance of the noses of the Shi'a who walk every dark path.

We say, and with Allah is success, and in His hand are the reins of verification:

Both readings are mutawatir (transmitted through an unbroken chain of mass transmission), by the consensus of both groups, indeed by the unanimous agreement of all the people of Islam. Among the principles of usul al-fiqh (the foundations of jurisprudence) held by both groups is that when two mutawatir readings conflict in a single verse, they have the status of two verses. Therefore we must strive and exert ourselves first to apply both of them, as far as possible, because the default in evidences is to act upon them rather than to disregard them, as is established among the scholars of usul. Then we seek to weigh one against the other (tarjih). If we cannot manage to weigh one against the other, we set both aside and turn to other evidences from the Sunnah.

The usulis have mentioned that when verses conflict in such a way that it is impossible to reconcile them and then to weigh one against the other, the matter is referred to the Sunnah. For when we cannot act upon them, they are, as far as action is concerned, nonexistent for us. If the Sunnah itself conflicts in the same way, we refer to the statements of the Companions and of the Ahl al-Bayt, or we refer to qiyas (analogical reasoning) according to those who hold that the qiyas of a mujtahid is acted upon when there is a conflict.

When we reflected on these two readings in the verse, we found their application to one another through our principles in two ways:

The first: that masḥ (wiping) be understood as ghasl (washing), as Abu Zayd al-Ansari and others among the lexicographers have stated. It is said of a man who has performed wudu: tamassaha (he wiped himself). It is also said: "God wiped away what is upon you" (masaha Allah ma bika), meaning He removed the illness from you; and "the rain wiped the earth" (masaha al-matar al-ard) when it washed it. So when the feet are conjoined to the heads in the reading with the genitive (jarr), it is not necessary that they be wiped in the sense that the Shi'a claim.

This has been objected to in several ways:

The first: the function of the two terms differs in language and in the Shari'ah, and God has distinguished between the washed limbs and the wiped limbs. How, then, can the meaning of washing and wiping be one?

The second: if the feet are conjoined to the heads, and the obligation regarding the heads is wiping, which is not washing, by unanimous agreement, then the ruling for the feet must also be the same; otherwise it would entail combining literal and metaphorical meaning.

The third: if masḥ (wiping) meant ghasl (washing), the argument from the report that "he (ﷺ) washed his feet" would be invalidated, because according to this view it would be possible that he wiped them and called wiping "washing."

The fourth: Abu Zayd's citation of the expression "I have wiped myself for prayer" (tamassahtu li'l-salah) is of no benefit, because it is possible that when they wished to report on purification in a concise term, and it was not permissible for them to say "I have bathed (taghassaltu) for prayer" since that would give the impression of full bathing (ghusl), they said instead "I have wiped myself," because the washed limbs are also wiped. Thus they used a figurative expression, relying on the understanding of the intended meaning. That does not imply that they made masḥ one of the names of ghasl.

This is answered as follows. As to the first: we do not deny that the two terms differ in function, linguistically and in the Shari'ah, nor God's distinguishing between the washed and wiped limbs. But we maintain that applying masḥ to ghasl in some contexts is permissible, and there is nothing in language or the Shari'ah that forbids it. Moreover, this usage has occurred in their speech.

As to the second: we assume the word "wipe" (imsahu) before "your feet" as well, and when a word is repeated there is no harm in its meaning being repeated, and there is no prohibition in this. Al-Shari' of Zubdat al-Usul from the Imamiyya has quoted that this type of combining literal and metaphorical meaning is permissible: the word in the conjoined element is taken in its literal sense, and in the conjoining element in its metaphorical sense.

They have said of the verse: "Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor (approach it) in a state of major impurity, except for passing through (the mosque)" (4:43): the word "prayer" (salah) in the conjoined element has its literal Shari'i meaning, which is the specific acts of worship, and in the conjoining element it has its metaphorical meaning, which is the mosque, since it is the place of prayer. That commentator claimed that this is a type of istikhdam (a double usage). On this basis a group of Imamiyya exegetes and jurists interpreted the verse. Accordingly, this conjunction is, in reality, a conjunction of clauses, and the wiping connected with the heads is in its literal sense, while the wiping connected with the feet is in its metaphorical sense. Moreover, it is among the principles of the Imamiyya, as among the Shafi'is, that combining literal and metaphorical meaning is permissible, as is using a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its meanings. It is also possible here to suppose an elided preposition following the verb. So reflect on this.

It is not objectionable that the verse, on this reading, contains an ambiguity, and that such a thing is unlikely in revelation. For we say: the verse was revealed after wudu had been prescribed, and Gabriel (the Holy Spirit) had taught it to him (ﷺ) years before the beginning of the mission. There is no harm, then, in employing this type of ambiguity in it, for those addressed knew the manner of wudu, and their knowledge of it did not depend on deriving it from the verse. The verse was not revealed to teach them; rather its purpose was to substitute tayammum for wudu and ghusl in appearance, and the mention of wudu before tayammum is for preparation. What is generally mentioned for such purposes is not a fully sufficient explanation.

As to the third: applying masḥ to ghasl for a reason does not entail applying ghasl to masḥ without a reason. How, then, could the argument be invalidated? Glory be to God! This is truly a marvel and a wonder.

As to the fourth: we do not concede that the avoidance of "I have bathed (taghassaltu)" is because it suggests washing, since "I have wiped myself (tamassahtu)" also suggests that, on the basis of what they said, that the washed limbs are also wiped. Even granting that, we did not limit ourselves to that in citing evidence, and "the rain wiped the earth" (masaha al-matar al-ard) suffices for the point.

The second way is that masḥ remain in its apparent sense, and that the feet, in that reading, be taken as conjoined to the washed limbs, as in the reading with the accusative and the genitive by proximity (li'l-mujawara). This too has been objected to in several ways:

The first, second and third: what al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned, that the genitive by proximity is a grammatical error (lahn), and that it is only resorted to when there is no risk of confusion, and there is no such safety in our case, and that it occurs only without the conjunctive particle.

The fourth: that conjoining to the washed limbs, whether the conjoined term is in the accusative or the genitive form, involves separating the conjoined and the conjoining element by an unrelated clause that is not parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), which the grammarians do not permit. Moreover, the sentence in that case would be like: "I struck Zayd and honored Khalid and Bakr," with Bakr conjoined to Zayd, or with the intention that he was struck and not honored, which is extremely objectionable; natures recoil from it and ears do not accept it. How, then, could one incline to it, or how could the speech of God Most High be interpreted in that way?

It is answered to the first: the imam of the grammarians al-Akhfash, Abu'l-Baqa and all the masters and leaders of Arabic grammar permitted the genitive by proximity, and said that it occurs in eloquent speech, as you will hear, God willing. Only al-Zajjaj denied it, and his denial, despite its being attested in their speech, indicates shortcomings in his survey. From this they said: the affirmative takes precedence over the negative.

As to the second: we do not concede that it is resorted to only when there is no risk of confusion, and nothing to that effect is reported from the grammarians in the authoritative books. Yes, some of them said: the condition for its goodness is the absence of confusion together with the inclusion of a point of rhetoric, and here it is so, since the limit (ghayah) indicates that this genitive element is not wiped, for wiping is never found limited (by a terminus) in their speech; that is why it was not limited in the verse of tayammum, whereas washing is limited, and that is why it was limited in this verse when it was needed. So it is not objectionable that the washing of the face was not limited, because the matter is evident in it. Nor is the statement of al-Murtada objectionable: that there is no barrier to limiting wiping, and the point in it is to indicate the lightening of washing, to the extent that it is as if it were wiping.

As to the third: they have explicitly stated that it occurs in the adjective (na't), as in the examples mentioned earlier, and in His saying: "the punishment of an encompassing day" (11:84), where "encompassing" (muhit) is in the genitive although it is an adjective of "punishment." It also occurs in emphasis (tawkid), as in the verse: "Remind all the possessors of wives (dhawi'l-zawjat) that there is no union when the bonds of sin are dissolved," with "kulli-him" in the genitive according to what al-Farra' related. And in the words of al-Nabigha:

"There remained only a captive who was not freed,
and a bound one in the thongs of hide, pinioned."

The grammarians have devoted a separate chapter to this on account of its frequency and because of the parallelism it contains. It has become frequent in eloquent speech to the point that they went beyond taking it into account in case-endings to (matching) in dual and feminine forms and other things. The statement of Ibn al-Hajib on this matter is not worth attention.

As for the verse being among the examples mentioned of the forbidden type, it may well be so if the wording were: "and wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles." But the actual wording is not like that. So he is wiping the sock in reality and in ruling. Moreover, wiping the sock does not, by unanimous agreement, extend to the ankles. It was answered that it is possible that this is to indicate the place on which wiping suffices, since it does not suffice on the shank. Yes, this view is not free from remoteness, and the heart does not incline to it, even though al-Jalal al-Suyuti claimed that it is the best of what has been said about the verse.

The second way: the waw in it has the meaning of "with" (ma'a), as in the expression "the water and the stick levelled" (istawa al-ma'u wa'l-khashaba).

In both ways there are objections from the Ahl al-Sunnah on several grounds:

The second: if "and your feet" were conjoined to the grammatical position of "with your heads," it would be possible to understand from it the meaning of washing. For among the established principles of the Arabic sciences: when two verbs of different meanings come together, each having its own complement, one of them may be elided and the complement of the elided one conjoined to the complement of the mentioned one, as though it were its complement. An example is his saying:

"Would that your husband had gone out
wearing a sword and carrying a spear."

What is meant is "and carrying a spear."

Another example is his saying:

"When the women who are without husbands come forth on a day,
and draw their eyebrows and their eyes (with kohl)."[Page 75]

Both readings are mutawatir by the consensus of both groups, indeed by the unanimous agreement of all the people of Islam.
