Therefore we must strive and exert ourselves first to apply both of them, as far as possible, because the default in evidences is to act upon them rather than to disregard them, as is established among the scholars of usul. Then we seek to weigh one against the other (tarjih, preponderance). If we cannot manage to weigh one against the other, we set both aside and turn to other evidences from the Sunnah (the Prophetic practice and sayings).

The usulis have mentioned that when verses conflict in such a way that it is impossible to reconcile them and then to weigh one against the other, the matter is referred to the Sunnah. For he intended: "and anointing the eyes" (*wa-kahhalna al-'uyun*).

And his saying:

*You see him as though his master were slitting his nose ∗∗∗ and his two eyes, if his master had any wealth (wafr) at all.*

That is, he is gouging out his eyes, and so on in countless instances.

The third point: making *wa* (and) mean *ma'a* (with) without a qarina (contextual indicator) is something that scarcely can be permitted. And there is no qarina here indicating that it necessarily applies, as was said: "He did the two wipings together in time," and no one holds this by consensus.

It remains that someone might say: "I am not satisfied with this degree of argument for washing the feet from this verse, unless something is added to it from outside that strengthens the application of the Ahl al-Sunnah. Their statement and the statement of the Imamiyyah on this are perhaps two horses in a race." It is answered: the Sunnah of the best of creation, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the narrations of the Imams, may Allah be pleased with them, bear witness to what the Ahl al-Sunnah claim. These are, from their path, more than can be counted. As for the path of that people, al-Ayyashi narrated from 'Ali, from Abu Hamza, who said: "I asked Abu Hurayra about the two feet?" He said: "They are washed, washing."

Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man narrated from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "If you forget to wipe your head until you have washed your two feet, then wipe your head and then wash your two feet." This hadith was also narrated by al-Kalbi and Abu Ja'far al-Tusi through chains that are sound, such that it is not possible to weaken them, nor to read them as taqiyyah (dissimulation); for the one addressed in it is a specifically Shi'i person.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali, from his father, from his grandfather Amir al-Mu'minin, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "I sat performing wudu, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, came, and when I washed my feet he said: 'O 'Ali, separate the fingers (between the toes).'"

Al-Sharif al-Radi transmitted from Amir al-Mu'minin, may Allah ennoble his face, in Nahj al-Balagha, the description of the wudu of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and he mentioned in it the washing of the two feet. This indicates that the meaning of the verse is as the Ahl al-Sunnah said, and none of them claimed abrogation (naskh) so that it would need to be forced into proof, as one who has no grounding supposed.

What the Imamiyyah claim, attributing wiping to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Anas ibn Malik and others, is a lie fabricated against them. For none of them has been reported by a sound route that he permitted wiping. Except that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said by way of wonder: "We find in the Book of Allah only wiping, but they refused except washing." His intention was that the apparent sense of the Book requires wiping according to the reading in the genitive (*jarr*), which was his reading. But the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his Companions did only washing. So in this statement there is an indication that the reading in the genitive is to be interpreted, its apparent sense set aside by the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

The attribution of permitting wiping to Abu al-'Aliyah, Ikrimah, and al-Sha'bi is also falsehood and calumny. Likewise the attribution to al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, of combining washing and wiping or of giving a choice between them. The same goes for attributing the choice to Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, author of the great History and the famous Tafsir.

[p. 78]

The narrators of the Shi'ah have spread these various lies, and some of the Ahl al-Sunnah, who did not distinguish the sound from the weak among reports, transmitted them without verification or chain. The tear has widened beyond the patcher's ability to mend. Perhaps the Muhammad ibn Jarir who holds the choice is Muhammad ibn Jarir ibn Rustam, the Shi'i author of *al-Idah li-l-Mutarashshid fi al-Imamah*, not Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir ibn Ghalib al-Tabari al-Shafi'i, who is one of the leading figures of the Ahl al-Sunnah. What is mentioned in his tafsir of this is washing only, not wiping, nor combining, nor the choice that the Shi'ah attributed to him.

There is no proof for them in the claim of wiping from what is related "from Amir al-Mu'minin 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he wiped his face and his hands, and wiped his head and his two feet, and drank the leftover of his water for purification standing, and said: 'People claim that drinking standing is not permissible, and I have seen the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, do the same as I have done.'" This is the wudu of one who has not become impure, because the discussion concerns the wudu of the one who is impure, not mere cleaning by wiping the extremities, as the report itself indicates by its wiping of what is washed, by consensus.

As for what is related from 'Abba ibn Tamim, from his paternal uncle, in weak narrations, "that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, performed wudu and wiped over his two feet," it is, as the memorizers of hadith (huffaz) said, shadhdh (anomalous) and munkar (rejected), not fit for use as proof. Along with the possibility of reading "the two feet" as "the two leather socks" even metaphorically, and the possibility that the two feet of one wearing light footwear were mistaken for those without it, which is a remote possibility.

Similar to that, according to one who knows the circumstances of the narrators, is what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id al-Ahwazi narrated from Fadala, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Ghalib ibn Hudhayl, who said: "I asked Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, about wiping over the two feet, and he said: 'It is what Jibril, peace be upon him, brought down.'"

And what is related from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, who said: "I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, about how wiping over the two feet is done. He placed his palms on the toes, then wiped them up to the ankles. I said to him: 'If a man wiped with two of his fingers like this up to the ankles, would it suffice?' He said: 'No, unless with his whole palm.'" And other things the Imamiyyah narrated in this chapter. Whoever considers the circumstances of their narrators will not rely on any of their reports.

We have mentioned a portion of this in our book *al-Nafahat al-Qudsiyyah fi Radd al-Imamiyyah*. Moreover, we can say: if it were supposed that the ruling of Allah the Exalted is wiping, as the Imamiyyah claim from the verse, then washing suffices in its place. But if the ruling were washing, wiping would not suffice in its place. Thus with washing one is certainly discharged of the obligation, but not with wiping. This is because washing achieves the purpose of wiping, which is the arrival of moisture, and more. This is the meaning of those who express it as "wiping and more." So what is said, that washing and wiping are opposites that cannot be combined in one place, like black and white, does not apply. Also, the Shi'ah would be obliged to washing, because it is more fitting to the rational purpose of wudu, which is cleanliness for standing before the Lord of Lords, glorified and exalted; and it is more cautious as well, since its basis is agreed upon by both groups, as you have heard, while wiping is not, due to disagreement about its basis.

Some of the researchers said: "It may be incumbent upon them, according to their own principles, to permit both washing and wiping, and not restrict themselves to wiping alone." Al-Jalal al-Suyuti claimed that there is no difficulty in the verse according to the two readings for those who hold the choice. However, it is possible to claim for others that this was legislated at first and then abrogated (*nusikha*) by the specification of washing, while the two readings remained established in the written text, just as the choice between fasting and the expiation (*fidyah*) was abrogated by the specification of fasting, while the written form of that remained established. And it is not hidden that this is weaker than a spider's house, and indeed the weakest of houses.

Now, as for the reading in the nominative (*raf'*), it is not suitable as proof for either group, since each can supply whatever it wishes. From this, al-Zamakhshari said regarding it that it means: "And your feet are washed or wiped." But al-Tibi noted that there is no doubt that changing the sentence from a verbal to a nominal form, and deleting its predicate, indicates the intention of its affirmation and manifestness, and that its content is a settled ruling, established and unambiguous. And this is only so when the qarina is taken to be what is known from the explicit and implicit content of both readings, and what has been witnessed and customarily done from the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and heard from them, and made known among them.

[p. 79]

'Ata' has said: "By Allah, I do not know that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, wiped over the two feet." All of this rejects interpreting this reading by saying "your feet" are "washed or wiped" in alternation, especially since the shift from the imperative (*insha'iyyah*) to the declarative (*ikhbariyyah*) suggests that the people hastened to it, and He is informing about it, end of quote. So it is better to supply something of the nature of washing in a way that leaves the imperative intact.

From the totality of what we have mentioned, one can know what is in the words of Imam al-Razi, may Allah sanctify his secret, and his transmission from what we have presented earlier. So know men by the truth, not the truth by men. And Allah the Exalted is the Guide to the straight path.

Then know that they differed over whether the verse requires the obligation of intention (niyyah) or not. The Hanafis said: its apparent sense does not require that, and saying that intention is obligatory requires adding to the text, and adding to it requires abrogation (naskh), and abrogating the Qur'an by a report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid) does not occur, rather it is not permissible according to the majority; likewise by analogy (qiyas), according to the preferred school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, as al-Marwazi said. Therefore, establishing intention cannot be valid.

Some of the Shafi'is said: the verse requires obligation, because the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, "When you rise" (*idha qumtum*) is "when you intend to rise while you are impure," and the washing occurred as a consequence of that, and the consequence is caused by the condition, so it indicates the obligation of washing for the sake of intending prayer, and by this the desired conclusion is established.

Others said, and on this they rely: the basis of the requirement is that wudu is commanded, which is evident, and everything commanded must be an act of worship, otherwise it would not be commanded; and every act of worship is not valid without intention, due to His saying, the Exalted: "They were only commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion" (Qur'an 98:5). And sincerity is not attained except by intention, and it has been made a state (*hal*) of those who worship, and states are conditions, so every act of worship is conditioned on intention. They also analogized wudu to tayammum (dry ablution) on the basis that both are purifications for prayer, and intention was obligatory in the analogized base (*maqis 'alayh*), so likewise in the analogized (*maqis*). Our answer is the argument by the implication of the ratio (*qawl bi-mujib al-'illah*), meaning: we grant that every act of worship requires intention, and wudu does not occur as an act of worship without it. But that is not our discussion. Rather, it concerns whether, if one does not intend, so that it does not occur as an act of worship that is a cause of reward, the condition required for prayer is nevertheless fulfilled, so that the prayer is valid by it or not. Neither the verse nor the well-known hadith they cite on this point indicates either its negation or its affirmation. We say yes, because a condition is intended to be realized for something else, not for its own sake. So how is the purpose achieved and it becomes like covering the private parts?! The remaining conditions of prayer do not require that one intend them. Whoever claims that the condition, which is wudu, is itself an act of worship, the burden of proof is on him.

The analogy mentioned to tayammum is faulty. For it is agreed that a condition of analogy is that the legislation of the ruling of the base is not later than the ruling of the branch, otherwise the ruling of the branch would be established without evidence. And the legislation of tayammum came later than wudu, so wudu cannot be analogized to tayammum in its ruling.

Yes, if what is intended is the argument from the verse of tayammum, in the sense that when tayammum was legislated with the condition of intention, the obligation of intention in wudu became apparent, and the meaning of the analogy would be that there is no difference, that would not be rejected.

Some researchers mentioned two points in distinguishing between wudu and tayammum:

The first: tayammum linguistically indicates intent (*qasd*), so it is not realized without it, unlike wudu.

The second: dust was made a purifier in a specific circumstance, whereas water is a purifier in itself, as is derived from His saying, the Exalted: "pure water" (Qur'an 25:48) and His saying, glorified be He: "to purify you by it" (Qur'an 8:11). In that case the analogy is also faulty.

The objection to the first position is that the intention (niyyah) that is required is not the intention of the act itself, but rather that one intends by it purification and prayer, even if it is the funeral prayer or the prostration of recitation, as has been explained in its proper place. If that is so, then what it indicates is an intention that does not count as a valid niyyah, so the text does not thereby require the valid niyyah.

From this it becomes clear what is wrong with the argument of some Shafi'is from the verse of wudu' for the obligation of intention in it, which was mentioned just above. This is because what is implied by the implied construction is only the obligation of washing for the sake of wanting to pray while in a state of minor impurity (hadath), not the requirement that one wash for the sake of prayer. For the consequent of a conditional sentence expressed as a command conveys the demand for the content of the consequent once the content of the condition is realized, and its obligation is considered to be caused by that. So where is the demand for it in a specific manner, that one does it with the intention that it be for the content of the condition? So reflect. This has been hidden from some of the eminent scholars, to the extent that he did not answer it with a reply.

The second position: if by the specific state is meant the state of prayer, then it is based on the premise that the wanting (irada) is governed by the sentence joined to it, the sentence of tayammum.

You have now learned that there is no indication in it of the condition of intention. If by it is meant the state of inability to use water, then it is evident that this does not require the obligation of intention nor its negation. He derived from what was mentioned that water is purifying in itself, because the intent of its sending down is purification by it, and calling it "tahur" (purifying) does not imply considering it to purify in itself, that is, to remove the legal ruling without intention, and that is what is sought. This is unlike its removal of filth (khabath), because that is perceived to be a natural property of it, and there is no necessary connection between its sensory removal of an observable attribute and its being that by whose use a legal ruling is lifted.

What is implied by "liyutahhirakum" (so that He may purify you) is that the intent of its sending down is purification by it, and this holds true whether intention is a condition, as al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said, or not, as we have said. The general does not indicate the particular in its specificity, as is established. So reflect.

They also differed as to whether it requires the obligation of the order (tartib) or not. The Hanafis went to the second, because the particle in it is "wa" (and), which is for mere joining according to the sound view relied upon by them. The Shafi'is went to the first, because the "fa" (then) in "fa-ghsilu" (so wash) is for sequence, so it implies that standing to prayer is followed immediately by washing the face, so the order between the face and other parts is required, and so it is required for all of them, because there is no one who holds a distinction.

It was answered that we do not accept that it indicates that standing is followed immediately by it, but rather by the whole of the limbs. Its verification is that the verb of washing that is subsequent has complements, of which the first is reached in mention directly and the rest through the shared particle, so all of them are joined in it without implying a demand that the attachment of one be prior to another in existence. Thus the implication of the construction becomes a demand that the washing of all the limbs be done in succession. This is like your saying: "Enter the market and buy for us bread and meat," where what is meant is that after entering one buys what was mentioned in whatever way it occurs.

Some claimed that the arrangement of the text indicates order, because if it did not indicate that, it would require placing the wiped part before or after the washed part, and because they put the more important before the less important. But there is a question about this, because the most that the arrangement indicates is the preferability of order, and we do not deny that.

Others said: the evidence for order is his action, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, for he performed wudu' in order, then said: "This is a wudu' which God does not accept prayer except with." But there is a question about this, that the reference was to an ordered wudu' in which there was continuity (muwalah), so if it indicated the obligation of order, it would indicate the obligation of continuity, and no one holds that according to both parties. Yes, the strongest evidence for them is his saying, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Begin with what God has begun with," on the basis that the command is for obligation, and the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. It was answered in the same way as before, but caution is not hidden.

This amount suffices for the discussion of this verse. Going beyond that by explaining the sunan of wudu', its nullifiers, and what is connected to it, which the verse does not convey, as some exegetes did, is superfluous rather than virtuous, and a display of knowledge through which ignorance shows.

﴿And if you are in a state of janabah﴾, that is, at the time of standing up to prayer, ﴿then purify yourselves﴾, that is, wash yourselves thoroughly. It was read: "fa-thharu," that is, purify your bodies. Rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose are obligatory here just like washing the rest of the body, because He, glorified is He, attributed purification to the name "waw" (the whole body), which is the entire body of every responsible person, so every part to which water can reach is included, except what involves hardship, such as the inside of the eyes, which is excused for hardship. There is no hardship in the inside of the mouth and nose, so the text of the Book includes them without any opposition, just as the saying of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, in what Abu Dawud narrated, included them: "Under every hair is janabah, so moisten the hair and cleanse the skin." That they are part of fitrah as came in the report does not negate obligation, because fitrah is the religion, and it is more general than that. The verse suggests that washing is not required for one in janabah immediately unless some act is intended that is not permitted without it. This is supported by what is authentically reported: that he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, went out for the dawn prayer forgetting that he was in janabah, until when he stood he remembered, so he turned back and washed, and went out with his noble head dripping water.

﴿And if you are sick﴾, a sickness by which you fear destruction, or its increase by using water.
﴿Or on a journey﴾, that is, settled upon it.
﴿Or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it﴾. The "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit, and it was said it is for partitive, and it is connected to "fa-msahu" (wipe).

ʿAbd Allah read: "fa-ummu sa'idan," and the interpretation of the verse has already been given in Surat al-Nisa', so refer to it there.

Perhaps the repetition is so that the discussion can continue on explaining the types of purification, and so that it is not thought to be abrogation (naskh), as has been said, based on the premise that this surah is among the last to be revealed.

﴿God does not intend﴾ by what He has obligated upon you of wudu' when you stand to prayer, and washing from janabah, or by the command of tayammum, ﴿to put upon you any hardship﴾, that is, narrowness in complying. The word "ja'l" (putting/making) may mean creation and bringing into being, so it takes one object, which is "min haraj" (of hardship), where "min" is extra and "'alaykum" is then connected to "ja'l," and it is permitted that it be connected to "haraj" even though it is a deferred verbal noun. It may also mean making/designating, so "'alaykum" would be the second object. ﴿But He intends﴾, that is, by that, ﴿to purify you﴾, that is, to cleanse you, so purification is linguistic, or ﴿to remove from you the filth of sins﴾, for wudu' by which God expiates sins.

For Malik, Muslim, and Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "When the Muslim servant performs wudu' and washes his face, every sin he looked at with his eyes comes out of his face with the water, or with the last drop of water. When he washes his hands, every sin that his hands seized comes out of his hands with the water, or with the last drop of water. When he washes his feet, every sin that his feet walked to comes out with the water, or with the last drop of water, until he comes out pure from sins." So purification is spiritual, in the sense of expiating sins, not in the sense of removing impurity (najasah), because hadath is not an impurity by unanimous agreement. Its application to it is in consideration that it is a legal impurity, in the sense of being a barrier to prayer, not in the sense that it makes food or moist drink impure upon contact with one in hadath, or that prayer is invalidated by carrying it. As for the impurity of water, as is widely reported from the Imam al-A'zam, may God be pleased with him, and it is narrated that he retracted from it, it is due to the transfer of the barrier and sins to it legally. It was also said that the meaning is purifying the heart from the filth of rebellion against obedience to God.

It is also permitted that the meaning of "liyutahhirakum" is with earth when purification with water is unavailable, and purification means lifting hadath and the legal barrier.

As for what was reported from some Shafi'is, such as Imam al-Haramayn, that saying that earth purifies is a weak statement, his meaning by it is denying sensory purification, so it does not contradict the authentic hadith: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a purifier." The irada (will/intention) is an attribute of essence, and its interpretation is well known, and its object in both places is omitted, as was pointed out. The lam is for causation, and to this some verifiers went. It was also said that it is extra, and the meaning: God does not intend to put upon you any hardship so that He does not grant you the concession of tayammum, but He intends to purify you. This was deemed weak because "an" (that) is then to be assumed after the extra particle, and it was objected that this contradicts the statements of the grammarians, for al-Radi said:
[p. 82]
The apparent view is that "an" should be assumed after the extra lam that follows the imperative verb and the verb of will, and likewise in al-Mughni and elsewhere. The occurrence of this lam after the imperative and will in the Qur'an and Arabic speech is widespread and analogical, and it is among the issues of the Book (Sibawayh's). He said in it: I asked him (i.e., al-Khalil) about the meaning of "uridu li-an yaf'ala" (I want that he do)? He said: You only want to say: "uridu lihadha" (I want this), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And she commanded: "that I be the first of the Muslims"﴾, end.

The grammarians differed about it. Al-Sirafi said: in it are two views:
One of them, which the Basrans chose, is that its object is omitted, that is: I want what I want in order that you do, so the lam is causal and not extra.
The second is that it is extra for emphasis of the object.

Abu 'Ali said in al-Ta'liq from al-Mubarrad: the verb indicates the verbal noun, so it is omitted, that is: I wanted and my wanting is for such-and-such, so "my wanting" is omitted and the lam is extra, and this is a remote affectation.

The positions are three:
The closest is the first.
The easiest is the second, and it is from the eloquent ancient speech, like his saying:
"I want to forget her remembrance, but it is as if Layla appears to me on every path."
The eloquence in it is something the sound taste recognizes, said al-Shihab.

﴿And that He may complete﴾ by His legislation what is a means of purification for your bodies ﴿His favor upon you﴾ in religion, or that He may complete by the concession of His bestowal upon you through the strict obligations (al-'aza'im) ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, giving thanks for His favor by your obedience to Him in what He has commanded you and forbidden you.

Among the subtleties of this noble verse, as some verifiers said, is that it contains seven matters, all of them in pairs:
Two purifications: the original and the substitute.
The original is of two kinds: comprehensive, and non-comprehensive.
The non-comprehensive, with regard to the action, is washing and wiping; with regard to the place, limited and unlimited; and their instrument is liquid and solid; and what makes them obligatory is minor and major hadath; and what permits the resort to the substitute is illness or journey; and what is promised upon them is purification and completion of the favor.

Some added other pairs: the unlimited is the head and face, and the limited is the hand and foot, and the end-points are the ankle and elbow, and gratitude is verbal and practical.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 7:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾: it is the favour of Islam, or, more generally, the favour in the sense of the genus. They were commanded to do so that the Benefactor would remind them and encourage them to give thanks for it. ﴿And His covenant with which He bound you﴾: that is, the pledge He took from you.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) modifying (wa-thaqakum bihi) ("with which He bound you"), or modifying an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (bihi) or from (mithaqihi) ("His covenant"). That is: being at the time of your saying, "We hear and we obey." The purpose of restricting it to this time is to emphasize the obligation to observe it, by reminding them of their saying and of their commitment to safeguard it.

The covenant meant here is the one He took from the Muslims when the Prophet (ﷺ) gave them the pledge at the Second Pledge of al-Aqabah in the thirteenth year of prophethood, to hear and obey in ease and hardship, in what pleases and what displeases them, as recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim from the hadith of Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

It has also been said that it is the covenant made at the First Pledge of al-Aqabah in the eleventh year, or the Pledge of al-Ridwan at al-Hudaybiyah. The attribution of the covenant to Allah, although it proceeded from the Prophet (ﷺ), is because the return is to Him, glorified is He, as His saying expresses: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Humayd related from Mujahid who said: "It is the covenant which He made with the children of Adam when He brought them out from the loins of their father, peace be upon him." And in this there is remoteness.

﴿And fear Allah﴾: regarding forgetting His favour and breaking His covenant, or regarding everything you do and leave undone, so that what has been mentioned enters into it as a primary application.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾: that is, of its concealed contents, those that are intimately connected with it in a complete connection that justifies applying the term "companion" to them, so He will recompense you for them. So what then of your manifest deeds?!

The sentence is a parenthetical insertion and a justification of the command, and the mention of the Glorious Name instead of a pronoun is for what has passed more than once.

O you who believe: this begins an explanation of the rulings concerning what occurs between them and others, following what concerns themselves. ﴿Be persistent in standing firm for God﴾, meaning: be often steadfast in fulfilling His necessary rights. It was also said: let it be among your habits to uphold the truth in yourselves through righteous deeds, and in others through enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil, seeking the pleasure of God, exalted is He. ﴿Witnesses in justice﴾, meaning: with fairness. It was also said: callers to God, exalted is He, making His religion clear through sound proofs. ﴿And let not﴾, meaning: let not ﴿the enmity of a people﴾, meaning: the intensity of your hatred for them, ﴿lead you to not act justly﴾, so that you do not bear witness fairly concerning their rights, or so that you do not transgress against them by committing what is unlawful. ﴿Act justly﴾, O believers, toward your friends and your enemies alike. Some scholars restricted it to enemies, based on what is reported: when Mecca was conquered, God, exalted is He, charged the Muslims through this verse not to repay the Meccan disbelievers for what they had previously done, but to act justly in speech and in deed. (The word "huwa") refers back to the justice implied by the verb, and it is either absolute justice, which includes the justice pointed to by the occasion of revelation, or justice specifically toward disbelievers. ﴿It is nearer to God-consciousness﴾, meaning: it is more fitting to it, for God-consciousness (taqwa) is the culmination of obedience, and justice is the most suitable of acts of obedience to it. Thus the nearness between them, on this view, is the suitability of one act of obedience to another. It is also possible that its nearness to God-consciousness is considered in terms of it being a means of grace (lutf) toward it, so the relation is that of a cause leading to its effect, and this is like the last component of a cause (ʿilla). The particle "lam" here is like it in your saying "he is close to Zayd" (huwa qarībun li-Zayd), denoting specification and not completion, for it would otherwise be with "min" or "ilā".

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) strained in explaining the verse, saying: If it is asked, how does He, glorified is He, say ﴿nearer to God-consciousness﴾, when the comparative form (afʿal) is only used for two things that share one matter, one of which has an advantage, and we know that nothing of God-consciousness or doing good is other than part of justice? It is answered: although the comparative form is as you have mentioned, it may be used by framing the speech according to the addressee's belief about the matter itself, to cut off his argument and to expose his confusion. So one says to someone who believes Zayd has a certain merit, though there is no merit in him, but he cannot deny that ʿAmr is superior to him: "Serve ʿAmr, for he is better than Zayd." Upon this manner comes His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾ though it is known that there is no good in what they associate.

The sentence is in the position of giving the reason for the command to act justly, and He stated this to them for emphasis and reinforcement. Then, glorified and exalted is He, commanded God-consciousness by His saying: ﴿And fear God﴾, after clarifying that justice is nearer to it, out of care for its importance and as an alert that it is the foundation of the whole matter.

﴿Indeed God is Acquainted with what you do﴾ of deeds, so He will recompense you accordingly. The like of this verse has already occurred in al-Nisa'. It was not limited to this for greater emphasis on justice and for intensifying the extinguishing of the flame of anger. It was also said: the reason is different, for the first was revealed concerning the polytheists, and this one concerning the Jews.

Some verifying scholars mentioned a reason for placing "justice" first there and last here: the verse of al-Nisa' came in the context of acknowledging against oneself, one's parents and relatives, so it began there with justice, which is fairness without favoring oneself, a parent, or a relative. This one came in the context of abandoning enmity, so it began with standing firm for God, exalted is He, because that is more effective in restraining the hostile, and then followed with bearing witness in justice. Thus each context received what suits it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 9:

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, [i.e., from among the obligatory and recommended acts, and among them justice and piety], ﴿for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) explaining the second object (maf'ul thani) of "promised" (wa'ada), which has been omitted, as if it were said: "What did He promise them?" So it is said: "Forgiveness," and so on.

It is also possible that the object is left unstated, and the meaning is: "He granted them a promise," which is what is explained by the sentence mentioned. It is also permitted that it be the object of "promised" on the basis that it has the sense of "said" (qala), or that the intended meaning is its quotation, since according to the Kufans it is quoted by what has the meaning of speech. It is also possible that the word "said" is implied, i.e., "He promised them, saying this concerning them," in which case it is an affirmation of its being established for them, and this is more emphatic. It has also been said that this statement is addressed to them at the time of death, to ease matters for them and to make the agonies of death lighter upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 10:

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾ — the Qur'anic signs, among which are the explicit texts I have recited that enjoin justice and piety. Some have understood the signs to refer to the miracles with which Allah, exalted is He, supported His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. ﴿Those﴾ — who are described by what has been mentioned — ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾; that is, those who are continually and perpetually connected with the intensely blazing fire. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the first subject (mubtada' awwal), the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is the second subject (mubtada' thani), and what follows them is its predicate (khabar), and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject. The sentence was not presented in the context of threat as the sentence before it was presented in the context of promise, in order to cut off their hope. And mentioning the state of the disbelievers after the state of the believers, as is the case in the noble Sunnah and the Qur'an, fulfils the duty of the call and gladdens the hearts of the believers by making the companions of the Fire their enemies rather than them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 11:**

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ is a reminder of the favour of being saved from evil, following the reminder of the favour of bestowing good, which is the favour of Islam and the covenant that accompanies it. Alternatively, it is a reminder of a particular favour after the reminder of the general favour, out of concern for its importance. "Upon you" (ʿalaykum) is connected either to "favour of Allah" or to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) modifying it.

As for His, exalted is He, saying ﴿when a people resolved﴾: according to the first view, it is an adverbial clause of time (ẓarf) for the favour itself; according to the second, it is an adverbial clause for what the adverbial phrase is attached to. It is not permissible for it to be an adverbial clause of time for "remember" (udhkurū), because the two tenses conflict: "when" (idh) refers to the past, while "remember" refers to the future. The meaning is: remember His, exalted is He, bestowal upon you; or "remember" His favour existing upon you at the time when a people intended ﴿to stretch out their hands against you﴾, that is, to strike you with killing and destruction. It is said: "He stretched out his hand against him" when he attacked him, and "he stretched out his tongue against him" when he insulted him. Basṭ (stretching out) in its original sense means simply extending, and when it is used with hand and tongue it becomes a metonymy (kināyah) for what has been mentioned. The placement of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for the purpose of hastening to show that the harm and consequence of the stretching out returns to them, thereby leading them from the outset to count the favour of averting it.

﴿But He restrained their hands from you﴾ is coordinated with "resolved" and is the favour that is intended to be recalled. Mentioning the resolve serves to indicate that the favour came at the time of greatest need for it. The particle "fa" (then) denotes sequence, which conveys the completion and perfection of the favour. The explicit mention of "hands" is for added emphasis, and the placement of the direct object before its usual position. The meaning is: He prevented their hands from being extended toward you immediately after their resolve, and protected you from them. It is not intended that He restrained them from you after they had extended them toward you. In this is what is not hidden of the perfection of the favour and the abundance of kindness.

The verse alludes to what Muslim and others transmitted from the hadith of Jabir: "The polytheists saw that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were at ʿUsfān, and they stood for the noon prayer together. When they prayed, they regretted that they had not fallen upon them, and they resolved to attack them when they stood for the afternoon prayer. So Allah, exalted is He, turned back their plot by sending down the prayer of fear."

It is also said that it alludes to what Abu Nuʿaym transmitted in al-Dalāʾil through the route of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When ʿAmr ibn Umayyah al-Ḍamrī returned from the well of Maʿūnah, he met two men from the Banu Kilab who had a safe-conduct from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He killed them, not knowing that they had a safe-conduct. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) paid their blood money, and he went to the Banu al-Nadir, and with him were Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, ʿUmar, and ʿAli. They met him and said, 'Welcome, O Abu al-Qasim! Why have you come?' He said, 'A man from my companions killed two men from Kilab who had a safe-conduct from me, and he asked me for their blood money, so I want you to help me.' They said, 'Yes. Sit until we gather it for you.' So he sat beside the fortress, with Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli. The Banu al-Nadir had plotted to drop a stone on him (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him). Jibril (peace be upon him) came and informed him, so he rose, and those with him rose."

It is also said that it alludes to what more than one transmitted from the hadith of Jabir: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stopped at a place, and the people dispersed among the thorny trees seeking shade beneath them. The Prophet (ﷺ) hung his weapon on a tree. A bedouin came to his sword, took it, drew it, then turned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'Who will protect you from me?' He said, 'Allah.' The bedouin said it twice or three times, while the Prophet (ﷺ) in each case said, 'Allah.' Then the bedouin sheathed the sword. The Prophet (ﷺ) called his companions and informed them of the bedouin's deed, while the bedouin was sitting at his side, and he did not punish him."

There is no concealment in the fact that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) may be multiple, and that the word "qawm" (people) may be applied to one individual, as with "people" (al-nās) in His, exalted is He, saying ﴿those to whom the people said﴾. Also, the harm and benefit of a leader return to those he leads. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is coordinated with "remember" (udhkurū), meaning: fear Him in observing the rights of His favour, and do not neglect its thanks; that is, in the more general sense of that, and it enters into it primarily.

﴿And upon Allah﴾ alone, to the exclusion of others, whether independently or jointly, ﴿let the believers put their trust﴾. Indeed He, glorified is He, is sufficient for repelling corruptions and bringing about benefits. The clause is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) that confirms what precedes it. The choice of the third-person imperative form and attributing it to the believers is to make trust in Allah obligatory upon the addressees by a demonstrative method, and to highlight what calls to compliance and restrains from neglect, while observing the rhyme (fāṣilah). The mention of the majestic matter is to give the reason for the ruling and to strengthen the independence of the concluding clause. Similar examples have passed. This verse, as transmitted from Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, is to be recited seven times in the morning and seven times in the evening to ward off plague.

[Page 85]

[Page 85]

﴿And God certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) containing an explanation of some of what the Children of Israel did. It is brought to remind the believers of God's blessing and to urge them to honour the covenant, and to warn them against breaking it. Or it is brought to confirm what was mentioned of the intent to stretch out the hand (al-hamm bi-l-batsh), and to establish it, on the basis that it came from their forefathers. It shows that treachery and betrayal were in them, a trait of the lineage of Akhzam (shinshinah akhzamiyyah). The Name here is mentioned explicitly to cultivate awe, to magnify the covenant, and to emphasise the gravity of breaking it, along with preserving the right of the resumption, which calls for a break from what came before.

The shift of grammatical person (al-iltifat) in His words ﴿And We raised up from them twelve chiefs﴾ is for the sake of following the customs of majesty. The fronting of the indirect object over the direct object is for the reason already mentioned more than once: concern and arousing eagerness. As for the word naqib (chief): it has been said that it is faʿil in the sense of fāʿil, derived from naqb in the sense of investigation, and from it comes His words ﴿So they roamed through the lands﴾. He was called that because he investigated the conditions and secrets of the people. It has also been said that it is in the sense of mafʿūl, as if the people chose him with knowledge of him and by investigating their conditions.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its origin is from al-naqb, which is a wide hole, and a path through a mountain. It is said: "So-and-so has a good naqibah," meaning a good disposition. A naqqab is one who knows things, who is sharp of heart and who searches much into affairs. This whole root carries the meaning of making an impression on a thing that has depth. From this comes: "I pierced the wall," meaning I reached its far end by piercing it.

It is reported that when the Children of Israel had finished with the matter of Pharaoh, God commanded them to march to Ariha, a land of Syria, which was inhabited by the tyrants, the Canaanites. He, glorified is He, said to them: "Indeed I have written it for you as a dwelling and a home, so go out to it, and strive against those who are in it, for I am your helper." And He, majestic is His affair, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to take from each tribe a guarantor over them for fulfilling what they were commanded. So he took the covenant from them,

[Page 86]

and he chose from them the chiefs, and set out with them. When he drew near to the land of Canaan, he sent the chiefs to spy out the news, and forbade them to tell their people. They saw huge bodies and fierce might, and they were afraid. So they returned and told their people, except Kalib ibn Yuqanna of the tribe of Judah, and Yusha ibn Nun of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Yusuf, peace be upon him. At that point the Children of Israel said to Moses, peace be upon him: ( Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here ).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported, from Mujahid, that when the chiefs entered upon the tyrants, they found that two of them could enter into the sleeve of one of them, and that five persons among them could carry a single bunch of their grapes on a pole, and that five persons, or four, could enter into half a pomegranate once its seeds had been removed.

Al-Baghawi mentioned that a man from among those people met them, called ʿŪj ibn ʿUnuq. His height was three thousand three hundred and thirty-three and a third cubits. He would hold back the clouds, drink from them, and reach for the fish from the bottom of the sea, roast it by the sun's rays, lifting it up to them and then eating it. It is related that the water covered everything on the earth of mountains, and it did not reach beyond the knees of ʿŪj. He lived three thousand years, until God destroyed him at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him. That was because he came and hollowed out a rock from the mountain to the measure of Moses' army, which was a farsakh by a farsakh, and carried it to throw upon them. So God sent the hoopoe, which pierced the rock with its beak, and it fell upon his neck and felled him. Moses, peace be upon him, came while he was felled, and killed him. His mother was ʿUnuq, one of the daughters of Adam, peace be upon him, and her seat was a jarib of land. When they met ʿŪj, with a bundle of firewood on his head, he took them all and placed them in his bundle, and went off with them to his wife and said: "Look at these people who claim that they want to fight us," and he threw them down before her, and said: "Shall I not grind them under my foot?" His wife said: "No, rather let them go until they inform their people of what they saw." So he did so. End of quotation.

I say: The matter of ʿŪj has spread among the common people, and they have transmitted sensational tales about him. In the fatawa of the scholar Ibn Hajar, the memorizer al-ʿImad Ibn Kathir said: The story of ʿŪj and all that they relate about him is nonsense with no basis, and it is from the fabrications of the People of the Book. He was never in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, and no unbeliever was saved from among them.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: Among the matters by which it is known that a hadith is fabricated is that sound evidences establish its falsehood, such as the lengthy hadith of ʿŪj. There is no wonder at the audacity of the one who fabricated this hadith and lied against God, the Exalted. The wonder is at the one who includes this hadith in books of knowledge, of tafsir and others, and does not clarify its status. Then he said: There is no doubt that this and its like are from the fabrication of the heretics among the People of the Book, who intended to mock and ridicule the noble messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, and their followers. End of quotation.

Ibn al-Mundhir cited from Ibn ʿUmar something amazing from his story, and some authors criticised it, saying that this is something one is ashamed to attribute to Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with both of them. The author of al-Qamus also held that its reports are fabricated.

al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Hibban in his book al-ʿAzamah reported in it reports. The memorizers said, concerning the longest of them, which contains strange things about his circumstances: It is false and a lie. The memorizer al-Suyuti said: The closest account regarding ʿŪj is that he was a remnant of ʿĀd, and that he had a stature in general of about a hundred cubits, or something like that, and that Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, killed him with his staff. This is the extent that can be accepted. End of quotation.

How right he is! For his survival through the flood, despite his manifest disbelief, since no faith of his has been transmitted, and the supplication of Noah, peace be upon him, which encompassed the earth, is something that the fair-minded hardly accepts. Likewise his survival after the flood, together with the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And We made his offspring the survivors﴾, is something the knowing person cannot justify. And his roasting of the fish by the sun's rays is something that can hardly be conceived, according to what the philosophers have mentioned. Al-Khalkhali mentioned that they held that the sun is not hot, for otherwise the mountain peaks would be hotter than the valleys because of the peaks' nearness to the sun and the distance of the valleys from it. Rather, heat arises from the arrival of the sun's rays on the surface of the earth and their reflection from it, and for this reason the valleys are seen to be hotter, due to the accumulation of the reflected rays in them. Whatever the ray reaches of the surface of the earth becomes hot, and otherwise not. The commentator on Hikmat al-ʿAyn mentioned something similar to this. An objection to this, that some people narrated that such-and-such angels pelt the sun with ice when it rises, and that without this the earth would be burned, does not arise, because that is not established according to the memorizers, and it is closer to fabrication than to authenticity.

Furthermore, the one who holds that this ʿŪj existed would not say that there is the zamharir layer, which is the third of the seven layers of the elements and what is above it. Otherwise, how could there be a holding back by clouds, when thunder, lightning and lightning-bolts arise only from that cold layer, which the effect of the sun's rays does not reach by reflection from the surface of the earth?

They also mentioned that above it there are two layers:

The first is that which mixes with fire, and in it the rising smoke from below dissipates, and in it the comets with tails and the meteors form.

The second is that which is nearly pure, since neither the heat of what is above it nor the coldness of what is below it from the earth and water reaches it, and in it shooting stars occur. So if this man held back the clouds, his head would reach, according to their claim, one of those two layers. How would his condition then be with that cold and that heat?

I do not think any human, however he might be, could endure that. Moreover, the very fact of holding back is something that cannot be done on the basis of the statements of the philosophers, since you know that the source of clouds is the zamharir layer.

In the book Nuzhat al-Qulub, quoting the sage Abu Nasr, it is stated that the furthest extent of its height is twelve farsakhs and six hundred cubits, and from the earlier scholars that it is eighteen farsakhs. The farsakh is three miles, and the mile is three thousand five hundred cubits. End of quotation.

They also differed about the furthest extent of its descent, and none of them mentioned that it descends to the point where one could imagine that a man of the stature they mentioned could be held back by clouds, unless it is meant that the cloud did not reach this height. Despite all this, they erred in their saying "Ibn ʿUnuq." It is in fact Ibn ʿŪq, like Nuh, as is stated in al-Qamus. And it is also the name of his father, not his mother, as is mentioned there too. So let this be noted.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-ʿĀliyah that he said concerning the verse: "God took the covenant of the Children of Israel that they would devote themselves to Him and not worship other than Him. He raised up from them twelve guarantors, who guaranteed over them the fulfilment to God of what they had pledged to Him of covenants concerning what He commanded them and forbade them." This was the view chosen by al-Jubbai. The chiefs at that time could be messengers, or they could be leaders, as al-Balkhi said. Abu Muslim held that they were raised up as prophets to establish the religion, to teach the tribes the Torah, and to command them with what God had obligated upon them.

Al-Tibi reported, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that they were ministers, and that they became prophets after that.

﴿And God said﴾, that is, to the chiefs, according to al-Rabiʿ, and al-Samin preferred this because it is closer. According to most of the commentators, it was to the Children of Israel, and Abu Hayyan preferred this, since they are the ones in need of what has been mentioned of encouragement and warning, as the shift of person indicates, together with what it contains of cultivating awe, and of stressing what the speech includes of promise: ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾, hearing your speech, seeing your deeds, and knowing your inner thoughts, so I will repay you for that. It has been said: "with you" in terms of support, and it has been said: in terms of knowledge. The generality is preferable.

﴿If you establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and believe in My messengers﴾, that is, in all of them. The lam is preparatory for the omitted oath. The placing of faith after the establishing of the prayer and giving of zakat, although these two are branches that follow from it, is because they, as more than one said, were acknowledging the obligation of both as was intended from them, while committing the denial of some of the messengers, peace be upon them. It is also to preserve the parallel between it and His words: ﴿and you help them﴾.

Some of them said: The clause "and believe in My messengers" to its end is an allusive metonymy (kinayah ima'iyyah) for struggle and support of the religion of God, His messengers, peace be upon them, and spending in His cause, as if it were said: "If you establish the prayer, give the zakat, and strive in the cause of God." This is indicated by His words: ﴿And do not turn back on your heels, for you would become losers﴾. The meaning is: Do not turn back on your heels in your religion, by opposing the command of your Lord and disobeying your Prophet, peace be upon him. The concern was placed on this connection rather than on the first two, and it was expressed in the form of an allusion, because the people were shrinking back from fighting and saying to Moses, peace be upon him: ( Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here ). End of quotation. And this is not free from scrutiny.

Some said: He placed the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat first because they are the outward signs of their condition, indicating their faith. Ta'zir (ta'zir) is originally about preventing and repelling. It was also said that ta'zir means strengthening, and it derives from ʿazr, which is of the same root as azr (support). There is no doubt that strengthening involves preventing whoever you strengthen from others, so the two meanings are close. Then it was used figuratively for support, because support contains that, and for discipline (ta'dib), which in the Shariah is what falls short of a prescribed punishment (hadd), since it deters and restrains from committing an ugly act. For this reason it was called support (nusrah) in a hadith. It is authentically reported from him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Support your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I support him when he is oppressed, but if he is an oppressor, how can I support him?" The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "You restrain him or prevent him from oppression; that is his support."

Al-Raghib said: ta'zir is support together with honouring. Al-Hasan and Mujahid explained it only as support, while Ibn Zayd and Abu 'Ubaydah explained it only as honouring. It was read as ('azartumuhum) with the lighter form. "And you lend to Allah" means: by spending in the way of good. It was also said: by giving voluntary charities. Whichever is meant, it is a metaphor, because when He, glorified is He, promised its recompense and reward, it was likened to a loan that is repaid in kind. In ancient Arabic speech, "good deeds are loans" (al-salihat qurud). ﴿A goodly loan﴾, which, as al-Akhfash said, is what is given with a willing soul. It was also said: that which is not followed by reproach or harm. It was also said: that which is from lawful wealth.

Many have noted that "qardan" may be a verbal noun (masdar) or an object (maf'ul bihi). ﴿Surely I will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ answers the omitted conditional, and it stands in its place in meaning. It is not the answer to the condition, contrary to Abu al-Baqa', but rather the answer to the oath. It has been established that when a condition and an oath come together, the one that comes first is answered, unless it is preceded by something with a predicate. It was also permitted that this be the answer to what is implied in His words, ﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, as an oath. It was also said that its answer is: ("If you establish"), so the lam is not an introductory lam, or it has two aspects, and this is strange. The clause of the conditioned oath and its answer explains that covenant mentioned earlier.

﴿And I will surely admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, included with it in its ruling, and later than it in attainment, since clearing (takhliyah) necessarily precedes adorning (tahliyah). ﴿Then whoever disbelieves﴾ means: in My messengers, or in any of what has been enumerated within the scope of the condition. The fa' indicates that the statement of the ruling for the one who disbelieves follows the statement of the ruling for the one who believes, to strengthen encouragement through warning. ﴿After that﴾ refers to the emphasized condition on which the great promise is contingent, namely "I will surely remove." It was also said: after the emphasized condition attached to the great promise, namely "I am with you," based on interpreting being-with as being-with in support and aid, or in granting success in good. The condition is attached to it in meaning, like saying: "I am attentive to your affair if you serve me; I will raise your standing." It was also said: the meaning is "after I stipulated this condition, promised this promise, and bestowed this favour."

Page 89

His words ﴿among you﴾ are connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "disbelieves." Perhaps the change in construction, where He did not say "and if you disbelieve" as a conjunction to the preceding conditional sentence, is—as Shaykh al-Islam said—to remove the disbelief of all from the realm of possibility, and to drop "whoever disbelieves" from the level of direct address. Moreover, disbelief here does not mean initiating it after faith, but includes continuing in it as well, as if it were said: "whoever is characterized by disbelief after that." However, by using a form that indicates occurrence, he intended to show their progression through the stages of disbelief, for being characterized by something after the arrival of what requires abandoning it—even if it is continuation in terms of the label—is a new act and a fresh deed.

﴿Then he has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ means: from the middle of the path, and it has encompassed him, a straying with no doubt in it and no excuse with it, unlike one who disbelieved before that, for perhaps he may have some doubt, and an excuse may be imagined for him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 13 (part 1 of 3):

﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾, that is, because of their breaking their solemn covenant and not because of anything else, either alone or combined with it. The *ba'* here is causal, and *ma* is redundant, serving to emphasise the statement and fix it firmly in the soul. Alternatively, *ma* means "a thing," as Abu al-Baqa' said. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb in God's words ﴿We cursed them﴾, meaning: We expelled them and removed them from Our mercy as a punishment for them. This is the view of Ata' and a group of scholars. From al-Hasan and Muqatil, the meaning is: We transformed them into apes and swine. From Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), the meaning is: We punished them by imposing the jizya (poll tax) upon them.

It is not hidden that what Ata' said is closer to the real meaning, because the true sense of *la'n* (cursing) in the language is expulsion and removal. Using it in the last two meanings is metaphorical, through employing it for its necessary implication, which is abasement through what was mentioned. However, there is no indication in the statement pointing to this. Restricting the explanation to what was mentioned, although the proper order would be to explain first the realisation of the cursing and the breaking, by saying for example: "So they broke their covenant, so We cursed them," is because of the priority of the simple quiddity (*huwiyya*) over its compound quiddity, as Shaykh al-Islam said. This is to indicate that the realisation of both is a clear matter that needs no explanation; what requires explanation is the causal relation between them.

﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, dry and coarse, rejecting the acceptance of truth and not softening. This was said by Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).

It was said: the meaning is that We deprived them of divine success (*tawfiq*) and the subtle grace by which their breasts are expanded, so that rust (*ran*) settled upon their hearts because of what they used to earn. This is like when you say to someone else: "You have ruined your sword when its care is abandoned until it rusts," and "You have made your fingernails your weapon when you do not trim them."

Al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is that We made clear the condition of their hearts and their hardness, and We judged that they do not believe and that admonition does not benefit them. It is not hidden that this contradicts the apparent meaning, and only the Mu'tazilite doctrine led him to it.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *qasiyya*. This is either an intensive form of *qasiya*, being on the pattern *fa'il*, or it means *radiyya* (defective), from their saying "a dirham is *qasiyy*" when it is adulterated. This also derives from *qaswa* (hardness), since in an adulterated coin there is dryness and hardness. It was also said that *qasiyy* is not Arabic but is a loanword (*mu'arrab*). It was read as *qisiyya*, with a kasra on the qaf, for harmony (*ittiba'*).

﴿They distort words from their places﴾. This is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) explaining the degree of hardness of their hearts, for there is no degree greater than what results from their audacity in distorting the speech of the Lord of the worlds and inventing lies against Him, exalted and majestic. The use of the present tense is for narration, to bring the scene to mind, and to indicate renewal and continuity. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object of "We cursed them," or from the genitive in "their hearts." This was deemed weak for the reasons given. Making it a circumstantial clause from the hearts or from its pronoun in "hard," as has been said, is not valid because there is no returning pronoun linking it to the subject. Making "hearts" mean "their owners" is something their owners would not accept.

﴿And they forgot a portion﴾, that is, they abandoned an ample share. The use of *nisyan* (forgetting) in this sense is common.

﴿of what they were reminded of﴾, from the Torah, or of what they were commanded in it regarding following Muhammad (ﷺ).

*[Page 90]*

It was said: they distorted the Torah, so certain things fell from their memory because of the evil consequence of that.

Ibn al-Mubarak and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "I think a man forgets the knowledge he used to know because of a sin he commits."

Regarding the meaning of this is the saying of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him):

I complained to Waki' of the badness of my memory,
so he guided me to abandon sins,
and informed me that knowledge is light,
and the light of God is not given to a disobedient one.

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾, that is, treachery (*khiyana*), as it was read, being a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'ila*, like *al-kadhiba* and *al-laghiya*. Or it is the pattern *fa'la*, *khai'ina*, meaning possessing treachery. The words of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) point to this. Or it means a group (*firqa*) that is treacherous, or a soul (*nafs*) that is treacherous, or a person (*shakhs*) that is treacherous, taking it as an adjective, with the *ta'* for emphasis, though this is rare in the pattern *fa'il*. The phrase "from them" is connected to an omitted word that serves as an adjective to it. Except that in the first two views *min* is for the starting point, meaning: a treachery or a treacherous act issuing from them and proceeding from them. In the other views *min* is partitive. The meaning is that deceit and treachery are a continuous habit for them and their forefathers, as is known from their description with distortion and what accompanies it, such that they scarcely abandon it or conceal it. Thus you will not cease to see this from them.

﴿except a few of them﴾. This is an exception from the pronoun in "from them." The few meant are Abdullah ibn Salam and his like, those who gave sincere counsel to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). Some made it an exception from "treacherous" according to the second view. Thus the few means a few acts, and *min* is for the starting point, as already explained, meaning: except a few acts issuing from them. It was also said that the exception is from His words, "And We made their hearts hard."

﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾, that is, if they repent or pay the jizya, as was reported from al-Hasan and Ja'far ibn Mubashshir, and al-Tabari chose it. The pronoun in "pardon them" returns to what its counterparts return to. From Abu Muslim, it returns to the exceptional few, meaning: pardon them as long as they remain on your covenant and have not betrayed you. According to both views, the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). It was said the pronoun returns to what al-Tabari chose, and the verse is unrestricted (*mutlaqa*), except that it was abrogated (*nuskhat*) by God's words, "Fight those who do not believe in God," and so on. This was reported from Qatada. From al-Jubba'i, it was abrogated by God's words: "And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms."

﴿Indeed, God loves the good-doers﴾. This is an explanation for the command and an exhortation to comply, and a notice that pardon absolutely is a part of goodness.

* * *

This, and from the allusive (*ishara*) sense of the verses:

﴿O you who believe, when you rise to the prayer, wash your faces﴾. This is a command to purification for one who wishes to stand before the Great King, exalted is His majesty and great His dominion. He began with the face, because He, glory be to Him and exalted, impressed upon it the imprint of the seal of His attributes. In the *Futuhat* (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya of Ibn Arabi), there is no disagreement that washing the face is obligatory. Its ruling inwardly is watchfulness (*muraqaba*) and modesty before God, absolutely. Then the outward ruling has been disputed regarding the limits of washing the face in ablution in three places:

The whiteness between the sideburn and the ear; the second is what hangs down from the beard; the third is the combing of the beard (*takhlil*). As for the mentioned whiteness, some say it is obligatory to let water pass over it, and others say it is not obligatory. Likewise the combing of the beard: some say it is obligatory, and others say it is not. The ruling for this is inward. As for washing the face generally, without regard to delimiting the matter, there is among it what is obligatory and among it what is not. The obligatory part is modesty before God that He sees you where He has forbidden you, or that He does not find you where He has commanded you. As for the sunna of it, it is modesty before God that you look at your private parts or the private parts of your wife, even though this has been permitted to you. However, practising modesty regarding them is better and more fitting. Whatever is determined from it is obligatory upon you, and whatever is not determined but you do it is sunna and recommended. A person should watch over his actions outwardly and inwardly, and watch over his Lord in his inward self, for the face of his heart is what is considered. The face of a person in reality is his essence. It is said: "the face of a thing" meaning its reality, its essence and its self. Thus modesty is all good, modesty is from faith, and it brings only good.

As for the whiteness between the sideburn and the ear, which is the dividing limit between the face and the ear, it is the boundary between what a person is charged with doing with his face and what he is charged with doing with his hearing. The action in this is to include the limit within what is limited. Thus it is better for a person to direct his modesty to his hearing as he directs it to his sight. Just as modesty is the lowering of the gaze, as God said: "Say to the believers that they lower their gaze" (24:30), likewise modesty before God requires that one not hear what is not lawful for him, such as backbiting and evil speech from a speaker saying what is not fitting. That whiteness lies between the sideburn and the ear, and it is the place of doubt, which is that one says: "I inclined to him in order to reply to him." This is the meaning of *iadhar* (sideburn), for it derives from *udhr* (excuse). A person makes an excuse when asked: "Why did you incline your ear to this speech?" He says: "I wanted to verify what he said so that I could forbid him from it." Thus it is called *idhar* by metonymy. Whoever sees it as obligatory washes it, and whoever does not see it as obligatory, if he wills he washes it and if he wills he leaves it.

As for washing what hangs down from the beard and combing it, these are accidental matters. The beard is something that appears on the face and is not of its original structure. Whatever matters arise for you concerning this aspect of the face, you are in them under the ruling of that accident. If purifying that accident is required of you, this is the view of those who say its washing is obligatory. If purifying it is not required of you, but you purify it as recommended, or leave it because it was not required of you, this is the view of those who do not say that purification of it is obligatory. It has been made clear that the ruling of the inner differs from the outer, in that there is an aspect toward the obligatory and an aspect toward the sunna and recommendation. The obligatory part of this must be performed, and doing what is not obligatory is better than leaving it. This applies to all acts of worship. End.

Some of the gnostics said: this is an address to believers with knowledge-based faith (*iman 'ilmi*), when they rise from the sleep of heedlessness and aim for the prayer of presence, intimate conversation and true turning toward the Truth, that they purify the faces of their faculties with the water of beneficial, pure knowledge that purifies from the knowledge of the laws, morals and dealings, which is related to removing the barriers against the defilement of the attributes of the soul.

The first of this is the hands, in God's words "and your hands" (5:6), meaning with the powers and the capacities. That is: purify also your powers and capacities from the filth of indulging in appetites and of dealing with the substances of impurity. "To the elbows" means to the measure of rights and benefits. The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, said: people agreed on washing the two hands and forearms, but differed about including the elbows in this washing. Some say it is obligatory to include them, and some say inclusion is not obligatory, yet no one disputed that it is recommended. The inward ruling regarding this is that washing the two hands and forearms is an indication of washing them with generosity, bounty, liberality, giving, holding fast, and reliance upon God. These and similar qualities are attributes of the hands and wrists by correspondence.

What remains is washing the elbows, which is seeing the means by which the servant takes support and finds comfort for himself. Whoever sees the inclusion of the elbows in his self sees that means were placed by God as wisdom in His creation, so he does not want God's wisdom to be nullified, not by way of relying upon them, for that would detract from his reliance upon God. Whoever sees that they are not obligatory in washing sees the soul's tranquillity in means, and that the state of reliance upon God is not sincerely attained for him while the sight of means persists. Everyone who says washing them is not obligatory says it is recommended. Likewise, seeing means is recommended according to all, although their rulings differ regarding them, for God tied wisdom to their existence.

"And wipe your heads" (5:6). Some gnostics said: that is, with the directions of your spirits, from the dust of the cloudiness of the heart and the grime of its change through turning toward the lower world and love of this world, by the light of guidance. For the spirit is not defiled by attachment, but its light becomes veiled from the heart, so the heart blackens and darkens. It suffices for the spread of its light to polish the high face to which it turns. For the heart has two faces:

One is toward the spirit, and the head here is an indication of it.

The second is toward the soul and its faculties, and it is most fitting that the foot be an indication of it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 13 (part 2 of 3):

The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar), may God sanctify his secret, said, after explaining the disagreement of the scholars about the amount that must be wiped: As for the ruling on wiping the head in its inner sense, its root lies in *riyasa* (leadership), which means height and elevation. Since the highest part of the body, in outward appearance, and the whole body beneath it, is called a "head" (*ra's*), for the leader (*ra'is*) is above the one led (*mar'us*), and he has the direction of "above." God, exalted is He, has described Himself as being "above" His servants with the attribute of domination, saying, glorified is He: ﴿And He is the Irresistible over His servants﴾. Therefore the head is the limb of the body closest to the Real, exalted is He, because of the correspondence of "aboveness." Then it has another nobility, in the sense by which it is made head over the whole body: it is the seat of all the powers, sensory and spiritual. Since it has this leadership from this aspect, it is called a head. Then the intellect, which God, exalted is He, made the noblest thing in the human being, is placed in its seat, the *yafukh* (crown of the head), which is the highest point of the head. He, glorified is He, placed it on the side of "aboveness." Since it is the seat of all the outer and inner powers, and each power has a rule, authority and pride that gives it dignity over the others, and since the seats of these powers in the head differ, the whole head is covered. Therefore the wiping of the entire head is obligatory in this expression, because of this leadership flowing through all of it from the aspect of these powers, with humility and submission. Thus each power has a particular wiping suited to the correspondence of its claim. This is the perspective of the one who holds that wiping the entire head is obligatory.

And whoever sees that the powers differ in leadership: the imaginative-formative power, for example, has authority over the representational power, so it is its leader. And if the representational power has leadership too, he says: the obligation on him is to wipe part of the head, which is the one designated as "the highest."

Then they differed about this part. Every knower spoke according to what God, exalted is He, gave him of perception in the ranks of these powers, so he wipes according to what he sees. The meaning of wiping is submission, and removing arrogance and haughtiness through humility and servanthood. This is because the one performing ablution is about to commune with his Lord and seek His connection. A mighty leader, when he enters upon the one who granted him that might, dismisses his own might and leadership before the might of the one he enters upon.
