He stands before Him in the position of servants, in a place of abasement, not with the attribute of abasement. So whoever has the leadership of some powers over others dominating his mind must wipe that part, for the sake of the connection sought through this worship. For this reason wiping the head is not prescribed in *tayammum* (dry ablution), because placing dust on the head is one of the signs of separation: you see the one who has lost his beloved through death placing dust on his head. The details of the leaderships of the powers are known to the people of this discipline. As for the partial wiping of the hand with which one wipes, and the disagreement about that, deal with it just as you deal with what is wiped, for the remover of this leadership has various causes in its ability to do so, and its seat is the hand. Some remove it by way of domination, and some by policy and encouragement, to the end of what he said.

(﴿and your feet﴾) These are pointed to as the natural, bodily powers, immersed in desires and excessive pursuit of pleasures. Washing them with the water of the science of ethics and the science of mathematics (*al-riyadiyyat*), until they return to the purity by which the heart becomes prepared for presence and intimate communion.

In the *Futuhat* [al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya], they differed about the manner of their purification, after agreement that they are among the limbs of ablution: is it by washing, by wiping, or by choice between them? Our school holds the choice, and combining is better. There is no opinion without someone holding it. Wiping is supported by the apparent text of the Book, and washing by the Sunna. The wording of the verse can bear a departure from its apparent sense. As for the ruling on this in the inner sense, know that striving to the congregations, multiplying steps to the mosques, and steadfastness on the day of battle are among the things by which the feet are purified. So let the purity of your two feet be by what we have mentioned and the like, and do not behave like a tale-bearer among people, do not walk in arrogance, moderate your walk, and lower your voice. Among these there is what is obligatory, like one time in washing the limb of ablution, the foot and others. And among them there is what is Sunna, which is what exceeds the obligatory: your walking toward what the Law has urged you to, and what it has obligated upon you. So what is obligatory for you is moving your feet to your prayer place. The recommended, the desirable, and the Sunna, and whatever you wish to call it, is moving the feet to the mosques from near or far, for that is not obligatory, although what is obligatory in this matter, according to some people, is a particular mosque and a particular congregation. On this basis, washing your two feet in the inner sense is by way of meaning.

Know that washing includes wiping, so whoever washes has incorporated wiping within it, just as the light of the stars is absorbed into the light of the sun. Whoever wipes has only washed according to the view of one who holds that. It is reported from the Arabs that *al-mash* (wiping) is a linguistic synonym for *al-ghasl* (washing), so they are synonymous terms. The correct meaning, in the ruling of the inner sense, is that wiping is used for what requires specificity among actions, and washing for what requires generality. For this reason our school holds the choice according to the circumstance. A person may strive for a particular virtue in the need of a specific individual, and that is like wiping. He may also strive before the king for a need that encompasses the subjects, and that person enters into this generality, and this is like washing, in which wiping is absorbed. End of quotation.

﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾. Major impurity (*janaba*) is the estrangement of the servant from his rightful homeland, and there is nothing but servanthood, and the estrangement of a divine attribute from its homeland. All of this necessitates purification. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are sick﴾, etc., its parallel has already been mentioned.

In the *Futuhat*: It has been disputed about the limit of the hands mentioned in this purification. Some say its limit is the same as the limit of ablution. Others say it is only the palm, and this is what I say. Others say the recommended extent is to the elbows, and the obligatory is the palms. Others say the obligatory extent is to the shoulders.

The consideration in this is that since dust in the earth is the origin of human emergence, and it realizes his servanthood and lowliness, he is commanded to purify his self from arrogance by means of the dust, which is the reality of his servanthood. This is by considering the origin of his creation. Since among what he claims is power and giving, although he is naturally disposed to weakness and miserliness, and these are attributes of the hands, it is said to him at this claim and his seeing himself in the apparent power and generosity and giving: purify yourself from this attribute by considering what you were made of, namely your weakness and your miserliness. God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿He created you from weakness﴾, ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾, ﴿And when evil touches him, he is grudging﴾. So when he looks at this origin, his self becomes pure and is cleansed of pretension.

They differed about the number of strikes on the earth for *tayammum*. Some say one, and some say two. Among those who say two, some say one strike for the face and one for the hands, and some say two strikes for the hands and two for the face. Our school holds that whoever strikes once has sufficed, and whoever strikes twice has sufficed. The hadith of the single strike is more authentic. The consideration in this is directing attention to what this purification is by. Whoever gives precedence to Divine unity in actions speaks of a single strike. Whoever gives precedence to the ruling of the cause that God established, and attributes the act to God while acknowledging the causes, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God created you and what you do﴾, affirming and negating, speaks of two strikes. And whoever says that this applies to every act speaks of two strikes for each limb. End of quotation.

The Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, has extended his discussion of the types of purification, and has brought forth wonders.

(﴿God does not intend to make for you any difficulty﴾) That is, narrowness and hardship through the abundance of struggles. (﴿But He intends to purify you﴾) from the wicked attributes.

From Sahl: Purification has seven aspects: purity of knowledge from ignorance, purity of remembrance from forgetfulness, purity of certainty from doubt, purity of intellect from foolishness, purity of assumption from accusation, purity of faith from what is beneath it, and purity of the heart from the desires.

He said: Perfecting the purity of the outer self produces the purity of the inner self, and completing the prayer produces understanding from God, exalted is He. Purity exists in several things: in purity of food, in separation from people, in truthfulness of the tongue, and in humility of the secret. Each of these four corresponds to what God, exalted is He, commanded to be purified and washed among the outer limbs.

Ibn 'Ata said: The inner things are places where the Real, glorified is He, looks. It has been reported from him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, that: "God, exalted is He, does not look at your forms, nor at your deeds, but He looks at your hearts." So the place of the Real's gaze, majestic and exalted is He, is most worthy of purity. This happens only by removing kinds of treachery, transgressions, varieties of whisperings, deceit, spite, showing off, seeking reputation, and other prohibited things. There is nothing more difficult for the knowers than gathering the concern and purifying the secret. In attributing the purification to Him, exalted is He, there is an evident subtlety.

(﴿And to complete His favor upon you﴾) by perfecting. Some knowers said: The completion of favor for one people is their salvation through their piety, and for others, their salvation from their piety. How far apart are one people and another. (﴿And that you may be grateful﴾) for the favor of perfection, through steadfastness and standing by the right of justice when remaining after annihilation. (﴿And remember the favor of God upon you﴾) through guidance to the path of arrival at Him. (﴿And His covenant with which He bound you﴾) and that is the binding of His resolutions mentioned above. (﴿When you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾) That is: when you accepted them from the source of prophethood with purity of nature. Some of them said: The intended meaning of God's favor is His guidance, glorified is He, which preceded from eternity for the people of happiness, and the covenant is the covenant by which God bound His servants that they should not occupy themselves with anything other than Him, glorified is He. Abu 'Uthman said: The favors are many, and the greatest of them is knowledge of Him, glorified is He. The covenants are many, and the greatest of them is faith.

(﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of God upon you when a people had determined﴾) That is: from the powers of your concealed selves and their attributes. (﴿to extend their hands to you﴾) by seizing and domination, to attain their objectives and pleasures. (﴿but He withheld their hands from you﴾) That is: He prevented them from you, by what He showed you of the way of purification and sanctification. (﴿And fear God﴾) Make Him, glorified is He, your protection in subduing and restraining them. (﴿And upon God let the believers rely﴾) by seeing all actions as from Him, mighty and majestic is He.

(﴿And God had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾) They are, in the souls, the five apparent senses, the five inner senses, the rational theoretical faculty, and the practical faculty. Many of our masters among the Sufis mentioned that the *nuqaba'* (leaders) are of one type among the saints, may God benefit us by their blessings. In the *Futuhat*: Among them are the *nuqaba'*, who are twelve leaders in every age, neither more nor fewer, corresponding to the twelve signs of the celestial sphere. Each leader knows the property of each sign, and what God, exalted is He, has deposited in his station of secrets and influences, and what is given to the sojourners therein from the wandering planets and the fixed stars. For the fixed stars have movements and a passage through the signs that are not perceived by the senses, because this appears only over thousands of years, and the lifespans of observers fall short of witnessing that.

واعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى قَدْ جَعَلَ بِأيْدِي هَؤُلاءِ النُّقَباءِ عُلُومَ الشَّرائِعِ المُنَزَّلَةِ، ولَهُمُ اسْتِخْراجُ خَبايا النُّفُوسِ وغَوائِلِها، ومَعْرِفَةُ مَكْرِها وخِداعِها، وإبْلِيسُ مَكْشُوفٌ عِنْدَهُمْ، يَعْرِفُونَ مِنهُ ما لا يَعْرِفُهُ مِن نَفْسِهِ، وهم مِنَ العِلْمِ بِحَيْثُ إذا رَأى أحَدُهم أثَرَ وطْأةِ شَخْصٍ في الأرْضِ عَلِمَ أنَّها وطْأةُ سَعِيدٍ أوْ شَقِيٍّ، مِثْلَ العُلَماءِ بِالآثارِ والقِيافَةِ، وبِالدِّيارِ المِصْرِيَّةِ مِنهم كَثِيرٌ، يُخْرِجُونَ الأثَرَ في الصُّخُورِ، وإذا رَأوْا شَخْصًا يَقُولُونَ: هَذا الشَّخْصُ هو صاحِبُ ذَلِكَ الأثَرِ، ولَيْسُوا بِأوْلِياءَ، فَما ظَنَّكُ بِما يُعْطِيهِ اللَّهُ تَعالى لِهَؤُلاءِ النُّقَباءِ مِن عُلُومِ الآثارِ؟! انْتَهى.

The author (al-Alusi) said: And know that God Most High has placed in the hands of these chiefs (nuqaba', "the leaders") the sciences of the revealed laws. They have the ability to extract the hidden depths of souls and their treacheries, and the knowledge of their deceit and trickery. Iblis is laid bare before them: they know of him what he himself does not know of his own self. They possess such knowledge that when one of them sees the trace of a person's footstep on the ground, he knows whether it is the step of one who is happy or one who is wretched, like the scholars of traces and of tracking (qiyafa, "the art of tracing footprints and deducing lineage from them"). In the Egyptian lands there are many of them; they bring out the trace in rocks, and when they see a person they say: "This person is the owner of that trace." They are not saints (awliya'), yet how then do you imagine what God Most High gives to these chiefs of the sciences of traces?! End of quotation.

وقَدْ عَدَّ الشَّيْخُ - قُدِّسَ سِرُّهُ - فِيها أنْواعًا كَثِيرَةً، والسَّلَفِيُّونَ يُنْكِرُونَ أكْثَرَ تِلْكَ الأسْماءِ، فَفي بَعْضِ فَتاوى ابْنِ تَيْمِيَّةَ: وأمّا الأسْماءُ الدّائِرَةُ عَلى ألْسِنَةِ كَثِيرٍ مِنَ النُّسّاكِ والعامَّةِ، مِثْلُ الغَوْثِ الَّذِي بِمَكَّةَ، والأوْتادِ الأرْبَعَةِ،
[Page 95]
والأقْطابِ السَّبْعَةِ، والأبْدالِ الأرْبَعِينَ، والنُّجَباءِ الثَّلاثِمِائَةٍ فَهي لَيْسَتْ مَوْجُودَةً في كِتابِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، ولا هي مَأْثُورَةٌ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ - صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ - لا بِإسْنادٍ صَحِيحٍ ولا ضَعِيفٍ مُحْتَمَلٍ، إلّا لَفْظُ الأبْدالِ، فَقَدْ رُوِيَ فِيهِمْ حَدِيثٌ شامِيٌّ مُنْقَطِعُ الإسْنادِ، عَنْ عَلِيٍّ - كَرَّمَ اللَّهُ تَعالى وجْهَهُ - مَرْفُوعًا إلى النَّبِيِّ - صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ - أنَّهُ قالَ: ««إنَّ فِيهِمْ - يَعْنِي أهْلَ الشّامِ - الأبْدالَ أرْبَعِينَ رَجُلًا، كُلَّما ماتَ رَجُلٌ أبْدَلَ اللَّهُ تَعالى مَكانَهُ رَجُلًا»» ولا تُوجَدُ أيْضًا في كَلامِ السَّلَفِ، انْتَهى.

The author also mentioned in it (the book of the Shaykh) many categories. The Salafis (al-Salafiyyun, "those who follow the early generations") reject most of these names. In one of the fatwas of Ibn Taymiyyah (may God have mercy on him): "As for the names that circulate on the tongues of many ascetics and common people, such as the Ghawth (the Helper, the chief saint) who is in Mecca, the four Awtad (pegs),
[Page 95]
the seven Aqtab (poles), the forty Abdal (substitutes), and the three hundred Nujaba' (noble ones), these are not found in the Book of God Most High, nor are they transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), neither by a sound chain nor by a weak but acceptable chain, except for the term Abdal. Concerning them a Syrian hadith has been related with a broken chain (munqati' al-isnad), from Ali (may God honor his face), traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Among them, meaning the people of Syria, are forty men, the Abdal; whenever one of them dies, God Most High replaces him with another man." Nor are these terms found in the speech of the early generations (salaf)." End of quotation.

وأنا أقُولُ:
وما أنا إلّا مِن غَزِيَّةَ إنْ غَوَتْ غَوَيْتُ وإنْ تَرْشُدْ غَزِيَّةُ أرْشُدِ
( ﴿وقالَ اللَّهُ﴾ ) تَعالى ( ﴿إنِّي مَعَكُمْ﴾ ) بِالتَّوْفِيقِ والإعانَةِ ( ﴿لَئِنْ أقَمْتُمُ الصَّلاةَ﴾ ) وتَحَلَّيْتُمْ بِالعِباداتِ البَدَنِيَّةِ ( ﴿وآتَيْتُمُ الزَّكاةَ﴾ ) وتَخَلَّيْتُمْ عَنِ الصِّفاتِ الذَّمِيمَةِ مِنَ البُخْلِ والشُّحِّ فَزَهِدْتُمْ وآثَرْتُمْ ( ﴿وآمَنتُمْ بِرُسُلِي﴾ ) جَمِيعِهِمْ مِنَ العَقْلِ، والإلْهاماتِ، والأفْكارِ الصّائِبَةِ، والخَواطِرِ الصّادِقَةِ مِنَ الرُّوحِ والقَلْبِ، وإمْدادِ المَلَكُوتِ (﴿وعَزَّرْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ ) أيْ: وعَظْتُمُوهم بِأنْ سَلَّطْتُمُوهم عَلى شَياطِينِ الوَهْمِ، وقَوَّيْتُمُوهم ومَنَعْتُمُوهم مِنَ الوَساوِسِ، وإلْقاءِ الوَهْمِيّاتِ والخَيالاتِ والخَواطِرِ النَّفْسانِيَّةِ ( ﴿وأقْرَضْتُمُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا﴾ ) بِأنْ تَبَرَّأْتُمْ مِنَ الحَوْلِ والقُوَّةِ والعِلْمِ والقُدْرَةِ، وأسْنَدْتُمْ كُلَّ ذَلِكَ إلَيْهِ عَزَّ شَأْنُهُ، بَلْ ومِنَ الأفْعالِ والصِّفاتِ جَمِيعِها، بَلْ ومِنَ الذّاتِ بِالمَحْوِ والفَناءِ وإسْلامِها إلى بارِيها جَلَّ وعَلا ( ﴿لأُكَفِّرَنَّ عَنْكم سَيِّئاتِكُمْ﴾ ) الَّتِي هي الحُجُبُ والمَوانِعُ لَكم ( ﴿ولأُدْخِلَنَّكم جَنّاتٍ﴾ ) مِمّا عِنْدِي ( ﴿تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ﴾ ) وهي أنْهارُ عُلُومِ التَّوَكُّلِ والرِّضاءِ والتَّسْلِيمِ والتَّوْحِيدِ، وتَجَلِّياتِ الأفْعالِ والصِّفاتِ والذّاتِ ( ﴿فَمَن كَفَرَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ﴾ ) العَهْدِ وبَعْثِ النُّقَباءِ مِنكم ( ﴿فَقَدْ ضَلَّ سَواءَ السَّبِيلِ﴾ ) وهَلَكَ مَعَ الهالِكِينَ.

And I say:
"I am only of the tribe of Ghazziyya: if they go astray, I go astray; and if Ghazziyya is rightly guided, I too am rightly guided."

(God said: ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾) by granting success and help, (﴿if you establish the prayer﴾) and adorn yourselves with the bodily acts of worship, (﴿and give zakah﴾) and empty yourselves of blameworthy qualities such as stinginess and avarice, so that you renounce the world and prefer others, (﴿and believe in My messengers﴾), all of them, through the intellect, the inspirations, the correct thoughts, and the true intuitions of the spirit and the heart, and the support of the malakut (the realm of the unseen dominion), (﴿and support them﴾), i.e., honor them, by empowering them over the devils of illusion, strengthening them and protecting them from whisperings and from the casting of imaginary notions, fancies and carnal intuitions, (﴿and lend God a goodly loan﴾) by disavowing power, strength, knowledge and capacity, attributing all of that to Him, exalted is His majesty, and even (disavowing) actions and attributes altogether, and even the essence itself through annihilation (fana') and submitting it to its Creator, may He be glorified and exalted; (﴿I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾), which are the veils and barriers for you; (﴿and I will surely admit you to gardens﴾) of what is with Me, (﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾), and these are the rivers of the sciences of trust (tawakkul), contentment (ridaa), submission (taslim) and unity (tawhid), and the manifestations (tajalliyat) of the acts, attributes and essence. (﴿But whoever disbelieves after that﴾), after the covenant and the sending of the chiefs from among you, (﴿has certainly strayed from the right way﴾) and perished with those who perish.

(﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾) which they had confirmed, (﴿We cursed them﴾) and expelled them from the presence (al-hadrah), (﴿and made their hearts hard﴾) by the domination of the qualities of the self over them and their inclination toward earthly matters, (﴿they distort words from their places﴾), since they were veiled from the lights of the malakut and jabarut, which are the words of God Most High, and they substituted the powers of their souls for them, and used their illusions and imaginings instead of their realities. (﴿And they have forgotten a portion﴾), a generous share, (﴿of what they were reminded of﴾) in the later covenant, which is what they had been given in the earlier covenant of the perfections latent in their predispositions, existing in them potentially. (﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾), in breaking covenants and withholding trusts, because the devil of the self has dominated them and their hearts have hardened, (﴿except a few of them﴾), namely those whose predisposition has led them to what is good for them. (﴿So pardon them and overlook, for indeed God loves the doers of good﴾) toward His servants, with gentleness and good dealing. May God Most High make us and you among the doers of good.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 14:

﴿And among those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾ This begins the explanation of the abominations and crimes of the Christians, following the explanation of the abominations and crimes of their brethren the Jews. "Min" (from, among) is connected to "akhadhna" (We took), and placing the prepositional phrase first serves emphasis. Also, mentioning one of the two groups raises in the listener's mind the question of what the state of the other is. It is as if it were said: "And from the other group too, [We] took their covenant." The pronoun in "their covenant" refers either to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who"), or it refers back to the Children of Israel, to whom the earlier pronouns have returned. This is similar to your saying: "I took from Zayd the covenant of 'Amr," meaning: the like of his covenant.

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted element that stands as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the clause "akhadhna" is a qualifier (sifah), meaning: "And among those who say, 'We are Christians,' are a people from whom We took their covenant." It has also been said that the omitted subject is "min" as a relative (mawsulah) or descriptive (mawsufah) word. It should not be overlooked that the permissibility of omitting the relative pronoun while retaining its complement was held only by the Kufan grammarians.

God, glory be to Him, said "they say, 'We are Christians'" and did not say "and from the Christians," as would be the apparent expression, without elaboration, to indicate (as some have said) that they are upon the religion of Christianity by their own claim, and they are not truly upon it, because they do not act upon its requirements, and they oppose what is in the Gospel (Injil) of the good tidings of our Prophet (ﷺ).

Page 96

It has also been said that it is to indicate that they gave themselves this title on the meaning that they are the helpers (ansar) of God, while their deeds require support for Satan. Thus the deviation from the apparent expression serves to form that state in the listener's mind and to establish that they claimed the support of God while they were far removed from it. The reason for singling out this place for attributing Christianity to their claim is that, since the aim of this verse is to censure them for breaking the covenant taken from them regarding supporting God, it was fitting that the speech begin with what indicates that they did not support God, and did not fulfil what they pledged regarding support. The outcome of their affair was nothing but uttering a claim, and their saying rather than their doing.

It should not be overlooked that this is based on the view that the reason for their being called Christians is that they are the helpers of God, which is a well-known opinion; for this reason they are also called "Ansar."

In other places it is mentioned that Jesus (peace be upon him) was born in the year 304 (of the Seleucid era), owing to the conquest of Alexander, in Bayt Lahm (Bethlehem) of al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Then his mother (peace be upon her) carried him to Egypt (Misr). When he reached twelve years of age, she returned with him to al-Sham (Syria), and he dwelt in a town called al-Nasira or Nasura, and from it the Christians were named and attributed to it. It has also been said that they are the plural of Nasran, like nadama and nadman (companions), or the plural of Nasri, like mahri and maha.

Al-Nasraniyya, al-Nasrana, and al-Nasraniyya are the singular of the Christians, and al-Nasraniyya is also their religion. They are called Nasara and Ansar. "Tanassara" means he entered into their religion.

﴿But they forgot﴾ immediately after the taking of the covenant, ﴿a portion﴾ a large share ﴿of what they had been reminded of﴾ within the terms of the covenant, namely faith in God, the Exalted, and other obligations. It has also been said that it refers to what was written for them in the Gospel concerning faith in the Prophet (ﷺ), but they cast it behind their backs, followed their own desires, and split into seventy-two sects.

﴿So We stirred up﴾ that is, We bound and attached (them), and its root meaning is adhesion. It is said: "gharRitu bi-l-rajul gharan" when you cling to a man, as al-Asma'i said. Others said: "gharītu bihi ghara'an" with a long vowel, and "aghraytu Zayda bi-kadha hatta ghariya bihi," and from it comes al-ghira' (glue), by which things are stuck. God's words "between them" are a locative adverb (zarf) for "aghrayna," or are connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of its object, meaning: "We stirred up enmity and hatred" existing between them.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "There is no way to make it a locative adverb for both, because the verbal noun does not govern what precedes it." You know that some of them permitted that when the governed element is an adverb.

God's words ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ are either a limit for the stirring up or for the enmity and hatred, meaning: they will be hostile and hateful toward one another until the Day of Resurrection, in accordance with their differing desires and their deviant opinions, which lead to division into many sects, among them the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyya), the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyya), and the Melkites (al-Malkaniyya), and the discussion of them has already passed. The pronoun in "between them" refers to the Christians, as narrated from al-Rabi' and chosen by al-Zajjaj and al-Tabari. And from al-Hasan and a group of the exegetes it is related that it refers to the Jews and the Christians.

﴿And God will inform them of what they used to do﴾ in the world, of breaking the covenant and forgetting the great share of what they had been reminded of. The statement is directed toward a severe threat of reward and punishment. So "inform" is a metaphor for the occurrence of that and its disclosure to them, not that there are actual reports there. The point of the expression "inform" is to tell them that they do not know the reality of the evil deeds they perform and what they entail of punishment, so the arrangement of punishment upon them in conveying knowledge of the reality of their state is like informing them of it. The shift to mentioning the Glorious Name is for what has passed many times, and the expression of the work as "making" (sun') is to announce their firmness in it. "Sawfa" (surely/will) is for emphasising the threat.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 15:

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is a shift (iltifat) to addressing both groups, the Jews and the Christians. The word "scripture" (al-kitab) is a generic noun that applies to one book, to two, and to more. Referring to them by the title "people of the Scripture" serves as a rebuke, for being people of the Scripture requires that they uphold it, act according to what it requires, and make clear the rulings contained in it. Yet they did this while knowing (better). ﴿Indeed there has come to you Our Messenger﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ). Describing him this way, together with attributing him to the Majestic "Our," honors him and signals that it is obligatory to follow him, upon him be peace. ﴿makes clear to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to "Our Messenger." The use of the verbal form (al-fi'liyya) indicates the renewal of the clarifying, meaning: while he is making clear to you, in stages as the public interest requires, ﴿much of what you used to conceal from the Scripture﴾, that is, from the Torah and the Gospel. This includes the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), the verse of stoning, and the good news of Jesus concerning Ahmad, upon both of them be peace.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ikrima that he said: "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) was approached by the Jews, who asked him about stoning. He, upon him be peace, said: 'Which of you is the most knowledgeable?' They pointed to Ibn Suriya. He adjured him by Him who sent down the Torah to Musa, upon him be peace, and by Him who raised the Mount, and by the covenants that were taken from them, until he (Ibn Suriya) was seized with trembling (afkal). He said: 'When it became widespread among us, we would flog the one (guilty) with a hundred lashes and shave the heads, so he (the Prophet) judged them to be stoned.' Then Allah the Exalted sent down this verse."

The placement of (kathiran) after the prepositional phrase is for a reason already mentioned more than once. The combination of the past and the present tense forms indicates their continuous persistence in concealment and hiding. (mimma) is connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of (kathiran). (ma) is a relative noun, and what follows it is its relative clause. The returning pronoun is omitted, and (min al-kitab) is a circumstantial clause (hal) of that omitted element, meaning: He makes clear to you much of what you conceal continuously, while it is from the Scripture to which you belong and upon which you are devoted.

﴿and pardons much﴾ means: he does not disclose much of what you conceal, when no religious motive calls for it, to protect you from further disgrace. Al-Hasan said: he overlooks much of you, and does not hold to account the one who repents and follows him. Ibn Humayd reported from Qatada something similar.

It has been objected that this is contrary to the apparent sense, since the apparent sense is that this "much" is the same as the earlier "much." There is room for debate on this, as al-Shihab said, because when an indefinite noun is repeated as an indefinite, it is different (from the first). Yes, al-Jubba'i and a group of exegetes preferred the first interpretation. The sentence is conjoined to the circumstantial clause, and falls under its ruling.

﴿There has come to you from Allah a light﴾, great, which is the light of lights and the chosen Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatada, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i said: by "the light" he means the Qur'an, because it reveals and makes manifest the paths of guidance and certainty. Al-Zamakhshari confined himself to this. On this view, the conjunction in His saying, ﴿and a clear Book﴾, serves to treat the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence. As for the first view, it is clear.

Al-Tibi said: this is more fitting for the repetition of His saying, glorified is He, "there has come to you," without a conjunction. Thus the description of the Messenger is attached first, and the description of the Book second. Better than this is the path taken by al-Raghib, who said: In the first and second verses he mentioned the three blessings with which the servants were singled out: prophethood, reason, and the Book. In the third verse he mentioned three rulings, each of which returns to one of the blessings previously mentioned. ﴿by which He guides﴾ to the end returns to His saying, glorified is He, "there has come to you Our Messenger." ﴿He brings them out﴾, etc., returns to His saying, "there has come to you a light." ﴿He guides them﴾ returns to His saying, exalted is His affair, "and a clear Book," like His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾. End of quotation.

You know that there is no evidence for this correspondence except the consideration of the verbal order. If you had made the three rulings return to the first, there would be no objection. In my view it is not far-fetched that by "the light" and "the clear Book" what is meant is the Prophet (ﷺ), and the conjunction to him is like the conjunction in what al-Jubba'i said. There is no doubt about the validity of applying each of the two designations to him, upon him be peace. Perhaps you hesitate to accept it as a matter of literal expression, so let it be taken as a matter of allusion (ishara).

The prepositional phrase is connected to (jaa'a, has come). The (min) is for the starting point of the action, used figuratively. Alternatively, it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "light." Placing this before the subject serves to hasten the explanation that the coming is from His lofty Majesty, and to create anticipation for what comes. Also, placing it before the subject would disturb the harmony of the noble composition, because there is a kind of length in it.

Al-Mubin, derived from (bana), which is intransitive and means "to become manifest," means "the manifest in its inimitability." It may also be derived from the transitive form, in which case it means "the one who makes manifest to people what was hidden from them."

﴿يَهْدِي بِهِ اللَّهُ﴾ [by which Allah guides]: The pronoun (الضمير, *al-damir*, pronoun) is singular (بِهِ, *bihi*), though the antecedent is plural in meaning, because the two (the Book and the Messenger, or the Light and the Clear Book) are one in essence, or because they are treated as one thing, or because the intended meaning is "by what has been mentioned" (يَهْدِي بِما ذُكِرَ). The prepositional phrase (بِهِ) is placed first for emphasis, in view of the context. The Divine Name (اللَّهُ) is stated explicitly to show the full importance given to the matter of guidance. The clause (الجملة, *al-jumla*) has a position in grammar (محل, *mahall*) of nominative (الرفع, *al-raf'*), as a second adjective (صفة, *sifa*) of (كِتابٌ, "a Book"), or of accusative (النصب, *al-nasb*) as a circumstantial qualifier (حال, *hal*) of it, since it is particularized by the description.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier (حال) of (رَسُولُنا, "Our Messenger"), or a substitute (بَدَل, *badal*) for (يُبَيِّنُ, "makes clear"), or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in (يُبَيِّنُ), or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in (مُبِينٌ, "clear"), or an adjective (صفة) of (نُورٌ, "a Light").

﴿مَنِ اتَّبَعَ رِضْوانَهُ﴾ [those who follow His good pleasure]: that is, whoever Allah knows wishes to follow the pleasure of Allah by believing in Him. The word (مَن, *man*) is a relative pronoun (مَوْصُولَة, *mawsula*) or a qualifying noun (مَوْصُوفَة, *mawsufa*).

﴿سُبُلَ السَّلامِ﴾ [the paths of peace]: that is, the ways of safety from every fear, as said by al-Zajjaj. So (السَّلامُ, *al-salam*) is a verbal noun (مَصْدَر, *masdar*) with the meaning of (السَّلامَة, *al-salama*, safety).

According to al-Hasan and al-Suddi, (السَّلامُ) is one of the Names of Allah, may He be exalted. Placing the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is a refutation of the Jews and Christians who attribute deficiencies to Him, exalted is He far above what they say. In this case, (سُبُلِهِ, "His paths") means His laws (شَرائِعُهُ) which He prescribed for His servants, and established. It has been said that (سُبُلَ) is a second object of (يَهْدِي, "guides") with the preposition dropped, as in ﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ [And Musa chose from his people...].

It has also been said that (سُبُلَ) is a substitute (بَدَل) for (رِضْوانَهُ), a substitute of the whole for the whole, or of a part for a whole, or of inclusion (اشْتِمال, *ishtimal*). The word (الرِّضْوانُ, *al-ridwan*) is read with a kasra or a damma on the letter ra', and both are dialectal forms, and both have been recited. The word (السُّبُلُ, *al-subul*) has a damma on the ba', and the sukun (silent pronunciation) is a dialectal form, and it has been recited with it.

﴿ويُخْرِجُهُمْ﴾ [and brings them out]: the object pronoun refers to (مَن, "whoever"), and the plural is used in view of the meaning, just as the singular of the subject pronoun in (اتَّبَعَ, "follows") is used in view of the wording.

﴿مِنَ الظُّلُماتِ إلى النُّورِ﴾ [from darknesses into light]: that is, from the varieties of disbelief and error into faith. ﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾ [by His permission]: that is, by His will, or by His grace.

﴿ويَهْدِيهِمْ إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ [and guides them to a straight path]: which is the religion of Islam, which leads to Allah, exalted is He, as al-Hasan said. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, it is said: this guidance is the very same as the guidance to (سُبُلِ السَّلامِ, "the paths of peace"). It is joined to it by conjunction only because the descriptive difference is treated as though it were an essential difference, as in His saying: ﴿ولَمّا جاءَ أمْرُنا نَجَّيْنا هُودًا والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ بِرَحْمَةٍ مِنّا ونَجَّيْناهم مِن عَذابٍ غَلِيظٍ﴾ [And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and saved them from a severe punishment].

Al-Jubba'i said: the straight path (الصِّراط المُسْتَقِيم) means the path to Paradise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 5, verse 17:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ It means only the Messiah, just as one says, "Generosity is piety," and "Allah, exalted is He, is fate," meaning the one who brings about events and no other. So the restriction here is of the predicate to the subject. This differs from your saying, "Zayd is the one who departs," whose meaning is "none other than Zayd."

Those who say this, according to what is well known, are the Ya'qubiyya (the Jacobites, a Monophysite Christian sect), who claim that Allah, glorified is He, may incarnate in the body of a specific human being or in his soul.

It was said: No one among the Christians has explicitly stated this view. Rather, since they claimed that there is a *lahut* (divinity) in him, along with their explicit affirmation of unity and their saying, "There is no god but One," it follows for them that Allah, glorified is He, is the Messiah. So the necessary implication of their saying was attributed to them, to expose their ignorance and to disclose their creed.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, "No one has said that Allah, exalted is He, is the Messiah, but they have said that the Messiah is Allah, exalted is He. This is because, in their view, the Messiah is composed of *lahut* and *nasut* (humanity). So it is valid to say, 'The Messiah is the *lahut*, and he is *nasut*,' just as it is valid to say, 'The human being is an animal,' despite being composed of the elements. But it is not valid to say, 'The *lahut* is the Messiah,' just as it is not valid to say, 'The animal is the human being'?" It is answered: They said "he is the Messiah" in a way other than what you have mentioned, namely what has been related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: "When Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised, a group of the scholars of the Children of Israel gathered and said, 'What do you say about Jesus, peace be upon him?' One of them said, 'Do you know anyone who gives life to the dead except Allah, exalted is He?' They said, 'No.' He said, 'Do you know anyone who heals the blind and the leper except Allah, exalted is He?' They said, 'No.' They said, 'Then Allah, exalted is He, is none other than the one who has this attribute,' meaning that the reality of divinity is in him. This is like your saying, 'The generous one is Zayd,' meaning that the reality of generosity is in Zayd." Based on this is their saying: "Indeed Allah is the Messiah." End of quotation.

You know that, with the claim that those who hold incarnation say that the worshipped is restricted to the Messiah, as is the apparent meaning of the structure, nothing is objectionable.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to rebuke them, to show the falsehood of their corrupt saying, and to silence them. It has also been said that the address is to everyone who is capable of it. The *fa'* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then who could prevent Allah at all﴾, is conjunctive, coordinating with an implied clause, or it is the answer to an omitted condition. The *man* (who) is interrogative, for denial and reproach. *Milk* means complete control and firm preservation. Here the meaning is: who can prevent or who is able, as in the verse of poetry:

*I have come to carry no weapon, and I do not control even the halter of a camel, if a group [attacks].*

The phrase ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to it, with an omitted noun: the matter is not as they say, or, if it is as you claim, then who can prevent from His power and His will anything? ﴿If He willed to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth, all together.﴾ It is due to the one who is God that he not be affected by anything, nor by any of his affairs; rather, the power of another over any existent thing is greater, let alone that he would be unable to repel any of them when they are affected by his destruction. Since his incapacity is clear and beyond doubt, it becomes evident that he is far removed from what you say about him.

By destruction is meant death and annihilation in general, not out of wrath or anger. The Messiah is mentioned in the manner in which they attributed divinity to him, and the attribute is included with him in a place where a pronoun would have been expected, to increase the affirmation and to make explicit that he, from that very aspect, is included under His power and dominion, glorified is He. It has been said: Describing him thus alerts to the fact that he is created, subject to the power of God without doubt, because he was born from a mother. The mention of the mother specifically, though she is included in the general scope of what is coordinated, serves to further emphasize the incapacity of the Messiah. Perhaps her placement among those whose destruction is supposed, though her destruction had already occurred, is for the emphasis of the rebuke and for the increased affirmation of the content of the statement, by making her condition an example of the condition of the rest of those whose destruction is supposed. The generalization of the will to destroy, though the purpose is achieved by restricting it to Jesus, peace be upon him, serves to magnify the matter and to show complete incapacity by explaining that all are under His power and dominion, exalted is He; none can repel what is willed against him, let alone what is willed against others. It also serves to notify that the Messiah is an example for the rest of the creatures in being exposed to destruction, just as he is an example for them in incapacity and in not deserving divinity. This was said by the scholar Abu al-Su'ud.

﴿All together﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the coordinated items, and it is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of *man* alone, due to its generality.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, means what is between the two extremes of the physical world. It includes what is in the heavens, such as the angels and others, and what is in the depths of the earth and the seas of created beings. It has been said: This is an explicit statement that all are under His power and dominion, following the indication that some are so. That is, to Him alone belongs the dominion of all existents, and the absolute disposal over them by bringing into being and annihilating, giving life and causing death, not to anyone else, either independently or in partnership. So this is a confirmation of the exclusivity of divinity to Him, exalted is He, following the statement of its negation from anything else. It has been said: It is another proof of the negation of the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him, because if he were God, he would have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. It has been said: It is a proof of the negation that he, peace be upon him, is a son, by showing that he is owned, since he falls under the general scope, and it is known that ownership contradicts sonship.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought to explain some of the rulings of dominion and divinity in a manner that removes the doubts that afflicted them concerning the matter of the Messiah, peace be upon him: his birth without a father, the creation of the bird, the healing of the blind and the leper, and the raising of the dead. The *ma* is an indefinite, qualified noun, in the accusative place as a verbal noun. That is: He creates whatever creation He wills. So at times He creates from no origin, as with the creation of the heavens and the earth, for example, and at other times from an origin, as with the creation of some of what is between them. This too is varied. At times He originates from an origin that is not of its own kind, as with the creation of Adam and many animals, and at other times from an origin of its own kind: either from a male alone, as with the creation of Eve, or from a female alone, as with the creation of Jesus, peace be upon him, or from both, as with the creation of all other people. He creates without the intermediary of any created being, and He may create through the intermediary of another created being, as with the creation of the bird by the hand of Jesus, peace be upon him, as a miracle for him, and the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper. So all of that should be attributed to Him, exalted is He, not to the one through whose hand it was accomplished. This was said by more than one scholar.

It has been said: The sentence has been brought here to clarify what is meant by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, etc., according to what the context requires. The *ma* is also in the accusative as a verbal noun. It has been said: It is permissible that it be relative, in the accusative place as object: He creates whomever He wills to create. The sentence is brought to show that His power, exalted is He, is broader than the world of existence.

In every case, His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a concluding statement confirming the content of what precedes it. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name is for the reason mentioned before, and to strengthen the independence of the sentence.

[Page 100]

**Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 5, verse 18 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿The Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved."﴾ This is a report of the false claim each of the two groups made for itself, and an explanation of its falsehood, following the mention of the false claim made by one of them about the other and the explanation of its falsehood. That is, each of the two groups said this false statement. By "sons" they meant those brought near, that is, "We are brought near to Allah the Exalted as children are near to their father." By "beloved" (plural of *habib*, meaning either one who loves or one who is loved) they meant the same. It is also possible that they meant by "sons" the special ones, as one says "the sons of this world" and "the sons of the Hereafter." It is also possible that they meant the followers (*ashya'*) of one who was described as a prophet. That is, the Jews said, "We are the followers of his son Uzayr," and the Christians said, "We are the followers of his son the Messiah, peace be upon them both." The word "sons" was applied to followers metaphorically, either by *taghlib* (the dominant term being used for the whole group) or by *tashbih* (likening them to sons in nearness of station). This is like the followers of a king saying, "We are the kings." It is also like the usage in the case of the followers of Abu Khubayb, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who are called "the Khubaybiyyun" in his line:

*"Enough for me of supporting the Khubaybiyyun, enough."*

According to the version that has it in the plural. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "He means Abu Khubayb and those who were with him." Since it is permitted to pluralize "Khubayb" together with the followers of his father, it is even more fitting to permit pluralizing "the son of Allah, may His name be exalted," together with the followers of the son, according to the claim of the two groups. Thus we reject what has been said: that they do not claim sonship for themselves. It is not interpreted as a distributive sense, meaning "we ourselves are the beloved and our sons are the sons," with the two sons pluralized to match "the beloved," because the address ﴿Nay, you are but human beings﴾ rejects this apparently, or indicates their claim of sonship in whatever sense it is taken.

It has also been said that the speech contains an omitted modifier (*mudaf* elided): "We are the sons of the prophets of Allah." This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The one who said this was some of the Jews, and it is attributed to all of them, as has been mentioned more than once.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "Nu'man ibn Aasi, Bahri ibn Amr, and Shas

[Page 101]

ibn Adi came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They spoke with him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with them, invited them to Allah the Exalted, and warned them of His punishment. They said, 'What do you frighten us with, O Muhammad? By Allah, we are the sons of Allah and His beloved.' The Christians had said this before them. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse concerning them."

It is related from al-Hasan that the Christians interpreted what is in the Gospel from the words of the Messiah, "I am going to my Father and your Father," and so they said what they said.

In my view, the application of "son of Allah" to the obedient was known in ancient times. In the Torah, Allah the Exalted said to Moses, peace be upon him: "Go to Pharaoh and say to him: The Lord says to you, Israel is My son, My firstborn. Send him that he may worship Me. If you refuse to send My son, My firstborn, I will slay your son, your firstborn." In the same book, in the story of the Flood: when the sons of Allah the Exalted looked upon the daughters of men, who were very beautiful, they were enamored of them, and they married from among them whomever they loved and chose. They begot giants, and they corrupted. So Allah the Exalted said: "My care shall not remain upon this people." The "sons of Allah the Exalted" are meant to be the children of Abel, and "the sons of men" the children of Cain. The women were very beautiful, and they turned the hearts of His servants away from the worship of Allah the Exalted toward the worship of idols.

In the Psalms: "You are My son, ask Me and I will give you." And also in it: "You are My son and My beloved." Isaiah, in his prophecy, said on behalf of Allah the Exalted: "Charge Me concerning My sons and My daughters," meaning the righteous male and female servants of Allah the Exalted.

John the Evangelist said in the second chapter of the First Epistle: "Behold the love of the Father for us, that He has given us to be called sons." In the third chapter: "Beloved, now we are the sons of Allah the Exalted. It is fitting for us to revere Him as He is. Whoever has this hope, let him purify himself by abandoning sin and wrongdoing. Know that whoever commits sin has not known Him."

Matthew said: The Messiah said, "Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father who makes His sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous."

John the Disciple said in the Acts of the Apostles: "O my beloved, we are the sons of Allah the Exalted; He has named us thus." Paul the Apostle said in his epistle to the King of the Romans: "The Spirit bears witness with our spirits that we are the sons of Allah the Exalted and His beloved," and other things beyond counting.

The term "son" has also been applied to the disobedient, but in the sense of consequence and the like. In the Fifth Epistle of Paul: "Beware of foolishness, abuse, and play, for the adulterer and the impure, like the idol-worshipper, has no portion in the kingdom of Allah the Exalted. Beware of these evils, for because of them the wrath of Allah comes upon the sons who do not obey Him. Do not be partners with them, for you were before in darkness; now strive as the sons of light."

The intended meaning of the two groups in saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ is the sense that includes praise. The summary of their claim is that they have a superiority and distinction with Allah the Exalted over the rest of creation. So He, glorified is He, rejected this from them, and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿Say﴾ as a reproach and rebuke: ﴿Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾ That is: if what you claim is true, then for what reason does He punish you on the Day of Resurrection with the Fire for a number of days equal to the days you worshipped the calf? You have acknowledged this on more than one occasion. This contradicts your claim of nearness and of Allah's love for you, or your love for Him, which entails His love for you, as it has been said: "What is the reward of one who loves except to be loved?" Or: "For what reason did you sin, as evidenced by the fact that you will be punished?" The term "sons of Allah the Exalted," if used in a context of pride, applies to the obedient, as your books affirm. Or: if what you claim is true, then why has He punished you with transformation (*maskh*), which you cannot deny?

Some have counted the punishments as trials and afflictions, such as killing and captivity. This has been objected to on the grounds that it is not suitable as a proof, for trials and afflictions have been abundant among the righteous. It has been reported: "The people most severely tried are the prophets, peace be upon them, then the best and then those next best." The poet said:

*"But they are the people of guardianship and high station, so they are the adversaries of the calamities of time."*

[Page 102]

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Nay, you are but human beings﴾ is a conjunction with an understood premise to which the speech is linked; that is: the matter is not so, rather you are human beings. If you wish, you may supply something similar at the beginning of the speech and make the fa' a conjunctive particle. His statement, glorified is He: ﴿of those He has created﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as a descriptor of "human beings," meaning: human beings who are of the kind of those Allah the Exalted has created, without any distinction for you over them.

﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ among those created beings, namely the believers in Him, the Exalted, and His messengers, peace be upon them. ﴿And punishes whom He wills﴾, namely those who disbelieved in Him, glorified is He, and in His messengers, peace be upon them, like you. What indicates the specification is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him﴾, if we take its generality, as is well known. Among the strange things in the commentary of Muslim by al-Nawawi is that it is possible that this is specific to this community. There is room for examination in this.

Furthermore, some of the verifying scholars raised a problem here, which he said is strong: if the meaning of ﴿We are the sons of Allah﴾ is that they are the followers of His sons, then at most they would be on the path of the son, to establish following. But from where does it follow that they must be of the same kind as the Father, as al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated, in the absence of committing abominations, and the absence of human nature and createdness, so that the rebuttal against them would be fitting: that they are ﴿human beings of those He has created﴾? Yes, what they mentioned in this context, that love entails the absence of disobedience and punishment, may perhaps hold, because it is the nature of a lover not to disobey the beloved and not to deserve punishment from him. From here it has been said:

*"You disobey God while you show His love; by my life, this is a wondrous thing in deeds.*
*Had your love been true, you would have obeyed Him; indeed the lover is obedient to the one he loves."*

But there is an objection to this, since this is the way of lovers, and "the beloved" are the lovers. He answered the problem of establishing humanness by saying that it is not an establishment of absolute humanness, so that the rejection of their claim would have to be by its negation. Rather it is an establishment that they are human beings like the rest of human beings, and of the kind of the rest of created beings, among them the disobedient and the obedient, and those who deserve forgiveness and punishment, not as they claim, that they are the followers specially distinguished by greater nearness and special favor not found among the rest of humankind. For this reason He, glorified is He, described human beings with His words ﴿of those He has created﴾, so that it is not far-fetched that ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ is also in the position of a descriptor, with the returning pronoun elided, meaning: whom He wills among them.

As for the problem of the kind, it has been said in its answer: the meaning is that if you were followers of the sons of Allah the Exalted, you would be upon their attribute in abandoning abominations and not deserving punishment, because it is the nature of followers and adherents to be upon the attribute of those they follow. Those followed here are the sons by claim, and it is the nature of sons to be upon the attribute of the father. Thus it is the nature of followers to be upon the attribute of the father by intermediation. It has also been said: the speech of one who said "it entails that they must be of the same kind as the Father" is by an elision of a modifier: that is, if you were followers of the sons of Allah the Exalted, you would be of the kind of the followers of the Father, meaning the people of Allah the Exalted who do not commit abominations and do not deserve punishment.

In *al-Kashf*: their statement "We are the sons of Allah the Exalted" involves affirming the Son, and that they are among His followers, deserving the Father's love for that. So the rebuttal should include the demolition of both claims. It is said: the one to whom you attribute sonship is not fit for it, since abomination is possible for him and transgression may proceed from him, and he may be taken to account for a slip. Your claim of love is false, otherwise you would not be punished.

Also, if it is refuted that He the Exalted has a son, it is refuted that they are His followers, and likewise the love founded upon that. Then he said: It is permissible to say that this is to refute that they are sons in the literal sense, as the apparent wording indicates, or in the figurative sense, as al-Zamakhshari explained. End of quotation.

You know that everything he mentioned is nothing, as is not hidden from one who has the least reflection. What we have mentioned suffices for the purpose.

[Page 103]

Yes, al-Shihab, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned an interpretation that is not objectionable, which is that the fitting meaning of their saying that they are the sons of Allah the Exalted is that when He sent to them the son, according to their claim, and sent to others the messengers of His servants, this indicates their distinction over the rest of creation, and that they have a complete affinity with Allah the Exalted and nearness that entails a dignity with no dignity above it. Just as when a king sends one of his soldiers to call a people and sends his son to others, they know that he intends to bring them near, and that they are safe from every harm that visits others.

The rebuttal is that you have no distinction between yourselves and others before Allah the Exalted, for if it were as you claim, He would not have punished you and placed transformation upon you. Likewise, if the meaning is "those brought near," the intended nearness is a special nearness, and the rebuttal matches it, and the two answers embrace, so understand it. End of quotation.

The answer to the objection that some made is known from what we have pointed to earlier, so do not be heedless.

{Part 2 of 2 of the commentary; this passage begins mid-argument}

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is a continuation of the refutation; that is, all of that belongs to Allah, the Exalted. Nothing of it is attributed to Him, glorified is He, except as a thing owned, a servant, and subjugated, under His sovereignty (malakut), which He disposes as He wills: bringing into being and annihilating, giving life and causing death, rewarding and punishing. So how can these people claim what they assert?! It may be said that this, together with what preceded, is a refutation of their being "sons of Allah," in the sense of "partisans of His sons": He first denied that they were partisans, and then denied that He has any sons, exalted is His majesty.

﴿And to Him is the final return﴾ that is, the return in the Hereafter, not to anyone else, whether independently or jointly; so He will recompense each of the good-doer and the wrongdoer with what His knowledge requires, without any deterrent that turns Him away or any inclination that sways Him.

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is a repetition of the address through a shift of grammatical person (iltifat), and an gentle appeal. It is also said that the address here is to the Jews specifically. ﴿Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you﴾ "making clear" means that he explains, gradually as the benefit requires, the laws and rulings beneficial for both the Hereafter and this world, accompanied by promise and threat. The object is omitted because it is evident, since it is known that what the Messenger makes clear is the laws and rulings. It is also permissible to treat the verb as intransitive, meaning that he performs and dispenses clarification to you in everything you need regarding matters of religion. As for keeping it transitive with the object supplied, as in ﴿much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾, as has been said, then it has been said against it that, besides being a repetition without benefit, it is refuted by His words, exalted is He: ﴿after a interval [fatrah] in the messengers﴾. For the interval in the sending of messengers and the cutting off of revelation only necessitates the clarification of laws and rulings, not the clarification of what they had concealed. The phrase ﴿after an interval﴾ is linked to ﴿has come﴾ in the sense of a time adverb, as in His exalted words: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾. That is, he has come to you at a time of interval in the sending of messengers, and the cutting off of revelation, and the greater need for clarification.

It is also permitted that it be linked to an omitted element, as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿makes clear﴾ or from the pronoun in ﴿to you﴾. That is: ﴿makes clear to you﴾ while being in a state of interval, or while you are in a state of interval. ﴿From the messengers﴾ is an attribute of ﴿interval﴾, and ﴿from﴾ is for origin, meaning an interval consisting of messengers, originating from their side. The fatrah (interval) is a noun of the form fa'lah from "fatara" regarding his work, yafturu futuran, when it becomes still. Its basic meaning is cessation from the earnestness that one had in work. According to all the exegetes, it is the cessation between two messengers.

They differed about its duration between our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and Jesus, peace be upon him. Qatadah said: between them was five hundred and sixty years. al-Kalbi said: five hundred and forty years. Ibn Juraij said: five hundred years. al-Dahhak said: four hundred and thirty-some years.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was six hundred years. It is also said that between our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his brother Jesus, peace be upon him, there were three prophets, who are the ones referred to by His exalted words: ﴿We sent to them two, and they denied them both, so We strengthened them with a third﴾. It is also said that between them, peace and blessings be upon them both, there were four: the three referred to, and one Arab man from the tribe of Banu 'Abs, who is Khalid ibn Sinan, peace be upon him, concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "That is a prophet whom his people neglected."

It is not hidden that the three referred to in the verse were messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the attribution of their sending to Him, exalted is He, is based on the fact that it was by His command, glory and majesty be to Him. Its verification will come, Allah willing. As for Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi, al-Raghib hesitated about him in his Muhadarat, and some did not affirm him, and some said that he was before Jesus, peace be upon them both, because it occurred in a hadith: "There is no prophet between me and Jesus," may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.

However, the histories affirm him, and he has a detailed story in the books of narrations, and it is mentioned that his daughter came to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and believed in him. The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, engraved for him a bezel in his book Fusus al-Hikam. al-Shihab affirmed that he, peace be upon him, is among the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and that he was before Jesus, peace and blessings be upon them both. According to this, the meaning of his daughter who came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, if the report is sound, is his daughter by intermediary, not a daughter of his loins, for her survival until that time, with no one mentioning that she was among the long-lived, is very distant.

Between Moses and Jesus, peace and blessings be upon them both, there were, according to what is well known, one thousand seven hundred years, but revelation did not cease during them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, related that Allah, exalted is He, sent during them one thousand prophets from the Children of Israel, besides those sent from others.

﴿Lest you say﴾ is a reason for the coming of the Messenger with clarification, meaning: out of aversion that you should say, as the Basrans (al-Basriyyun) estimated, or "lest you say," as the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun) estimate, making excuses for your negligence in the rulings of religion on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿There came to us no bringer of good tidings nor warner﴾. The traces of the previous law had been obliterated and its reports cut off. The addition of "min" to the subject is for emphasis in negating the coming, and the indefiniteness of "bringer" and "warner," according to what Shaykh al-Islam said, is for minimization. The phrase ﴿Indeed there has come to you﴾ etc. following this implies that what is estimated or intended in what preceded is the laws and rulings, not in whatever form, but accompanied by mention of promise and threat. The fa' in His exalted words ﴿so there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ reveals an omitted element, which is its cause, and the estimate here is: "Do not make excuses, for there has come to you." This fa' is called the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasihah), and the wording of the element estimated before it varies: sometimes it is a command or prohibition, sometimes a condition, as in His exalted words: ﴿This is the Day of Resurrection﴾, and the words of the poet:

"So we have come to Khurasan"

and sometimes it is what is governed by a preceding verb, as in His exalted words: ﴿so it burst forth﴾. Sometimes recourse is made to estimating a saying, as in al-Furqan, in His exalted words: ﴿for they have denied you﴾. And if you wish, it may be estimated here too, so we say: "Do not make excuses, for there has come to you," etc. Some scholars of Arabic have stated that the reality of this fa' is that it is linked to an omitted condition, and estimating a saying does not conflict with that, because when the omitted element is made explicit, there is no escape from an implied verb in order to connect it to what precedes. So it is said in the verse, for example: "And we said," or "So we said: If what you mentioned is sound, then we have come to Khurasan." Likewise in what we are dealing with: "So we said: Do not make excuses, for there has come to you." Then, in meaning, it is the answer to an estimated condition, whether that is stated or not, because when speech contains two things where one is in a relation of causation to the other, it is in the sense of condition and consequence. So there is no contradiction between the estimates, and the different estimates; and even if a contradiction were granted, they are two aspects, one of which they mentioned in one place and the other in another place, as verified in al-Kashshaf. The allusion to the matter of this fa' has already been made from a distance, so remember. The tanwin on "bringer" and "warner" is for magnification.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾, so He is able to send messengers in succession, and to send after the interval.

[p. 104]

[Page 105]

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾ is a resumed clause, brought to explain what the Children of Israel did after the covenant was taken from them, and to detail how they broke it, while also indicating that there was a gap between the messengers, peace be upon them, among them. The word ﴿إذ﴾ (idh, "when") is in the accusative as the object of an omitted verb. It is addressed to the master of those addressed, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, through the method of shifting the address (iltifat). He turned it away from the People of the Book in order to enumerate against them the crimes that some of them had committed earlier. The meaning is: "And mention to them, O Muhammad, the time when Musa, peace be upon him, said, giving counsel and seeking to win them over by attributing them to himself: ﴿O my people, remember the favour of God upon you﴾." Directing the command to remember toward the time is more eloquent than directing it toward what occurred in it, even though the latter is the primary intended meaning, as the indication of it has already passed. The phrase ﴿upon you﴾ (ʿalaykum) is connected either to "favour" if it is taken as a verbal noun (maṣdar), or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it if it is taken as a noun. The meaning is: "Remember His bestowal upon you with gratitude," or "Remember His favour being upon you." Likewise, the word ﴿إذ﴾ in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when He made among you prophets﴾, is connected to what the prepositional phrase is connected to. The meaning is: "Remember His bestowal upon you at the time He made it," or "Remember the favour of God being upon you at the time He made among you, from among your kinsmen, prophets." The plural form is taken in its literal sense, as is apparent. Those meant by it are Musa, Harun, Yusuf, and the rest of the sons of Ya'qub, according to the view that they were prophets, or the earlier ones, and the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time of his Lord. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said that they were prophets.

Al-Mawardi and others said: those meant are the prophets who were sent afterward among the Children of Israel, and the past-tense verb is turned away from its literal meaning. It was said: those meant are those who came before and those who came after, and no nation among the nations was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel were, peace be upon them. ﴿And made you kings﴾ is coordinated with ("made among you") and the style in it is changed, because there were many kings among them, or because all of them became, from among them, as if they were kings, by following their way in abundance and luxury. Therefore the attribution of kingship to all of them is permitted, unlike prophethood, for although it was numerous, no one follows the way of the prophets, peace be upon them, because it is a divine matter that God specifies for whom He wills. Therefore it is not permitted to use figurative language in attributing it.

It was said: there is no figurative usage (majāz, metaphor) in the attribution; rather the figure is in the word "kings," for the people had been enslaved in the hands of the Copts, and God rescued them, so that rescue was called kingship. It was also said: there is no majāz at all; rather they were all made kings in the literal sense, and a king is one who has a house and a servant, as was reported from Zayd ibn Aslam, traced to the Prophet.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: «When one of the Children of Israel had a servant, a mount, and a wife, he was recorded as a king.»

Ibn Jarir reported, from al-Hasan: "Is kingship anything but a mount, a servant, and a house?"

Al-Bukhari reported, from Abdullah ibn Amr, that a man asked him, saying: «Are we not among the poor emigrants?» Abdullah said: "Do you have a wife you resort to?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling you live in?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "Indeed I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."»

It was also said: the king is one who has a spacious dwelling in which there is flowing water.

It was said: one who has wealth with which he does not need to burden himself with labours and endure hardships. This is the view of Abu Ali al-Jubba'i.

You know that the apparent meaning here is the view that there is majāz, and what was mentioned in the context of argumentation is also open to that interpretation.

﴿And gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds﴾, namely the splitting of the sea, the drowning of the enemy, the shading of the clouds, the gushing of water from the stone, the sending down of the manna and quail, and other particular matters that God, exalted is He, gave them. The address is to the people of Musa, peace be upon him, as is apparent. The definite article in ﴿the worlds﴾ is for prior reference, and the meaning is the worlds of their time; or it is for comprehensiveness (istighraq). Preference in one respect does not require preference in every respect, for the less excellent may possess what the more excellent does not. On either reading, it does not follow that they are preferred over this Muhammadan nation, upon its prophet be the best of blessings and the most complete greetings. Giving what no one else was given does not necessarily entail preference, but the immediate understanding from its use is preference, and therefore it was interpreted in the way it was.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik, that the address here is to this nation[Page 106] — and this is very contrary to the apparent meaning, and such a thing is hardly ever ventured in the Glorious Book, because the address before and after this passage is to the Children of Israel, so the presence of an address in the midst to others would disrupt the noble structure. It seems that what motivates the view of it is the assumption that preference is necessarily entailed, with no way to avoid it other than that; and you know that this is from some kinds of conjecture.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 21:

﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land﴾. The call (nida') is repeated together with the honorific attribution (idafah tashrifiyyah), out of concern for the matter and in emphasis of urging them to comply with it. The "Holy Land" (al-ard al-muqaddasah) is, as related from Ibn 'Abbas - may Allah be pleased with both of them - and al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

Al-Zajjaj said: Damascus, Palestine, and Jordan.

Mujahid said: It is the land of Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it.

And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: It is what lies between the Euphrates and the Brook of Egypt ('Arish Misr).

Taqdis (sanctification) means purification (tathir), and that land was described as such either because it is purified from polytheism (shirk), since it was made the dwelling place of the Prophets - upon them be prayers and peace - or because it is purified from calamities, and the domination of the tyrants (jabbarin) over it does not remove it from being holy, or because it was purified from drought and hunger. It was also said: it was called holy because in it is the place where one is made holy from sins.

﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾. That is: He decreed it and allotted it to you, or He wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) that it would be a dwelling place for you.

It is related that Allah the Exalted commanded the Friend (al-Khalil) - upon him be prayers and peace - to ascend the mountain of Lebanon, and whatever his gaze reached would be for him and his offspring, so that land was the extent of his sight.

And from Qatadah and al-Suddi: the meaning is: the land which Allah the Exalted has commanded you to enter and has imposed upon you. So the writing (al-katb) here is like His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾. Many of the exegetes took the first two possibilities.

The writing, according to the first of them, is metaphorical (majaz), and according to the second, literal (haqiqah). They restricted it by "if you believe and obey," because of His saying to them after they disobeyed: ﴿Therefore it is forbidden to them﴾.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and do not turn back on your heels, lest you turn about as losers﴾. The ordering of loss and ruin upon turning back indicates, decisively, that the writing is conditioned on the striving (mujahadah) that follows from faith. The "adbar" is the plural of "dubur," which is what lies behind them of places, from Egypt and other than it. The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "tartaddu" - that is: do not return from your intended destination as ones who turn back, out of fear of the tyrants. It was also permitted that it be connected to the verb itself. It may be intended by "turning back" the diverting of their hearts from what they held of belief, a diversion not perceptible, that is: do not return from your religion through disobedience and lack of trust in Allah the Exalted. This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿fa-tanqalibu﴾ is either jussive by conjunction (ma'tuf), which is the more apparent, or subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition. Al-Shihab said: on the basis that it is of the type of: "Do not disbelieve, you will enter the Fire." This is impermissible, contrary to al-Kisa'i, and there is a consideration in it that is not hidden. The intended meaning of "loss" (al-khusran) is the loss of both abodes.

They said, "O Moses, indeed in it is a people of tyrants." (Those who are) severe in their force, dominating, whose opposition cannot be countenanced, and whose forelocks are not to be cut. *Al-jabbar* is an intensive form (*sigha mubalaghah*) from the basic triliteral *jabara*, according to the regular pattern, not from *ajbarahu* (to compel him), which is contrary to it, like *al-hassas* from *al-ihsas*. It means one who overpowers people and compels them, whoever they are, to do what he wills, whatever it may be. Its meaning regarding stinginess is what the hand cannot reach in length. These people were among the Amalekites, remnants of the people of 'Ad, and they had bodies that were not like those of others.

Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam related in *Futuh Misr*, from Ibn Hujayrah, who said: Seventy men of the people of Moses, peace be upon him, sheltered in the skull of one man from the Amalekites.

Al-Bayhaqi related in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: It reached me that a hyena and her young were seen resting in the wide openings of the eye of one of them, and other reports of this kind. In my view these are like the reports about Uj ibn Unuq, and they are a fabricated tale.

﴿And indeed we will never enter it until they leave it.﴾ Either by others fighting them, or by a cause through which God Most High makes them leave; for we have no power to drive them out of it. This is a refusal to fight in the most complete form.

[Page 107]

﴿So if they leave it﴾ by one of the causes with which we have no connection, ﴿then indeed we will enter﴾ it at that time. They used this conditional sentence, although its content was already understood from what preceded, as an explicit statement of the intended meaning and as a specification that their refusal to enter it was only because of their presence in it.
