In the consequent they used a nominal sentence introduced by *inna*, indicating the certainty and firmness of entering when the condition is certainly fulfilled, and showing their complete eagerness for it and for complying with the command.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 23:**

﴿Said two men from among those who feared﴾: that is, who feared God, Exalted is He. It is also read with the verb in this form. The intended meaning is two men from among the God-fearing. They were, as Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him and his father) reported, along with Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Rabi', Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yuqanna. Describing them in this way implies that anyone else among the people does not fear God, Exalted is He, but rather fears the enemy.

It has also been said that the two men are as mentioned, and that "from among those who feared" refers to the Children of Israel, meaning that they feared the enemy. That the two men were "from them" means that they were from them by lineage, not in fear. It has also been said that they were from them in fear as well, and the meaning is that fear did not prevent them from speaking the truth.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, on the authority of Ibn Jubayr, that the two men were among the tyrants (jabbarun). They became Muslims and went to Musa (peace be upon him). According to this view, "those who" refers to the tyrants, the waw (in "yakhafun") refers to the Children of Israel, and the relative pronoun's returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "they fear them."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "yukhafun" with a dammah on the ya'. al-Zamakhshari took this reading as evidence that the two men were among the tyrants (al-jabbarin), as if it were said: "from among those who inspire fear," meaning that the Children of Israel feared them.

This reading carries two other possibilities:

The first is that it derives from *al-ikhafa* (causing fear), meaning: "from among those who warn about God through reminder and admonition," or "whom the threat of God's punishment frightens."

The second is that the meaning of "yukhafun" is "they are revered and held in awe," and that people turn to them for their merit and goodness. With these two possibilities, there is no preference for the tyrant reading in this recitation. The preference for it based on His saying ﴿God bestowed favour upon them both﴾, meaning with faith and steadfastness, is also not clear, because this attribute is shared between Yusha', Kalib and others. Moreover, it is only fitting to say this of one who has become Muslim from among the disbelievers, not of one who is already a believer in a state of restraint. The clause is a second attribute of "two men," or a parenthetical clause. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), with "qad" implied, either from the pronoun in "yakhafun" or from "two men," in order to specify them by the attribute, or from the hidden pronoun in the prepositional phrase. The meaning is: they both said, addressing them and encouraging them,

﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾: that is, the gate of their city. The fronting of "upon them" before "the gate" is for emphasis, because the intention is entering the gate while they are in their own land. The meaning is: surprise them and press upon them in the narrow passage, and do not give them respite so that they may gather themselves and find room for war.

﴿When you have entered it﴾ upon them through the gate, ﴿then you will surely be victorious﴾ without need for fighting. We have seen them and witnessed that their hearts are weak, though their bodies are large, so do not fear them. Attack them in the narrow passages, for they cannot advance and retreat freely.

It has also been said that they judged on the basis of victory because they knew it from Musa (peace be upon him) and his saying ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾. It has also been said that it was from the dominance of supposition, and from what they had observed of God's custom in supporting His messengers, and from what they had known of God's dealings with Musa (peace be upon him) in subduing his enemies. It has been said that the first view is more appropriate given that victory is linked to entering.

﴿And upon God alone﴾, Exalted is He, ﴿so put your trust﴾ after arranging the means, and do not rely upon them, for they have no effect without His permission.

﴿If you are believers﴾ in God, Exalted is He. This is meant as incitement and encouragement; otherwise their faith is already established. Faith may also be understood as affirmation of God and what follows from it, which is affirmation of what He has promised. That is, "if you are believers" in Him, Exalted is He, affirming His promise, for this is what necessitates trusting in Him.

"They said," paying no heed to them or to what they had said, addressing Musa (peace be upon him) to show their persistence in the first position and to openly declare their opposition to him (peace be upon him): "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it," meaning the land of the tyrants, let alone entering upon them while they are in their own land, "ever," meaning for a long time, or for all of future time, "as long as they remain in it," meaning in that land. This is a substitute (badl) for "ever," a substitute of part (badl al-ba'd). It has also been said that it is a substitute of the whole for the whole, or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), since it occurs between two indefinite nouns. A similar example of substitution is the poet's saying:

"And honour your brother all your days, so long as you both live together; death is enough of a separation and a distance."

Here his saying "so long as you both live" (ma dumtuma) is a substitute for "all your days" (al-dahr).

"So go," meaning: if the matter is as such, then "go, you and your Lord, and fight," meaning: fight them and drive them out until we enter the land. They said this in contempt and mockery of Him (glorified is He) and of His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and with indifference. They intended their going to be literal, as the extreme of their ignorance and the hardness of their hearts indicates, and it is contrasted with His saying (exalted is He): "Indeed we are sitting right here."

It has also been said: they meant the desire and intention of the two of them, as you say, "I spoke to him, so he went to answer me," as if they had said: "Then desire to fight them and intend them."

Al-Balkhi said: the meaning is "go, you and your Lord, and He will help you." The waw is then for the state (lil-hal), and "you" (anta) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate has been omitted. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and "fight" (faqatila) does not support it. They did not mention his brother Harun (peace be upon them both), nor the two men who had spoken, as if they had not been certain of their going, or did not care about fighting them. By "sitting" they meant not advancing, not also not lagging behind.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 5, verses 25–26:**

﴿He said﴾: Musa, peace be upon him, when he saw from them what he saw of obstinacy, resorted to expressing his distress and grief and complaining to Allah, the Exalted, together with a tenderness of heart by which mercy is drawn down and victory is brought near. So his purpose was not to inform, and likewise every statement addressed to the Knower of the unseen is intended to convey some meaning other than informing about a ruling or its implication. Therefore his words were neither a rejection of what Allah, the Exalted, had commanded, nor an excuse for not entering: ﴿My Lord, I have no power except over myself and my brother﴾ Harun, peace be upon him. The phrase "and my brother" is coordinated with "myself," meaning: no one responds to me in obeying You or agrees with me in carrying out Your command except myself and my brother. He did not mention the two men upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, even though they would agree with him if he called upon them, because he saw the people's fickleness and the shifting of their opinions. It is as if he trusted those two but did not rely upon them.

It has been said: the purpose is not restriction (qasr, exclusive limitation), but rather to state how few are those who agree with him, likening his situation to that of one who has no power except over himself and his brother. It has also been allowed that "my brother" may mean one who is a brother to me in religion, so that the two of them are included in it; but this is complete only by interpreting it as every brother of his in religion, or as the category of brother, and this is far-fetched.

There are other possible readings (i'rab, grammatical analysis) of "my brother":

The first: it is in the accusative, by coordination with the subject of ("inna," indeed).

The second: it is in the nominative, by coordination with the subject of ("amliku," I possess), with a separating element (fasl) intervening.

The third: it is a nominative subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted.

The fourth: it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of the noun of ("inna") which is at a distance, since it comes after the completion of the predicate; the majority hold that this is permissible in that case.

The fifth: it is in the genitive, by coordination with the pronoun in the genitive, according to the view of the Kufans.

Then, on some of these readings, there is no requirement of unity of object. Rather, a different object is supposed for the coordinated element, meaning: "and my brother possesses nothing except himself." So what has been said is not a valid objection, namely that coordinating it with the noun of "inna" or the subject of "amliku" would necessitate that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, possess only the self of Musa, peace be upon him, and nothing more. The meaning is not that, as is clear. Nor is it a coordination of sentences, with the supposition: "and my brother does not possess except himself," as some have imagined. Its verification is that coordination with an object of the verb requires only sharing in the general meaning and concept of that verb, not sharing in a specific individual instance with its particular connections; that depends on the contextual indicators.

﴿So separate between us﴾: he means himself and his brother, peace and blessings be upon them both. The "fa" (so) indicates the sequence of separation and of the supplication for it upon what precedes it. It has also been read "fafriq" with a kasra on the ra'.

﴿and between the wicked people﴾: that is, those who depart from Your obedience, by ruling for us what we deserve and against them what they deserve. This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Jubba'i said: Musa, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to separate them by distancing them in the Hereafter, by making him and his brother in Paradise and placing them in the Fire. Most exegetes adopted the first view, and what supports it is that the supplication is followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said: "Indeed, it is﴾, for the "fa" there indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it of the supplication. So that was a consequence of the supplication and a type of what was asked for.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, became angry when the people said to him what they said, so he made supplication, and that was a haste on his part, which he hastened. When the wandering was imposed upon them, he regretted it, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the wicked people﴾. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the Holy Land, meaning: indeed it, by your supplication, is ﴿forbidden to them﴾, they will not enter it nor possess it. The prohibition is a prohibition of prevention (man'), not a prohibition of worship (ta'abbud). A similar example is the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing his horse:

*She circled to throw me down, so I said to her: "Desist, for I am a man whose being thrown is forbidden to you."*

He means: I am a horseman, and it is not possible for you to throw me.

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i allowed (and al-Balkhi's words point to this) that it may be a prohibition of worship. The first is more apparent.

﴿forty years﴾: it is related to ("muharramah," forbidden), so the prohibition is temporary, not perpetual. Thus it does not contradict the apparent meaning of His words: ("God has ordained for you"). The meaning of their prohibition is that none of them enters it during this period. But this does not mean that all of them will enter it afterward; rather some of those who remained will, according to what is reported: that Musa, peace be upon him, led those of the Children of Israel who remained to the Holy Land, with Yusha' ibn Nun at its vanguard, and he conquered it, and remained there as long as Allah willed, then Musa, peace be upon him, was taken. This is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It has been said that none of those who said ("We will never enter it") entered it, but there entered with Musa, peace be upon him, only the young ones from their descendants. Accordingly, the time limit of forty years is in reality a prohibition upon their descendants. It is made a prohibition upon them because of the complete connection between them.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they wander in the land﴾ are a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of their deprivation. It has been said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ("'alayhim," upon them). The "tih" is bewilderment. It is said: "taha yatihu" and "yatuhu," and "huwa atwah" and "atyah," so it is among the words in which waw and ya' have interchanged. The meaning is: they travel bewildered, and their bewilderment is their failure to find the way.

It has been said: the adverbial phrase is related to ("yatihun," they wander), and this is related from Qatadah. Then the wandering is temporary, and the prohibition is unrestricted, admitting of perpetuity or its absence. The extent of the land in which they wandered was thirty farsakhs by a width of nine farsakhs, as Muqatil said. It has been said: twelve farsakhs by a width of six farsakhs; it has been said: six by nine; it has been said: its length was thirty miles by a width of six farsakhs, and it is what lies between Egypt and Syria. It is mentioned that they were six hundred thousand fighting men, and they would travel, so that they woke up where they had gone to sleep, and went to sleep where they had woken up, as al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

It has been said: the wisdom in their being tested with wandering is that when they said ("Indeed, we will remain seated here"), they were punished with something resembling sitting, and it was forty years, because it is the furthest limit of time in which the ignorant one comes to his senses.

It has been said: because they worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment for each day was made one year of wandering. But this is nothing. That was among the extraordinary events beyond customary habit, for bewilderment over such a distance among many intelligent people for this long a period is something that custom deems impossible. Perhaps that was by the erasing of the signs by which one might be guided, or the likeness of some of them was cast upon others.

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: it was by the land they were on being transformed at the time they slept, and Allah, the Exalted, is above needing to accept this.

It is related that the cloud shaded them from the heat of the sun, and manna and quails descended upon them, and the stone of Musa, peace be upon him, was with them, from which water gushed forth to repel their thirst. It is said: at night a column of light rose over them, illuminating for them. Their hair did not grow long, and their garments did not wear out, as related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Their children would grow up along with them when they grew up, as related from Tawus.

Several storytellers (qussas) mentioned that when a child was born to them, he had a garment like a fingernail which grew with his growth and did not wear out, along with other things they mentioned.

Customary habit makes much of this remote, so nothing is accepted except what is authentically related from Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ). I once asked one of the rabbis of the Jews about the clothing of the Children of Israel during the wandering, and he said: they left Egypt with much of the garments of the Copts and their goods, and Allah, the Exalted, preserved them for their elders and their young. I mentioned to him the story of the fingernail, and he said: "We did not attain it," and denied it. I said to him: "It is a virtue, so why did you not establish it for your people?" He said: "I do not accept a garment of lies."

The treatment of them with these blessings has been raised as a difficulty, along with their being punished with bewilderment. It is answered that this punishment is from His generosity, the Exalted, and their chastisement was only for discipline, just as a man beats his son while loving him, and does not cut off his kindness from him. Perhaps they sought forgiveness for disbelief, if it had occurred from them.

Most exegetes hold that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, were with them in the wandering, but the hardship that reached them did not reach them as it reached the others, and that was for them a ease and safety, like the fire for Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Perhaps the two men were also like that.

It is related that Harun died during the wandering, and Musa, peace be upon them both, was accused of it. They said: "He killed him out of love for us." So Allah, the Exalted, brought him back to life through Musa's supplication, and cleared him of what they said, and he returned to his resting place. Musa, peace be upon him, died after him by one year. It has been said: by six and a half months; it has been said: by eight years. Yusha' entered Jericho (Arihaa) three months after him. Qatadah said: two months. Musa had previously been made a prophet to those of the Children of Israel who remained, and the responsible ones at the time of the command were not left among them. It has been said: the noble arrangement of the verses does not support this, for after he (peace be upon him) had received his supplication against the Children of Israel and punished them with the wandering, it is far-fetched that those who were saved would be saved, and that the deaths of the two prophets, peace be upon them both, would be considered to have occurred apparently in the place of punishment, even if that was for them a station of ease and rest. You know that the reports of their deaths, peace be upon them both, during the wandering are numerous, especially the reports of the death of Harun, peace be upon him. I see no room for denying this, and perhaps that was more grievous to the Children of Israel.

It has been said: the two of them, peace be upon them both, were not with the Children of Israel during the wandering, and that the supplication, which was answered, concerned separation in the sense of distance in place in this world. I consider this view to be almost unsound, for many of the verses are explicit in establishing Musa's presence with them in it, as is not hidden.

﴿So do not grieve﴾: that is, do not be sorrowful over their death, or over what befell them in it, from grief (asa), which is sorrow.

﴿over the wicked people﴾: those whose supplication against them was answered because of their wickedness. So the address is to Musa, peace be upon him, as is apparent, and this is the view of the distinguished exegetes.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and by "the wicked people" are meant his contemporaries from the Children of Israel. It is as if it were said: these are the deeds of their ancestors, so do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for they inherited that from them.

﴿He said﴾: Musa, peace be upon him, when he saw from them what he saw of obstinacy, resorted to expressing his distress and grief and complaining to Allah, the Exalted, together with a tenderness of heart by which mercy is drawn down and victory is brought near. The second: it is in the nominative, by coordination with the subject of ("amliku," I possess), with a separating element (fasl) intervening.

The third: it is a nominative subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted.

The fourth: it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of the noun of ("inna") which is at a distance, since it comes after the completion of the predicate; the majority hold that this is permissible in that case.

The fifth: it is in the genitive, by coordination with the pronoun in the genitive, according to the view of the Kufans.

Then, on some of these readings, there is no requirement of unity of object. Rather, a different object is supposed for the coordinated element, meaning: "and my brother possesses nothing except himself." So what has been said is not a valid objection, namely that coordinating it with the noun of "inna" or the subject of "amliku" would necessitate that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, possess only the self of Musa, peace be upon him, and nothing more. The meaning is not that, as is clear. Nor is it a coordination of sentences, with the supposition: "and my brother does not possess except himself," as some have imagined. Its verification is that coordination with an object of the verb requires only sharing in the general meaning and concept of that verb, not sharing in a specific individual instance with its particular connections; that depends on the contextual indicators.

﴿So separate between us﴾: he means himself and his brother, peace and blessings be upon them both. The "fa" (so) indicates the sequence of separation and of the supplication for it upon what precedes it. It has also been read "fafriq" with a kasra on the ra'.

﴿and between the wicked people﴾: that is, those who depart from Your obedience, by ruling for us what we deserve and against them what they deserve. This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Jubba'i said: Musa, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to separate them by distancing them in the Hereafter, by making him and his brother in Paradise and placing them in the Fire. Most exegetes adopted the first view, and what supports it is that the supplication is followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said: "Indeed, it is﴾, for the "fa" there indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it of the supplication. So that was a consequence of the supplication and a type of what was asked for.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, became angry when the people said to him what they said, so he made supplication, and that was a haste on his part, which he hastened. When the wandering was imposed upon them, he regretted it, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the wicked people﴾. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the Holy Land, meaning: indeed it, by your supplication, is ﴿forbidden to them﴾, they will not enter it nor possess it. The prohibition is a prohibition of prevention (man'), not a prohibition of worship (ta'abbud). A similar example is the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing his horse:

*She circled to throw me down, so I said to her: "Desist, for I am a man whose being thrown is forbidden to you."*

He means: I am a horseman, and it is not possible for you to throw me.

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i allowed (and al-Balkhi's words point to this) that it may be a prohibition of worship. The first is more apparent.

﴿forty years﴾: it is related to ("muharramah," forbidden), so the prohibition is temporary, not perpetual. Thus it does not contradict the apparent meaning of His words: ("God has ordained for you"). The meaning of their prohibition is that none of them enters it during this period. But this does not mean that all of them will enter it afterward; rather some of those who remained will, according to what is reported: that Musa, peace be upon him, led those of the Children of Israel who remained to the Holy Land, with Yusha' ibn Nun at its vanguard, and he conquered it, and remained there as long as Allah willed, then Musa, peace be upon him, was taken. This is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It has been said that none of those who said ("We will never enter it") entered it, but there entered with Musa, peace be upon him, only the young ones from their descendants. Accordingly, the time limit of forty years is in reality a prohibition upon their descendants. It is made a prohibition upon them because of the complete connection between them.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they wander in the land﴾ are a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of their deprivation. It has been said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ("'alayhim," upon them). The "tih" is bewilderment. It is said: "taha yatihu" and "yatuhu," and "huwa atwah" and "atyah," so it is among the words in which waw and ya' have interchanged. The meaning is: they travel bewildered, and their bewilderment is their failure to find the way.

It has been said: the adverbial phrase is related to ("yatihun," they wander), and this is related from Qatadah. Then the wandering is temporary, and the prohibition is unrestricted, admitting of perpetuity or its absence. The extent of the land in which they wandered was thirty farsakhs by a width of nine farsakhs, as Muqatil said. It has been said: twelve farsakhs by a width of six farsakhs; it has been said: six by nine; it has been said: its length was thirty miles by a width of six farsakhs, and it is what lies between Egypt and Syria. It is mentioned that they were six hundred thousand fighting men, and they would travel, so that they woke up where they had gone to sleep, and went to sleep where they had woken up, as al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

It has been said: the wisdom in their being tested with wandering is that when they said ("Indeed, we will remain seated here"), they were punished with something resembling sitting, and it was forty years, because it is the furthest limit of time in which the ignorant one comes to his senses.

It has been said: because they worshipped the calf for forty days, so the punishment for each day was made one year of wandering. But this is nothing. That was among the extraordinary events beyond customary habit, for bewilderment over such a distance among many intelligent people for this long a period is something that custom deems impossible. Perhaps that was by the erasing of the signs by which one might be guided, or the likeness of some of them was cast upon others.

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: it was by the land they were on being transformed at the time they slept, and Allah, the Exalted, is above needing to accept this.

It is related that the cloud shaded them from the heat of the sun, and manna and quails descended upon them, and the stone of Musa, peace be upon him, was with them, from which water gushed forth to repel their thirst. It is said: at night a column of light rose over them, illuminating for them. Their hair did not grow long, and their garments did not wear out, as related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Their children would grow up along with them when they grew up, as related from Tawus.

Several storytellers (qussas) mentioned that when a child was born to them, he had a garment like a fingernail which grew with his growth and did not wear out, along with other things they mentioned.

Customary habit makes much of this remote, so nothing is accepted except what is authentically related from Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ). I once asked one of the rabbis of the Jews about the clothing of the Children of Israel during the wandering, and he said: they left Egypt with much of the garments of the Copts and their goods, and Allah, the Exalted, preserved them for their elders and their young. I mentioned to him the story of the fingernail, and he said: "We did not attain it," and denied it. I said to him: "It is a virtue, so why did you not establish it for your people?" He said: "I do not accept a garment of lies."

The treatment of them with these blessings has been raised as a difficulty, along with their being punished with bewilderment. It is answered that this punishment is from His generosity, the Exalted, and their chastisement was only for discipline, just as a man beats his son while loving him, and does not cut off his kindness from him. Perhaps they sought forgiveness for disbelief, if it had occurred from them.

Most exegetes hold that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, were with them in the wandering, but the hardship that reached them did not reach them as it reached the others, and that was for them a ease and safety, like the fire for Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Perhaps the two men were also like that.

It is related that Harun died during the wandering, and Musa, peace be upon them both, was accused of it. They said: "He killed him out of love for us." So Allah, the Exalted, brought him back to life through Musa's supplication, and cleared him of what they said, and he returned to his resting place. Musa, peace be upon him, died after him by one year. It has been said: by six and a half months; it has been said: by eight years. Yusha' entered Jericho (Arihaa) three months after him. Qatadah said: two months. Musa had previously been made a prophet to those of the Children of Israel who remained, and the responsible ones at the time of the command were not left among them. It has been said: the noble arrangement of the verses does not support this, for after he (peace be upon him) had received his supplication against the Children of Israel and punished them with the wandering, it is far-fetched that those who were saved would be saved, and that the deaths of the two prophets, peace be upon them both, would be considered to have occurred apparently in the place of punishment, even if that was for them a station of ease and rest. You know that the reports of their deaths, peace be upon them both, during the wandering are numerous, especially the reports of the death of Harun, peace be upon him. I see no room for denying this, and perhaps that was more grievous to the Children of Israel.

It has been said: the two of them, peace be upon them both, were not with the Children of Israel during the wandering, and that the supplication, which was answered, concerned separation in the sense of distance in place in this world. I consider this view to be almost unsound, for many of the verses are explicit in establishing Musa's presence with them in it, as is not hidden.

﴿So do not grieve﴾: that is, do not be sorrowful over their death, or over what befell them in it, from grief (asa), which is sorrow.

﴿over the wicked people﴾: those whose supplication against them was answered because of their wickedness. So the address is to Musa, peace be upon him, as is apparent, and this is the view of the distinguished exegetes.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and by "the wicked people" are meant his contemporaries from the Children of Israel. It is as if it were said: these are the deeds of their ancestors, so do not grieve, you, because of their wicked deeds with you and their rejection of you, for they inherited that from them.

[Page 111]

﴿And recite to them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with an implied clause, to which his saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when Moses said﴾ etc., is connected. Its connection to that has been said to be because it serves as a preface to what will come, if God Most High wills, of the transgressions of the Children of Israel after what was prescribed for them and after the messengers came to them with the clear proofs they brought. It has also been said that the connection is because the first (passage) concerns cowardice in the face of killing, while this one concerns daring to commit it, although each of them is a disobedience.

The pronoun in ﴿to them﴾ refers to the Children of Israel, as is apparent, since they are the ones spoken of first. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to recite this to them, to inform them of what is in the obscure texts of their earlier scriptures, of which the Messenger (peace be upon him) has no knowledge except through revelation, so that the proof may be established against them by it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to this community, meaning: recite, O Muhammad, to your people ﴿the account of the two sons of Adam﴾: Habil (may God have mercy on him) and Qabil (may He give him what he deserves). By the consensus of most exegetes, they were the two sons of Adam (peace be upon him) from his own loins.

Al-Hasan said: they were two men from the Children of Israel, and God's hand is with the community. Among their story is what Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Masʿud and a number of the Companions, may God be pleased with them all: "Adam (peace be upon him) would not have a child born without a girl being born with him. He would marry the boy of one womb to the girl of the other womb, and the girl of one womb to the boy of the other womb. The separation of the wombs was treated as the separation of lineage, out of necessity at that time. Then he had two sons, called Habil and Qabil. Qabil was a tiller of crops and Habil a herder of livestock. Qabil was the elder. Qabil had a sister named Iqlima, who was more beautiful than Habil's sister. Habil asked to marry Qabil's sister, but he refused and said: 'She is my sister, born with me, and she is more beautiful than your sister, and I have more right to marry her.' So their father ordered him to let Habil marry her, but he refused. Then he said to them both: 'Offer a sacrifice, and whichever of you is accepted shall marry her.' He ordered this only because he knew that Qabil's offering would not be accepted, not because, had it been accepted, it would have been permissible. Then Adam (peace be upon him) went away from them, going to Mecca to look at it. Adam said to the sky: 'Guard my son with trust,' but it refused; he said it to the earth, but it refused; he said it to the mountains, but they refused. Then he said to Qabil, and he said: 'Yes. Go and return, and you will find your family as pleasing to you as you wish.' When Adam (peace be upon him) had departed, the two offered a sacrifice. Habil offered a young she-camel, and it was said a ram, and Qabil offered a bundle of ears of grain. He found in it one large ear, rubbed it and ate it. Then fire descended and consumed Habil's offering, and that was the sign of acceptance. Eating the offering was not permitted in the earlier law. It left Qabil's offering, and he became angry and said: 'I will surely kill you.' Habil answered him with what God Most High related."

﴿in truth﴾ is connected to an implied element that occurs as a qualifier of the verbal noun of (recite). That is: recite a recitation accompanied by truth and correctness. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of (recite) or from its object, meaning: you, or their account, being accompanied by truth and sincerity, in agreement with what is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when they offered an offering﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of (account), and it operates in it, because it is originally a verbal noun, and the adverbial complement suffices for it the trace of the verb. It has been permitted that it be connected to an implied element occurring as a circumstantial clause from it. This was rejected on the grounds that then it would be a restriction on its governing word, which is (recite) in the future, while (when) refers to the past, so they do not meet. Therefore it is not connected to it despite its being apparent. This may be answered by distinguishing between the two aspects, so consider this carefully.

It has also been said that it is an apposition (badal) of (account), with an omitted noun, so that it may be correctly described as recited: that is, recite to them their account, the account of that time. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr rejected this, arguing that (when) is only prefixed by a time word, such as (on that day) and (at that time), and (account) is not a time. It was answered by denial, and there is no difference between the account of that time and the account of (when). Both are correct in meaning and grammatical analysis. The claim that the first is permissible by transmission but not the second, without establishing it, is a thorny reach.

The qurbān (offering) is a name for what one draws near to God Most High with, whether a slaughtered animal or other things, just as ḥulwān is the name for what is given as a gift. Its being singular is because it is originally a verbal noun. It has been said that its implied sense is: when each of them offered an offering. ﴿So it was accepted from one of them﴾, who was Habil, ﴿and it was not accepted from the other﴾, because he was angered by God's ruling, which was the impermissibility of marrying a twin. ﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive statement arising from the preceding speech, as if it were said: What did the one whose offering was not accepted say? So it was answered: He said to his brother, out of excessive envy at the acceptance of the other's offering and the elevation of his rank with his Lord, exalted and majestic is He, as the following speech indicates. It has also been said that it refers to what would happen of taking his beautiful sister.

﴿I will surely kill you﴾: that is, by God Most High, ﴿I will surely kill you,﴾ with a doubled nun, and it has been read with the single nun. ﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive statement like the previous one: the one whose offering was accepted said, when he saw his brother's envy: ﴿God only accepts from the righteous﴾, that is, the offering and obedience, ﴿from those who are mindful (of God)﴾ in that, by sincerity of intention toward God Most High, not from others. The meaning of piety here is not the piety of avoiding polytheism, which is the first of the levels, as has been said. His purpose in this answer is: you only came from yourself, because you stripped off the garment of piety, not from me, so why do you kill me? And why do you not rebuke yourself and make it act in fear of God Most High, which is the cause of acceptance? This is a wise, concise answer comprising several meanings.

It also contains an indication that the envious person should see his deprivation as a result of his own shortcoming, and strive to acquire what made the envied one fortunate, rather than trying to remove his good fortune and blessing, for his striving in the matter mentioned harms him and does not benefit him.

It has also been said that his purpose is a metaphor (kināya) that he does not refrain from God's judgment and its threat, because he is mindful of God, and the one mindful of God prefers obedience over life. Or it is a metaphor that he will not kill him in defence against his killing, because he is mindful of God, so that this serves as a preparation for what follows. Its remoteness is not hidden.

This verse has been cited to admonish those who do deeds. It is reported from Amir ibn ʿAbd Allah that he wept when death came to him. He was asked: "What makes you weep, when you were such and such?" He said: "I hear God Most High say: ﴿God only accepts from those who are mindful (of Him)﴾."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 28:

﴿Even if you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you.﴾ It is said that Habil (Abel) was stronger than him, but he refrained from killing him and submitted to him out of fear of Allah, the Exalted; for defence was not permissible at that time and in that law, as Mujahid narrated.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "The Children of Israel had been prescribed that when a man stretched out his hand against another man, he could not refrain from him until he killed him or left him."

Or it was out of seeking what is best and most rewarding, namely being the one killed rather than the killer, by defending oneself, on the basis that defence was permissible at that time.

Some researchers said: The matter has been disputed now, as expounded by the Imam al-Jassas. The correct view of the school is that a man is obliged to repel corruption from himself and others, even if it leads to killing. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: the meaning of the verse is: "Even if you stretch out your hand against me in the manner of injustice and aggression to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you in the manner of injustice and aggression." The verse, according to what Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said, is abrogated (mansukhah). Was it abrogated before our law or not? There is discussion on this. The evidence for it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ (49:9), and other verses and hadiths.

It has also been said: it is not obligatory, rather it is permissible. It was cited as evidence the narration recorded by Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat, from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, from him (ﷺ), that he mentioned a time of strife: "The one sitting in it is better than the one standing, the one standing in it is better than the one walking, and the one walking in it is better than the one running. If you encounter that, then be the servant of Allah who is killed, and do not be the servant of Allah who kills." They interpreted it as abstaining from fighting in strife and avoiding it, and the beginning of the hadith indicates this. As for those who prohibited it now, citing the hadith: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire," it has been refuted by saying that what is meant is that each of them intended to kill his brother, even if he did not fight him, and they met with this intention. End of quotation, with addition.

On the authority of al-Sayyid al-Murtada: the verse is not a point of dispute, because the lam that enters upon the verb "to kill" is the lam of purpose (kay), which indicates will and objective, and there is no doubt in the ugliness of that, first and last; for the one defending himself is only praised for repelling the wrongdoer seeking to escape, without intending to kill him. It is as if he said to him: "If you wrong me, I shall not wrong you."

Allah, glorified is He, said "ما أنا بباسط يدي" (I shall not stretch out my hand) as the answer to "لئن بسطت" (even if you stretch out) for emphasis that this is not part of his character, nor is he among those who are described by it. For this reason he emphasised the negation with the bi- (ba'), and did not say "ما أنا بقاتل" (I am not a killer), but said "بباسط" (one who stretches out), to disclaim even the preliminaries of killing, let alone killing itself. The prepositional phrase governed by "بسطت" was placed first, to signal, as it is said, that from the outset the harm and danger of the stretching out returns to him. It occurs to me that it was placed first to hasten his reminder of himself, which leads to a reminder of the brotherhood that prevents killing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a reason for refraining from stretching out his hand to kill him, and in it is guidance to Qabil towards fear of Allah in the most complete manner, and an implicit suggestion that the killer does not fear Allah, the Exalted.

﴿Indeed, I wish that you should bear my sin and your sin﴾: this is another reason for his refraining from stretching out his hand. Since each of the two is an independent cause, neither is joined to the other by a conjunction, to signal their independence and to rule out the suspicion that one is only part of the cause and not a complete cause. The root of *bawa'* is "to be bound to" (*al-luzum*). In the *al-Nihayah* (of Ibn al-Athir): "I return with Your blessing upon me and I return with my sin," meaning: I take on, return, and acknowledge. The meaning is: "By my submission and my refraining from confronting you, I wish that you would return with my sin, that is, that you would bear it, if I stretched out my hand against you, since you were the cause of it, and it was you who taught me to strike and to kill, and [that you would bear] your sin, since you stretched out your hand against me."

This is parallel to what Muslim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two who revile each other: what they say falls upon the one who initiates it, so long as the wronged one does not transgress." That is, upon the initiator falls the sin of his own abuse, and a sin like that of the abuse he directed at his companion, because he was the cause of it. However, the sin is removed from his companion and forgiven him, because he is a counterpart who defends his honour. Do you not see the phrase: "so long as the wronged one does not transgress"? For when he goes beyond the bounds of retaliation and transgresses, he is not safe. Thus [it is stated] in the *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari).

It is said: there is a problem with this. The essence of what he established is that upon the initiator falls his sin and a sin like that of his companion, unless the companion transgresses, in which case this whole amount does not fall upon the initiator. There is no indication in it that when the wronged one does not transgress, the particular sin arising from his cause is removed from him, except with an additional element joined to it, and there is nothing in the wording that suggests it. He (the author of *al-Kashf*) refuted this, saying: "How is it not indicative of his being relieved of it? His peace and blessings be upon him saying 'upon the initiator' is a clear specifier."

And the statement of the *al-Kashshaf*, "but the sin is removed," is an explanation of his saying "upon the initiator," and his saying "upon him is the sin of his abuse and a sin like that of the abuse of his companion" is an explanation of his saying "what they say." So just as it indicates that upon him is a doubled sin, it indicates that the sin of his companion is removed.

This is it. Then he said: "Perhaps the more apparent reading of the hadith is that the 'like' is not to be supposed, and the meaning is: the sin of their reviling falls upon the initiator. This was so that one would not be obliged to combine literal and metaphorical meanings." And the claim that, since what he said has no sin for anyone other than the initiator, how can it be said "the sin of their reviling," and how can sin be attributed to him when the obligation is shared? The realization of this is that what he said has a sin for someone other than the initiator, but it does not fall upon the initiator. This is not contrary to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, because by his inciting him to it, he is counted as a party to it. This is like what is reported regarding one who establishes a good custom or a bad custom. Yes, in what we are discussing, the doer has no sin; rather, it belongs to the instigator. The conclusion is that the abuse by one other than the initiator entails two things:

The first, in relation to its doer, is removed if it is by way of defence and not transgression.

The second, in relation to its instigator, is not removed; that is, it is established initially, not that it is not pardoned.

And it was raised in *al-Tahqiq* (of Ibn al-Humam) that what he mentioned about the removal of sin from the wronged one because he is a counterpart is not correct, because when a person is reviled, he does not take his recompense except through the judge. The answer: the explicit wording of the hadith indicates what is mentioned in the *al-Kashshaf*, and the reconciliation between it and the legal ruling is that abuse is either by a wording that entails the legal hadd punishment, in which case its path is referral to the judge; or by other than that, and then it is either a word of alienation, of boasting, or of pride in lineage and the like that includes disparagement of his companion's lineage without vulgar insult, such as accusing him of unbelief or wickedness, in which case he may retaliate in kind. The hadith of Zaynab and 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with them both) indicates this, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'A'ishah: "Go ahead, and defend yourself." Or it includes vulgar insult, in which case it too is referred to the judge so that he may discipline him.

The hadith is to be understood as referring to the category in which retaliation applies. His saying (ﷺ): "so long as the wronged one does not transgress" indicates this, because when his right is referral to the judge and he busies himself with retaliation, he is counted as a transgressor. End of quotation. This is a fine distinction.

It is said: the meaning of "with my sin" is with the sin of my killing, and the meaning of "with your sin" is your sin that was before my killing. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak (may Allah be pleased with them both). These [authorities] left the sin that preceded it unspecified.

And from al-Jubba'i and al-Zajjaj: it is the sin on account of which the offering was not accepted, which is not being content with the judgment of Allah, the Exalted, as has passed. It is also said: its meaning is: with the sin of my killing and your sin, which is the killing of all people, since you established killing as a custom.

The attribution of sin in all these statements to the pronoun of the speaker is because it arose from him, or it is by way of an implied noun. There is no need to posit an implied noun in the genitive, as was said at first. However, it is clear that there is no good parallelism between the first person and the second person on this reading, because both sins are the sin of the addressee. But the matter is easy.

The prepositional phrase with what it is conjoined to is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of *tabu'a*, meaning: you return laden with the two sins, carrying both of them. Perhaps his intention, essentially, is only that he himself is not burdened with sin, not that his brother is burdened, since wishing sin upon another is not permissible. It is also said: the intended sin is what he is bound to and what results from it of punishment. It is not clear, on this reading, how the Exalted's statement ﴿so you will be among the companions of the Fire﴾ follows as a consequence, for being among the companions of the Fire results from returning with the two sins, not from being afflicted with the punishment of them, and this is evident.

Interpreting the punishment as another kind that results in the Fire is refuted, as Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) said, by the Glorified's statement ﴿and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, for it is explicit that being among the companions of the Fire is the complete and perfect punishment. The sentence is a concluding clause confirming what precedes it, and it is from the speech of Habil, according to what is apparent. It is also said: rather it is a report from the Exalted to the Messenger (ﷺ).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 30:**

﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him﴾: it made it easy for him and facilitated it for him. It is from *ta'a lahu al-marta'* (the pasture became wide for him) when it became spacious. The ordering of *taw'een* (making easy) after what preceded it, namely the statements of Habil, is with the certainty of his [Qabil's] resolve beforehand, as his saying "I will surely kill you" reveals. This is because the continuation of the act after the removal of what would have prevented it, although apparently a continuation of the same state, is in reality a new occurrence and a fresh act. Alternatively, this degree of making it easy had not existed before that, on account of his hesitation about his ability to kill, since his brother was stronger than him. It came about after he perceived his brother's submission and his non-resistance to him. The explicit mention of their brotherhood serves to fully condemn what his soul had embellished for him.

Al-Hasan recited *fa-tawa'at* (فَطَاوَعَتْ), and in this there are two possibilities:

The first is that *fa'ala* (فَاعَلَ) here means *fa'ala* (فَعَلَ), as Sibawayh and others mentioned. This is more consistent with the *mutawatir* (widely transmitted) recitation.

The second is that the *mufa'alah* (the form of reciprocal action) is figurative, by making the killing call the soul to undertake it, while the soul was resisting it. Thus each of the killing and the soul seems to want its companion to obey it, until the killing overcame the soul. So *fatawa'at-hu* (فَطَاوَعَتْهُ) and *lahu* (لَهُ) are for emphasis and clarification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾.

The claim that it is there to exclude the possibility that the soul made it easy for someone else to kill him is not worth considering.

﴿So he killed him﴾. Ibn Jarir reported, from Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj: "Qabil did not know how to kill Habil, so the accursed Iblis appeared to him in the form of a bird. He took a bird and placed its head between two stones and crushed it, and thus taught him killing. He then killed him in this manner while he was submissive."

He also reported, from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them: "Qabil sought his brother in order to kill him, and he was evading him in the tops of the mountains. One day he came upon him while he was tending his sheep and was asleep, so he lifted a rock and crushed his head with it, and he died. He left him in the open, not knowing how to bury him, until Allah sent the crow. Habil had been twenty years old when he was killed."

The location of his killing is disputed. According to Amr al-Sha'bani, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, he was killed on the mountain of Dayr al-Mirran. In another report from him, he was killed on the mountain of Qasiyun. It is also said: near the pass of Hira'. It is also said: in Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad reported, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Fadala, that when Qabil killed Habil, Allah deprived him of his reason and removed his heart, so he kept wandering until he died.

It is narrated that when he killed him, his body turned black, and it had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said: "I was not a guardian over him." He [Adam] said: "Rather, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black."

Ibn Asakir and Ibn Jarir reported, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: "When one of Adam's sons killed the other, Adam, peace be upon him, remained for a hundred years without laughing, out of grief for him. Then, at the completion of the hundredth year, he was told: 'May Allah greet you and make you well,' and he was given the glad tidings of a boy. At that point he laughed."

Muhyi al-Sunnah mentioned that after the killing of his son, Adam, peace be upon him, had another son fifty years later, Shith, peace be upon him, and his name means "gift of Allah," meaning that he was a replacement for Habil. Allah taught him the hours of the night and day and the worship of creation at each hour of them, and He sent down to him fifty scrolls. He became the successor of Adam and his appointed heir.

Ibn Jarir reported, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "When the son of Adam, peace be upon him, killed his brother, Adam, peace be upon him, wept and lamented him in verse."

Al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir reported something similar from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is well known.

It is narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran, from the Habr (the learned one), may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever says that Adam, peace be upon him, composed poetry has lied. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and all the Prophets, peace be upon them, are alike in the prohibition of poetry." But when Qabil killed Habil, Adam lamented him in Syriac. It continued to be transmitted until it reached Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, who spoke Arabic and Syriac. He examined it, rearranged parts of it, and made it into Arabic poetry. Some scholars of Arabic mentioned that in that poem there are grammatical errors (*lahn*), or *iqwa'* (a defect in rhyme), or the commission of a poetic necessity (*darurah*). The more appropriate view is not to attribute it to Ya'rub either, because of the evident weakness of its composition.

﴿So he became among the losers﴾, in this world and in the Hereafter.

Al-Shaykhan and others reported, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share (*kifl*) of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing."

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Indeed we find that the son of Adam who killed will share with the people of the Fire a portion of punishment that is exact, and upon him is half of their punishment."

It has been reported that he was one of the wretched. This and similar reports are explicit that the man died a disbeliever.

Even more explicit than that is what is narrated: when he killed his brother, he fled to Aden in the land of Yemen. Iblis, may the curse of both of them be upon him, came to him and said: "The fire only consumed the offering of Habil because he used to serve it and worship it. If you also worship it, you will achieve your aim." So he built a house of fire and worshipped it. He was thus the first to worship fire. Apparently, upon him is also the burden of everyone who worships fire, and indeed it is not far-fetched that upon him is the burden of everyone who worships other than Allah, exalted is He, until the Day of Resurrection.

Some scholars cited His saying, glorified is He: (﴿فَأَصْبَحَ﴾ *fa-asbaha*) as evidence that the killing occurred at night. This is not valid, for it is the custom of the Arabs to say: *asbaha fulan khasira al-saftah* (so-and-so became one who lost the deal) when he does something whose outcome is loss, and by this they mean attainment, without regard to one time over another. And the reason He, glorified is He, did not say *fa-asbaha khasiran* (فَأَصْبَحَ خَاسِرًا) is for emphasis, even though at that time there was no one else who was a loser.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 31:

﴿Then God sent a raven, scratching in the earth, to show him how to conceal the corpse of his brother.﴾ ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿAṭiyya, who said: "When he killed him, he regretted it. He carried him on his back until he began to rot, while the birds and beasts gathered around him, waiting for when he would throw him down so they could eat him. He disliked bringing him to Adam (peace be upon him) and grieving him, and he was perplexed about the matter, since he was the first dead person among the children of Adam (peace be upon him). So God Most High sent two ravens; one of them killed the other while he watched. Then it dug a hole for it with its beak and its foot until it had made a grave for it, then it pushed it with its head until it threw it into the hole, then it scratched the earth over it with its foot until it had covered it." It was also said: one of the two ravens was dead.

The raven is a well-known bird. It was said: the wisdom in God sending this particular creature, and not any other animal, is that it is regarded as a bad omen in separation and estrangement, and this is appropriate to this story.

Some of them said: it was an angel who appeared in the form of a raven. The pronoun in ﴿يُرِيَهُ﴾ refers either to God Most High or to the raven. If it refers to God, the lām is necessarily connected to ﴿بَعَثَ﴾; if it refers to the raven, it is connected to ﴿يَبْحَثُ﴾, though it may also be connected to ﴿بَعَثَ﴾. The word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿يُوارِي﴾, and it was placed before it because it has the front position (ṣadr). The clause ﴿كَيْفَ يُوارِي﴾ is in the place of the second object of ﴿يُرِيَ﴾, the visual verb that takes two objects by means of the hamza, and it is suspended (muʿallaqah) from the second. It was also said that ﴿يُرِيَهُ﴾ means "teach him", for if it were taken to mean "see", the clause ﴿كَيْفَ يُوارِي﴾ would have no good position, and the clause would then be in the place of two objects. But there is consideration in this.

Al-baḥth (searching) originally means searching for a thing in general, or searching in the dust; what is meant here is digging. What is meant by al-sawʾah (the shameful thing) is the body of the dead person. al-Jubbāʾī restricted it to the decomposing body. It was said: it means the private parts (al-ʿawrah), because they cause shame to the one who looks at them. It was specified by mention, though the intended meaning is concealing the whole body, for the sake of emphasis upon it, because its covering is more binding. The first is preferable. The reason for the naming is shared, and the pronoun in ﴿أخِيهِ﴾ refers to the one being searched for, not to the searcher, as some have wrongly supposed.

The sending of the raven was by way of inspiration if what is meant by it is the apparent meaning; it was an actual sending if what is meant is an angel who appeared in its form. On both assumptions, most scholars held that the searcher covered the corpse, and Qabil learned, so he did the same with his brother. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, and Ibn Masʿud, and others.

al-Aṣamm held that God Most High sent whoever He sent, so he searched in the earth and covered Habil. When Qabil saw what God Most High had honoured his brother with, ﴿he said: "Woe is me!"﴾ — an expression of distress and grief. The waylah, like the wayl, means destruction. It is as if the one lamenting calls out to his destruction and death, and asks for its presence after making it like one who is called. Wishing for death is only done by one who is in a state worse than it. The alif is a substitute for the first-person yāʾ, meaning "O my woe", and al-Ḥasan read it thus — "Come, for this is your time."

﴿"Am I unable to be like this raven, and to conceal the corpse of my brother?"﴾ This is an expression of wonder at his inability to be like it, since it was not guided to what the raven was guided to, despite being nobler than it. ﴿So that I conceal the corpse of my brother﴾ is coordinated with ﴿أكُونَ﴾ ("to be"). al-Zamakhsharī made it a subjunctive after the interrogative, and many grammarians objected to this. Abū Ḥayyān said: it is a gross error, because the condition for this accusative is that it be formed from an interrogative clause, while the answer here is a conditional clause, like: "Will you visit me so that I honour you?" — its implied sense being: "If you visit me, I will honour you." If it were said here: "Am I unable to be like this raven, [so that] I conceal the corpse of my brother?", the meaning would not be correct, because concealing is consequent upon not being unable, not upon being unable. Al-Kashshāf answered that the interrogative is for reproachful denial, and it is of the type of: "Do you disobey your Lord so that He pardons you?" in the accusative, so that the denial applies to both matters. This indicates that he is engaged in disobedience, and that expecting pardon is a violation of what is reasonable. When it is put in the nominative, it is an apparent statement of the denial applying; when it is put in the accusative, there is exaggeration by reversal, since the cause of punishment is made the cause of pardon. In what concerns us here, he blames himself for his inability, and places it in the position of one who makes inability the cause of concealment, to show the emphatic reversal of inability and shortcoming in comparison to what a raven is guided to.

Then he said: If you say: reproachful denial applies only to what has occurred or is expected, so reproach for disobedience and inability has a basis, but as for pardon and concealment, it does not. I say: the reproach is for making each one a cause, or for placing it in the position of one who made it a cause, not for the pardon and concealment. So understand. End.

Perhaps the command to understand is an indication of the remoteness in it. It was also said in explaining this: the interrogative is for denial, and it has the sense of negation, and it is a cause; the meaning is: "If I were not unable, I would have concealed." This was objected to as not valid, because for the accusative it is not sufficient that the negation be a cause; rather, the cause must be the negated matter before the negation entered. Do you not see that: "What you do not come to us and speak to us" is explained by them to mean "there is no coming from you and then speaking"? Al-Shihab said: the answer to this is that there is a difference between what is put in the accusative after a negation and what is put in the accusative after an interrogative, and the discussion concerns the second, so how could the first be raised as a counterexample? And if it were taken as after a negation, what was mentioned would not arise either, because there is no need to derive negation from the reproachful interrogative, given the clarity of interpreting "I was unable" as "I was not guided." Al-Tashīl states: it is in the accusative after an explicit and an implied negation, and what we are dealing with is of the second kind, so its ruling applies. So consider. End.

Perhaps the command to consider is an indication that what is in the claim of a difference between the reproachful interrogative which means negation, and negation itself, is of obscurity; and likewise in interpreting "I was unable" here as "I was not guided". So let it be understood.

It is read ﴿أعْجِزْتُ﴾ with a kasra on the jīm, which is an anomalous dialect for ʿajaza. It is also read ﴿فَأُوارِيَ﴾ with a sukūn, on the basis that it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), in which case they assume a subject to clarify the break from the coordination; or it is coordinated, but it was made quiescent for lightness, as many have said. Abū Ḥayyān objected to this in al-Baḥr, saying that the fatḥah is not burdensome enough to be dropped for lightness, and the quiescence of the accusative is not a dialect according to the grammarians, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed, and it is not permissible except in poetic necessity, so the recitation should not be interpreted that way when a meaning of new sentence is available for it. End.

On the claim of necessity, there is an obvious objection, for quiescence of the accusative is frequent in their speech. al-Mubarrad claimed that this is among the good poetic licences which may be allowed in prose similarly.

﴿So he became among the regretful.﴾ That is, he was counted among them. His regret was over killing him, because of what he endured in his perplexity over the matter, and carrying him on his neck for forty days, or a year, or more, as it was said, and the raven's instruction of him; for this is humiliation. For this reason he was not inspired at first with what he was inspired with later; and his face blackened, and his parents disowned him — not because of the sin itself, for that is repentance.

**Because of that** (i.e., because of what was mentioned in the course of the story), **min** (ﷺ no) — correction: **min** here is *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating the starting point), and it is connected to the words **kataba** ("We prescribed"), meaning *qada* ("decreed"). It has also been said that it is connected to **al-nadimin** ("the regretful"), which is the apparent meaning of what is narrated from Nafi', and **kataba** would then be a new sentence (*istinaf*). Abu al-Baqa' and others found this unlikely.

**Al-ajl** is pronounced with a fatha on the hamza, and it may also be pronounced with a kasra. It has been read with the kasra, but with the kasra moved onto the nun. Similarly, it has been read with the fatha moved onto the nun, originally. Its meaning is *al-jinayah* (crime, offence). One says *ajala 'alayhim sharran* when he commits an offence against them. Its equivalent meaning is *jarra 'alayhim jarirah* (he brought a wrong upon them). Then it was used to mean the cause of offences, and then it was extended to be used for any cause. So the meaning is: from that began the prescribing, and from it it arose, and not from anything else.

**"Upon the Children of Israel"**: They are singled out for mention because envy was the source of that corruption, and it was prevalent among them.

It has also been said that they were mentioned rather than "people" in general, because the Torah was the first book in which the grave nature of killing was affirmed. Despite this, they were the most rebellious and persistent in it, to the extent that they killed the prophets, upon them be peace. It is as if it were said: because of this great matter, We prescribed in the Torah the gravity of killing, and We made it strict for them, yet after that they still did not care.

From here you know that this verse does not support, as al-Hasan, al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim said, the view that the two sons of Adam, upon him be peace, were from the Children of Israel. The sending of the crow, which clearly teaches something that was unnecessary at their time since they were not ignorant of burial, rules this out.

**"That whoever"** (*annahu*), i.e., the matter is: **"whoever kills a soul"**, one single soul among human souls, **"not for a soul"**, i.e., not for a killing of a soul that requires retaliation (*al-iqtisas*). The **ba'** here is *lil-muqabalah* (of exchange) and is connected to **qatala** ("kills"). It has also been permitted that it be connected to a omitted word that stands as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: transgressing, unjustly. **"Or corruption in the land"**, i.e., corruption in it that requires the forfeiture of blood, such as polytheism for example. It is conjoined to what is annexed to **ghayr** ("not").
[Page 118]
The negation here is used in a disjunctive sense, because the permissibility of killing is conditional upon one of the mentioned causes: killing or corruption. It necessarily follows that its prohibition is conditional upon the absence of both together. It is as if it were said: whoever kills a soul without either of them, **"it is as if he had killed all of mankind"**, because the two acts share the violation of the sanctity of blood, defiance against God Most High, tyranny in killing so as to entail retaliation, and drawing down the great wrath of God Most High.

Ibn Jarir narrated, from Ibn Mas'ud, that this comparison applies to the one killed, just as the comparison that follows applies to the one rescued. The first is more appropriate and more fitting for the purpose for which the comparison was made. It has been read as **"or corruption"** in the accusative (*fasadan*), with the implied meaning: "or he did corruption," or "he corrupted with corruption."

**"And whoever gives it life"**, i.e., causes the survival of one single soul described by the absence of the mentioned killing and corruption, either by forbidding its killer from killing it, or by rescuing it from any of the causes of destruction in any way. **"It is as if he had given life to all of mankind."** It has also been said that the meaning is: whoever helps in carrying out retaliation, it is as if, etc. In both places, **ma** is *kaffah muhayyi'ah* (a particle that prepares the verb to follow it). **Jami'an** ("all") is either a circumstantial state of "mankind" or an emphasis. The purpose of the comparison is to instil fear and deter from killing one soul, by depicting it in the form of killing all of mankind, and to encourage and urge the saving of it, by depicting it in the form of giving life to all of mankind.

**"And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs"**, i.e., the manifest verses that clearly state what We prescribed for them, as an affirmation of the obligation to observe it and as a confirmation of the necessity of safeguarding it.

This sentence is independent and not conjoined to **kataba** ("We prescribed"). It is emphasised with an oath for the complete concern with its content. He did not say "and certainly We sent to them," etc., in order to make explicit that the message reached them, since that is more indicative of their extreme obstinacy and stubborn arrogance.

**"Then indeed many of them, after that"**, i.e., after the mentioned prescription and the emphasis on the command with the sending of messengers. The use of the demonstrative (*dhalika*) in place of a pronoun serves to indicate that it has become fully distinguished and placed, because of that, among well-known matters, and what it contains of the sense of distance indicates the elevation of its rank and the remoteness of its station in great importance. **Thumma** ("then") indicates a delay in rank and a sense of astonishment.

**"In the land"** is connected to the words **"surely transgressors"** (*lamusrifun*). Likewise, what follows it is connected, as has been said, and the displaced lam (*al-lam al-muzahlaqah*, the lam shifted from the predicate to the emphatic position) does not prevent this.

*Al-israf* in any matter is excessive departure from the limit of moderation, combined with indifference to it. The intended meaning: they are transgressors in killing, indifferent to it. Since their excess in the matter of killing entails their negligence in the matter of giving life, whether existing or absent, and since killing was the more ugly and more horrible of the two matters, it sufficed to mention it in the context of censure for which the verses were brought.

It is narrated from al-Kalbi that the meaning is: those who exceed the bounds of truth through polytheism. It has also been said that the meaning is something more general than excess through killing, polytheism, and other things. God Most High said **"then indeed many of them"** because He, exalted be His affair, as in al-Khazin, knew that among them were those who would believe in God Most High and His Messenger, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, and they were few among the many. The mention of **"the land"**, although excess occurs only in it, serves to indicate that the excess of that great number is not a matter specific to them, but that its evil spread throughout the land and reached others besides them.

When He, glorified be He, had explained the great gravity of killing without right, He began to explain the ruling on one type of killing, and what is related to it of corruption through taking property and its like, and the determination of its consequence. He included in it an explanation of what had been alluded to in general terms of the corruption that makes killing permissible. So He, majestic be His affair, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 33:

﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ Most of the exegetes—as al-Tabarsi said, and as the majority of the jurists also hold—have taken the view that it was revealed concerning highway robbers (qutta' al-tariq). The statement, as al-Jassas said, contains an elision (hadhf) of a modifier (mudaf), meaning: those who wage war against the friends (awliya') of Allah the Most High and His Messenger—upon him be blessings and peace. It is thus like His saying, the Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾.

Page 119
This is indicated by the fact that if they waged war against the Messenger of Allah—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace—they would become apostates by openly declaring war against him and opposing him, upon him be blessings and peace. It has also been said: the intended meaning is "those who wage war against the Messenger of Allah—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace." The mention of Allah the Most High serves as a preface (tamhid) and an alert to the exalted station of his position—upon him be blessings and peace—with Him, Mighty and Majestic. Warring against the people of his sharia and those who follow his path among the Muslims is a warring against him—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace. Thus the ruling encompasses whoever wages war against them after the Messenger—upon him be blessings and peace—even after many ages, by way of the expression (ibarah), not by way of implication (dalalah) or analogy (qiyas) as is supposed; for the revelation of the text was not by way of direct address (khitab al-mushafahah) so that it would be restricted to those obligated at the time of revelation and would need another proof for its generalization, as has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul).

It has also been said: there is no elided modifier; rather, the intended meaning is warring against the Muslims, except that their warring was made a warring against Allah—Mighty and Majestic—and His Messenger—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace—in honour of them and elevation of their status. And the mention of the Messenger in this view serves as a preface upon a preface (tamhidan 'ala tamhid), and there is in it what is not hidden.

Ḥarb ("war") originally means plundering and seizing; it is said: "harabahu" when he plundered him. Here it means cutting the road (qat' al-tariq). It has also been said: it is an open assault with banditry, even if it occurs within a city (misr).

﴿And they strive﴾ is a conjunction upon (yuharibun), and to it is attached His saying, the Most High: (fi al-ardi, "in the land"). It has been said that it is attached to His saying, Glorified is He: (fasadan, "corruption"). The word fasadan is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject of (yas'awna), by interpreting it as "those who cause corruption" or "those possessed of corruption," or it is without interpretation for the purpose of emphasis (mubalagha), as has been said; or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lah), meaning: for the sake of corruption; or it is an absolute object (masdar mu'akkid) for (yas'awna), since it carries the meaning of (yufsidun). And fasadan is either a verbal noun (masdar) from which the augmentations have been dropped, or an ism al-masdar. His saying, the Most High: (innama jaza'u, "indeed the penalty of") is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the clause formed by His saying, the Most High: ﴿an yuqattalu﴾, "that they be killed," meaning as a prescribed punishment (hadd) without crucifixion if they commit murder alone. There is no difference whether it is by a cutting instrument or not. The use of the form of the intensive (tafil) is because of the added severity beyond retaliation (qisas), in that, being a right of the Sharia, it is not dropped by the pardon of the guardian. Likewise the crucifixion in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿or be crucified﴾, because of the killing within it, meaning: they are to be crucified along with being killed if they combined killing and taking property.
