It has been said that the intensive form in both verbs is for multiplicity, and that crucifixion is before killing, by their being crucified alive, and their bellies being pierced with a spear until they die. The more correct of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i—may Allah have mercy on him—is that crucifixion is for three days after killing; it has been said it is a single day.

It has been said: until its pus flows. The better view is that it be done on the road in the thoroughfare of people, so that this serves as a deterrent to others from undertaking such disobedience.

According to the apparent narration (zahir al-riwaya), the imam has discretion: if he wishes, he may suffice with that, and if he wishes, he may cut off their hands and feet from opposite sides, and kill them and crucify them.

﴿or their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides﴾ meaning: they are cut off in differing manner, such that their right hands and left feet are cut off, if they confine themselves to taking property from a Muslim or a dhimmi, since he has what we have and is subject to what is upon us, and the amount was such that if it were divided among them, each would receive ten dirhams or what is equal to it in value. This is for the first offence; if they repeat, the remaining limbs are cut off. The cutting of hands is for taking property, and the cutting of feet is for terrorising the road and destroying its security.

﴿or be banished from the land﴾ if they did nothing beyond terrorising and striving for corruption. By banishment (nafy) according to us is meant imprisonment and confinement, and the Arabs use nafy in this sense, because the person is separated from his home and family by it. One of the imprisoned has said:

We went out from the world while we were its people, so we are not among the dead in it, nor among the living.
When the jailer came to us one day on some need, we were amazed and said: "This one has come from the world!"

They are also disciplined (yu'azzarun) for their direct involvement in terrorising the road and removing its security. According to al-Shafi'i—may Allah have mercy on him—banishment means exile from one city to another, and he is constantly sought while fleeing in fear until he repents and returns. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi—may Allah the Most High be pleased with them—Ibn Jubayr and others, and the Imamiyya also hold this view.

From 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and in another narration from Ibn Jubayr, that he is banished only from his own land. It has been said: to a more distant land. They used to banish them to Dahlak, which is a town at the farthest edge of Tihama, and Nasi', which is a town in the lands of Abyssinia.

The first view is supported by the argument that the purpose of banishing the highway robber is to restrain him and repel his evil; if he is banished to another land, that cannot be assured, and expelling him from the world is impossible, and from the abode of Islam is not permissible. If he is imprisoned in another land there is no benefit in it, since by imprisoning him in his own land the aim is achieved, and it is more severe for him.

Furthermore, since warring and corruption are of differing degrees and diverse forms, a specific punishment has been prescribed for each of those degrees by way of distribution, as we have indicated. So "or" (aw) is for distribution (taqsim) and for the law of wrapping and unfolding (laff wa-nashr), as is assumed according to the sound view. It has been said that it is for choice (takhyir), and that the imam has discretion among these punishments for every highway robber. The first is known from revelation; otherwise there is nothing in the wording that indicates it, beyond choice. Also, because the verse contains varying penalties in severity and leniency, they must correspond to varying crimes, so that the recompense of each evil is a like evil; and because there is no great meaning in giving choice between the most severe and the mildest for a single offence.

The apparent view is that this arrangement and detailing was revealed to him—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace. This is supported by what al-Kharaʼiti related in Makarim al-Akhlaq from Ibn 'Abbas—may Allah the Most High be pleased with them both. Some have claimed that choice is closer to the truth, and that the variation between the most severe and the mildest is with regard to the persons and the times, since punishments are for deterrence and reforming creation, and people may differ in being deterred, so that matter was left to the opinion of the imam. In this there is reflection; so reflect.

﴿That﴾ meaning: what has been detailed of the rulings and penalties. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, the Most High: ﴿for them is disgrace﴾ is a clause made of a fronted predicate and a subject, in the position of a predicate for the subject. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿in this world﴾ is attached to an implied element that serves as an attribute of (khizy, "disgrace"), or is attached to it adverbially, as just mentioned. It has been said: (khizy) is the predicate of (dhalika), and (lahum, "for them") is attached to an implied element serving as a circumstantial (hal) of (khizy), because originally it was an attribute of it, and when it was fronted it took the accusative as a circumstance; and (fi al-dunya) is either an attribute of (khizy) or attached to it, as passed a moment ago. Khizy means humiliation and disgrace.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ which its measure cannot be gauged, and that is due to the extreme greatness of their crimes. Disgrace is mentioned alone for this world, though they also have punishment in it, and punishment alone for the Hereafter, though they also have disgrace in it; because disgrace in this world is greater than its punishment, and punishment in the Hereafter is more severe than its disgrace. This verse is the strongest proof for those who say that the prescribed penalties (hudud) do not remove the punishment in the Hereafter. Those who hold that they remove it cite the words of the Prophet—may Allah the Most High bless him and grant him peace—in the sound hadith: "Whoever commits something and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him," for it implies the removal of sin from him and that he will not be punished in the Hereafter. This is problematic alongside this verse. Al-Nawawi answered that the prescribed penalty expiates the right of Allah the Most High, but not the rights of people; and here there are two rights, that of Allah the Most High and that of people. And there is consideration in this.

Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. This exception applies specifically to what is among the rights of God Most High, as His saying indicates: "Know that God is Forgiving and Merciful."

As for what is among the rights of people, such as the rights of the heirs (awliya') to retaliation (qisas) and the like, its obligation upon the ruler (imam) falls away through repentance insofar as it is qisas. Its permissibility, however, does not fall away with regard to the heirs insofar as it is qisas, for if they wish they may pardon, and if they prefer they may exact it.

Al-Baydawi said: Killing by way of qisas loses its obligation through repentance, not its permissibility. He was criticized for this because of the narrowness of the expression of the scholar Ibn Hajar in his book al-Tuhfa, and he devoted a note (tanbih) to it. Ibn Hajar, after quoting him, said: "This is strange. More strange is the silence of our shaykh about it in his gloss, despite its evident corruption, because repentance has no bearing on qisas at all. For it is inconceivable, with the qualification that it is qisas, that there be two states of obligation and permissibility. If we look at the heir, then his demand is permissible for him, not obligatory absolutely. Or if we look at the imam, then if the heir demands it from him, it becomes obligatory; otherwise it is not obligatory insofar as it is qisas. And if it is permissible or obligatory insofar as it is hadd (fixed penalty), then consider it." End of quote.

Ibn al-Qasim responded to him, saying: "His claim of corruption is evidently corrupt, for he did not claim what was mentioned. He only claimed that repentance has a bearing on the nature of killing as qisas, namely its obligation. As for his saying, 'For it is inconceivable, etc.,' we say: he did not claim that it has two states of obligation and permissibility with this qualification. Rather he claimed that it has two states in itself, which is correct. It is possible, however, that it has two states with that qualification, but from two perspectives: the perspective of the heir and the perspective of the imam when it is demanded from him. As for his saying, 'For if we look, etc.,' it is a fallen statement, and there is no doubt that looking at both of them requires the establishment of the two states as qisas. As for his saying, 'Then consider it,' we considered it and found that his words arose from little consideration." End of quote.

Our master, the shaykh of all in all, Sibghatullah al-Haydari, held that the source of the scholar's criticism is what appears from the expression, namely that it is an explanation of the delegation of qisas to the heirs. But if it were made an explanation of the falling of the hadd in the killing of a highway robber through repentance before power, rather than killing as qisas, then the criticism does not arise. So reflect. Restricting repentance to before power implies that after power it does not drop the hadd, though it does drop the punishment (in the Hereafter).

Some people held that the verse refers only to apostates, because warring against God and His Messenger is used only of unbelievers.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Anas: "A group from 'Ukl came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), became Muslim, and found Medina unhealthy for them. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them to go to the camels of charity and drink from their urine and milk. They killed its herdsman and drove off the camels. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a party (qafa) in pursuit of them, and they were brought back. He cut off their hands and feet, branded (samala) their eyes, did not cauterize them, and left them until they died." Then God revealed: "The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger..." up to the end of the verse.

You know that the view of specification is baseless and contrary to the ijma' (scholarly consensus) of those whose opinion counts among the early and later scholars. What indicates that the intended are highway robbers from among the people of the religion is His saying: "except those who repent," etc. It is known that apostates do not differ in their ruling regarding the removal of the punishment through repentance after power, just as it is dropped from them before power. Yet God distinguished between their repentance before power and after it. Also, Islam does not drop the hadd from one who is liable to it. Also, the punishment of apostates is not like this.

The claim that muharaba (warring) is used only of unbelievers is refuted by the fact that the hadiths use it of sinners as well. And the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) cannot serve as a specifier, for the consideration, as established, is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Abi Hatim, and others narrated from al-Sha'bi who said: "Haritha ibn Badr al-Tamimi, of the people of Basra, had spread corruption on earth and waged war. He spoke to men of Quraysh asking them to seek safe-conduct for him from 'Ali, but they refused. So he went to Sa'id ibn Qays al-Hamdani, who came to 'Ali and said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, what is the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption on earth?' He said: 'That they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land.' Then he said: 'except those who repent before you gain power over them.' Sa'id said: 'Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr?' He said: 'Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr.' He said: 'This is Haritha ibn Badr, who has come repentant. Is he safe?' He said: 'Yes.' So he brought him to him, he pledged allegiance to him and accepted it from him, and he wrote him a guarantee of safety." Something of the same meaning was narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

Then, the branding of eyes which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) carried out was not done to anyone other than those men. Muslim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those because they had branded the eyes of the herdsmen."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Walid ibn Muslim who said: I discussed with al-Layth ibn Sa'd the branding of their eyes by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his leaving them without cauterizing until they died. He said: I heard Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan say: "This verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as a rebuke concerning that, and he was taught the punishment of their like: killing, crucifixion, amputation, and exile. He did not brand the eyes of anyone after them." He said: I mentioned this statement to Abu 'Umar, who denied that it was revealed as a rebuke and said: "Rather, that was the punishment of those particular men. Then this verse was revealed as the punishment of others who waged war after them, and so branding was lifted from them."

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusions (ishara) in the verses:

"And from those who said, 'We are Christians,' We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of, so We stirred up among them enmity and hatred" — i.e., We made that binding upon them, because of the divergence of the impulses of their faculties, through their veiling from the light of unity and their distance from the holy world. "Until the Day of Resurrection" — i.e., until the time of their rising through the manifestation of the light of the Spirit, or the Greater Resurrection through the manifestation of the light of unity. "And God will inform them of what they used to do" — that is at death, and the manifestation of loss through the manifestation of the ugly, harmful states firmly rooted in them.

"O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal" — according to the impulses and requirements — "of the Book, and pardoning much" — if no call to it calls. "There has come to you from God a light" — brought forth by divine care from the hiding-places of blindness — "and a Book" — inscribed by the Pen of the Creator upon the pages of possibility, comprehensive of every perfection. These two are an allusion to the Prophet (ﷺ), and therefore the pronoun is singular in His saying: "by which God guides" — i.e., through him — "whoever follows His good pleasure" — i.e., whoever desires that — "to the paths of peace" — which are the ways leading to Him, mighty and majestic.

Some of the knowers said: "The ways to God Most High are closed, except to those who follow the Prophet (ﷺ)."

"And brings them out of darknesses" — the darknesses of doubt, the objections of the soul, and the satanic suggestions — "into light" — the light of contentment and submission — "and guides them to a straight path" — the way of ascent through the lofty stations. It may be said: the first clause alludes to the unity of acts, the second to the unity of attributes, and the third to the unity of the Essence.

"Certainly they have disbelieved who said, 'God is the Messiah, son of Mary'" — they confined divinity to him and restricted the God to His determination, which is the Absolute Being, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. "Say: Who then has any power against God if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth together?" — for all of that is among the determinations and states, and God is encompassing behind them.

"And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them" — i.e., the world of spirits, the world of bodies, and the world of forms — "He creates what He wills" — and manifests whatever states He wishes. "The Jews and the Christians said, 'We are the sons of God and His beloved'" — they claimed the sonship of secrets and nearness to the presence of the light of lights. Some of the earlier people said this, as the allusion has passed, and some of the later ones said something close to it. Al-Wasiti said: "Son of the pre-eternal and the everlasting." But these people did not know the realities, nor did they taste the subtleties, so God refuted their claim by His saying: "Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?" The sons and the beloved do not sin so as to be punished, or they are not tested, since they have left the place of testing as far as bodily forms are concerned. "Rather you are human beings of those He has created" — like the rest of God's servants, with no distinction for you over them in anything, as you claim. "He forgives whom He wills" — among them, by grace — "and punishes whom He wills" — among them, by justice.

"And when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, remember God's favor upon you when He made among you prophets and made you kings'" — through guardianship (wilaya) and knowledge of the attributes, or through the sovereignty of ecstasy (wajd), the strength of state, and the might of the knowledge of gnosis. Or "kings" means possessors of your own souls, by restraining them from anything other than my obedience. The kings, in our view, are the free from the bondage of the two worlds and what is in them. "And gave you what He had not given anyone of the worlds" — i.e., of the worlds of your time. Of this is the beholding of the light of manifestation from the face of Moses (peace be upon him). "O my people, enter the Holy Land" — which is the presence of the heart
[Page 123]
"which God has prescribed for you" — in the preceding decree, according to readiness — "and do not turn back on your heels" — by inclining toward the city of the body and turning to it by pursuing its pleasures — "lest you turn back as losers" — by your forfeiting the lights and goodness of the heart.

"They said, 'O Moses, in it are a people of tyrants'" — these are the qualities of the soul — "and we will never enter it until they leave it" — by God turning them away without discipline or struggle from us, or by their weakening from seizing it by nature. "If they leave it, then we will enter" — at that time. "Two men of those who feared" — the evil outcome of remaining with the body — "on whom God had bestowed favor" — with guidance to the upright path, and these two are the theoretical intellect and the practical intellect — "said: Enter upon them through the gate" — i.e., the gate of the town of the heart, which is trust through the manifestation of the acts, just as the gate of the town of the Spirit is contentment — "for when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious" — by your emerging from your acts and your own power. What indicates that the gate is trust is His saying: "And upon God rely, if you are believers" — truly, which is faith with presence, and its lowest degree is the manifestation of the acts.

"They said, 'O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here'" — i.e., we remain in our place in the station of the soul, devoted to desire and pleasures. "He said: It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land" — i.e., the land of nature. That is the duration of their remaining in the station of the soul, and the light of the bond of livelihood used to descend upon them from the heaven of the Spirit, so they benefited by its light.

(﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam﴾) — the heart (al-qalb), which are Habil (the intellect, al-'aql) and Qabil (the imagination, al-wahm). (﴿When they both offered a sacrifice﴾) — and this, as some of the gnostics (al-'arifin) said, is because the twin of the intellect is the practical reasoning faculty (al-'aqilah al-'amaliyyah), which directs the affairs of livelihood and the hereafter through sound opinions that necessitate righteous deeds and noble morals, and which devises the various crafts and governments; and the twin of the imagination, namely the faculty of representation (al-quwwah al-mutakhayyilah), which acts upon sensible things and particular meanings, in order to obtain satanic opinions. So Adam, the heart, ordered the marriage of the imagination to the intellect, so that the intellect might govern it through submissive disciplines (al-riyadat al-idh'aniyyah) and spiritual policies (al-siyasat al-ruhaniyyah), and accompany it with rational demonstrative syllogisms (al-qiyasat al-'aqliyyah al-burhaniyyah), thereby subjugating it to the intellect; and the marriage of the intellect to the imagination was so that it would make her righteous, keep her from the desires of corrupt imaginings and false self-talk, and be used for what benefits, so that her father rests and benefits. But Qabil (the imagination) envied Habil (the intellect), because his twin was more beautiful and dearer to him, owing to her suitability for him. Then they were commanded at that time to offer a sacrifice, and they offered a sacrifice; one of them was accepted, namely Habil (the intellect), by a fire descending from heaven which consumed it. What is meant by the fire is the Active Intellect (al-'aql al-fa''al), descending from the heaven of the world of spirits, and its consuming is its bestowing the conclusion upon the syllogistic form, which is the intellect's sacrifice and its work by which one draws near to God Most High. (﴿And it was not accepted from the other﴾) — namely Qabil (the imagination); for the acceptance of the imaginary form is impossible, since it does not correspond to what is in reality.

(﴿He said: "I will surely kill you."﴾) — out of increased envy, due to the intellect's greater nearness to God Most High and the imagination's distance from its rank in its perceptions and operations. His killing him is an indication of preventing him from acting and cutting off from him the support of the spirit and the light of divine guidance, by which there is life, through introducing imaginary doubts and objections in obtaining theoretical matters. (﴿He said: "Surely God accepts only from the righteous."﴾) — those who take God Most High as a shield (wiqayah), or who beware the dark bodily states, the ruinous desires, and the destructive deceptions.

(﴿If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you.﴾) — that is, I do not nullify your deeds, which are sound in their places. (﴿Indeed I fear God, Lord of the worlds.﴾) — that is, because I know God, glory be to Him, so I know that He created you for a purpose and brought you into existence for a wisdom, and among that is that the means of livelihood are not obtained except by the imagination, and were it not for hope, work would cease. (﴿I desire that you bear my sin and your sin﴾) — that is, the sin of my killing and the sin of your deeds from false opinions. (﴿and so become of the companions of the Fire﴾) — which is the fire of veiling and deprivation. (﴿Such is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾) — those who place things in other than their proper place, just as the sensible judgments were placed in the position of intelligibles. (﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him, and he killed him﴾) — by preventing him from his proper actions
Page 124
and veiling him from the light of guidance. (﴿So he became of the losers﴾) — because of the harm he suffered by seizing control over the intellect; for when the imagination is cut off from the support of the intellect, it drives the soul toward matters by which it is harmed.

(﴿Then God sent a crow﴾) — and this is the crow of greed (al-hirs) (﴿scratching in the earth﴾) — that is, the earth of the soul (﴿to show him how to conceal his brother's shame﴾) — and this is the intellect, cut off from the life of the spirit, mixed with imagination and desire, veiled from its world in the darknesses of the earth of the soul. (﴿He said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal my brother's shame?"﴾) — by hiding it in the darkness of the soul, so that he might benefit by it. (﴿So he became of the regretful﴾) — when the loss became manifest and deprivation occurred.

(﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had killed all mankind﴾) — because the one comprises what all the individuals of the species comprise, and the subsistence of the species in the one is like its subsistence in all of them in external existence; and number is of no account, for the reality of the species does not increase with the increase of individuals nor decrease with their decrease. The same is said regarding the side of giving life.

(﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾) — that is, their allies (awliya'ahuma) (﴿and strive upon the earth to cause corruption﴾) — by discouraging the travelers (al-salikin) (﴿is that they be killed﴾) — by the sword of abandonment (al-khidhlan) (﴿or crucified﴾) — by the rope of separation (al-hijran) upon the trunk of deprivation (al-hirman) (﴿or that their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides﴾) — from the skirts of union (al-wisal), by way of disagreement and hesitation toward the travelers (﴿or that they be banished from the land﴾) — that is, the land of nearness and harmony, so that the traveler does not turn to them nor direct himself toward them (﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾) — because of the greatness of their crime. It has been reported that God Most High becomes angry for His friends as a lion becomes angry in battle, and: "Whoever harms a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him."

We ask God for pardon and well-being in religion, in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ When He, glorified is He, mentioned the recompense of the one who wars (against Allah and His Messenger) and the greatness of his crime, and alluded, within the course of that, to His forgiveness, exalted is He, for whoever repents, He commanded the believers to have taqwa of Him, mighty and majestic is He, in everything they do and leave undone, by abandoning what must be guarded against of the sins, among which are warring and corruption, and by performing acts of obedience, among which are repentance, seeking forgiveness, and repelling corruption. ﴿And seek means of approach to Him﴾ That is, seek for yourselves nearness to His reward and closeness to Him. ﴿The means (al-wasilah)﴾ is a form (fa'ilah) meaning that by which one seeks means and draws near to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, through performing acts of obedience and abandoning acts of disobedience, from "wasala ila kadha" meaning he drew near to it by means of something. The adverbial phrase is connected to it, and it was placed before it for emphasis. It is an adjective, not a verbal noun, so that the prohibition of its complement preceding it would not apply. It was said: it is connected to the verb before it. It was said: it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial modifier of it, meaning "being directed toward Him." Perhaps what is meant by it is the taqwa commanded, as the words of Qatadah indicate, for it is the essence of the whole matter, the means to every good, and the refuge from every harm. The sentence in that case runs in relation to what precedes it in the manner of explanation and emphasis. It was said: the first sentence is a command to abandon sins, and the second is a command to perform acts of obedience.

Ibn al-Anbari and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that al-wasilah means need (hajah), and he recited the verse of 'Antarah:
"Indeed, men have a means (wasilah) toward you; if they seize you, then adorn yourself with kohl and dye."
The meaning then seems to be: seek your needs, turning toward Him, for in His hand, mighty is His affair, are the keys of the heavens and the earth; and do not seek them turning toward other than Him, lest you be like the weak one who takes refuge in a cluster of colocynth.

Some have explained al-wasilah as a rank in Paradise. Its being in this sense is not apparent, since it is specific to the prophets, peace be upon them, based on what Muslim and others narrated: "It is a rank in Paradise which Allah has granted to one of His servants, and I hope that I will be he, so ask Allah for al-wasilah for me." And for the seeking here to be directed to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is something no sound mind would readily incline to; and on this basis the attachment of the adverbial phrase to it is impossible, as is not hidden.

Some people have used this verse as evidence for the legitimacy of seeking help from the righteous, and making them a means between Allah, the Exalted, and the servants, and swearing by Allah, the Exalted, by them, by saying: "O Allah, we swear to You by so-and-so that You give us such-and-such." Among them are those who say to an absent or dead righteous servant of Allah, the Exalted: "O so-and-so, pray to Allah, the Exalted, that He grant me such-and-such," and they assume that this falls under the category of seeking the means. They also narrate from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "When matters overwhelm you, then resort to the people of the graves," or "seek help from the people of the graves." All of this is far from the truth by great distances.

The detailed truth in this matter is that seeking help from a created being and making him a means, in the sense of asking him to supplicate, is without doubt permissible if the one asked is alive, and it is not conditioned upon his being superior to the petitioner; indeed, the superior may ask from the inferior. It is sound that "he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he asked his permission for 'umrah: 'Do not forget us, my brother, in your supplication'." And he also commanded him to ask Uways al-Qarani, may Allah have mercy on him, to seek forgiveness for him; and he commanded his community, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to seek al-wasilah for him as mentioned just above, and to send blessings upon him.

As for when the one asked is dead or absent, no scholar doubts that it is impermissible, and that it is among the innovations which none of the early generation (al-salaf) did. Yes, greeting the people of the graves is legislated, and addressing them is permissible. It is sound that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to teach his companions, when they visited graves, to say: "Peace be upon you, people of the abodes from among the believers, and we, if Allah wills, will join you. May Allah have mercy on those of us who went before and those who came after. We ask Allah for well-being for us and for you. O Allah, do not deprive us of their reward, and do not test us after them, and forgive us and them."

And none of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who are the most eager of creation for every good, is reported to have asked anything of a dead person. Indeed, it is sound from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when he entered the Prophet's chamber as a visitor, he would say: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Abu Bakr. Peace be upon you, O my father," then he would depart and would add nothing to that, and he would not ask anything of the master of the worlds, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, or of his two honored companions, may Allah be pleased with them both. They are the most honored of those whom the earth has embraced and the highest in rank of all whom the encompassing spheres surround.

Yes, supplication in that noble presence and that exalted garden is a legislated matter. The Companions used to supplicate to Allah, the Exalted, there, facing the qiblah, and it is not reported of them that they faced the noble grave during supplication, although it is more excellent than the Throne.

The imams differed regarding facing it at the time of greeting. From Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, it is that one does not face it but turns his back to it while facing the qiblah. Some said: one faces it at the time of greeting, faces the qiblah and turns his back to it at the time of supplication. The sound and relied-upon view is that one faces it at the time of greeting, and at the time of supplication one faces the qiblah, and the noble grave is placed to the right or left.

If this is what is legislated in visiting the master of creation and the very cause of existence in reality, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, then how far does visiting anyone else reach in comparison with his visit, peace and blessings be upon him, so that something may be added to it, or something be requested from the one visited that is not among the duties of servants?!

As for swearing by Allah, the Exalted, by one of His creatures, such as saying: "O Allah, I swear to You, or I ask You by so-and-so, except that You fulfill my need," it is reported from Ibn Abd al-Salam that this is permissible regarding the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the master of the sons of Adam, but it is not permissible to swear upon Allah, the Exalted, by anyone else among the prophets, angels, or saints, because they are not at his rank. Al-Manawi transmitted this from him in his large commentary on al-Jami' al-Saghir. Its evidence is what al-Tirmidhi narrated, and he said: "a hasan sahih hadith," from Uthman ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a blind man came to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: 'Pray to Allah that He cure me.' He said: 'If you wish, I will supplicate, and if you wish, you may be patient, and that is better for you.' He said: 'Then supplicate.' So he commanded him to perform ablution, performing it well, and to supplicate with this supplication: 'O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet, the Prophet of mercy, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. O Messenger of Allah, I have turned to you toward my Lord in this need of mine, that it be fulfilled for me. O Allah, then let him intercede for me.'" And the like of this is narrated from Ahmad.

Among the people is one who prohibited seeking means through the essence (of the Prophet) and swearing upon Allah, the Exalted, by any of His creatures absolutely, and this is what the words of Majd Ibn Taymiyyah suggest, and he transmitted it from Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Yusuf and other distinguished scholars. He answered the hadith by saying that it is on the omission of an annexed term, meaning "by the supplication or intercession of Your Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him," so in it is the making of supplication a means, which is permissible, indeed recommended. The evidence for this interpretation is his saying at the end of the hadith: "O Allah, then let him intercede for me," and even at its beginning there is what indicates this. Al-Taj al-Subki, as is his habit, criticized Majd harshly, saying: "Seeking means and help through the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, toward his Lord is good, and none of the early or later generations denied it, until Ibn Taymiyyah came, denied it, deviated from the straight path, and innovated what no scholar had said, and became an example among mankind." End of quote.

You know that the supplications reported from the Pure People of the House and others among the imams contain no seeking of means through the noble essence, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. Even if we suppose the existence of what appears to be such, it is interpreted by an omitted annexed term as you have heard, or something similar as you will hear, Allah willing. Whoever claims a explicit text bears the burden of proof. As for what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan and others, that "a man said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: 'We seek your intercession with Allah, and we seek Allah's intercession through you.' So the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, glorified Allah until it was seen in the faces of his Companions, and he said: 'Woe to you! Do you know what Allah is? Indeed Allah is not interceded through by anyone of His creation; the affair of Allah is greater than that.'" It is not suitable as evidence for what we are discussing, since he denied his saying "we seek Allah's intercession through you," and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not deny his saying "we seek your intercession with Allah," because the meaning of seeking intercession through him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is asking him to supplicate, not swearing by him upon Allah, the Exalted. And if swearing were the meaning of seeking intercession, why did the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, deny the content of the second sentence and not the first? On this basis, neither the report nor what precedes it is suitable evidence for one who claims the permissibility of swearing by his essence, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, whether living or dead, and likewise by the essence of other holy spirits absolutely, by analogy with him, peace be upon him, on the basis of honor, though they differ in strength and weakness. That is because what is in the second report is seeking intercession, not swearing, and what is in the first report is not an explicit text on the point in dispute, and even granting it, it contains only swearing by the living and seeking means through him.

The equality of his two states, life and death, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, in this matter requires a text, and perhaps the text indicates the opposite. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Anas, that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever they suffered drought, would seek rain through al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "O Allah, we used to seek means to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain; and now we seek means to You through the uncle of our Prophet, so give us rain," and they were given rain.

For if seeking means through him, peace and blessings be upon him, after his departure from this world were legislated, they would not have turned to anyone else, but would have said: "O Allah, we seek means to You through our Prophet, so give us rain." And far be it from them to turn away from seeking means through the master of mankind to seeking means through his uncle al-Abbas, while they found the slightest latitude for that. Their turning away, despite their being the foremost early ones, and their being more knowledgeable than us about Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and about the rights of Allah and His Messenger, peace be upon him, and what supplication is legislated and what is not, and they being in a time of necessity and hunger, seeking the relief of distress, the easing of hardship, and the sending down of rain by every means, is clear evidence that what is legislated is what they followed rather than other than it.

And as for what was mentioned about analogy of other holy spirits to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, despite the difference in honor

Which none but a hypocrite denies, is something that can hardly be accepted. Moreover, you already know that swearing by the Prophet (ﷺ) before his Lord, may He be exalted, whether he is alive or dead, is something the text does not establish. It cannot be said that the report in al-Bukhari indicates the validity of swearing by him (ﷺ) while he was alive, nor by anyone else in the same way.

As for the first, it rests on the words of ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) in it: "We used to seek a means (tawassul) through your Prophet (ﷺ)."

As for the second, it rests on his words: "We seek a means through the uncle of your Prophet." It has been said that this tawassul is not a form of swearing but is of the type of seeking intercession (istishfaʿ), which means asking a person for supplication and intercession, and asking God to accept his supplication and intercession. This is supported by the fact that al-ʿAbbas used to supplicate while they said "Amen" to his supplication, until they were given rain.

Al-Majd has mentioned that the term tawassul through a person, and turning toward him and by him, is ambiguous and shared in its usage according to convention. Its meaning in the language of the Companions is to ask him for supplication and intercession, so that tawassul and turning are in reality through his supplication and intercession. There is no objection to that. But in the language of many people, its meaning is to ask God by that and to swear by it upon Him, and this is the point of dispute, and you have already known the discussion of it.

Among the impermissible forms of swearing is the saying of the one who says: "O God, I ask You by the standing (jah) of so-and-so." It has not been reported from any of the early predecessors (salaf) that they supplicated in this way. It has been said: one swears only by Him, by His names and attributes. So one says: "I ask You, by the fact that all praise is Yours, there is no god but You, O Allah, the Bestower, Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of majesty and honor, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting," and "I ask You, by the fact that You are Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him," and "I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You named Yourself," the hadith, and similar of the transmitted supplications.

As for what some of the common folk mention, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you have a need with God, then ask God by my standing, for my standing with God is great," no one among the people of knowledge has transmitted it, nor is it in any of the books of hadith.

As for what al-Qushayri transmitted from Maʿruf al-Karkhi (qaddasa sirruhu), that he said to his disciples: "If you have a need with God, then swear by me upon Him, for I am now the intermediary between you and Him, may His majesty be glorified," there is no chain of narration for it that the scholars of hadith rely upon.

As for what Ibn Majah transmitted from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the supplication of one who goes out to prayer: 'O God, I ask You by the right of those who ask You, and by the right of this walk of mine. For I did not go out out of insolence, nor out of pride, nor out of showing off, nor for reputation, but I went out out of fear of Your wrath and seeking Your pleasure, that You rescue me from the Fire and admit me to Paradise,'" in its chain is al-ʿAwfi, and there is weakness in it. And on the supposition that it is from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), it is said concerning it: the right of those who ask Him, may He be exalted, is that He answers them, and the right of those who walk in His obedience is that He rewards them. "Right" here means a promise that is established and certain to occur, as a favor and not as an obligation, as in His words: ﴿And it was ever a duty upon Us to help the believers﴾.

In the Sahih, from the hadith of Muʿadh: "The right of God upon His servants is that they worship Him and not associate anything with Him, and their right upon Him, if they do that, is that He will not punish them." So the request then is by reward and answer, and these are among the active attributes of God, may He be exalted, and asking by them is not disputed. So this supplication is like the seeking of refuge in his words (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in Your good pleasure from Your wrath, and in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You." So whenever seeking refuge by His pardon is valid, asking by its establishment and its answering is valid.

In a similar manner, the request of the three (from the cave) to God, may He be exalted and glorified, by their deeds, is understood, since tawassul by deeds means seeking a cause for the attainment of the desired object. There is no doubt that righteous deeds are a cause for God's reward to us, but the persons themselves are not so.

Today people have gone to excess in swearing upon God, so they have sworn upon Him, may His majesty be glorified, by those who were not in the caravan nor in the army, and who have not the least bit of standing (qiṭmir) with Him. Even more serious, they ask the dwellers of graves for things like curing the sick, enriching the poor, returning the lost, and facilitating every difficulty. Their devils inspire them with the report "When matters are difficult for you…," etc., and it is a fabricated hadith upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by the consensus of those who know his hadith. No one among the scholars has transmitted it, nor is it found in any of the authoritative books of hadith.

The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade taking graves as places of worship and cursed those who did so. So how can it be imagined that he (ﷺ) would command seeking aid and requesting from their occupants?! Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander.

It is reported from Abu Yazid al-Bistami (qaddasa sirruhu) that he said: "The seeking of aid by a created being from a created being is like the seeking of aid by a prisoner from a prisoner."

From the words of al-Sajjad (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu): "The request of the needy from the needy is folly in its judgment and misguidance in its reason."

From the supplication of Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam): "And by You is the seeking of aid."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiyallahu ʿanhuma): "If you seek aid, then seek aid from God," the report (khabar).

And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.﴾

After all of this, I do not see any harm in seeking a means to God through the standing (jah) of the Prophet (ﷺ) with God, whether he is alive or dead. By "standing" is meant a meaning that returns to one of God's attributes, such as love of him being complete, which requires that He not reject him and that He accept his intercession. So the meaning of the saying of one who says, "My God, I seek a means through the standing of Your Prophet (ﷺ) that You fulfill my need," is: "My God, make Your love for him a means for the fulfilling of my need." There is no difference between this and your saying: "My God, I seek a means through Your mercy that You do such-and-such," since its meaning is also: "My God, make Your mercy a means for doing such-and-such."

Indeed, I see no harm even in swearing upon God by his standing (ﷺ) in this sense. The discussion concerning its prohibition is like the discussion concerning standing. This does not apply to seeking a means or swearing by the pure essence (dhat).

Yes, seeking a means through standing and sanctity (ḥurma) has not been known from any of the Companions (raḍiyallahu ʿanhum). Perhaps that was out of their avoidance of what might have stuck in the minds of people at that time, since they were recently converted from seeking a means through idols. Then the pure imams who came after them followed them. And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) "left off demolishing the Kaʿba and rebuilding it upon the foundations of Ibrahim, because the people were recently converted from disbelief," as is established in the Sahih.

What I have mentioned is only to remove hardship from people, and to flee from the claim that they are misguided, as some allege, in seeking a means through the standing of the one of greatest standing (ﷺ). It is not because I incline to the view that supplication in this manner is better than using the transmitted supplications that the Book has brought and that the tongues of the Sunnah have uttered. For no fair-minded person doubts that what God and His Messenger (ﷺ) taught, what the noble Companions (raḍiyallahu ʿanhum) practiced, and what those after them received with acceptance, is better, more comprehensive, more beneficial, and safer. So whatever has been said has been said, whether true or false.

Two matters remain here:

The first: seeking a means through the standing of someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ) is also not objectionable, if the one through whose standing one seeks a means is known to have standing with God, such as one whose righteousness and sainthood (wilaya) are certain. As for one whose case is not certain, one should not seek a means through his standing, because this involves an implicit judgment upon God regarding something whose realization from Him, may He be exalted, is not known. And in that is a tremendous audacity against God.

The second: people have greatly increased their calling upon other than God, whether living or dead saints and others, such as: "O my master so-and-so, help me!" This is not in any way among the permissible forms of tawassul. It is proper for the believer's condition not to utter such things and not to hover around its sacred boundary. Some scholars have counted it as polytheism (shirk), and if it is not that, it is close to it. I do not see anyone who says this except that he believes that the one called upon, whether living and absent or dead and hidden, knows the unseen or hears the call, and is able, by himself or by another, to bring benefit and avert harm. Otherwise he would not call upon him nor open his mouth. And in that is a great trial from your Lord.

So prudence lies in avoiding that, and not requesting except from God, the Strong, the Self-Sufficient, the Doer of what He wills. And whoever comprehends the secret of what al-Tabarani transmitted in his Majma' (Majma' al-Zawa'id), that "in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) there was a hypocrite who harmed the believers, so al-Siddiq (raḍiya [Page 129] Allahu ʿanhu) said: 'Come, let us seek aid from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) against this hypocrite.' They came to him, and he said: 'I am not called upon for aid, only God is called upon for aid.'" will not doubt that seeking aid from the dwellers of graves, some of whom are fortunate, whose bliss and whose movement in the gardens distract them from attending to what is in this world, and some of whom are wretched, whose punishment and confinement in the fires distract them from answering their caller and listening to the people of their assembly, is a matter that must be avoided, and it does not befit people of intellect to commit.

Do not be deceived by the fact that one who seeks aid from a created being has his need fulfilled and his request granted, for that is a trial and a test from Him, may He be exalted and glorified. Often Satan appears to the one seeking aid in the form of the one from whom he sought aid, so he thinks that this is a miracle (karama) for the one he called upon. Far, far from it! It is only a devil who has misled and seduced him and made his desire seem good to him. This is like the devil speaking through idols to mislead their stupid worshippers. Some ignorant people say that this is due to the spiritual development (tatawwur) of the soul of the one called upon, or due to an angel appearing in his form as a miracle for him. Evil is what they judge! For the development and the appearing, though possible, are not possible in such a form, and at the commission of this sin. We ask God by His names to protect us from that, and we seek a means through His gentleness that He lead us and you on the best of paths.

﴿And strive in His way﴾ with your enemies by whatever means you can.

﴿So that you may succeed﴾ by attaining the bliss of eternity and deliverance from every hardship.

**Page 130**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ is an independent sentence (*kalam mubtada'*), brought to emphasise the obligation to comply with the preceding commands, and to encourage the believers to hasten to obtain the means of reaching Him, exalted is His majesty, before its time passes. It does so by showing the impossibility of the disbelievers seeking means of salvation on the Day of Resurrection through what is among the strongest means of escape from punishment, let alone attaining reward. ﴿Even if they had﴾, i.e. each one of them, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And even if every soul that has wronged had﴾, and so on. In this there is a magnification of the matter and a dreadfulness of the state that is absent from our saying "for all of them." ﴿Whatever is on the earth﴾, i.e. of its kinds of wealth, its treasures and all its benefits, in their entirety. It is the subject (*ism*) of *anna*, and *lahum* ("for them") is its predicate (*khabar*). Its position is nominative according to them (the majority of grammarians). However, according to Sibawayh it is nominative as an inceptive (*mubtada'*), and no predicate is needed for it, since its relative clause contains both the predicate and the subject. It is specifically distinguished, among all the other items that are interpreted as nouns, by occurring after *law* ("if"). It is also said that the predicate is omitted, and two opinions exist as to whether it is to be taken as preceding or following. According to al-Zajjaj, al-Mubarrad and the Kufans, it is nominative as the agent (*fa'iliyya*), i.e. "if there were to be established for them whatever is on the earth."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿all together﴾ are either an emphasis of the relative pronoun (*mawsul*) or a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of it. His words, glorified is He: ﴿and the like of it﴾ are in the accusative and are conjoined to it (*'atf*). His words, exalted is His majesty and glorified is He: ﴿with it﴾ is an adverbial phrase (*zarf*) that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of the conjoined item, and the pronoun refers back to the relative pronoun. The purpose of stating explicitly—on the assumption that both of them are in their possession—that they are together (*ma'iyya*) and not in succession (*ta'aqub*), is to affirm the full extent of the horror of the matter.

The *lam* in His words, exalted is He: ﴿so that they may ransom themselves with it﴾ is connected to what the predicate of *anna* is connected to, namely the implied stability (*istiqrar*) in *lahum*, and to the implied predicate according to the one who holds that view, and to the implied verb after *law* according to al-Zajjaj and those who follow his approach. It has been said: there is no doubt that the basis of seeking ransom through what has been mentioned is that it belongs to them, not that it is established as belonging to them, although the latter entails the former. The *ba'* in ﴿with it﴾ is connected to "ransoming," and the pronoun refers to the relative pronoun. [The singular pronoun is used] ﴿and the like of it with it﴾ because the two, by being together, are considered one thing, or because the pronoun is treated in the manner of a demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*), as the reference to this has already passed. It is also said that it refers to the relative pronoun, and the one that refers back to the conjoined item, namely ﴿the like of it﴾, is "its like," which is omitted, just as the predicate is omitted from *Qayyar* in the verse:

*"Whoever has his camel-saddle in Medina tonight, / then I and Qayyar there are indeed strangers."*

It has also been allowed that ﴿and the like of it﴾ is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*), its governing element being the verb implied after *law*, following the opinion of al-Zajjaj, and whoever holds his view. In that case the singularity of the pronoun is clear, since the rule for a pronoun following an object of accompaniment is singularity. Al-Akhfash permitted that it be given the status of two conjoined items, so the pronoun would be dual. Some grammarians said: the correct view is that it is permissible, though rare. Abu Hayyan raised an objection to this aspect: the meaning would become "with its like, *ma'ahu*," and if what is on the earth is with its like, then its like is necessarily with it; so there is no point in mentioning "with it" alongside, since each of them is necessarily with the other. Al-Tibi answered that "with it" in this case is an emphasis. Al-Safaqisi said: his reply is that the implied element is not the same as the explicit one, and the *waw* includes the meaning of "with," and it would only be objectionable if "with" were stated explicitly. Often the implied form differs from the explicit, as in the expression "*rabb shatan wa-sakhlatuha*" [the owner of a ewe and her lamb]; if you stated "*rabb*" explicitly and said "*wa-rabb sakhlatiha*," it would not be permitted. Al-Halabi answered that the pronoun in "*ma'ahu*" refers back to "*mithlahu*," and the meaning becomes "with two like things," which is more emphatic than being with a single like thing. Yes, indeed, the claim that the governing element is "*thabata*" [was established] is not correct, because the governing element of the object of accompaniment is the governing element of the item accompanied, as they have explicitly stated; here that is "*ma*" [whatever] or its pronoun, and neither of these governs "*thabata*" in its implied form. As for its validity on the supposition of making it for them or its complement—as has been said—this is also impossible, based on what is transmitted from Sibawayh, that he said: "As for '*hadha laka wa-abaka*' [this is yours and your father's], it is ugly, because no verb has been mentioned, nor a particle carrying the meaning of a verb, so that it would be as if he had spoken with a verb. For in it there is an explicit statement that the demonstrative, the prepositional particle, and the adverbial phrase do not govern an object of accompaniment."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection﴾ are also connected to "ransoming," i.e. "even if whatever is on the earth and its like were theirs, so that they might make it a ransom for themselves from the punishment that befalls them on that Day."

﴿Not one of it would be accepted from them﴾—that is the response (*jawab*) of *law*. Its arrangement, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is based on that belonging to them, for the sake of their ransoming with it, without mentioning the ransoming itself—such as saying "and they ransomed with it." [This is so] although the rejection and acceptance are only consequent upon the act itself and not upon its preliminaries, in order to signify that it is a certainly occurring matter, independent of mention, and what requires the supposition is only their capacity for what has been mentioned. Or it is for the sake of intensifying the certainty of the rejection, and to imagine that it occurred before the ransoming, following the pattern of His words, exalted is He: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.﴾ So when he saw it settled beside him…﴾, where it did not say "so he brought it, and when he saw it…" and so on; and His words, glorified is He: ﴿And she said: Come out before them,﴾ and when they saw him they exalted him﴾, without mentioning his (peace be upon him) coming out before them or their seeing him.

Some eminent scholars said: The reason it was not sufficient to say, "Indeed, those who disbelieve, if they were to ransom themselves with whatever is on the earth, all of it, from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them," is that the noble structure indicates that if they had obtained whatever is on the earth and its like with it, for this purpose, and had been fearful of Allah, exalted is He, and had guarded the ransom and reflected on ransoming and attended to its means—as is the condition of one who is preparing for a matter—it would not be accepted from them. How much less would it be if they were heedless of obtaining the ransom and sought the ransom suddenly. For this reason it did not say, "If they had whatever is on the earth, all of it, and its like with it, and ransomed themselves with it, it would not be accepted," and so on. The conditional clause remains in its state as the predicate of "*inna alladhina kafaru*" [indeed, those who disbelieve]. It is a metonymy for the necessity of punishment for them, and that there is no way for them to escape from it. For the necessity of punishment entails that whatever is on the earth, all of it, and its like with it, if they were to ransom themselves with it, would not be accepted from them. So when this clause—indeed, this implication—was a necessary consequence of the necessity of punishment, it was expressed by means of it.

Some people applied to this clause the term "*tamthil*" [illustrative expression]. Perhaps their intention—as mentioned by al-Qutb—was what he mentioned. Some researchers said: they do not mean by it the illustrative metaphor (*al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah*), but rather the presentation of an example and a judgment from which the necessity of punishment for them is understood. That is, this statement was not intended to establish this conditional proposition, but rather the mind moves from it to this meaning. In this sense it is called a metonymy. It may be interpreted as the technical illustrative expression, by saying that their situation in seeking escape from punishment is like the situation of one who possesses that great matter and tries by it to free himself from punishment, yet it is not accepted from him and he is not freed.

﴿And for them there is a painful punishment﴾. It has been said: its position is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). It has been said: nominative, conjoined to the predicate of *inna*. It has been said: it is conjoined to *inna alladhina* [indeed those who], so it has no place in grammatical analysis, like the former. The purpose of the sentence is to make explicit what was meant by the first sentence, for the sake of increasing its establishment and explaining its terror and severity. It has also been said: the purpose of it is to signify that just as their punishment is not averted by that, it is also not lightened; rather, for them after this there is a punishment in the utmost painfulness. Likewise is His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 37:

﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾. This is to convey that, just as their punishment is not averted by that ransom, its continuance is not averted either, nor is it cut off. This, as already stated, is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to explain their condition in the midst of enduring the punishment, based on a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "How will their condition be?" or "What will they do?" So it was said: "They wish" etc.

It has been made clear within this that their punishment is the punishment of the Fire. The wishing (al-irada) – it has been said – is in its real, well-known meaning: the flame of the Fire lifts them up, so they wish to come out, but how can they! This is narrated from al-Hasan. Al-Jubba'i said: the wishing (al-irada) is in the sense of longing (al-tamanni), i.e., they long for that.

It has also been said: the meaning is that they nearly come out of it because of its intensity and the increase of its lifting them up, and this is like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and they found therein a wall that wanted to collapse﴾, i.e., it nearly and almost (did so). One may ask: how is it permissible that they wish to come out of the Fire while they know they will abide forever? We say: the terror of that Day makes them forget that, and even if they do not forget, it is said: knowledge that a thing will not occur does not divert one from wishing for it, just as knowledge that it will occur does not either, for the motive for wishing is the goodness of the thing and the need for it.

﴿And they will not be out of it﴾. It is either a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of (they wish), or a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). In either case, the choice of the nominal sentence over the verbal one, introduced by (ma), the Hijazi negation, which by the preposition (ba') in its scope indicates the emphasis of negation, is to show the full extent of their wretched condition through the continuance of their not coming out of it. For the affirmative nominal sentence, as has already been indicated, while it conveys by the aid of context the permanence of establishment, also conveys negation by the aid of the permanence of negation, not the negation of permanence.

Abu Waqid read: (an yukhraju) with the passive form, from ikhraj (causing to come out). The reading of the majority is supported by His saying: (bi-kharijin) rather than (bi-mukhrajin). This verse, as you see, concerns the disbelievers, so it does not contradict the view that intercession is granted to sinful believers to come out of it, as is not hidden from anyone who has the least faith.

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Jabir ibn Abdullah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A people will come out of the Fire and enter Paradise." Yazid al-Faqir said: I said to Jabir: "Allah, exalted is He, says: (They wish to come out of the Fire, and they will not be out of it)?" He said: "Recite the beginning of the verse: (Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby...). Surely they are the ones who disbelieved."

Ibn Jarir related from Ikrimah that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "You claim that a people will come out of the Fire, and Allah, exalted is He, has said: (and they will not be out of it)?" Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Woe to you! Read what is above it; this is for the disbelievers."

The report that he said to him: "O you blind of sight, blind of heart, you claim etc." is related by al-Zamakhshari, who then reviled the People of the Sunnah, accusing them of lying and fabrication. So examine what has been said: "She accused me of her own ailment and slipped away."

We are not obliged to authenticate this report, nor did Allah, exalted is He, make the soundness of the creed depend on its soundness. How many authentic hadiths do we have that bear witness to the truth of what we say and to the falsehood of what the Mu'tazilah say. Woe to them!

﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾. This is an explicit statement of what was alluded to: the non-cessation of the duration of the punishment after clarifying its severity, i.e., a constant, established punishment that does not cease nor pass away, ever.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 38 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And as for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ This begins the explanation of the ruling on the minor theft (al-sariqa al-sughra), after the explanation of the major rulings, and the circumstance requiring the placement of what came between them of speech has already been explained. The utterance consists of two clauses according to Sibawayh, since the estimated sense is:
Page 132
"In what is recited to you: the male thief and the female thief," i.e., their ruling. It is one clause according to al-Mubarrad. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it in the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the majority because of the imperative, since "Zayd, so strike him" (zaydan fa-adribhu) is better than "Zayd, so strike him" (zaydun fa-adribhu). Al-Zamakhshari said, and those who followed him, including Ibn al-Hajib, followed this.
Al-ʿAllama Ahmad in al-Intisaf criticized him with words that are all excellent, so there is no harm in quoting it in full. We say:
He said in it: What is established from the varieties of readings is that the common reading never agrees on deviating from the more eloquent form, and it is fitting for the Qur'an to secure the most eloquent of the modes, and not to be devoid of the most eloquent and to include it, in the speech of the Arabs, which none of them reached the peak of its eloquence, nor clung to its fringes. Sibawayh shields the reading of the masters of the Qur'an from neglecting the most eloquent and from including the irregular (shadh), which is not counted as part of the Qur'an. We shall cite the passage from Sibawayh's words on this verse so that its hearer may see clearly Sibawayh's innocence of responsibility for this transmission.
Sibawayh said, in the chapter-heading of the chapter on the command and prohibition, after he mentioned the positions in which the accusative is preferred and summarized them: "Whenever the noun is built upon a verb of command, that is the position where the accusative is preferred." Then he said, as one clarifying the distinction of this verse from what he chose the accusative for: "As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ and His saying, Exalted: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog them﴾, this is not built upon the verb, but it came on the pattern of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing are promised﴾, then He, glorified, said after it: ﴿Therein are rivers﴾, of which..." Sibawayh intends by this the distinguishing of these verses from the positions in which he indicated the choice of the accusative. The point of distinction is that where the accusative is chosen the noun is built upon the verb, whereas in these verses it is not built upon it, so the choice of the accusative is not required. Then he said: "The example was only placed for the narrative he mentioned after it, so he mentioned reports and stories, as if he said: among the stories is 'the likeness of the Garden,' and it is carried upon this implied meaning. And God Exalted knows best."
Likewise ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾: when He, whose praise is great, said: ﴿A surah which We sent down and made obligatory﴾, He said, Majestic and Exalted, among the obligations: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾, then came ﴿flog them﴾ after the nominative had passed over them. Sibawayh means: the noun was not built upon the verb mentioned after it, but was built upon an earlier omitted element, and the verb came as an incidental. Then he said, as in the line:
"And a speaker said: Khawlan, marry their young women,"
so he brought the verb after the pronoun had governed it. Likewise ﴿And the thief, male and female﴾ in what is enjoined upon you: "the thief, male and female." These nouns entered after stories and narratives. Some people read ﴿the thief, male and female﴾ in the accusative, and it is, in Arabic, of the strength I have mentioned to you, but the common people refused anything but the nominative. Sibawayh means: in the accusative reading the noun is built upon the verb without depending upon an earlier element, so the accusative is strong relative to the nominative, where the noun is built upon the verb and not upon an earlier element. It does not mean that it is strong relative to the nominative where the noun depends upon an omitted earlier element, for he has made clear that this removes it from the category in which the accusative is chosen, so how can his preference of it over that be understood? The category, together with the contexts, differs, and preference occurs only after equality within the category. So the accusative is preferred over the nominative where the noun is built upon the verb, while the nominative is required, not merely preferred, where the noun is built upon a preceding speech. The words of Sibawayh were confused for al-Zamakhshari, since he believed that it was one category for him. Do you not see his saying: "Because 'Zayd, so strike him' is better than 'Zayd is, so strike him'": how he preferred the accusative over the nominative, where the speech in both cases is built upon the verb?
Sibawayh has explicitly stated that the speech in the verse, with the nominative, is built upon an earlier speech, then he verified this estimated element by saying that the speech falls after stories and reports. Had it been as al-Zamakhshari supposed, Sibawayh would not have needed an estimate, but would have made it nominative as a beginning (mubtada') and made the command its predicate, as al-Zamakhshari parsed. So the summary according to this is that the accusative has one way, namely building the noun upon the imperative verb, while the nominative has two ways: one of them weak, namely beginning and building the speech on the verb, and the other strong and sound like the way of the accusative, namely making it nominative as the predicate of an omitted beginning, indicated by the context. When two ways of nominative present themselves to us, one strong and the other weak, it is necessary to carry the reading upon the strong one, as Sibawayh parsed it, may God Exalted have mercy on him and be pleased with him. End.
The fa' (fa) when the speech is built on two clauses is causal (sababiyya), not conjunctive; it has been said it is superfluous (za'ida), and likewise on the weak way, since the subject (mubtada') contains the sense of the conditional, for the meaning is: "and he who stole and she who stole."
Some verifiers claimed that such a construction can only be justified by one of two things: the insertion of the fa' as is reported from al-Akhfash, or the estimate of "amma" (as for), because the entry of the fa' into the predicate of the subject is either because it includes the sense of the conditional, or because the subject occurs after "amma"; and since the first is not present, the second is required. The flaw in this is not hidden.
On the reading of ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar the accusative is by an implied verb which the apparent word explains, and the fa' also, as Ibn Jinni said, is because of the conditional sense in the speech; and for this it is fine with the imperative, since it has its meaning. Do you not see that its response is jussive for this reason, since the meaning of "Submit, you will enter Paradise" is "If you submit, you will enter Paradise"?
The intended meaning, as some commentaries on the Kashshaf indicate, is: "If you want the ruling on the thief, male and female, then cut off etc.," and for this one may not say "Zayd, so I struck him," because the fa' does not enter the response of a conditional when it is past; and its estimate, "If you want knowledge of" etc., is better than its estimate "If you cut" because the latter does not indicate the intended obligation. Abu Hayyan said that the fa' is in response to an implied command, i.e., "Be mindful of their ruling, so cut off." It has been said that the fa' entered because it is the right of the explanation to be mentioned after what is explained, like the detail after the summary in His saying: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾. This is not worth anything.
From what Sahib al-Intisaf mentioned, the falsity is known of what has been said: that the cause of the earlier disagreement about this construction is that Sibawayh and al-Khalil require, for the entry of the fa' into the predicate, that the subject be joined to something that accepts direct contact with the conditional particle, while others do not require that. The apparent cause of this is failure to grasp the intended meaning, so let it be remembered.
Theft (sariqa) is taking the property of another secretly. It obliges amputation only when the taking is from a secure place (hirz), and the item taken is worth ten dirhams or more, with conditions which the books of jurisprudence have undertaken to explain. The school of al-Shafiʿi, al-Awzaʿi, Abu Thawr and the Imamiyya, may God be pleased with them all, hold that amputation applies to what is worth a quarter dinar or more. Some said: five is not cut except for five dirhams, and Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i chose this. It has been said: amputation is obligatory for little and much, and the Kharijites went this way. By "hands" (aydi) is meant the right hands, as was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and the generality of the Successors, may God be pleased with them all; and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, "aymanahuma" ("their right hands") supports this. For this reason the plural was placed in the position of the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Your hearts have inclined﴾, relying on the dual of the pronoun governed, so they said.
Al-Zajjaj said: The reality of this matter is that whatever a thing has only one of, is not dualized, and the word is in the plural, since the addition makes it clear; so when you say "I filled their bellies," it is known that the two have only two bellies.
Al-Tibi drew from this that comparing what is here with what is in the other verse is not correct, since each thief has two hands, so the plural is permissible, and that all the hands could be cut off by the apparent sense of the language; and Abu Hayyan said likewise. This is open to question, since the proof has shown that by "hand" is meant a specific hand, namely the right hand, and it is treated like the heart and the back, while "yad" is the name of the whole limb. For this the Kharijites went to the view that the cut is at the shoulder, while the Imamiyya hold that it is cut from the roots of the fingers, leaving the thumb and palm, and they narrated this from ʿAli, may God honour his face. They also argued for it by His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their hands﴾, since there is no doubt they write with their fingers. You know that this does not complete the argument for that claim, and the state of their narrations is too clear to be hidden. The majority hold that the cut is at the wrist (rusgh).
Al-Baghawi and Abu Nu'aym in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba related from the hadith of al-Harith ibn Abi ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a: "That he, upon him be prayer and peace, was brought a thief and ordered that his right hand be cut off from him."
The addressee of His saying, glorified: ﴿cut off﴾ is, according to al-Bahr, the Messenger (ﷺ), or the rulers such as the sultan and whoever is authorized to carry out the prescribed punishments, or the judges and rulers, or the believers; these are four views. The feminine thief is not subsumed under the masculine thief by way of precedence (taghlib), as is well known in such cases, for greater attention to clarity and for intensifying the deterrence.
﴿A recompense﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu): i.e., "cut off for the recompense," or as an infinitive of "cut off" from its meaning, or for an implied verb of the same root. It is also permitted to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "cut off," meaning "requiting them" ﴿for what they earned﴾, i.e., because of their earning, or what they earned of theft which is carried out by the hands.
His saying: ﴿an exemplary punishment﴾ is also an object of purpose, as most grammarians said, and al-Samin said it is in the accusative as "recompense" is.
