The first possibility was objected to as not good, since the object of purpose does not multiply without conjunction or following, because it is in the sense of the preposition "li" (for), so it would be like two prepositions with one governing verb, which is impermissible. It was answered that the exemplary punishment is a kind of recompense, so it is an apposition to it. Al-Halabi and some verifiers said: conjunction was omitted only to indicate that the cutting is for the recompense, and the recompense is for the exemplary punishment and for the prevention of repetition; accordingly it is an object of purpose nested within another, like nested circumstantial clauses, and with this the objection is also dismissed, and it is good.
Izam al-Milla said: it was not conjoined because the cause is the two together, as in "this is sweet-sour." "Recompense" indicates that it contains the right of the servant, and "exemplary punishment" indicates that it contains the right of God Exalted. The flaw in this is not hidden, so consider it.
It is also related from some grammarians that they permitted the object of purpose to multiply without following, and then the question does not arise at all. His saying, Exalted: ﴿from God﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as an attribute of "exemplary punishment," meaning an exemplary punishment proceeding from Him, Exalted.
﴿And God is Mighty﴾ in legislating deterrence ﴿Wise﴾ in prescribing amputation; or Mighty in His vengeance against the thief and others among the people of disobedience, Wise in His obligations and His prescribed punishments. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for what has passed more than once.

Among the strange things is that it is reported from Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) that he recited: (والسَّرَّقُ والسَّرَّقَةُ) without the alif and with a shadda on the rā’, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this reading is a corruption (taṣḥīf), because al-sāriq and al-sāriqa were written in the muṣḥaf without an alif. It was also said in their explanation that they are the plural of sāriq and sāriqa, but it was said: this plural form is not reported in the feminine plural, so if it were said that they are a form of intensity (ṣīghat mubālagha), it would be closer.

The heretic al-Maʿarrī objected to the obligation of cutting off the hand for stealing a small amount, and said:

A hand that was valued at five hundred gold dinars as blood-money, why was it cut off for a quarter of a dinar?
It is arbitrary; for us there is nothing but silence about it, and that we seek refuge with our Lord from the Fire.

But ʿAlam al-Dīn al-Sakhāwī answered him, and how excellent his answer is, with his words:

The honour of trustworthiness: its price is highest and cheapest is the humiliation of betrayal, so understand the wisdom of the Creator.

In Ibn ʿArabī's Aḥkām it is stated that the punishment of the thief in the law of those before us was enslavement, and it was said that this lasted until the time of Mūsā (peace be upon him) and was abrogated (nusikha). According to the first view, our law abrogates what came before it; according to the second, it confirms the abrogation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 5, verse 39:

﴿Whoever repents﴾ among the thieves, turning to Allah, the Exalted, ﴿after his wrongdoing﴾, which is his theft. The explicit mention of it serves to show the greatness of Allah's favor by reminding one of the greatness of his offense. ﴿And makes amends﴾ for his affair by freeing himself from the consequences, by returning the stolen property if possible, or by seeking the pardon of its owner (istihlal), or by spending it in the way of Allah, the Exalted, if he cannot identify the owner. It has also been said that the meaning is: and he does a good, beautiful deed, namely that he remains steadfast in repentance, as is required of him.

﴿Then indeed Allah will accept his repentance﴾, that is, He will accept his repentance, so He will not punish him in the Hereafter. As for the amputation (qat'), repentance does not remove it according to us, because it involves the right of the one from whom the property was stolen. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, in one of his two opinions, it is removed. There is no concealing what this sentence contains of encouragement for the sinner to repent. This is reinforced by His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and this is in the position of giving a reason for what precedes it. It also contains an indication that the acceptance of repentance is an act of grace from Him, the Exalted.

[Page 135]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 40:

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to receive it. Its connection with what precedes it, according to what al-Tabarsi said, is the connection of argument and clarification concerning the truth of what came before of promise and threat. Shaykh al-Islam said: what is meant by it is to cite this as evidence of His power, exalted is He, over what will follow of punishment and forgiveness in the most eloquent and complete manner. That is: Do you not know that Allah, exalted is He, possesses the overpowering authority and the dominating control, which necessitate complete power over the total disposal of both of them, and over what they contain, by creating and annihilating, giving life and causing death, and beyond that, according to what His will requires. The prepositional phrase "lahu" is a predicate placed first, and "mulku al-samawati" is the subject; the sentence is the predicate of "anna," and it together with what is within its scope occupies the place of the two objects of "ta'lam" according to the majority of scholars. The repetition of the predication is to strengthen the ruling.

As for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills﴾, it is either a confirmation that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, glorified is He, or another predicate of "anna." The apparent order, in light of the hadith "My mercy has preceded My wrath," would be to mention forgiveness before punishment. It is reversed here because punishment is for the one who persists in theft, and forgiveness is for the one who repents from it. Theft was mentioned first in the verse, then repentance was mentioned after it, so this subsequent clause follows the order of the preceding one. Or, because punishment here means amputation, and forgiveness means overlooking the right of Allah, exalted is He; the first occurs in this world and the second in the Hereafter, so it is placed in the order of existence. Or, because the context is one of warning, or because the intended aim is to describe Him, exalted is He, with power, and power in punishing whom He wills is more manifest than power in forgiving, since there is no reluctance in forgiving on the part of the one forgiven, whereas in punishment there is clear reluctance.

﴿And Allah is over all things Powerful﴾, so He is capable of what has been mentioned of punishment and forgiveness. The sentence is a concluding clause confirming the content of what precedes it. The manner of its manifestation is like daylight.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 41 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾. He (ﷺ) is addressed with the title of Messenger to honour him and to signal what necessitates the absence of grief. Al-musara'ah fi al-shay' (hastening toward something) means falling into it quickly and eagerly. The choice of the preposition fi ("in") over ila ("to") indicates that they are firmly settled in disbelief and do not leave it. They only move, through haste, from some of its branches and rulings to others, such as displaying loyalty to the polytheists, showing the effects of plotting against Islam, and similar things.

Referring to them by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) points to the cause of grief through what its clause contains. Although this apparently forbids the disbelievers from grieving him (ﷺ) by their hastening into disbelief, in reality it is a prohibition to him (ﷺ) from being affected by this and from caring about it. Its purpose is merely consolation in the most emphatic and eloquent form, for forbidding the causes and beginnings of a thing that lead to it is a forbidding of the thing itself by demonstrative argument and a cutting of it at its root.

It is also read as yuhzinka (with a dammah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the zayn, from ahzana), which is a dialect form. It is also read as yusri'una, from the expression asra'a fihi al-shayb ("grey hair appeared in him quickly"), meaning that he fell into it quickly. That is: do not grieve, and do not care about their rushing into disbelief, out of caution, as it has been said, against their evil and their loyalty to the polytheists,
(Page 136)
for Allah the Exalted is your Supporter against them, or out of compassion for them, since they were not granted success in guidance; for Allah guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills. ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths﴾ is an explanation of "those who race to disbelief." Abu al-Baqa' said that it is connected to a deleted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of yusari'un or from the relative pronoun, meaning: being among those who... etc. The preposition bi- is connected to qalu ("they said"), not to amanna ("we believed"), because the latter's invalidity is evident. Its connection to amanna is in the sense of: with their mouths, i.e., they believe in what they utter with their mouths, without their hearts being attached to it, which is something that anyone with even minimal discernment should not pay attention to.

﴿And their hearts have not believed﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) from the pronoun in qalu. It has been said that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with qalu. The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among those who are Jews﴾ are coordinated with ﴿among those who said﴾, and with this the division of those who race ahead is completed into two groups: hypocrites and Jews. Then His words, Exalted is He, ﴿who listen to falsehood﴾ are the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: they are listeners. The pronoun refers to both groups, or to those who race ahead. It has been permitted that it refers to those who are Jews, but this was objected to on the grounds that it undermines the general scope of the forthcoming threat and its beginnings for everyone, as you will see, Allah willing.

Similarly, many have made ﴿and among those who﴾ and so on a predicate, with ﴿who listen﴾ being an attribute of a deleted subject, meaning: and among them is a people who listen to its delivery, pointing to the exclusivity of what has been enumerated of the ugly deeds and their consequences of worldly and otherworldly calamities as belonging to them. Moreover, it has been read as sammaʿin in the accusative, as a form of censure, and this clearly indicates that coordination is more preferred. Therefore, that is the correct reading. The lam is for emphasis, as in His words: ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾. It has also been said that the lam is to imply the meaning of acceptance in listening, meaning: they accept what the rabbis fabricate of falsehood about Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ), and the distortion of His Book. Al-Shihab objected to this on the grounds that it implies that listening was interpreted as acceptance only so that it could govern the lam.

Al-Zajjaj had said: it is said, "Do not listen to so-and-so," meaning, do not accept (from him). From this comes "Allah hears whoever praises Him," meaning, He accepts his praise. The words of al-Jawhari contradict this as well, and imply that it is not based on implication. ʿIsam al-Millah said: acceptance is also transitive by itself, for in al-Qamus: qabilahu, like ʿamilahu, and taqabbalahu, mean akhadhahu ("took it"). Yes, listening in the sense of acceptance is transitive with the lam in the sense of min ("from"), as in "Allah hears whoever praises Him," meaning, Allah accepted from whoever praised Him. But this lam enters the one from whom something is heard, not the thing heard.

It has also been permitted that the lam is for causation, with the object deleted, meaning: listeners to your speech in order to lie about you concerning it, by distorting it through addition, subtraction, substitution, and alteration, or [listeners to] the speech of people circulating among themselves in order to lie, by spreading news of the killing of believers and the defeat of their expeditions, or something similar that causes them harm. Whatever the case, the sentence is a new clause, functioning, as has been said, as a justification for the prohibition, or it is directed merely toward censure, as the accusative reading indicates.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿listeners on behalf of another people who have not come to you﴾ are a second predicate for the subject deleted from the first, and an explanation of what is meant by lying, given the reading of emphasis and implication. The lam here is like its counterpart in "Allah hears whoever praises Him." The meaning: exaggerating in accepting the speech of another people. Shaykh al-Islam chose this reading.

It has been permitted that it is the lam of cause: listeners to his speech (ﷺ) that issues from him, in order to lie about him on behalf of another people. The meaning is that they were spies on him (ﷺ) for those people. This was narrated from al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj, and Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i chose it. Nothing in the composition prevents it, and it is not far-fetched.

Yes, what has been said, that the lam may be connected to lying, with the second sammaʿun being a repetition for emphasis, meaning: listeners in order to lie for another people, is far-fetched. ﴿Other﴾ is an attribute of ﴿people﴾, and the clause ﴿who have not come to you﴾ is another attribute. The meaning: they did not attend your presence. It has been said that it is a metaphor meaning that they were not able to look at you, and this indicates the intensity of their hatred for him and the extremity of their enmity. The possibility that it is an attribute of
(Page 137)
sammaʿun (listeners), meaning: listeners who did not intend to come to you, but intended to listen in order to relay to another people matters that should not be paid attention to, is also possible.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They distort words after their places﴾ are another attribute of ﴿people﴾. They are described first by their difference from the listeners, to draw attention to their independence and originality in opinion; then by their not attending the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), signalling the completeness of their insolence in error, or by their inability to look at him (ﷺ), signalling what has been mentioned above; then by their continuing to distort, to explain the extremity of their arrogance, obstinacy, and audacity against Allah the Exalted, and to specify the lie that the listeners heard, in some respects, as the apparent meaning indicates.

It has been said that the clause is a new sentence, having no place in grammatical analysis, condemning their vile acts. It has also been said that it is the predicate of a deleted subject referring to the people, or to both groups. The meaning: they deviate and remove the Torah, or the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ), or both, or the word in general, according to one opinion, from the places where it was placed, either verbally by neglecting it or changing its arrangement, or in meaning by applying it to what is not intended and placing it in a context where it does not belong.

From here the rationale for the Exalted's words ﴿after its places﴾ rather than ﴿from its places﴾ becomes clear. ʿIsam al-Millah said: the inclusion of the word "after" serves to indicate that the words have been relocated to a position lower than where they were placed, since this is the nullification of the beneficial by the harmful, not by the beneficial or the more beneficial. So it is as if the distorter stands at a position lower than the place of the word, and moves it to his own position. This far-fetched interpretation is not hidden.

Some said: "from" indicates the starting point, and the word "after" indicates that the distortion moves from what is distant to a position further away, and there is in this an exaggeration in censure that is not hidden. Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) read: ﴿They distort words away from their places﴾.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿they say﴾ are like the preceding clause in its possibilities. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿distort﴾. It has been permitted that it is, like the one before it, an attribute of ﴿listeners﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in it. Shaykh al-Islam objected to this, saying that it is in no way possible at all. How can it be, when the content of the speech itself shows that its speaker is among those who do not attend the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ), while the addressee is among those who attend? How could the listeners, who frequently visit him (ﷺ), say it to someone who never approaches his presence, certainly? To claim that the listeners said it to their descendants who mixed with the Muslims is an obvious contrivance that undermines the eloquence of the noble composition.

Therefore, the truth from which there is no escape, and upon which most exegetes have proceeded, is that those who distort and those who say it are the other people, meaning: they say to their followers, the listeners to them, ﴿If you are given this﴾ from the Messenger's side (ﷺ), as is apparent, ﴿then take it﴾ and act upon its ruling, for it conforms to the truth; ﴿but if you are not given it﴾ from his side, but are given something else, ﴿then beware﴾ of accepting it, and keep yourselves and it away, or beware of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In arranging the command to beware upon the mere absence of giving the distorted matter, there is an exaggeration and a warning that is not hidden.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, and others narrated, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said: "Two groups of the Jews: one of them had overpowered the other in the Jahiliyyah, until they agreed and reconciled on the condition that for every slain man whom the mighty group killed from the humble group, the blood-money (diyah) would be fifty wasq (a unit of measure), and for every slain man whom the humble group killed from the mighty group, the blood-money would be a hundred wasq. They remained upon this until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, and both groups became humbled at the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had not yet prevailed over them that day. Then the humble group killed a man from the mighty group, and the mighty group sent to the humble group: 'Send us a hundred wasq.' The humble group said: 'Has this ever happened between two tribes, whose religion is one, whose lineage is one, and whose land is one, and the blood-money of some of them is half the blood-money of others? We only gave you this as oppression from you and force upon us. But now that Muhammad (ﷺ) has come, we will not give you that.' War was almost about to erupt between them. Then they agreed to make the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) an arbiter between them. The mighty group thought, and said: 'By Allah, Muhammad will not give them, from us, double what he gives them from us.' They spoke the truth, for they had given it to us only as oppression and subjugation of them. So send to Muhammad (ﷺ) someone to inform you of his opinion. If he gives you what you want, you will make him the judge; but if he does not give it to you, you will be wary of him and will not make him the judge. So they sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) some hypocrites to test the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) opinion for them. When they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah the Exalted informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of all their affairs and what they intended. So He revealed: ﴿O Messenger﴾ (the verse)." According to this, the matter of distortion is not clearly part of the narrative.

And Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "The rabbis of the Jews gathered in the *bayt al-midras* (the house of study) when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina. A man had committed adultery after his marriage (*ihsan*) with a Jewish woman, who was also married. They said: 'Send this man and this woman to Muhammad (ﷺ) and ask him how the ruling is concerning them. Make him their judge. If he judges between them with your method of *tajbiyah*, which is flogging with a rope of palm fiber smeared with pitch, and then blackening their faces and mounting them on two donkeys with their faces toward the rear of the donkeys, then follow him. But if he judges between them with something else, then he is a prophet, so beware of him, lest he strip you of what is in your hands.' They came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, this man has committed adultery after his marriage with a woman who was also married. Judge between them, for we have made you the judge concerning them.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked until he came to their rabbis in the house of study, and he said: 'O assembly of Jews, bring out to me your scholars.' They brought out to him 'Abdullah ibn Suriya, Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, and Wahb ibn Yahudha. They said: 'These are our scholars.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) questioned them, and then their affair reached the point where they said to 'Abdullah ibn Suriya: 'This is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in the Torah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then took him aside. He was a young man, one of the youngest of them in age. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pressed the question upon him, saying: 'O Ibn Suriya, I adjure you by Allah, and I remind you of His days among the Children of Israel. Do you know that Allah has ruled, in the Torah, concerning one who committed adultery after his marriage, with stoning?' He said: 'By Allah, yes. O Abu al-Qasim, indeed they know that you are a prophet sent by Allah, but they envy you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then went out and ordered that the two be stoned, and they were stoned at the gate of his mosque." Then Ibn Suriya disbelieved afterward and denied the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah revealed: "O Messenger..." etc.

And al-Humaydi in his *Musnad*, Abu Dawud, and Ibn Majah related from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "A man from the people of Fadak committed adultery. They wrote to some Jews in Medina: 'Ask Muhammad (ﷺ) about this. If he orders you to flog, then take it from him, and if he orders you to stone, then do not take it from him.' They asked him about it, and he said: 'Send to me the two most knowledgeable men among you.' They brought a one-eyed man called Ibn Suriya, and another. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: 'Is there not in your possession the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I adjure you by the One who split the sea for the Children of Israel, shaded you with the clouds, saved you from the household of Pharaoh, sent down the Torah upon Moses (peace be upon him), and sent down the manna and quail upon the Children of Israel: what do you find in the Torah concerning the matter of stoning?' One of them said to the other: 'I have never been adjured with the like of this.' They said: 'We find that repeated glancing is suspicion, embracing is suspicion, and kissing is suspicion. When four witnesses testify that they saw him inserting and withdrawing it like a kohl stick entering a kohl pot, then stoning is obligatory.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It is so.' He then ordered that he be stoned, and he was stoned."

[Page 139]

As for the validity of the legally binding *ihsan* (marital condition) that necessitates stoning in the case of a disbeliever, it is as mentioned in the *Furu'* (the works of positive law, lit. "branches"). Perhaps this is the view of those who stipulate Islam, such as Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was based on the law of Moses (peace be upon him), or that it was before the revelation of the *jizyah* (poll tax). So let it be pondered.

﴿And whomever Allah wills to test (*fitnah*)﴾, i.e., His punishment, as related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, and preferred by al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim; or His destruction, as related from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak; or His disgrace and exposure by revealing what he conceals, as transmitted from al-Zajjaj; or His testing of him by what He afflicts him with of the duty of upholding His limits, so he repels that and distorts it, as has been said, but this is not correct.

The intended meaning is general, and those mentioned are included in it in the first instance. The absence of an explicit statement that they are of this kind is to indicate that it is evident and needs no mention. ﴿then you will not be able to avail for him﴾, i.e., you will not be able to do anything for him, ﴿anything from Allah﴾, in repelling that trial. The *fa'* (فَ) is a responsive particle (*jawabiyyah*), and (*min Allah*, مِنَ اللَّهِ, "from Allah") is connected to (*tamliku*, تَمْلِكُ, "you possess") or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of (*shay'an*, شَيْئًا, "anything"), since it is originally its descriptor, meaning: anything coming from the kindness of Allah, Exalted is He; or it is a substitute (*badal*) for (*Allah*). (*Shay'an*, شَيْئًا, "anything") is the direct object of (*tamliku*). Some grammarians permitted that it be an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), and the sentence is then a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it, or explaining that those people never cease from the aforementioned vices.

﴿Those﴾, i.e., the aforementioned hypocrites and Jews. The meaning of distance in the demonstrative is because they have been referred to repeatedly. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is His, Glorified is He, saying: ﴿those whose hearts Allah did not will to purify﴾ from the filth of disbelief and the impurity of misguidance. The sentence is a new clause explaining that His will for their trial is conditional upon their own bad choice, which requires it, and is not an initial act from Him, Glorified is He. In it, as in the preceding one, according to one of the interpretations, is evidence against the claim of the Mu'tazilah that evils are not by the will of Allah, Exalted is He, and that they come only from the servants.

As for the statement of some of them that the meaning is: He did not will to purify their hearts from distress by blame, contempt, and punishment; or He did not will to purify them from disbelief by judging them to be free of it and praised with faith, as al-Balkhi said, this is not something that one with even minimal taste for the styles of speech would proceed to.

It is strange that al-Zamakhshari, when he saw what was mentioned contradicted his doctrine, said: "The meaning of (*man yurid Allahu fitnatahu*, مَن يُرِدِ اللَّهُ فِتْنَتَهُ, "whomever Allah wills to test") is whomever He wills to leave tested and forsaken (*khidhlanahu*). (*Fa-lan tamlika lahu min Allahi shay'an*, فَلَنْ تَمْلِكَ لَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا, "then you will not be able to avail for him anything from Allah") means you will not be able to avail for him anything of the kindness of Allah and His success. The meaning of (*lam yurid Allahu an yutahhira qulubahum*, لَمْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أنْ يُطَهِّرَ قُلُوبَهم, "Allah did not will to purify their hearts") is that He did not will to bestow upon them of His favors that by which He would purify their hearts, because they are not among its people, since He knows that this does not benefit them or take effect in them." End of quotation.

Ibn al-Munir responded to him with his words:

*How long he stammers, while the truth is clear!*

This verse, as you see, conforms to the creed of the People of the Sunnah that Allah, Exalted is He, willed the trial of those who are tested, and did not will to purify their hearts from the filth of trial and the stain of disbelief. It is not as the Mu'tazilah claim, that Allah, Exalted is He, did not will trial for anyone, and willed for everyone faith and purity of heart; that what occurs of trials is contrary to His will, Glorified is He; and that the purity of the hearts of the disbelievers, which does not occur, is willed but simply did not happen. This verse and its like are sufficient for them, even if Allah, Exalted is He, willed to purify their hearts from the stain of innovations. *"Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?"* (Qur'an 47:24). How grievous is al-Zamakhshari's diversion of this verse from its apparent meaning with his words: "Allah, Exalted is He, did not will to grant them His kindness, since He knows that His kindness does not take effect." Exalted is Allah above what the wrongdoers say! And if the kindness of Allah, Exalted is He, does not take effect nor benefit, then whose kindness does benefit? And whose will takes effect?

*Beyond Allah there is no hope for the servant.*

End of quotation. Their evasion from this is difficult.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾. As for the hypocrites, their disgrace is their exposure and the tearing away of their veil, by the manifestation of their hypocrisy among the Muslims, and the increase of their distress with the greater spread of Islam, the strengthening of its power, and the elevation of its word. As for the disgrace of the Jews, it is humiliation, the *jizyah*, and public exposure by the manifestation of their lying in concealing the text of the Torah, and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir from their homes.

The indefiniteness of (*khizyun*, خِزْيٌ, "disgrace") is for magnification. It is the subject, and (*lahum*, لَهم, "for them") is its predicate, and (*fi al-dunya*, فِي الدُّنْيا, "in this world") is connected to what the predicate implies of settledness. The sentence is a resumptive clause based on a question arising from their conditions that necessitate punishment, as if it were said: "What then is their punishment for that?" So it was said: "For them in this world is disgrace." The situation is similar in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and for them in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., in addition to worldly disgrace, ﴿is a great punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured, which is eternal abiding in the Fire, together with what has been prepared for them therein. The pronoun in (*lahum*, لَهم, "for them") in both clauses refers to (*ulaika*, أُولَئِكَ, "those") of the hypocrites and Jews together. It is said that it refers to the Jews specifically, and it is said: it refers to them if the sentence is resumed with His statement, Exalted is He, (*wa-min alladhina hadu*, وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هادُوا, "and among those who are Jews"); otherwise it refers to both groups.

The repetition, despite the unity of the referent, is for the increase of confirmation and emphasis, and for this reason His statement, Exalted is He, was repeated:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 42:**

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾. It has been said: the apparent meaning is that this is an explanation (ta'lil) of His words, exalted is He, ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, and so on; or it is a preparation (tawti'ah) for what follows. Or the intended meaning of "falsehood" here is false claims, and what was mentioned earlier includes what the rabbis fabricate. The separation between the two phrases supports this.

﴿Devourers of the unlawful gain (suht)﴾, that is, the forbidden. It comes from "sahatahu," when he uprooted it entirely. According to al-Zajjaj, the forbidden is called suht because it is followed by the punishment of uprooting and ruin. Al-Jubba'i said: because there is no blessing for its people, so they are usually destroyed with a destruction that uproots them. Al-Khalil said: because in the way of earning it there is shame, so it strips a person of his honour (muruwwah). The intended meaning here, according to the well-known view, is bribery in judgement. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every flesh that grows from unlawful gain, the Fire is more deserving of it." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the unlawful gain?" He said: "Bribery in judgement."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The gifts of rulers are unlawful gain."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Masruq, who said: I said to Umar ibn al-Khattab (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu): "Do you consider bribery in judgement to be of the unlawful gain?" He said: "No, but it is disbelief. The unlawful gain is only that a man has standing and position with the ruler, and another man has a need from the ruler, and he does not fulfil his need until he gives him a gift."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ali (karrama Allahu wajhahu): that he was asked about unlawful gain, and he said: "Bribery." It was said to him: "In judgement?" He said: "That is disbelief."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in his Sunan something similar from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Six things are of the unlawful gain: the bribe of the leader, which is the worst of all of them; the price of a dog; the stallion's fee; the wages of a prostitute; the earnings of a cupper; and the gift of a soothsayer." Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, in the narration of Ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi from him, counted other things besides these.

It has been said: because of the gravity of the matter of bribery, those who limited themselves to it did so. And it has come through several chains from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who gives a bribe, the one who takes a bribe, and the broker who walks between them are cursed."

And because the matter has grown severe in these times through taking bribes, the order was issued from the presence of our master, the shadow of Allah, exalted is He, over creation, and renewer of the order of the customs of the Shari'ah and the Haqiqah, the just Sultan Mahmud Khan, may he always remain under the protection of Allah, exalted is He, wherever he may be, in the year one thousand two hundred and fifty-four, to hold the taker of bribes and his two brothers to account in the most complete manner, and to set a limit for gifts, so that they are not used as a means to bribery, as many of the rulers do today.

For Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "After me there will be governors who will make lawful wine, nabidh, the rigging of prices by charity, and unlawful gain by means of gifts, and killing by way of admonition. They will kill the innocent so that they may please the common people. Respite will be given to them so that they increase in sin."

This. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿al-suhut﴾ with two dammas, and they are two dialects, like "al-unq" and "al-unuq."

Page 141

It was also read ﴿al-sahtu﴾ with a fatha on the sin, in the form of the verbal noun, meaning the thing that is uprooted, like "al-sayd" in the sense of "al-masid." And ﴿al-sahatu﴾ with two fathas, and ﴿al-sihtu﴾ with a kasra on the sin.

﴿So if they come to you﴾: this is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the fa' is a fa' of explanation (faṣīḥah), meaning: if their condition is as explained, ﴿if they come to you﴾ seeking judgement from you concerning the disputes that have arisen among them, ﴿then judge between them﴾ by what Allah has shown you, ﴿or turn away from them﴾, not caring for them and not troubled by them. This, as you see, is an option given to him (ﷺ) between the two matters, and it conflicts with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has sent down﴾. The verification of the position, as al-Jassas mentioned in his book Al-Ahkam, is that the scholars differed. A group held that the option is abrogated (mansukh) by the other verse (naskh: abrogation), and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas, and most of the early generation (salaf) followed this view. They said: he (ﷺ) was initially given the option, then he was commanded, peace be upon him, to enforce the rulings upon them, and such a thing cannot be said on the basis of personal opinion. It was also said: this verse concerns those who have not been granted a covenant of protection (dhimmah), and the other verse concerns the people of the dhimmah, so there is no abrogation. Some affirmed it in the sense of specification (takhsis), because whoever pays the jizya (poll tax) has the rulings of Islam applied to him. This too was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

Our companions said: the people of the dhimmah are held to the rulings of Islam in sales, inheritance and all other contracts, except in the sale of wine and pork, for they are left to it, and they are prevented from fornication like the Muslims, for they have been forbidden from it. They are not stoned, because they are not muhsan (protected by marriage). The report about stoning mentioned earlier has already had its interpretation explained.

It has been disputed concerning their marriages. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are left to them. Muhammad and Zufar differed with him in some of that. We have no objection to them before they agree to our rulings. Whenever they agree to them and bring their disputes to us, it becomes obligatory to enforce the rulings upon them. The full detail is in the books of furu'.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾: this is an explanation of the condition of the two matters after his (ﷺ) being given the option between them. The mention of the case of turning away first is to hasten to show that there is no harm in it, since it could be a cause of the arising of enmity, which requires confronting the harm. So the meaning comes to this: if you turn away from them and do not judge between them, and they become hostile to you and intend your harm, ﴿then they will not harm you﴾ by that ﴿at all﴾, for Allah, exalted is He, will protect you from their harm.

﴿And if you judge, then judge between them with justice﴾, that is, with the justice you were commanded to, which is what the Qur'an contains and what the Shari'ah of Islam comprises. And what was narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "If the cushion were folded for me, I would give fatwa to the People of the Torah by their Torah, and to the People of the Gospel by their Gospel," if it is authentic, the intended meaning of it is its necessary implication.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾, that is, those who are just, so He protects them from every disliked thing and magnifies their standing.

[Page 142]

"How can they make you judge when they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?" This is an expression of wonder at their making judgment the responsibility of one in whom they do not believe, while the ruling is explicitly stated in their own Book, which they claim to believe in. It also indicates that such appeal to judgment was not for the sake of knowing the truth, but for seeking the easier ruling. Even if that ruling is, in their claim, the judgment of Allah the Exalted, His statement "while they have the Torah" (﴿وعِنْدَهُمُ التَّوْراةُ﴾) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative) relating to the subject of "they make you judge." His statement "in which is the judgment of Allah" (﴿فِيها حُكْمُ اللَّهِ﴾) is a circumstantial clause relating to "the Torah," if "the Torah" is taken as raised by the adverbial phrase (ẓarf, a prepositional complement). That this is weak because the adverbial phrase does not depend on a preceding element is a mistake, since, as al-Samīn (al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī) said, it depends on the element it modifies (dhū al-ḥāl). However, he said: "Making 'the Torah' raised by the adverbial phrase introduced by the conjunction 'wa' is open to question," and perhaps its reason is that it makes it an independent sentence not dependent on anything, or that it is not connected with "wa." If "the Torah" is taken as the subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence), then the phrase is a circumstantial clause from its pronoun that is hidden in the predicate (khabar, the comment of a nominal sentence), because it is not valid, according to Sībawayh, for a circumstantial clause to come from the subject.

It has been said: it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), brought to explain that they have with them what suffices them from judgment. The word "the Torah" is treated as feminine, after its Arabization, in the manner of Arabic nouns that match it, such as "mawmāh" and "dawdāh."

"Then they turn away" (﴿ثُمَّ يَتَوَلَّوْنَ﴾) is a coordination with "they make you judge," and falls within the scope of the expression of wonder. This is because appealing to judgment, despite the presence of what contains the truth that makes judgment unnecessary, although it is a place for wonder and astonishment, is even more wonderful with turning away from that. The "then" (thumma) indicates delay in rank. Al-Ajhūrī permitted that the clause be a new sentence not falling under the scope of the expression of wonder, i.e., "then they turn away," meaning their custom, whenever the truth is made clear to them, is to turn away and withdraw. The first is preferable.

His statement, glory be to Him, "after that" (﴿مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾), i.e., after they have made you judge, is an explicit statement of what is already known, for the emphasis of astonishment and wonder. His statement, mighty and majestic is He, "and those are not believers" (﴿وما أُولَئِكَ بِالمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾), is a concluding clause that confirms the implication of what precedes it. The placing of the demonstrative noun "those" in the position of their pronoun is intended to bring them to mind with the ugly qualities they have been described with, indicating the cause of the ruling, along with an indication that they have been distinguished from others in this respect in the most complete distinction, until they were gathered into the rank of observable matters. That is: "and those" who are described by what was mentioned "are not believers" in their Book, because of their turning away from it, which points to the absence of inner acceptance of it at first, and of your judgment that agrees with it second. Or: they are not believers in you and in it. It has been said: this is information from Him, exalted is He, about those Jews that they do not believe in the Prophet (ﷺ) and in his judgment at all.

It has been said: the meaning is "and those are not the perfect ones," in mockery of them.

[p. 143 begins mid-passage; see below]

﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to confirm the increased enormity of the state of those Jews by explaining the supreme status of the Torah in the most complete manner. ﴿In it is guidance﴾, meaning direction for people to the truth. ﴿And light﴾, meaning illumination by which what was confusing and dark to them is made clear. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said.

Al-Zajjaj said: "(In it is guidance)" means an explanation of the ruling about which they came to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for a verdict. "(And light)" means an explanation that the matter of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is true. Perhaps generalising the guidance to refer to him, as in the words of Ibn ʿAbbas, is better, and what al-Zajjaj mentioned of the ruling falls under it at an initial level of inclusion.

The application of "light" to what is in the Torah is a figurative usage (majaz). Perhaps its application to this, rather than to the Qur'an, is based on the view that light is a term used with gradation (maqul bi'l-tashkik). It may also be said that its application to that by which the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) is explained, according to what al-Zajjaj said, is on account of the explained matter being connected to the first of the lights, without which the revolving sphere would not have been created (ﷺ). In that case the difference between the two applications is as clear as the morning. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), "guidance" is the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Torah, meaning: being in it is that. Similarly, the sentence ﴿by which the prophets judge﴾ is, according to one view, a circumstantial clause, though it is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah). However, most scholars hold that it is a resumed sentence explaining the high rank of the Torah and its lofty standing. By "the prophets" is meant those among them from Moses to Jesus (peace be upon them both), as narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim from Muqatil, and there were a thousand prophets between the two prophets (peace be upon them both).

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿIkrimah that the intended meaning is our Prophet (ﷺ) and those before him from the prophets of the Children of Israel (peace be upon them). On this basis, whoever said that the law of those before us is law for us, as long as it has not been abrogated (naskh), built his argument from the verse. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is for the reason already mentioned more than once. The intended meaning is: the prophets judge by its rulings.

﴿Who submitted﴾ is a descriptive attribute applied to "the prophets," as has been said, for the purpose of praise, and it applies to them openly. Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that praise is generally given through distinctive attributes by which the one praised is distinguished from others, whereas submission (islam) is a general matter that encompasses the nations of the prophets and their followers just as it encompasses them. Do you not see that it is not fitting, in praising the Prophet (ﷺ), to limit him to being a Muslim man, since the least of his followers are like that? He then said: the correct view, and Allah knows best,

[p. 144]

is that an attribute may be mentioned to magnify it in itself, and to make it known when it is ascribed to someone of great rank, just as it is mentioned to draw attention to the rank of the one described. On this style the description of the prophets (peace be upon them) with righteousness occurs in more than one verse, to draw attention to the magnitude of righteousness, since it is made an attribute of the prophets (peace be upon them), and to urge ordinary people to strive to acquire its attribute. Likewise it was said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾. So He, glorified be He, informed about the near angels with the attribute of faith, to magnify its worth and to urge humans to enter into it, so that they may equal the near angels in this attribute. Otherwise, it is well known that the angels are simply believers. How could they not be, when they are "with their Lord," as stated in the report?

Then the Exalted, may He be high, said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾, meaning from among humankind, because the bond of brotherhood in faith is established between the two groups. Therefore, and Allah knows best, the description of the prophets in this verse with submission (islam) occurs to draw attention to it. The poet has rightly said: "The descriptions of the noble are the noblest of descriptions." Hassan, the versifier, in praising him (peace be upon him), said:

"I did not praise Muhammad with my words;
rather, I praised my words by Muhammad."

Submission, though it is among the most noble attributes, since its essence is knowing Allah as is required for Him, impossible for Him, and permissible in His judgment, nonetheless prophethood is more noble and more exalted, because it includes the generality of submission together with special gifts that language cannot contain. So if we did not go with the benefit mentioned for mentioning submission after prophethood, we would depart from the known rule of eloquence in the Noble Book and in the eloquent speech of the Arabs, which is ascent from the lower to the higher, not descent in the reverse. Do you not see how Abu al-Tayyib deviated from this path in his words:

"A sun whose forenoon is a crescent at night,
its pearls of pearls and its emeralds."

He descended from the sun to the crescent, and from the pearl to the emerald, so tongues chewed at the honour of his eloquence and tore the hide of his craft. So it is incumbent upon us to ponder the miraculous verses until our understanding attaches to the heights of their eloquence known to them. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right. End of quotation.

In al-Miftah and al-Takhlis there is an indication of what he mentioned, and al-Tibi's objection to it is not sound. Indeed, it may be said that whoever holds that these attributes praise the one they are applied to may claim that this is not objectionable if other benefits are intended together with the praise, such as drawing attention to the high rank of the Muslims here, and implicitly reproaching the Jews by showing that they are far removed from submission. Moreover, in eloquent speech, indeed in the most eloquent, the mention of a less eloquent attribute after a more eloquent one has occurred, and among that is "the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," where it contains a subtle point.

ʿIsam al-Milla said: submission for the Prophet is the perfection of praise, because submission by the one who is followed, to countless creatures, is an attribute above which there is none. It is possible that describing him with it here is an indication of the source of the ruling, so that the community preserves it, does not violate it, and does not suppose that the ruling belongs to prophethood. Apart from the Prophet (ﷺ), no one is excluded from this path. End of quotation. In this there is room for reflection, since ascent from the lower to the higher has not yet appeared, and the final outcome is a return to something like what was previously stated. So understand.

﴿For those who became Jews﴾, meaning repented from disbelief, as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said, and the intended meaning of them is the Jews, as al-Hasan said. The prepositional phrase is either related to "judge," meaning they judge among themselves; and the lam is either to indicate that the ruling is specific to them, whether it is for them or against them, as if it were said: for the sake of those who became Jews; or to indicate that it benefits the one judged against as well by removing responsibility from him; or to indicate the perfection of their contentment with it and their submission to it, as if it were a matter beneficial to both groups, and so there is an implicit reproach to the distorters. It was also said that it is of the type of ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾. Or it is related to "We sent down," and perhaps the intervening element is not a foreign one so as to cause harm. It was also said that it is related to "was sent down" in the passive form, with the agent omitted because the context indicates it, and the sentence is then parenthetical. On this view the verse is explicit in restricting "the prophets" to the prophets of the Children of Israel, since their being sent down to them does not necessarily entail that it is restricted to them. It was also said that the prepositional phrase is related to "guidance and light," though this involves separating a verbal noun from its object; it was said that it is related to an omitted term that serves as a descriptive attribute of both, meaning: guidance and light belonging to them. The words of al-Zajjaj may allow this and what came before it.

﴿And the rabbis and the scholars﴾, meaning the worshippers and the learned, as Qatadah said. Mujahid said: "the rabbis" are the learned jurists, who are above the scholars (al-ahbar). ʿAn Ibn Zayd: "the rabbis" are the rulers, and "the scholars" are the learned. The singular of "ahbar" is "habr," with a fatha or a kasra. Al-Farra' said: the most I have heard of it is with a kasra. It is derived from ornamenting and beautifying, for scholars adorn and beautify knowledge and make it clear. From this comes "al-hibr" with a kasra on the ha' only, meaning what is written with. This is a coordination with "the prophets," meaning they too judge by its rulings. The placement of the group being judged between the two coordinated terms, as Shaykh al-Islam said, indicates that the original basis for judging by it and compelling people to follow it is the prophets, while the rabbis and scholars are their successors and deputies in this, as the Exalted's words indicate: ﴿by what they were entrusted with﴾, meaning by what was entrusted to them from the prophets, which is the Torah, since they asked them to preserve it from alteration and change without restriction. There is no doubt that this entrustment from them (peace be upon them) indicates their succession in implementing its rulings without neglecting any part of it. The prepositional phrase is related to "judge," and "what" is a relative pronoun, and the plural pronoun refers to the rabbis and scholars.

The Exalted's words ﴿of the Book of Allah﴾ explain "what." In this indefiniteness and specification there is the evident magnification of the Torah's status in essence and in attribution. Also in it is emphasis on the obligation to preserve it and act by what is in it. The preposition "bi" attached to the relative is causal, so there is no requirement that two prepositions of the same meaning relate to one verb. The meaning is: the rabbis and scholars also judge by the Torah because of what they preserved from the Book of Allah, as their prophets enjoined on them and asked them to preserve it. The causality here is not intended in terms of its essence, but in terms of its being preserved, since linking their judgment to the relative clause indicates the causality of the preservation which necessarily follows what is in the relative clause of the entrustment to it. Some have thought that "what" means "a matter," and "from" explains an omitted object of "were entrusted," the meaning being: because of a matter with which they were entrusted, something from the Book of Allah. This is not something by which the Book of Allah should be interpreted. It was said that it is better to make "what" a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, so that the omission of a returning pronoun is avoided, and in that case it cannot be said that "from" explains it. Some permitted "bi-ma" to be a substitute for "bi-ha," with the preposition repeated because of the long separation, which is also permissible even without long separation. Some have referred the implicit subject pronoun to the prophets and those coordinated with them, so the one entrusted is then Allah, the Exalted, and the narrative of the reports (hadith al-anba') would not apply in that case. It was said that "the rabbis" is the subject of an omitted verb, the preposition is attached to it, and the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the rabbis and scholars judge by the ruling of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, which their prophets asked them to preserve from alteration.

﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾ is coordinated with "were entrusted." The meaning of "witnesses" is guardians, who protect it from anything of change or alteration encroaching upon its sacred boundary in any way. Or "witnesses" means witnesses that it is true.

The first interpretation is preferred because it implies that "the rabbis and scholars" would be guardians over themselves, not allowing themselves to change and distort the Torah, since a distorter could only be from among them and not from the common people. This, as you see, adds no further meaning. Referring the pronoun in "they were" to the prophets is something that barely can be permitted. It was said that it is coordinated with an omitted "judge," the intended meaning of which is recounting a past state: the rabbis and scholars judged by the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and were witnesses over it. On this view it is clearly permissible that witnessing is used figuratively for explaining, meaning clarifying what is hidden from it. The matter of transitivity with "over" is easy, and perhaps the intended meaning is something beyond judgment. It was said that the implicit subject pronoun here, like the previous one, refers to the prophets and those coordinated with them, and the coordination is either with "were entrusted" or with "judge."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

The misconception of some commentators, when one of them said, "and because of their being witnesses," that the conjunction is upon (mā) the relative pronoun, so that (kānū) is construed as a verbal noun (maṣdar, a noun derived from the verb), seems to intend a summary of the meaning. This is because what was mentioned is weak where the conjoined term is not an event (ḥadath). As for conjoining upon "the Book of God" by supposing a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī) so that the conjoined term falls under the command, it is as you see (fa-kamā tarā), which is far-fetched.

Returning the pronoun in (ʿalayhi) to the ruling of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning stoning, as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), is something that Arabic grammar rejects in some of the possibilities. Although it is grammatically permissible in another of them, it contradicts the apparent meaning, and there is no indication for it. Perhaps the intent of the scholar (al-Ḥabr) is to explain some of what the Book contains, to which they are witnesses. In sum, the possible readings of this verse are many.

﴿So do not fear the people﴾: this is addressed to the leaders and scholars of the Jews, by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. The prohibition also includes, by implication (dalāla), others than those addressed. The fa' (then) is the response to an omitted condition, meaning: if the matter is as has been mentioned, O rabbis, then do not fear the people, whoever they may be. Follow, in observing and preserving the rulings of the Torah, those who came before you among the prophets, the rabbanis (rabbinic teachers) and the rabbis, and do not deviate from that, and do not distort it out of fear of anyone. ﴿And fear Me﴾ in abandoning My command, for benefit and harm are in My hand; or in neglecting the rights of observing it, let alone attacking it with harm.

﴿And do not exchange My signs﴾: that is, do not substitute My signs, which are in it, by removing them from it, or by abandoning acting upon them, and take for yourselves ﴿a small price﴾ from bribery, status and the other worldly portions. For these, however great they may be, are small and base in themselves, especially compared with what is lost to them by disobeying the command. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held that the address is to the Muslims, and this is what the statement of al-Shaʿbi seems to indicate.

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿud (this is the preferred reading, as in al-Kashshaf) that the verse is general, and the fa' is in both readings a fa' faṣīḥa (a fa' that indicates an implied condition), meaning: and when you know what the prophets and rabbis were upon, and what the successors agreed upon regarding distortion and alteration for bribery and fear, then do not fear the people, and do not be like those latecomers who deviated. What the statement of some of the Arabic grammarians implies is that it is also a fa' faṣīḥa in this reading. The discussion of this kind of construction has already preceded, so recall it.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ of rulings, ﴿those are﴾: the demonstrative refers to (man), and the plural is used according to its meaning, just as the singular in the preceding is used according to its wording. It is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is the clause of His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿they are the disbelievers﴾.

It is also possible that (hum) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and (al-kāfirūna) is the predicate. The clause is then a tadhyīl (concluding statement) that confirms the content of what precedes in the most eloquent confirmation, and a warning against neglecting it in the strongest warning.

The Kharijites argued with this verse that the grave sinner (fāsiq) is a disbeliever and not a believer. The basis of their argument is that the word (man) in it is general, comprising everyone who does not judge by what Allah has revealed, so the sinner who affirms the truth is also included, since he is not judging by and acting upon what Allah has revealed. It is answered that the verse does not have its apparent sense, for judging, although it includes the actions of the heart and the limbs, is here meant as an action of the heart, namely affirmation (taṣdīq). There is no dispute about the disbelief of one who does not affirm what Allah has revealed. Also, the intent is the generality of negation by taking (mā) as a genus, and there is no doubt that one who does not judge by anything that Allah has revealed can only be one who does not affirm it, and there is no dispute about his disbelief.

Also, Ibn Manṣur, Abu al-Shaykh,

[Page 146]

and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that he said: "Allah only revealed ﴿and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers, the wrongdoers and the defiantly disobedient﴾ concerning the Jews specifically."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Salih, who said: "The three verses in al-Ma'ida, ﴿and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ etc., contain nothing that applies to the people of Islam; they are about the disbelievers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿIkrima, and Ibn Jarir from al-Ḍaḥḥak, something similar.

Perhaps their being described by the three attributes is due to different considerations: for their denial of that they are described as disbelievers; for their placing the ruling in other than its place they are described as wrongdoers; and for their departure from the truth they are described as defiantly disobedient. Or they are described by these attributes according to their conditions and states that accompany their refusal to judge, so at times they were in a state that requires disbelief, and at other times in a state that requires wrongdoing or defiant disobedience.

Abu Ḥumayd and others narrated from al-Shaʿbi that he said: "The three verses in al-Ma'ida: the first of them is for this nation, the second is about the Jews, and the third is about the Christians." It follows from this that the believers would be in a worse state than the Jews and Christians. However, it has been said that when disbelief is attributed to believers it is understood as intensification and severity, while when a disbeliever is described with defiant disobedience or wrongdoing, it indicates his excess and rebellion in it.

This is supported by what Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), concerning the disbelief in the first of the three: "It is not the disbelief you are thinking of; it is not disbelief that removes one from the religion; it is a lesser disbelief." The apparent meaning is that this is like a general address to the Jews and others, and it is expressed in the form of severe warning; or one adopts one of the two answers. The difference in the descriptions is due to the difference in considerations. The latter two, according to some verifiers, also mean disbelief, by interpreting them as complete defiant disobedience and complete wrongdoing.

And what al-Ḥakim (who authenticated it), ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ḥudhayfa (may Allah be pleased with him), that "the three verses were mentioned in his presence, and a man said: this is about the Children of Israel. Ḥudhayfa said: What a fine brotherhood you have with the Children of Israel! If you have all the sweetness and they have all the bitterness! No, by Allah, you will surely follow their path step by step (qadda al-shirāk)." This may be an inclination on his part toward the view of generality, and it may be, as has been said, an inclination toward the view that it applies to Muslims. And it was narrated the first (view) from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn (may Allah be pleased with both of them), except that he said: "It is a disbelief that is not like the disbelief of polytheism, a defiant disobedience that is not like the defiant disobedience of polytheism, and a wrongdoing that is not like the wrongdoing of polytheism."

Now, some of the knowers (ʿārifīn) have spoken about what is indicated in some of these verses, and said: (﴿O you who believe, fear Allah﴾) that is, fear Him, glory be to Him, by purifying your souls from blameworthy character traits (﴿and seek the means of access to Him﴾), that is, seek nearness to Him, the Exalted, by adorning yourselves with praiseworthy traits (﴿and strive in His cause﴾) by erasing the attributes and passing away into the Essence (﴿that you may succeed﴾), that is, so that you may attain the goal. It has also been said: seeking the means is drawing near to Him by means of His past beneficence and His great mercy, and this is in the manner of his saying:

O generosity of Maʿn, convey my need on my behalf,
for there is no intercessor to Maʿn other than him.

(﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved, even if they had all that is in the earth﴾), that is, what is in the lower direction, (﴿and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection﴾), the greatest (Day), (﴿it would not be accepted from them﴾), because it is a cause of increasing veiling and distance, and nothing benefits there except what is in the higher direction of knowledge and luminous realities.

(﴿And the thief, male and female﴾), that is, the one who takes from the souls, and the one who takes from the psychic powers the desires that are forbidden to them (﴿cut off their hands﴾), that is, restrain them by severing their capacity with the sword of striving and the knife of discipline (as a recompense for what they earned), that is, from taking what is not lawful for them to take (﴿as an exemplary punishment﴾), that is, a punishment from Allah, Mighty and Majestic (﴿listeners to falsehood﴾), and the whisperings of the soul's devil (﴿listeners to other people﴾), who are the psychic powers (﴿who have not come to you﴾), that is, who do not submit to you,

[Page 147]

or: listeners to people who establish evil traditions (﴿they distort words﴾), which are the divine determinations (﴿from their places﴾), so they remove them from what they indicate of the existence of the true Reality; or they change the laws of the Shariʿa by deceptions of nature, like one who interprets the Qur'an and the hadiths according to his own desire. What we are dealing with is not of this kind, as those veiled ones claim, because that happens only by denying that the apparent meaning is what Allah intends, and restricting His intent, glory be to Him, to these interpretations. We disown that before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for it is plain disbelief. Rather, we say: the intent is the apparent meaning, and by it Allah has required His creatures to worship Him, but in it there is an indication to other things that the bounds of enumeration cannot encompass; what has been mentioned is likely to be only some of them.

(﴿And whoever Allah desires to test, you cannot avail him anything against Allah﴾). Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: whoever Allah veils from the benefits of his times, no one can bring him to Him. (﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not desire to purify﴾), that is, through watchfulness and attentiveness. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the purity of the heart lies in two things: removing envy and deceit, and having good opinion of the community of Muslims. (﴿They are consumers of unlawful gain﴾), which is what they eat by means of their religion. (﴿So if they come to you, judge between them﴾) as a physician for their disease, if you see that treatment is a cause of their healing. (﴿Or turn away from them﴾) if you are certain that cure is unattainable because of their wretchedness. (And if you judge, judge between them with justice), that is, treat them according to what they deserve and what their disease requires. The discussion of the remaining verses is clear, and Allah is the One who grants success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 45:

﴿And We prescribed﴾ is coordinated with (We sent down the Torah). The meaning is: We decreed and obligated. ﴿upon them﴾, i.e., upon those who became Jews (al-ladhina hadu). In the codex of Ubayy it reads: (and We sent down upon the Children of Israel). ﴿therein﴾, i.e., in the Torah. The prepositional phrase is connected to (We prescribed). It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: We obligated these matters clearly stated therein. It was also said that it is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning (We prescribed) a writing clearly stated ﴿therein﴾.

﴿That the life for the life﴾, i.e., taken, or killed, or subjected to retaliation (qisas) with it, if it kills it without right. In each of what follows in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and the eye for the eye and the nose for the nose and the ear for the ear and the tooth for the tooth﴾, what is suitable to it is to be understood, such as gouging out, cutting off, severing, and extracting. Some of them understood a general state of being, and said: it is what they intend, i.e., the taking of it for the eye is established, and similar.

Al-Kisa'i read: (the eye) and what is coordinated with it in the nominative case (raf'). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi explained this by saying that the speech in that case is sentences coordinated with the sentence (that the life for the life), but in terms of meaning, not in terms of wording. For the meaning of (We prescribed upon them that the life for the life) is: We said to them, "The life for the life." So the sentence falls under what was prescribed for the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Atiyya, on this view, regarded it as coordination by way of (tawahhum), which is not a regular usage.

It was also said that it is to be taken as a resumption (isti'naf), in the sense that the sentences are nominal, coordinated with the verbal sentence, and this would be the beginning of legislation and the statement of a new ruling, not falling under what was written in the Torah. It was also said that it falls under it as well on this view, and the implied meaning is: "And likewise the eye for the eye," etc., so that the two readings agree.

Al-Khatib said: there is no coordination; the resumption is in its apparent sense, and the speech is an answer to a question, as if it were said: "What is the status of other than the life?" And He, glory be to Him, said: (the eye for the eye), etc. It was also said that the eye, and likewise all the nominative items, are coordinated with the hidden nominative pronoun in the prepositional phrase that functions as a predicate, and the prepositional phrase after them is a circumstantial qualifier clarifying the meaning. This was deemed weak, because it entails coordinating upon a connected nominative pronoun without separation or emphasis, and that is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians except by necessity.

It was answered that it is separated by implication, since its original form is: "the life is taken or subjected to retaliation, it being for the life," because the pronoun is hidden in the element connected before the prepositional phrase according to the original arrangement, and it was only placed after deletion and movement to the adverbial position, as was said. This implies that the implied separation suffices for coordination, and there is discussion of this. On this view the connected element is to be understood as general so that the coordination is valid, for if it were understood as "the life killed for the life and the eye," the meaning would not be sound, as is not hidden.

Know that the word nafs (life/soul) in their speech, when it refers to the person himself, is masculine, and they say "three nafs," in the sense of three persons. When it refers to the spirit (ruh), it is feminine only, and its diminutive is nufaysa only. The eye, in the sense of the specific organ, is feminine. The general claim of feminine gender does not appear to have a basis, for it is not valid to say "this is the eye of these men" while meaning the best of them. The ear is similar to it. The nose is masculine only. The tooth (sinn) is feminine and not masculine, though when it refers to age it is different. However, Ibn al-Shihna mentioned that sinn is applied to the molar and the canine, and they explicitly stated that both are masculine, and likewise the molar (nasij), the incisor (dahik), and the premolar (arid). Ibn 'Usfur explicitly stated that the molar permits both. He versified what is permitted in this regard in his saying:

"Take from the organs what I have enumerated: some are feminine at times and masculine at other times.
The tongue of the youth, the armpit, the neck, the nape, and the shoulder, the back, and the molar are masculine."

"And in my view the forearm, the shank, and the intestine, along with the buttock of the youth, and then the adorned poetry."

"Thus every grammarian who narrated in his book, except Sibawayh, who among them is esteemed,
holds that the feminine form of the forearm is what came, though the masculine form is rejected in that."

It is well known that those organs that come in pairs in the body, like the hand, the rib, and the leg, are feminine, and those that are single, like the head, the mouth, and the belly, are masculine. This is not consistent, for the eyebrow, the temple, the cheek, the elbow, and the wrist are each masculine, though the body has two of each. The liver and the stomach are feminine, though the body has only one of each.

The detailed account of which organs are masculine and not feminine, and which are feminine and not masculine, would lead to extended discussion, and restraint is more appropriate to the situation.

(And) the injuries (al-jurah) are retaliation (qisas), in the nominative case as read, coordinated with the subject of (that). Qisas is the predicate. Because it is a verbal noun, like qital, and is not the same as the subject it describes, it is interpreted by one of the known interpretations in such cases. Al-Kisa'i, who read in the nominative earlier, read so here as well. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr, though they read in the accusative earlier, read in the nominative here, on the basis that it is a general statement of the ruling on injuries after the ruling on other organs was detailed. This ruling applies where equivalence can be known, as detailed in the books of jurisprudence.

Those who said that a Muslim is killed for a non-Muslim, a free person for a slave, and a man for a woman, took as evidence the generality of "that the life for the life." Those who disagreed took as evidence His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾, and His statement, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "A believer is not killed for an unbeliever." One of our companions answered that the text is a specification by mention, so it does not indicate the negation of what lies beyond it. What was narrated refers to the combatant (harbi), by its context, and not to one who has a covenant in its covenant. Coordination requires difference, and it has been narrated that "he, upon whom be prayer and peace, killed a Muslim for a dhimmi."

Ibn al-Faras mentioned that the verse concerns free Muslims, because the Jews to whom this was prescribed in the Torah were one religious community, not divided into Muslim and unbeliever, and all of them were free with no slaves among them. For the covenant of protection (dhimma) and enslavement were permitted only to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, among all the prophets, because enslavement is from the spoils of war, and this was not lawful to anyone other than him, upon whom be prayer and peace. The covenant of protection is for the continuance of unbelievers, and this did not occur in the time of any prophet, rather those who denied were all destroyed by punishment, and this was delayed for this nation as a mercy. End of quotation.

You know that the wording is apparent in generality, but they did not keep it on that basis. The companions said: a Muslim is not killed for one under safe-conduct (musta'man), nor a dhimmi for him, because he is not one whose blood is protected permanently, and likewise his unbelief inspires hostility, since he intends to return. Nor is a musta'man killed for a musta'man, by juristic preference (istihsan), because of the presence of what permits it; and by analogy (qiyas) he is killed for equality. Nor is a man killed for his son, because of His statement, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "A parent is not subjected to retaliation for his child." This, in its unrestricted form, is evidence against Malik in his view that he is retaliated against if he slaughtered him by slaughter. Also, because he is the cause of the son's existence, it is absurd that he should deserve his destruction. For this reason it is not permitted for him to kill him even if he finds him fighting in the ranks of the enemy, or committing adultery while married.

Retaliation is owed first to the one killed, and then his heir succeeds to it. The paternal or maternal grandfather, however high, is in this matter in the position of the father, and likewise the mother and the paternal or maternal grandmother, however near or distant, for the reason we have stated. Nor is a man killed for his slave, nor for his mudabbar (one freed upon death), nor for his mukatab (one under a contract of manumission), nor for the slave of his son, because he cannot be owed retaliation from himself for himself, nor can his son be owed it from him. Likewise he is not killed for a slave of whom he owns a part, because retaliation is not divisible. Understand this.

It has been cited as evidence for what is narrated from Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, that a group is not killed for one person, because of His statement in it: "that the life for the life," in the singular. It was answered that the wisdom of retaliation, which is the preservation of blood and of lives, requires killing, and turning the verse away from what was mentioned: for if it were so, they would be killed together so that retaliation would lapse for them, and then blood would be wasted and corruption would increase. Thus it has been said.

﴿Then whoever forgoes﴾, i.e., of those entitled to retaliation, ﴿it﴾, i.e., the retaliation, meaning whoever pardons it.
