The expression of that as forgoing (tasaddaq) is for emphasis in encouraging it. ﴿then it﴾, i.e., the forgoing mentioned, ﴿is an expiation for him﴾, for the one who forgoes, as Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Sha'bi, and most exegetes hold this view.

Al-Daylami related from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, recited the verse and said: "It is the man whose tooth is broken, or who is wounded in his body, and he forgoes it, so that from his sins is removed an amount equal to what he forgave of his body. If it is half the blood-money, then half of his sins; if it is a quarter of the blood-money, then a quarter of his sins; if it is a third of the blood-money, then a third of his sins; and if it is the whole blood-money, then all his sins."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and others related from 'Adi ibn Thabit that a man broke the mouth of another man in the time of Mu'awiya, may Allah be pleased with him. He was given blood-money, but he refused except to take retaliation. He was given double, and refused. He was given triple, and a man from the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, narrated from the Messenger of Allah, upon whom be prayer and peace, that he said: "Whoever forgoes a blood-claim or less than it, it is an expiation for him from the day he was born until the day he dies."

It was said: the pronoun refers to the offender. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as related by Ibn Jarir, and of Mujahid and Jabir as related from them by Ibn Abi Shaybah. The meaning of its being an expiation for him on this reading is that what was obligatory on him falls away by it. On this reading it is necessary that the predicate of the subject be the whole conditional clause and its consequent, since the returning pronoun occurs only in the condition. This is the view of the second 'Allamah.

It was also said that there is a returning pronoun in the consequent as well, by considering that (anna) means its forgoing, so that it includes, in meaning, the pronoun of the subject. Therefore the determination is not established. Some said it is possible that the meaning of the verse is that everyone who forgoes and acknowledges what is owed to him of retaliation and submits to it, it is an expiation for the wrong he committed, and the statement of His, exalted is He, fits this completely: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers." On this view the pronoun in (for him) refers to the one who forgoes, intending the offender himself. This has a clear remoteness.

Ubayy read: (then it is his expiation for him). The pronoun in the nominative then refers to the one who forgoes, not to the forgoing. Likewise the two pronouns in the genitive. The genitive construction is one of particularity, and the lam emphasizes that. That is: the one who forgoes, his expiation which he deserves by forgoing, for him, nothing is reduced from it, because part of a thing is not that thing. This is an exaltation of what he did, since it was made to entail the due entitlement without any reduction. In this is encouragement to pardon.

The verse was revealed, as more than one has said, when the Jews agreed not to kill the noble for the base, nor the man for the woman, and so they did not give the wronged their right against the wrongdoer.

From al-Sayyid al-Sanad it is related that retaliation was obligatory upon them in their law, so forgoing is among what was added in our law. Al-Dahhak said: in the Torah no blood-money was prescribed for a life or for a wound; there was only pardon or retaliation, and this is what the apparent meaning of the verse requires.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 46:

﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps﴾ This begins the explanation of the rulings of the Injil (Gospel), as it has been said, after the explanation of the rulings of the Tawrat (Torah). It is coordinated (ʿatf) with "We sent down the Torah," and the pronoun of plurality in the genitive refers to the prophets who submitted (aslamū), as most of the exegetes have said, and ʿAli ibn ʿIsa and al-Balkhi chose this view. It has also been said that it refers to those upon whom the ruling mentioned earlier was imposed, and this is related from al-Jubba'i, but it is not the preferred view. The taqfiyah (following) is the act of coming after. One says "qafa fulan athar fulan" when he follows him, and "qaffaytuhu bi-fulan" when you make him follow him. The estimate here is: "We made them follow in their footsteps."

﴿with ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾ So the verb, as it has been said, is transitive to two objects, one directly and the other by the preposition bi, and the first object is omitted, and "ʿala athararihim" (in their footsteps) takes the place of it, since when he is made to follow in their footsteps with him, he has made them follow with him. It has been objected that the verb before intensification was transitive to one object, and making a verb transitive to one object into two by means of bi is not permissible, whether by the hamzah or by intensification. It has been answered that the correct view is that it is permissible, but it is rare, and words of this kind have come from it: they said "ṣakka al-ḥajaru al-ḥajara" (the stone struck the stone) and "ṣakaktu al-ḥajara bi-l-ḥajari" (I struck the stone with the stone), and "dafaʿa Zaydun ʿAmran" (Zayd repelled ʿAmr) and "dafaʿtu Zaydan bi-ʿAmrin" (I made Zayd repel ʿAmr), meaning I made him one who repels it.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) went to the view that the intensification in what we are dealing with is not for transitivity, and that the attachment of the prepositional phrase to the verb is due to its being given the meaning of coming, meaning: "We came with ʿIsa son of Maryam in their footsteps, following them." He is then transitive to one object only, by means of bi, and the sum of the meaning is: We sent ʿIsa, peace be upon him, after them, ﴿confirming what was before him of the Torah﴾, a circumstantial clause (hal) from "ʿIsa" that is emphatic, for that is among the necessary qualities of a messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿And We gave him the Injil﴾ is coordinated with "qaffayna."

Al-Hasan read it with a fatḥah on the hamzah. The justification for this is that it is a foreign (aʿjamī) name, so there is no harm in its being in a pattern not found in Arabic forms. It is either afʿīl or faʿlīl with fatḥah; as for ifʿīl with kasrah, it has parallels such as ibzīm and ihlīl and other things. ﴿In it is guidance and light﴾ as in the Torah. The sentence is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the Injil. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and confirming what was before it of the Torah﴾ is coordinated with the circumstantial clause, and it is also a circumstantial clause. The coordination of a single-word circumstantial clause with a sentence-form circumstantial clause, and the reverse, is permissible because each is interpreted as a single word. This repetition is for the increase of affirmation.

His statement, glorious and mighty is He: ﴿and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾ is coordinated with what preceded it, joined with it in the same series of circumstantial clauses. Making all of it guidance after it was made to include it is for the sake of exaggeration in extolling its status, since in it is the more evident glad tidings of our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. The God-fearing are singled out for mention because they are the ones guided by its guidance and the ones who benefit from its gain. It is permitted to read "hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan" (guidance and admonition) in the accusative as objects of purpose, coordinated with another implied object of purpose, meaning: "for affirming his prophethood and as guidance," and so on. It is also permissible that both are causal complements of an omitted verb governing them, meaning: "and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing" — We gave him that.

[Page 151]

﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein.﴾ This is a new imperative (amr mubtada'), commanding them to judge and to know by what is in it, including matters among which are the proofs of his prophethood, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and what his noble law established of its rulings. As for the abrogated rulings (mansukh, those cancelled by later revelation), judging by them is not judging by what Allah the Exalted has revealed. Rather, it is their nullification and suspension, since the Gospel bears witness to their abrogation and to the end of the time for acting upon them. This is because its testimony to the truth of what abrogates them in the Ahmadan law (the law of Muhammad) is testimony to their abrogation, and because its rulings are what that law, whose truth it attests, has established. Thus Shaykh al-Islam, may his secret be sanctified, stated, and al-Jubba'i chose, that it is a new imperative.

Others said: it is a report of the command that was directed at them, with a verb coordinated with (We gave him) understood as: "And We said: 'Let the People of the Gospel judge...'" The omission of the verb "said" because what precedes it indicates it is common in speech, and from it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. Peace be upon you.﴾ 'Ali ibn 'Isa chose this view.

Hamzah recited (wa-liyahkuma) with the preposition lam of purpose and the verb put in the subjunctive by an implied (an), with the verbal noun coordinated with (guidance and admonition), on the basis that both are causative. The lam is made explicit because the subject differs: the subject of the implied verb is the pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, while the subject of this is the People of the Book. It is attached to an omitted element on the first reading of (guidance and admonition), meaning: "And We gave it so that they might judge," and so on. It was not coordinated because coordinating a cause with a state is not valid. Some permitted the coordination, on the basis that the state here has the meaning of a cause, but this is weak. Some of them supposed, on the assumption of the causative reading, that it is connected to (revealed), so that it may be a cause for the giving of the Gospel to 'Isa, peace be upon him, of what has been mentioned.

From Abu 'Ali, it is reported that he recited (wa-an liyahkuma), with (an) as a relative particle joined to the imperative, as in your saying: "I commanded him that he should stand." The meaning of joining is that (an) completes with what follows it a unit of speech, like (alladhi) and its sisters. The joining of the verbal (an) to an imperative verb is among what has been repeatedly discussed in al-Kashshaf, where it mentions a report from Sibawayh. Here "We commanded" is understood, as if it were said: "And We gave him the Gospel and commanded that he judge." An objection was raised against Sibawayh, which the author of al-Kashf examined carefully in answering, and he brought what dispels many of the objections to the (an) of the verbal and explanatory types.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun).﴾ That is, the rebellious who depart from His judgment, or from faith, and its verification has already passed. The sentence is a concluding statement confirming the content of the preceding sentence and emphasising the obligation of compliance with the command. The verse indicates that the Gospel contains rulings, and that 'Isa, peace be upon him, was independent in the law, commanded to act by what is in it of rulings, whether few or many, not merely by what is in the Torah specifically. The hadith of al-Bukhari also supports this: "The People of the Torah were given the Torah and acted upon it, and the People of the Gospel were given the Gospel and acted upon it." Some excellent scholars disagreed. In al-Milal wa'l-Nihal of al-Shahrastani: All the Children of Israel were obliged to the law of Musa, peace be upon him, charged with the obligation of the rulings of the Torah, and the Gospel revealed to the Messiah, peace be upon him, contains no rulings and does not embody lawful and unlawful matters, but is symbols, parables and admonitions, and whatever else of laws and rulings is deferred to the Torah. For this reason the Jews would not submit to 'Isa, peace and blessings be upon him. The opponent interpreted this verse as (let them judge by what Allah has revealed) therein, concerning the obligation to act by the rulings of the Torah, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning, like the restriction of what was revealed concerning the prophethood of our Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him.

And We have sent down to you the Book (al-Kitab), meaning the perfect individual (al-fard al-kamil) truly deserving to be called "the Book" without qualification, owing to its superiority over all the other heavenly scriptures; it is the Great Qur'an. The article in "al-Kitab" is for specific reference (lil-'ahd), and the sentence is coordinated (ataf) upon "anzalna" and what is coordinated with it.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿with the truth﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida) from "al-Kitab," meaning: while being clothed in truth and sincerity. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of "anzalna" (the agent), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the kaf in "ilayka" (to you).

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "al-Kitab," meaning: while being a confirmer of what preceded it. The discussion of the manner of its confirmation of that has already passed. Abu al-Baqa' claimed that it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause of what has been mentioned, since two circumstantial clauses cannot belong to a single governing element, and he held that it must be a circumstantial clause of the pronoun concealed in the preposition-and-object preceding it. His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿from the Book﴾ is an explanatory specification (bayan) of "ma" (what), and the article in it is for the genus (lil-jins), based on the claim that the books other than the heavenly scriptures are not a "book" in relation to it. It is permissible, as more than one commentator has said, that it be for specific reference (lil-'ahd), in view of the fact that it did not intend the genus of the meaning of the word "Kitab," but rather a particular type of it, which, considered in terms of the absolute "Kitab," is known (ma'hud) with respect to the attribute of being heavenly. The point is that its specific reference is not to the degree of individual particularity, but to a type-specific particularity more restricted than the absolute "Kitab"; this is evident. And it is also from the heavenly Book, since it has been restricted to what is other than the Qur'an.

﴿And as a guardian over it﴾. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, a watchful overseer (raqib) over the other heavenly books that are preserved from alteration, in that it bears witness to their soundness and authenticity, affirms the fundamentals of their laws and what of their branches is perpetual, and specifies their abrogated rulings.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada — may Allah be pleased with them — said: that is, a witness over it that it is the truth. The conjunction (ataf) in that case is for emphasis. Its ha' is original (asliyya), and its verb is haymana. It has analogues: bayqara, khaymara and saytara. al-Zajjaj added: bayqara, and there is no sixth to them. It has also been said that it is substituted from a hamza, and its root derives from amn (security), like haraqa. al-Mubarrad and Ibn Qutayba said: the muhaymin originally was mu'min, and it is one of His names, the Exalted; so it was diminutivized and its hamza was changed to a ha'. al-Samin and others criticized this, saying that it is an error, indeed unbelief or something akin to it, since the names of Allah, the Exalted, are not diminutivized, and likewise every name that is legally venerated.

It is reported from Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid that they both read "muhaymanan" with a fatha on the mim, in the pattern of the passive participle (bina' al-maf'ul). On this reading, the pronoun in "'alayhi" returns to the first Book, and the meaning is that it was preserved from distortion and alteration, and the one who preserves it is Allah, the Exalted, as He, the Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardians﴾.

﴿So judge between them﴾, that is, between the People of the Book, as Ibn 'Abbas — may Allah be pleased with them both — said. The fa' is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, since the Great Qur'an's being of that status is among the requirements of the judgment commanded, that is: if the Qur'an is as has been mentioned, ﴿then judge between them by what Allah has sent down﴾, that is, by what He sent down to you, for it is the truth from which there is no escape, and which encompasses all the legal rulings remaining in the divine books. The placing of "between them" first is for the sake of attention to generalizing the judgment to them; and placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun is to alert to the causality of what is within the relative clause for the ruling, and as a warning against opposition. The shift to the explicit mention of the Glorified Name is for what has passed many times.

﴿And do not follow their desires﴾, the deviant ones. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas — may Allah be pleased with them both — that he meant what they had distorted and altered regarding the matter of stoning, ﴿away from the truth that has come to you﴾, from which there is no turning aside. "'An" is connected to "la tattabi'" on the basis of implying the sense of deviating or the like, as if it were said: do not deviate from the truth that has come to you, following their desires. It has also been said: it is connected to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from its subject, that is: do not follow their desires while deviating from what has come to you; or from its object, that is: do not follow their desires while being one who deviates from what has come to you. This was objected to on the ground that what occurs as a circumstantial clause must necessarily be a general verb; perhaps the one who said it does not accept that. And "min," as Abu al-Baqa' said, is connected to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the nominative subject of "jaa'aka," or from "ma." The relative pronoun is placed in the position of the first relative pronoun in order to allude, through what is within the relative clause, to what necessitates complete avoidance of following desires. The prohibition may be addressed to one from whom the forbidden act is not conceivable, so it is not said: how could the Prophet — may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — be forbidden to follow their desires, when he is protected from committing what is less than that? It has also been said: the address is to him — may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — and what is meant is all the rulings.

﴿For each of you, We have appointed a law and a path﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to move the People of the Book among his contemporaries — may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — to submit to his judgment, by what Allah, the Exalted, sent down to him of the truth, by clarifying that it is what they were charged to act upon, not what is in their own books, and that those charged to act upon it were only those who passed before the abrogation.

The address — as a number of the commentators said — is to all people, those present and those who passed, by way of prevalence (taghlib). The word "shir'a" — with a kasra on the shin; Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a fatha — is the "shari'a," and it is originally the apparent path through which one reaches water. What is meant by it is the religion, and its use for it is because it is a path leading to what is the cause of eternal life, just as water is the cause of transient life; or because it is a path to the act which purifies the doer from moral filth, just as the shari'a is a path to the water which purifies its user from sensory filth.

Al-Raghib said: religion was called "shari'a" by analogy with the watering-place of water, in that whoever truly enters upon it is quenched and purified. By quenching I mean what some of the sages said: "I used to drink and not be quenched; when I knew Allah, the Exalted, I was quenched without drinking." By purification, I mean His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and to purify you thoroughly﴾.

The "minhaj" is the clear path in religion, from "nahaja al-amr" when it became clear. The conjunction is in view of the plurality of attributes. al-Mubarrad said: "shir'a" originally means the path, and "minhaj" the straight path. It has been said: both have the same meaning, which is the path, and the repetition is for emphasis; the conjunction is like it in the saying of al-Hutay'a:

"And Hind, between her and me stand distance and remoteness"

and the saying of 'Antara:

"Greetings to you from a ruin whose traces have grown old, emptied and desolate after Umm al-Haytham."

It has been said: "shir'a" is the path in general, whether clear or not. It has also been said: "minhaj" is the guide. It has been said: "shir'a" is the Prophet — may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — and "minhaj" is the Book. It has been said: "shir'a" is the practical legal rulings and "minhaj" the doctrinal rulings, but this is nothing.

The "li" is connected to "ja'alna," which is transitive to one object, and it is a report of a past making, not an act of creation; its being placed before it is for specification. "Minkum" is connected to an elided element that occurs as an attribute of what the tanwin of "kullin" replaces, that is: and for every community existing among you, O communities remaining and those passed, We have determined and placed a law and a path specific to that community, such that no community can easily transgress its law.

The community that existed from the sending of Moses to the sending of Jesus — upon both be blessings and peace — had as its law what is in the Torah; and the community that existed from the sending of Jesus — upon him be peace — to the sending of Ahmad — upon him be blessings and peace — had as its law what is in the Gospel. As for you, O present ones, your law is what is in the Furqan; there is nothing but: believe in it and act upon what is in it.

Abu al-Baqa' required that "minkum" be connected to an elided element whose estimate is "a'ni" (I mean), and he did not permit the attributive function, because that would necessitate separating the attribute from the modified by a foreign element that does not tighten the speech, and would also necessitate separating "ja'alna" from its object, which is "shir'a." Shaykh al-Islam said: there is no harm in the placing of "ja'alna" between the attribute and the modified, as in His saying: ﴿Shall I take other than Allah as a protector, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?﴾ etc. The separation between the verb and its object is necessary in every case. What has been mentioned, that the address is to the communities, is the apparent meaning. It has been said that it is to the prophets who were alluded to in the verses before. The distance of this is not hidden.

More distant than it is making the address to this Muhammadan community, which neither the preceding context nor the following supports. Those who hold that we are not bound by the laws of those before us have used this verse as evidence, since the address, as you know, encompasses the communities, and the "li" is for exclusivity, so each community has a religion specific to it; and if one were bound by another law, that exclusivity would not exist.

Allamah al-Taftazani answered, after granting that the "li" indicates restrictive exclusivity, by denying the implication, since it is permissible that we be bound by the law of those before us together with additional particularities in our religion by which exclusivity is achieved. And in it: there is no need, for conveying restriction in what has been mentioned together with the fronting of the complement. Also, the particularities mentioned do not contradict our being bound by the law of those before us, since its proponents claim that it applies in what has not been known to be abrogated, and our religion's differing from it is only absolute, since no one has said it applies absolutely. For this reason the verification-scholars combined this verse, and its like, which indicates the difference of laws, with what contradicts it, such as His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ etc., and His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾, by holding that every verse indicating non-difference is to be understood as referring to the fundamentals of religion and the like. The verification in this matter is that we are bound by the rulings of the remaining laws insofar as they are rulings of our law, not insofar as they are a law for the earlier ones.

﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made you one community﴾, that is, a group agreed upon one religion in all eras, or possessing one creed without difference among you at any time regarding any of the religious rulings, with no abrogation and no alteration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas — may Allah be pleased with them both. The object of "shaa'a" is elided, relying on the indication of the conditional clause, that is: had Allah willed your gathering upon Islam, He would have compelled you to it. It is reported from al-Hasan something similar. al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Maghribi said: the meaning is: had Allah willed, He would not have sent a prophet to you, so you would be bound by what is in reason, and you would be one community. ﴿But that He might test you﴾ is connected to an elided element required by the context, that is: but He did not will that making, rather He willed something else, so that He, the Glorified, would deal with you as one who tests you.

﴿In what He has given you﴾ of the differing laws, for divine wisdoms which each age requires; whether you will know by them, submitting to them, believing that in their difference there is benefit returning to you in your livelihood and your return, or you will turn away from them, pursuing desire, and trading guidance for error. And by this — as Shaykh al-Islam said — it has become clear that the basis for the absence of the aforementioned willing is not merely testing; rather the principal thing in that is what was pointed to of the difference containing what is in their interest in livelihood and return, as His, the Glorious and Majestic's, saying indicates: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, that is: since the matter is as mentioned, then hasten to what is better for you in both abodes, of the sound creeds and the righteous deeds contained in the Noble Qur'an, and seize them, grasping the opportunity and securing the merit of precedence and advancement. ﴿So the foremost are the foremost; those are the ones brought near﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 48 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought in the manner of a causal explanation for the urging to race towards good deeds, given what it contains of promise and threat. The word "jami'an" (all of you) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in the genitive position, and its governing element is either the verbal noun (masdar) in construction, which is analysable into a verb in the active voice or in the passive voice, or the implicit state of being (istiqrar) contained in the prepositional phrase. It has also been said, though this is far-fetched, that the clause is a response to an implied question, as if it were said: "What is the ruling in that?" So it was answered: "Verily you will be returned to Allah, exalted is He, and gathered to the abode of recompense in which the realities are unveiled and the wisdoms become clear."

﴿Then He will inform you of that about which you used to differ﴾, that is, He will then deal with you with a recompense that separates truth from falsehood, leaving you no trace of doubt, concerning that about which you used to differ in the world regarding matters of religion. Thus "inform" (al-inba') here is a metaphor for requiting, because of what it involves of the realisation of the matter.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 49:**

﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires.﴾ It is coordinated (*ʿatf*, conjunction) with "the Book" (*al-Kitab*), as if it had been said: "And We sent down to you the Book, and Our saying: 'Judge.'" The imperative "judge" (*ihkum*) means that the command to judge is what is meant, not the judging itself, because what was sent down is the command to judge and not the judging, and so that the demand is not entirely voided. You may also take the command to judge as being from the start of the command without the need to supply a verb of saying (*idmar al-qawl*), as he verified in *al-Kashshaf*. It has also been permitted that it be coordinated with "the truth" (*al-haqq*). In its grammatical position there are two possibilities, the genitive and the accusative, according to the well-known difference of opinion. It has been said that the clause may be a nominal sentence with an implied subject, meaning: "And We commanded that you judge." Some claimed that this "an" (*an*) is explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), and Abu al-Baqa justified this by saying the meaning is: "And We commanded you," then this command was explained as judging. Abu Hayyan rejected its soundness on this basis, because the omission of what is explained by "an" has not been preserved from their speech, and the matter is as he mentioned.

Al-Tibi said: "If this clause were made coordinate with 'so judge' (*fahkum*) in meaning, so that the repetition would serve to attach His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾, it would be better." This was rejected on the basis that "an" is what prevents that coordination, and the matter of the attachment is necessary in every case.

Some said: The command to judge was repeated only because seeking judgment from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, occurred twice: once concerning the adultery of a married person, and once concerning a slain man among them. So each command came regarding a separate matter. This is related from al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. The nun of "an" in it may be vowelled with a *damma* or a *kasra*. The clause formed from "an yaftinukum" (that they tempt you) is a substitute for the object pronoun, a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), meaning: "And beware of their temptation of you, and that they divert you from some of what Allah, exalted is He, has revealed to you, even if it is the least of little, by portraying falsehood in the form of truth."

Ibn Zayd said: [They tempt you] by lying about the Torah, that this ruling is not in it. It has also been permitted that it be an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), meaning: "Beware of them out of fear that they tempt you." The repetition of "what Allah has revealed" (*ma anzala Allah*) ... "to you" (*ilayka*) is to emphasize the warning by magnifying the gravity of the matter. Perhaps this is to cut off their hopes.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that: "The rabbis of the Jews said: 'Come, let us go to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion.' So they said: 'O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis of the Jews, and that if we follow you, all the Jews will follow us, and that there is a dispute between us and our people, so we will seek judgment from you, and you will rule for us against them, and we will believe in you and affirm you.' But the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, refused that, so this was revealed."

﴿Then if they turn away﴾, that is: they refuse to accept the judgment by what Allah, exalted is He, has revealed to you, and desire other than it, ﴿know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾, and that is the sin of turning away and refusing. It is a particular "some." Expressing it this way indicates that they have many sins, and this one, despite its great magnitude, is one of them. In this vagueness there is an exaltation of turning away, as in his saying:

*Leaver of places when I do not like them, or whose souls' death-appointment is bound to some souls.*

He means by "some" himself, that is, a great soul, and a soul of what a soul! Al-Jubba'i said: "Some" is mentioned while the whole is meant, just as a generality is mentioned while a specific is meant. It was also said: The intended meaning is an indefinite "some," as an intensification of the punishment, as if it were indicated that it suffices that they be seized for some of their sins, whichever some it is, and be destroyed and annihilated thereby.

Some claimed that it is not sound to intend the whole, because the intended meaning of this affliction is the worldly punishment, and this is specific to some sins and not others. What encompasses all is only the punishment of the Hereafter. This affliction, according to what is related from al-Hasan, is the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It was said: it is the killing of Banu Qurayza. It was said: it is more general than that, and it includes what befell Banu Qaynuqa, the people of Khaybar, and Fadak. Perhaps this is the preferable view.

﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, that is: transgressors in disbelief, persisting in it, going beyond the known limits. This is a concluding parenthetical statement (*i'tiradh tadhyili*) confirming the content of what precedes it. In it there is consolation for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which is not hidden. It was said: It is coordinated with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾, meaning: We prescribed the ruling of retaliation in the Torah, and confirmed it in the Gospel, and We sent down to you the Book confirming what is in both of them. ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾ regarding the divine rulings established in the religions. Its remoteness is not hidden. The intended meaning of "the people" is generality. It was said: it means the Jews.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 50:

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam)?﴾ is a denunciation and a expression of wonder at their condition, and a rebuke to them. The fa' (fa) is for conjunction with an implied element that the context requires, meaning: Do they turn away from accepting your judgment with what Allah the Exalted has sent down to you, and so seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah?! It has been said: the position of the hamzah (interrogative particle) is after the fa', and it was placed first because it has the right of initial position. The fronting of the object is for specification, which conveys the emphasis of denunciation and wonder; for turning away from the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and seeking another judgment is a denounced and wondrous matter, and seeking the judgment of the Jahiliyyah is more ugly and more wondrous.

Page 156

By al-Jahiliyyah is meant the Jahili creed (millah), which is the following of desire, which entails inclination and flattery in judgments; or the Jahili community, and their judgment is what they were upon of preferring one over another among the slain. It has been said: the speech is by elision of a modifier, meaning the people of the Jahiliyyah, and their judgment is what has been mentioned.

It is narrated that when the Banu al-Nadir referred to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dispute over a slain man which occurred between them and the Banu Qurayzah, some of them asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to judge between them by what the people of the Jahiliyyah had of preference (in blood-money), so he, peace be upon him, said: "The slain are equal (bawa')." The Banu al-Nadir said: "We do not accept that," and so it was revealed.

Ibn 'Amir recited (tabghun) with the ta', and this is either by iltifat (shift of grammatical person) to intensify the rebuke, or by implying a verb of saying, meaning: (Say to them: Do they seek the judgment) etc. Ibn Wathhab, al-A'raj, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and others recited (Afahukmu) with the damma, as a mubtada' (subject), with (yabghuna) as its predicate, and the returning pronoun is elided. It has been said: the predicate is elided, and what is mentioned is its attribute, meaning: a judgment they seek. The elision of the returning pronoun from the predicate was considered weak, but Ibn Jinni mentioned that elision from it occurs just as elision occurs from the relative clause and the qualifier, as in the verse:

Umm al-Khiyar has begun to claim against me a sin, all of which I did not commit.

Abu Hayyan said: the goodness of the elision in the verse is due to the resemblance of (yabghuna) to the rhyme-final position, so it functions as sharing; and the claim that the aforementioned reading is an error is itself an error, as is not hidden.

Qatadah recited (Afahakama) with a fatha on the fa', the ha' and the kaf, meaning: are there judges like the judges of the Jahiliyyah (yabghuna). The Jahiliyyah used to be called before this, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Urwah, "ʿālamiyyah" (worldly), until a woman came and said: O Messenger of Allah, in the Jahiliyyah such-and-such occurred, so Allah the Exalted revealed the mention of the Jahiliyyah and judged them by this title.

﴿And who is better in judgment than Allah?﴾ is a denial that anyone's judgment could be better than the judgment of Allah the Exalted, or equal to it, as the usage indicates, although the apparent construction does not directly address the negation or denial of equality. ﴿For a people who are certain﴾: that is, with a people (inda qawm), so the lam means "with" (inda), and al-Jubba'i went to this view, and it was weakened by him in al-Durr al-Masun, who held that it is for explanation, connected to an elided element, as in (hayta laka) and (saqyan laka), meaning: the content of this denying interrogative became clear and manifest to a people who reflect on matters and verify things by their insight; as for others, they do not know that there is no better judgment than the judgment of Allah the Exalted. Perhaps whoever explained it as (inda) intended to clarify the resultant meaning. It has been said: the lam is on its original basis and is a complement, meaning: the judgment of Allah the Exalted for the believers over the disbelievers is the best and most just of judgments, and this clause is a circumstantial clause confirming the meaning of the preceding denial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 51:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an address whose ruling covers all the believers, the sincere and others alike, although its occasion of revelation concerned a particular group, as you will learn, God willing. Describing them with the title of faith serves to move them, from the outset, to refrain from what they have been forbidden, through His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. Reminding them that they are characterized by the opposite of the qualities of the two groups is among the strongest deterrents from allying with them. That is, let none of you take them as an ally, meaning: do not show them the friendship of loved ones, and do not seek their support.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: When the battle of Uhud took place, it weighed heavily on a group of people, and they feared that the disbelievers would gain the upper hand over them. One man said to his companion: "As for me, I will join that Jew, take safe-conduct from him, and become a Jew with him, for I fear the Jews will gain the upper hand over us." The other said: "As for me, I will join so-and-so the Christian in some part of the land of Syria, take safe-conduct from him, and become a Christian with him." So God, exalted be He, revealed concerning the two of them, forbidding them: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and so on.

[Page 157]
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Atiyyah ibn Sa'd, who said: "Ubadah ibn al-Samit of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have many allies among the Jews, in great number, and I disavow to God, the Exalted, and to His Messenger (ﷺ) the alliance with the Jews, and I take God, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ) as my allies.' Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: 'I am a man who fears reversals of fortune, and I will not disavow the alliance of my allies.' So it was revealed:" ﴿Some of them are allies of others﴾. That is, some of the Jews are allies of other Jews, and some of the Christians are allies of other Christians. The general expression was chosen because the intended meaning is clear, since it is evident that the Jews do not ally with the Christians, nor the reverse. The sentence is resumed, serving as a reason for the prohibition preceding it and as a confirmation of the obligation to avoid what is forbidden. That is: some of them are allies of others, united in one word in everything they do and everything they leave undone. It follows necessarily that all of them are united in opposing you and harming you, such that they inflict evil upon you and seek to destroy you. How, then, could any friendship be conceived between you and them? Al-Hawfi claimed that the sentence is in the position of a qualifier for ﴿allies﴾, but the apparent reading is the first.

As for His words, exalted be He: ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is indeed one of them﴾, that is, one of their number, and his ruling is their ruling, as a conclusion drawn from what precedes it. It is expressed in this form for emphasis and intensification in deterrence, because if the one who allies with them were literally one of them, he would be a disbeliever, and that is not the intended meaning. It has been said that the intended meaning is: whoever among you takes them as allies is literally a disbeliever like them, and this is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. Perhaps that applies when their alliance is on the basis of their being Jews or Christians. It has also been said that, rather, the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the meaning is that by alliance with them they become openly declared disbelievers.

As for His words, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, [meaning those who wrong] themselves by allying with the disbelievers, or the believers by allying with their enemies. This is another reason, as it is said, which implies that alliance with the disbelievers yields no benefit, but rather entails harm resulting from it. It has also been said that it is a reason for the statement that whoever allies with them is one of them, that is, He does not guide them to faith, but leaves them to themselves, so they fall into disbelief and misguidance. The explicit noun was placed in the position of their pronoun to draw attention to the fact that their alliance is an act of wrongdoing, since it exposes the self to the everlasting punishment, and it is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

And His saying, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning hypocrisy, like ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his kind, as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. It is an explanation of how they take allies, an indication of its cause, and of what their affair leads to. The fāʾ (فَ, "so") indicates that the seeing follows from their lack of guidance, and it is purely causal (لِلسَّبَبِيَّةِ الْمَحْضَةِ, expressing pure causation).

Al-Karkhi permitted that it is coordinated (لِلْعَطْفِ) with ﴿Indeed Allah﴾ and so on, in terms of meaning. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) by way of talwīn (a shift of address), or to everyone who is qualified to be addressed. Using the relative pronoun (al-ladhīna) rather than a pronoun for the people indicates that what they committed of allying themselves was due to what lay hidden in them of disease. The seeing may be visual (بَصَرِيَّةٌ), and His saying ﴿they hasten to them﴾ is then a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, حال) from the object, which is the most fitting given the clear manifestation of their hypocrisy. Or it may be mental (قَلْبِيَّةٌ, "to know/consider"), and the clause is in the position of the second object. The meaning in both cases is: hastening in their allegiance. However, it was said "in them" (فِيهِمْ) to emphasise their eagerness for it and their rushing headlong into it. The choice of فِي ("in") over إِلَى ("to") indicates that they are firmly established in the allegiance, and their hastening is only from one level of it to another.

Al-Zamakhshari explained al-musāraʿah (hastening) as inqimāsh (shrinking/diving into), because of how frequently it is used with فِي. Some scholars (al-muḥaqqiqīn) differed from him, because that would be explaining by something less clear. It was preferred that musāraʿah is construed here with إِلَى, because it includes the meaning of entering.

It is read as ﴿fa-yara﴾ with the ya of the third person, on the basis that the pronoun refers, as Abu al-Baqa' said, to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that it refers to whoever is able to see. It was also said that the subject is the relative pronoun and the object is the clause, with the deletion of the verbal particle أَنْ, and the seeing is mental. That is: "those in whose hearts is a disease will see that they hasten among them." When أَنْ was deleted, the verb became marfūʿ (nominative), as in his saying:

*Ah, you who forbid me from attending the battle.*

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿they say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us."﴾ is a ḥāl from the subject of ﴿they hasten﴾. The word al-dāʾirah (calamity, الدَّائِرَةُ) is one of the descriptive words that have become predominant, so that the thing it qualifies is not mentioned with it. Its original form is dawwārah, since it derives from dāra yadūr (to turn). Its meaning linguistically, according to the Qāmūs (the dictionary), is what surrounds a thing. In Sharḥ al-Mulakhkhaṣ it says: al-dāʾirah is a level plane surrounded by a curved line, such that a point can be imagined inside it whose distance from every direction of the line is equal. The word dāʾirah is sometimes also used for that surrounding line itself, and this is the end of the quotation.

Scholars differed over which of the two meanings is the primary (ḥaqīqah) one. It was said that it is primary in the first meaning and figurative (majāz) in the second, and it was said the reverse. Al-Barjandi said: The verification of this is that when one end of a straight line is fixed and it is turned one full revolution, it produces the surface of a circle, which is called dāʾirah because the shape of this surface has a turning. Moreover, the form of the active participle (dāʾirah) is used for attribution. And when the motion of a point around a fixed point is imagined as one full revolution, such that the distance of the moving point from the fixed point does not vary, the circumference of a circle is produced, which is also called dāʾirah, because the point was turning, so what results from its turning is called dāʾirah. If the first is considered, it is fitting that the use of dāʾirah for the surface is primary and for the circumference figurative. If the second is considered, it is fitting that the matter is the reverse. End of quotation.

Some learned scholars objected to this, saying: it is not hidden what is problematic in it, because its use for the circumference in the second consideration is also figurative, since it is from the naming of the effect by the name of the cause. Unless it is said that he intended by its being primary for the circumference that its use for it is not figurative in the manner in which it was figurative in the first consideration. For the basis of the figurativeness in the first case is naming the surrounding thing by the name of the surrounded, and here it is not so, as you have heard. But this is a far-fetched strain. And if he had said, regarding the reason for the naming in the later case, "because the shape of the line has a turning", in accordance with his saying regarding the reason for the naming in the earlier case, this objection would not have arisen. So reflect.

However that may be, the word has been borrowed (istuʿīrat) for the calamities of time, with regard to its surrounding nature. And their saying this was an excuse for allying themselves with the disbelievers, meaning: "We fear that a calamity from the calamities of time will turn against us, and a turn of its turns, by which the matter will be reversed in favour of the disbelievers, and the dominion will belong to them over the Muslims, so we will need them." This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

It is also reported from al-Kalbi that the meaning is: "We fear that time will turn against us with something disliked, such as drought and famine, so they will not supply us with provisions and will not lend to us." It is not far-fetched that the hypocrites were showing the believers that they meant by the calamity what al-Kalbi said, while concealing in the circles of their hearts what the group (the majority) said, which indicates doubt about the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah, the Exalted, frustrated their false excuses and cut off their empty hopes, and gave the believers good news of the fulfilment of their wish by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so perhaps Allah will bring the victory﴾. For ʿasā (perhaps) from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, is a binding promise, because the generous, when he gives hope, gives. So what do you think of the most generous of the generous?

By "the victory" (al-fatḥ) is meant the conquest of Mecca, as was narrated from al-Suddi. It was also said: the conquest of the lands of the disbelievers, and al-Jubbaʾi chose this. Qatadah and Muqatil said: it is the decisive judgement by His granting victory to him (peace be upon him) over whoever opposed him, and the honouring of the religion. The phrase ﴿an yaʾtiya﴾ (that He bring) is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is the predicate of ʿasā according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, and an object according to the opinion of Sibawayh, so that the event is not predicated of the essence. The matter in this is easy according to al-Akhfash.

﴿or a command from Him﴾, which is the killing and taking captive of the descendants of the Banu Qurayza, and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, according to Muqatil. It was also said: the exposure of the hypocrites' hypocrisy together with the command to kill them. It was narrated from al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj. It was also said: the death of the head of hypocrisy, and this is reported from al-Jubbaʾi.

﴿and they will become﴾, meaning those hypocrites. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿yaʾtiya﴾, and is included with it in the predicate of ʿasā. The fāʾ of causation makes the two clauses like a single clause, dispensing with the pronoun returning to the noun. The meaning is: they will become ﴿regretful for what they concealed within themselves﴾ of disbelief and doubt about the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Regretful﴾ is the predicate of yuṣbiḥu (to become), and ﴿for what they concealed﴾ is connected to it. The restriction of the regret to this, and not to what they used to display of allying themselves with the disbelievers, is because it is what used to drive them to that alliance and incite them to it. This indicates that their regret was over the alliance in its root and cause.

Ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAmr that he heard Ibn al-Zubayr reading: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring the victory or a command from Him, and they will become, the wicked ones, regretful for what they concealed within themselves.﴾ ʿAmr said: I do not know whether that was from him a recitation or an explanation.

[Page 160]

﴿And those who believe will say﴾: this is a resumed sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), brought in to show the full extent of the wretched condition of the group already mentioned.

Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir read it without the conjunction *wa* (and), treating it as an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnaf bayani*), as if it were said: "Then what will the believers say at that time?" Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read *wa-yaqula* (and [that] they say) in the subjunctive, as a conjunction with *fa-yusbihu* (so that they become). It has also been said that it is conjoined with *an yaʾtiya* (that He bring) according to the sense, as if it were said: "It may be that Allah brings victory" (*ʿasa Allahu an yaʾtiya bil-fath*), "and [that] those who believe say," with the verb *yaʾtiya* attributed to the Glorious Name rather than to its pronoun. This was taken into account because conjoining with the predicate of *ʿasā* (it may be) or its object requires that the pronoun of God, exalted is He, be present in it so that the predication is valid, or so that it may follow its usage. Here there is no pronoun and nothing that replaces it. In the case of conjunction according to the sense, *ʿasā* is complete (*tāmma*), since it is predicated of *an* and what falls within its scope, so no pronoun is needed. This, as has been said, is close to *ʿaṭf al-tawahhum* (conjunction by apparent imagination), and they expressed it in that way rather than by the pronoun out of courtesy. Some have permitted that *an yaʾtiya* be a substitute (*badal*) for the Glorious Name, with the conjunction being to the substitute, and *ʿasā* also complete, as al-Farisi stated explicitly. Others make the conjunction to the predicate of *ʿasā* and suppose a pronoun, meaning: "and those who believe say concerning it." Ibn al-Nahhas held that the conjunction is to *al-fath* (the victory), and this is like the line of verse:

"And the wearing of a cloak, and my eye being cooled."

It has been objected that this involves separating the parts of the relative clause (*al-fasl bayna ajzaʾ al-silah*), which is not permitted; and that the meaning would then be "It may be that Allah brings about the saying of the believers," which is weak. The first objection is answered by distinguishing between separation by an actual element and separation by an implied element; the second is answered by saying that the intended meaning is: "It may be that Allah, glorified is He, brings about what necessitates the saying of the believers, namely the victory that manifests their condition."

Shaykh al-Islam (may God sanctify his secret) chose what we have already set forth, and it does not need the burden of supposing a pronoun, because *fa-tusbihū* (so that you become), as you know, is conjoined to *yaʾtiya*, and the *fa* (so) suffices in that place for the pronoun, so it also suffices for the pronoun in the conjoined element, since the two conjoined things are like one thing. And with this there is no need to say that the conjunction to it is based on its being in the accusative as the answer to the expression of hope, treating it as if it were an expression of wish, as Ibn al-Hajib said, because this is permitted only by the Kufans, unlike the way we have mentioned.

The meaning is: "And those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, who used to be allied with them, hoping for their dominance, and showing them the utmost love and inseparability in both ease and hardship, when they witness the frustration of their hopes and the reversal of their calculations by the occurrence of the opposite of what they were awaiting and boasting of," in wonder at the addressees concerning their condition and as an allusion to them: ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that they were surely with you?﴾ That is, [who swore that they would be with you] in support and aid, as they said concerning what is related of them: "And if you are fought, we will surely support you." So the demonstrative *hāʾulāʾ* (these) is the subject, and what follows it is its predicate. The meaning is a denial of what they did, a rebuke of it, and a correction of them in that matter. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam and others.

Many have chosen that the meaning is: "The truthful believers say to one another," ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah﴾ (exalted is He) to the Jews, ﴿that they were surely with you?﴾ The address, on both suppositions, is to the Jews, except that on the first it comes from the side of the believers, and on the second from the side of those who swore.

In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is stated that on the second supposition the address is to the believers, that is: "Those who believe say to one another, marvelling at the condition of the hypocrites, since they swore strongly to them and swore that they were with you, and that they would support you against your enemies, the Jews. But when what befell the Jews befell them, they showed what they had been concealing of their allegiance to them and of their conspiring against the believers." Ata's statement points to this, but it is nothing, as is not hidden.

The clause ﴿that they were surely with you﴾ has no place in the grammatical structure, because it is an explanation and a report of the meaning of *aqsamū* (they swore), but not in their own words, for otherwise it would have been said: "Indeed we are with you." Al-Samin and others mention that it is permissible to say: "Zayd swore: I will surely do it, and he will surely do it." *Jahda aymānihim* (with their utmost oaths) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of *aqsamū*, derived from its sense: "they swore an oath strenuously exerted in," or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) in the sense of "striving." Its original form is "they strive with the utmost of their oaths," so the circumstantial clause is in reality the whole sentence. For this reason it is valid for it to be a circumstantial clause, as in their saying: "Do that with your utmost effort" (*ifʿal dhālika jahdaka*), even though a circumstantial clause should be indefinite; because it is not a circumstantial clause in its original form.

Others have said: the definiteness of the circumstantial clause here is not a problem, because it is in interpretation indefinite. It is a metaphor from "he exerted himself" (*jahada nafsahu*) when he reached its limit. The overall meaning is: "Are these the ones who confirmed the oaths and made them strong?"

﴿Their deeds have come to nothing, and so they have become losers.﴾ It is possible that this is a resumed sentence brought from His side, exalted is He, to explain the outcome of what they did in claiming allegiance and swearing to be with them in every condition, following the allusion to its falseness by the interrogative. It is also possible that it is part of what the believers say, by making it a second predicate of the demonstrative. Some grammarians have allowed the like of this, and among its instances is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾. Or it may be made the predicate, with the relative pronoun and what falls within its relative clause being an attribute of the subject. In that case the interrogative is for affirmation (*taqrīr*), and it carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How their deeds have come to nothing! How great their loss!" The meaning is: their deeds that they performed concerning your allegiance, and in which they strove with great effort, have come to nothing, since there is no dominion for you, as they supposed, so that they might benefit from what they did of exertions and endured the hardships of toil. There is in this, from the ridicule of the hypocrites and the rebuke of the addressees, what is not hidden. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam.

Some have gone to the view that if it is part of what is said, then it is in the accusative position governed by "said," with the supposition that a speaker asks: "What did the believers say after that statement of theirs?" So it is said: "They said: *their deeds have come to nothing*," and so on. The sentence is either informative, and the believers' testimony to its content, on the supposition that what is meant is worldly loss, and the going of the deeds without benefit that results from them is the hope they placed in the dominion of the Jews, which presents no difficulty; or, on the supposition that what is meant is an otherworldly matter, it may be taken in regard to what appears of the condition of the hypocrites in committing what they committed, or in regard to the Prophet's (ﷺ) informing of that. Or it is a supplicatory sentence, and there is no harm in invoking the like of that, as has been indicated. The statement of some has suggested that there is in the sentence a sense of wonder absolutely, whether it is part of the speech or part of the speech of God, exalted is He. Perhaps this is far-fetched for one who reflects.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 5, verse 54 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾. This begins an explanation of the state of apostates in general, after Allah, glorified is He, had earlier forbidden allegiance to the Jews and Christians, and had explained that such allegiance leads to apostasy from the religion. He also detailed the fate of the hypocrites who give them their allegiance. It has been said: this is one of the events that the Qur'an reported before they occurred.

It is narrated that eleven groups apostatized from Islam, three of them during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

The Banu Mudlij, whose leader was Dhu al-Himar, namely al-Aswad al-'Ansi. He was a soothsayer who claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized control of its lands. He expelled from them the governors of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen. Allah destroyed him at the hands of Fayruz al-Daylami, who attacked him by night and killed him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of his killing on the night he was killed, and the Muslims rejoiced at it. The Prophet (ﷺ) passed away the following day, and the news arrived in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal.

The Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima al-Kadhdhab ibn Habib, who claimed prophethood. He wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "From Musaylima, Messenger of Allah, to Muhammad, Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Peace be upon you. To proceed: I have been made a partner in the affair with you, and to us belongs half the earth, and to Quraysh belongs half the earth, but Quraysh are a people who transgress." Two of his messengers came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with this letter. When he (ﷺ) read his letter, he said to them: "What do you two say?" They said: "We say what he said." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, were it not that messengers are not killed, I would have struck off your necks." Then he (ﷺ) wrote to him:

"In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, Messenger of Allah, to Musaylima the liar: Peace be upon the one who follows guidance. To proceed: Indeed the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good end is for the God-fearing."

This was in the tenth year (of the Hijra). Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) fought him with the armies of the Muslims, and he was killed at the hands of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza (may Allah be pleased with both of them). Wahshi used to say: "In my pre-Islamic days I killed the best of people, and in my Islam I killed the worst of people." It was also said that he and Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Ansari took part in killing him: Wahshi stabbed him, and Abdullah struck him with his sword. He himself said:

*People ask me about his killing, so I say: "I struck him, and that was a stab."*

[The verses continue in several lines.]

The Banu Asad, the people of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against him, and after the fighting he fled to Syria. He then embraced Islam, and his Islam was sound.

Seven groups apostatized during the time of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): Fazara, the people of Uyayna ibn Husayn; Ghatafan, the people of Qurra ibn Salama al-Qushayri; the Banu Sulaym, the people of al-Fujaa'a ibn Abd Yalil; the Banu Yarbu', the people of Malik ibn Nuwayra; some of the Banu Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, the soothsayer, who claimed prophethood and married herself to Musaylima in a well-known story. It is established that she later embraced Islam and her Islam was sound; Kinda, the people of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays; and the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il in Bahrain, the people of al-Hatm ibn Zayd. Allah sufficed them through the hands of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

One group apostatized during the time of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): Ghassan, the people of Jabala ibn al-Ayham, who became a Christian, joined Syria, and died upon his apostasy. It was also said that he embraced Islam.

It is narrated that Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to the scholars of Syria when Jabala joined them a letter in which he said: "Jabala came to me with the nobles of his people and embraced Islam, so I honored him. Then he set out for Makkah and performed the tawaf, and a man from the Banu Fazara stepped on his waist-wrapper. Jabala slapped him and broke his nose and knocked out his front teeth." In another narration: "He gouged out his eye." The Fazari complained against Jabala to me, so I ruled either for pardon or for retaliation. He said: "Will you take retaliation against me while I am a king and he is a commoner?" I said: "Islam has made you and him equal; you have no superiority over him except through well-being." Jabala asked for a delay until the next day. When night came, he rode off with his cousins and joined Syria as an apostate.

It is also narrated that he regretted what he had done and recited:

*I became a Christian after the truth, out of shame at a slap, though had I been patient with it there would have been no harm.*

*Then the obstinacy of zealous pride overtook me, so I sold my sound eye for a blind one.*

*Would that my mother had not borne me, and that I had been patient with the word that Umar said.*

This view has been objected to on the ground that this is one of the matters that Allah reported before they occurred, since *man* (مَن) is conditional, and a condition does not imply that the event happens, as its basic use is for hypothetical matters. The answer is that the conditional may be used for matters that are certain, to indicate that they should not occur, and that they should rather have been placed among the hypothetical matters. This usage is common. It is known from the occurrence of these events after this verse that the intended meaning is this.

Nafi' and Ibn Amir read *wa-man yartadid* (ومَن يَرْتَدِدْ) with the doubled letters unmerged (فك الإدغام), which is the original form, because the second of the two identical letters is vowelless. It is also so in some copies of the Imam's codex.

Allah's words, ﴿then Allah will bring forth﴾, are the response (jawab) of the conditional *man* (مَنِ), which is the subject of the sentence. Scholars differ regarding its predicate. It has been said that the predicate is the whole conditional clause together with its response. It has been said that the predicate is the response alone. On the first view the response does not need a pronoun linking it back, but on the second view it does, and here it is implied. The sense is: "then Allah will bring forth, in their place, after their destruction, a people whom He loves with a love befitting His majesty, according to the meaning He intended; ﴿and they love Him﴾, that is, they incline to Him, glorified is His majesty, with a true inclination, so they obey Him in carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions." The phrase ﴿and they love Him﴾ is coordinated with the preceding *yuhibbuhu* (يُحِبُّهم, He loves them). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in it, meaning: "while they love Him."

In *al-Kashshaf*: The love of the servants for their Lord is obedience to Him and seeking His pleasure, and not doing what brings about His anger and punishment. The love of Allah for His servants is that He rewards them with the best reward for their obedience, honors them, praises them, and is pleased with them.

As for what the most ignorant of people believes, and the most hostile to knowledge and its people, the most opposed to the Sharia, and the worst in conduct (though their way is esteemed among the like of them, the ignorant and foolish), it is nothing. They are the contrived and agitated group among the Sufis, and what they profess of love and passion, and of singing upon their chairs (may Allah ruin them) and in their dance-halls (may Allah render them idle), with verses of amorous poetry composed about beardless youths. Indeed, those whom they call martyrs, and their swoons, compared to which the swoon of Musa (peace be upon him) is nothing, and then the crumbling of the mountain (Sinai)—exalted is Allah far above that by a great exaltation! Among their sayings: Just as He loves them in His essence, so they love His essence, for the pronoun refers to the essence and not to the attributes and qualities. And among them: love has the condition that the intoxications of love overtake it; when that does not happen, there is no reality in it. End of his words.

He has mixed the worthless with the valuable in this. He spoke in an utterly disgraceful manner of disparagement against the Sufis, and attributed to them things that no one who commits them would be regarded, nor counted even among animals, let alone among the elite of mankind. But it does not follow that because a group has taken this name—usurping it from its people, and then committing what is reported of them, and indeed multiplying many times over what we know of this group in our time, which contradicts the state of those truly named by it—that we should hold the righteous accountable for the wicked, and strike the heads of some with others. ﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

The verification of this matter, according to what Ibn al-Munir mentioned in *al-Intisaf*, is that there is no doubt that interpreting the servant's love for Allah as obedience to Him, glorified is He, is contrary to the apparent meaning. It is a kind of figurative usage (majaz), in which the effect is named by the name of its cause. Figurative usage is not turned to from the literal meaning (haqiqa) except when the literal meaning is impossible. So let the literal reality of love (mahabba) be examined linguistically according to the rules, to see whether it is established for the servant, connected to Allah, or not. Love linguistically is the inclination of one who is characterized by it toward something pleasurable. The pleasures that arouse love are divided into those perceived by the senses, such as the taste of food and the pleasure of looking at beautiful forms, and others; and into pleasures perceived by the intellect, such as the pleasure of rank, leadership, and knowledge, and what resembles them. It is established that among the pleasures that arouse love there are some that only the intellect perceives and not the senses. Then love necessarily varies according to the variation of its motives. The pleasure of a person's leadership over the people of one village is not like his pleasure in leadership over notable regions. If love varies according to the variation of its motives, then the pleasures of knowledge also vary according to the variation of the things known. Nothing known is more perfect or more majestic than the true object of worship. So the pleasure that results from knowing Him and knowing His majesty and perfection is greater, and the love that springs from it is stronger. When this love arises, it stirs up acts of obedience and conformity.

From this it is established that the servant's love for his Lord, glorified is He, is possible, indeed it actually occurs in every believer. It is one of the necessary requirements and conditions of faith. People vary in it according to the variation of their faith. Since this is so, it is necessary to interpret the servant's love for Allah, mighty and majestic is He, according to its true linguistic meaning. Acts of obedience and conformity are then like its consequence and different from it. Do you not see the Bedouin who asked about the Hour, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What have you prepared for it?" He said: "I have not prepared for it great deeds, but I love Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A person is with whom he loves." This clearly shows that what is understood by love for Allah is other than deeds and the commitment to acts of obedience, because the Bedouin negated the deeds and affirmed love, and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved of this. Then he (ﷺ) affirmed that the servant's love for Allah is to be taken in its literal reality. When love becomes intensified, it is called ishq (passionate love). So ishq is intense and firmly established love. The claim that it is an expression for love beyond the measure of the beloved, so that whoever says "I am a lover (ʿashiq) of Allah or of His Messenger (ﷺ)" becomes an unbeliever, as some of our Hanafi masters have said, is in my view something to be rejected.

Those who acknowledge the conceivability of the servant's love for Allah in its true meaning consider those who deny it to be ignorant, and so they deny it. Just as a child denies that there is any pleasure beyond play, such as intercourse or other things, and a person absorbed in desires and passion for women thinks there is no pleasure beyond that, such as rank or dignity or the like. Every group mocks what is above it, believing that they are occupied with nothing.

The Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali (may Allah refresh his spirit) said: "Those who love Allah say to whoever denies this about them: ﴿If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock﴾," end of his words, with some slight addition. He did not, however, speak about the meaning of Allah's love for the servant. You know that this belongs to the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses), and the positions on it are well known. We have already presented some of the discussion on this matter, so remember it.

The intended referent of "these people" in the well-known view is the people of Yemen. Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from the hadith of Iyad ibn Umar al-Ash'ari that "when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who was of the pure stock of Yemen, and said: 'They are the people of this man.'"

And from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak: they are Abu Bakr and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who fought the people of apostasy (ahl al-riddah).

And from al-Suddi: they are the Ansar. It was also said: they are those who fought at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah: two thousand from al-Nakha', five thousand from Kindah and Bajilah, and three thousand from the various tribes. There, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas fought Rustam the wretched, commander of the army of Yazdajird.

The Imamiyyah said: they are Ali, may Allah honour his face, and his partisans at the Battle of the Camel and at Siffin. And it is reported from them that they are the Mahdi and those who follow him, but they have no basis for this except their false narrations. It was also said: they are the Persians, "because the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about them, so he struck his hand on the shoulder of Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: 'This man and his people.'" Al-Iraqi criticised this, saying: "I have not found a report containing this, and here it is a mistake; rather, this was related regarding His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾, as al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. Whoever mentions it here has erred."

﴿humbly (adhillah) toward the believers﴾: showing compassion toward them and humbling themselves before them. It is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul, for its plural is dhulal. The apparent expression would have been "adhillah li-l-mu'minin," as one says "tadhallala lahu" (he humbled himself to him), and not "tadhallala 'alayhi," because of the incompatibility between humbling oneself and superiority. However, it is construed with ʿalā because it is made to imply the meaning of compassion and tenderness (al-'atf wa-l-hunuww), which is construed with it. It was also said: this is to draw attention to the fact that they, despite their high rank and their superiority over the believers, are lowering their wings to them.

Perhaps the intended meaning is that ʿalā is used in the sense of li (for), to indicate that they outdid the other believers in humility, to the point that they surpassed them in this attribute. But there is some obscurity in deriving this from that. As for the view that the meaning is that the attribute implies the meaning of excellence and superiority, i.e., that their being humble is not because they are inherently humble, but because they intend to combine with the loftiness of their station and honour the virtue of humility, there is much to be said against it, for the one who makes this claim contrasted it with implication (tadmin), which requires that it be a different aspect with no implication in it.

As for the view that the prepositional phrase, on this reading, is attached to a deleted element occurring as a further attribute of "a people," and "together with the loftiness of their rank," etc., is an explanation of His saying "upon the believers," and "lowering their wings" etc. is an explanation of "humble," this is not something worth considering.

It was also said: the humility is construed with ʿalā because ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ (aʿizzah ʿalā al-kafirin) is construed with it, as its usage requires, and it accompanies it, so the parallelism (al-mushakalah) is taken into account. They have stated explicitly that the order may be inverted. It was also said: because "might" (al-ʿizzah) is construed with ʿalā and humility is its opposite, so it is treated in the same way as it; for just as a counterpart is treated by analogy to its counterpart, so an opposite is treated by analogy to its opposite, as Ibn Jinni and others stated explicitly.

The genitive forms of ﴿humble﴾ and ﴿mighty﴾ are in agreement as two attributes of "a people," like the preceding clause, and the conjunction between them is omitted to indicate that they are independently characterised by each of them.
