This indicates the validity of placing the explicit attribute after the non-explicit one, and this occurs in other verses. Whoever does not permit this makes the clause here a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradiyyah), and it is not hidden that this is a strained interpretation.

The meaning of their being ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ is that they are firm and prevail over them, from ʿazzahu (he overpowered him) when one overcomes him. Al-'Allamah al-Tibi stated that this attribute was brought for completion (al-takmil), because the attribute before it may give the impression that they are humble and despised in themselves, so this illusion is dispelled by stating it, in the manner of the poet's words:

They sit in their assemblies, dignified, and if a guest comes upon them, they are light and gentle (khufuf).

It is read as aʿizzatan and adhillatan in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of "a people," to specify it by the attribute.

﴿striving in the way of Allah﴾ by fighting, to raise high His word, and to strengthen His religion, may His glory be great. This is another attribute of "a people," following from what precedes it, and clarifying, together with what follows, the manner of their might. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial state from the pronoun in ʿizzah, meaning: they are made mighty while striving; and that it be a new independent clause.

﴿and they do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾ in what they undertake of striving, or in everything they do and leave undone. It is conjoined to "striving," meaning that they combine striving with steadfastness in religion. Herein is an allusion to the hypocrites. It was permitted that it be a circumstantial state of the subject of "striving," meaning: they strive while their state is not the state of the hypocrites; the allusion is then clearer. It was said that on the first reading there is no allusion, but rather it is a completing addition to the meaning of "striving," conveying emphasis and comprehensiveness; but this is not sound.

The circumstantial reading was objected to on the grounds that they have stated that the present tense negated by "la" or "ma," like the affirmative, does not admit the conjunction "wa" before it. It was answered that this rule is based on the view of al-Zamakhshari, who held that the present negated by "la" and "ma" may be conjoined with "wa," for the grammarians permitted this in the case of the negation by "lam" and "lamma," and there is no difference between them.

The word "lawmah" is a single instance of blame, from "lawm," i.e., objection, and it is in the genitive by annexation to its agent. The original form of "lā'im" is "lāwim," an active participle like "qā'im." With the singular "lawmah" and the indefinite "lā'im," there are two intensifications, as it is said; al-'Allamah al-Tibi explained that the non-fear of one instance of blame does not negate the fear of all blamings, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is general; then, when its indefiniteness is joined with the indefiniteness of its agent, it comprehends the negation of fear of all blamers. Thus this is completion upon completion: they do not fear anything of blame from any of the blamers.

It was objected to this: how can "lawmah" be more intensive than "lawm," with the meaning of unity it carries? Had it been said "lawmu lā'im" it would have been more intensive! It was answered: it is originally for the single instance, but what is meant here is the genus, and the ta' was brought to indicate that the genus of blame, in their estimation, is like a single instance of blame. It was objected that this does not resolve the question, for there is no indication of this figurative usage while the ambiguity remains. It may be said that the context of praise is a strong indication of this.

﴿That﴾ refers to the qualities previously mentioned, not to some of them, as it was said; the singular is for what has preceded, and likewise the sense of distance in it. ﴿is the bounty of Allah﴾, that is, His kindness and beneficence, ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, giving it to them, not that they are independent in being characterised by it. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, abundant in bounty, or generous, whose resources are never feared to be exhausted, may He be glorified, ﴿All-Knowing﴾,

صفحة 165

emphatic in the knowledge encompassing all things, among which is the one who is worthy of bounty and its locus. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it. The mention of the Majestic Name here is to indicate the cause and to emphasise the independence of the parenthetical sentence, as has passed more than once.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusions (al-isharah) in the verses, according to what some of the gnostics have said:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what is before it of the Book﴾: it may be that the first "Book" is an allusion to the knowledge of the Criterion (ʿilm al-Furqan), and the second to the knowledge of the Qur'an. The first is the manifestation of the details of perfection, and the second is the general knowledge established in the readiness. The meaning of its being "guardian over it" (muhayminan ʿalayhi) is preserving it by manifestation. It may also be that the first refers to what is between our hands of the codex, and the second refers to the genus that encompasses the Torah, whose call is toward the outward, and the Gospel, whose call is toward the inward; and our Book comprises both, preserving each of the two Books.

( ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ ) from justice, which is the shadow of love, which is the shadow of unity, which has been unveiled to you. ( ﴿And do not follow their desires﴾ ) in favouring one of the two sides, either the outward or the inward. ( ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law﴾ ) a source, like the source of the soul, the source of the heart, the source of the spirit. ( ﴿And a way﴾ ) a path, like the knowledge of the rulings and the cognitions that relate to the soul, and the traversing of the path of the inward that leads to the Garden of Attributes, and the knowledge of Unity and contemplation, which relates to the spirit, and the traversing of the path of annihilation that leads to the Garden of the Essence. Some have said: Allah, glory be to Him, has seas for spirits, rivers for hearts, and streams for minds, and for each of them there is a law in that from which one drinks: like the law of knowledge, the law of power, the law of self-sufficiency, the law of love, and so on. And He, Mighty and Majestic, has paths equal to the breaths of creatures, as Abu Yazid, may his secret be sanctified, said. By these are meant the personal paths, not absolutely, and all of them lead to Him, may He be glorified. This is an allusion to the diversity of the drinking-places of people and the non-unity of their roads. He, may He be exalted, has said: ﴿Each people has known its drinking-place﴾, and He distinguished between the righteous and the drawn-near in this. Rarely do two agree on one drinking-place and one method. From here the problem is resolved concerning what is related from His eminence the white falcon, our master Muhyi al-Din ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified, that he said: "I kept travelling in the wildernesses of holiness until I had traversed the traces, and a trace of a footstep appeared to me from afar, and my soul nearly departed; then a call came: 'This is the footstep of your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)!'" For its apparent meaning requires that he (ﷺ) preceded the prophets and messengers, the lords of legislation, peace be upon them, and others of the perfect, and this, as you see, is not so.

Its explanation is that he, may his secret be sanctified, traversed the traces on the path in which he was, and that requires precedence only over the travellers of that path, and no more. So it is possible that he was preceded by those mentioned of travellers on a different path from that one. This is the best that occurs to me in answer to that problem, considering my own drinking-place, and the drinking-places of people are diverse.

( ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation﴾ ) agreeing in drinking-place and path. ( ﴿But He tests you in what He has given you﴾ ) that is, to manifest upon you what He has given you according to your readiness, in proportion to the acceptance of each of you. ( ﴿So race to good works﴾ ) that is, to the matters that lead you to your perfection, which has been decreed for you according to the readinesses that bring you near to it by bringing it into act.

( ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ ) in the unity of the totality of existence according to the levels. ( ﴿Then He will inform you of that about which you used to differ﴾ ) and that is by manifesting the effects of what that difference requires. ( ﴿And judge between them﴾ ) according to what wisdom requires and what readiness accepts. ( ﴿By what Allah has revealed﴾ ) to you of the Qur'an, which comprises the outward and the inward. ( ﴿And do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed﴾ ) so that you are restricted to the pure outward or the pure inward, and deny the other. ( ﴿But if they turn away, know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ ) like the sin of veiling the acts for the Jews, and the sin of veiling the attributes for the Christians. ( And indeed many of the people are defiantly disobedient ) and the kinds of defiance vary: the defiance of the Jews is their departure from the rule of the manifestations of the Divine acts, through seeing

صفحة 166

...the self's actions. The disbelief of the Christians is their departing from the judgment of the manifestations (tajalliyat) of the Real attributes (al-sifat al-haqqaniyya), by the self's seeing its own attributes. The iniquity that afflicts some of this community is turning toward their own essences and departing from the judgment of the essential Oneness (al-wahda al-dhatiyya), (﴿Do they seek the judgment of ignorance?﴾), which is the judgment issuing from the station (maqam) of the self in ignorance, not from divine knowledge. (﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾) of Truth, so he is veiled by some of the veils (hujub). (﴿Then Allah will bring a people whom He loves﴾) from eternity, not for a cause, (﴿and who love Him﴾) likewise. The source of the love that does not change, according to the Sufis, is the Essence without the attributes, as al-Wasiti said, and al-Zamakhshari criticized it, as we have already mentioned. Since He loved them, and they did not exist except in knowledge, the lover and the beloved were one in the state of collective unity (ayn al-jam').

Al-Sulami said: "They loved Him by the grace of His love for them. Otherwise, from where would they have love for Allah, the Exalted? What does dust have to do with the Lord of lords!" The condition of love, as he said, is that it be touched by the intoxications (sakarat) of love; otherwise it is not truly love. A Bedouin woman said in describing love: "It is hidden from being seen, and it is too exalted to be concealed. It is latent like fire in a stone: if you strike it, it appears, and if you leave it, it hides. Even if it is not a branch of madness, it is the essence of magic." This is the nature of love for the created. How then is the love of the Eternal, may His majesty be exalted? The discussion of this is lengthy.

(﴿Humble towards the believers﴾) because of their intrinsic kinship (al-jinsiyya al-dhatiyya), the bond of eternal love, and the natural affinity among them. (﴿Mighty towards the disbelievers﴾), the veiled ones, for the opposite of what has been mentioned. (﴿They strive in the way of Allah﴾) by effacing their attributes and annihilating their essences, which are the veils of contemplation (mushahada). (﴿And they do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾) because of the excess of their love, which is the greatest right guidance (rashad a'zam) for the one who possesses it:

"When a young man recognizes right guidance for himself,
the blame of the blamers becomes easy for him."

Indeed, when love is true, the lover delights in blame, as it is said:

"I find blame in Your love sweet,
out of love for Your remembrance, so let the blamers blame me."

(﴿That is the grace of Allah﴾), whose extent cannot be reached, (﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾) of His servants whom divine care has preceded. (﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾) in grace (al-fadl), (﴿All-Knowing﴾) as to where He places His grace. We ask Allah, the Exalted, to bestow upon us of His vast grace and His generosity, which has no preventer.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 55 (part 1 of 2):

Then, when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾, and gave the reason for it that He gave, He then mentioned, right after that, the one who truly deserves to be taken as an ally, by way of restriction (qasr), saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Your only ally is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. It is as if it were said: Do not take those people as allies, for some of them are allies of one another and are not your allies. Your allies are only Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the believers. So confine your allegiance to them and do not overstep them to others. He used the singular word walī (ally) although it is in a plural sense, in order to convey, as has been said, that allegiance belongs to Allah, exalted is He, in the primary sense, and to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the believers by extension. Thus the sense is: Your only ally is Allah, glorified is He, and likewise His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and those who believe. In the speech there is therefore a principal and a subordinate, and not that walīyukum (your ally) is singular used in the manner of the plural, as the author of al-Fara'id (Sahib al-Fara'id) supposed. He objected that what was mentioned is far from the rule of speech, since it makes what does not admit of singular and plural into a plural. Then he said: It may be said that the sense is: ﴿Your only ally is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾ are your allies, so the predicate has been omitted because the preceding indicates it. The benefit of the separate mention of the predicate is to draw attention to the fact that their being allies comes after His, glorified is He, being the ally, and then after His making them allies; so in reality He is the ally. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from the careful reader that the outcome is one and the source is one. From what has been established it is known that the words of al-Halabi may bear another meaning, namely that walī is of the form fa'īl, and the people of the language have stated that it applies to the one, the two, and the plural, masculine and feminine, with a single form, like ṣadīq, without being used in its proper place. This does not conflict with what we have presented, that if the sense were as such it would contradict restricting allegiance to Allah, exalted is He, and then affirming it for the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and for the believers; because the restriction is in regard to His, glorified is He, being the ally in the primary and true sense, while the allegiance of others is only by attribution to Him, exalted is His majesty.

﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakah﴾ is a substitute for the first relative pronoun, or a qualifier of it, considering it as functioning like nouns; for the relative clause is a link to describing definites by sentences, and a descriptive cannot be described except with an interpretation. It is also permissible to regard it as accusative by way of praise, or nominative by way of praise too. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is ﴿wa-alladhīna yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh﴾ with a waw.

﴿And they are bowing (rāki'ūn)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of the two verbs, meaning: they do what was mentioned of establishing prayer and giving zakah while they are humble and submissive before Allah, exalted is He.

It has been said: it is a circumstance specifically concerning the giving of zakah, and rukūʿ means the rukūʿ of prayer, and the purpose is to show the completeness of their eagerness for good and their hastening toward it. Most of the transmitters of reports hold that it was revealed concerning ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face. Al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and others transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, with a connected chain, that he said: "Ibn Salam and a group of his people who had believed in the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, came and said: O Messenger of Allah, our dwellings are far away, and we have no gathering or place to converse except this gathering, and when our people saw that we had believed in Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and had confirmed him, they abandoned us, and swore upon themselves that they would not sit with us, nor marry us, nor speak to us, and this grieved us. So the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿Your only ally is Allah, and His Messenger﴾. Then he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, went out to the mosque while the people were standing and bowing, and he saw a beggar and said: Has anyone given you anything? He said: Yes, a silver ring. He said: Who gave it to you? He said: That one standing, and he gestured toward ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: In what state did he give it to you? He said: While he was bowing. So the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said takbir, then recited this verse." Then Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, composed:

O Abu Hasan, my self and my soul are ransom for you, and every one slow in guidance and every one hastening to it.
Shall your praise, finely woven, go to waste? Yet praise is not wasted in the presence of God.
You are the one who gave, when you were bowing, a zakah; may the soul be ransomed for you, O best of those who bow.
So God revealed concerning you the best of allegiance, and affirmed it in the two books of the laws.

The Shi'a have used this as evidence for his imamate, may Allah ennoble his face. The basis of their argument, in their view, is that it is agreed that it was revealed concerning him, may Allah ennoble his face, and the word innama (only) conveys restriction, and the word walī means one who manages affairs and who has the right to dispose of them; and it is evident that what is meant here is the general disposal equivalent to the imamate, by the indication of the linking of his allegiance with the allegiance of Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. So his imamate is established and the imamate of others is negated, for otherwise the restriction would be void. There is no difficulty in expressing one by the plural, for it has come in more than one place. The scholars of Arabic have mentioned that it has two purposes: glorifying the agent, and that whoever does that act is of great standing, like a group; as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾, so as to encourage people to do the like of his deed. And glorifying the act as well, so that his act becomes a natural disposition of every believer; and this is a subtle point, to be considered in every place according to what suits it.

The Sunnis have answered this with several arguments:

The first: a counter-argument, that this proof, as they claim, indicates the negation of the imamate of the earlier caliphs, and likewise indicates the removal of the imamate from the later imams, such as the two grandsons and the rest of the Twelve, may Allah be pleased with them all, by the very same reasoning. So the proof harms the Shi'a more than it harms the Sunnis, as is not hidden. It cannot be said that the restriction is relative to those who preceded him, for we say: the restriction of allegiance to one who possesses those qualities is not beneficial unless it is absolute; indeed it is not valid, because those qualities are not found in those who came after him, may Allah ennoble his face. And even if they answer the counter-argument by saying that what is meant is the restriction of allegiance to the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, during some period, namely the period of his imamate, not the period of the imamate of the two grandsons and those after them, may Allah be pleased with them, we say: then welcome to agreement; for our school also holds that general allegiance belonged to him during the time of his being imam, not before it, which is the period of the rule of the three, nor after it, which is the period of the rule of those mentioned.

If they say: if the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, had not been the possessor of general allegiance during the time of the caliphs, a deficiency would follow for him, unlike the time of the rule of his noble descendants, may Allah be pleased with them, for when he was no longer alive, the imamate of another did not become a cause of diminishing his complete nobility, because death removes all worldly rulings. It is said: this is flight and a shift to another argument, which is not understood from the verse, for it rests on two premises:

The first: that the holder of general allegiance being under the allegiance of another, even for a period of time, is a deficiency in him, as he is not independent in allegiance.

The second: that the holder of general allegiance is not subject to any deficiency in any respect, at any time whatsoever. Neither of these two is understood from the verse at all, as is not hidden from anyone of understanding. Moreover, this argument is refuted by the two grandsons during the period of the Commander's rule, and even by the Commander himself during the time of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.

The second: we do not grant the consensus that it was revealed concerning the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face. The scholars of tafsir have differed on this. Abu Bakr al-Naqqash, author of the well-known tafsir, related from Muhammad al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was revealed concerning the Muhajirun and the Ansar. And one speaker said: We have heard that it was revealed concerning ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face; and he (al-Baqir) said: He is among them, meaning that he, may Allah ennoble his face, is also included among the Muhajirun and the Ansar and is one of them.

Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, related from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, something similar, and this report is more in accord with the plural forms in the verse.

A group of exegetes related from ʿIkrimah that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: we do not grant that the meaning of walī is one who manages affairs and has the right to dispose of them with general disposal; rather the meaning is the helper, because the discourse concerns strengthening the hearts of the believers and comforting them, and removing fear from them concerning the apostates; and this is a stronger indication of what he mentioned, and the conjunction does not contradict it, as is not hidden from one whom Allah has opened the eye of his insight.

And whoever is fair to himself knows that His saying, exalted is He, afterward: ﴿O you who believe, do not take those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game, from among those who were given the Book before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies﴾, refuses to take walī in the sense of one equal to the supreme Imam; because no one has taken the Jews, the Christians, and the disbelievers as imams for himself, and they too have not taken one another as imams, but they took helpers and friends. The particle innama, which conveys restriction, also demands that meaning; for restriction occurs in what admits of belief in partnership, hesitation, and dispute; and there was not, by consensus, at the time of the revelation of this verse, any hesitation or dispute concerning the imamate and the right of disposal, but rather concerning support and love.

The fourth: even if it is granted that the meaning is what they mentioned, the word of plural is general or equal, as al-Murtada mentioned in al-Dhari'a and Ibn al-Mutahhar in al-Nihaya; and the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, as both parties agree.

So the import of the verse then is the restriction of general allegiance to several men, among whom the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, enters; and taking the general in its particular sense is contrary to the original, and is not valid to resort to without necessity, and there is no necessity.

If they say: necessity is established here, since almsgiving to the beggar while bowing was done by no one other than the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face. We say: the verse is not explicit that the almsgiving occurred during the bowing of prayer, since it is permissible that the rukū' means humility and submissiveness, not in the commonly known sense in the usage of the people of the sharia, as in his words:

Do not humiliate the poor man, perhaps you will one day bow, while fate has raised him up.

It has also been used in this sense in the Qur'an, as has been said regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, since in the prayer of those before us from the peoples of the earlier laws there is no rukū' that is one of the pillars by consensus; and likewise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he fell down bowing﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, bow, they do not bow﴾, as some of the learned have explained. And taking rukū' in the verse to mean other than its sacred legal meaning is no further-fetched than taking zakah, which is joined with prayer, to mean such almsgiving; and this is necessarily binding upon the claimants of Imamism, with certainty.

[Page 169 continues]

Some of us, the People of the Sunna, have said: Taking *ruku'* (bowing) in its technical legal sense (*shar'i*), and making the clause a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the subject of *ya'tuna* ("they come"), necessarily results in a clear deficiency in the meaning of *yuqimuna al-salah* ("they establish the prayer"). The praise and virtue of prayer lie in its being free of movements that have no connection to it, whether many or few. The only difference is that many movements invalidate the prayer, while few do not. But they do not in any way diminish the meaning of establishing the prayer. Therefore, the words of the Exalted God should not be interpreted in this way. End of quotation.

It has reached me that it was said to Ibn al-Jawzi (may Allah have mercy on him): How could 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) give away a ring while he was in prayer, when the assumption, indeed the certain knowledge, is that he (may Allah honour his face) was absorbed in prayer, so that he would not turn his attention to anything unconnected with it? Many reports support this. He then composed verses:

*He gives drink and drinks, and his intoxication does not distract him*
*from the boon companion, nor does he neglect the people.*

*His drunkenness obeys him, so that he is able*
*to act like the sober. This one is the unique man among people.*

Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurdi (may Allah sanctify his secret) answered the basis of this argument by saying that the evidence lies outside the point of dispute. That point is that 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) was the imam after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) without any distinction. This is because the guardianship of "those who believe", according to the claim of the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shi'a), was not intended at the time of address, since that was the era of prophethood, whereas the Imamate is a deputyship (*niyaba*) and cannot be conceived except after the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away. When the time of address is not what is intended, it is necessarily the time later than the time of his passing. There is no limit to the delay. Let that then apply to the Commander of the Faithful (may Allah honour his face) after the passing of the three imams. Thus the Imamiyya's claim is not established.

Among the strange things is that the author of *Izhar al-Haqq* has exerted the utmost effort to correct the argument according to his own claim, yet has offered nothing more than what would make the bereaved laugh and terrify the dead when they hear it. He said: The command to love Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) is necessarily in the form of obligation. So the command to love the believers who possess the mentioned attributes, and their guardianship, is likewise. For in a single speech, the ruling regarding a subject, whether it is single, multiple, or connected by conjunction, cannot be partly obligatory and partly recommended. Otherwise, the word would be used with two meanings. Therefore, when the love and guardianship of those believers are obligatory, just as the love of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) is obligatory, it is impossible that this refers to all Muslims and the whole community on the basis that it is their nature to possess those attributes. This is because it is impossible for any accountable person to know each of them in order to love and befriend them. Moreover, opposing some believers for a certain reason may be permissible, and even obligatory. Therefore, it is determined that the reference is to some of them, namely 'Ali al-Murtada (may Allah honour his face). End of quotation.

It is objected: Even granting the premises, where is the necessary connection between the proof and the claim? How can the specific be inferred from the general? Furthermore, it is not hidden from anyone with even slight reflection that befriending believers, insofar as they are believers, is a general matter without restriction or aspect, and it returns to befriending their faith in reality, and to hating them for a reason that does not harm it. Moreover, what does he say about the words of the Glorious One: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾? Furthermore, how is the opposition of the unbelievers to be answered, and how does it stand, when they are many times more numerous than the believers? If general consideration is sufficient there, then let it suffice here.

You know that considering a plurality under the heading of a unity is something whose occurrence is beyond doubt, let alone its possibility. Reference to the science of lexical meanings (*'ilm al-wad'*) guides to this. The problem is that the three kinds of guardianship would be on one level. But that is not the case. The first is a principle, the second is subordinate, and the third is subordinate to the subordinate. So the predicates differ, and the subjects likewise differ, since guardianship belongs to general matters, is like graded (*mushakkika*) accidents, and conjunction requires sharing in the ruling but not in its aspect. Thus what exists externally, the Necessary Being, the substance, and the accident, all share existence, yet the relation of existence to each is not its relation to the others, and the aspects differ beyond doubt. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: This is my way. I call to Allah upon insight, I and whoever follows me﴾, although calling to Allah is obligatory upon the Messenger (ﷺ) and recommended for others. For this reason the scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) said: Juxtaposition in wording does not require juxtaposition in ruling. They counted this type of argument among the rejected methods of inference.

Then he (the author of *Izhar al-Haqq*) answered the point about the absence of any doubt, given that *innama* ("only") requires it, by saying that it appears from some hadiths of the People of the Sunna that some Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) requested from the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) the appointment of a successor.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Hudhayfa that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would appoint a successor!" He said: "If I appointed one over you and you disobeyed him, you would be punished. But whatever Hudhayfa narrates to you, believe him, and whatever Abd Allah teaches you to recite, recite it."

Also, they asked him (peace be upon him) about who would be imam after him (ﷺ). Ahmad related from 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) that he said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, whom shall we appoint after you? He said: If you appoint Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), you will find him trustworthy, ascetic in the world, and desirous of the Hereafter. If you appoint 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), you will find him strong and trustworthy, who fears no blame in the cause of Allah. And if you appoint 'Ali (and I do not see you doing so), you will find him a guide, rightly guided, who will lead you upon the straight path." This request and this inquiry both imply that there was doubt in his presence (ﷺ) at the time the verse was revealed, so the meaning of *innama* was not invalidated.

The reply is that the mere question and inquiry do not imply the occurrence of doubt. Yes, if they had consulted about this matter, and some had disputed with others after hearing from the Prophet (ﷺ) the answer to what they had asked, then the implication would be established. But that is not the case. A mere question and inquiry do not necessitate *innama* nor belong to its contexts. Rather, they belong to the contexts of *inna*. The difference is as clear as the morning.

Furthermore, even if we grant that there was doubt, how can we know that it came after the verse or before it, whether it was connected or separate, whether it was the cause of revelation or coincidental? The priority, the connection, and the causal relation must be proven, and where is that? A mere possibility is neither accepted nor sufficient for inference.

After all this, the second hadith explicitly contradicts the restriction (*hasr*). For in a context of asking about the one deserving the caliphate, he (ﷺ) mentioned the two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and 'Umar). If the verse came earlier, it would follow that the Messenger (ﷺ) contradicted the Qur'an. If the reverse, it would follow that he was lying. Abrogation (*naskh*) is not conceivable in reports, as established. Moreover, the sequence of one relative to the other is unknown, so the argument collapses.

If they say: The hadith is a single report (*khabar al-wahid*), and that is not accepted in the matter of the imamate. We reply: Likewise, the argument from the verse is not accepted in establishing a doubt and a dispute upon which the reliance on the verse is based. The first hadith indicates that leaving the appointment of a successor is better. So leaving it, as the verse is understood by their claim, is what is meant. Yet they do not permit this. So reflect.

Al-Tabarsi, in *Majma' al-Bayan*, mentioned another aspect, different from what the author of *Izhar al-Haqq* mentioned, regarding the claim that guardianship is restricted. It is that He (the Exalted) said: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah﴾, addressing all the believers, and the Prophet (ﷺ) and others entered into the address. Then He said: ﴿and His Messenger﴾, thereby excluding His Prophet (peace be upon him) from among them, since they were attributed to his guardianship. Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿and those who believe﴾. Therefore, the one addressed by the verse must be other than the one to whom guardianship was given. Otherwise, the one attributed would be the same as the one to whom it is attributed, and each believer would be his own guardian, which is impossible. End of quotation.

You know that what is meant is the guardianship of some believers over others, not that each of them is his own guardian. How could it be imagined from your saying, for example: "O people, do not backbite people", that it is a prohibition for each person against backbiting himself? And in the report also: "Fast on the day the people fast." It does not occur to the heart that it is a command for everyone to fast on the day the people fast. Many similar examples occur in their speech. What we have mentioned regarding the occasion of revelation is clear that those addressed by it were Ibn Salam and his companions. On this there is no difficulty, except that this is not considered a specifying qualifier, as is not hidden. Therefore, the verse in any case does not indicate the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful (may Allah honour his face) in the manner the Imamiyya claim. This is evident to whoever Allah, the Exalted, has protected in his mind from the dust of partisanship.

[Page 171 continues]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 56:

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies⦆ That is: whoever takes them as allies. The explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun (al-idmar, the pronominal form) in observance of the subtle point, mentioned earlier, of demonstrating that the wilaya (guardianship, allegiance) belongs originally to Allah, Exalted is He, as is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the party of Allah – they are the victorious﴾, where the word ḥizb (party, group) – meaning a company and a community in general, or a community that has strength – is attributed to Allah, Exalted is He, alone. And in this – according to the view that a noun is placed in the position of a pronoun – there is also the referent of "whoever" (man), that is: indeed they are the victorious. However, they have been made the party of Allah, Exalted is He, to honor them and to establish their victory by way of demonstrative proof, as if it were said: whoever takes these as allies, then indeed they are the party of Allah, Exalted is He, and the party of Allah, Exalted is He, they are the victorious. The sentence is the answer-indicating clause (dalil al-jawab) according to many of the grammarians (al-mu'rabin).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 57:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as ridicule and play (from) among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies; and fear Allah, if you should be believers.﴾ Ibn Ishaq and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) who said: Rifa'a ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had outwardly professed Islam and then acted hypocritically, and some of the Muslims were friendly with them. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. He, glorified is He, attached the prohibition to a description that encompasses both of them and others, generalizing the ruling, alerting to the cause ('illah), and giving notice that one whose condition is this is deserving of enmity, so how (much more so) of alliance?!

Al-huzu' (ridicule), as in al-Sihah, is mockery. One says: "hazi'tu minhu" and "hazi'tu bihi" (according to al-Akhfash), "istahza'tu bihi," "tahazza'tu," and "hza'tu bihi" also, with "huzu'an" and "mahza'atan" (according to Abu Zayd). A man is "huz'ah" (with sukun), meaning one who is mocked, and "huza'ah" (with fatha on the za'), meaning one who mocks people.

Al-Zajjaj mentioned that four forms are permissible for "huzuwan":

The first: "huzu'" with a damma on the zay and the hamza; this is the original and the most preferred.

The second: "huzuw" with a damma on the zay, with the hamza replaced by waw because of the preceding damma.

The third: "huz'" with sukun on the zay and the hamza.

The fourth: "hazy" like "hady"; reading with any of these except the last is permitted.

"Al-la'ib" (play), with fatha on its first letter and kasra on its second, is like "al-dahik" (laughter). Al-la'b and al-la'b, with fatha or kasra on the lam and sukun on the 'ayn, and al-tal'ab, are the verbal noun of la'iba (like sami'a), and it is the opposite of seriousness (al-jidd), as in al-Qamus. In Majma' al-Bayan: it is taking something not in the way of seriousness, and its equivalent is "al-'abath" (idle play). Its origin is from a child's saliva; it is said: la'iba (like sami'a and mana'a) when his saliva flowed and went in a direction other than its own. The two verbal nouns are either in the sense of the passive participle, or the statement is elliptical with an omitted genitive, or it is for emphasis (mubalagha).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the preceding "alladhina," or relating to the subject of "takhadhu." The mention of the description of being given the Scripture serves to explain the completeness of their wickedness and the extremity of their misguidance, since being given the Scripture should restrain them from taking the religion of the believers who confirm their Scripture as ridicule and play.

﴿and the disbelievers﴾
That is, the polytheists. This meaning occurs in several places in the Qur'an, and they were singled out because of the multiplication of their disbelief. It is conjoined to the first relative clause, and according to this there is no explicit statement of their mockery here, even though it is affirmed of them in the verse ﴿Indeed We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾, since the intended ones there are the polytheists of Arabia. In that case the prohibition is not, with regard to them, grounded in mockery; rather they were forbidden from allying with them from the outset.

Al-Kisa'i and the people of Basra read "wal-kuffari" with a kasra, conjoining it to the last relative clause. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy ("and from the disbelievers") and the reading of 'Abd Allah ("and from those who associated partners"), and thus they too are among those explicitly mocking.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿allies﴾ is the second object of "la tattakhidhu," and the intended meaning is: distance yourselves from them entirely. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in this matter by abandoning allegiance to them, or by abandoning the prohibited things in general, so that abandoning allegiance to them enters into it in the first place.

﴿if you should be believers﴾ truly, for the requirement of faith necessarily entails taqwa.

(Tafsir commentary text translated below.)

﴿And when you call﴾: i.e., some of you call others ﴿to the prayer, they take it﴾, i.e., the prayer or the call to it, ﴿as a mockery and a game﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi related in *al-Dala'il*, through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The caller of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, when he called to the prayer and the Muslims stood up for it, the Jews said: 'They have stood up; may they never stand up!' And when they saw them bowing and prostrating, they mocked them and laughed at them."

Ibn Jarir and others related, from al-Suddi, who said: "There was a man among the Christians in Medina who, whenever he heard the caller calling, 'I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' would say: 'May the liar be burned.' One night his servant came in with a fire while he was asleep and his family were sleeping, and a spark fell and burned the house, and he and his family were burned."

The discourse is directed to explain their mockery of a particular ruling of the religion, after explaining their mockery of the religion in general, to show the completeness of their wretchedness. ﴿That﴾, i.e., the taking mentioned, is ﴿because they are a people who do not reason﴾, for foolishness leads to ignorance of the excellences of the truth and to mocking it. Had they possessed any reason at all, they would not have dared against such a great matter.

It has been said: in the verse there is evidence that the adhan (the call to prayer, *adhan*) is established by the explicit text of the Book, not by the dream alone. It has been objected that His saying, ﴿And when you call﴾, does not indicate the adhan. Except it may be said: since it came after its establishment, it is a reference to it, and so it is an affirmation of it. In *al-Kashf* he said: I say concerning this: taking the call as a mockery is one of the reprehensible things, for it is among the recognized matters of the Sharia; from this aspect it indicates that the call they were practicing was a legitimate matter prescribed by Him, exalted is He, and this is what is meant by its being established by the text after it had been established initially by the Sunnah, and by the dream of 'Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Ansari, the hadith in full. It is not contradicted by the fact that this occurred when they first arrived in Medina, while al-Ma'ida is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed.

His saying "not by the dream alone" does not imply that the Sunnah is not independent in its indication, for the legal evidences are indicators and signs, not causes and obligating agents, and the coincidence of indicators is not to be denied. Here ends the quotation.

Abu Hayyan has a statement on this point which should not be paid attention to, because of the manifest obstinacy in it. The adhan was called "a calling" (*munadah*) because of the caller's words in it: "Hasten to the prayer, hasten to success."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 59:

﴿قُلْ يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ﴾ "Say: O People of the Book." This is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), addressed in the manner of *talwin al-khitab* (shifting of address), after the prohibition on the believers from speaking as the mockers did. He is commanded to address them, to make clear that the religion is free of anything that would justify what they did of mockery, to reveal to them the cause of what they committed, and to silence them. They are described with the attribute of being People of the Book as a preparation for what Allah, glory be to Him, will mention of their rebuke and their being held to account for their disbelief in their own Book. That is: "Say, O Muhammad, to those wicked ones: ﴿هَلْ تَنْقِمُونَ مِنّا﴾ 'Do you resent us?'" That is: do you disapprove of and find fault with us? It is from *naqama minhu kadha* (to resent something from someone), meaning that he denied it and hated it, in the pattern of *daraba* (to strike).

Al-Hasan read *tanqamuna* with a fatha on the qaf, from the pattern of *ʿalima*, and this is a rare dialect. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *naqima* with fatha and kasra, and its meaning is that he went to great lengths in hating the thing. He recited for ʿAbd Allah ibn Qays:

*"They did not resent the Banu Umayya for anything, except that they are forbearing when they are angry."*

In *al-Nihaya* (of Ibn al-Athir) it is said: *naqama yanqimu* when hatred reaches the limit of wrath. It is also said: *naqima min fulan al-ihsan* when he regards it as something leading to ingratitude for the blessing. From this is the hadith on zakat: "Ibn Jamil resents nothing except that he was poor and Allah made him rich," meaning: he resents nothing in refusing zakat except that he is ungrateful for the blessing; so his wealth led him to ingratitude toward the blessing of Allah, the Exalted.

From al-Raghib: the interpretation of *naqama* as *ankara* (denied) and *aʿaba* (found fault with) is because *al-niqma* means denial by the tongue or by punishment, since one is only punished for what one denies. So it is in the manner of his saying:

*"We curse with deeds, not with speech."*

This, as al-Shihab said, is among the verbs that take *min* and *ʿala*.

Abu Hayyan said: its original construction is with *ʿala*, then the derived form *if'al* from it takes *min*, because it includes the meaning of afflicting with something disliked. Here *faʿala* is used with the meaning of *if'al*, and he did not cite any evidence for this.

﴿إلا أنْ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ وما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْنا﴾ "Except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us," from the glorious Qur'an, ﴿وما أُنْزِلَ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ "and what was revealed before," that is, before its revelation, from the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books revealed to the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿وأنَّ أكْثَرَكم فاسِقُونَ﴾ "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient," that is, rebellious, outside the circle of faith in what has been mentioned. For disbelief in the glorious Qur'an entails disbelief in all the other books, as is clear. The *waw* is for conjunction (*ʿataf*), and what follows it is conjoined to *an amanna* (that we believe).

Some eminent verifiers chose that it is an object of purpose (*maful lahu*) for *tanqimuna*, and the object (*maful bihi*) is the religion, which is omitted, relying on the clear indication of what precedes and what follows it. For taking the religion as a mockery and a game is the very same as resenting it and denying it, and believing in what has been detailed is the very same as the religion they resented. Except that it is in the context of the cause of their resentment toward them, a record against them of complete obstinacy and reversal, since they made it the reason for resenting it while in itself it is the reason for accepting and approving it. Thus the exception on this reading is from the most general of causes: "You resent our religion for no cause except our belief in Allah, the Exalted, and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before from your books; and because most of you are rebellious, not believing in anything of what has been mentioned, even if you believed in your own Book, which states the truth of our book, you would believe in it." Some of them estimated the omitted object to be something specific, and I see no harm in it.

It has been said: the conjunction is to *an amanna* considering it as the object (*maful bihi*), but not on the basis that the excepted item is the combined two conjuncts, since they do not acknowledge that most of them are defiantly disobedient, so as to deny it. Rather it is what the two entail of opposition. So it is as if it were said: "Do you resent us for anything except that we are in a state that opposes your state, since we entered Islam and you left it?" It has been said: the speech is with an omitted modifier, that is, "and the belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said: the conjunction is to the thing believed in, that is: "Do you resent us except our belief in Allah, and in what was revealed to us, and in what was revealed before, and that most of you are disbelievers?" This is in meaning like the view before it.

It has been said: the conjunction is to an omitted cause, and the preposition has been omitted on the side of the conjunct, and its position is either genitive or accusative according to the well-known disagreement. That is: "Do you resent us except the belief, due to the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient?" It has been said: it is accusative by a negated verb omitted, indicated by what was mentioned: "and you do not resent that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said: it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, and it is estimated as preceding according to some, because *anna* with a fatha does not occur with what follows it as a subject unless the predicate precedes it.

Abu Hayyan said: *anna* is not begun with when preceding, except after *amma* only. He opposed most of the grammarians in this condition, though in estimated matters what is not tolerated in other matters is tolerated. The clause, on both estimates, is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) or a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtiraḍ*), that is: "and your defiant disobedience [is] established or known."

[Page 174]

It has been said: the *waw* means "with" (*maʿa*), that is: "Do you resent us except the belief, along with the fact that most of you…" etc.

Al-Allama al-Taftazani objected to this, that it is not complete according to the apparent statement of the grammarians, that the object of accompaniment (*maful maʿahu*) must have accompaniment in the governance of the verb. In that case the problem returns, which is that they resented the fact that most of them are defiantly disobedient. Yes, it is valid according to the view of al-Akhfash, who was satisfied in the object of accompaniment with co-existence in time, citing their saying: "I traveled along with the Nile," and "I came to you at sunrise." There is a point of discussion in this: that the condition regarding the object of accompaniment does not require the condition for every *waw* meaning *maʿa*. So let the *waw* be with the meaning of *maʿa* without being an object of accompaniment, since its condition, which is accompaniment of the verb's governed noun, is absent, and rather it is for conjunction.

It has been said: the *waw* is extra, and "and that most of you…" etc. is in the position of causal explanation, that is: "Do you resent us except the belief, because most of you are defiantly disobedient?"

Naʿim ibn Maysara read *wa-inna akthSarakum* with a kasra on the hamza, and the clause in that case is resumed, explaining that most of them are rebellious. What is meant by "most" is those who did not believe, and those among them who believed are few.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

"Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that?" This is a further rebuke of those wicked people, by making clear that the truly deserving of vengeance and censure is the distorted religion they hold to. In it there is a reproach directed at them by way of allusion, concerning their crimes and the consequences and punishments that befell them. God, glorified be He, did not state this explicitly, lest the explicit statement drive them to persist in obstinacy and stubbornness. He addressed them, before the explanation, with words that indicate the great importance of what is to be explained, and that call for their attention to receiving it: the interrogative sentence that arouses their longing for the one who will be informed, and the verb "unabbi'u" (inform), which suggests that it is a weighty matter, since al-naba' (the news) is the report that has significance and importance. It also refers to the religion that sustains them. The word "sharr" (worse, evil) is applied in relation to it, although it is pure good, entirely free of any admixture of evil, so as to accommodate them in their false belief that its evil is complete, and God forbid. This is to establish that their religion is worse than every evil. God, glorified be He, did not say "anqam" (more deserving of vengeance) explicitly, to specify the basis of the evil, because mere vengeance does not establish it at all, since censure may come from the fault of the censurer:

"How many a censurer has spoken a correct word, while his flaw lies in a sickly understanding."

In this there is confirmation of the evil of what will be mentioned, and an increase in its affirmation. It has been said: he said "bi-sharr" (with something evil) because it occurs in the phrasing of the addressees. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A group of Jews came to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, among them Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi', Ghazi ibn 'Amr, Zayd, Khalid, and Izar ibn Abi Izar. They asked him, peace be upon him, about which of the messengers he believes in. He said: 'We believe in Allah, and in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting.' When he mentioned Jesus, peace be upon him, they denied his prophethood and said: 'We do not believe in Jesus, nor do we believe in whoever believes in him.' Then they said, as in the narration of al-Tabarani: 'We do not know of a religion worse than your religion.' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed the verse." By this report those who held that the addressees of "unabbi'ukum" (I will inform you) are the People of the Book found support.

Some said: the addressees are the disbelievers in general. It was said: they are the believers. Just as there is disagreement about the addressees, there is disagreement about what the demonstrative "dhalika" (that) refers to. The majority hold the view we have already mentioned. It was said: the reference is to the most rebellious wrongdoers. The noun was made singular either because the demonstrative may be used for one and for other than one, unlike the pronoun, or because it is interpreted as referring to "the mentioned" and the like.

It was said: the reference is to the individuals previously mentioned, who are the People of the Book, and the meaning is that the earlier generation is worse than the later one. "Mathuba 'inda Allah" (a recompense with Allah) means a lasting reward with Him, exalted be He. It is a mimi noun (a noun beginning with mim) with the meaning of "thawab" (reward), and it is used of both good and evil, because it is what returns to a person of the recompense of his deeds. It was named thus by the imagining that what one has done returns to him, as His saying, exalted be He, indicates: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it." Here He did not say "will see its recompense." However, the more commonly used form is in regard to good, and similarly "mathuba" in that respect. Its use here in regard to evil is in the manner of mockery, as in the poet's words:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz) from "bi-sharr." It was said: it may be made an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for "unabbi'ukum," meaning: "Shall I inform you, seeking a recompense with Allah, exalted be He, in this informing?" It may also become the cause of your fear and lead to your guidance. On this reading, "mathuba" is in its commonly used sense. Although this has some validity, it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It has been read: "mathbatan" with the thā' sukun and the wāw fatha, and similar to it are "mashura" and "mashwara," contrary to al-Hariri, who required "mashura" like "ma'una."

His saying, glorified be He: "Whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry" is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an annexed noun suppressed before it that suits what is indicated by "dhalika," meaning: the religion of him whom Allah cursed, etc. Or, with an annexed noun suppressed before the demonstrative that suits "man" (whoever), meaning: "bi-sharrin min ahli dhalika" (something worse than the people of that). The sentence, on both assessments, is a resumptive clause (istinaf) that came as an answer to a question arising from the interrogative sentence, as al-Zajjaj said, either in its own form or according to the supposition within it. It is as if it were said: "What is it that is worse than that?" and it was answered: "It is the religion of him whom Allah cursed, etc." Or: "Who is it that is worse than the people of that?" and it was answered: "He whom Allah cursed, etc."

It was permitted, and it should not be permitted upon reflection, that it be an apposition (badal) of "sharr," and an annexed noun must also be supposed, in the manner mentioned just before. The need for it here is to avoid it being an apposition of error (badal ghalat), which does not occur in eloquent speech. As for the first aspect, it is too clear to be hidden. When that is made a reference to the individuals, the sentence does not need that supposition, as is evident. The placing of the noble Name in the position of the pronoun is to instil awe, to bring in dread, and to magnify the matter of the curse and what follows it. The relative pronoun refers to the People of the Book, since Allah, exalted be He, removed them from His mercy and was angry with them for their disbelief and their immersion in sins after the signs had become clear and the proofs had shone forth.

"And He made among them apes and swine" (wa-ja'ala minhumu al-qiradata wal-khanazir): that is, He transformed some of them into apes, and they are the people of the Sabbath, and some of them into swine, and they are the disbelievers of the table of Jesus, peace be upon him.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that both transformations were among the people of the Sabbath: their young men were transformed into apes and their elders into swine. The pronoun in "minhum" refers to "man" according to its meaning, just as the first two pronouns refer to it according to its wording. Likewise the pronoun in His saying, glorified be He: "and who worshipped the Taghut," for it is coordinated with the relative clause of "man," as al-Zajjaj said. Al-Farra' claimed that there is an omitted relative pronoun in the sentence, meaning "and whoever worshipped," and it is coordinated with the object of "ja'ala," meaning: "and He made among them whoever worshipped," etc. It is not hidden that this is valid only according to the Kufans.

The meaning of "al-taghut" (the transgressor/false object of worship) according to al-Jubba'i is the calf which the Jews worshipped. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Hasan, that it is Satan. It was said: the soothsayers and everyone whom they obeyed in disobedience to Allah, exalted be He. Worship, apart from the first opinion, is a metaphor for obedience.

Shaykh al-Islam said: The mentioning of their attributes first, in order to establish the evil of their religion, before their attribute of this (worship of the Taghut), although that is the origin which entails them in existence, and its indication of their evil is essential, since the worship of the Taghut is the very essence of their religion, which is manifestly false. Its indication of it is by way of inference from the evil of the effects to the evil of what produces them of belief and action. Either this is for the purpose of rebuking them from the outset by describing them with what gives them no way to deny, neither its evil and enormity nor their being characterized by it; or it is to signal that each of the front and the back independently indicates the evil mentioned. Had the order of existence been observed, and it were said: "Whoever worshipped the Taghut, and whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry, etc.", it might have been understood that the cause of the evil is the whole combined. End of quotation.

You know that the attribute being the origin is not evident according to what al-Jubba'i held, and that the characterization with the curse and anger is among the things they have no way to deny, in the sphere of prohibition. How, when they say: "We are the children of Allah and His beloved"? Unless it is said: the effects that follow from that and indicate it are most evident, so that denying its implication would be obstinacy.

It was said: he mentioned the two attributes of curse and anger first, because they are explicit that the people are deserving of vengeance, and indicate that this matter is great. He followed them with the mentioned making, as if it were an argument for that, and he added the worship of the Taghut, which indicates the evil of their religion most completely, so that it might settle in the mind most fully, since what indicates it was previously mentioned in general terms. This also is not evident according to the opinion of al-Jubba'i, and perhaps observing it is not necessary, given the lowering of its rank in this context. The apparent sense of Shaykh al-Islam's words is that he built his speech upon this opinion, when he said, after saying: "The intended by the Taghut is the calf; it was said: the soothsayers and everyone whom they obeyed in disobedience to Allah, exalted be He", so that the judgment encompasses the religion of the Christians too. The wisdom of delaying their worship until after the mentioned punishments becomes clear, for had it been placed before them, the two groups would have shared those punishments. End of quotation. So reflect on it carefully.

In the verse, as several scholars have said, there are several readings: two of the seven, and what is other than them is irregular. The majority, other than Hamzah, read "'abada" (he worshipped) in the active past form, and "al-taghut" in the accusative, and this is the reading upon which the interpretation has been built. Hamzah read "wa-'abuda al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', a fatha on the dal, and al-taghuti in the genitive, on the basis that "'abud" is a singular noun intended as a genus, not a plural, since no such form is heard in its patterns, but rather is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah). For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is excessiveness in servitude, and he cited as evidence the verse of Tarafah:

"O sons of Lubayna, your mother is a slave-woman, and your father is an 'abud (a utterly servile one)."

He meant "'abd" (slave), and Ibn al-Anbari and al-Zajjaj mentioned something similar, saying: the ba' was given a damma for intensification, as they say of the clever and the cautious: "fatun" and "hadhurun" with a damma on the ayn. So the criticism by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' of this reading, and the attribution of its reader to error, is itself an error. The accusative is by coordination with "al-qiradah wal-khanazir."

It has been read "wa-'abudi" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', a kasra on the dal, and al-taghuti in the genitive by annexation, and coordinated with "min," on the basis that it is governed by an omitted annexed noun, or by apposition, as has been said, but this was not accepted.

Ubayy read "'abadu" with the plural pronoun referring to "man" according to its meaning, and the coordination is like it in the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan read "'ibad," the plural of "'abd," and "'abd" in the singular, with al-taghuti in the genitive or the accusative. The genitive is by annexation, and the accusative is either on the assumption that the original is "'abada" with a fatha on the ba', or "'abdun" with tanwin, from which it was elided, as in his saying:

"And not remembering God except a little,"

with the noble Name in the accusative, and the coordination is clear.

Al-A'mash, al-Nakha'i and Aban read "'ubida" in the passive past form with al-taghutu in the nominative, as its deputy subject, and the coordination is with the relative clause of "min," and the returning pronoun of the relative is omitted, meaning "'ubida fihim" (was worshipped among them) or "baynahum" (among them). Some read likewise, except that he made it feminine: "'ubidat" with the silent feminine ta', and al-taghut is masculine and feminine, as has passed. The matter of the coordination and the returning pronoun is according to the pattern of the reading mentioned before.

Ibn Mas'ud read "'abuda" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', a fatha on the dal, with al-taghutu in the nominative as the agent of "'abuda," and it is like "sharufa," as if worship had become his disposition, or that it means "became worshipped," like "umira" meaning "became a commander." The returning pronoun to the relative is, on this too, omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read "'ubud" with damma on the ayn and the ba', a fatha on the dal, and al-taghuti in the genitive. According to al-Akhfash, it is a plural of "'abid," the plural of "'abd," so it is a plural of a plural; or the plural of "'abid" like "sharif" and "sharuf"; or the plural of "'abd" like "saqf" and "suquf"; or the plural of "'ibad" like "kitab" and "kutub," so it is also a plural of a plural, like "thimar" and "thumur."

Al-A'mash also read "'ubbad" with a damma on the ayn, a shadda on the ba' which is fatha, a fatha on the dal, and al-taghuti in the genitive, the plural of "'abid" and "'abd," on the pattern of "huttam" and "zuffar," in the accusative, annexed to al-taghut, singular.

Ibn Mas'ud also read ('ubbida) with a damma on the ʿayn, a fatha on the doubled bāʾ, a fatha on the dāl, and the nasb of (al-ṭāghūt), on the pattern of the line:

"wa-lā dhākiri Allāha illā qalīlan"

with the noun of majesty (Allah) in the accusative.

It was also read (wa-ʿābida al-shayṭān), with the nasb of (ʿābid) and the jarr of (al-shayṭān) in place of al-ṭāghūt. According to some, this is an explanation (tafsir), not a reading (qirāʾa).

It was also read (ʿUbbād), like (juhhāl), and (ʿibād), like (rijāl), the plural of ʿābid or ʿabd. In this there is an attribution of "servants" (ʿibād) to other than God Most High, and some have forbidden it.

It was read (ʿābidu) with the raf on the basis that it is the predicate of an implied subject, with the jarr of al-ṭāghūt.

It was read (ʿābidū) in the plural with an idafa.

It was read (ʿābada) in the accusative.

It was read (ʿabada al-ṭāghūt), with fatahat and an idafa, on the basis that its original form is (ʿabadah), like (kafarah), and its tāʾ was dropped for the idafa, as in the line:

"wa-akhlafūka ʿidā al-amri alladhī waʿadū"

meaning ʿidatahu, like (iqāmu al-ṣalāh). Or it is a plural, or a collective noun for ʿābid, like khādim and khadam.

It was read (aʿbuda), like (aklub), and (ʿabīd), which is a plural or a collective noun, and (ʿābidī), a plural with the yāʾ.

Ibn Mas'ud also read (wa-man ʿabadū).

(Ulāʾika): that is, those described by those ugly and shameful traits. It is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and His words (Glorified is He): (sharrun) are its predicate. His words (Exalted is He): (makānan) are a tamyiz transferred from the agent. Attributing evil to their place is to make the evil of their condition more emphatic in indicating their wickedness. The scholars have stated that attributing evil to the place of a thing is a metonymy for attributing it to the thing itself, as in their saying:

"salāmun ʿalā al-majlis al-ʿālī"

and "al-majdu bayna burdayhi."

So it is as though their evil had affected their place, or it became so great that it took on a bodily form.

It has been permitted that the attribution is metaphorical, as in (jarā al-nahr). It was also said: the place may mean the abode of settling and dwelling, where their affairs come to be established, that is, "worse in position," and the intended meaning is Hell, "and evil is the destination." The sentence is independent, coming from Him, Exalted, as a testimony against them of the completeness of their evil and error. It falls under the command, as an emphasis on the obligation and an intensification of the rebuke. Making it an answer to the question arising from the interrogative sentence, so that the earlier possibility of apposition holds together, is something that barely holds together.

(Wa-aḍallu ʿan sawāʾi al-sabīl): that is, more astray from the balanced path of truth, which is the religion of Islam and the ḥanīfiyya. It is coordinated with (sharrun) as a confirmation of it. This indicates that their religion is pure evil, far from the truth, because the way they follow is their religion; so if they are more astray, their religion is manifest error with no end beyond it. The intended meaning of the two comparative forms is an absolute increase, without regard to others sharing in that. It was said: it is comparative according to their own claim. It was also said: it is relative to other unbelievers.

Some have said: there is no objection to saying that their place in the Hereafter is worse than the place of the believers in this world, because of the hardships of time, the bearing of harm, and the oppression they suffered at the hands of their enemies.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on surah 5, verse 61:

﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe."﴾ It was revealed, as Qatadah and al-Suddi said, concerning some Jews who used to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and show him faith and contentment with what he had brought, out of hypocrisy. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the plural is for honour. Or it is addressed to him (peace and blessings be upon him) together with those of his Companions who were with him (may Allah be pleased with them all). That is: when they come to you, they display Islam to you.

﴿And they had entered with disbelief, and they had gone out with it﴾: that is, they leave from your presence as they entered. They gained nothing from their presence before you, and what they heard from you had no effect on them. The two clauses are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, circumstantial state) relating to the pronoun in "qalu" (they said), according to the most apparent view.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that they be two circumstantial clauses relating to the pronoun in "amanna" (we believed). The "ba'" in "bil-kufr" and "bihi" would be for accompaniment (mulabasah), and the prepositional phrases would be circumstantial clauses relating to the subject of "dakhalu" and "kharaju." The waw attached to the nominal circumstantial clause is the waw of the circumstantial state (waw al-hal). Whoever prohibits multiple circumstantial clauses without a conjunction says that the waw is a conjunctive waw, and the item conjoined to a circumstantial clause is also a circumstantial clause.

The entry of "qad" (a particle) into a past-tense circumstantial clause, as the second scholar (al-Allamah al-Thani) said, serves to bring the past closer to the present, so that it breaks the sense of distance between the past and the present in the clause. Otherwise, "qad" only brings things close to the time of speaking.

This points to what al-Sayyid al-Sanad clarified in the margins of *al-Mutawassit*, that it has been said: the past tense indicates only the passing of a time before the time of speaking, whereas the circumstantial state, which describes the condition of the doer or the object, is a restriction on its governing verb. So if the governing verb is past, the circumstantial clause is also past in meaning; if the governing verb is present, it is present; and if it is future, it is future. Therefore, what they (the grammarians) mentioned is an error that arose from the shared usage of the term "hal" between the present tense, which is the opposite of the past, and what expresses the described state. Then he said: It may be said that when a verb occurs as a restriction on something whose being past, present or future is considered with respect to that restricted thing, then when one says, "Zayd came to me riding," it is understood from it that the riding was before the coming, so "qad" must be present to bring it closer to the time of the coming so that it coincides with it. Al-Allamah al-Kafiyaji mentioned something similar in his commentary on *al-Qawa'id*. Then he said: As for the excuse that prefacing the affirmative past with "qad" is merely for verbal elegance, this is a concession to that objection, so it is neither acceptable nor approved. End of quotation.

There is a further detailed discussion of this in its proper place. Another meaning has been mentioned for "qad" in the verse, other than bringing close, namely expectation (tawaqqu'), so it conveys that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was expecting the entry and exit of those wicked people. He was (as clean as a hand that wipes off what is wet, so that nothing clings to them) of what they heard from his admonition (ﷺ) with the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of his supposition, based on the evident signs upon them, of their firmly rooted hypocrisy. For this reason, He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾, and in it is a warning that is not hidden.

In *al-Kashshaf*: the signs of hypocrisy were manifest upon them, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was expecting Allah to reveal what they had concealed, so the particle of expectation entered for this purpose. Al-Tibi objected to this, saying: "qad" is set for the expectation of what follows it, and here what follows it is the very hypocrisy. So how can it be said that it is for Allah's revelation of what they concealed? He answered that there is no doubt that what is expected should be something already occurring, and that they were hypocrites was known to him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) by the evidence of his (al-Zamakhshari's) saying: "the signs of hypocrisy," etc. Therefore it is necessary to resort to metaphor, and to the claim that Allah revealed what they concealed. In *al-Kashf* he said, implicitly criticizing this: the entering into disbelief and the going out with it is itself a manifestation of it, and for this reason the particle of expectation was introduced into it. It is not that it is the very hypocrisy, which would require a metaphorical extension in the return of the expectation to its manifestation. The appearance of its sign is other than Allah's manifestation of it through His informing about them, that they are involved in disbelief and vacillate in it, going out and coming in. End of quotation. So let this be considered carefully.

He, glory be to Him, did not say "and they had gone out" in the same pattern as the first clause, for the purpose of emphasizing the disbelief at the time of going out. This is because it is contrary to the apparent sense. Since their eyes had been illuminated by seeing the rising sun of the Message, and their ears delighted by the pearls of the words of the sea of valour (peace and blessings be upon him), the apparent expectation was that they would turn back from their error and remove from the pure hearts, which lack the adornment of guidance, the fine jewels of disbelief. Furthermore, when they heard the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) and denied it, their disbelief increased and their misguidance multiplied.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 62:

﴿And you see many of them﴾ i.e., of those Jews, as narrated from Ibn Zayd. The address is to the master of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The seeing is visual (basariyyah), and it has been said that it is mental (qalbiyyah). His saying: ﴿hastening into sin and transgression﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from (kathiran) "many," which is described by the prepositional phrase, and it has been said that it is a second object of (tara) "you see." Al-musara'ah (hastening) is rushing to a thing swiftly. The preference of (fi) "in" over (ila) "to" indicates their being firmly immersed in what they hasten toward, as something contained is within its container, and its encompassing their deeds. This point has already been mentioned.

By al-ithm (sin) is meant what is forbidden. It has been said that it means lying in general. It has been said that it means lying through their saying "We believed," since that is either a report or a performative statement that includes a report of the attainment of the quality of faith for them. Specification (of lying) has been argued for by the later verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and their saying sinful speech﴾, though you know that it does not necessitate this. It has been said that what is meant by it is disbelief, and this was narrated from al-Suddi. Perhaps the reason for specifying it as such is that it is the complete instance.
