By al-'udwan (transgression) is meant injustice, or exceeding the limit in acts of disobedience. It has been said that al-ithm is what is specific to them, and al-'udwan is what extends to others. The speech is directed to describing them with evil deeds after describing them with evil belief.

﴿And their consumption of unlawful gain (al-suht)﴾, i.e., what is forbidden in general. Al-Hasan said: it is bribery in judgment. The explicit mention of this, despite its being included in what came before, is for the sake of emphasis in condemnation. ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do﴾, i.e., evil indeed is the thing these matters they were doing. So (ma) is an indefinite descriptive noun that serves as a specification (tamyiz) for the hidden pronoun of the subject in (bi'sa) "evil is." The object of dispraise is omitted, as we have indicated. It is permitted to make (ma) a relative pronoun serving as the subject of (bi'sa), and the combination of the past and present forms indicates continuity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 63:

﴿Why do the rabbis (rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (ahbar) not forbid them from their saying sin and their consuming of illicit gain?﴾ Al-Hasan said: The rabbaniyyun (those devoted to God) are the scholars of the Gospel, and the ahbar (rabbis, scholars of the Law) are the scholars of the Torah. Others said: all of them refer to the Jews, because it is connected to the mention of them. The particle lawla (why not), when it precedes the imperfect verb, as Ibn al-Hajib and others have established, expresses urging (tahdid), and when it precedes the perfect verb, it expresses reproach (tawbikh). What is meant here is urging those whose subordinates follow them, who know the ugliness of what they are engaged in and the evil of its outcome, to forbid their inferiors.

﴿from their saying sin and their consuming of illicit gain﴾ Despite their knowledge of its ugliness and their awareness that they themselves are directly engaged in both. In al-Bahr it is said: this urging includes a reproach for their silence and their abandonment of prohibition. ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do﴾. The discussion here is like the earlier discussion of its counterpart, except that this is more emphatic than what came before regarding the common people, because it is established in language and usage that an act (fi'l) is whatever proceeds from a living being in general; if it proceeds from intention it is called 'amal (deed). Then, if it is acquired through practice and repetition until it becomes firmly rooted and becomes a habit for him, it is called sun' (craft), sun'ah (skill), and sina'ah (craftsmanship). Therefore sun' is more emphatic, as it implies firm establishment. For this reason a skilled person is called sani' (craftsman), and a well-woven garment is called sani'; as al-Raghib said. Thus the verse indicates that abandoning prohibition is uglier than committing the act. It has been explained that the one who commits the sin derives pleasure and fulfillment of desire from it, unlike the one who approves of it. For this reason it is reported: indeed the sin of the cuckold (dayyuth) is greater than that of the two adulterers.

This has been objected to, since it would follow from this that abandoning prohibition of fornication and murder is a greater sin than them, which is far-fetched. It has been answered that it is not far-fetched that the sin of abandoning prohibition, on the part of one whose prohibition restrains the one prohibited from doing what is forbidden, is greater than the sin of the one who commits it, whatever the act committed may be, whether murder, fornication, or otherwise.

Al-Shihab said: the qualifier of greater severity varies according to the perspective. Its being greater from the viewpoint of committing what has no benefit in it contradicts the commission itself being a greater sin than it. So reflect.

In the verse there is, among what is censured in the scholars, their laxity in forbidding evil deeds, which is evident. For this reason al-Dahhak said: how I fear this verse. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: there is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in reproach than this verse.

It was also recited: "Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their saying transgression (al-'udwan) and their consuming of illicit gain? Evil indeed is what they used to do."

﴿The Jews said﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak reported that they said: "Allah had expanded provision for the Jews. When they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He withheld from them what He had expanded for them." At that point Finhas ibn 'Azura, the chief of the Jews of Qaynuqa', said, and in another report from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) it was al-Nabbash ibn Qays: ﴿The Hand of Allah﴾, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿is chained﴾.

[Page 180]

Since the others did not object to the speaker and accepted his words, that grave statement is attributed to all of them. There are many similar cases earlier. By this, and may Allah curse them, they meant that He, glory be to Him, withholds what He has and is stingy with it, exalted is He far above what they say. The chaining and the spreading of the hand are both figurative (majaz) expressions for stinginess and generosity, or metonymies (kinaya) for them. The hand is used where a literal hand cannot apply, as in the verse:

*The sanctuary was generous, spreading both hands with heavy rain; its hills and valleys gave thanks for its bounty.*

They also attributed a hand to the north wind, as in the verse:

*It lost its herd, and a gusting wind, whose affair lies in the hand of the north wind, took it in as a guest.*

And the words of Labid:

*And on a morning of wind and biting cold, I faced it, when its reins were in the hand of the north wind.*

It is also said: "Despair spread its two palms over the chest of so-and-so." Here despair, which is a meaning and not a physical thing, is given two palms. The poet said:

*The weakness of my hopes and their contraction disturbed me, and the fresh despair spread its two palms over my chest.*

It is also said that the meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is poor, as in His saying: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said, "Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾ It is also said that "hand" here means blessing, so the meaning is: "His blessing is withheld from us."

It is reported from al-Hasan that the meaning is: "The hand of Allah is restrained from punishing us, so He punishes us only with what fulfils His oath, to the extent that our fathers worshipped the calf." It seems that he took "hand" to mean power and "chained" to mean not being attached to anything.

It is also said that it is not far-fetched that they meant the literal hand, since they were anthropomorphists (mujassima). It has been related about them that they claimed their Lord had white hair and a white beard, sat on a throne, finished creating the heavens and the earth on Friday, and lay on His back, placing one foot over the other and one hand on His chest, to rest from the fatigue He had suffered in creating that, exalted is Allah far above what they say. All these statements are as you see. And how strange it is that al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) should be quoted on this! I wish he had not said it, and perhaps the attribution to him is not correct. What rhetoric requires, and what the context of the speech supports, is the first view. It is not far-fetched that people who said to Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾, and who worshipped the calf, believed Allah to be described by stinginess and said what they said.

Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi said: It is possible that the Jews uttered a statement and held a doctrine whose meaning leads to the claim that Allah, exalted is His majesty, is stingy at one time and generous at another. So this was related about them in a manner of wonder at them and denial of them.

Another said: They said it as mockery, since He, glory be to Him, did not widen provision for the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions. But what is related about the occasion of revelation does not support this. It was also said: They said it in the form of a question and surprise, and the meaning is: "The hand of Allah, glory be to Him, is chained from us, since He has restricted our livelihood." Its distance is not hidden.

﴿Their hands are chained﴾: this is a curse upon them with the blameworthy stinginess, as al-Zajjaj said. Cursing them with it is an expression of Allah's placing miserliness in their hearts and tightness in their hands, and there is no impossibility in this according to the doctrine of the People of the Truth (Ahl al-Haqq). It is also possible that it is a curse upon them with poverty and humiliation. It is also said: Their hands are literally chained, shackled in this world as captives, and in the Hereafter tormented in the fetters of Hell. The connection of this to what precedes it in that case is through wording, so it is a paronomasia (tajnis). It is also said that the connection is through wording and the consideration of the root of the figurative usage, as when you say: "He cut off my tail (sabbani)," meaning "Allah cut off his descendants (dabir)," because the root of sabb is cutting. Al-Zamakhshari took this view and al-Tibi found it pleasing, and he said: This is a subtle mushakala (a rhetorical correspondence), unlike the saying:

*They said: "Propose something, and we will find you a dish for it." I said: "Cook me a robe and a shirt."*

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i chose that this is a report about their state on the Day of Resurrection, meaning: their hands are bound to their necks in Hell as recompense for this monstrous word. Al-Tabarsi related it from al-Hasan, then said: On this view there must be an implied fa' or wa' (conjunction), their speech is complete, and another statement is begun after it. It is their custom to omit in such cases, as in His saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow," they said, "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾. You know that this is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), and there is no need to bear the burden of supplying an implied word. Moreover, in our view, the statement of al-Hasan is not explicit that the sentence is informative, since at most he said: "Their hands are chained" in Hell, and it may be a curse upon them with that.

﴿And they are cursed﴾, i.e. they are removed far from the mercy of Allah and His reward, ﴿for what they said﴾, i.e. because of their saying, or because of that monstrous statement they uttered. This is a second supplication, joined to the first. Whoever takes it as informative also holds that it is a good statement. It was also read as "wa-lu'nu" (with a sukun on the 'ayn).

[Page 181]

﴿But His hands are both outspread﴾: this is coordinated with an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Not so; the matter is not as they claim, but He is at the utmost of generosity." It is to this, as it is said, that the dual of "hand" points, since the furthest that the resolve of the generous reaches is to give with both their hands. It is also said: "Hand" here also means blessing, and the dual refers to the blessings of this world and of the Hereafter, or the apparent blessings and the hidden blessings, or what is given as a gradual enticement (istidraj) and what is given as honour. It was also said, and related from al-Hasan, that the hands mean power, like the first "hand," and their being dual is with regard to their connection to reward and their connection to punishment. It was also said: The dual is intended as multiplicity, as in His saying: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾, and multiplicity here means only exaggeration in the perfection and vastness of power, not that they are actually more than one. A parallel is the poet's saying:

*The two sides of his forelock were made to shine, and it was hidden in his waist, and it aided his highland.*

He did not mean that this guidance had two forelocks, since a person has only one forelock. He only meant exaggeration.

The Salaf of the Ummah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: This is among the ambiguous verses (mutashabih), and entrusting its interpretation to Allah is the safest course. It has been authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he affirmed two hands for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and said: «Both His hands are right hands». No one from among his Companions (ﷺ) is related to have interpreted that as blessing or power. Rather they left it as it came and remained silent. And if speech is of silver, silence is of gold, especially in such places.

In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "But His hands are both open (bussatan)." It is said: "A hand, busut" in the sense of the familiar form, similar to "a gait, sujuh" and "a she-camel, surah."

﴿He spends as He wills﴾: this is a resumed sentence brought to affirm the perfection of His generosity, glory be to Him, because it indicates the generalisation of states, which is derived from "how" (kayfa). The phrase also draws attention to the secret of the straitened circumstances they were tested with, which they took, from the extreme of their ignorance and error, as a pretext for daring a word whose ugliness filled the expanse. The meaning is that this is not due to a deficiency in His bounty, but because His spending follows His will, which is based on subtle wisdoms upon which the orbits of livelihood and the Hereafter turn. Wisdom required, since they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and denied His Messenger (ﷺ), that they be restricted. "How" (kayfa) is an adverbial complement of "wills" (yashaa'), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "spends", meaning: he spends being in whatever state He wills, that is, according to His will, that is, desiring. It is also said that the clause "spends" is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the genitive pronoun in "His hands". It was objected that this involves separation by the predicate, and that the circumstantial clause cannot come from a possessed noun. It was answered that separating the circumstantial clause from its owner is not impermissible, as in His saying, quoting: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾, where it is said that "old man" (shaykhan) is a circumstantial clause from the demonstrative, and what governs it is the indication. What is forbidden is a circumstantial clause coming from the possessor when the possessed is not a part, or like a part, or an agent. Here the possessed is part of the possessor, or like a part, so there is no prohibition.

It was also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the two hands, or from their pronoun. This was refused on the ground that they have no pronoun in it. It was answered that there is no barrier to supposing a pronoun for them, meaning: he spends with them. From here it was said that it is permissible for it to be a second predicate of the subject. Yes, supposing an implied element goes against the original and the apparent reading, and that only implies disfavour, not impossibility. Allah, glory be to Him, omitted mention of what He spends in order to generalise.

﴿And surely many of them will increase﴾: they are their scholars and leaders, or the persistent disbelievers among them in general. ﴿What has been sent down to you﴾: from the Qur'an, which includes these verses. The object is placed first for the sake of emphasis. ﴿From your Lord﴾: it is connected to "sent down", just as "to you" is. Its placement after it, although the subject ought to precede the predicate in the context, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is for the sake of drawing attention to the endpoint, since the focus of the increase is the descent upon him (ﷺ). In using the title of Lordship with the addition to his pronoun, peace be upon him, there is an honour that is not hidden.

The relative clause is the subject of "will increase", the attribution is figurative (majaz), "many" (kathiran) is its first object, "of them" (minhum) is its descriptive modifier, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿rebellion and disbelief﴾ is its second object. That is: it will surely increase them in rebellion beyond their former rebellion and in disbelief beyond their former disbelief, since increase requires that what is increased already existed before. This increase is either in terms of intensity and excess, or in terms of quantity and multiplicity, since whenever a verse descends they disbelieve in it, and their rebellion and disbelief grow in proportion to its measure. This is like how food suitable for the healthy increases the sickness of the sick. It is also possible that "what has been sent down" means the blessings that Allah granted His Prophet, peace be upon him. That is: they disbelieved and persisted in disbelief and said what they said, since Allah restricted them and withheld from them what He had extended to them. So when they saw, along with that, the spreading of His favours and the continuous succession of His bounties upon His Prophet (ﷺ), who is the most hostile of their enemies, they increased in rage and resentment against their Lord, glory be to Him. Thus they added to their former rebellion a further rebellion, and to their disbelief a further disbelief. In that case the verse agrees with what precedes it very closely. However, this is not free from distance, and I have not seen anyone mention it.

﴿And We have cast among them﴾: i.e. among the Jews. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: the pronoun refers to the Jews and the Christians, since their mention has already occurred in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians﴾, and because His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O People of the Book﴾ includes both groups. This was related from al-Hasan and Mujahid.

﴿the enmity and the hatred﴾. Thus their hearts rarely agree and their word is not united. Among the Jews are the Jabriyyah (determinists), among them the Qadariyyah (those who affirm human free will), among them the Murji'ah (those who postpone judgment on the believer's faith), and among them the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists). The enmity and hatred between one sect and another are firmly established. The same holds among the Christians: the Melkites, the Jacobites and the Nestorians, and their state is like their state in this respect. The state of the Jews with the Christians is too evident to be hidden. It has been preferred that the pronoun refers to the Jews, since the discussion concerns them. The purpose of this information here is to remove what might be suspected from mentioning their rebellion and disbelief, namely that they unite upon a matter that would harm the Muslims.

Abu Hayyan said, after he had made the pronoun refer to the two groups: the meaning is that the Jews and the Christians remain mutually hateful and hostile, and rarely does one of the two groups agree with the other. They do not unite to fight you and wage war against you. In this there is a report of the unseen, for no army of Jews and Christians has gathered to wage war against the Muslims since the sword of Islam was drawn.

Page 183

Al-Samin (al-Halabi) distinguished between enmity and hatred, saying that enmity is more specific than hatred, because every enemy is a hater, while one may hate someone who is not an enemy. ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to "We cast" (alqayna). It has been permitted that it be connected to "hatred", meaning that the mutual hatred among them is continuous for as long as they exist, and the literal sense of the limit is not intended. It was not permitted that it be connected to "enmity", lest this result in separating the verbal noun from its complement by a foreign element.

﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾. This is an explicit statement of what was alluded to, namely that the harm of their situation does not reach the Muslims. The meaning is: whenever they intended to fight the Messenger (ﷺ) and arranged its beginnings, Allah turned them back and subdued them, by scattering their opinions, dissolving their resolve, and casting terror into their hearts. Thus "kindling the fire" is a kinaya (an allusion by which the thing meant is denoted indirectly) for intending war. The Arabs, when they agreed upon fighting, would make their signal the kindling of a fire on a mountain or a hill, and they called it "the fire of war", and it was one of their well-known fires. Its extinguishing is an expression for repelling their evil.

Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) reports two opinions concerning the verse. According to some, the kindling is literal, and so is the extinguishing: whenever they kindled a fire for fighting, terror was cast upon them, so they held back and extinguished it. The attribution of the extinguishing to Him, Exalted, is the attribution of the effect to its primary cause.

According to the majority, the speech is in the form of an isti'ara (metaphor). The kindling of the fire means displaying plots against the believers, which resemble fire in causing harm, and its extinguishing means turning that away from the believers. Perhaps the view of kinaya is subtler than these two. That the war in question is the fighting of the Messenger (ﷺ) is what is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It is also said that it is more general than that: whenever they intended to fight anyone, they were defeated. When the Jews opposed the judgment of the Torah, Allah, Exalted, empowered Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them. Then they corrupted again, so He, glory be to Him, empowered over them Futrus the Roman. Then they corrupted again, so He, Exalted in majesty, empowered over them the Magians. Then they corrupted again, so He, Mighty and Majestic, empowered over them His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, who destroyed their power, uprooted their strength, scattered their assembly, and humbled them. He expelled the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Qaynuqa', killed the Banu Qurayza, took captive the people of Khaybar, prevailed over Fadak, the people of Wadi al-Qura submitted to him, and he imposed the jizya (poll tax) upon the protected people (ahl al-dhimma). Allah, Exalted, left them in a humiliation after which they will never be honoured. The extinguishing of the fire according to this is an expression for victory over them, may Allah fight them.

﴿for war﴾ is connected to "they kindled". The lam is for causation (ta'lil), or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a description of "fire", and this latter is more fitting to the naming.

﴿And they strive throughout the land to cause corruption﴾. That is, they exert themselves in plotting against Islam and its people, and in stirring up evil and sedition among themselves. This is different from what was expressed by kindling the fire of war, such as altering the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), introducing doubts to the weak among the Muslims, and walking about with tale-bearing together with slander, and the like. "Corruption" (fasadan) may be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), as Abu al-Baqa' restricted himself to, or it may be in the position of a verbal noun, or it may be a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "they strive", meaning: they strive for corruption, or in a striving of corruption, or as corrupters.

﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾. Rather, He hates them, and for this reason He extinguished the blaze of their corruption. The lam is either for the genus, and they are included in it initially, or it is for a specific reference (al-'ahd). Placing the apparent noun in the place of their pronoun serves as a causal explanation and shows that they are firmly established in corruption.

The independent sentence is brought to remove what might be suspected, that their striving might have some effect of harm. Some scholars placed it in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). Its benefit is to intensify the ugliness of their condition and the gravity of their affair.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 65:

﴿If the People of the Scripture had believed﴾, that is, the Jews and the Christians. The intended meaning of "the Scripture" here is the genus that includes the Torah and the Gospel, though it is possible that only the Jews are meant. The mention of the Gospel is not explicit in requiring generality, but the view held by the majority of exegetes (mufassirun) is generality. They were addressed with this title to emphasise the censure against them. Those meant are the contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning: even if they, despite what they had committed of various kinds of crimes, both in word and deed, ﴿had believed﴾, in what was denied to them, which is faith. This includes the obligation of their believing in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The object was omitted, relying on its being evident from His words, exalted be He: ﴿Do you blame us except that we believed in God?﴾ etc., and from what follows in His words, glorified be He: ﴿If only they had established the Torah﴾ etc.

Restricting the object of belief to belief in him (ﷺ) is rejected by the context, as Shaykh al-Islam said, because what was mentioned before and after of their disbelief in him (ﷺ) was mentioned coupled with their disbelief in their own Scripture as well, with the intention of obligating and rebuking them, by showing that disbelief in him (ﷺ) entails disbelief in their Scripture. Therefore, reading "belief" here as belief in him (ﷺ) disrupts the coherence of the noble composition. Qatadah, in what Ibn Humayd and others related from him, estimated the object to be "what God has sent down", which inclines toward generality. Likewise he generalised in His words: ﴿and been conscious of God﴾, saying: that is, [of] what God has forbidden.

Shaykh al-Islam said: All the sins that we have enumerated, of which their violation of their Scripture is one, ﴿We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾, which they committed and hastened towards, even if they were extremely great, and We would not have called them to account for them. The plural used for them is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), either with regard to the types, or with regard to the fact that they, though numerous, are few in comparison to the generosity of God. We have indicated earlier that the plural of paucity may stand in place of the plural of abundance when the context requires it. ﴿And We would have admitted them﴾ together with that ﴿into Gardens of Bliss﴾.

Abu Hayyan made the expiation of misdeeds correspond to faith, and the admission into Gardens of Bliss correspond to piety, and he interpreted it as performing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. So the verse is of the type of distribution (al-tawzi'), though the apparent reading is that it is not. The repetition of the particle of emphasis (lam) is for emphasising the promise. In it there is an alert to the perfect greatness of their sins and the multitude of their disobediences, and that Islam erases what came before it, however great it is and however far it exceeds the limit. In the annexation of "Gardens" to "Bliss" there is an alert to what they would deserve of punishment had they not believed and been conscious of God.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Malik ibn Dinar that he said: "The Gardens of Bliss are between the Gardens of Firdaws and the Gardens of Eden, and in them are maidens created from the rose of Paradise." It was said: "Who will dwell in them?" He said: "Those who intended to commit sins, but when they remembered the greatness of God, exalted be His majesty, they feared Him." It is not hidden that such a thing is not said on the basis of opinion (ra'y), and what the apparent reading requires is that it be said of all the gardens: "Gardens of Bliss", even if the degrees of bliss differ within them.

[Page 184]

**[Part 1 of 2]**

﴿Had they truly upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾: that is, had they fulfilled their rights by observing the rulings contained in them, among which are the signs of his prophethood (ﷺ) and the good tidings of his mission (ﷺ). What is meant is not observing all the rulings in them, whether abrogated (naskh) or not, for that is not "upholding" in any sense. ﴿And what was sent down to them from their Lord﴾: that is, the glorious Qur'an, which confirms what is before it. This is as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and it was chosen by al-Jubba'i and others. It has also been said that what is meant by the relative clause is the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as the Book of Isaiah, the Book of Ezekiel, the Book of Habakkuk, and the Book of Daniel, for they are full of good tidings of his (ﷺ) coming. This was chosen by Abu Hayyan. It is also permissible that it refers to both of these and to the great Qur'an.

To send down a book to someone means merely that it reaches them, and that acting upon it becomes obligatory for them, even if revelation was not descending upon them. The expression of the Qur'an by this title is to announce the obligation of upholding it upon them because it has been sent down to them, and to state explicitly the falsity of their claim that it was not sent down to the Children of Israel. The placement of ﴿to them﴾ before its verb is because of what has passed just above. And the attribution of "Lord" to their pronoun carries an extra kindness toward them in the call to uphold it.

﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾: that is, the sky would have given them its rain and its blessing, and the earth its plants and its good. As Allah the Glorified said: ﴿We would have opened for them blessings from the sky﴾. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Mujahid said. It has also been said that what is meant is that they would have benefited from the abundance of fruit on the trees and the produce of the crops. It has been said: from the fruits that hang down from the tops of the trees and what falls from them to the ground. It has been said: from what would come to them from their great ones and their kings, and what their lowly and common people would give them. It has also been said that what is meant is an exaggeration in describing abundance and fertility, not specifying the two directions; as if it were said: "They would have eaten from every direction." al-Tabarsi made it like your saying: "So-and-so is in good from his horn to his foot," meaning good comes to him from every direction he seeks it from. What is meant by "eating" is benefiting in general, and it was expressed by it because it is the greatest of benefits, and it entails all the others. The object of "they ate" is omitted either for the purpose of generality, or for directing attention to the act itself, as in your saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds." The "min" in both places denotes the starting point of the extent.

We will allude, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the section on allusion (ishara), to the secret of mentioning the feet. In the first conditional there is an encouragement toward an otherworldly matter, and in the second an encouragement toward a worldly matter, and an alert that what befell those wicked ones of hardship and constriction was only due to the ill omen of their misdeeds, not to any shortfall in the outpouring of the Bountiful. The encouragement toward the otherworldly matter is placed first because it is more important, since through it comes eternal salvation and lasting bliss. The two expressions were varied: first it said "they believed and feared Allah," and second "they upheld," in both cases following the path of eloquence. It has been said: it is likely that the "ma" in the second conditional is an allusion to what was done to the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, namely cutting down their palm trees, ruining their crops, and expelling them from their homelands. So it is as if it were said about them: "If only they had remained in their dwellings and benefited from their palm trees and crops! But they transgressed from upholding, so they were deprived and wandered in the deserts of hardship, because they had wronged."

Some have distinguished between the two conditionals by saying that the first is necessarily fulfilled for the People of the Book until the Day of Resurrection, for there is no doubt that when a person of the Book believes and fears Allah, Allah the Exalted expiates his misdeeds and admits him - Glorified be His majesty - into His mercy, whether he was a contemporary of the Prophet (ﷺ) or not. The second conditional is not like that, for it appears that the necessary fulfilment is restricted to the contemporaries, since we see many of the People of the Book today who are far from the upholding mentioned, and yet they have been given more abundance than many who did uphold it. We also see many of them uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, and believe in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) in the proper manner, while they were previously in hardship of life, and their condition does not change; and perhaps they were in comfort, until when they upheld it the boat of life stopped with them, and they fell into a state of distress.

To make it like the first conditional, and to take the expansion (tawsi'ah) in a sense more general than the apparent material expansion and the spiritual expansion, such as that Allah the Glorified grants them contentment and satisfaction with what is in their hands, so that what they have is like much even if it is little, I do not think this takes a place in your heart, nor do I reckon it decisive for what is being said. And to say that the second is like the first, except that the connection between all of them upholding what has passed and all of them benefiting in the same way, i.e., if they all upheld the Torah etc., they would all have eaten from above them etc., and not that if some of them upheld it, I do not see it to be anything but an objectionable statement and a falsehood.

Some verifiers have mentioned that some commentators interpreted His saying, "they would have eaten" etc., as "provision would have been expanded for them," and interpreted the expansion in several ways which they mentioned, and did not make it inclusive of the provision of both abodes. If it were taken as an ascent and a detailing of what was summarized in the first, as condition and consequence, it would be a valid view. End of quote.

By this view I say, and toward it I turn, and I see it as almost required. Yet the two conditionals, according to it, are not equal, and the difficulty remains in one respect. I see no way out of it except by holding that the two conditionals differ. Perhaps the matter will lead, if Allah the Exalted wills, to a verification of what pertains to this station, so reflect.

﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾: that is, a just party, neither extreme nor negligent,
[p.186]
as has been narrated from al-Rabi'. They are those among them who embraced Islam and followed the Prophet (ﷺ), as Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said, and al-Jubba'i chose it. Such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like from the Jews, and eighty-some from the Christians. It was also said that what is meant by them is al-Najashi and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The sentence is a new (independent) clause, built upon a question arising from the content of the two conditionals introduced by the particle of impossibility, which indicate the absence of the faith, fear, and upholding mentioned. As if it were said: "Are all of them devoted to disbelief and its two companions?" So it was said: "Among them..." etc. Interpreting moderation as being balanced in hostility is far-fetched. ﴿And many of them﴾: and they are the boorish, fanatical ones, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his like, and the Romans.

﴿Evil is what they do﴾: of obstinacy, arrogance, distorting the truth, and turning away from it.

It has also been said: of excessive hostility. "Many" is a subject (mubtada'), "of them" is its description, and "saa'a" (evil is) is like "bi'sa" (wretched is), for dispraise.

It is related from some grammarians that it carries the meaning of wonder, like "qadwa Zayd" (how judicious is Zayd), i.e., "how judicious he is!" So the meaning here is: "How evil is their deed!" Some say that it is merely for dispraise, and the wonder is derived from the context. Its specification (tamyiz) is omitted, and "ma" is a relative pronoun serving as its subject, meaning: "evil is the deed they do." It is also permissible for "ma" to be an indefinite in the place of the specification, and the verbal sentence (of the imperative type) is a predicate of the subject. The discussion of this is well-known.

* * *

Now, among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses:

("﴿Your only guardian is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe, who establish prayer﴾") that is, the prayer of witnessing and inner presence ("﴿and give zakah﴾") that is, the zakah of their existence ("﴿while bowing﴾") that is, humbling themselves in abiding by Allah.

The verse, according to most of the narrators, was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. The Imamiyyah, as you know, use it as evidence for his caliphate after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) immediately without interval. You have known from us the refutation of their claim, all praise be to Allah the Glorified. Many of the Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, allude to the view of his caliphate, may Allah ennoble his face, after the Messenger, peace be upon him, also immediately without interval. But that caliphate, according to them, is the inner caliphate, which is the caliphate of guidance, education, support, and spiritual governance, not the outward caliphate, which consists of establishing the apparent limits, equipping armies, defending the egg of Islam, and fighting its enemies with the sword and the spear. The outward caliphate, according to them, occurred in the order that actually happened, as is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. The distinction between the two caliphates in their view is like the distinction between the husk and the kernel. The inner caliphate is the kernel of the outer caliphate, and through it the reality of Islam is defended, and through the outer it is defended in its form. The station of the pole (qutb) in every age is this inner station, and it may combine with the outer caliphate, as it combined in 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, during his reign, and as it combines in the Mahdi during his appearance. It and prophethood are like two infants at one breast. To this the saying narrated from him, peace be upon him, alludes: "I and 'Ali were created from one light." This caliphate was in him, may Allah ennoble his face, in its most complete form.

From here the chains of the people of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, all terminate with him, except what is rarer than the egg of the female raven; for that terminates with al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, like the chain of our masters of the Naqshbandiyyah, may Allah benefit us by their knowledge. Yet despite this, objections are raised against it, may Allah ennoble his face, as well.

By dividing the caliphate into these two parts, some of the gnostics reconciled the traditions which imply or explicitly state the caliphate of the three imams, may Allah be pleased with them, after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the known order, with the traditions which imply or explicitly state the caliphate of the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, after him, peace be upon him, immediately without interval. He interpreted the traditions concerning the caliphate of the three caliphs as the outer caliphate, and the traditions concerning the caliphate of the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, as the inner caliphate. He did not nullify any of the reports, and he affirmed the reality of the caliphate of the four, may Allah be pleased with them all.

You know that this implies the superiority of the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, over the three caliphs. Some of them state this explicitly, and they say it is permissible for a less excellent person to hold the outward caliphate in the presence of the more excellent. But we have already quoted from the Greatest Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, that he said: "There is no man between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him." His intent was nothing but to explain the rank in excellence. So understand.

("﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies﴾") for he is of the party of Allah the Exalted, that is, the people of His special care, who stand with Him upon the conditions of uprightness ("﴿indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾") over their inner and outer enemies. It has been authentically reported: "A group of my community will not cease standing by the command of Allah the Glorified, unharmed by those who forsake them, until the command of Allah the Exalted comes, while they are upon that."

( ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَتَّخِذُوا الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا دِينَكُمْ﴾ ) That is, your state in which you are in the journey and the spiritual path ( ﴿هُزُوًا ولَعِبًا﴾ ) [i.e., they mocked it and played with it], so they reproached it ( ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ مِنَ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ ) [meaning] those who were given the Book before you, and they are those who restrict themselves to the outward alone, like the Jews, or to the inward alone, like the Christians ( ﴿والكُفّارَ﴾ ) those who have veiled themselves from the Truth by their own selves ( ﴿أوْلِياءَ﴾ ) [as allies], because of their opposition in states ( ﴿واتَّقُوا اللَّهَ إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ) [i.e., fear] Allah, exalted is His majesty, if you are believers ( ﴿وإذا نادَيْتُمْ إلى الصَّلاةِ﴾ ) that is, presence in the presence (ḥaḍrah) of the Lord ( ﴿اتَّخَذُوها هُزُوًا ولَعِبًا ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم قَوْمٌ لا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ) the secrets; and they did not understand what is in the prayer of attaining one's goals. For it is authentically related: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer."

( ﴿قُلْ يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ هَلْ تَنْقِمُونَ﴾ ) and deny ( ﴿مِنّا إلا أنْ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ وما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْنا وما أُنْزِلَ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ) [Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us only because we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before?"] So we combined the outward and the inward, and we flew with these two wings to the holy presence (al-ḥaḍrah al-qudsiyyah) ( ﴿وجَعَلَ مِنهُمُ القِرَدَةَ والخَنازِيرَ﴾ ) [And made some of them apes and swine], that is, He changed their attributes into the attributes of those animals, in cunning, greed, lust, and lack of jealousy ( ﴿وعَبَدَ الطّاغُوتَ﴾ ) [and worshipped the Taghut], and it is everything that transgresses beyond what is other than Allah, exalted, that is, they submitted to it and humbled themselves before it, and among them is one who is a worshipper of the dirham and the dinar ( ﴿أُولَئِكَ شَرٌّ مَكانًا﴾ ) [Those are worse in position], because they nullified their innate capacity, and they went astray with a far-reaching error ( ﴿وتَرى كَثِيرًا مِنهم يُسارِعُونَ في الإثْمِ والعُدْوانِ وأكْلِهِمُ السُّحْتَ﴾ ) [And you see many of them hastening into sin and transgression and their consuming of unlawful gain], that is, they rush quickly into all the vices, because of their habituation to them, their training in them, and their becoming settled dispositions (malakāt) of their souls. Sin is the vice of the rational faculty (al-quwwah al-nuṭqiyyah), transgression is the vice of the irascible faculties (al-quwwā al-ghaḍabiyyah), and consuming unlawful gain is the vice of the appetitive faculties (al-quwwā al-shahawiyyah). ( ﴿وقالَتِ اليَهُودُ﴾ ) [And the Jews said], because of their deprivation from the secrets that the people of the outward do not perceive, ( يَدُ اللَّهِ ) [the Hand of Allah], exalted above what they say, ( ﴿مَغْلُولَةٌ﴾ ) [is chained], so He does not bestow except what we are in of the outward knowledge ( ﴿غُلَّتْ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ ) [Their own hands are chained], and they were deprived until the Day of Resurrection from partaking of the fruits of the trees of secrets ( ﴿ولُعِنُوا﴾ ) that is, they were distanced from the divine presence ( ﴿بِما قالُوا﴾ ) [for what they said], from that great word. ( ﴿بَلْ يَداهُ مَبْسُوطَتانِ يُنْفِقُ﴾ ) [Rather, His hands are both outstretched; He spends] with them ( ﴿كَيْفَ يَشاءُ﴾ ) [however He wills], so He bestows, according to wisdom, of the kinds of knowledge, outward and inward, upon whomever He finds worthy of it. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicated the outward and the inward with the night and the day in what al-Bukhari and others transmitted: "The Hand of Allah, exalted, is full; expenditure does not diminish it, pouring forth night and day."

( ﴿ولَوْ أنَّ أهْلَ الكِتابِ آمَنُوا﴾ ) with true faith ( ﴿واتَّقَوْا﴾ ) the shirk of their actions, their attributes, and their essences. And if they had believed in the outward sciences and avoided denial and objection to whoever relates from the inward sciences, and submitted to them in their states, as it has been said:

"If you do not see the crescent, then submit to people who have seen it with their eyes."

( ﴿لَكَفَّرْنا عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ﴾ ) which they committed ( ﴿ولأدْخَلْناهم جَنّاتِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ ) [We would have expiated from them their misdeeds and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss], in return for their faith and their being mindful. ( ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم
صفحة 188
أقامُوا التَّوْراةَ﴾ ) [And if they had upheld the Torah] through the realization of the outward sciences, and attending to the rights of the manifestations of the actions, and preserving their rulings in transactions ( ﴿والإنْجِيلَ﴾ ) [and the Gospel] through the realization of the inward sciences, and attending to the rights of the manifestations of the attributes, and preserving their rulings in the unveilings (mukāshafāt) ( ﴿وما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْهِمْ مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ) [and what was revealed to them from their Lord], of the knowledge of the origin and the return, and the unity of the dominion and the kingdom of the realm of Lordship, which is the realm of the Divine Names ( ﴿لأكَلُوا مِن فَوْقِهِمْ﴾ ) that is, they would have been provided from the spiritual realm with divine sciences, intellectual realities, and true gnosis ( ﴿ومِن تَحْتِ أرْجُلِهِمْ﴾ ) [and from beneath their feet], that is, from the lower, corporeal world, with the natural sciences and sensory perceptions. Through the first they are guided to knowledge of Allah, exalted, and knowledge of the dominion and the might; through the second they are guided to knowledge of the world of dominion. Thus they come to know Allah, exalted, when both matters are complete for them through His inward and outward names, indeed through all the Names and Attributes.

Al-Tayyibi has a fine statement here suitable to this chapter. After relating from some that he said regarding "they would have eaten" etc., that is, the best of both abodes would have been widened for them, he said: "I say: this is in the case of those who count the misdeeds of the People of the Book if they merely uphold the limits of the Torah and the Gospel. So what is your opinion about the gnostic traveler when he subdues the desire of the self and withdraws from this world to the landmarks of holiness, holding fast to the rope of Allah, exalted, and the Sunnah of His beloved, may Allah bless him and grant him peace? For He, exalted, pours upon his heart buckets of His virtues and clouds of His blessings, so that it lies hidden within him as rain lies hidden in the earth, and springs of wisdom appear from his heart upon his tongue."

In the attachment of eating from above and from beneath the feet to upholding what was mentioned, and in the specification of the initial "min" (from), there is an allusion to the meaning of his words, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah makes him inherit the knowledge of what he did not know." For when they uphold action according to the Book of Allah, glorified is He, blessings descend upon them from above; then when they strive in action for those descended blessings and stand upon them with the firmness of their established steps, Allah, exalted and mighty, causes greater blessings, purer than the first, to descend upon them. So knowledge and action continue to alternate until the traveler reaches the station of nearness and the abodes of the gnostics. In the mention of the feet there is an indication of the attainment of steadfastness of the foot and the firmness of knowledge; and in its conjunction with "beneath" there is an indication of greater steadfastness, and that they are of those firmly rooted, who draw their knowledge from the niche of prophethood, not of those who waver, who took their knowledge from illusions. For this reason, some gnostics wrote to the Imam, concerning this verse, as guidance to him toward knowing the way of the people of Allah, exalted is His majesty. End of quote.

Some of the people of expression, from among those who are to me in the place of the crown upon the head, may he remain, have explained the mention of the feet here as indicating that what is meant by His, glorified is He, words "from beneath their feet" are the lower matters acquired through striving and effort, just as what is meant by His, exalted, words "from above them" are the matters attained through mere overflowing. In that case, the antithesis between the two conjoined phrases becomes stronger.

Perhaps you may derive from what al-Tayyibi mentioned other than this interpretation, which also agrees with the approach of the people of the outward, so reflect.

( ﴿مِنهم أُمَّةٌ مُقْتَصِدَةٌ﴾ ) [Among them is a moderate community]. It has been said: just and attaining to the unity of the Names and Attributes ( ﴿وكَثِيرٌ مِنهم ساءَ ما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ) [and many of them, evil is what they do]. They are those completely veiled, who have not yet attained to the unity of actions, let alone the unity of attributes. And Allah, exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 5):

﴿O Messenger﴾ to ﴿both jinn and humankind, all of them﴾. This is an address of honour, because the message is Allah the Exalted's greatest favour and His supreme honour. This title also signals what requires him (ﷺ) to carry out what he was commanded: conveying what was revealed to him.

﴿Convey﴾, that is, deliver to the creation ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾, that is, all that has been sent down, whatever it may be, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the Owner of your affair, who brings you to the perfection that befits you. Within this is an implicit promise of his protection and safeguarding (peace be upon him). The meaning is: convey it without fearing anyone's watchfulness over you in this, and without fearing that any harm will ever befall you. ﴿And if you do not do so﴾, that is, what you were commanded to convey of all of it,

[p. 189]

﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾, that is, you have not delivered any part of His message. This is because no part of it is more deserving of delivery than another. So if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you have neglected delivering all of it. Likewise, whoever does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, since each part conveys what the others convey, and they are therefore in the ruling of one thing. And one thing cannot be both conveyed and not conveyed, believed and not believed. Also, concealing part of it nullifies what has been delivered of it, like omitting some pillars of the prayer, for the purpose of the call is undone by that.

It has been objected to the claim that no part is more deserving of delivery than another, that priority is established in terms of obligation, definitively and speculatively, clearly and obscurely, as principle and as derivative. Al-Kashf answered that he denied priority by looking at the basic obligation. Moreover, that refers to what is conveyed, whereas the discussion is about conveying, and conveying does not differ in obligation, since it is one thing considered in its essence. Then, concealing part indicates that he did not consider that he was commanded to convey, but rather considered the benefit in what is conveyed. So it is as if he did not comply with this command at all, and thus did not convey. And even if he informed the people, it would not benefit him, since in that case he would be a reporter, not a conveyer.

The second justification was challenged on the grounds that the Lawgiver regarded the prayer as one unit, unlike conveying. But this objection does not hold, because God obligated him (peace be upon him) to convey all of it, so He has made it like the prayer without doubt.

From what we have said in explaining the conditional sentence, it is known that there is no identity between the condition and the consequence. Whoever claims it, on the basis that the outcome of "if you do not convey the message, you have not conveyed the message," has compared it to the saying:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

Here the predicate is the very same as the subject, without any addition to the wording. "My poetry is my poetry" is famed for its eloquence and widely known for its fluency. But he has spoken by remaining silent about those attributes through which the benefit is achieved, relying on the fact that they are among the necessary qualities of his poetry in the understanding of listeners, due to its fame for them, and that he is independent of mentioning them because of their renown and wide circulation. Likewise, as Ibn al-Munir said, it is intended in the verse, because not conveying the message is a matter known to people, firmly established in minds as something grave and shameful, condemned in the one who commits it. Do you not see that the failure of a scholar to spread knowledge is a dreadful thing? So how much more is the concealment of the message by the Messenger! Thus the additions by which the condition and consequence differ are dispensed with, since they are attached to the consequence in people's understanding, and whoever hears "not conveying the message" understands what lies behind it of threat and warning. This style is made beautiful in the Mighty Book by mentioning the condition in general terms, where He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And if you do not do so﴾, and did not say: "And if you do not convey the message, then you have not conveyed the message." Thus the two differ in wording, even if they are one in meaning. This is more lustrous and more manifestly graceful than repeating the same word in condition and consequence. Abu al-Najm fell short of this pinnacle by mentioning the subject with the wording of the predicate, and it is fitting that his eloquence should shrink next to the eloquence of the Inimitable. So there is no fault in him for that.

It has also been said: the meaning is, "If you do not do so, then for you is what the concealment of the whole revelation necessitates," so the cause is placed in the position of the effect. This is supported by what Ishaq ibn Rahawayh recorded in his Musnad from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and what Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Hibban recorded in their Tafsir from the mursal narration of al-Hasan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent me with the message, and I was distressed by it. Then Allah revealed: If you do not convey My messages, I shall punish you. He guaranteed me protection, and so I was strengthened."

It has also been said: the meaning is, "If you abandon conveying what has been sent down to you, you will be judged as not having conveyed at all." It has also been said, and would that it had not been said, that what is meant by "what has been sent down" is the Qur'an, and what is meant in the answer is the rest of the miracles. Other views have also been stated.

The verse has been cited as evidence that he (ﷺ) did not conceal anything of the revelation. It is attributed to the Shi'a that they claim he (ﷺ) concealed part of it out of taqiyya (dissimulation).

It is reported from some Sufis that what is meant is conveying what concerns the interests of the servants among the rulings, and that its sending down was intended for them to know it. As for what was specially given to him of the unseen which did not concern the interests of his community, he had the right, or rather the duty, to keep it concealed. Al-Sulami narrated from Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾, that he said: "He revealed without intermediary, between Him and him, secretly, into his heart, and no one else knows of it except in the Hereafter, when He gives him intercession for his community." Al-Wasiti said: "He cast to His servant what He cast, and did not reveal what He revealed, because He, glorified be He, specified it for him (ﷺ). What was specific to him (peace be upon him) was hidden, and what Allah the Exalted sent him with to the creation was manifest." Al-Tibi said: "The meaning of what we have narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said, 'I memorised from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) two vessels. As for one of them, I spread it; as for the other, if I spread it, this throat of mine would be cut,' points to this." He meant his neck, and the original meaning of al-bula'um is the passage of food. Al-Bukhari explained it thus. They call this the knowledge of divine secrets and the knowledge of reality. To this the leader of the gnostics, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, alluded when he said:

"Indeed I conceal from my knowledge its precious jewels,
lest one ignorant of the Truth see them and be tempted by us.
Abu Hasan had already gone before this to al-Husayn,
and before him he had bequeathed it to al-Hasan.
For many a jewel of knowledge, were I to disclose it,
I would be told: 'You are of those who worship idols.'
And men who are Muslims would make my blood lawful,
seeing as good the foulest of what they do."

Among this is the knowledge of the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud). They have explicitly stated that it is a level beyond the level of reason, and they said that it is something the spirit knows without the mediation of reason. From here they spoke of the hidden knowledge, in the sense that it is hidden with respect to the people of thought and the minds immersed in the states of obstacles and attachments, not with respect to those who are stripped of them and ascend to the presences of holiness and the gardens of lights.

Shaykh Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani, may Allah refresh his spirit, mentioned in his book al-Durar al-Manthura fi Bayan Zubad al-Ulum al-Mashhura the following text: "As for the essence of the science of Sufism, in which the people have written their treatises, it is the fruit of acting upon the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever acts on what he knows speaks as they spoke, and all that they said becomes part of what is with him. For whenever the servant advances in the station of courtesy with Allah the Exalted, his speech becomes subtle to people's understanding, until one of them said to his shaykh: 'The speech of my brother so-and-so is subtle to my understanding!' He said: 'Because you have two shirts and he has only one; he is higher in rank than you.' This is what moved the jurists and their like among the people of veiling to call the science of the Sufis the science of the inner. But it is not inner, for the inner is only the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. As for everything He has taught creation, across its different levels, it is of the outer science, for it has appeared to the creation. Know this." End of quotation.

Some have understood that what is meant is conveying the rulings and what relates to them of benefits, not what includes the science of secrets, from His words, glorified be He: ﴿What We have sent down to you﴾, rather than: ﴿what We have made known to you﴾. They mentioned that the science of secrets was not sent down by revelation, but by way of inspiration and unveiling. It has also been said that this is understood from the word "message," for a message is what is sent to others.

Some Sufis, sanctified be their secrets, have extended their discourse on this matter. My own verification is that what the Prophet (ﷺ) possesses of divine secrets and other legal rulings is comprised in the Qur'an that was sent down. For the Exalted has said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾, and He, exalted be He, said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as recorded by al-Tirmidhi and others: "There will be trials." It was said: "What is the way out of them?" He said: "The Book of Allah the Exalted: in it is the news of what came before you, the report of what comes after you, and the judgement of what is among you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In this Qur'an every knowledge has been sent down, and everything has been made clear to us in it, but our knowledge falls short of what has been made clear to us in the Qur'an."

Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Everything the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled by, he understood from the Qur'an." This is supported by what al-Tabarani recorded in al-Awsat from the hadith of A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I permit only what Allah the Exalted has permitted in His Book, and I forbid only what Allah the Exalted has forbidden in His Book."

Al-Mursi said: "The Qur'an has gathered the sciences of the first and the last, such that no one truly encompasses it in knowledge except the One who spoke it, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), apart from what He, glorified be He, has kept to Himself. Then the greater part of this was inherited from him by the leading Companions and their eminent figures, such as the four caliphs, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), to the extent that he said: 'If the tether of a camel were lost to me, I would find it in the Book of Allah the Exalted.' Then the Successors inherited it from them with excellence. Then aspirations fell short, resolutions weakened, and the people of knowledge diminished, and they became too weak to bear what the Companions and the Successors carried of its sciences and all its branches. So they diversified its sciences, and every group took charge of one of its branches."

Some said: "There is nothing that cannot be extracted from the Qur'an for one whom Allah the Exalted has granted understanding." To the extent that someone derived the age of the Prophet (ﷺ) as sixty-three years from the words of the Exalted in Surah al-Munafiqun: ﴿And Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come﴾, for it is the beginning of the sixty-third surah. And He followed it with Surah al-Taghabun, so that the loss (taghabun) would become manifest in the loss of that Prophet (ﷺ) himself. This is something over which two rams would hardly clash. Since it is established that all of that is in the Qur'an, conveying the Qur'an is conveying it. The only point is that the identification of these details, secret by secret and ruling by ruling, has not been established by explicit wording for everyone. How many a secret and a ruling have been indicated by allusion, without being stated by explicit expression! And whoever claims that there are secrets outside the Book of Allah the Exalted, which the Sufis received from their Lord by whatever means, has committed a great slander, and Ibn al-Sabhlal has come with misguidance without any doubt.

[p. 192]

As for the saying of some of them, "You took your knowledge dead from dead men, while we took it from the Living who does not die," it does not prove that claim, because that taking may have been from the Qur'an through a holy understanding (*fahm qudsi*) that God Most High gave to that recipient. What supports this is what is authentically related from Abu Juhayfa, who said: "I said to Ali, may God honor his face: 'Do you have a book that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) singled you out with?' He said: 'No, except the Book of God Most High, or an understanding given to a Muslim man, or what is in this sheet,' and it was hanging from the hilt of his sword. I said: 'And what is in this sheet?' He said: 'The blood-money (*al-'aql*), the ransoming of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.'"

It is understood from this, as al-Qastallani said, that a scholar may derive from the Qur'an, by his own understanding, what has not been transmitted from the exegetes, provided it agrees with the foundations of the Shari'ah. What the Sufis (*al-Sufiyya*, the mystics) have, in my view, is all of this kind, except that the apparent meaning of some of their expressions contradicts what the noble Shari'ah has brought. But these are built on technical terminologies (*istilahat*) among themselves, and when their intended meaning is known, the dust settles. Whether they are to be blamed for those terminologies, on the basis of the saying of Ali, may God honor his face, as in Sahih al-Bukhari: "Speak to people in what they know. Would you like God and His Messenger (ﷺ) to be called liars?", or whether they are not to be blamed because there was a motive for them, as their good opinion requires, is another question, and we are not concerned with it.

Close to the report of Abu Juhayfa is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Antarah, who said: "I was with Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, when a man came to him and said: 'Some people come to us and inform us that you have something that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not reveal to the people!' He said: 'Do you not know that God Most High said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾? By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not bequeath us a black [mark] on white.'"

The restriction of Abu Hurayra's (may God be pleased with him) "vessel," which he did not disseminate, to knowledge of secrets is not definite, because what may be meant by it is reports about trials (*fitan*) and the signs of the Hour, and what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed of regarding the corruption of religion at the hands of a few foolish youths of Quraysh. Abu Hurayra used to say: "If I wished to name them by their names, I would have done so."

[p. 192 continued]

Or what is meant is the hadiths that specify the names of tyrannical rulers, their conditions, and their blame. He used to allude to some of that without stating it openly, out of fear for himself from them, saying: "I seek refuge in God, glory be to Him, from the head of the sixties and the rule of youths," pointing to the caliphate of Yazid the Outcast, may God curse him in spite of his supporters, since it began in the year 60 AH. God answered the supplication of Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, and he died a year before it.

Al-Qastallani also said: "If it were so, Abu Hurayra would not have been able to conceal it, given what al-Bukhari transmitted from him, that he said: 'People say: Abu Hurayra has narrated much hadith. Had it not been for two verses in the Book of God Most High, I would not have narrated a single hadith.' Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾," and so on to the end of what he said. What he recited indicates the condemnation of concealing knowledge, especially the knowledge they call the knowledge of secrets, for many of them claim that it is the essence and fruit of knowledge. Moreover, Abu Hurayra denied disseminating that vessel in general, without specification, so how can it be used as evidence for that? Abu Hurayra, as far as I know, did not reveal what was concealed, so from where is it known that what he knew is this? Whoever claims must provide proof, and beyond that is cutting off necks."

So the argument from this report for the path of those people has what it has. Similar to it is what is related from Zayn al-Abidin (may God be pleased with him). Yes, there is for them another basis, which is explained in its proper place. But it is not granted to anyone, whoever he may be, that what they hold, which is absent from the Book of God the Glorious, or that it is a matter beyond the Shari'ah. Whoever proves this by his own claim has gone far astray. Al-Sha'rani, may his secret be sanctified, said in *al-Ajwiba al-Mardiyya* concerning the jurists and the Sufis: "I heard my master 'Ali al-Marsafi say: 'A man does not become perfect in the station of gnosis (*ma'rifa*) and knowledge until he sees the Reality (*haqiqa*) confirming the Shari'ah, and that Sufism is not something added to the Prophetic Sunnah, but is its very essence.'"

And I heard my master 'Ali al-Khawwas say many times: "Whoever thinks that the Reality opposes the Shari'ah, or the reverse, has erred, for among the realized scholars there is no Shari'ah that ever opposes a Reality. They even said: 'A Shari'ah without a Reality is idle, and a Reality without a Shari'ah is void,' contrary to what the deficient among the jurists and the poor (*fuqara'*) hold." Whoever claims a contradiction between Reality and Shari'ah may rely on the story of al-Khidr with Musa, peace be upon them both. Its verification will come, God willing, in a manner by which the opponent cannot open his lips.

From what we quoted from al-Qastallani concerning the report of Abu Juhayfa, the answer becomes known to the objection raised against the Sufis: that what they have, if it agrees with the Book and the Sunnah, then both are in our hands; and if it opposes them, it is a rejection of them, and after the truth there is only error.

The answer, by choosing the first part, is that the Book and the Sunnah being in our hands does not require that nothing further can be derived from them, nor does it entail that what is in them is confined to what scholars knew before. It is possible that God gives some of His special servants an understanding through which they grasp from them what no exegete or jurist among the mujtahids in religion has reached. How much the first has left for the last! Since the four Imams, for example, were granted their ijtihad and their derivation from the verses and hadiths, even though some of them differed from others, what prevents granting to these people what has been opened to them of the meanings of the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ)? Even if it differs from what some Imams held, provided it does not oppose what the explicit consensus (*ijma'*) of the infallible Community has established? I consider the distinction between the two groups, while each one's acceptance and rejection are established, to be a purely arbitrary judgment, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

The Shi'a claimed that what is meant by "what has been sent down to you" is the caliphate of Ali, may God honor his face. They relate with their chains from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with both of them, that "God Most High revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should appoint Ali, may God honor his face, as successor. He feared that this would be hard on a group of his companions, so God Most High sent down this verse as an encouragement to him, peace be upon him, regarding what he had been commanded to convey."

[p. 193]

And from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Ali, may God honor his face, when God, glory be to Him, commanded him to inform the people of his guardianship (*wilaya*). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) feared that they would say: 'He favored his cousin,' and that they would object to it. So God revealed this verse to him, and he stood up for his guardianship on the day of Ghadir Khumm, took his hand, and said, peace be upon him: 'Whoever I am his master (*mawla*), Ali is his master. O God, befriend whoever befriends him and oppose whoever opposes him.'"

Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, transmitted from Abu Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir, all transmitting from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "This verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Ghadir Khumm concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We used to recite in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, [that] Ali is the guardian of the believers. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message.'"

The report of Ghadir is the cornerstone of their proofs for the caliphate of the Commander (*al-Amir*), may God honor his face. They have added to it, to complete their aim, objectionable additions, inserted into it fabricated words, composed poems on it, and attacked the Companions, may God be pleased with them, claiming that they opposed the explicit text of the Chosen Prophet (ﷺ). Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Himyari, may God treat him with His justice, said in a long qasida:

I marvel at a people who came to Ahmad
with a plan that has no place.
They said to him: "If you wished, you would inform us
who is the final refuge and the place of recourse,
When you die and part from us,
while among them are those who covet rule."
He said: "If I informed you of a refuge,
you would perhaps act with it
as the people of the Calf acted when they abandoned
Harun, so leaving him is more scrupulous."
Then after him came a resolve
from his Lord that has no repelling.
"Convey! Otherwise you would not be a conveyor,
and God protects you from them."
Then the Prophet stood up, the one who
was, by what He commanded him, proclaiming openly,
Delivering a sermon commanded, and in his hand
the hand of Ali, whose light shines.
Lifting it high—how honored is the hand of the one
who raises and the hand that is raised!
"Whoever I am his master, this one is his master."
They were not pleased, nor were they content with him.
A people was enraged by his words,
as if their noses were being cut off.
Until, when they buried him in his grave,
and turned away from his religion, they lost it.
They forgot what he said the day before and what he enjoined,
and bought harm in exchange for what benefits.
They severed their kinship after him,
so they will be repaid for what they severed.
They resolved on treachery against their master.
Perdition to what they resolved upon!
Neither will they come to his Pool
tomorrow, nor will he intercede for them.

And so on to the end of what he said. May God forgive his slip and pardon him. You know that the reports of Ghadir that contain the command to appoint a successor are not authentic according to the People of the Sunnah, nor are they accepted by them at all. We will explain what occurred there with the fullest explanation, and clarify the weak from it and the strong. Then we return to the Shi'a's argument, refuting it. From God, glory be to Him, is the seeking of aid, and upon Him is reliance.

[p. 194]

We say: The Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon in a place between Mecca and Medina, on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage, near al-Juhfa, called Ghadir Khumm. In it he explained the virtue of Ali, may God honor his face, and the vindication of his honor from what some who were with him in the land of Yemen had spoken of, because of what had come from his justice, which some thought was oppression, narrowness, and stinginess. The truth was with Ali, may God honor his face, in that matter. This was on Sunday, the eighteenth of Dhu al-Hijja, under a tree there.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 3 of 5):

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yahya ibn Abdullah, from Yazid ibn Talha, who said: "When Ali, may Allah honour his face, was coming from Yemen to meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Makkah, he hastened ahead to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and appointed over the troops who were with him a man from among his companions. That man set about dressing every man in a ḥulla (a suit of clothing) from the bazz (striped cloth) that was with Ali, may Allah honour his face. When his army drew near, he went out to meet them and saw that they were wearing the ḥulla. He said: 'Woe to you! What is this?' He replied: 'I clothed the people so that they might look splendid with it when they enter among the people.' He said: 'Woe to you! Take it off before we reach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So he took the ḥulla off the people, returned it to the bazz, and the army expressed their complaint about what he had done to them."

And he (al-Tabari) also transmitted from Zaynab bint Ka'b, who was the wife of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The people complained about Ali, may Allah honour his face. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us delivering a sermon, and I heard him say: 'O people, do not complain about Ali, for by Allah, he is indeed too harsh (akhshan) in the cause of Allah, or in the path of Allah.'" Imam Ahmad also narrated it.

He also narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "From Buraydah al-Aslami, who said: 'I campaigned with Ali in Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness (jafwa). When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali, may Allah honour his face, and I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change. He said: "Buraydah! Am I not closer (awlā) to the believers than their own selves?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Whoever I am his mawla (master/patron), then Ali is his mawla."'" Al-Nasa'i likewise narrated it with a good, strong chain whose narrators are all trustworthy (thiqat). It is also narrated by another chain, which is unique to it.

Al-Dhahabi said: "It is authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: 'When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the Farewell Pilgrimage and alighted at Ghadir Khumm, he ordered that the large trees be cleared away. Then he said: "It seems as though I have been called and I have answered. Indeed, I have left among you the two weighty things (al-thaqalayn): the Book of Allah and my family (ʿitrah), the people of my household. So see how you will deal with me regarding them, for they will not separate until they come to me at the Basin (al-Ḥawḍ). Allah is my mawla, and I am the wali of every believer." Then he took the hand of Ali, may Allah honour his face, and said: "Whoever I am his mawla, then this one is his wali. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him."' There was no one among the large trees except that he saw him with his own eyes and heard him with his own ears."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ali ibn Zayd, Abu Harun al-Abdi, and Musa ibn Uthman, from al-Bara', who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the Farewell Pilgrimage. When we came to Ghadir Khumm, a place was swept for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) beneath two trees, and it was proclaimed among the people: 'Al-salat jami'ah' (prayer is gathering).
