The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Ali, may Allah honour his face, took his hand, and made him stand on his right side. He said: 'Am I not closer to every person than his own self?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Indeed, this one is the mawla of whoever I am his mawla. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him.' Then Umar ibn al-Khattab met him and said, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Congratulations to you! You have become the mawla of every believing man and woman, morning and evening.'" This report is weak (ḍaʿīf), for they (the scholars) have stated explicitly that Ali ibn Zayd, Abu Harun, and Musa are weak narrators, whose reports are not relied upon. Also in the chain is Abu Ishaq, who was a Shi'i whose narrations are rejected.

Ḍimra narrated with his chain from Abu Hurayra, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the hand of Ali, may Allah honour his face, he said: 'Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾." Then Abu Hurayra said:

[p. 195]

"That was the day of Ghadir Khumm. Whoever fasts on the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, Allah will record for him the fasting of sixty months." This is an extremely rejected (munkar) report, and al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya explicitly states that it is fabricated (mawdu').

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir al-Tabari took special care with the hadith of Ghadir. He compiled on it two volumes in which he included all its chains and wordings, and he brought together the weak and the strong, the sound and the unsound, in accordance with the habit of many hadith scholars, who report whatever reached them on the subject without distinguishing between sound and weak. Likewise, the great hafiz Abu al-Qasim ibn Asakir reported many hadiths in this sermon, but what is relied upon in it is what we have indicated and similar material that does not contain the report of the succession (istikhlaf), as the Shi'a claim.

It is narrated from al-Dhahabi that: "Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla" is mutawatir (narrated by so many chains that its transmission is certain), and it is certain that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it. As for "O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him," it is an addition with a strong chain. As for "fasting the eighteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah," it is not sound. And by Allah, that verse was not revealed except on the Day of Arafah, a few days before Ghadir Khumm.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate the report of Ghadir in their Sahihs because they did not find it fulfilling their conditions. The Shi'a claim that this is due to deficiency and partisanship in them, but may they be far from that.

The Shi'a's argument from the report "Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla" is that mawla means "the one more entitled to disposal" (al-awla bi-al-tasarruf), and priority in disposal is identical with the imamate. It is not hidden that the first error in this argument is their making mawla mean awla, which the grammarians (ahl al-ʿArabiyyah) all deny. Indeed they said: "The pattern maf'al has never come with the meaning of af'al at all." Only Abu Zayd the lexicographer permitted it, relying on the statement of Abu Ubayda in explaining the verse ﴿It is your mawla﴾, meaning "more worthy of you."

It is replied: this implies the validity of "so-and-so is a mawla of so-and-so," just as "so-and-so is awla than so-and-so" is valid, and the implication is false by consensus (ijma'), so what implies it is likewise false. Abu Ubayda's explanation is a clarification of the resulting meaning, i.e., "the Fire is your abode and your destination, the place fitting for you," and it is not explicit proof that the word mawla there means awla.

Second: even if we concede that mawla means awla, it does not follow that its connection is disposal. It may be that the intended meaning is "more worthy of love," "more worthy of honour," and the like. The word awla has come in many speeches where the sense of disposal cannot be applied, such as the verse ﴿Indeed the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who believe﴾.

Moreover, we have two indications that the intended meaning of wilaya (from the word mawla or awla) is love:

The first is what we have related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq concerning the complaint of those who were with the Commander, may Allah honour his face, in Yemen, such as Buraydah al-Aslami, Khalid ibn al-Walid, and others. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not forbid the complainants specifically, in order to exaggerate in seeking his friendship and to be gentle in calling to it, as is generally his way in such matters. For this gentle approach he (ﷺ) opened the sermon with the words: "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?"

The second is his statement, upon him be prayers and peace, according to some narrations: "O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him." For if the intended meaning of mawla were "one who disposes of affairs" or "one more entitled to disposal," he would have said: "O Allah, befriend whoever is under his disposal and be an enemy to whoever is not." Since he (ﷺ) mentioned love and enmity, he indicated that the purpose is the obligation of loving him, may Allah honour his face, and warning against enmity and hatred towards him, not disposal or its absence. Had the intended meaning been the caliphate, he (ﷺ) would have stated it explicitly.

What supports this is the report narrated by Abu Nu'aym from al-Hasan al-Muthanna ibn al-Hasan al-Sibt, may Allah be pleased with them both, that people asked him whether this report was an explicit text on the caliphate of the Commander, may Allah honour his face. He said: "If the Prophet (ﷺ) had intended his caliphate, he would have said: 'O people, this is the guardian of my affair and the one who will govern you after me, so listen to him and obey.'" Then al-Hasan said: "I swear by Allah, the Exalted, that if Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) had preferred Ali for this matter, and Ali had not advanced himself, he would have been the greatest of people in error."

Also, it may be argued that the intended meaning of wilaya is love, since the word "after me" (ba'di) was not used in it, and it is apparent that the two wilayas (of love and of disposal) would then be combined at one time. Such combination cannot be conceived if the intended meaning were priority in disposal, unlike when the intended meaning is love.

The Shi'a also relied, to establish that the intended meaning of mawla is "more entitled to disposal," on the wording found at the beginning of the report in one of its versions, namely his statement (ﷺ): "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?" We say: the intended meaning of this too is "more worthy of love." That is: "Am I not more beloved to the believers than their own selves?" Indeed, it may be said that awla here is derived from wilaya in the sense of love, and the meaning is: "Am I not more beloved to the believers than themselves?" So that the parts of the speech harmonize, the arrangement is good, and the overall meaning is this: "O assembly of believers, you love me more than your own selves, so whoever loves me should love Ali. O Allah, love whoever loves him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him."

It is indicated that the intended meaning of awla in that sentence is not "more entitled to disposal," because it is derived from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and those of relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾. This verse is directed at negating the lineage of adopted sons from those who adopt them. Its explanation: it is not proper to say that Zayd ibn Harithah is the son of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Prophet's (ﷺ) relation to all believers is like that of a compassionate father, and more so. His wives are their mothers, and relatives by blood are more entitled and closer than others, even if compassion and reverence for strangers are greater. But the basis of lineage is kinship, and it is absent in adopted sons, not compassion and reverence. This is what is in the Book of Allah, i.e., in His ruling. The notion of priority in disposal has no bearing on the intended matter at all. So the meaning intended in our case is the meaning intended in the source from which it was taken. Even if we suppose that awla in the opening of the report means "more entitled to disposal," it is possible that this was to alert the addressees with that address, so that they would turn fully to listen to his speech (ﷺ) and attend to it with utmost care, and so that what it contains of guidance would be established most firmly. This is like a man saying to his sons in a context of admonition and advice: "Am I not your father?" And when they acknowledge this, he commands them with what he intends from them, so that they accept the authority of fatherhood and prophethood and act in accordance with both.

Accordingly, his statement, upon him be prayers and peace, in this context: "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?" is like: "Am I not the Messenger of Allah to you?" or "Am I not your Prophet?" It is not possible to apply the same to what follows it, in order to preserve the coherence of the context.

[p. 197]

Among the Shi'ah (the partisans of Ali) is one who offered an argument against the meaning of love (*maḥabba*). It runs as follows: the love of al-Amīr (Ali) — may Allah honour his face — is already established within the verse ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾. So if this hadith also conveyed that same meaning, it would be superfluous (*laghw*). Its corruption is not hidden. The source of this error is that the one who makes the argument did not understand that obligating the love of someone within a general statement is one thing, and obligating his love specifically is another. The difference between them is as clear as the sun. What makes this even more evident is that if a person believed in all of Allah's prophets and messengers — peace be upon them — but did not mention our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically, his faith would not be considered valid. Furthermore, even if we assume that the content of the verse and the report is the same, it does not follow that there is superfluity. At most, it entails confirmation and emphasis, and that is the role of the Prophet (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) often confirmed and reaffirmed the contents of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an itself repeats its contents for this very reason. No one has said that this is superfluous — Allah forbid. Also, the explicit designation of the succession (*imāma*) of al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — has been repeated many times in Shi'ite sources, so if that is authentic, then it would entail superfluous speech, and the speech of the Lawgiver (Allah) is far above that.

Then, what al-Himyarī indicated in his poem, in which he went to excess, namely that the Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in this collective manner and requested from him the appointment of an imam after him, is something the historians and biographers from both groups have not mentioned, as far as I know. Rather, it is pure falsehood and slander. We seek refuge in Allah from it.

Whoever has read that abominable poem in its entirety, and what the Shi'ah narrate in it, and has even a little knowledge, will see a marvel, and will realise that the clanging of these people is like the creaking of a door or the buzzing of a fly.

Furthermore, the reports coming through the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) indicating that this verse was revealed concerning Ali — may Allah honour his face — even if they are authentic and reach the level at which they can be used as evidence, contain no more than an indication of his excellence, may Allah honour his face, and that he is the friend (*walī*) of the believers in the sense we have established. We do not deny this, and whoever denies it is cursed. Likewise, what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud — may Allah be pleased with him — contains nothing more than this. And the explicit mention of him — may Allah honour his face — by name is for the reason we have already presented.

Some of our companions said, by way of concession: the verse refers to the report of Ibn Mas'ud, and likewise the report of Ghadir (Ghadir Khumm) according to the well-known narration. Granting that both indicate that what is meant is that he is the one with the greater right to disposal (*awlā bi-l-taṣarruf*), they must both be restricted by what indicates this in the final outcome. In that case, welcome to agreement, because the People of the Sunnah also say this at the time of his imamate. The reason for specifically mentioning al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — at that time is what the Prophet (ﷺ) knew through revelation about the occurrence of corruption and rebellion during his caliphate, and the denial of his rightful imamate by some people. That this would happen right after death without any interval is something for which there is no proof.

The report introduced by "It is as if I have been called and I have answered" is not explicit regarding the intended meaning, as is not hidden. And among the things that weaken the claim of the Shi'ah that the verse was revealed specifically concerning the caliphate of Ali — may Allah honour his face — and that the relative pronoun in it is specific, is the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. For although "the people" here is general, what is meant by them is the disbelievers. And [the verse continues]: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. This is in the position of a reason for His protecting the Prophet (ﷺ), and it contains the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun. That is: because Allah does not guide them to their wish concerning you. And when the intended meaning of "them" is the disbelievers, how can this be after the intention of the caliphate?! Indeed, if it were said that it is not valid, it would not be far-fetched. This is because the fear that the Shi'ah attribute to the Prophet (ﷺ) — and he is far above that — regarding conveying the matter of the caliphate actually came from the Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — since among them, Allah forbid, there were those who coveted it for themselves. And when such a person sees himself deprived of it, it is not far-fetched that he would intend to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And committing oneself to the statement — we seek refuge in Allah the Mighty and Majestic — that those who hinted at attributing coveting of the caliphate to him are disbelievers entails comprehensive dangers. The least of them is declaring al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — a sinner, and he is who he is; or attributing cowardice to him, while he is the victorious lion of Allah; or ruling that he practised taqiyya (dissimulation), while he is the one who fears no blame in the cause of Allah and fears none but Allah, glorified is He; or attributing the act of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and rather the divine command, to futility. All of this, as you see, is unacceptable.

It may be said: we have two matters which indicate that what is meant by the relative pronoun is the caliphate:

The first is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded with the most eloquent expression to convey the legal rulings that he was commanded to convey, as He, glorified is He, said addressing him — peace be upon him: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾. So if the intended meaning here were not a single item that is the most important of the items and the greatest in standing — and that is none other than the caliphate, since through it the affair of religion and the world is ordered — the speech would be devoid of benefit.

The second is that Ibn Ishaq mentioned in his biography that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed the people during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Ḥijjat al-Wadā') with the sermon in which he made clear what he made clear. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, listen to my words, for I do not know, perhaps I will not meet you after this year at this place ever. O people, your blood and your wealth are forbidden to you until you meet your Lord, as the sanctity of this day of yours, and as the sanctity of this month of yours. You will meet your Lord, and He will ask you about your deeds, and I have conveyed." Then he (ﷺ) enjoined [kindness] to the women. Then he (ﷺ) said: "Understand my words, for I have conveyed. I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ)." Until he said, with my father and mother as his ransom, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O Allah, have I conveyed?" Ibn Ishaq said: It was mentioned to me that the people said: "O Allah, yes." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, bear witness." End of quote.

This report is clear that the sermon was on the Day of Arafat, the Greatest Day of Hajj, as in the narration of Yahya ibn 'Abbad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. And the day of Ghadir was the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, after the Prophet (ﷺ) had finished and completed the matters of the rites and turned towards Medina the Illuminated. In that case, what he was commanded to convey would be a different matter from what he had conveyed before (ﷺ), and he made the people witness his conveying it, and he made Allah witness this. And this is none other than the Great Caliphate and the Supreme Imamate. So it is as if He, glorified is He, were saying: "O Messenger, convey that Ali — may Allah honour his face — is your successor and your deputy after you. And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message." And even if the people said to you when you said, "O Allah, have I conveyed?": "O Allah, yes."

Because we say: the conditional statement in the first matter, after closing our eyes to what is in it, is disputed, since it is possible that what is meant by the relative pronoun in the two verses is the legal rulings related to the welfare of the servants in their livelihood and their return. Nor does it follow that there is no benefit, for how many verses have been repeated in the Qur'an, and commands and prohibitions mentioned many times for emphasis and confirmation. Moreover, some have mentioned that the benefit of the command here is to remove the suspicion that the Prophet (ﷺ) had left, or would leave, conveying some part of revelation out of taqiyya.

Against the second matter, two objections arise:

The first is that the fact that the day of Ghadir came after the day of Arafat is accepted. But we do not accept that the verse was revealed on it, so that what he was commanded to convey would be a different matter. Rather, what the content of the sermon and the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it require, "O Allah, have I conveyed?", is that the verse was revealed before the two days of Ghadir and Arafat. And what has been transmitted in other reports that the chapter of al-Mā'idah was revealed between Mecca and Medina during the Farewell Pilgrimage is not suitable as evidence for either being after or before, since there is no mention in it of the return or the going. The apparent state of the Prophet (ﷺ) during that pilgrimage, in showing the rites, and in abolishing usury and the blood-vengeance of the Jahiliyyah, and other matters too long to mention — which the biographers have recorded — indicates that the revelation was during the going.

The second is that even if we grant that the revelation was on the day of Ghadir, we do not accept that what he was commanded to convey is a different matter. What necessarily follows in that case is repetition, and you have already learned its benefit and how frequently it occurs. And even if we grant that what he was commanded to convey is a different matter, we do not accept that it is none other than the caliphate. How many other verses did the Prophet (ﷺ) convey after that, from what was revealed to him — peace be upon him. And what is understood from some reports is that this verse was before the Farewell Pilgrimage. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diyā' in al-Mukhtārah transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: Which verse that was sent down from the heaven was the hardest on you? He said: I was at Mina during the days of the season, and the polytheists of the Arabs and the scattered people gathered at the season. Then Gabriel — peace be upon him — came down to me and said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord, and if you do not do it, then you have not conveyed His message﴾, the verse. He said: So I stood at the Aqaba and called out: O people, who will support me so that I may convey the messages of my Lord, and for you is Paradise? O people, say: There is no god but Allah, and I am the Messenger of Allah to you; you will prosper and succeed, and for you is Paradise." He (ﷺ) said: "No man, woman, slave girl, or child remained but that they threw dust and stones at me, saying: 'Liar, apostate!' Then an apparition appeared to me and said: 'O Muhammad, if you are the Messenger of Allah, then it is time for you to curse them as Noah cursed his people with destruction.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know; and help me against them, so that they answer my call to Your obedience.' Then his uncle al-'Abbas came and rescued him from them and drove them away from him."

Al-A'mash said: "For this, the Banu al-'Abbas take pride and say: 'Concerning them was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾.' The Prophet (ﷺ) loved Abu Talib, and Allah willed for 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib."

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 5 of 5):

Clearer than this is what Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym in (al-Dala'il), Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was guarded, and his uncle Abu Talib used to send with him every day men from Banu Hashim to guard him, until there was revealed ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. His uncle then wished to send with him someone to guard him, but he said: 'O uncle, indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has protected me.'" Abu Talib died before the Hijra, and the Farewell Pilgrimage was many years after it, and the apparent reading is that the verse is connected (to the context).

It is also reported from some of them that the verse was revealed at night, based on what 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was guarded until there was revealed ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. He then put his head out of the dome and said: 'O people, disperse, for Allah the Exalted has protected me.'" It is not hidden that this is not explicit regarding the intended meaning.

What I incline to, in reconciling the reports, is that this verse was revealed more than once, and Allah the Exalted knows best. The intended meaning of protection from the people is the preservation of his blessed soul (upon him be prayers and peace) from killing and destruction. Therefore it is not objected that his noble face was wounded and his front tooth was broken at the Battle of Uhud.

Some held the general view, claiming that the verses were revealed only after Uhud. Both points are challenged by the fact that the Jews poisoned him, peace be upon him, to the extent that he said: "The morsel of Khaybar continues to trouble me, and now is the time when it has severed my aorta." It is answered that He, glorified and exalted, guaranteed him protection from being killed or the like by reason of conveying the revelation, while what was done to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and to the prophets, peace be upon them, was for defending wealth, lands and lives. Its remoteness is not hidden.

Al-Raghib said: The infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, is their being preserved by what they were singled out with of purity of substance (safa' al-jawhar), then by the noble character and virtues bestowed upon them, then by victory and the firming of their feet, then by the sending down of tranquility upon them, and by the guarding of their hearts, and by success (tawfiq).

It was also said: the intended meaning of infallibility is protection from committing sin, and the meaning is: "Convey, and Allah will grant you protection from committing sin among the people," that is, He will protect you by means of that from them. It is not hidden that this interpretation is one that could only come from someone whom Allah the Exalted has not preserved from error.

Similar to this is what was reported from 'Ali ibn 'Isa regarding His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, where he said: He does not guide them by assistance, success and kindnesses toward disbelief, but rather He guides them to faith. He claimed that what prompted him to this interpretation is that Allah the Exalted guided the disbelievers to faith by showing them it, encouraging them to it, and warning them against opposing it. And you have known the intended meaning of the verse. Moreover, in his statement there is what is not hidden of disputability.

Al-Jubba'i said: the intended meaning is: He does not guide them to Paradise and reward. In this there is heedlessness of the fact that the clause is in the position of causal explanation.

Some claimed that the intended meaning is: upon you is only the conveying, not the guidance; whoever I have decreed to disbelief and to die upon it will never be guided. This is as you see. So let all that we have mentioned regarding this verse be understood and memorized, for I do not think you will find it in a book.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (risalatihi) in the plural form. The placement of the verse among the verses addressing the People of the Book is because all of them are harsh warnings that the disbelievers dislike hearing, and it is difficult for the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to address them with them, especially what follows them of the text lamenting upon them their utter misguidance. For this reason the command is repeated, and He, glorified be He, said:

﴿Say: O People of the Book﴾. By them is meant the Jews and Christians, as some exegetes said. Others said that by them is meant only the Jews. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Rafi' ibn Haritha, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf and Rafi' ibn Huraymila came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion and creed of Abraham, and that you believe in what we have of the Torah, and that you testify that it is truth from Allah the Exalted?' The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Yes, but you have innovated and denied what is in it of the covenant taken from you, and you concealed from it what you were commanded to make clear to the people, so I am free of your innovations.' They said: 'Then we hold to what is in our hands, for we are upon guidance and truth, and we do not believe in you nor follow you.'" So Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you are not upon anything﴾, that is, a religion that is considered valid and worthy of being called "something," due to the manifestness of its falsehood and the clarity of its corruption. In this expression there is what is not hidden of contempt; and among their sayings is "less than nothing." ﴿Until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that is, you observe them and preserve what is in them of matters, among which are the proofs of the Messenger of Allah's prophethood and the evidences of his prophecy. For establishing them and fulfilling their rights is only by that, not by acting upon everything in them, whether abrogated or otherwise, for observing the abrogated is nullifying them and rejecting their testimony.

﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, that is, the glorious Qur'an, and establishing it is by believing in it. The establishing of the two Books was mentioned before the establishing of it, although it is the principal intended matter, out of regard for the right of testimony and to bring them down from the rank of opposition. It was also said: the intended meaning of the relative clause is the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel, peace be upon them. It was said: the divine books, for they all affirm the obligation of believing in one who claims prophethood and displays a miracle, and the obligation of obeying the one sent to them. The full discussion of this noble structure has already passed, as has that of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And surely much of them will increase in transgression and disbelief by what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. The clause is resumptive, as Shaykh al-Islam said, explaining the severity of their obstinacy, their excess in arrogance and enmity, and that conveying the message benefits them nothing. Its opening with an oath is to emphasize and affirm its content. And the attribution of sending down to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, along with its attribution to them earlier, is to indicate their detachment from that attribution. And if by the relative clause is meant the blessings given to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, the matter of attribution is quite evident.

﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, that is: do not be sorrowful or grieved over their increase in transgression and disbelief, for the harm of that is connected to them and its consequence returns to them, and in the believers there is sufficiency for you regarding them. The placement of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to record upon them their firm rootedness in disbelief. It was said: the intended meaning is: do not grieve over their destruction and punishment; and placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to draw attention to the cause that necessitates the absence of grief, and it is not free from

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 5):

﴿O Messenger﴾ to ﴿both jinn and humankind, all of them﴾. This is an address of honour, because the message is Allah the Exalted's greatest favour and His supreme honour. This title also signals what requires him (ﷺ) to carry out what he was commanded: conveying what was revealed to him.

﴿Convey﴾, that is, deliver to the creation ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾, that is, all that has been sent down, whatever it may be, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the Owner of your affair, who brings you to the perfection that befits you. Within this is an implicit promise of his protection and safeguarding (peace be upon him). The meaning is: convey it without fearing anyone's watchfulness over you in this, and without fearing that any harm will ever befall you. ﴿And if you do not do so﴾, that is, what you were commanded to convey of all of it,

[p. 189]

﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾, that is, you have not delivered any part of His message. This is because no part of it is more deserving of delivery than another. So if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you have neglected delivering all of it. Likewise, whoever does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, since each part conveys what the others convey, and they are therefore in the ruling of one thing. And one thing cannot be both conveyed and not conveyed, believed and not believed. Also, concealing part of it nullifies what has been delivered of it, like omitting some pillars of the prayer, for the purpose of the call is undone by that.

It has been objected to the claim that no part is more deserving of delivery than another, that priority is established in terms of obligation, definitively and speculatively, clearly and obscurely, as principle and as derivative. Al-Kashf answered that he denied priority by looking at the basic obligation. Moreover, that refers to what is conveyed, whereas the discussion is about conveying, and conveying does not differ in obligation, since it is one thing considered in its essence. Then, concealing part indicates that he did not consider that he was commanded to convey, but rather considered the benefit in what is conveyed. So it is as if he did not comply with this command at all, and thus did not convey. And even if he informed the people, it would not benefit him, since in that case he would be a reporter, not a conveyer.

The second justification was challenged on the grounds that the Lawgiver regarded the prayer as one unit, unlike conveying. But this objection does not hold, because God obligated him (peace be upon him) to convey all of it, so He has made it like the prayer without doubt.

From what we have said in explaining the conditional sentence, it is known that there is no identity between the condition and the consequence. Whoever claims it, on the basis that the outcome of "if you do not convey the message, you have not conveyed the message," has compared it to the saying:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

Here the predicate is the very same as the subject, without any addition to the wording. "My poetry is my poetry" is famed for its eloquence and widely known for its fluency. But he has spoken by remaining silent about those attributes through which the benefit is achieved, relying on the fact that they are among the necessary qualities of his poetry in the understanding of listeners, due to its fame for them, and that he is independent of mentioning them because of their renown and wide circulation. Likewise, as Ibn al-Munir said, it is intended in the verse, because not conveying the message is a matter known to people, firmly established in minds as something grave and shameful, condemned in the one who commits it. Do you not see that the failure of a scholar to spread knowledge is a dreadful thing? So how much more is the concealment of the message by the Messenger! Thus the additions by which the condition and consequence differ are dispensed with, since they are attached to the consequence in people's understanding, and whoever hears "not conveying the message" understands what lies behind it of threat and warning. This style is made beautiful in the Mighty Book by mentioning the condition in general terms, where He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And if you do not do so﴾, and did not say: "And if you do not convey the message, then you have not conveyed the message." Thus the two differ in wording, even if they are one in meaning. This is more lustrous and more manifestly graceful than repeating the same word in condition and consequence. Abu al-Najm fell short of this pinnacle by mentioning the subject with the wording of the predicate, and it is fitting that his eloquence should shrink next to the eloquence of the Inimitable. So there is no fault in him for that.

It has also been said: the meaning is, "If you do not do so, then for you is what the concealment of the whole revelation necessitates," so the cause is placed in the position of the effect. This is supported by what Ishaq ibn Rahawayh recorded in his Musnad from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and what Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Hibban recorded in their Tafsir from the mursal narration of al-Hasan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent me with the message, and I was distressed by it. Then Allah revealed: If you do not convey My messages, I shall punish you. He guaranteed me protection, and so I was strengthened."

It has also been said: the meaning is, "If you abandon conveying what has been sent down to you, you will be judged as not having conveyed at all." It has also been said, and would that it had not been said, that what is meant by "what has been sent down" is the Qur'an, and what is meant in the answer is the rest of the miracles. Other views have also been stated.

The verse has been cited as evidence that he (ﷺ) did not conceal anything of the revelation. It is attributed to the Shi'a that they claim he (ﷺ) concealed part of it out of taqiyya (dissimulation).

It is reported from some Sufis that what is meant is conveying what concerns the interests of the servants among the rulings, and that its sending down was intended for them to know it. As for what was specially given to him of the unseen which did not concern the interests of his community, he had the right, or rather the duty, to keep it concealed. Al-Sulami narrated from Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾, that he said: "He revealed without intermediary, between Him and him, secretly, into his heart, and no one else knows of it except in the Hereafter, when He gives him intercession for his community." Al-Wasiti said: "He cast to His servant what He cast, and did not reveal what He revealed, because He, glorified be He, specified it for him (ﷺ). What was specific to him (peace be upon him) was hidden, and what Allah the Exalted sent him with to the creation was manifest." Al-Tibi said: "The meaning of what we have narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said, 'I memorised from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) two vessels. As for one of them, I spread it; as for the other, if I spread it, this throat of mine would be cut,' points to this." He meant his neck, and the original meaning of al-bula'um is the passage of food. Al-Bukhari explained it thus. They call this the knowledge of divine secrets and the knowledge of reality. To this the leader of the gnostics, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, alluded when he said:

"Indeed I conceal from my knowledge its precious jewels,
lest one ignorant of the Truth see them and be tempted by us.
Abu Hasan had already gone before this to al-Husayn,
and before him he had bequeathed it to al-Hasan.
For many a jewel of knowledge, were I to disclose it,
I would be told: 'You are of those who worship idols.'
And men who are Muslims would make my blood lawful,
seeing as good the foulest of what they do."

Among this is the knowledge of the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud). They have explicitly stated that it is a level beyond the level of reason, and they said that it is something the spirit knows without the mediation of reason. From here they spoke of the hidden knowledge, in the sense that it is hidden with respect to the people of thought and the minds immersed in the states of obstacles and attachments, not with respect to those who are stripped of them and ascend to the presences of holiness and the gardens of lights.

Shaykh Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani, may Allah refresh his spirit, mentioned in his book al-Durar al-Manthura fi Bayan Zubad al-Ulum al-Mashhura the following text: "As for the essence of the science of Sufism, in which the people have written their treatises, it is the fruit of acting upon the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever acts on what he knows speaks as they spoke, and all that they said becomes part of what is with him. For whenever the servant advances in the station of courtesy with Allah the Exalted, his speech becomes subtle to people's understanding, until one of them said to his shaykh: 'The speech of my brother so-and-so is subtle to my understanding!' He said: 'Because you have two shirts and he has only one; he is higher in rank than you.' This is what moved the jurists and their like among the people of veiling to call the science of the Sufis the science of the inner. But it is not inner, for the inner is only the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. As for everything He has taught creation, across its different levels, it is of the outer science, for it has appeared to the creation. Know this." End of quotation.

Some have understood that what is meant is conveying the rulings and what relates to them of benefits, not what includes the science of secrets, from His words, glorified be He: ﴿What We have sent down to you﴾, rather than: ﴿what We have made known to you﴾. They mentioned that the science of secrets was not sent down by revelation, but by way of inspiration and unveiling. It has also been said that this is understood from the word "message," for a message is what is sent to others.

Some Sufis, sanctified be their secrets, have extended their discourse on this matter. My own verification is that what the Prophet (ﷺ) possesses of divine secrets and other legal rulings is comprised in the Qur'an that was sent down. For the Exalted has said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾, and He, exalted be He, said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as recorded by al-Tirmidhi and others: "There will be trials." It was said: "What is the way out of them?" He said: "The Book of Allah the Exalted: in it is the news of what came before you, the report of what comes after you, and the judgement of what is among you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "In this Qur'an every knowledge has been sent down, and everything has been made clear to us in it, but our knowledge falls short of what has been made clear to us in the Qur'an."

Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Everything the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled by, he understood from the Qur'an." This is supported by what al-Tabarani recorded in al-Awsat from the hadith of A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I permit only what Allah the Exalted has permitted in His Book, and I forbid only what Allah the Exalted has forbidden in His Book."

Al-Mursi said: "The Qur'an has gathered the sciences of the first and the last, such that no one truly encompasses it in knowledge except the One who spoke it, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), apart from what He, glorified be He, has kept to Himself. Then the greater part of this was inherited from him by the leading Companions and their eminent figures, such as the four caliphs, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), to the extent that he said: 'If the tether of a camel were lost to me, I would find it in the Book of Allah the Exalted.' Then the Successors inherited it from them with excellence. Then aspirations fell short, resolutions weakened, and the people of knowledge diminished, and they became too weak to bear what the Companions and the Successors carried of its sciences and all its branches. So they diversified its sciences, and every group took charge of one of its branches."

Some said: "There is nothing that cannot be extracted from the Qur'an for one whom Allah the Exalted has granted understanding." To the extent that someone derived the age of the Prophet (ﷺ) as sixty-three years from the words of the Exalted in Surah al-Munafiqun: ﴿And Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come﴾, for it is the beginning of the sixty-third surah. And He followed it with Surah al-Taghabun, so that the loss (taghabun) would become manifest in the loss of that Prophet (ﷺ) himself. This is something over which two rams would hardly clash. Since it is established that all of that is in the Qur'an, conveying the Qur'an is conveying it. The only point is that the identification of these details, secret by secret and ruling by ruling, has not been established by explicit wording for everyone. How many a secret and a ruling have been indicated by allusion, without being stated by explicit expression! And whoever claims that there are secrets outside the Book of Allah the Exalted, which the Sufis received from their Lord by whatever means, has committed a great slander, and Ibn al-Sabhlal has come with misguidance without any doubt.

[p. 192]

As for the saying of some of them, "You took your knowledge dead from dead men, while we took it from the Living who does not die," it does not prove that claim, because that taking may have been from the Qur'an through a holy understanding (*fahm qudsi*) that God Most High gave to that recipient. What supports this is what is authentically related from Abu Juhayfa, who said: "I said to Ali, may God honor his face: 'Do you have a book that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) singled you out with?' He said: 'No, except the Book of God Most High, or an understanding given to a Muslim man, or what is in this sheet,' and it was hanging from the hilt of his sword. I said: 'And what is in this sheet?' He said: 'The blood-money (*al-'aql*), the ransoming of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.'"

It is understood from this, as al-Qastallani said, that a scholar may derive from the Qur'an, by his own understanding, what has not been transmitted from the exegetes, provided it agrees with the foundations of the Shari'ah. What the Sufis (*al-Sufiyya*, the mystics) have, in my view, is all of this kind, except that the apparent meaning of some of their expressions contradicts what the noble Shari'ah has brought. But these are built on technical terminologies (*istilahat*) among themselves, and when their intended meaning is known, the dust settles. Whether they are to be blamed for those terminologies, on the basis of the saying of Ali, may God honor his face, as in Sahih al-Bukhari: "Speak to people in what they know. Would you like God and His Messenger (ﷺ) to be called liars?", or whether they are not to be blamed because there was a motive for them, as their good opinion requires, is another question, and we are not concerned with it.

Close to the report of Abu Juhayfa is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Antarah, who said: "I was with Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, when a man came to him and said: 'Some people come to us and inform us that you have something that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not reveal to the people!' He said: 'Do you not know that God Most High said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾? By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not bequeath us a black [mark] on white.'"

The restriction of Abu Hurayra's (may God be pleased with him) "vessel," which he did not disseminate, to knowledge of secrets is not definite, because what may be meant by it is reports about trials (*fitan*) and the signs of the Hour, and what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) informed of regarding the corruption of religion at the hands of a few foolish youths of Quraysh. Abu Hurayra used to say: "If I wished to name them by their names, I would have done so."

[p. 192 continued]

Or what is meant is the hadiths that specify the names of tyrannical rulers, their conditions, and their blame. He used to allude to some of that without stating it openly, out of fear for himself from them, saying: "I seek refuge in God, glory be to Him, from the head of the sixties and the rule of youths," pointing to the caliphate of Yazid the Outcast, may God curse him in spite of his supporters, since it began in the year 60 AH. God answered the supplication of Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, and he died a year before it.

Al-Qastallani also said: "If it were so, Abu Hurayra would not have been able to conceal it, given what al-Bukhari transmitted from him, that he said: 'People say: Abu Hurayra has narrated much hadith. Had it not been for two verses in the Book of God Most High, I would not have narrated a single hadith.' Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾," and so on to the end of what he said. What he recited indicates the condemnation of concealing knowledge, especially the knowledge they call the knowledge of secrets, for many of them claim that it is the essence and fruit of knowledge. Moreover, Abu Hurayra denied disseminating that vessel in general, without specification, so how can it be used as evidence for that? Abu Hurayra, as far as I know, did not reveal what was concealed, so from where is it known that what he knew is this? Whoever claims must provide proof, and beyond that is cutting off necks."

So the argument from this report for the path of those people has what it has. Similar to it is what is related from Zayn al-Abidin (may God be pleased with him). Yes, there is for them another basis, which is explained in its proper place. But it is not granted to anyone, whoever he may be, that what they hold, which is absent from the Book of God the Glorious, or that it is a matter beyond the Shari'ah. Whoever proves this by his own claim has gone far astray. Al-Sha'rani, may his secret be sanctified, said in *al-Ajwiba al-Mardiyya* concerning the jurists and the Sufis: "I heard my master 'Ali al-Marsafi say: 'A man does not become perfect in the station of gnosis (*ma'rifa*) and knowledge until he sees the Reality (*haqiqa*) confirming the Shari'ah, and that Sufism is not something added to the Prophetic Sunnah, but is its very essence.'"

And I heard my master 'Ali al-Khawwas say many times: "Whoever thinks that the Reality opposes the Shari'ah, or the reverse, has erred, for among the realized scholars there is no Shari'ah that ever opposes a Reality. They even said: 'A Shari'ah without a Reality is idle, and a Reality without a Shari'ah is void,' contrary to what the deficient among the jurists and the poor (*fuqara'*) hold." Whoever claims a contradiction between Reality and Shari'ah may rely on the story of al-Khidr with Musa, peace be upon them both. Its verification will come, God willing, in a manner by which the opponent cannot open his lips.

From what we quoted from al-Qastallani concerning the report of Abu Juhayfa, the answer becomes known to the objection raised against the Sufis: that what they have, if it agrees with the Book and the Sunnah, then both are in our hands; and if it opposes them, it is a rejection of them, and after the truth there is only error.

The answer, by choosing the first part, is that the Book and the Sunnah being in our hands does not require that nothing further can be derived from them, nor does it entail that what is in them is confined to what scholars knew before. It is possible that God gives some of His special servants an understanding through which they grasp from them what no exegete or jurist among the mujtahids in religion has reached. How much the first has left for the last! Since the four Imams, for example, were granted their ijtihad and their derivation from the verses and hadiths, even though some of them differed from others, what prevents granting to these people what has been opened to them of the meanings of the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ)? Even if it differs from what some Imams held, provided it does not oppose what the explicit consensus (*ijma'*) of the infallible Community has established? I consider the distinction between the two groups, while each one's acceptance and rejection are established, to be a purely arbitrary judgment, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

The Shi'a claimed that what is meant by "what has been sent down to you" is the caliphate of Ali, may God honor his face. They relate with their chains from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with both of them, that "God Most High revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should appoint Ali, may God honor his face, as successor. He feared that this would be hard on a group of his companions, so God Most High sent down this verse as an encouragement to him, peace be upon him, regarding what he had been commanded to convey."

[p. 193]

And from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Ali, may God honor his face, when God, glory be to Him, commanded him to inform the people of his guardianship (*wilaya*). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) feared that they would say: 'He favored his cousin,' and that they would object to it. So God revealed this verse to him, and he stood up for his guardianship on the day of Ghadir Khumm, took his hand, and said, peace be upon him: 'Whoever I am his master (*mawla*), Ali is his master. O God, befriend whoever befriends him and oppose whoever opposes him.'"

Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, transmitted from Abu Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir, all transmitting from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "This verse was revealed upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Ghadir Khumm concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We used to recite in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, [that] Ali is the guardian of the believers. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message.'"

The report of Ghadir is the cornerstone of their proofs for the caliphate of the Commander (*al-Amir*), may God honor his face. They have added to it, to complete their aim, objectionable additions, inserted into it fabricated words, composed poems on it, and attacked the Companions, may God be pleased with them, claiming that they opposed the explicit text of the Chosen Prophet (ﷺ). Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Himyari, may God treat him with His justice, said in a long qasida:

I marvel at a people who came to Ahmad
with a plan that has no place.
They said to him: "If you wished, you would inform us
who is the final refuge and the place of recourse,
When you die and part from us,
while among them are those who covet rule."
He said: "If I informed you of a refuge,
you would perhaps act with it
as the people of the Calf acted when they abandoned
Harun, so leaving him is more scrupulous."
Then after him came a resolve
from his Lord that has no repelling.
"Convey! Otherwise you would not be a conveyor,
and God protects you from them."
Then the Prophet stood up, the one who
was, by what He commanded him, proclaiming openly,
Delivering a sermon commanded, and in his hand
the hand of Ali, whose light shines.
Lifting it high—how honored is the hand of the one
who raises and the hand that is raised!
"Whoever I am his master, this one is his master."
They were not pleased, nor were they content with him.
A people was enraged by his words,
as if their noses were being cut off.
Until, when they buried him in his grave,
and turned away from his religion, they lost it.
They forgot what he said the day before and what he enjoined,
and bought harm in exchange for what benefits.
They severed their kinship after him,
so they will be repaid for what they severed.
They resolved on treachery against their master.
Perdition to what they resolved upon!
Neither will they come to his Pool
tomorrow, nor will he intercede for them.

And so on to the end of what he said. May God forgive his slip and pardon him. You know that the reports of Ghadir that contain the command to appoint a successor are not authentic according to the People of the Sunnah, nor are they accepted by them at all. We will explain what occurred there with the fullest explanation, and clarify the weak from it and the strong. Then we return to the Shi'a's argument, refuting it. From God, glory be to Him, is the seeking of aid, and upon Him is reliance.

[p. 194]

We say: The Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon in a place between Mecca and Medina, on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage, near al-Juhfa, called Ghadir Khumm. In it he explained the virtue of Ali, may God honor his face, and the vindication of his honor from what some who were with him in the land of Yemen had spoken of, because of what had come from his justice, which some thought was oppression, narrowness, and stinginess. The truth was with Ali, may God honor his face, in that matter. This was on Sunday, the eighteenth of Dhu al-Hijja, under a tree there.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 3 of 5):

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yahya ibn Abdullah, from Yazid ibn Talha, who said: "When Ali, may Allah honour his face, was coming from Yemen to meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Makkah, he hastened ahead to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and appointed over the troops who were with him a man from among his companions. That man set about dressing every man in a ḥulla (a suit of clothing) from the bazz (striped cloth) that was with Ali, may Allah honour his face. When his army drew near, he went out to meet them and saw that they were wearing the ḥulla. He said: 'Woe to you! What is this?' He replied: 'I clothed the people so that they might look splendid with it when they enter among the people.' He said: 'Woe to you! Take it off before we reach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So he took the ḥulla off the people, returned it to the bazz, and the army expressed their complaint about what he had done to them."

And he (al-Tabari) also transmitted from Zaynab bint Ka'b, who was the wife of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The people complained about Ali, may Allah honour his face. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us delivering a sermon, and I heard him say: 'O people, do not complain about Ali, for by Allah, he is indeed too harsh (akhshan) in the cause of Allah, or in the path of Allah.'" Imam Ahmad also narrated it.

He also narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "From Buraydah al-Aslami, who said: 'I campaigned with Ali in Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness (jafwa). When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali, may Allah honour his face, and I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change. He said: "Buraydah! Am I not closer (awlā) to the believers than their own selves?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Whoever I am his mawla (master/patron), then Ali is his mawla."'" Al-Nasa'i likewise narrated it with a good, strong chain whose narrators are all trustworthy (thiqat). It is also narrated by another chain, which is unique to it.

Al-Dhahabi said: "It is authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: 'When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the Farewell Pilgrimage and alighted at Ghadir Khumm, he ordered that the large trees be cleared away. Then he said: "It seems as though I have been called and I have answered. Indeed, I have left among you the two weighty things (al-thaqalayn): the Book of Allah and my family (ʿitrah), the people of my household. So see how you will deal with me regarding them, for they will not separate until they come to me at the Basin (al-Ḥawḍ). Allah is my mawla, and I am the wali of every believer." Then he took the hand of Ali, may Allah honour his face, and said: "Whoever I am his mawla, then this one is his wali. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him."' There was no one among the large trees except that he saw him with his own eyes and heard him with his own ears."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ali ibn Zayd, Abu Harun al-Abdi, and Musa ibn Uthman, from al-Bara', who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the Farewell Pilgrimage. When we came to Ghadir Khumm, a place was swept for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) beneath two trees, and it was proclaimed among the people: 'Al-salat jami'ah' (prayer is gathering). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Ali, may Allah honour his face, took his hand, and made him stand on his right side. He said: 'Am I not closer to every person than his own self?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Indeed, this one is the mawla of whoever I am his mawla. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him.' Then Umar ibn al-Khattab met him and said, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Congratulations to you! You have become the mawla of every believing man and woman, morning and evening.'" This report is weak (ḍaʿīf), for they (the scholars) have stated explicitly that Ali ibn Zayd, Abu Harun, and Musa are weak narrators, whose reports are not relied upon. Also in the chain is Abu Ishaq, who was a Shi'i whose narrations are rejected.

Ḍimra narrated with his chain from Abu Hurayra, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the hand of Ali, may Allah honour his face, he said: 'Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾." Then Abu Hurayra said:

[p. 195]

"That was the day of Ghadir Khumm. Whoever fasts on the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, Allah will record for him the fasting of sixty months." This is an extremely rejected (munkar) report, and al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya explicitly states that it is fabricated (mawdu').

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir al-Tabari took special care with the hadith of Ghadir. He compiled on it two volumes in which he included all its chains and wordings, and he brought together the weak and the strong, the sound and the unsound, in accordance with the habit of many hadith scholars, who report whatever reached them on the subject without distinguishing between sound and weak. Likewise, the great hafiz Abu al-Qasim ibn Asakir reported many hadiths in this sermon, but what is relied upon in it is what we have indicated and similar material that does not contain the report of the succession (istikhlaf), as the Shi'a claim.

It is narrated from al-Dhahabi that: "Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla" is mutawatir (narrated by so many chains that its transmission is certain), and it is certain that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it. As for "O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him," it is an addition with a strong chain. As for "fasting the eighteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah," it is not sound. And by Allah, that verse was not revealed except on the Day of Arafah, a few days before Ghadir Khumm.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate the report of Ghadir in their Sahihs because they did not find it fulfilling their conditions. The Shi'a claim that this is due to deficiency and partisanship in them, but may they be far from that.

The Shi'a's argument from the report "Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla" is that mawla means "the one more entitled to disposal" (al-awla bi-al-tasarruf), and priority in disposal is identical with the imamate. It is not hidden that the first error in this argument is their making mawla mean awla, which the grammarians (ahl al-ʿArabiyyah) all deny. Indeed they said: "The pattern maf'al has never come with the meaning of af'al at all." Only Abu Zayd the lexicographer permitted it, relying on the statement of Abu Ubayda in explaining the verse ﴿It is your mawla﴾, meaning "more worthy of you."

It is replied: this implies the validity of "so-and-so is a mawla of so-and-so," just as "so-and-so is awla than so-and-so" is valid, and the implication is false by consensus (ijma'), so what implies it is likewise false. Abu Ubayda's explanation is a clarification of the resulting meaning, i.e., "the Fire is your abode and your destination, the place fitting for you," and it is not explicit proof that the word mawla there means awla.

Second: even if we concede that mawla means awla, it does not follow that its connection is disposal. It may be that the intended meaning is "more worthy of love," "more worthy of honour," and the like. The word awla has come in many speeches where the sense of disposal cannot be applied, such as the verse ﴿Indeed the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who believe﴾.

Moreover, we have two indications that the intended meaning of wilaya (from the word mawla or awla) is love:

The first is what we have related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq concerning the complaint of those who were with the Commander, may Allah honour his face, in Yemen, such as Buraydah al-Aslami, Khalid ibn al-Walid, and others. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not forbid the complainants specifically, in order to exaggerate in seeking his friendship and to be gentle in calling to it, as is generally his way in such matters. For this gentle approach he (ﷺ) opened the sermon with the words: "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?"

The second is his statement, upon him be prayers and peace, according to some narrations: "O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him." For if the intended meaning of mawla were "one who disposes of affairs" or "one more entitled to disposal," he would have said: "O Allah, befriend whoever is under his disposal and be an enemy to whoever is not." Since he (ﷺ) mentioned love and enmity, he indicated that the purpose is the obligation of loving him, may Allah honour his face, and warning against enmity and hatred towards him, not disposal or its absence. Had the intended meaning been the caliphate, he (ﷺ) would have stated it explicitly.

What supports this is the report narrated by Abu Nu'aym from al-Hasan al-Muthanna ibn al-Hasan al-Sibt, may Allah be pleased with them both, that people asked him whether this report was an explicit text on the caliphate of the Commander, may Allah honour his face. He said: "If the Prophet (ﷺ) had intended his caliphate, he would have said: 'O people, this is the guardian of my affair and the one who will govern you after me, so listen to him and obey.'" Then al-Hasan said: "I swear by Allah, the Exalted, that if Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) had preferred Ali for this matter, and Ali had not advanced himself, he would have been the greatest of people in error."

Also, it may be argued that the intended meaning of wilaya is love, since the word "after me" (ba'di) was not used in it, and it is apparent that the two wilayas (of love and of disposal) would then be combined at one time. Such combination cannot be conceived if the intended meaning were priority in disposal, unlike when the intended meaning is love.

The Shi'a also relied, to establish that the intended meaning of mawla is "more entitled to disposal," on the wording found at the beginning of the report in one of its versions, namely his statement (ﷺ): "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?" We say: the intended meaning of this too is "more worthy of love." That is: "Am I not more beloved to the believers than their own selves?" Indeed, it may be said that awla here is derived from wilaya in the sense of love, and the meaning is: "Am I not more beloved to the believers than themselves?" So that the parts of the speech harmonize, the arrangement is good, and the overall meaning is this: "O assembly of believers, you love me more than your own selves, so whoever loves me should love Ali. O Allah, love whoever loves him and be an enemy to whoever is an enemy to him."

It is indicated that the intended meaning of awla in that sentence is not "more entitled to disposal," because it is derived from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and those of relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾. This verse is directed at negating the lineage of adopted sons from those who adopt them. Its explanation: it is not proper to say that Zayd ibn Harithah is the son of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Prophet's (ﷺ) relation to all believers is like that of a compassionate father, and more so. His wives are their mothers, and relatives by blood are more entitled and closer than others, even if compassion and reverence for strangers are greater. But the basis of lineage is kinship, and it is absent in adopted sons, not compassion and reverence. This is what is in the Book of Allah, i.e., in His ruling. The notion of priority in disposal has no bearing on the intended matter at all. So the meaning intended in our case is the meaning intended in the source from which it was taken. Even if we suppose that awla in the opening of the report means "more entitled to disposal," it is possible that this was to alert the addressees with that address, so that they would turn fully to listen to his speech (ﷺ) and attend to it with utmost care, and so that what it contains of guidance would be established most firmly. This is like a man saying to his sons in a context of admonition and advice: "Am I not your father?" And when they acknowledge this, he commands them with what he intends from them, so that they accept the authority of fatherhood and prophethood and act in accordance with both.

Accordingly, his statement, upon him be prayers and peace, in this context: "Am I not closer to the believers than their own selves?" is like: "Am I not the Messenger of Allah to you?" or "Am I not your Prophet?" It is not possible to apply the same to what follows it, in order to preserve the coherence of the context.

[p. 197]

Among the Shi'ah (the partisans of Ali) is one who offered an argument against the meaning of love (*maḥabba*). It runs as follows: the love of al-Amīr (Ali) — may Allah honour his face — is already established within the verse ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾. So if this hadith also conveyed that same meaning, it would be superfluous (*laghw*). Its corruption is not hidden. The source of this error is that the one who makes the argument did not understand that obligating the love of someone within a general statement is one thing, and obligating his love specifically is another. The difference between them is as clear as the sun. What makes this even more evident is that if a person believed in all of Allah's prophets and messengers — peace be upon them — but did not mention our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically, his faith would not be considered valid. Furthermore, even if we assume that the content of the verse and the report is the same, it does not follow that there is superfluity. At most, it entails confirmation and emphasis, and that is the role of the Prophet (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) often confirmed and reaffirmed the contents of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an itself repeats its contents for this very reason. No one has said that this is superfluous — Allah forbid. Also, the explicit designation of the succession (*imāma*) of al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — has been repeated many times in Shi'ite sources, so if that is authentic, then it would entail superfluous speech, and the speech of the Lawgiver (Allah) is far above that.

Then, what al-Himyarī indicated in his poem, in which he went to excess, namely that the Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in this collective manner and requested from him the appointment of an imam after him, is something the historians and biographers from both groups have not mentioned, as far as I know. Rather, it is pure falsehood and slander. We seek refuge in Allah from it.

Whoever has read that abominable poem in its entirety, and what the Shi'ah narrate in it, and has even a little knowledge, will see a marvel, and will realise that the clanging of these people is like the creaking of a door or the buzzing of a fly.

Furthermore, the reports coming through the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) indicating that this verse was revealed concerning Ali — may Allah honour his face — even if they are authentic and reach the level at which they can be used as evidence, contain no more than an indication of his excellence, may Allah honour his face, and that he is the friend (*walī*) of the believers in the sense we have established. We do not deny this, and whoever denies it is cursed. Likewise, what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud — may Allah be pleased with him — contains nothing more than this. And the explicit mention of him — may Allah honour his face — by name is for the reason we have already presented.

Some of our companions said, by way of concession: the verse refers to the report of Ibn Mas'ud, and likewise the report of Ghadir (Ghadir Khumm) according to the well-known narration. Granting that both indicate that what is meant is that he is the one with the greater right to disposal (*awlā bi-l-taṣarruf*), they must both be restricted by what indicates this in the final outcome. In that case, welcome to agreement, because the People of the Sunnah also say this at the time of his imamate. The reason for specifically mentioning al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — at that time is what the Prophet (ﷺ) knew through revelation about the occurrence of corruption and rebellion during his caliphate, and the denial of his rightful imamate by some people. That this would happen right after death without any interval is something for which there is no proof.

The report introduced by "It is as if I have been called and I have answered" is not explicit regarding the intended meaning, as is not hidden. And among the things that weaken the claim of the Shi'ah that the verse was revealed specifically concerning the caliphate of Ali — may Allah honour his face — and that the relative pronoun in it is specific, is the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. For although "the people" here is general, what is meant by them is the disbelievers. And [the verse continues]: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. This is in the position of a reason for His protecting the Prophet (ﷺ), and it contains the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun. That is: because Allah does not guide them to their wish concerning you. And when the intended meaning of "them" is the disbelievers, how can this be after the intention of the caliphate?! Indeed, if it were said that it is not valid, it would not be far-fetched. This is because the fear that the Shi'ah attribute to the Prophet (ﷺ) — and he is far above that — regarding conveying the matter of the caliphate actually came from the Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — since among them, Allah forbid, there were those who coveted it for themselves. And when such a person sees himself deprived of it, it is not far-fetched that he would intend to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And committing oneself to the statement — we seek refuge in Allah the Mighty and Majestic — that those who hinted at attributing coveting of the caliphate to him are disbelievers entails comprehensive dangers. The least of them is declaring al-Amīr — may Allah honour his face — a sinner, and he is who he is; or attributing cowardice to him, while he is the victorious lion of Allah; or ruling that he practised taqiyya (dissimulation), while he is the one who fears no blame in the cause of Allah and fears none but Allah, glorified is He; or attributing the act of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and rather the divine command, to futility. All of this, as you see, is unacceptable.

It may be said: we have two matters which indicate that what is meant by the relative pronoun is the caliphate:

The first is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded with the most eloquent expression to convey the legal rulings that he was commanded to convey, as He, glorified is He, said addressing him — peace be upon him: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾. So if the intended meaning here were not a single item that is the most important of the items and the greatest in standing — and that is none other than the caliphate, since through it the affair of religion and the world is ordered — the speech would be devoid of benefit.

The second is that Ibn Ishaq mentioned in his biography that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed the people during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Ḥijjat al-Wadā') with the sermon in which he made clear what he made clear. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, listen to my words, for I do not know, perhaps I will not meet you after this year at this place ever. O people, your blood and your wealth are forbidden to you until you meet your Lord, as the sanctity of this day of yours, and as the sanctity of this month of yours. You will meet your Lord, and He will ask you about your deeds, and I have conveyed." Then he (ﷺ) enjoined [kindness] to the women. Then he (ﷺ) said: "Understand my words, for I have conveyed. I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ)." Until he said, with my father and mother as his ransom, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O Allah, have I conveyed?" Ibn Ishaq said: It was mentioned to me that the people said: "O Allah, yes." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, bear witness." End of quote.

This report is clear that the sermon was on the Day of Arafat, the Greatest Day of Hajj, as in the narration of Yahya ibn 'Abbad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. And the day of Ghadir was the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, after the Prophet (ﷺ) had finished and completed the matters of the rites and turned towards Medina the Illuminated. In that case, what he was commanded to convey would be a different matter from what he had conveyed before (ﷺ), and he made the people witness his conveying it, and he made Allah witness this. And this is none other than the Great Caliphate and the Supreme Imamate. So it is as if He, glorified is He, were saying: "O Messenger, convey that Ali — may Allah honour his face — is your successor and your deputy after you. And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message." And even if the people said to you when you said, "O Allah, have I conveyed?": "O Allah, yes."

Because we say: the conditional statement in the first matter, after closing our eyes to what is in it, is disputed, since it is possible that what is meant by the relative pronoun in the two verses is the legal rulings related to the welfare of the servants in their livelihood and their return. Nor does it follow that there is no benefit, for how many verses have been repeated in the Qur'an, and commands and prohibitions mentioned many times for emphasis and confirmation. Moreover, some have mentioned that the benefit of the command here is to remove the suspicion that the Prophet (ﷺ) had left, or would leave, conveying some part of revelation out of taqiyya.

Against the second matter, two objections arise:

The first is that the fact that the day of Ghadir came after the day of Arafat is accepted. But we do not accept that the verse was revealed on it, so that what he was commanded to convey would be a different matter. Rather, what the content of the sermon and the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it require, "O Allah, have I conveyed?", is that the verse was revealed before the two days of Ghadir and Arafat. And what has been transmitted in other reports that the chapter of al-Mā'idah was revealed between Mecca and Medina during the Farewell Pilgrimage is not suitable as evidence for either being after or before, since there is no mention in it of the return or the going. The apparent state of the Prophet (ﷺ) during that pilgrimage, in showing the rites, and in abolishing usury and the blood-vengeance of the Jahiliyyah, and other matters too long to mention — which the biographers have recorded — indicates that the revelation was during the going.

The second is that even if we grant that the revelation was on the day of Ghadir, we do not accept that what he was commanded to convey is a different matter.
