What necessarily follows in that case is repetition, and you have already learned its benefit and how frequently it occurs. And even if we grant that what he was commanded to convey is a different matter, we do not accept that it is none other than the caliphate. How many other verses did the Prophet (ﷺ) convey after that, from what was revealed to him — peace be upon him. And what is understood from some reports is that this verse was before the Farewell Pilgrimage. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diyā' in al-Mukhtārah transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: Which verse that was sent down from the heaven was the hardest on you? He said: I was at Mina during the days of the season, and the polytheists of the Arabs and the scattered people gathered at the season. Then Gabriel — peace be upon him — came down to me and said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord, and if you do not do it, then you have not conveyed His message﴾, the verse. He said: So I stood at the Aqaba and called out: O people, who will support me so that I may convey the messages of my Lord, and for you is Paradise? O people, say: There is no god but Allah, and I am the Messenger of Allah to you; you will prosper and succeed, and for you is Paradise." He (ﷺ) said: "No man, woman, slave girl, or child remained but that they threw dust and stones at me, saying: 'Liar, apostate!' Then an apparition appeared to me and said: 'O Muhammad, if you are the Messenger of Allah, then it is time for you to curse them as Noah cursed his people with destruction.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know; and help me against them, so that they answer my call to Your obedience.' Then his uncle al-'Abbas came and rescued him from them and drove them away from him."

Al-A'mash said: "For this, the Banu al-'Abbas take pride and say: 'Concerning them was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾.' The Prophet (ﷺ) loved Abu Talib, and Allah willed for 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib."

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verses 67–68 (part 5 of 5):

Clearer than this is what Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym in (al-Dala'il), Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was guarded, and his uncle Abu Talib used to send with him every day men from Banu Hashim to guard him, until there was revealed ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. His uncle then wished to send with him someone to guard him, but he said: 'O uncle, indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has protected me.'" Abu Talib died before the Hijra, and the Farewell Pilgrimage was many years after it, and the apparent reading is that the verse is connected (to the context).

It is also reported from some of them that the verse was revealed at night, based on what 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was guarded until there was revealed ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. He then put his head out of the dome and said: 'O people, disperse, for Allah the Exalted has protected me.'" It is not hidden that this is not explicit regarding the intended meaning.

What I incline to, in reconciling the reports, is that this verse was revealed more than once, and Allah the Exalted knows best. The intended meaning of protection from the people is the preservation of his blessed soul (upon him be prayers and peace) from killing and destruction. Therefore it is not objected that his noble face was wounded and his front tooth was broken at the Battle of Uhud.

Some held the general view, claiming that the verses were revealed only after Uhud. Both points are challenged by the fact that the Jews poisoned him, peace be upon him, to the extent that he said: "The morsel of Khaybar continues to trouble me, and now is the time when it has severed my aorta." It is answered that He, glorified and exalted, guaranteed him protection from being killed or the like by reason of conveying the revelation, while what was done to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and to the prophets, peace be upon them, was for defending wealth, lands and lives. Its remoteness is not hidden.

Al-Raghib said: The infallibility (ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, is their being preserved by what they were singled out with of purity of substance (safa' al-jawhar), then by the noble character and virtues bestowed upon them, then by victory and the firming of their feet, then by the sending down of tranquility upon them, and by the guarding of their hearts, and by success (tawfiq).

It was also said: the intended meaning of infallibility is protection from committing sin, and the meaning is: "Convey, and Allah will grant you protection from committing sin among the people," that is, He will protect you by means of that from them. It is not hidden that this interpretation is one that could only come from someone whom Allah the Exalted has not preserved from error.

Similar to this is what was reported from 'Ali ibn 'Isa regarding His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, where he said: He does not guide them by assistance, success and kindnesses toward disbelief, but rather He guides them to faith. He claimed that what prompted him to this interpretation is that Allah the Exalted guided the disbelievers to faith by showing them it, encouraging them to it, and warning them against opposing it. And you have known the intended meaning of the verse. Moreover, in his statement there is what is not hidden of disputability.

Al-Jubba'i said: the intended meaning is: He does not guide them to Paradise and reward. In this there is heedlessness of the fact that the clause is in the position of causal explanation.

Some claimed that the intended meaning is: upon you is only the conveying, not the guidance; whoever I have decreed to disbelief and to die upon it will never be guided. This is as you see. So let all that we have mentioned regarding this verse be understood and memorized, for I do not think you will find it in a book.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (risalatihi) in the plural form. The placement of the verse among the verses addressing the People of the Book is because all of them are harsh warnings that the disbelievers dislike hearing, and it is difficult for the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to address them with them, especially what follows them of the text lamenting upon them their utter misguidance. For this reason the command is repeated, and He, glorified be He, said:

﴿Say: O People of the Book﴾. By them is meant the Jews and Christians, as some exegetes said. Others said that by them is meant only the Jews. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Rafi' ibn Haritha, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf and Rafi' ibn Huraymila came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion and creed of Abraham, and that you believe in what we have of the Torah, and that you testify that it is truth from Allah the Exalted?' The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Yes, but you have innovated and denied what is in it of the covenant taken from you, and you concealed from it what you were commanded to make clear to the people, so I am free of your innovations.' They said: 'Then we hold to what is in our hands, for we are upon guidance and truth, and we do not believe in you nor follow you.'" So Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you are not upon anything﴾, that is, a religion that is considered valid and worthy of being called "something," due to the manifestness of its falsehood and the clarity of its corruption. In this expression there is what is not hidden of contempt; and among their sayings is "less than nothing." ﴿Until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that is, you observe them and preserve what is in them of matters, among which are the proofs of the Messenger of Allah's prophethood and the evidences of his prophecy. For establishing them and fulfilling their rights is only by that, not by acting upon everything in them, whether abrogated or otherwise, for observing the abrogated is nullifying them and rejecting their testimony.

﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, that is, the glorious Qur'an, and establishing it is by believing in it. The establishing of the two Books was mentioned before the establishing of it, although it is the principal intended matter, out of regard for the right of testimony and to bring them down from the rank of opposition. It was also said: the intended meaning of the relative clause is the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel, peace be upon them. It was said: the divine books, for they all affirm the obligation of believing in one who claims prophethood and displays a miracle, and the obligation of obeying the one sent to them. The full discussion of this noble structure has already passed, as has that of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And surely much of them will increase in transgression and disbelief by what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. The clause is resumptive, as Shaykh al-Islam said, explaining the severity of their obstinacy, their excess in arrogance and enmity, and that conveying the message benefits them nothing. Its opening with an oath is to emphasize and affirm its content. And the attribution of sending down to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, along with its attribution to them earlier, is to indicate their detachment from that attribution. And if by the relative clause is meant the blessings given to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, the matter of attribution is quite evident.

﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, that is: do not be sorrowful or grieved over their increase in transgression and disbelief, for the harm of that is connected to them and its consequence returns to them, and in the believers there is sufficiency for you regarding them. The placement of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to record upon them their firm rootedness in disbelief. It was said: the intended meaning is: do not grieve over their destruction and punishment; and placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to draw attention to the cause that necessitates the absence of grief, and it is not free from

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 69 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to encourage faith and righteous deeds.

The disagreement concerning the intended meaning of "those who believed" has already been mentioned in the verse of al-Baqarah. It is related from al-Thawri that they are those who believed with their tongues, namely the hypocrites, and this is what al-Zajjaj chose. The judge (al-Qadi) chose that what is meant by them are those who adhere to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), whether sincere or hypocritical. It has also been said otherwise.

﴿And those who were Jews﴾, that is, those who entered Judaism. ﴿And the Sabians﴾, who are, as Hasan Jalabi and others said, a people who departed from the religions of the Jews and the Christians and worshipped the angels. The discussion of this has already passed.

In Husn al-Muhadara fi Akhbar Misr wa al-Qahira by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, there is the following statement: The imams of history have mentioned that Adam (peace be upon him) bequeathed to his son Shith, in whom and in whose descendants were prophethood and religion, and there was sent down to him twenty-nine scrolls. He came to Egypt, which was called Bayluna, and he and the sons of his brother settled there. Shith dwelt above the mountain, and the sons of Qabil dwelt at the bottom of the valley. Shith appointed as successor his son Anush; Anush appointed as successor his son Qawnan; Qawnan appointed as successor his son Mahla'il;
صفحة 201
and Mahla'il appointed as successor his son Yard, and handed the bequest to him, taught him all the sciences, informed him of what would happen in the world, looked into the stars, and into the Book that was sent down to Adam (peace be upon him). To Yard was born Ukhnukh, who is Idris (peace be upon him), and he is called Hurmus. The king at that time was Mahwil son of Ukhnukh son of Qabil. Idris (peace be upon him) received prophethood at the age of forty, and the king intended him harm, but God Most High protected him. There was sent down to him thirty scrolls, and his father handed him the bequest of his grandfather and the sciences that he had. He had been born in Egypt, and he left it, traveled the whole earth, and returned. He called the creation to God Most High, and they responded to him until his community covered the earth. His community was the Sabians, which is the affirmation of the oneness of God Most High, purity, fasting, and other rites of worship. During his journey to the East, all its kings obeyed him, and he built one hundred and forty cities, the smallest of which was al-Ruha. Then he returned to Egypt, its king obeyed him, and believed in him, to the end of what he said, transmitted from al-Tifashi. From this one understands an opinion concerning the Sabians other than the previously mentioned opinions.

In Shadharat al-Dhahab by Abd al-Hayy ibn Ahmad ibn al-Imad al-Hanbali, in the biography of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi, the text reads: "Al-Sabi, with a hamza at its end, is said to be a relative noun (nisba) to Sabi ibn Mattushalakh ibn Idris (peace be upon him), who was upon the first hanifiyya. It is also said: Sabi ibn Mawi, who lived in the time of Khalil (peace be upon him). It is also said: among the Arabs, the Sabi is one who departs from the religion of his people." End of quotation.

"Al-Nasara" is the plural of "Nasran," and its derivation has already passed. "Al-Sabiun" is put in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, because the predicate of "inna" indicates it. The intention in it is delay (ta'khir) from what is in the predicate of "inna." The estimate is: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, their ruling is such and such, and the Sabians likewise," based on the view that the omitted element in "inna Zaydan wa 'Amrun qa'im" is the predicate of the second, not the first, as is the view of some grammarians. This is supported by the verse of Sabi ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi:

Whoever has his camp in Medina, indeed I and Qayyar there are strangers.

For his saying "la-gharib" is the predicate of "inna," and therefore the lam entered upon it, since it enters upon the predicate of "inna" and not upon the predicate of the subject except rarely. It has also been said that "gharib" here is a predicate for both nouns together, since the form fa'il is used for the singular and other than it, like: "and the angels after that are a helper" (Qur'an 66:4). Al-Khalkhali rejected this, saying it does not come for the dual, although it comes for the plural. Ibn Hisham answered him that they said regarding the verse "on the right and on the left, a sitter" (Qur'an 50:17) that the intended meaning is two sitters, and this indicates its use for the dual as well. The correct position is to prohibit this aspect, because it entails two governing elements acting upon one governed element, and such a thing is not valid according to the most correct view, in contrast to the Kufans. Bishr ibn Abi Hazim says:

When the forelocks of the family of Badr are cut, then pay their ransom, and the captives in bondage,
And otherwise know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in dissension.

For his saying "bughat ma baqina" is the predicate of "inna." Had it been the predicate of "antum," he would have said "ma baqitum." "Bughat" is a plural in the sense of "seekers," and it has been said that it is the plural of "baghin," from transgression and aggression. "Antum bughat" is a parenthetical clause, because he would not say of his own people that they are transgressors. "Ma baqina fi shiqaq" is the predicate of "inna." In that case the verse is not suitable as evidence for what was mentioned. The clause has been placed here between "inna" and its predicate, with the consideration of intended delay, so that the speech is free from separating the subject and the predicate, and so that it is known that the predicate indicates—as has been said—that the Sabians, despite the manifest error and deviation from all religions, whose repentance is accepted if faith and righteous deeds are genuinely found in them, then others are more deserving of this.
صفحة 202
Therefore it has been said that the clause is like a parenthetical insertion, by which it indicates what has been mentioned. It was not made a parenthesis in the strict sense because it is conjoined to the clause "inna alladhina" and its predicate. Ibn Hisham's objection was raised against this: that it involves placing a conjoined clause before part of the clause it is conjoined to, and a conjoined element precedes its conjunct only in poetry. So likewise it should not be placed before part of the conjunct; rather, this is more deserving of prohibition. As for his answer that the waw is the waw of resumption, which enters upon parenthetical clauses, as in His saying: "And if you do not, and you will never do, then guard against the Fire" (Qur'an 2:24), and this clause is parenthetical, not conjoined, it does not hold in our matter, because it loses the nuance of delay that was pointed out, for if it is parenthetical it cannot be a delayed element. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) directed the aforementioned predicate to His saying "and the Sabians," and made the predicate of "inna" omitted, which is the other view of the grammarians regarding such a construction, and it also accords with usage, as in the verse:

We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, and opinions differ.

For his saying "radin" is the predicate of "anta," and the predicate of "nahnu" is omitted. It was preferred because attaching to the nearer is nearer, and because it is free from what follows from the first explanation. Yes, the most that can be objected to it is that the more common is omission from the second because the first indicates it, and the reverse is rare but permissible. It has been countered that the discussion in our matter is directed to the explanation of the People of the Book, so directing the predicate to them is more appropriate. Also, in directing the predicate to the second, there is a separation of the Christians from the Jews and a distinction among the People of the Book, because then it becomes a conjunction upon His saying "and the Sabians" definitively. Yes, if it were correct that the hypocrites and the Jews are the most extreme among those counted in error, and the Sabians and the Christians are more lenient, then their conjunction would be good, and what is mentioned would be made a predicate for both, and the omission of the word of confirmation mentioned in the first two would be evidence for this meaning. It has also been said that "al-Sabiun" is a conjunction upon the place (mahall) of "inna" and its subject. Some permitted this absolutely, some prohibited it absolutely, and others made distinctions, saying: it is impossible before the predicate is completed, and permissible after it.

Al-Farra' held that if the case ending of the noun is hidden, it is permissible, because the verbal disliked feature is removed, as in: "Indeed you and Zayd are going." Otherwise it is prohibited. The preventing factor according to the majority is that it entails two governing elements, "inna" and the beginning (ibtida'), or the subject, acting upon one governed element, which is the predicate. For this reason they regarded this view as weak in the verse, and they built upon the school of the Kufans. That the predicate of the conjoined element in it is omitted—in which case there is no entailment of two governing elements—is not valid, because then the clause would be conjoined upon the clause, and that would not be conjunction upon the place at all. As for one who says that the predicate of "inna" is raised by what was raised by it before it entered, the entailment of two governing elements does not arise for him.

It is related from al-Kisa'i that the conjunction is upon the pronoun in "hadu," and al-Zajjaj rejected it on two grounds: that one does not conjoin upon the attached raised pronoun without a separator, and that if it were conjoined upon the subject, the sense would be "and the Sabians became Jews," which implies that they are Jews, and this is not so. Perhaps al-Kisa'i holds the correctness of conjunction without a separator, so the first objection does not apply to him. It has also been said that "inna" here means the affirmative "na'am" (yes), and it has no governing effect then, so what follows it is raised in place by beginning, and the raised element is conjoined upon it. Abu Hayyan judged this weak, because the establishment of "inna" in the sense of "na'am" is disputed among the grammarians. And even if it is established, it requires something preceding it that it would confirm, and it does not come at the beginning of speech. The answer that there is an assumed, distant and weak question is far-fetched. It has also been said that "al-Sabiun" is a conjunction upon the relative clause (silah) by deletion of the antecedent, that is, "those who are the Sabians," and its remoteness is not hidden,
صفحة 203
even if it is counted among the best of the views.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative with a presumed fatha upon the waw, and the conjunction then is clear. It was objected that the dialect of Bal-Harith and others, who made the dual always with the alif, as in "I saw al-Zaydan" and "I passed by al-Zaydan," and parsed it with presumed vowels, is only regarding the dual specifically, and nothing like this is reported from them regarding the plural, contrary to what the expression of Abu al-Baqa' suggests. The matter is one to which analogy (qiyas) does not apply, so one should not derive the Great Qur'an upon it.

Ibn Kathir and Ubayy read "wa-l-Sabi'in," which is the apparent reading, and "wa-l-Sabiyyun" with the hamza changed to ya' contrary to analogy, and "wa-l-Sabun" with its deletion, from sabaa with the hamza changed to alif; so it is like "ramun" from "rama." Abdullah read: "O you who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians."

As for His saying, glorified and exalted: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds":

Either it is in the place of raising, as a beginning whose predicate is His saying, "then there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve," and the fa' is because the beginning includes the meaning of a condition, and the plural of the final pronouns is according to the sense of the relative, just as the singular of what is in its relative clause is according to its wording. The clause is the predicate of "inna," or the predicate of the subject, and in either case the returning pronoun must be estimated, that is: "whoever of them believes."

Or it is in the place of accusative, as a substitute (badal) for the noun of "inna" and what is conjoined to it, or for what is conjoined to it alone, and it is a partial substitute. A pronoun must be present in it, as established in Arabic, so it is also estimated. His saying, exalted: "then there is no fear" and so on, is the predicate, and the fa' is as in His saying, glorified and exalted: "Indeed those who tempted the believing men and believing women, then did not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell" (Qur'an 85:10), and the verse continues. The meaning, as many have said, on the assumption that what is intended by "those who believed" is those who believe with their tongues, namely the hypocrites, is: whoever of these groups newly acquires sincere faith in the origin and the return, in the proper manner, not as the People of the Book claim—for that is far from it—and does righteous deeds as faith requires: "then there is no fear for them" when the unbeliever fears punishment, "nor will they grieve" when the negligent grieve over the squandering of life and the loss of reward. The intention is to explain the negation of the two matters, not the negation of their continuance, as the indication to this has passed more than once.

In the case where those who believe are understood as those adhering to the religion of the Prophet (ﷺ), whether sincere or hypocrites, then "whoever believes" (man amana) refers to whoever among them is characterized by sincere faith in the sense mentioned, absolutely. This applies whether it is by way of steadfastness and continuance, as with the sincere ones, or by way of initiation and beginning, as is the case with the hypocrites and the rest of the groups. There is no combining of the literal and the metaphorical here, as is not hidden, because steadfastness in faith and beginning it are two instances of faith in its general sense. However, in this view the sincere ones are placed alongside the disbelievers, and this involves a diminishing of their honor. It may be said that the purpose of this is to strongly encourage the rest to embrace faith, by showing that their delay in attaining it does not detract from their being exemplars alongside those foremost, distinguished predecessors. The full discussion has already passed in the commentary on the verse of al-Baqarah, so refer back to it.

[Page 204]

﴿Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel.﴾ This is a new statement, brought to explain another of their crimes, which implies that they were far from faith. Some scholars took it as connected to what God opened the surah with, namely His words: ﴿Fulfil the contracts.﴾ But its remoteness is clear.

The covenant (mithaq) taken here means the firm pledge that their prophets took from them to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and follow him in what he commands and forbids. Or it means the pledge to affirm monotheism and all the laws and rulings written for them in the Torah.

﴿And We sent to them messengers﴾ of great number and great standing, who made them aware of this, admonished and reminded them, and informed them of what to do and what to avoid in their religion. ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire﴾, that is, with what their souls did not incline towards from the laws and the burdensome obligations. The expression "what their souls did not desire" is used instead of "what their souls disliked" in order to intensify their condemnation. As Abu Hayyan said, the word "kullama" (every time) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), because it is governed by "ma" (what) as a temporal verbal noun (maṣdariyya ẓarfiyya), and it is not a conditional word (kalimat shart). The jurists and the rationalists nevertheless call it a conditional word. As-Saffaqsi justified this by saying that calling it a conditional word is because it requires an answer, like the non-jussive conditional, so it is like "idha" (when), and there is no problem with that. Its answer, as it is said, is His words: ﴿a group they denied and a group they killed.﴾

It is also said that the answer is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned, and Ibn al-Munir estimated it as "they were arrogant", because this is evident in His words: ﴿Is it, whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, that you were arrogant, so that a group you denied and a group you kill?﴾ etc. Some took the word as governing an object (nasabuhu), because it is more emphatic in rebuking what they did in response to the coming of the messenger who guided them, and more fitting to what is described in the detail as extremely reprehensible, namely killing, as we will indicate, God willing. For arrogance leads to it only through opposition.

As for the other verse, the intention was to make arrogance itself reprehensible, considering it in itself, as the context requires. Some claimed that the use of the particle "fa" (then) in the verse about arrogance indicates that an intermediary is considered, as if it were said: "You were arrogant, so you opposed, so a group..." etc. There is a question about this, and the sentence in that case is a resumption (isti'naf) explaining the answer.

Az-Zamakhshari made this view the definite one, because the discourse is a detailing of the ruling on the individual members of the plural "messengers" mentioned earlier, meaning: every time a messenger from the messengers came to them. What is stated in His words: ﴿a group they denied﴾ etc. requires that the one who came each time was two groups, so there is a contradiction between them. Setting this aside, it is not good in such a context to estimate the object, as in: "If you honour my brother, you honour him", because this implies particularity, which necessitates certainty about the occurrence of the act itself while the object is in dispute, and linking it to a condition implies doubt about the act itself. Also, placing the object first, as some say, requires the particle "fa", either because it makes the verb distant from its agent and so requires a connector, or because by fronting the object it resembles a nominal sentence which needs "fa". It is also said that there is another obstacle: the meaning is that whenever a messenger came to them, one of two things occurred, not both. So if it were the answer, the expected form would be "aw" (or) instead of "wa" (and). Those who made the sentence the answer did not consider these obstacles.

Some of the scholars said:

As for the first, it is because, for the purpose of severity, the killing of one was made like the killing of a group. It is also said that the word "messenger" is meant generically, covering the many, and this is supported by "kullama" (every time), which indicates multiplicity.

As for the second, the rules of Arabic do not require the like of it, and what has been mentioned of these arguments are illusions that are not to be heeded, and the like of them is not found in the books of grammar. From this the rejection of the last point is known.

Our master Shihab al-Din followed up on this, saying: It is strange that one so deeply learned should overlook such a matter. He said in the commentary on at-Tashil: "It is permissible that 'khayran yasubb' (he would pour good) be conjugated..." differing from al-Farra'. Its commentators said: Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i permitted fronting the object of the answer while its jussive ending remains. Al-Kisa'i recited:

"For good there are days, so whoever endures them, and knows their good days, will be rewarded with good."

Its estimate is: "good follows (ya'qub al-khayr)". Al-Farra' prohibited this while the jussive ending remains, and said: rather, the nominative must be used through inversion, or by assuming an omitted "fa". He interpreted the verse as meaning that "good" is a qualifier of "days", as if he had said: "its righteous days."

Ibn Malik chose this position in some of his books. When az-Zamakhshari saw that the obstacle is shared between the conditional with jussive and what is similar to it, he inclined to it, especially since the strength of the meaning requires it. It is the truth. End of quote.

The conditional clause is a qualifier (sifa) of "messenger", and the connecting pronoun is omitted, meaning: a messenger from among them. Most of the grammarians followed this view.

Our master Shaykh al-Islam chose that the conditional clause is a new sentence (isti'naf), coming as an answer to a question arising from the report of taking the covenant and sending the messengers. As if it were said: "What did they do to the messengers?" So it was said: "Every time a messenger from those messengers came to them with what their souls, immersed in error and corruption, do not love of the true laws and sharia, they disobeyed him and opposed him." And he (may God have mercy on him) objected to the view of the majority that it is a qualifier, saying that this does not fit the context, because when a declarative sentence is made a qualifier or a relative clause, its ruling is cancelled, and it becomes a title for the described one and a complement to it. For this reason it is required that its attribution to him be known. Hence they said: qualities before they are known are reports, and reports after they are known are qualities. There is no doubt that what the composition is intended for is to show that they made every messenger who came to them a target for killing and denial, as its being a new sentence in the most eloquent and emphatic way indicates. It does not show that He sent to them messengers described as each being such, which is what making it a qualifier would imply. End of quote.

Shihab (al-Alusi) responded that this is an imagined notion with no benefit. For His words: ﴿Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ etc. are sent to explain their crimes and to blame them for them, as the objector himself acknowledged. This would only imply the point through considering the qualifier, which is the aim of the speech, as with all restrictions. As for it being known, there is no harm in that. If you rebuke someone and say to him: "You did such and such", while he knows what he did, that does not harm the rebuke or reproach, rather it is stronger, as is not hidden from one expert in the styles of speech. So do not turn to such illusions. End of quote.

What he said, "it implies this only by considering the qualifier", contains an evident denial, and likewise, equating our case with your saying to a person you want to rebuke, "You did such and such, while he knows what he did", is obscure. What the fairness of reflection judges, after consideration, is that both options are permissible, and that what Shaykh al-Islam chose is better. So reflect and be fair.

[Page 205]

The use of "yaqtulun" (they kill) instead of "qatalu" (they killed), like "kadhdhabu" (they denied), although the apparent form would be "qatalu", serves to bring the past situation of their forefathers into the present for the sake of marvelling at it. This was not intended in the denial, for the purpose of giving more emphasis to the killing. In this there is also the observance of the rhyme (fawasil). Some explained the use of the present form in it as indicating that this is their constant custom, for they still hover around the killing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Others limited it to the purpose of narrating the situation, on the basis of the pronouns of the third person. The fronting of "fariqan" (a group) in both positions is for emphasis and to arouse the listener's interest in what they did to them, not for restriction.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 71:

﴿And they thought there would be no fitnah﴾ That is, the Children of Israel supposed that no trial or punishment from God Most High would befall them for what they had done, because of their claim—as al-Zajjaj said—that they were the sons of God Most High and His beloved, or because of God Most High's granting them respite, or for something similar. And it is narrated from Muqatil that fitnah was interpreted as hardship and famine. The better view is to take it in its general sense. On both of these interpretations, the intended meaning is not its well-known meaning.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿أن لا تكون﴾ with the nominative (tukuna is then read with raf'), taking ﴿أن﴾ to be the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah, the lightened form of inna). Its original form was annahu la takunu, so the particle was lightened and the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), which is its subject, was deleted. Attaching the verb of supposition (al-husban) to it, though it denotes certainty, is because of treating it as knowledge, owing to the completeness of its strength. The particle ﴿أن﴾ together with what follows it fills the place of both its objects. It has also been said that ﴿حسب﴾ here means ʿalima (knew), and that ﴿أن﴾ is lightened only after something that conveys certainty. It has also been said that the second object is omitted, meaning: "and they supposed the non-occurrence of fitnah to be existent," and this is transmitted from al-Akhfash. And ﴿تكون﴾ is a complete verb (tammah) on every interpretation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فعموا﴾ is coordinated with ﴿حسبوا﴾, and the fa' indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it. That is: they felt secure from God's punishment, so they persisted in all kinds of error and corruption, ﴿and were blind﴾ to the religion after the Messengers had guided them to its landmarks and explained to them its methods, ﴿and deaf﴾ to listening to the truth which they had been given. This refers to the first of the two times the Children of Israel corrupted, when they opposed the rulings of the Torah, committed what is forbidden, and killed Sha'ya, and it has been said Irmiya, peace be upon them both.

﴿Then God turned to them in mercy﴾ when they repented and returned from the corruption they had been in, after they had been in Babylon for a long time, under the domination of Bukhtunassar (Nebuchadnezzar), as captives in the utmost humiliation and abasement. So God, mighty and majestic, sent a great king from the kings of Persia to Bayt al-Maqdis, and he rebuilt it, and he returned those of the Children of Israel who remained in captivity under Bukhtunassar to their homeland, and those of them who had scattered into the regions returned, so they settled, increased in number, and became as good as they had ever been.

It has also been said: when Bahman ibn Asfandiyar the king inherited from his grandfather Kasif, God cast into his heart compassion for them, so he returned them to al-Sham and appointed Daniel, peace be upon him, as their ruler, and they overpowered those who were there from the followers of Bukhtunassar. The prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, then arose among them, and they returned to the best state they had been in. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave you back the return of victory over them﴾. He, glory be to Him, did not attribute the repentance to them as He did with their other states—supposing, blindness and deafness—out of reluctance to explicitly ascribe good to them; it was only alluded to within the statement of God Most High's turning to them in mercy, as a preparation for explaining their breaking of it by His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿Then they became blind and deaf﴾. This refers to the last of the two times of their corruption, which is their audacity in killing Zakariya and Yahya, and their intent to kill ʿIsa, peace be upon them all. Al-Zamakhshari made the blindness and deafness in the first instance a reference to their worship of the calf, and in the second a reference to their demand to see God. In this there is the objection that the worship of the calf, though a great sin arising from complete blindness and deafness, occurred in the time of Musa, peace be upon him, and has no connection with what is related of them regarding what they did to the Messengers who came after him, peace be upon him, by ages. Likewise the claim—according to his view—about the demand to see God: the demand to see was from the people who were with Musa, peace be upon him, when he set out for the secret conversation, while the worship of the calf was from the people who stayed behind, so his being later than it is not established. And taking ﴿thumma﴾ to mean a delay in rank rather than in time is something for which there is no necessity.

It has also been said: the blindness and deafness in the first instance refer to what occurred in the time of Zakariya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, and in the second instance refer to the disbelief and disobedience that occurred in the time of our Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace. He began with blindness because it is the first thing that befalls one who turns away from the laws: he does not see the one who brought them from God Most High, and does not heed his miracles; then, even if he saw him, he would not hear his speech, so deafness comes after the onset of blindness.

It is also read ﴿عُمُوا وصُمُّوا﴾ with a damma, on the reckoning: God made them blind and deaf (ʿamahum Allah wa-sammahum), that is, He struck them and smote them with blindness and deafness, as one says: "nazaktuhu" when you strike him with the nayzak (a spear-like tool), and "rakabtuhu" when you strike him with your knee.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿كثير منهم﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the two verbs. It has been said that it is the subject (fa'il), and the waw is a sign of the plural, not a pronoun; this is a dialect of some Arabs, which the grammarians express with "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me). Or it is the predicate of a deleted subject, that is: "the blindness and deafness are many among them."

It has been said: that is, "the blindness and deafness are many among them," meaning: such conduct proceeds from many of them. This is contrary to the apparent sense. It has been permitted that it be the subject (mubtada'), with the preceding clause as its predicate; but this has been deemed weak, because a verbal predicate may not precede the subject due to its ambiguity with the agent. It is answered that the prohibition of preceding is conditional on the agent being a concealed pronoun, since there is no ambiguity when it is explicit; and its ambiguity with the agent in the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" they did not regard as an impediment, because that dialect is weak and not to be considered. From here the grammarians stated the permissibility of preceding in examples like "al-Zaydani qama" (the two Zaydis stood), yet they stated that it is not permissible to precede the predicate where the subject could serve as an emphatic for the agent, as in: "ana qumtu" (I, I stood); for if "ana" were postponed it would be ambiguous with emphasis of the agent. What we are dealing with is similar to this, except that the ambiguity here is with another follower, namely the substitute (badal). So reflect.

He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿many of them﴾ because some of them were not like that. ﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾, that is, of what they did. The form of the present tense is for narrating a past state, to bring its dreadful image vividly to mind, along with what this involves of observing the rhyme endings (fawasil). The clause is a concluding remark (tadhyil) by which the falsity of their supposition mentioned above is indicated. The befalling of punishment from where they did not reckon is a general allusion, with which one is content, relying on what was explained in some detail in Surat Bani Isra'il. And the placement of "Seeing" (basir) here, alongside His saying, glory be to Him: "they became blind," is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 72:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ This begins the detailing of the abominations of the Christians and the refutation of their corrupt statements, after the detailing of the abominations of the Jews. The sayers of this are a group among them, as has been related from Mujahid. We have already thoroughly discussed the detailing of their statements and sects earlier, so refer back to it.

﴿And the Messiah said﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of (qalu) with an implied (qad), serving to add to the ugliness of their state by showing that they denied the Messiah and did not desist from what they insisted upon despite the threat directed at them. That is: they said that, while the Messiah, peace be upon him, had said to them, addressing them: ﴿O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾, for I am a servant nourished (marbub) like you, so worship my Creator and your Creator. ﴿Indeed, he﴾, i.e., the matter, ﴿whoever associates others with Allah﴾, i.e., anything in His worship, or in what is specific to Him of attributes and actions, such as ascribing knowledge of the unseen and giving life to the dead essentially to Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿then Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾, because it is the abode of the monotheists. What is meant is that he is prevented from entering it, just as one who is forbidden from something is prevented from it. So the "forbidding" is a metonymy (majaz mursal), or a subsequent metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) for prevention, since there is no obligation (taklif) there. The mention of the glorious Name in the place of the pronoun serves to magnify the matter and to instill awe.

﴿And his refuge is the Fire﴾, for it is prepared for the polytheists. This is an explanation of their being afflicted with punishment after the explanation of their being deprived of reward. What this sentence contains of an indication of the strength of the factor requiring his entry into the Fire is not hidden.

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, i.e., they have no one who helps them by rescuing them from the Fire and admitting them into Paradise, either by way of overpowering or by way of intercession. The plural is used to observe the correspondence with "the wrongdoers."

It has been said: the negation of helpers is known a fortiori, for if the great multitude does not help them, how would a single one of them help them? It has also been said: this is in accordance with their claim that they have many helpers, so this is negated as a mockery of them. The definite article (al-) is either for specific reference (ʿahd), in which case the plural is in view of the meaning of (min), just as the singularity of the three pronouns is in view of its wording; or it is for the genus (jins), into which they enter primarily. Placing it in the first sense in the position of their pronoun serves to record against them that they wronged by associating partners with Allah and deviated from the path of truth. The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhil) confirming what precedes it, and it is either a continuation of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, or it comes from the side of the Exalted, as an affirmation of the statement of Jesus, peace be upon him, and a confirmation of its content.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ This begins the explanation of the disbelief of another group among them, and you have already been told who they are. "The third of three" cannot occur except in the genitive construction (idafa), as al-Farra' said; and likewise "the fourth of four" and the like. Its meaning is that he is one of those numbers, not specifically the third or the fourth. If you say, for example, "the third of two" or "the fourth of three," both the idafa and the accusative are permissible; al-Zajjaj also explicitly stated this.

By "the three," according to what is related from al-Suddi, they meant the Creator, exalted is His name, and Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both. So each of the three is a god by their claim, and divinity is shared among them. This is reinforced by the words of the Exalted to the Messiah, peace be upon him: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ This is also what is immediately apparent from the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ That is: while the reality is that there is no necessary existent in the existents deserving worship, since He is the origin of all existents, (except a god) described by unity, exalted above accepting partnership in any respect; for plurality necessitates the negation of divinity, as the proof of mutual hindrance (burhan al-tamanu') indicates. Since divinity negates any plurality at all, what then is your opinion about the Trinity?! And "min" (min) is extra (zā'ida), for the sake of comprehensiveness (istighraq), as the grammarians stated, and they said regarding its reason: because it is originally the "min" of beginning, whose counterpart has been omitted, indicating non-finitude; so the origin of "there is no man (la rajul)" is "there is not from a man," extending to what has no end.

This is the summary of what the author of al-Iqlid mentioned on this. It was also said: they say that Allah, glory be to Him, is one substance (jawhar wahid) of three hypostases (aqanim): the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus). By the first they mean the essence (dhat), and it was said: existence (wujud); by the second, knowledge (ilm); and by the third, life (hayat). Among them are those who said that these are embodied. So the meaning of His words, "And there is no god except one God," is: there is no god in essence, exalted above any trace of plurality in any of the aspects they claim. The verification of this matter has already been made with nothing further to add, so return to it if you wish.

﴿And if they do not desist from what they say﴾: that is, if they do not turn back from what they are upon to its opposite, which is monotheism and faith, ﴿a painful punishment will surely afflict those of them who disbelieved.﴾ The answer is to an omitted oath, serving in place of the answer to the condition, as Abu al-Baqa' stated. By "those who disbelieved" is meant either those who persist in disbelief, as al-Jubba'i and al-Zajjaj chose, or the Christians, as has been said. Placing the relative pronoun in the place of their pronoun is to repeat the testimony against them regarding disbelief. Here "min" is explicative (bayaniyya), and on the first view it is partitive (tab'idiyya). The verb indicating occurrence (huduth) was used to alert that persisting in it, after what has come that requires abandoning it, is a fresh disbelief and an additional excess beyond the original disbelief they were already upon.

The interrogative form (al-istifham) in His saying, ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾, is for rebuke (al-inkar). It expresses wonder at their persistence or at their failure to hasten to repentance (al-tawbah). The fa' here is a conjunction (al-'atf) over an implied clause that the context requires, meaning: "Will they not desist from those deviant beliefs and false statements, and so not repent to Allah the True and seek His forgiveness by glorifying Him above what they have attributed to Him, Mighty and Majestic? Or will they hear these repeated testimonies and emphatic warnings and still not repent after them?" ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, so He will forgive them and bestow upon them of His bounty if they repent. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it reinforces the rebuke and the wonder. The use of the apparent noun (al-izhar) in place of the pronoun (al-idmar) is for the reason already mentioned more than once.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 5, verse 75:

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger﴾ is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*, a new sentence that is not grammatically linked to what precedes it), brought to establish the truth from which there is no escape, and to explain the true condition of him (peace be upon him) and of his mother. This is done first by pointing to the qualities of perfection in which they excelled, to the point that they became among the most perfect individuals of their kind, and then by pointing to the attribute they share with human beings and even with animals. In this there is a gradual drawing of them away from their obstinacy, and a guidance to repentance and seeking forgiveness. That is, he (peace be upon him) is restricted to the office of messenger and does not go beyond it to what the Christians claim about him (peace and blessings be upon him). This is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Messengers had passed away before him﴾. The phrase "messenger" is qualified by a clause indicating that he is not characterized by anything that contradicts divinity. For the passing away of messengers before him points to his passing away too, and that requires the impossibility of divinity. That is: he is only a messenger like the messengers who passed away before him. Allah, exalted is He, specially gave him some signs, just as He gave each of them some other signs. Perhaps what He gave to others is more wondrous and more astonishing than what He gave to him. For if he (peace be upon him) brought back to life those among bodies that are capable of life, then Moses (peace be upon him) brought inanimate matter to life. And if he was created without a father, then Adam (peace be upon him) was created without a father or a mother. So from where do you derive his attribution of divinity?!

﴿And his mother was a true woman (*siddiqa*)﴾. That is: his mother too was only like the rest of women who keep to truthfulness or to affirming the truth (*tasdiq*), and who go to great lengths in being characterized by it. So from where do you derive an attribute for her that is not shared by her like? The truthfulness meant here is the truthfulness of her state with Allah, exalted is He. It has also been said that it means her truthfulness in her innocence of what the Jews accused her of. The affirmation (*tasdiq*) meant is her affirming the words of her Lord and His books, as Allah, exalted is He, related of her in His saying: ﴿and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾. This was narrated from al-Hasan, and was preferred by al-Jubba'i. It has also been said that it means her affirming the prophets. The form (*sigha*, the morphological pattern) is in any case intensive (*lil-mubalagha*, for emphasis of degree), like *shirrib* (شِرِّيبٍ, one who drinks a great deal).

[Page 209]

It has been preferred that it derives from truthfulness, because the analogy for intensive forms is that they are derived from the triliteral root, but what has been related may support that it derives from the doubled root. The restriction (*hasr*) pointed to above is understood from the context and from the conjunction, as the second Allamah said. Some scholars hesitated about this, but this is not the right place for that doubt. Those who hold that Mary (peace be upon her) was not a prophet have used this verse as evidence. For He, exalted is His majesty, mentioned her in the context of pointing out the most noble of her attributes, which is being a *siddiqa*, just as He mentioned the messengership of Jesus (peace be upon him) in the same context. So if she (peace be upon her) had the rank of prophethood, He would have mentioned it rather than *siddiqiyya*, because it is without doubt higher than that. Yes, most scholars hold that there is no rank between prophethood and *siddiqiyya*, but this is a separate matter, and it does not harm what we are concerned with.

﴿They both used to eat food﴾. This is a resumptive statement that has no place in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis), explaining what was pointed to, namely that they are like the rest of human beings, and even like animals, in needing the nourishment that sustains the body. So the eating of food is meant literally. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

It has also been said that it is an allusion (*kinaya*, a figurative expression) to relieving oneself, because whoever eats food needs to excrete. This is more bitter to the palates of those who claim their divinity, for in this, along with indicating the need that contradicts divinity, there is a conventional vulgarity. The only intention is to refute the Christians in their foul claim and their repugnant belief.

It has been said that the verse, in placing first what they have of the attributes of perfection, and placing last what belongs to their kind of human deficiencies, follows the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿May Allah pardon you; why did you grant them leave?﴾, where He, glorified is He, placed the pardon before the rebuke addressed to him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), so that the sudden reproach would not unsettle him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾ is a cause for wonder at the state of those who ascribe lordship to them both, and who do not refrain from that even after the true state has been made clear to them with a clarity that no trace of doubt approaches. The address is either to the master of those addressed (peace be upon him), or to everyone who is qualified for it. The word *kayfa* (كَيْفَ, "how") is the object of *nubayyinu* (نُبَيِّنُ, "We make clear"), and the clause is in the accusative position, suspending (*mu'allaqa*, blocking the effect of) the verb before it. By "signs" are meant the proofs, that is: look how We make clear to them the decisive proofs that refute what they say.

﴿Then look how they are turned away (*yu'fakun*)﴾. That is: how they are turned away from listening to them and reflecting upon them, because of their poor readiness and the corruption of their souls. The discussion of this is as it was in what preceded. The repetition of the command to look is for emphasis in expressing wonder. The word *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") serves to show the difference between the two wonders. That is: Our making the signs clear is a wondrous matter of its kind, reaching the furthest ends of verification and clarification, while their turning away from them, despite the absence of anything that would validate them and the convergence of what requires their acceptance, is more wondrous and more astonishing. It is also permissible that the word be taken in its literal sense, and what is meant is the indication of the continuance and extension of the time during which the signs are made clear, that is, that despite the long duration of that, they are not affected, (*wa-yu'fakun*, "and they are turned away").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 76:

﴿Say: Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾ This is a command to rebuke them immediately after expressing wonder at their condition. The phrase "that which does not possess" (ma la yamliku) refers to Jesus, or to him and his mother, upon them be peace. The meaning is: Do you worship something that is unable to do what Allah, exalted is He, is able to do, of afflictions, calamities, health and abundance? Or: Do you worship something that has no capacity at all, for all that humans are able to do is by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, and His empowering them to do it, not by their own essence. Allah, glorified is He, said "ma" (that which) in view of the state of the one spoken of in his essence, his beginning and his stages, as a preparation for denying him any power altogether, and as an alert that he is of this kind; and whoever shares with others a common nature and kind, how can he be a god?

It has been said: the intended meaning of "ma" is everything that is worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, such as idols and others, so the form for non-rational beings (ma la ya'qilu) was given precedence over the rational (man ya'qilu) for the sake of belittling. It has also been said: it is intended to denote the category, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ (4:3).

It has been said: it is possible that the intended meaning is an ascent from rebuking the Christians for worshipping Jesus, peace be upon him, to rebuking them for worshipping the cross, so "ma" is in its proper use. Its remoteness is not hidden. The placing of "harm" before "benefit" is because guarding against it is more important than seeking benefit, and because the lowest degree of influence is repelling evil, then bringing about good. The placing of the indirect object before the direct object is, as has been mentioned many times, for the sake of emphasizing the one placed first and creating anticipation for what is delayed.

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "do you worship", confirming the rebuke and containing a warning. The waw is the waw of circumstance. That is: "Do you worship" other than Allah, exalted is He, and associate with Him, glorified is He, that which has no power over anything, and you do not fear Him, while the state is that He, glorified and exalted is He, is the one exclusively encompassing all that is heard and known, of which is what you are upon of false sayings and deviant beliefs.

It may be said: the meaning is: "Do you worship" the powerless, "while Allah" is the One who is capable of hearing everything heard and knowing everything known; and He would not be like this unless He were living, powerful over everything, and from Him come harm and benefit and recompense for sayings and beliefs: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

A distinction has been made between the two aspects: "ma" in this aspect is for belittling, and the descriptive sense in this aspect is according to the meaning that turning to the vague expression is a form of contempt; however, "ma" for description and state confirms that. In the first aspect it is for mere belittling. The state is as you have known, so understand.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 77:**

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture"﴾ is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab, a change in the mode of address), directed to both groups of the People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab), with the generic sense of the definite noun (al-jins) being intended, through the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarsi chose that it is an address to the Christians specifically, because the speech with them is ﴿Do not commit excess in your religion﴾, meaning do not exceed the limit. This is a prohibition to the Christians from raising Jesus (peace be upon him) from the rank of messengership to what they have fabricated about him of great greatness, and likewise from raising his mother from the rank of truthfulness (siddiqiyyah) to what they have attributed to her (peace be upon her). It is also a prohibition to the Jews, on the assumption that they are included in the address, from belittling him (peace be upon him), and likewise his mother, from the lofty rank to what they have invented of falsehood and vile speech. Their being mentioned by the title "People of the Scripture" is an allusion to the fact that in their Book there is what forbids them from excess in their religion.

﴿other than the truth﴾ is in the accusative as a qualifier (sifah) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: excess of other than the truth, that is, falsehood. Describing it thus is for emphasis (lil-ta'kid), since excess is never anything but other than the truth, according to what al-Raghib said. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: it is for restriction (lil-taqyid). What al-Raghib mentioned is not accepted, for excess may be other than the truth and may also be the truth, such as deep investigation in theological (kalami) questions.

In al-Kashshaf: "Excess in religion is of two kinds: the true, which is to probe its realities and search out its remote meanings, and to strive to obtain its proofs, as the theologians of the People of Justice and Monotheism (ahl al-'adl wa'l-tawhid) do; and the false, which is to go beyond the truth and overstep it by turning away from the evidences and following doubts, as the people of desires and innovations (ahl al-ahwa' wa'l-bida') do." End of quotation.

It may be objected to this, despite its own excess in illustration, that excess is going beyond the limit, and there is no going beyond it unless it leaves the religion, and what was mentioned is not a leaving of it, so as to be excess. It is also permitted that ﴿other than﴾ (ghayr) be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject pronoun, meaning: ﴿do not commit excess﴾ going beyond the truth; or [it is a circumstantial clause] from ﴿your religion﴾, meaning: ﴿do not commit excess in your religion﴾ while it is falsehood, abrogated by the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that it is an exception, either connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati').

﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before﴾: they are their predecessors and leaders who had gone astray from both groups, or from the Christians before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) in their sharia.

(Page 211)

The "desires" (ahwa') are the plural of hawa, which is falsehood that agrees with the self. The meaning is: do not agree with them in their false doctrines, which were called for by nothing but appetite and for which no proof has been established. ﴿And they led many astray﴾, meaning many people who followed them and agreed with them in what they called to of innovation and error, or [it means] leading many astray, in which case the object is then deleted. ﴿And they strayed﴾ at the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the clarity of the path of truth and the manifestation of the methods of Islam, ﴿from the even way﴾, meaning the right path (qasd al-sabil), which is Islam. That was when they envied the Prophet (ﷺ), denied him, and transgressed against him. So there is no repetition between "they strayed" here and "had gone astray before". The apparent reading is that "from" (ʿan) is connected to the last verb. It is also permitted that it be connected to all three verbs, and that "the even way" means the true path, which, with reference to the last, is the religion of Islam. It has been said, regarding avoiding repetition, that the first refers to their straying from the requirement of reason, and the second to their straying from what the sharia brought. It has also been said that the pronoun in the last "they strayed" refers to the many, not to "a people", and the verb is intransitive corresponding to the causative of "to lead astray", meaning: those people led many of mankind astray, and those many have gone astray by the leading astray of those people, so there is no repetition.

It has also been said: the first straying may mean straying by excess in elevating and debasing, for example, and likewise the leading astray; and straying "from the even way" may mean straying from the evident principles of their religion and their complete departure from it. Al-Zajjaj said: the last straying means their straying in leading others astray, that is, these went astray in themselves and went astray by leading others astray, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they lead astray without knowledge﴾. This was transmitted from al-Raghib, as was the first opinion.

It is also permitted that His saying, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿from the even way﴾ be connected to ﴿had gone astray before﴾, except that since it was separated from what it relates to, it was repeated, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they have not done—do not think them safe from punishment﴾. Perhaps the censure of this people according to the view of the majority is more grievous than their censure according to the view of others. And God, exalted is He, knows best His intent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 78:

﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾ That is, Allah the Exalted cursed them. The verb is in the passive form (buna' al-fi'l li-ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), for the sake of following the customary manner of Majesty (al-jary 'ala sunan al-kibriya'). The prepositional phrase (al-jarr) is connected to an omitted element (muta'allaq bi-mahdhuf) that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), or to the subject of (kafaru). His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿upon the tongue of Dawud and Isa, son of Maryam﴾ is connected to (lu'ina), meaning: He, majestic and exalted, cursed them in the Injil and the Zabur, upon the tongue of these two prophets, peace be upon them, by Allah the glorified and exalted having sent down concerning them both: "Cursed is whoever among the Children of Israel disbelieves in Allah the Exalted or in any of His messengers, peace be upon them."

From al-Zajjaj: The intended meaning is that Dawud and Isa, may prayers and peace be upon them both, informed of the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and gave glad tidings of him, and commanded following him, and cursed whoever among the Children of Israel disbelieved in him. The first view is preferable, and it is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both. It has also been said: when the people of Ayla transgressed on the Sabbath, Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, clothe them in the curse like a cloak, and like a belt around the loins," so Allah the Exalted transformed them into apes. And as for the people of the table (ashab al-ma'ida), when they disbelieved, Isa, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, punish whoever disbelieves after eating from the table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the people of the Sabbath," so they became swine. They were five thousand men, among whom there was no woman or child. This view is narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah, and something similar is narrated from al-Baqir, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him. Many have chosen it. By "tongue" is meant the organ, and the use of the singular (ifrad) is one of the three well-known usages in such contexts.

Page 212
It has also been said: by "tongue" is meant language. ﴿That﴾, i.e., the aforementioned curse. The choice of the demonstrative (al-ishara) rather than a pronoun serves to indicate its complete manifestness, its distinction from its counterparts, and its inclusion by reason of it within the category of observed matters; and the distance indicated by (dhalika) serves to announce the utmost gravity of its heinousness and the remoteness of its rank in abomination and horror. ﴿Because they disobeyed﴾, i.e., because of their disobedience (issyan). The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a predicate (khabar) for the preceding subject, and the sentence is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) occupying the position of an answer to what arose from the speech, as if it were said: "For what cause did that occur?" So it was said: "That terrible, monstrous curse is because of their disobedience."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they used to transgress﴾ may be conjoined to (disobeyed), in which case it falls within the scope of the cause, meaning: and because of their continuous transgression. The combination of the past and present verb forms indicates the intention of continuity.

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the statement restricts the cause to what has been mentioned, i.e., "because of that and nothing else." Perhaps, as it has been said, this was derived from the deviation from the apparent form, namely attaching (bima 'asaw) to (lu'ina) without mentioning the demonstrative. When the demonstrative was brought, to belittle that curse and as an answer to the question raised, it indicates that its whole is due to this cause and not another. It has also been said: it is derived from the causal relation, since what is immediately understood from it is the cause in its complete sense, which conveys this. It is not objected to the restriction that their disbelief is also a cause, as the placement of it within the relative clause suggests, because what is mentioned in the causal position here includes their disbelief as well. It is also possible that it is a resumptive statement of information from Allah the Exalted that it was their condition and their matter to transgress and exceed the limit in disobedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 79:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed﴾ indicates the continuation of transgression, for it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that expresses the continuance of not forbidding wrong. This continuance cannot occur except with the continuance of committing wrongs. The intended meaning of "forbidding one another" (tanahi) is not that each of them forbids the other from the wrong he does, as is the well-known meaning of the verbal form (tafa'ul); rather, it is merely the issuing of a prohibition from several persons, without each one being both forbidder and forbidden at once, as in (they saw the crescent, ta'ra'aw al-hilal). It has also been said that tanahi is in the sense of intaha (ceasing), from the expression "he forbade the matter" (tanahā 'ani al-amr) and "he ceased from it" (intaha 'anhu), meaning he refrained. In that case the clause explains what precedes it, namely the disobedience and transgression, and expresses their continuance explicitly. On the first interpretation it only expresses the continuance of the absence of forbidding wrong, and necessarily the continuance of doing it. On both readings, this clause does not strengthen the possibility of a resumptive reading regarding what came before, contrary to Abu Hayyan.

As for the word "wrong" (munkar), it has been said that it refers to fishing on the Sabbath; it has been said that it refers to taking bribes in judgment; and it has been said that it refers to consuming usury and the price of fats. The better view is that it refers to the kind of wrong in general, and what the indefinite (tanwin) conveys is a generic unity, not a specific one. In that case, describing it with the past verb does not object to the prohibition's relation to it, because the object of the verb is only one instance of what the prohibition applies to; or the cessation from forbidding wrong in general is considered as its realization in any of its instances. Moreover, if the past tense in (they did it) is taken relative to the time of address rather than the time of the prohibition, no difficulty remains in the verse. Some, having overlooked this, said: the verse is problematic because it censures the people for not forbidding what had occurred, whereas prohibition cannot be conceived of in such a case at all, since prohibition concerns something before it occurs. Therefore it must be interpreted as meaning the prohibition of returning to it. This is either by supposing a genitive construction before "wrong," meaning "the repetition of a wrong," or it is understood from the context; or the meaning is that they did "its like"; or by taking "they did it" to mean "they intended to do it," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge﴾.

The first view has been objected to on the ground that repetition, like prohibition, does not apply to a wrong already committed, so one must turn to one of the last two options, and there is in both a forced interpretation that is not hidden. It has also been said: the difficulty arises only if the speech is not like our saying: "They did not forbid on Thursday a wrong they committed on Friday," for example, whose correctness is clear, and nothing in the speech rules it out, so it should be understood in that manner.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do﴾ is a condemnation of the badness of their deed and an expression of wonder at it; the oath serves to emphasize the wonder, or it concerns the act that is wondered at. In this verse there is a severe rebuke for whoever abandons enjoining good and forbidding wrong.

Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, you will surely enjoin good and forbid wrong, or else Allah will soon send upon you a punishment from Him, then you will call upon Him and He will not answer you."

Ahmad narrated from Adi ibn Umayra who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah, may He be exalted, does not punish the common people for the deed of the elite until they see wrong openly among them while they are able to denounce it, yet they do not denounce it. When they do that, Allah, may He be exalted, punishes the elite and the common people alike.'"

Al-Khatib narrated through the route of Abu Salamah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "By He in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad (ﷺ), there will surely come forth from my Ummah people from their graves in the form of monkeys and pigs, because they flattered the people of sins and withheld from forbidding them while they were able to do so."

The narrations on this subject are numerous, and they contain a great warning. How lamentable it is for the Muslims in their turning away from the gate of forbidding wrongs, and their little concern for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 80:

﴿You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve﴾. This is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of seeing. Here "seeing" (ru'yah) is visual, and the verbal clause following it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its object, since that object is qualified. The pronoun in "from them" refers to the People of the Book, or to the Children of Israel; al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan) favoured this. By "many" is meant Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and by "those who disbelieve" are meant the polytheists of Makkah. It is related that a group of Jews went out to Makkah in order to agree with its polytheists to fight the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, but this did not succeed for them.

It is related from al-Baqir (may Allah be pleased with him) that by "those who disbelieve" are meant the tyrannical kings, meaning: you see many of them, who are their scholars, allying themselves with the tyrants and adorning their desires for them, so that they might obtain some of their worldly gain. This is extremely far-fetched, and perhaps its attribution to al-Baqir (may Allah be pleased with him) is not sound.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Hasan and Mujahid that by "many" is meant the hypocrites among the Jews, and by "those who disbelieve" are meant their open ones. It was also said that they are the polytheists.

﴿Evil is what their souls have sent forward for them﴾. That is: evil is the thing they did in this world, so that they would meet its recompense in the Hereafter. ﴿That Allah has become wrathful towards them﴾ is the one particularly singled out for blame, by omitting the modified noun and placing the modifier in its position, to indicate the complete connection and linkage between the two, as if they were one thing, and for emphasis in blame. That is: evil is what they sent forward for their return, the cause that brings about Allah's wrath upon them. They took the modified noun into account because the very wrath of Allah, exalted is His station, by virtue of its attribution to Him, the glorified, is not blameworthy; rather what is blameworthy is what caused it among the means.
