Moreover, the wrath itself is something that was not done in this world so that its recompense might be seen in the Hereafter, as is not hidden.

Regarding the parsing of the one particularly singled out for blame or praise, there are well-known opinions among the grammarians. Abu al-Baqa' chose that the particularly singled out here is the predicate of an omitted subject, which the preceding clause indicates, as if it were said: what is it? Or what thing is it? Then it is said: it is that Allah has become wrathful towards them.

It is transmitted from Sibawayh that ﴿that Allah has become wrathful﴾ is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the one particularly singled out for blame, which is omitted; the clause ﴿they sent forward﴾ is its qualifier, and ﴿ma﴾ is a complete noun, definite, in the place of nominative as the subject of the verb of blame. The estimate is: evil is the thing that their souls sent forward for them, the wrath of Allah the exalted. It was also said that it is in the place of nominative as a substitute for "ma" if we say it is a definite subject of the verb of blame, or in the place of accusative from it if it is a specification (tamyiz). It was objected that this involves substituting a definite noun for an indefinite one. It was also said that it is according to an estimate of a preposition, and the one particularly singled out is omitted, meaning: evil is a thing, that for the reason that Allah the exalted became wrathful towards them.

﴿And in the punishment﴾, that is, the punishment of Hell, ﴿they will abide forever﴾, forever and ever. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and it is causally connected to what precedes it, and it is not included in the scope of the verbal particle (harf masdari) grammatically, as the expression of some people may suggest. Al-Isam Ibn Hamdan... [sic] defended this by making "an" a lightened (mukhaffafah) particle governing the pronoun of the matter, with the estimate "that He, the exalted, became wrathful towards them, and in the punishment they will abide forever." It was also permitted that this clause be coordinated with the second object of "tara" (you see), by making it a cognitive verb, meaning: you know that many of them take as allies those who disbelieve and will abide forever in the Fire. All of this is unnecessary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 81:

﴿And had they﴾ — that is, those who take the polytheists as allies — ﴿believed in Allah and the Prophet﴾, that is, their prophet Musa (peace be upon him), ﴿and what was revealed to him﴾, from the Tawrah (Torah). It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the Prophet" is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "what was revealed" is the Qur'an; that is, had the hypocrites believed in Allah the Exalted and in our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with a sound belief, ﴿they would not have taken them﴾, that is, the polytheists or the openly declared Jews, ﴿as allies﴾, for the belief mentioned would surely restrain them from taking such allies. ﴿But many of them are defiant transgressors﴾, that is, outside the religion, or persistently rebellious in hypocrisy and excessive in it.

[Page 2]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surat al-Ma'ida (The Sura of the Table Spread)**

﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*jumla musta'nafa*, a sentence that begins a new point) brought to confirm what precedes it concerning the ugly deeds of the Jews. It is emphasized with an oath, to draw attention to clarifying the certainty of its content. The address is either to the master of those addressed, the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to receive it, as a notice that their condition is one that no person among the people can fail to know. The verb *wajada* (to find) takes two objects: the first is *ashadda* (most intense), and the second is *al-Yahud* (the Jews) along with what is conjoined to it, as Abu al-Baqa' said. As-Samin preferred the reverse, because these two are originally a subject and predicate (*mubtada'* and *khabar*), and the point of the statement lies in the predicate. There is no harm in fronting and postponing when a sign indicates the order, and here that sign is clear, since the intent is to show that the two groups are the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers, not that the most intense of them in enmity toward them are the two groups mentioned. So let this be understood. The word *'adawatan* (in enmity) is a *tamyiz* (specification, a noun clarifying the sense of an adjective), and the *lam* that enters on the relative pronoun is connected to it, strengthening its governance. That it is feminine with the *ta'* does no harm, because it is built upon that, as in *rahbat 'iqabika* (the fear of your punishment). Abu al-Baqa' and as-Samin also permitted that it is connected to an omitted word that serves as a qualifier of it, meaning: enmity that exists toward those who believe. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense of "the Jews" is general, including those present with the Messenger (ﷺ) from the Jews of Madina and others. This is supported by what Abu ash-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Jew is alone with a Muslim but that he intends to kill him," and in another wording, "but that he speaks to himself about killing him." It has also been said that the intended meaning is the Jews of Madina, but this is far-fetched. Just as there is disagreement about the generality of "the Jews," there is disagreement about the generality of "those who associate partners." The intended sense of "the people," as Abu Hayyan said, is "the disbelievers," meaning: you will surely find the most intense of disbelievers in enmity to be these. Allah, glory be to Him, described them thus because of the severity of their obstinacy, the multiplication of their disbelief, their immersion in following desire, their closeness to blind imitation, their distance from verification, their habituation to rebellion and defiance against the prophets (peace be upon them), their audacity in denying them, and their opposition to them. It has been said that among the doctrines of the Jews is that it is obligatory for them to inflict harm upon anyone who differs from them in religion, by whatever means. In placing the Jews before the polytheists there is an indication of their precedence over them in enmity, just as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and [more eager] than those who associate partners﴾ there is a notice of their precedence over them in greed. It has been said that the fronting is because the discourse is about enumerating their ugly deeds. Perhaps the expression *alladhina ashraku* (those who associated partners) rather than *al-mushrikun* (the polytheists), although it is shorter, is for the sake of emphasizing blame. It has been said that it is in the pattern of *alladhina amanu* (those who believed), and the use of this expression rather than *al-mu'minun* (the believers) is because it is more apparent in the nobility of what falls within the scope of the relative clause. The relative pronoun with its clause is repeated in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe﴾. As for *ma* (in the phrase *ma li-ziyadat al-tawdih*, the "ma" in the sense of "for the increase of clarification and explanation"), and the expression with His saying, Glory be to Him and Exalted is He: ﴿Those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, rather than *al-Nasara* (the Christians), it is a notice of the nearness of their affection, since they claim that they are the helpers of Allah, Exalted is He, and the friends of the people of truth, even if they do not openly profess belief in the truth of Islam.

Ibn al-Munir said: He, glory be to Him, did not say *al-Nasara* as He said *al-Yahud*, as an allusion to the firmness of the former in disbelief and their refusal to submit. When the Jews were told: ﴿Enter the holy land﴾, they said: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight." And when the Christians were told, "Who are my helpers toward Allah?" they said: ﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾. Similarly, it occurs at the beginning of the sura, in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾. However, it is mentioned here as an alert to their submission, and that they did not confront the command with rejection in the manner of the Jews. It is mentioned there as an alert that they did not remain steadfast in the covenant. Allah, Exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His speech. The change, as Shaykh al-Islam said, from making the matter in which the two groups differ one single thing in which they differ by intensity and weakness, or by nearness and distance, is either by saying at the end: "you will surely find the weakest of them in affection," and so on, or by saying at the beginning: "you will surely find the most distant of people in affection," to indicate the complete contrast between the two groups in their difference, by showing that one of them is at the furthest degree of the two opposites, and the other is at the nearest degree of the other opposite. The discussion regarding the two objects of *latajidanna* (you will surely find) and the connection of the *lam* is as has preceded. The intended sense of "the Christians," according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', and as-Suddi, is the Negus (an-Najashi) and his companions.

And from Mujahid: they are those who came with Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him) as Muslims, and they were seventy men: sixty-two from Abyssinia and eight from the people of Syria, namely Buhayra the monk, Abraha, Idris, Ashraf, Tammam, Qatham, Duraid, and Ayman. The apparent meaning is generality, following the pattern of what has preceded, meaning that they are the nearest in affection to those who believe, because among them ﴿priests﴾, who are the scholars of the Christians, their devotees and their leaders. *Qissisin* (priests) is an intensive form derived from *taqassasa al-shay'* (he tracked the thing), when one follows it by night. They were named with it because of their great effort in pursuing knowledge, as ar-Raghib said. It has also been said: *al-qass* with a triply-vocalized initial letter means tracking a thing and seeking it, and from this the scholar of the Christians is called *qass* with a fatha and *qissis* because of his pursuit of knowledge. It has been said: *qass al-athar* (tracing a trace) and *qassuhu* have the same meaning. Qutrub said: *al-qass* and *al-qissis* mean the scholar in the language of the Romans, and the Arabs have spoken it and treated it like the rest of their words. They have said for the verbal noun *qususa* and *qissisiyya*, and for the plural *qusus*, *qissisun*, and *qasawisa*, like *mahalibah*. The original was *qassasa*, but since the sibilants multiplied, they replaced one of them with a *waw*. In Majma' al-Bayan, citing some of them, it is reported that the Christians lost the Gospel and inserted into it what is not part of it, and there remained among their scholars one who was upon the truth and uprightness, called *qissis*. So whoever was upon his guidance and religion is a *qissis*. And *ruhban* (monks) is the plural of *rahib*, like *rakib* and *rukban*, and *faris* and *fursan*. Its verbal noun is *rahbana* and *rahbaniyya*. It has been said that it is applied to the singular and the plural, and a poet's verse has been cited for it:

*If you were to see the monks of a monastery upon the hilltops, the monks would hasten forward and descend.*

The plural of *ruhban* in the singular sense, as in the Qamus, is *rahabin*, *rahabina*, and *rahbanun*. *Tarahhub* means worship in a cell, and its origin is from *rahba* (awe), meaning fear. Al-Fayruzabadi and al-Jawhari gave it the general sense of worship without restricting it to a cell. In a hadith: "There is no monasticism in Islam." What is meant by it, as ar-Raghib said, is excess in undertaking worship with extreme fear. In an-Nihaya: it is from the monasticism of the Christians, and its origin is from *rahba* (fear). They would practice monasticism by withdrawing from the concerns of the world, abandoning its pleasures, renouncing it, isolating themselves from its people, and deliberately undertaking its hardships, to the extent that some of them would castrate themselves, put a chain upon their necks, and other kinds of torment. The Prophet (ﷺ) negated it from Islam and forbade the Muslims from it. It is attributed to *ar-rahbana* with the addition of an *alif*. *Ar-rahbana* is of the pattern *fa'lana* or *fa'lala*, depending on whether the *nun* is considered original or augmentative. The indefiniteness in *ruhban* is to indicate multiplicity, and it is necessary to take this into account

[Page 4]

also in *qissisin*, since it is what indicates the affection of the class of Christians toward the believers. The attribution of many individuals of a class to a quality is an indication that the class as a whole possesses it. Otherwise, among the Jews too there are a people who are guided, but since they were not numerous like those among the Christians, their ruling did not extend to the class of Jews.

﴿And that they are not arrogant﴾ (*wa annahum la yastakbirun*) is a conjunction with (*anna minhum*, that among them), meaning: and that they do not behave arrogantly toward following the truth and submitting to it when they understand it, or that they are humble and do not act proudly, unlike the Jews. This quality, it has been said, includes all the individuals of the class. So its being the cause of their nearness in affection to the believers is clear. In the verse there is evidence that humility, devotion to knowledge and action, and turning away from desires are praiseworthy wherever they are found.

﴿When they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they are not arrogant﴾. The word (idha, "when") is in a position of accusative governed by (tara, "you see"), and the clause (tafidu, "overflowing") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The seeing is visual. The meaning is: this is due to the fact that they are not arrogant, and that when they hear the Qur'an you see their eyes overflowing with tears. Al-Samin and others permitted that it be a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf, a sentence beginning anew). In either case, it explains the softness of their hearts, the intensity of their fear, their hastening to accept the truth, and their not refusing it. The apparent reference of the pronoun in (sami'u, "they heard") is to those who said, "We are Christians."

It has already been mentioned that the apparent meaning of this includes generality. It has been said that here the intended meaning must be some of them, namely those who came from Abyssinia to the Prophet (ﷺ), because not all Christians are like that. Al-Faydh (faydh, "overflowing") is the pouring out of something from fullness, and it is used here in place of fullness, by mentioning the effect (musabbab) in place of the cause (sabab). That is, their eyes become full of tears. Or the intention is hyperbole, so that their eyes themselves are made to overflow because of the tears. This is what al-Zamakhshari stated in al-Kashshaf. According to what is in al-Kashf (a commentary on al-Kashshaf), the tears on the first reading are the specific water, and on the second reading they are the event (hadath). On the first reading it is a material origin (mabda' madiyy), and on the second it is a causal origin (sababi). In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir), it is said that this expression is the most eloquent of expressions, and it has three levels. The first is "fada damu 'aynihi" (the tears of his eye overflowed), and this is the original form. The second is a transformation of this, namely "fadat 'aynuhu damʿan" (his eye overflowed with tears), in which the verb has been transferred to the eye metaphorically and for hyperbole, and then the original and literal sense is pointed out by putting what was the subject in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz, specification). The third is what is in the noble text, which involves the same transformation, except that it is more eloquent than the second, by dropping the indication of the original and not putting the specifier in the accusative, and by presenting it in the form of a causal clause. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that one of these be the one with the preposition (min) that enters on the specifier. This is rejected. Although the Kufans went to the permissibility of making the specifier definite, and it is a condition that it be indefinite as is the position of the majority (al-Jumhur), because a specifier transferred from the subject cannot take (min) upon it, even if it is implied with it. So "tafaqqa'a Zayd min shahm" is not permitted. Let this be understood.

﴿from what they have recognized of the truth﴾: (min, "from") the first is for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya), and it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause of the tears. That is, the tears occur as a result of recognizing the truth. It is also permitted that it be causal (ta'lili), connected to (tafidu), meaning that their tears overflow because of their recognition.

It is also permitted, on the assumption that it is for the beginning, that it be connected to that as well. But on the assumption that the connection of this (min) and the (min) in ﴿from the tears﴾ is one, the meaning of the two is permitted to be unified, since two prepositions governing one meaning connect to one governing word. The second (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id), connected to (arafu, "they recognized"), in the sense that they recognized part of the truth and it made them weep, so how much more if they recognized all of it, read the Qur'an, and comprehended the Sunnah. Or it is for specifying (li-bayan) (ma, "what"), on the basis that (ma) is a relative pronoun. Abu al-Baqa explicitly stated that it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause of the omitted returning pronoun. He did not mention the first possibility.

It was recited as ﴿turā a'yunuhum﴾ (your eyes are seen) in the passive form. ﴿They say﴾ is a resumptive sentence built upon a question that arises from the description of their state when hearing the Qur'an, as if it were said: "What do they say?" Then the answer is given: "They say: 'Our Lord, we have believed'," in respect of what was sent down, or in respect of the one to whom it was sent down, or in respect of both.

Abu al-Baqa said: it is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in (arafu). Al-Samin said: both are permissible. It may also be a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in the genitive in (a'yunihim), since the one added is part of it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We removed what was in their breasts of rancor, as brothers﴾.

﴿So write us with the witnesses﴾ 38, that is, make us with you, together with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, those who will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Or: with those who bear witness to the truthfulness of your Prophet (ﷺ) and your Book, as was transmitted from al-Jubba'i, and something similar in meaning was narrated from al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 84:

﴿And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth?﴾ A group of scholars, including Shaykh al-Islam, took this as an independent (mustaʾnaf) sentence, confirming their faith and affirming it by denying the cause of its absence and negating it entirely. [They took it this way] on the basis that (nu'min) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (lana), and the governing element is what carries the meaning of settledness (al-istiqrar), i.e., "What has happened to us that we are not believers?" The denial is directed at both the cause and the effect together, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾ and its like, not at the cause alone while the effect is realized, as in His words: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ and similar.

It was also said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the first clause, falling under the same scope of speech, i.e., they say: "Our Lord, we have believed," etc., and they say "Why should we not believe," etc. It was also said that it is coordinated with an omitted clause, the implied meaning being: "Why do you not believe in God, and why should we believe, we ourselves, in God," etc. Some said that it is an answer to a questioner who asked: "Why have you believed?" This was preferred by al-Zajjaj.

It has been objected that the grammarians of Arabic have stated explicitly that an independent sentence that is the answer to an implied question is not joined with the conjunction (wa), and the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani) mentioned that it must be separated (al-fasl), since the answer is coordinated to the question. It was answered that the (wa) is superfluous, and al-Akhfash reported that it may be added to independent sentences; but it is not hidden that this requires a reliable transmission. The circumstantial clause mentioned, according to what al-Shihab stated explicitly, is obligatory, and the meaning is not complete without it. He said: For this reason it is correct for it to be joined with (wa) in (ma lana) and (ma balana la nafʿalu), and so on, because it is a statement in meaning while the thing inquired about is the predicate.

You know that the interrogation in this type of construction is mostly not literal; it is for denial, and its intended sense varies as we have indicated. The meaning of faith in God, exalted is He, is faith in His oneness in the manner brought by the Muhammadan Sharia, for these people were not monotheists in that manner. It was said: (it means faith) in His Book and His Messenger ﷺ, for faith in both is faith in Him, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is the first, and faith in the Book and the Messenger ﷺ is conveyed by the coordination, since the relative clause coordinated to the Divine Name certainly includes that. As for (min al-haqq), according to what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned, it is a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun; and he permitted that (min) be for the starting point of the end, i.e., "and with what has come to us from God," and that the relative pronoun be the subject with (min al-haqq) as its predicate, the clause also being in the position of a circumstantial clause. The distance in both views is not hidden.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people﴾ [48] are another circumstantial clause according to the majority, from the preceding pronoun with an implied subject, because the affirmative present tense takes the (wa), and its governing element is the governing element of the first, restricted by it; thus the meaning is multiplied, as was said of a similar construction in His words: ﴿Every time they are provided with fruit from it, [they say]...﴾ The meaning: "What has happened to us that we are not believers, while we hope for companionship with the righteous?" This is a synonymous circumstantial clause, and the necessity of the first does not remove it from synonymy. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (nu'min), meaning that they rebuked themselves for not believing while they hope for the company of the believers. It was also permitted that it be coordinated with (nu'min), or with (nu'min) in the sense of: "What is it with us that we combine not believing and hoping for that companionship?" Or in the sense of: "Why do we not combine faith and the aforementioned hope through entering Islam, since the disbeliever should not hope for that companionship?" The position of the verbal noun formed from (an) and what follows it is either in the accusative or the genitive, according to the disagreement between al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The intended sense in (an yudkhilana) is... Some of the grammarians chose that (na) is the first object of (yudkhila), and the second object is omitted, i.e., "Paradise." It was said: Were it not for the intention of this, He would have said (fi al-qawm) instead of "maʿa al-qawm."

﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, meaning: because of their saying, or for what they said out of conviction. When speech is not restricted to being free of conviction, what is meant by it is the conviction that accompanies it, as in the expression "this is the saying of so-and-so," because speech is only issued by its speaker to express conviction.

It has also been said that "saying" here is a figurative usage (majaz) for opinion, belief and doctrine, as one says, "this is the saying of the Great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him," meaning this is his doctrine and his belief. Many exegetes have held that the intended saying is their words: ﴿And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth?﴾ and so on.

Abu Hayyan preferred that it refers to their words: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed﴾. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ata that what is meant is ﴿so record us among the witnesses﴾, and their words ﴿and we hope that our Lord will admit us﴾ and so on. Al-Tabarsi said: "Then the saying, according to this, is in the sense of a request." But this requires examination.

The ithaba (reward) is recompense. In al-Bahr it is stated that it is more eloquent than giving (i'ta'), because it is not given except in return for an act, whereas giving does not necessarily entail that.

al-Hasan recited: ﴿So Allah gave them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, and this is a prospective circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah).

﴿And that﴾, the aforementioned matter of great dignity, ﴿is the recompense of the good-doers﴾ 58, meaning: their recompense. The apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun, as praise for them and an honouring of them with this noble description. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the category, and they are included in it by primary inclusion, meaning: the recompense of those who are accustomed to doing good in their affairs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 86:

﴿Those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ He joined denial of God's signs (takdhib) to disbelief (kufr), even though denial is a kind of disbelief, because the aim is to describe the state of those who deny and to mention them in contrast with those who affirm the signs, so that the threat is paired with the promise. Things are made clear by their opposites.
* * *
Furthermore, among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of some of the preceding verses is ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not conveyed His message.﴾ Many of our Sufi masters (al-Sufiyya) held that this is a command from Him, glorious is His majesty, that His Messenger ﷺ convey what He sent down to him that relates to the rulings of servanthood (ahkam al-ubudiyya). He did not command him, exalted is His majesty, to make people aware of the secrets between Him and him, for a single atom of His secrets is more than the heavens and the earth can bear. These secrets are what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. For this reason He, glorified is He, said ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾ and did not say "what We singled you out with" or "what We made you aware of."

Some scholars said, and this is the preferred view (al-mansur): the relative clause (al-mawsul) is general and includes revelation, inspirations (ilhamat), dreams (manamat), direct witnessings (mushahadat), and all other divine gifts (mawahib). The Messenger ﷺ is commanded to convey all of this, but the degrees of conveying differ according to the differences in receptive capacities (isti'dadat). So there is conveying by expression (tabligh bil-'ibara), conveying by allusion (tabligh bil-isharа), conveying by spiritual resolve (tabligh bil-himma), and conveying by spiritual attraction (tabligh bil-jadhba), and so on. Glory be to Him who sent down water from the sky, so valleys flow according to their capacity. ﴿And God protects you from the people﴾ by the secrets of divinity (asrar al-uluhiyya) that He deposited in you, so they cannot bring to you anything that would cut you off from God, exalted is He. Close to this is what has been said: He protects you from them so that you would not be occupied with them. It has also been said: He protects you from seeing anything of your own in them, but rather you see everything as from Him, glorified is He, and through Him.

﴿Say: O People of the Book, you stand on nothing﴾ that has any worth ﴿until you establish the Torah﴾, meaning you give the outward (zahir) its due and act by the Sharia in its most perfect form along with the unity of acts (tawhid al-af'al) ﴿and the Gospel﴾, meaning you give the inward (batin) its due and act by the Path (tariqa) in its most complete form along with the unity of attributes (tawhid al-sifat) ﴿and what has been sent down to you﴾, meaning you give the Reality (haqiqa) its due, and you witness the multiplicity within the oneness and the oneness within the multiplicity, and multiplicity does not veil you from oneness, nor oneness from multiplicity. ﴿But what has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾, because of their ignorance of it and their weak capacity to know its secrets.

On the authority of some of the masters, may God sanctify their secrets: the Qur'an sent down upon the Prophet, the one sent, ﷺ, has two aspects, the aspect of subjugation (qahr) and the aspect of gentleness (lutf). Whoever is shown the Qur'an through the aspect of gentleness, the light of his insight, his wisdom, the realities of its secrets, and the subtleties of its explanation increase, and through this both the outward and inward meanings of the address increase for him. Whoever is shown it through the aspect of subjugation, the darkness of his transgression increases, the door of gnosis (irfan) is closed to him, so that he does not perceive the secret of the address, and doubts and illusions multiply upon him. To this is the allusion in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it, and He leads none astray by it except the defiantly disobedient﴾. Some have likened this to the light of the sun: whoever benefits from it benefits, and it harms the bat and its like.

Among this is what many of the Sufis wrote, may God sanctify their secrets, for by their writings hearts that are pure have been guided, while many have gone astray through them, to the point that they abandoned prayer, followed their desires, nullified the laws of the Sharia, and deemed the forbidden permissible. They claimed, God forbid, that this is what the doctrine of the Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud), which is the belief of these people, necessarily entails. May God benefit us through their openings (futuhat). It has been related to me from someone whom God has led astray through occupation with the books of these people, one who did not grasp the reality of the matter, that there is no difference between a man putting his finger in his mouth and his putting his member into a forbidden private part, because all is one. Likewise, there is no difference between marrying a stranger and marrying his mother or his sister. This is clear disbelief (kufr sarih), and God preserve us and the Muslims from it. The source of this is reading the books of these people without understanding what they meant. This poor wretch did not realize that observing the degrees (murata'at al-maratib) is an obligation in their view, that neglecting it is heresy (zandaqa), and that they have explicitly stated that the Sharia is the greatest manifestation (mazhar a'zam), for it is the manifestation of the name of God, the Outward (al-Zahir), and that no one can reach God by neglecting it. Indeed, it has come from more than one of the gnostics (al-'arifin): "The paths to God are closed except to those who follow the footsteps of the Messenger ﷺ. If you see a man flying in the air while he has neglected a single ruling of the Sharia, say: he is a heretic (zindiq)." How excellent is the one who said, addressing the Muhammadan Presence (al-hadra al-Muhammadiyya):

"You are the Gate of God, that is, His command. Whoever comes to Him comes through you, not through another."

﴿You will surely find the most hostile of people toward those who believe﴾, meaning true faith, ﴿to be the Jews﴾. This is due to the intensity of their separation, for they are veiled from the unity of attributes and the unity of essence, and they have only the unity of acts. ﴿And those who associate partners with God﴾ are likewise, but they are even more separated from the believers and stronger, for they are veiled absolutely. The Jews were mentioned before them only because the discussion concerns them. This is contrary to what the people of literal expression (ahl al-'ibara) hold. ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe to be those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, because they have emerged from the veil of attributes and have left only the veil of essence. To this is the allusion in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant﴾. They are praised for knowledge, action, and not being arrogant, and this requires that they reached the unity of acts and attributes, and that they did not see their selves as qualified by the attribute of knowledge or action, nor attribute their deeds and knowledge to themselves, but to God, exalted is He. Otherwise they would have been arrogant and displayed self-admiration. ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾, among the kinds of unity of which
[Page 8]
the unity of essence is one, ﴿you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they recognized﴾ through proof and through spiritual discipline (riyada), ﴿of the truth﴾ that was sent down to the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿They say: Our Lord, we believe in this﴾, ﴿so write us down among the witnesses﴾, those who directly witness it. ﴿Why should we not believe in God﴾, collectively, ﴿and in what has come to us of the truth﴾, in detail, ﴿and hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people﴾, those who are steadfast in remaining after annihilation (baqa' ba'd al-fana'). ﴿So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, from the three manifestations (tajalliyyat al-thalath) along with their knowledge, ﴿and that is the reward of the good-doers﴾, those who witness the oneness within multiplicity through steadfastness in God, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿But those who disbelieved﴾, that is, were veiled from the Essence, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾, which point to the unity, ﴿they are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, because of their total deprivation and their being veiled by their selves and their attributes. And God is the Granter of success.

O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تُحَرِّمُوا طَيِّباتِ ما أحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾). That is, its delights and what hearts incline toward from it. It is as if, when the preceding passage included praise of the Christians for monasticism (*rahbaniyya*), it encouraged the believers to subdue the self and reject desires, so Allah, glorified is He, followed that with a prohibition against excess in this matter. That is: do not withhold them from yourselves by way of forbidding them. It has also been said: do not bind yourselves to forbidding them by means of an oath. It has also been said: do not say, "We have forbidden them to ourselves," as an exaggeration on your part in resolving to abandon them out of asceticism (*tazahhud*). As for the meaning being "do not forbid them to others through legal opinion (*fatwa*) and ruling," that is not something to be taken into account. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat one day and admonished the people and described the Resurrection, so the people were moved and wept. Ten of the Companions gathered in the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi, and they were: Ali, may Allah ennoble his face; Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him; Abdullah ibn Mas'ud; Abu Dharr al-Ghifari; Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa; Abdullah ibn Umar; al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad; Salman al-Farisi; Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin; and the owner of the house. They agreed to fast by day, stand in prayer by night, not sleep on beds, not eat meat or fat (*wadak*), not approach women or perfume, wear sackcloth (*musuh*), renounce the world, and travel across the earth. Some of them resolved to castrate himself, and this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He went to the house of Uthman but did not find him, so he said to his wife Umm Hakim: "Is it true what has reached me about your husband and his companions?" She disliked denying it when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked her, and she disliked revealing (something) against her husband, so she said: "O Messenger of Allah, if Uthman has told you, then he has told you the truth." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed. When Uthman entered and she informed him, he came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, together with his companions. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to them: "I have been informed that you agreed upon such-and-such." They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, and we intended only good." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, said: "I have not been commanded with that." Then he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep. For I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, I eat meat and fat, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me." Then he gathered the people and addressed them, saying: "What is the matter with people who forbid women, food, perfume, sleep, and the desires of this world? Behold, I do not command you to be priests (*qissisin*) and monks (*ruhban*), for there is no abandoning of meat and women in my religion, nor taking up of monasteries (*sawami'*). The wandering (*siyaha*) of my community is fasting, and its monasticism is jihad. Worship Allah, may He be exalted, and do not associate anything with Him; perform Hajj and Umrah, establish the prayer, give the zakat, fast Ramadan, and be upright, and you will be made upright. For those before you were destroyed only by excessive strictness: they were strict upon themselves, so Allah was strict upon them, and their remnants are in the dwellings and the monasteries." Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse.

It has also been narrated from Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the verse was revealed concerning Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Bilal, and Uthman ibn Maz'un. As for Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, he swore that he would never sleep at night, except as Allah wills. As for Bilal, he swore that he would never break his fast by day. As for Uthman, he swore that he would never marry. Other narrations have also been related, but we have not come upon any narration indicating that this prohibition was directed at others through legal opinion and ruling, as this speaker has held. Moreover, what follows concerning the command to eat distances this interpretation. And this prohibition does not contradict that Allah, may He be exalted, praised the Christians for monasticism, for a thing may be praised in relation to one people and blameworthy in relation to others.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ولا تَعْتَدُوا﴾ (And do not transgress): it is an emphasis (*ta'kid*) of the preceding prohibition, that is, do not exceed the bounds of what He, glorified is He, has made lawful for you by going into what He, great is His majesty, has forbidden to you. Or it is a prohibition against making lawful what is unlawful after the prohibition against forbidding what is lawful, in which case it is an establishment (*ta'sis*) of a new ruling. It is also possible that it is a prohibition against excess in what is lawful. It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mujahid and Qatada that the intended meaning is: do not castrate yourselves. It is not hidden that castration is one instance of transgression and exceeding the bounds, and taking the more general meaning is more comprehensive in benefit.

As for His saying, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ المُعْتَدِينَ﴾ (Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors): it stands as a causal explanation (*ta'lil*) of what precedes it. And it has already been indicated that negating Allah's love for something necessarily entails His hatred of it, since there is no intermediary state in relation to Him, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 88:**

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good.﴾ That is: eat what is lawful for you and good, of what Allah the Exalted has provided for you. So "حلالا" (ḥalālan, "lawful") is the direct object (maf'ūl bihi) of "كلوا" (kulū, "eat"). The phrase "مما رزقكم" (mimmā razaqakum, "of what He has provided for you") may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative) relating to it. It was originally a qualifier of it, but when the qualifier of an indefinite noun (nakirah) is placed before it, it becomes a circumstantial clause. Alternatively, it is connected to "كلوا" (kulū), with "من" (min) being partitive or inceptive (ibtidā'iyyah, indicating origin). It is also possible that it occupies the position of the object of "كلوا" (kulū), in the sense that it is a qualifier of an implied object standing in its place, meaning "something of what Allah has provided for you." Or one may take it as the object itself, by interpreting it as "some" (ta'wīl bi-ba'ḍ). However, this involves some strain (takallluf).

"حلالا" (ḥalālan) is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, or from its omitted resumptive pronoun, or it is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "eating that is lawful." In all these possibilities, the verse is evidence for us that provision (rizq) includes both the lawful and the unlawful. For if provision did not apply to the unlawful, mentioning the lawful would have no purpose except emphasis, and that goes against the apparent meaning in such a context.

﴿And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ (88) This is an invitation to piety (taqwā) and compliance with the command in a good manner. The verse clearly shows that enjoying pleasant foods does not contradict piety. The Prophet (ﷺ) ate meat stew (tharīd) and praised it, and he loved sweets (ḥalwā). The reports have detailed what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to eat, and the books of narrations are full of that.

It is narrated that al-Ḥasan used to eat falūdhaj (a sweet dish, falūdhaj). Farqad al-Sanjī entered upon him, and al-Ḥasan said: "O Farqad, what do you say about this?" He replied: "I do not eat it, nor do I like to eat it." Al-Ḥasan turned to someone else, as if astonished, and said: "Is the saliva of the bee mixed with the wheat and the ghee of the cow something a Muslim would find fault with?"

Al-Ṭabarsī mentioned that this verse indicates a prohibition of monasticism (tarahhub) and of abstaining from marriage (nikāḥ). It has come in more than one report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted did not send me with monasticism (rahbāniyyah)." He, peace and blessings be upon him, also said in a lengthy report: "The worst of you are your unmarried, and the basest of your dead are your unmarried." And from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to command us to marry (bā'ah) and forbade us strongly from celibacy (tabattul)."

And from Abū Najīḥ, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is able to marry and does not marry, he is not of me." And other reports besides these, too numerous to count.

[Page 9 continued]

﴿Allah will not hold you to account for the idle oaths (laghw) in your oaths.﴾ Laghw in an oath is the dropped oath that carries no legal consequence. According to us, it is that a person swears about a past matter, believing it to be so, when he in fact knows it to be otherwise. In that case the oath is a ghamus (a perjurious oath). This is reported from Mujahid.

According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, laghw is what the tongue utters without intending an oath. This is what is related from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them all. The evidence for both positions is set out at length in the books of the branches of law and its principles. Part of the discussion on this has already been given under ﴿in your oaths﴾.

[Page 10]

The phrase ﴿in your oaths﴾ may be connected to laghw, since it is said: "He uttered laghw in his oath" (laghā fī yamīnihi laghwan). It may also be connected to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "being in your oaths" or "occurring in your oaths." It has also been allowed that it is connected to ﴿will hold you to account﴾. It has been objected to this that its linkage to the holding to account is not evident, unless it is taken as a causal element, as in the hadith: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat."

﴿But He will hold you to account for what you have bound by oaths﴾, that is, for your binding of the oaths and their confirmation through intention and resolve. Here "mā" is a verbal-nominal (maṣdariyyah) particle. It has been said that it is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "for what you have bound the oaths upon." The first view is preferred, because the discourse stands in contrast to laghw, and because it is free of the burden of an extra estimate. Some have said that this estimate is misplaced, because the condition for omitting a returning pronoun in the genitive is that it be governed by the same preposition as the relative pronoun, both in form and in meaning and in its dependence. Here "mā" does not meet this condition, so let this be reflected upon. The meaning is: "But He will hold you to account for the breaking of what you have bound," or "But He will hold you to account for what you have bound them as, when you break them," and this has been omitted because it is understood. The holding to account here refers to the worldly consequence, which is sin and expiation (kaffārah), so there is no difficulty in the estimate of the adverbial phrase. The binding of oaths includes the ghamus according to the Shafi'is, and in it there is an expiation according to them. As for us, there is no expiation and no breaking of the oath.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ibn 'Ayyāsh from 'Āṣim read ﴿'aqadtum﴾ with the light pronunciation. Ibn 'Āmir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwān, read ﴿'āqadtum﴾ with the verbal pattern of mutual action (mufā'alah), and this reflects the root of the verb. Likewise the reading with the intensive doubling is for the same reason, because the readings explain one another. It has been said that the mufā'alah in it is for emphasis, in view of the fact that the binding is done by the tongue and the heart, and not that it refers to repetition by the tongue, as is wrongly imagined.

The verse, as Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, was revealed when the people were forbidden what they had been doing, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how shall we act regarding our oaths which we swore by?" It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawāḥah, who had a guest. His wife delayed his supper, so he swore that he would not eat of the food. The woman swore that she would not eat unless he ate, and the guest swore that he would not eat unless they both ate. Then 'Abd Allah ibn Rawāḥah ate, and they ate with him. He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You did well." And the verse was revealed.

﴿Then its expiation﴾: the pronoun refers either to the breaking (ḥinth) understood from the context, or to the binding that is contained within the verb, with an omitted noun, meaning "then the expiation of its breaking," or to "mā" as a relative pronoun with that same estimate. As for its returning to the oaths, because the word is singular like al-an'ām according to Sibawayh, or because it is interpreted as a singular, then it is as you see. The word kaffārah is meant in its verbal-noun sense, namely the act which is by its nature to cover over the sin and conceal it. Concealment here means erasure, because what is erased is seen as if it were concealed. This is the reason for its feminine form. Isam al-Dīn mentioned that the pattern fa''āl is common to masculine and feminine, except that when a pattern common to both, like fa'īl, has its described noun omitted, it takes the feminine form for a feminine referent, as in "I passed by the female slain of the Banū Fulān," and one does not say "qatīl" for it, to avoid ambiguity. He also mentioned that the ta' may be for transmission to the noun-form or for intensification. End of quotation.

What indicates that it is in the verbal-noun sense is the predication concerning it by the words of the Exalted: ﴿feeding ten needy persons﴾. The Shafi'is took as evidence the apparent meaning of the verse for the permissibility of making expiation with property before the breaking, whether the breaking was a sin or not. Restricting this, as al-Rafi'i did, to the case where it is not a sin, is not relied upon by them. The basis of the inference for what has been mentioned is that He, glory be to Him, placed the expiation right after the oath without mentioning the breaking, and He, mighty is His majesty, said: ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you swear.﴾ They restricted this to property, so as to exclude expiation by fasting, which according to them is only after the breaking, because it is resorted to when one is unable to do otherwise, and inability is realized without any breaking. They also analogized this to the advancing of zakāh before the year completes. They also took as evidence what Muslim reported from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath and sees something else as better than it, let him make expiation for his oath and let him do that which is better."

[Page 11]

We say: the verse includes the obligation of expiation at the time of the breaking, and it is not obligatory before it. Therefore it is established that what is meant by "what you have bound by oaths" is that you have broken them. They agreed that the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ is that he breaks his fast and then makes up a number of other days. Thus it is the same here. The hadith they cited can be used as evidence, because, granting that the consequential "fa" indicates sequence without delay, it may be said that what falls within its scope is the whole of the expiating and the giving, and it indicates an order between them. Do you not see that the words of the Exalted: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ require that hastening precede leaving off trade, by agreement? Also, in another narration it came: "Then let him do that which is better, then let him make expiation for his oath." Some have reported from the Shafi'is that they reconcile the two narrations by saying that one is for showing permissibility and the other for showing obligation. Isam al-Dīn said: the placing of the expiation before in one case and after in another indicates that precedence and sequence are equal.

You know that the Shafi'is are like the Hanafis in that they supply in the verse what we pointed out before in its interpretation, except that for them that supplying is a condition of obligation, and otherwise the inference from the verse is extremely obscure, as is not hidden, so reflect.

﴿Feeding﴾ (iṭ'ām) is a verbal noun whose object is annexed to it, and it is estimated by a preposition and a verb in the active voice. The subject of a verbal noun is often omitted, and there is no necessity to estimate the verb in the passive voice, because, besides being contrary to the original, that estimate is itself questionable. Al-Samin mentioned this. So the estimate here is: "its expiation is that the one who breaks or the one who swears feeds ten needy persons from the middle of what you feed your families," that is, from the average in kind or amount. For the Shafi'is this is one mudd for each needy person, and for us it is half a ṣā' of wheat or one ṣā' of barley.

Ibn Ḥumayd and others reported from Ibn 'Umar that the middle is bread and dates, and bread and olive oil, and bread and ghee, and the best is something like bread and meat. From Ibn Sīrīn he said: they used to say: the best is bread and meat, the middle is bread and ghee, and the lowest is bread and dates. The prepositional phrase has a place in the accusative case, because it is a description of the second object of ﴿feeding﴾, since that verb takes two objects, and its first object here is what was annexed to it. The estimate is: "food or provision of a kind from the middle." It has been said that it is a description of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "feeding of a kind from that." It has also been allowed that its place is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "their food is from the middle," or as a description of ﴿feeding﴾, or as an apposition (badal) to ﴿feeding﴾.

This has been objected to on the ground that the kinds of apposition can be conceived here. It was answered that it is an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) with an estimated qualifier, and that according to the opinion of Ibn al-Ḥājib, the author of al-Lubāb, and those who follow them, this is clearly so, because they are satisfied with a connection between the apposition and what it is an apposition to other than the relation of part and whole. As for the view of the majority, it is because they require that the follower include the followed, not in the way a container includes what it contains, but in the sense that it indicates it in general and calls for it in some way, so that the soul, when the first is mentioned, is eager for the second, and the second comes summarizing and explaining what the first left general. They count of this kind the saying: "I looked at the moon, its crescent," as Rukn al-Dīn stated in his commentary on al-Lubāb. It is not hidden that "feeding ten needy persons" indicates food in general and calls for it in some way. Some of the researchers chose that it is an apposition of whole to whole, with the estimate "feeding from the middle," like: "The hospitality of the guests impressed me, their hospitality being from the best of what was found." The "mā" is either a verbal-noun particle or a noun relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "from the middle of what you feed."

Abū al-Baqā' allowed estimating it governed by "min," meaning "you feed from it." Al-Samin criticized this, saying that the condition for an omitted returning pronoun in the genitive governed by a particle is that it be governed by the same kind of particle as the relative, in form, meaning, and dependence. Although the two particles here agree in one respect, the dependence differs, because the second "min" depends on "you feed," while the first does not depend on that. Then he said: If you say, "The relative is not in the genitive by annexation," the answer is that what is annexed to the relative is like the relative in this. Something like this examination was already raised a moment ago, and some answered it by saying that the omission is gradual. It is not hidden that this involves lengthening the distance.

﴿The families (al-ahlūn)﴾ is the plural of ahl against analogy, like arḍ and arḍūn, since the condition of this plural pattern is that it be a proper noun or an adjective, and ahl is a rigid noun. It has been said that what made it permissible is that it has been used frequently in the sense of "one who deserves," so it resembles an adjective. It is reported from Ja'far al-Ṣādiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read ﴿ahālīkum﴾ with the yā' vowelless, according to the dialect of those who make it quiet in all three cases, like the alif. This too is a plural of ahl against analogy, like layālin as the plural of laylah. Ibn Jinnī said: its singular is laylāh and ahlāh. This is possible, as has been said: it may mean that they have a presumed singular, which is what was mentioned, and it may mean that they have an actual singular heard from the Arabs, which is that. It has also been said that ahālī is the plural of ahlūn, but this is nothing.

﴿Or their clothing﴾ is conjoined, as Abū al-Baqā' said, to ﴿feeding﴾. This was preferred by many. Al-Zamakhsharī chose that it is conjoined to the place of ﴿from the middle﴾, and its reasoning, as attributed to him, is that ﴿from the middle﴾ is an apposition to the feeding, and the apposition is what is intended, so for this reason the appositioned element is in the position of what has been moved aside, as if it were said: "its expiation is from the middle of what you feed, or clothe." Ṣāḥib al-Taqrīb explained his departure from the apparent sense by saying that clothing is the name of something like a garment and not a verbal noun. Al-Rāghib said: al-kisā' and al-kiswah are clothing, so it is not appropriate to conjoin it to the earlier verbal noun, although both apply to the needy. He also said that it leads to omitting the mention of how the clothing is to be, namely that it be of middle quality. Then he said: It may be answered regarding the first point that clothing is either a verbal noun, as the words of al-Zajjāj suggest, or that a verbal noun is implied, like "clothing" (ilbās). And regarding the second, that it be estimated: "or we clothe them from the middle of what you clothe," and the omission of that is because of the indication of its mention in the conjoined element. Or that it be left in its general sense, either by intending its generality, or by leaving its explanation to another source. Also, conjoining to the place of ﴿from the middle﴾ conveys this intended meaning, namely the estimate of the middle in the clothing, so the obligation is shared, and it leads to the validity of its standing in place of the conjoined element. This is not sound. End of quotation.

Some of the researchers objected to what was attributed to al-Zamakhsharī as well: that conjoining to an apposition requires that the conjoined element also be an apposition, and the apposition of clothing to ﴿feeding﴾ would only be an error, since there is no relation between them at all. An apposition of error occurs in eloquent speech, let alone the most eloquent. Denying that it occurs is not something to be considered. Many also made this conjunction an instance of...

Alkafa'a

Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 2 of 2):

"I fed her straw and cold water."

It is as if it were said: "Feeding (ication) is the average of what you feed, or clothing is their clothing," in the sense that "feeding is the feeding of the average" and "clothing is the clothing of garments." There is in this both vagueness and explanation in both places.

It has been objected that the coordination on this reading would be to the substituted-for (mubdal minhu) and not to the substitute (badal). It was answered that what is meant is that, looking at the apparent wording, it is a coordination to the substitute; and that is as you see. Al-Shihab objected to the claim that the motive for al-Zamakhshari to depart from the apparent reading and choose coordination to the position of "min awsat" was to achieve harmony between the two types of expiation connected with the needy, saying: how can that be achieved when the coordination to "min awsat" has been made on the assumption of its being a substitute, and on that assumption it is an attribute of a supposed "feeding" (ita'am muqaddar)? End of quotation.

You know that this is the opinion of some of them. In general, what al-Zamakhshari held is problematic (daghdagha), to the extent that al-Ala' al-Iraqi said: it is an error, and the correct reading is coordination to "feeding" (ita'am). Al-Halabi said: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned works only in one way, namely that "min awsat" is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by what precedes it, its estimate being "their food is of the average [quality]". Then the sentence is complete at His words, "ten needy persons," and then He begins another statement that the food will be of such-and-such average. As for when we say that "min awsat" is the second object, it becomes impossible to coordinate "kiswatuhum" to it, because the two differ in i'rab. End of quotation.

Then, by "clothing" is meant that which covers most of the body, according to what is related from the Greatest Imam (Abu Hanifa), may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Yusuf. Thus, according to them both, trousers do not suffice, because one who wears them is called naked in common usage. But what does not suffice as clothing suffices as feeding, by way of its value. Here there are two reports concerning the condition of intention, and the apparent report is sufficiency whether or not one intends. It is also related that if one gives trousers to a woman it is permitted, and if given to a man it is permitted, because what is required is returning the naked to the extent that prayer is valid with it, and that is what achieves covering the 'awrah; the excess is a favour for beautification or the like, so it is not obligatory in clothing, like condiment in food. The report from Muhammad is that whatever permits prayer in it suffices absolutely. The sound and relied-upon view with us is the first. It is required that it be of the sort suitable for people of middling means and that it be usable for more than three months. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "A cloak used to suffice in that day." From Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: that a shirt, a robe, or a wrap suffices. From al-Hasan: that they are two white garments. The Imamiyya related from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that they are two garments for each needy person, and one garment suffices in case of necessity. Our companions stipulated for the needy person that he be an adolescent or older, so one who is not an adolescent does not suffice, according to what al-Haskafi reported from al-Bada'i in the expiation of zihar. It will come, God willing, in the verse of the expiation of zihar, that what is meant by "feeding" is enabling them to eat, and the full discussion of this is in its most complete form.

It is read "aw kus'watihim" with a damma on the kaf, and this is a dialect, like qudwa for qidwa and uswa for iswa. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Yamani read "aw ka-iswatihim" with the kaf of comparison attached to uswa. It is, as al-Raghib said, the state in which a person is in following another, whether good or bad. The hamza, as more than one said, is a replacement for a waw, because it derives from muwasah (consolation). The prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimate is "or their food is like the uswa of your families." Al-Sa'd said: the kaf is superfluous, meaning "or their food is the uswa of your families." It has been said that the better option is that the estimate is "food like their uswa," as an attribute, so it is again coordinated to "min awsat." On this reading, the choice between feeding and freeing is only in His words, "or freeing a neck," and clothing is established by the Sunnah. Abu Hayyan claimed that the verse negates clothing, but this is nothing. Abu al-Baqa' said: the meaning is "like the uswa of your families in clothing," so the verse is not devoid of clothing. But there is scrutiny in this, since nothing in the speech indicates that estimate.

By "freeing a neck" is meant manumitting a person of any kind. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, stipulated faith in it, taking the absolute here as qualified by the qualified text in the expiation for killing. With us it is taken as absolute because the cause differs. Some Shafi'is argued for this by saying that expiation is a right of Allah, and the right of Allah may not be diverted to an enemy of Allah, like zakat. We say: the text mentions "freeing a neck" and that has been realized.

The purpose of manumission is that the freed person be able to obey, by being released from service to a master and then from committing sin. His remaining in disbelief is attributed to his own bad choice. It has been objected: one might say, yes, his committing sin is attributed to that, but why should the supposition of it not be an obstacle to diverting it to him, as in zakat? It was answered: the analogy would permit diverting zakat to him as well, since it also involves consoling servants of Allah. But his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, "Take it from their rich and return it to their poor," removed them from the category of recipients.

Some of our companions set down a rule for what may be freed in expiation and what may not. He said: whenever a person frees a neck that is fully owned by him, with the intention of expiation, and the kind of benefit sought from it remains without substitute, it is permitted; and if not, then it is not permitted. Is manumitting a deaf person permitted or not? There are two opinions. In the Hidaya: it is permitted, and analogy says it is not, which is the report of al-Nawadir, because the lost thing is the kind of benefit. But we have approved permission, because the basic benefit remains, for when one shouts at him he hears, and even if he is in a state of not hearing at all, by being born deaf, the mute suffices. End of quotation.

The meaning of "or" is the obligation of one of the three choices absolutely, and the choice of the one bound in determining it. It is attributed to some Mu'tazilites that what is obligatory is the combination and one is dropped. It has been said: the obligation is determined in the sight of Allah, and it is what the bound person does, so it varies relative to the bound persons. It has also been said: the obligation is one specific item that varies, but by it and by the other it is discharged. Their difference in amount and reward does not contradict the option, whose variation is left to aspirations and the intention of increasing reward, since clothing is greater than feeding, and freeing is greater than both.

He, glorified and exalted, began with feeding, to ease matters for the servants. Many of our companions mentioned that if the bound person performs all of them together or in order, and does not form the intention except after completing them, one of them is counted, the one of greatest value. If he leaves all of them, he is punished with one, the one of least value, because the obligation falls by the lesser. The detailed treatment of this is in the books of principles.

"Then whoever does not find" means: anything of the matters mentioned. "Then fasting three days": that is, his expiation is that. It is required, according to us, that the days be consecutive, and it is nullified by menstruation, unlike the expiation for breaking the fast. To the requirement of consecutiveness went Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Nakha'i, may Allah be pleased with them.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When the verse of expiations was revealed, Hudhayfah said: O Messenger of Allah, are we free to choose? He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'You are free to choose: if you wish, free; if you wish, clothe; if you wish, feed. Whoever does not find, then fasting three consecutive days.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he used to read "fasting three days, consecutive." Most of these related from Ibn Mas'ud that he also used to read it so. Sufyan said: I looked in the codex of al-Rabi' and saw in it "whoever does not find anything, then fasting three days, consecutive." From all of this, the requirement of consecutiveness is established in the fullest way. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, permitted separation, and did not regard anomalous readings as evidence, and perhaps other reports did not reach him. He considered the lack of means and inability regarding the mentioned items at the time of performance, so that if one gives away his wealth and hands it over, then fasts, then takes back the gift, the fast suffices, as in al-Mujtaba. It is attributed to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that the inability is considered at the time of the oath being broken. It is required that the inability continue until the completion of the fast. So if an impoverished person fasts two days and then becomes wealthy before finishing, even by an hour, or by the death of his testator while he is wealthy, it is permitted for him to fast and he begins again when he has the money. If he fasts forgetting it, it does not suffice according to the sound view. Regarding the one who has means, there is disagreement. Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada: if he has fifty dirhams, he is one who has means and must feed; if he has less, he is one who lacks means and fasts. He related from al-Nakha'i: if he has twenty dirhams, he must feed in expiation. Abu Hayyan reported from al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Malik that whoever has a surplus beyond his sustenance and the sustenance of those whose maintenance is obligatory for him, for his day and night, and beyond his clothing to the extent of what he would feed or clothe, is one who has means. From Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him: if he has no nisab, he is one who lacks means.

"That" refers to what has been mentioned: "is the expiation of your oaths when you swear." That is, and break them, and its details have passed. The "idha" (when), according to al-Samin, is merely for temporal meaning and carries no conditional sense. He permitted that it be conditional, with its apodosis omitted according to the Basrans, the estimate being: "When you swear and break them, then that is the expiation of your oaths," and what precedes indicates this; or it is what precedes according to the Kufans. The dispute between the two camps is well known.

"And guard your oaths": that is, take care of them so that you may pay the expiation for them when you break them, or guard yourselves from breaking them even if breaking is not sinful, or do not make them common and reduce them, as His words indicate: "And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths." On this is the saying of the poet: "Few in oaths, guarding his oath; when an oath escapes him, he fulfils it." Or guard them, and do not forget how you swore, treating them lightly. Al-Shihab endorsed the first and objected to the second, saying it has no meaning, since one is not forbidden from breaking when the act is not sinful; and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Let him do what is better and make expiation." And He, glorified, said: "Allah has ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths." Thus it is established that breaking is not forbidden when it is not sinful, so "guard your oaths" cannot be a prohibition against breaking. He objected to the third as wholly weak and baseless: how can the command to guard an oath be a prohibition against swearing? It is nothing but like your saying "guard the wealth," meaning earn it. As for the line of poetry, there is no evidence in it, because the meaning of "guard his oath" is that he observes it by paying the expiation; and if its meaning were what was mentioned, it would be a repetition together with what precedes it, namely "few in oaths." He objected to the fourth as far-fetched, so reflect.

"Thus" means that wondrous explanation: "Allah makes clear to you His signs," that is, the announcement of His law and its rulings, not an explanation lesser than that. The placing of "lakum" before the direct object is for a reason already mentioned many times.

"Perhaps you will be thankful" (98): the blessing of instruction, or His blessings, whose thanks is obligatory.

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants﴾ means the intoxicant made from the juice of grapes, or anything of the drinks that covers the intellect and clouds it.

This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both. ﴿And gambling﴾ is qimar (gambling), and they counted among it playing with walnuts and knucklebones. ﴿And stone altars﴾ are the idols set up for worship. Some scholars distinguished between al-ansab (stone altars) and al-asnam (idols): al-ansab are stones that were not shaped into images, which they set up for worship and slaughtered beside, while al-asnam are what was shaped and worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And divining arrows﴾ are al-qidah (arrows used for divination), and the discussion of them has already been given in full. ﴿Are an abomination﴾ means filth, something that the intellects loathe. From al-Zajjaj: rijs is everything that is found disgusting of an ugly deed. Its original meaning is a loud sound, and for this reason the thundercloud is called rajjas because of its thunder. Some scholars take ar-rijz to have the same meaning.

[p. 16]

Ibn Duraid distinguished between rijs, rijz and riks: he made rijs to be evil, rijz to be punishment, and riks to be filth and stench. The singular rijs is used although it refers to plural things, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) in which the few and the many are equal. A similar usage is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are najas (impure)﴾. It has also been said that it is because it refers to the intoxicant, and the predicate of the coordinated items is omitted, relying on what has been mentioned. It has also been said that the speech contains an implied noun (mudaf) attached to those things, and the predicate refers to it, meaning: indeed, the affair of these things, or indulging in them, is an abomination. His statement, Glorified is He, ﴿from the work of Satan﴾, is in the place of raising, as an adjective of rijs, meaning it is from his work, because it is caused by his adornment and enticement. It has also been said that min here indicates origin, meaning it arises from his work. On either reading, there is no harm in describing that as a work, even though what was mentioned are objects. The claim that when the mudaf is supposed to be present there is no need to consider the causal relation nor to say that min is for origin is open to scrutiny.

﴿So avoid it﴾, that is, the abomination, or all that has passed by interpreting it as what has passed, or the indulgence that is implied, or Satan. ﴿That you may be successful﴾

[9]

Meaning: hoping for your success, or so that you may succeed by avoiding it. The discussion of this has already passed. Indeed, Glorified is He has emphasized the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling in this verse with the various forms of emphasis: the sentence begins with ﴿indeed﴾, they are coupled with the idols and the arrows, they are called an abomination from the work of Satan, alerting to the extreme ugliness of both, and avoidance of their very substance is commanded on the basis of some of the views, and it is made a cause from which success is hoped, so that committing them is a loss.

Then he confirmed this by explaining the corruptions of both, religious and worldly. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you through wine and gambling﴾. That is, through indulging in them, because the drunkard commits many ugly acts that produce this enmity, and he does not care. When he sobers up, he regrets what he did. A man may gamble until nothing remains to him, and the gambling may lead him to stake his children and his family. This brings him to become the greatest enemy of the one who beat him and defeated him. This is an indication of their worldly corruptions. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾ is an indication of their religious corruptions. The way Satan turns them away from these things, as mentioned, is that wine, because of the great joy it brings and the elation it produces in souls, and because of total immersion in bodily pleasures, distracts from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and from the prayer. As for gambling, if the player is the winner, his soul is delighted, and the love of victory, domination and gain keeps him from what was mentioned. If he is the loser, he is overcome by a constriction and a humiliation that drive him to scheme to become the winner, so nothing else barely occurs to his heart. We have witnessed many people who play chess, among whom there occur such quarrels, false oaths and heedlessness of Allah, exalted is He, that the elephant (the bishop) shrinks from them, the horse (the knight) stumbles because of them, the rook withers from their poison, its feathers even fall out, the pawn of understanding is bewildered by their ugliness, the sober mind is agitated, the shah (the king) of the heart dies, and the board of deeds turns black. The singling out of wine and gambling for repeated mention, and the explanation of the calamity in them, serves to draw attention to the fact that the purpose is to describe their condition. The mention of the idols (anṣāb) and the divining arrows (azlām) serves to show that these two are like them in prohibition and evil, as is indicated by what came from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) of reports loudly denouncing these things and condemning those who commit them.

The prayer was singled out for separate mention from the remembrance, even though whoever is turned away from the remembrance is also turned away from the prayer, because it is one of its pillars, to magnify it, as in the mention of the specific after the general, and to indicate that whoever turns people away from it is like one who turns them away from faith, since it is its pillar. The difference between this and disbelief is that inner belief is hidden, whereas the prayer is one of the most visible of its rites, seen at every time. For this reason congregation is prescribed in it,
Page 17
so that people may see faith and bear witness to it.
