So in the speech there is an indication that the aim of the accursed one, and the final goal of his hopes, in adorning the indulgence in drinking wine and playing with gambling, is to bring people into disbelief, which requires eternal dwelling in the Fire with it, and what an evil abode. Then He, glory be to Him, repeated the urging to desist, using the form of a rejecting interrogation together with a nominal sentence, arranged upon what preceded of the kinds of deterrents. So He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾

19

This indicates that the matter of restraint and prohibition has reached its utmost limit, and that excuses have been completely cut off, so much so that a sensible person, when left to himself after this, should hesitate to desist. The reason for these emphases is that the people, may Allah be pleased with them, as it is said, were hesitant about the prohibition after the revelation of the verse of al-Baqarah. For this reason ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Allah, make this clear to us with a healing explanation," and then this verse was revealed. When ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, heard ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, he said: "We have desisted, O Lord." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "The first thing revealed about the prohibition of wine was ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, the verse. Some people said: 'We will drink it for the benefits in it.' Others said: 'There is no good in anything that has sin in it.' Then ﴿O you who believe, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, the verse, was revealed. Some people said: 'We will drink it and sit in our houses.' Others said: 'There is no good in anything that stands between us and the prayer with the Muslims.' Then ﴿O you who believe, wine and gambling are only...﴾, the verse, was revealed, and they desisted."

He also narrated from Qatādah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, glory be to Him, has prohibited wine. Whoever has any of it, let him not eat it, and do not sell it.' So the Muslims remained for a time finding its smell in the streets of Medina from what they had poured out of it."

He also narrated from al-Rabīʿ that he said: "When the verse of al-Baqarah was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Your Lord is proceeding gradually in the prohibition of wine.' Then the verse of al-Nisāʾ was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your Lord is proceeding gradually in the prohibition of wine.' Then a verse in al-Māʾidah was revealed, and wine was prohibited at that time."

Something of the discussion at this point has already been mentioned under the verse of al-Baqarah, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 92:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ is a conjunction with (ijtanibuhu) (avoid it), meaning: obey both of them in all that they command and forbid. This includes their commands and prohibitions concerning wine and gambling by way of priority (dukhulan awwaliyyan). ﴿And beware﴾ means: beware of opposing them in that. This emphasizes the first command. It is also permissible that the meaning be: obey them in what they command and beware of what they forbid, in which case there is no emphasis. It is also permissible that no object be supplied for "beware" (al-hadhar), meaning: "and be wary and fearful." They were commanded to this because, when they are wary, wariness leads them to guard against every evil and to do every good. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ means: if you turn away and do not act upon what you were commanded. ﴿Then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾.

29

- That is: he did not fall short in that, so the proof has been established against you, the excuses have ended, the pretexts have been cut off, and nothing remains after that except punishment.

In this, as al-Tabarsi and others said, there is threat and severe warning that is not hidden. It has also been said that the meaning is: know that by your turning away you do not harm the Messenger ﷺ, because he was only charged with the clear conveyance of the verses, and he has done it; you have harmed only yourselves when you turned away from what you were charged with. But this is not right, since it would be supposed of them that they claim harm by their turning away, so that it would need to be refuted. Similar to this is what has been said: the meaning is, "If you turn away, then do not expect from the Messenger, peace be upon him, that he will leave you alone, because the Messenger's duty is only the clear conveyance, and it is not permissible for him to abandon conveyance."

[Page 18]

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ (لَيْسَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ جُناحٌ), meaning: no sin or constraint (أيْ إثْمٌ وحَرَجٌ).

﴿for what they have eaten, when they fear Allah, believe, and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah, believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ (فِيما طَعِمُوا إذا ما اتَّقَوْا وآمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ ثُمَّ اتَّقَوْا وآمَنُوا ثُمَّ اتَّقَوْا وأحْسَنُوا واللَّهُ يُحِبُّ المُحْسِنِينَ).

39

It has been said: When the prohibition of wine (al-khamr) and gambling (al-maysir) was revealed, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "What of our brethren who died while they had drunk wine and consumed gambling (the proceeds)?" So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning the people who forbade meat to themselves and adopted the path of asceticism, such as ʿUthman ibn Madh'un and others. The first view is the preferred one, and it has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Anas ibn Malik, al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and many others.

There is a lengthy discussion among the exegetes concerning the meaning of the verse. al-Tabarsi (the responsibility for this rests with him) transmitted from the exegesis of the Ahl al-Bayt that (مَا) refers to the permitted things (al-mubahat). This view was adopted by a number of later scholars, but it has been objected that it entails restricting the permission of these things to the condition of avoiding whatever else is forbidden, given His words, glory be to Him: ﴿when they fear Allah﴾. But that necessary implication is clearly untenable. Therefore the word (مَا) remains general in its scope, whether it is a relative or a descriptive term; it is specified only by that conditional qualifier that attaches to it. The word (الطُّعْمُ, "food/taste") is like (الطَّعامُ, "food"), used for both eating and drinking, as has already been indicated.

The meaning is: there is no blame upon them for whatever they have consumed, of food and drink, whatever it was, provided that, when they fear Allah, nothing of what is forbidden is in it, and they persist in faith and righteous deeds. Otherwise the negation of blame would not apply to everything they ate, but only to some of it. There is no objection to this, because what necessarily follows from it is the restriction of the permission of the whole by the presence of something forbidden in it, not the restriction of the permission of part of it by avoiding some other part, as the consensus (al-jama'ah) necessarily implies. The second (اتَّقَوْا, "they feared") is coordinated with its counterpart mentioned earlier and is included together with it within the scope of the condition. The intended meaning is: they feared what was forbidden to them after that, even though it had been permitted previously. As for the faith (الإيمانُ) mentioned coordinated with it, it is either faith in its prohibition, with the mention of fear placed before it either for the sake of emphasis or because fear is what indicates the new prohibition, which is what one believes in; or it means persistence in faith in what must be believed. The object of the third fear is: what was also forbidden to them after that, of what had been permitted before, on the basis that what is conditioned by fear each time is the permission of what they ate at that time, not the permission of what they ate before, because the permission of some of it was abrogated (naskh, "abrogation") at that point. By good deeds (الإحسان) is meant the performance of fine and beautiful actions that encompass all that has been mentioned of inner (قلبية) and outer (قالبية) acts.

The mention of these stages is not for the purpose of restricting the ruling to them, but to express repetition and recurrence, however many times it occurs. The meaning is that when they fear the forbidden things and persist in what they are upon of faith and righteous deeds, and are in obedience to Allah the Exalted, observing His commands and prohibitions, such that whenever something permitted is forbidden to them they avoid it, then there is no blame upon them for what they have eaten of foods and drinks each time, since there is nothing forbidden in it at the time of consumption. This was said by our master Shaykh al-Islam. Then he said: "You should know that other than avoiding the forbidden, the praiseworthy qualities mentioned have no bearing on the negation of blame. They were mentioned within the scope of (إذا) only as testimony to the attributes of those about whose condition the question was asked, and as praise for them for that and a commendation of their states. This has been indicated by the fact that those qualities are made to follow the fear each time, to distinguish them from what has a role in the ruling. For the context of the noble composition, though by way of expression it is for describing the condition of those who possess the attributes mentioned in what will come in future time, by the implication of (إذا ما), it has nevertheless been put in the form of an answer concerning the condition of those who passed away. The ruling's validity in respect of them is within the general legislation, in a demonstrative manner, by way of the implication of the text, based on their complete renown for being characterized by these qualities. It is as if it were said: There is no blame upon them for what they have eaten, if they are in obedience to Allah the Exalted, together with the praiseworthy qualities they possess, such that whenever they are commanded to something they respond with compliance. They used to consume wine and gambling in their lives only because these were not forbidden at that time. Had they been forbidden in their era, they would have avoided them entirely." End of quote.

[Page 19]

Among the things that indicate the verse is a general legislation is what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the verse ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'It has been said to me that you are among them.'"

It has also been said that what is within the scope of the condition, namely fear and other things, was mentioned by way of praise and commendation, to show that the people were characterized by that quality. This is because (مَا) refers to the permitted things, and the negation of blame in consuming the permitted thing that has not been forbidden is not restricted by a condition.

ʿAli ibn al-Husayn al-Naqib al-Murtada said: The exegetes occupied themselves with clarifying the reason for the repetition contained in this verse, thinking that this was the difficulty in it, and they neglected what is far more problematic than that. This is that He, the Exalted, negated blame from those who believe and do righteous deeds regarding what they eat, on condition of fear, faith and righteous deeds, even though the permitted thing, if it were consumed by an unbeliever, carries no sin or burden upon him. We have two ways of resolving this doubt. The first is to add to the mentioned condition another one not explicitly stated, so that the effect of the stipulated condition becomes evident. Thus the sense of the verse becomes: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ and [what is other than it] ﴿when they fear﴾ etc. This is because the condition for negating blame must have an effect, such that when it is absent, blame is established. We know that by fearing the prohibited things, blame is negated regarding what one eats, so that is the condition, with nothing beyond it. But since fear is followed by faith and righteous deeds, which have no effect in negating blame, we know that something previously mentioned has been left implicit, so that the condition is valid and corresponds to what is conditioned. For whoever fears the forbidden in what he eats has no blame regarding what he eats. It may, however, be that blame is established for him in respect of failing to perform an obligation or neglecting a duty. So when we stipulate faith and righteous deeds, the blame is lifted from him in every respect. It is not objectionable to omit what we have mentioned, since the context indicates it. It is the custom of the Arabs to omit what falls into this category, the strength of the indication making speech about it unnecessary. From this is the poet's saying:

You see him as though God were slitting his nose and his eyes, if his master has spent the night with abundance for him.

Here, since slitting belongs to the eye, and the eyes are coordinated with the nose to which slitting is appropriate, he left implicit what is appropriate to the eye, such as gouging, and what is similar to it.

The second way is to regard faith and righteous deeds not as a true condition, even though they are coordinated with the condition. It is as if He, the Exalted, when He wished to show the obligation of faith and what is coordinated with it, coordinated them with what is obligatory of avoiding the forbidden, because both share the same obligation, even though they do not share the same status as conditions for negating blame regarding what is eaten. This is an expansion in eloquence in which the intellect is bewildered by admiration and amazement. End of quote.

The defect of the second way is not hidden, and the first way is a burden. Such an omission, together with the indication he claims, is almost found in eloquent speech in similar situations. But it is not like the verse he cited, which belongs to the category of "I fed her straw and cold water," and that is something we are not concerned with. What is the relation of eggs to aubergines?

It has also been said in answer to this: The believer may rightly be described as having no blame upon him, whereas the unbeliever deserves punishment and is overwhelmed by it on the Day of Reckoning, so this description is not applied to him. Furthermore, the unbeliever has closed for himself the path of knowing what is lawful and what is unlawful, and therefore the believer is singled out for mention. But what is wrong with this is not hidden.

ʿIsam al-Milla said: The more evident view is that what is meant is that there is no blame for what they have eaten of things other than these prohibited items, if they fear Allah, and did not eat beyond their fill, and did not eat from the property of others. The mention of faith and righteous deeds is to indicate that fear necessarily requires them, for whoever has no faith does not fear, and likewise whoever has no righteous deed. He joined them to faith because they are the foundation of fear. The repetition of piety and steadfastness in faith is to indicate that the persistence of the negation of blame regarding what is eaten depends on the persistence of piety. The omission of mentioning righteous deeds a second time is to indicate that faith, after habituation to righteous deeds, does not call for abandoning deeds. The mention of good-doing afterwards is to indicate that the frequent practice of piety and righteous deeds culminates in ihsan, which is that you worship Allah the Exalted as if you see Him, and so on to the end of what is in the report. End of quote. In it there is both the poor and the good.

As for their statement that al-Murtada alluded to in clarifying the reason for repetition, it is abundant. Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: The first condition relates to past time; the second relates to continuing and persisting in that act; the third is specific to the wrongs done to people, and to injustice and corruption that transgresses onto others. He argued for the specificity of the third to this by His words: ﴿and do good﴾, since if good (al-ihsan) is transitive, the sins they were commanded to avoid before it must also be transitive. But this is extremely weak, because there is no explicit statement in the verse that the meaning of good is transitive good. It does not prevent that it means doing what is good and intensifying in it, even if it is confined to the agent and does not extend to others, as people say to one who excels in doing good, "You have done well and beautifully." Furthermore, even if it is conceded that the meaning is transitive good, why should it not be permissible to coordinate a transitive verb with an intransitive one? Had He, glory be to Him, explicitly said: "Avoid all vices and do good to people," it would not have been impermissible, and this is evident.

It has also been said: The first fear is the avoidance of rational sins that concern only the one who is responsible and do not extend to others. The first faith is faith in Allah the Exalted and in what makes faith in Him obligatory, and faith in the ugliness of these sins and the obligation to shun them. The second fear is the avoidance of sins known through revelation, and the second faith is faith in their ugliness and the obligation to shun them. The third fear is specific to the wrongs done to people. This is, as you see, weak.

It has also been said: The first is the avoidance of what was forbidden to them at first, together with persistence in faith and righteous deeds, since avoidance is of no benefit without that. The second is the avoidance of what was forbidden to them after that, such as wine and the like, and faith is the affirmation of the prohibition of that. By the third is meant persistence in avoiding all of that, both past and newly forbidden, together with the pursuit of beautiful deeds. This is what is meant by those who say that the repetition is with regard to three times.

It has also been said that it refers to the three stages of piety: the beginning, the middle, and the end, the details of which have already passed.

It has also been said that it refers to three states: that one fears Allah and believes in Him in secret, and avoids what harms himself, whether action or belief; that one fears Allah and believes in Him openly, and avoids what harms people; and that one fears Allah and believes in Him between himself and Allah the Exalted, in such a way that he removes intermediaries and reaches the highest levels. Because of the nearness to Allah the Exalted that this state involves, He mentioned good-doing (al-ihsan) in it, on the basis that, as the Prophet (ﷺ) explained in the authentic report: "It is that you worship Allah the Exalted as if you see Him."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 93 (part 2 of 2):

It has been said: [this is] in regard to what one guards against. One should abandon the forbidden things to guard against punishment, and the doubtful matters to guard against falling into what is unlawful, and some of the permissible things to preserve the soul from baseness and to refine it from the impurity of its natural disposition. It has also been said: the intended meaning of the first [taqwa] is guarding against disbelief (kufr), of the second guarding against major sins (kaba'ir), and of the third guarding against minor sins (saghair). It has also been said: the repetition is merely for emphasis (ta'kid), and it is permissible in this case to use the conjunction "then" (thumma), as Ibn Malik stated regarding the Almighty's words: ﴿Nay, you will soon know﴾.
﴿Then nay, you will soon know﴾. It is not hidden that most of these opinions are not suited to the context. The scholar al-Tibi mentioned that the meaning of the verse is: what is required of the believers is not abstention from pleasant things or the prohibition of good things. Rather, what is required of them is progress through the stages of piety and faith toward the levels of sincerity (ikhlas) and certainty (yaqin), and the ascents of holiness and perfection. This is achieved by their remaining steadfast in guarding against shirk, in believing in what must be believed, and in righteous deeds, so that complete uprightness is attained, by which they are able to advance to the rank of witnessing and the ascents of [worshipping] God as though you see Him. This is what is meant by the Almighty's words: ﴿And do good﴾ etc., and by it one is granted nearness to God and His love, which is indicated by the Almighty's words: ﴿God loves the good-doers﴾. In this arrangement there is a result drawn from what al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Asceticism in this world is not the prohibition of what is lawful, nor the squandering of wealth; rather, asceticism is that you be more confident in what is in the hand of God than in what is in your own hand." End of quotation.
This is very evident if the verse is taken to refer to the people who followed the path of asceticism (tarahhub), which is a less preferred view. So reflect on this.
The clause ﴿God loves the good-doers﴾, under all the interpretations, is a concluding clause (tadhyil, a closing phrase that appends a summarizing statement) confirming the content of what precedes it in the most emphatic way. Some have mentioned that the apparent wording would have been "God loves them," but He placed "the good-doers" in its place to indicate that they are characterized by this quality.

[Page 21]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 94:

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, He will surely deal with you as one who tests you, in order to learn your condition," ﴿with something of the game (al-sayd)﴾, that is, game of the land, as al-Kalbi said, whether it is edible or not, excluding the exceptions that will come, God willing. The definite article in al-sayd is the lam of reference (al-lam li'l-'ahd), meaning the known game.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil that the verse was revealed concerning the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyya, when Allah tested them with game while they were in ihram (the state of sacred consecration for pilgrimage). The wild animals would come close to them in their camps, and they were able to catch them by hand or spear them with their lances. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿that your hands and your lances can reach﴾. So they resolved to take them, and then this verse was revealed.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and also transmitted from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that what the hands can reach refers to the young of birds, the young of wild animals, and eggs, while what the lances can reach refers to the large game. Al-Jubba'i chose that what the hands and lances can reach refers to the game of the sacred precinct (haram) in general, because wherever it is, it is tame with people and does not flee from them as it does in the non-sacred area (al-hill). It was also said: what the hands can reach is what can be slaughtered, and what the lances can reach is what cannot be slaughtered. It was also said: the meaning is what is near and what is far. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that the apparent meaning is that He, glorified and exalted, singled out the hands for mention because they are the greatest means of action in hunting, and they include trained animals, snares, nets, and traps made by hand. He singled out the lances for mention because they are the most common means of wounding game, and they include the arrow and the like.

The indefiniteness of "something" (shay'), as many have said, is for belittlement, indicating that this is among the great trials in which the feet of the firmly rooted may slip, like being tested with the killing of souls and the destruction of wealth. It is only a kind of what the people of Aylah were tested with, namely the game of the sea. Its benefit is to alert that whoever does not stand firm in such a matter, how will he stand firm in the severe calamities? So "min" (in "min al-sayd") is explanatory (bayaniyya), meaning: with a small thing, which is game.

Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that this very formula has occurred in great trials, as in His words: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits. But give good tidings to the patient﴾. So the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that "min" is partitive, and what the wording suggests of lessening and partiality is an alert that all that with which trials of this kind occur is a part of the whole in relation to what Allah is able to do. He is able to make what He tests them with of such things greater and more terrible than what occurs. Whatever greater thing He may, in His power, turn away from them, He turns away only to what is lighter and easier, out of kindness and mercy toward them. This alert is meant to move them to patience and to bear it. What points to this is that the matter is announced before it befalls, to settle the souls for it, since a sudden encounter with hardships is very painful, while warning of them before they occur makes their occurrence easier. When a sensible person considers the kinds of afflictions he may be tested with, he finds that what is averted from him is greater than what has befallen him by multiples that no limit can reach. Glory be to the Subtle One with His servants. End.

The Shaykh (Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, in Dala'il al-I'jaz) pointed to this very point. Shihab al-Din, our master, critiqued him by saying: "shay'" is mentioned for the purpose of generality, as in His words: ﴿and there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him in praise﴾, or for vagueness and non-specification, or for belittlement, claiming that it is so small it is not known. Here, if it were said "He will surely test you with game," the meaning would be complete, so adding "shay'" requires a subtle purpose, and that is what was mentioned. As for what he cited from the other verse, it is a witness for him rather than against him, because the intent there is also belittlement in relation to what Allah has averted from them, as the objector himself stated. Moreover, the objection is not complete unless "naqs" (loss) is coordinated with the genitive noun after "min." If it were coordinated with "shay'," it would be exactly like this verse with no difference. End.

Isam al-Milla said: It is possible to say that the expression "shay'" is for vagueness, used as an allusion to admonition, and the tanwin (nunation) is for magnification, meaning: with a great thing, in a situation where one is held accountable for violating it, when Allah seizes those tested with it among earlier nations by transforming them into apes and swine. Then he deemed it likely that this expression is to convey partiality. From what we have already put forward, what is in it is known.

Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) read ﴿that your hands can reach﴾ with the ya (yanaluhu), and ﴿so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾, meaning: so that His knowledge may attach to whoever fears Him in actuality, so that he does not approach the game. His knowledge, glorified be He, that he will fear Him is attached to him, but the attachment of knowledge to his being in actual fear is what the matter of reward depends on, and it occurs only when fear is realized in fact. The words of al-Balkhi point to this. "Al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun in the position of an active participle, meaning: he fears Him in the place hidden from the creatures. So the prepositional phrase is attached to what precedes it.

Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) either from "man" or from the pronoun of the agent in "yakhafuhu," meaning: he fears Him while absent from the creatures.

Many have said: "knowledge" is a metaphor for the occurrence and manifestation of the known. The summary of the meaning is: so that the one who fears His punishment in the Hereafter, while unseen and expecting it, may be distinguished for the strength of his faith, and so that whoever does not fear Him may be distinguished for the weakness of his faith, and therefore he proceeds to it. It was also said that there is an omitted genitive, and the sense is: so that the friends of Allah may know. In every case "man" is a relative pronoun. The possibility that it is interrogative, meaning "so that the answer to 'who fears Him' may be known," is far-fetched.

It was read ﴿liyu'lima﴾ from the causative form (al-i'lam), with the first object omitted, meaning: so that Allah may inform His servants, and so on. Placing the glorious name in the position of a pronoun is to cultivate awe and to introduce majesty.

﴿Then whoever transgresses﴾, meaning: exceeds the limit of Allah, the Exalted, and approaches the game, ﴿after that﴾: after the announcement and the clarification that what has occurred is a trial from Him, glorified be He, for the wisdom mentioned. It was said: after the prohibition and the forbidding. This was refuted by saying that the prohibition and forbidding are not a new matter upon which the conditional clause with "fa" (then) is based. It was also said: after the trial. This was refuted by saying that the trial itself is suitable as the ground for severity and punishment, and indeed it may even be imagined that it is an excuse that justifies committing it.

Some interpreted the trial as the capacity of the pilgrim in ihram to hunt in the future, and said: the meaning is not that game surrounds them, for that has already passed. But you know that this meaning is not acceptable, and what is relied upon is what we have pointed to, namely: whoever approaches the game after we have made clear that the abundance of game and its lack of wildness toward them is a trial leading to the attachment of knowledge to the one who fears in actuality, or to the distinguishing of the obedient from the disobedient. ﴿For him there is a painful punishment.﴾

49

- Because approaching and transgressing at that point is pure defiance, a disregard for Allah's arrangement, a departure from His obedience, and a complete abandonment of fear and awe of Him. Whoever does not control his own self and does not observe the command of Allah in such trivial trials will hardly observe it in great dangers. The more evident sense, as has been said, is that this painful punishment is in the Hereafter. It was also said that it is in this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim related through Qays ibn Sa'd from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: it is that his back and belly are stretched by flogging, and his clothes are stripped off. The matter was the same in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) as well. It was also said that the meaning is the punishment of both abodes, and Shaykh al-Islam adopted this view.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it, as Ajhuri mentioned, is that when He, glorified be He, commanded them not to forbid the good things, and excluded from them wine and gambling and made them forbidden, He then excluded from the good things what is forbidden in one state but not in another, which is game.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 1 of 3):

Then, glorious is His name, He began to explain the rulings that make up for the transgression, following His explanation of the punishment that befalls it. So the Glorious, the Speaker said: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage)﴾. The explicit prohibition, although it is already known, especially from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿other than those who make game lawful while you are in the state of ihram﴾, is for emphasizing the sanctity and for establishing what follows from it. The alif-lam in (الصَّيْدِ), "the game," is for a previously mentioned reference (al-'ahd), as has passed. Its application to what is not edible is common. The Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'is) adopted the general meaning and recited for 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face:

*The game of kings are foxes and hares,*
*But when I ride, my game is the heroes.*

The Shafi'iyyah restricted it to edible game. They said: because that is what predominates in its customary usage. This is supported by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated: "Five are to be killed, both within the sanctuary and outside it: the kite, the crow, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog." In a narration of Muslim, "the snake" replaces "the scorpion." The completion of the discussion will come, God willing, later.

The word (الحُرُمُ) is the plural of (حَرامٌ), like (رُدُحٌ) is the plural of (رَداحٌ). (الحَرامُ) and (المُحَرَّمُ) have the same meaning. What is meant by it is one who has entered the state of ihram for hajj or 'umrah, even if he is outside the sanctuary (al-Haram). In its ruling is one who is within the sanctuary even if he is not in ihram. It has also been said: what is meant is one who is within the sanctuary even if he is not in ihram for a rite of worship, and in its ruling is the one in ihram even if he is outside the sanctuary.

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: the verse indicates the prohibition of killing game for one in ihram for a rite of worship wherever he is, and for one who is in the sanctuary wherever he is, together. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: it indicates only the prohibition of this for the first category exclusively. Perhaps the truth lies with 'Ali (ibn 'Isa), not with his father (al-Jubba'i).

The mention of "killing" rather than "slaughtering" or the like is to indicate that game, even if slaughtered, is in the status of carrion. This is the view of al-Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah), Ahmad, and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them. It is also the new opinion (al-qawl al-jadid) of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. In his old opinion (al-qawl al-qadim), it has the status of carrion, its eating is lawful for others, and it is forbidden for one in ihram.

﴿And whoever kills it﴾ being ﴿among you﴾, in the state of ﴿deliberately﴾, meaning remembering his ihram and knowing the prohibition of killing what he kills. Like this is one who kills by mistake, due to the Sunnah.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri, who said: "The Qur'an came down regarding intentional killing, and the Sunnah established the ruling for error." Al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "I saw all the people requiring compensation for error."

Some said: the restriction to deliberate killing is because it is the basic case, and error is attached to it by analogy (qiyas). It was objected that analogy in expiations (kaffarat) is disputed, and the Hanafiyyah do not accept it. It was also said: the restriction is because this is the occasion of revelation (al-mawrid). It is narrated that a wild donkey appeared to them, and Abu al-Yusr charged at it and struck it with his spear and killed it. It was said to him: "You killed it while you are in ihram!" So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about that, and Allah revealed the verse.

It was objected that the report, even if authenticated, only indicates that Abu al-Yusr's killing was intentional, and intentional here is other than deliberate in the earlier sense, since that includes knowledge of the prohibition, while Abu al-Yusr's act, by the testimony of the report, was free of that. Moreover, it also indicates that the prohibition on the one in ihram killing game was known after the revelation of the verse. It was answered: we do not concede that Abu al-Yusr was not aware of the prohibition at that time.

It is narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that game was forbidden in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyyah), where they would strike whoever killed game with a severe beating. What is known from the verse is that this is part of our Shari'ah. It has also been said that knowledge of the prohibition came in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿other than those who make game lawful﴾, and this is perhaps preferable.

From Dawud (al-Zahiri) it is narrated that there is nothing due for error, taking the apparent meaning of the verse. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Jarir and Tawus. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Sirin, who said: "Whoever kills it forgetting his ihram, then he owes the compensation. Whoever kills it deliberately, knowing it is killing, but not forgetting his ihram, then that is up to Allah, exalted is He: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him."
*Page 24*
Ibn Jarir narrated similarly from al-Hasan and Mujahid.

(مَن) may be conditional, which is the apparent reading, and it may be relative. The (فـ) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then the compensation is the equivalent of what he killed﴾ is, on the first reading, a response particle (jaza'iyyah) that is additional, due to the resemblance of the subject to the second conditional clause. (جَزاءٌ), with a nominative and tanwin, is the subject (mubtada'), and (مِثْلُ) is nominative as its attribute, while the predicate is omitted, meaning: "then upon him" (فَعَلَيْهِ). It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "then his obligation" (فَواجِبُهُ), or "then what is obligatory upon him is a compensation equivalent to what he killed."

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that (مِثْلُ) be an apposition (badal). Al-Zajjaj permitted that (جَزاءٌ) be the subject and (مِثْلُ) its predicate, since the implied meaning is: "the compensation for that act, or for the killed animal, is equivalent to what he killed." On this reading the Kufans and Ya'qub recited (the seven canonical readings are the alternative); the rest of the seven read (جَزاءٌ) in the nominative, construct-annexed to (مِثْلُ).

Al-Wahidi raised an objection to this, and even said: it should not be permitted, because the compensation is owed to the killed animal, not to its equivalent. There is no hiding that this is an attack on what is transmitted with mass transmission (mutawatir) from the Prophet (ﷺ), and that is an extreme of ugliness. As for what he mentioned, it has been answered: first, that (جَزاءٌ), as has been said, is a verbal noun annexed to its second object, meaning: "upon him is that he be recompensed with an equivalent of what he killed." Its first object is omitted, and the meaning is: "upon him is that he compensate the killed game with its equivalent." Then the first object was omitted because the context indicates it, and the verbal noun was annexed to the second. It may be said that there is no need to undertake this burden, by making it a verbal noun annexed to its object without assuming another object, on the basis that the meaning of "that he be recompensed with an equivalent" is "that equivalents be given as compensation."

Second, the annexation may be made explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: "a compensation which is the equivalent of what he killed."

Third, (مِثْلُ) may be an intrusive (muqhamah) element, as in their saying: "One like you does not do such a thing." This was objected to: it defeats the stipulation of equivalence between the compensation and the killed animal, and the requirement that the compensation prescribed be something that matches and equals it, and that requires equivalence, which is almost agreed to be understood from this sentence, as is not hidden.

Muhammad ibn Muqatil recited (جَزاءٌ) with tanwin and the accusative, and (مِثْلُ) in the accusative as well, meaning: "let him give a compensation," or "upon him is that he give a compensation equivalent to what he killed." Al-Sulami recited (جَزاءٌ) in the nominative with tanwin and (مِثْلُ) in the accusative. As for the nominative of (جَزاءٌ), it is clear. As for the accusative of (مِثْلُ), it is by a compensation, or by an omitted verb indicated by (جَزاءٌ), meaning: "he gives or pays an equivalent."

'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) recited (فَجَزاؤُهُ), with (جَزاءٍ) in the nominative, annexed to the pronoun, and (مِثْلُ) in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate.

According to al-Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah) and Abu Yusuf, the meaning of "equivalent" is in terms of value (al-qimah). The game is valued as game, not for what has been added to it by craftsmanship, in the place where the muhrim (one in ihram) struck it, or in the nearest places to it where it is bought and sold. Likewise, the time when he struck it is taken into account, because values differ according to places and times.

If its value reaches the value of a hady (sacrificial animal), the offender is given the choice between buying with it what is worth the value of the game and sacrificing it to the Haram, or buying with it food and giving each poor person half a sa' of wheat or one sa' of something else. It is not permitted to feed a poor person less than half a sa', and it is not prohibited to give him more, even if it is the whole of the food. However, if he does so, it suffices for feeding one poor person half a sa'. He must complete the rest in proportion, and the remainder counts as voluntary charity. He may also choose to fast one day for each poor person's share of food. If the surplus does not reach a poor person's food, he gives it in charity, or fasts for it a full day, because fasting less than a full day is not known in the Shari'ah.

If its value does not reach the value of a hady, then if it reaches what can buy a poor person's food, he is given the choice between feeding and fasting. If it reaches only what buys a mudd of wheat, for example, he is given the choice between feeding that amount and fasting a full day, for the reasons we have stated. So His saying, exalted is He, (مِنَ النَّعَمِ), "from the cattle," is an explanation of the hady purchased by value, according to one of the modes of choice, since whoever does that can truly be said to have been recompensed with an equivalent of what he killed from the cattle.

The author of al-Taqrib (Ibn Jamal?) objected to this, because the qira'ah (recitation) with the nominative of (جَزاءٌ) and (مِثْلُ) requires that the compensation be an equivalent from the cattle to the game. So if the compensation is the value, it is not equivalent to it from the cattle. Rather, the compensation is a value with which something equivalent is bought. Al-Kashf answered that what is bought with the compensation is also a compensation, for the food of the poor is a compensation by consensus, and it is bought with the value. The conclusion is that it is truly said of it that it is a compensation, and that it was bought with the compensation, and there is no contradiction between the two.

The author of al-Hidayah claimed that (مِنَ النَّعَمِ) is an explanation of (ما قَتَلَ), and that the meaning of the verse is: "the compensation is the value of what he killed from the cattle, in the sense of value." The cattle is understood as wild cattle, because the compensation is due only by killing it, not by killing domestic livestock. It has been established, as Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Asma'i said, that the term "na'am" (cattle) is applied in the language to domestic animals and also to wild ones.

As for the statement of Abu al-Baqa', where he said: "It is permitted that (مِنَ النَّعَمِ) be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (قَتَلَ), because the one killed is from the cattle, based on this," it is far from the intended meaning of the noble text, and contrary to what comes to mind. For the well-known meaning of (النَّعَمُ) in the language is camels, cows, and sheep, not what has been mentioned. Al-Zajjaj explicitly stated this, and he mentioned that when camels alone are mentioned they are also called (نَعَمٌ), and if cows and sheep alone are mentioned, they are called (نَعَمًا).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 2 of 3):

Muhammad (al-Shaybani) said, and it is attributed to al-Shafi'i, Malik and the Imamiyya as well: The intended meaning of "the like" (al-mithl) and "the equivalent" (al-nazir) is in appearance, in respect of what has an equivalent in that (appearance), not in value. So for the gazelle (zabi) there is a sheep (shah); for the hyena (dab') there is a sheep; for the hare (arnab) there is a female kid (anaq); for the jerboa (yarbu') there is a jafra (a young female goat); for the ostrich (na'āma) there is a camel (badana); and for the wild ass (himar al-wahsh) there is a cow (baqara). This is because God, exalted is He, required "the like of what was killed" restricted to livestock (al-na'am). Whoever considers value has contradicted the explicit text, because value is not livestock. Also, the Companions, such as 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, 'Umar, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and others, may God be pleased with them all, required a camel for the ostrich and a cow for the wild ass, and so on. It has also come from the Prophet ﷺ, as Abu Dawud related: "The hyena is game, and in it is a sheep." As for what has no equivalent in terms of creation, such as the sparrow and the dove, value is required in it according to Muhammad, as it is according to Abu Hanifa (al-Imam al-A'zam) and his companion. From al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, it is reported that he considers equivalence in terms of attributes, so he required a sheep for the dove, because the two resemble each other in that each of them coos (ya'ubb) and moans (yahdir). This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and Muqatil, may God be pleased with them. Ibn Abi Shayba related from 'Ata', who said: "The first to ransom a bird of the Haram with a sheep was 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him." For Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, may God be pleased with them both, God, exalted is He, stated the term unrestrictedly, and the unrestricted "mithl" is the like in form and meaning, which is the one that shares the species, and this is not intended here by consensus. So what remains is that the intended meaning is "mithl" in meaning, which is value. This is because the established usage in the Shari'a for the term "mithl" is that it refers to what shares the species or to value. God, exalted is He, said concerning compensation for aggression: ﴿So whoever aggresses against you, then aggress against him in the same manner as he aggressed against you﴾. The intended meaning is the more general of the two, namely the equal in species when the destroyed item is fungible (mithli), and value when it is non-fungible (qimi), on the basis that it is a homonym with a general meaning (mushtarak ma'nawi). Animals are, in the Shari'a, among the items valued (qimat), disregarding the equality present in the complete form, in favour of the internal difference among members of one species. So what do you think when sharing in species is also absent? Then nothing remains except resemblance in some aspect of form, such as the length of the neck and legs in the ostrich together with the camel, and similar things in other cases. When the Shari'a rules that equality is not considered together with resemblance in the complete form, and that the destroyed item is not compensated by what shares its entire species but by the intended equivalent, then when that is absent, and the resemblance is only in some aspect of the form, the disregard is even more evident, unless it is impossible. That would be the case if the word were to carry a meaning other than what is possible. Therefore, when the intended meaning of a word is known in the Shari'a and it is ambiguous in a context where it may be understood as that known meaning or otherwise, it is obligatory to understand it as the known meaning. What we are dealing with is of this kind, so it is necessary to turn to it. And what has come from the Prophet ﷺ and from his noble Companions, may God be pleased with them, concerning judgment by the equivalent should be understood as based on estimation by value. However, since the people at that time were owners of livestock, paying from it was easier for them, not in the sense that anything other than that would not suffice. As for the hadith restricting it to livestock, you already know the answer to it. Our master Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that the original cause of the offence and the compensation equal to the victim is in fact its value, but not in the sense that the offender intends it and spends it directly on the recipients. Rather, it is in the sense that it is made a standard by which one of the three options is estimated, and so it stands in its place. Thus His saying, ﴿like what was killed﴾, is a necessary attribute of the compensation, never separated from it in any state. As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿of the livestock﴾, it is an attribute of it that is considered in the subsequent state, on the basis of its first attribute, which is the standard for it and for what follows of food and fasting. So their right is that they be coordinated with the separable attribute, not with the necessary attribute, let alone being coordinated with the qualified noun, as will come, God willing. Among what indicates that the intended meaning of "mithl" is value is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿judging by it﴾, that is, by the like of what was killed, ﴿two just men from among you﴾, that is, two just arbiters from among the Muslims, because estimation is what requires examination and effort, not equality in form, which every person can know equally. This is clearly apparent when read in light of Muhammad's statement.

It may be said that this sentence also points to what we have said, according to the view of those who make the basis of equivalence between game and livestock the resemblance and analogy in some attributes and forms while the difference between them is established in the rest of the aspects. For that is something that the pillars of the leading imams of ijtihad and the champions of guidance and right direction do not reach, except those supported by holy power. Do you not see that Imam al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, and those we have mentioned, required a sheep for killing a dove, on the basis of the equality established between them in cooing and moaning, although the relation between them in all other respects is like that between the lizard (dabb) and the nun (fish), or rather the fish and the fishmonger? How then could the knowledge of these subtle and difficult details be entrusted to the opinion of two just men from ordinary people? Moreover, the ruling in this sense relates to species, not to individuals. So after each kind of game has been matched with a kind of livestock, the ruling is complete, and when the particular circumstances of incidents occur there is no need for any ruling at all.

Qira'a: Muhammad ibn Ja'far read (dhu 'adl) in the singular. Ibn Jinni explained it as intended for the imam. It was also said that "dhu" is used in the manner of "min" for few and many, and it is not meant here for unity but for plurality, and by it is meant two, because that is its lowest rank. In al-Hidaya they said: one just man suffices, but two is preferable because it is more cautious and further from error. On this basis there is no need to take "dhu" as plural or as referring to the imam. Rather, what is meant is one, whether he is an imam or otherwise. Whoever requires two takes the number in the verse to be in the mutawatir reading as a matter of preference. The sentence is an attribute of a compensation, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in its supposed predicate. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from it, because it is specified by the attribute. Ibn al-Humam allowed, on the reading of raising "jaza'" and its idafa, that it may be an attribute of "mithl" just as it may be an attribute of "jaza'", because "mithl" is not made definite by its idafa, so describing it and describing what is added to it by a clause is permissible. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as an offering (hadyan)﴾ is a circumstantial clause, presumptive, from the pronoun in "bihi", as al-Farisi said, or from "jaza'" on the basis that it is a predicate, or from it on the assumption that it is a subject according to one opinion, or it is an apposition to "mithl" according to those who read it in the accusative, or from its place according to those who read it in the genitive, or it is in the accusative as an infinitive, meaning he offers it as an offering. The sentence is another attribute of "jaza'". ﴿Reaching the Ka'ba﴾ is an attribute of "hadyan", because its idafa is verbal. ﴿Or an expiation (kaffara)﴾ is a conjunction on the place of "min al-na'am", on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is an attribute of "jaza'" according to what Shaykh al-Islam chose. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿food for the needy (ta'am masakin)﴾ is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to "kaffara" according to those who hold that view, like al-Farisi regarding indefinites, or an apposition to it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning it is the food of the needy. ﴿Or the equivalent of that in fasting (aw 'adl dhalika siyaman)﴾ is a conjunction on "ta'am", "dhalika" is a reference to it, and "siyaman" is a specification (tamyiz). The summary of the verse is as if it were said: then there is due a compensation equal to what was killed, which is of the livestock, or food for the needy, or fasting equal to their number. In that case equality is a necessary attribute of the compensation, by which the offering, the food and the fasting are estimated. The first two are without intermediary, and the third is through the second. So the offender chooses each of them as a substitute for the others. That the choice belongs to the offender is what Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, may God be pleased with them both, held. According to them, when the value of the game is determined by the ruling of the two arbiters and it amounts to an offering, he has the choice to make it an offering, food or fasting, because the option was prescribed as a concession to the one who is obliged, so the choice rests with him, that he may benefit by what he chooses, as in the expiation for oaths. Muhammad, and our companions relate it from al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him as well, said: the choice belongs to the two arbiters in determining one of the things. If they rule for an offering, the equivalent is due as explained above; if they rule for food or fasting, then it is according to what the Imam and his companion said, that value is considered in meaning.

It was argued, as has been said, from the verse on this point, and its basis is that it mentions the offering in the accusative as an explanation of the hidden pronoun referring back to "mithl" in His saying, ﴿judging by it two just men﴾, whether it is a circumstantial clause from it as we have said, or a specification according to what has been said. It thus establishes that the equivalent becomes an offering only by their choice and ruling. Or it is an object of "hukm" (judging), on the basis that it is a substitute for the pronoun, treated as in its place, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: My Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the community of Abraham﴾. In this there is an explicit statement that the determination belongs to the two arbiters. Then, when this was established for the offering, it was established for the food and fasting as well, since there is no one who makes a distinction, because He, glorified is He, conjoined them to it with the particle "aw" (or). This is according to those other than al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them, in one narration about the choice, so the choice belongs to the two of them. Many of our companions answered this by saying that the argument would be valid only if the expiation were conjoined to "hadyan", and it is not so, because their case endings differ. Rather it is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: "fa-jaza'" (then there is a compensation), as is shown by its being nominative, and likewise His saying "aw 'adl" and so on. So there is in the verse no indication that the two arbiters have a choice regarding food and fasting. When the choice is not established for the two arbiters in those two, it is not established for them in the offering either, since there is no one who makes a distinction. The two arbiters have only the right to weigh in on the destroyed item, and after that the choice belongs to the one who is obliged, for his ease. Moreover, in the direction of the argument according to what Akmal al-Din said in al-'Inaya there is a problem, because mentioning food and fasting with the particle "aw" would establish the intended point only if "kaffara" were in the accusative, as in the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Nahwi, and that reading is irregular (shadhdha). Al-Shafi'i does not regard an irregular reading as evidence, neither as Qur'an nor as a report, as is known in the principles of jurisprudence.

Our master Shaykh al-Islam objected to conjoining "kaffara" to "jaza'", although the eminent exegetes and jurists went that way, saying that in that case there would remain in the noble wording what could be used to estimate the food and fasting, and resorting to analogy with the offering is a clear artifice. You know what he chose, and the verse on that reading also can serve as evidence for the opponent's claim, as is evident. Moreover, the apparent meaning of it, as Ibn al-Humam said, is that the choice belongs to the one who is obliged, since the referent of the pronoun omitted from the predicate or from the subject of the sentence is to him, on the basis that the estimate is "then there is due upon him" or "the obligation is upon him." Then, if the choice falls on the offering, what suffices for it in the sacrifice is a jadha' (a male lamb of more than six months) from sheep, or a thaniyy from other animals, according to Abu Hanifa, because the unrestricted name "hadyan" refers to it, as in the offering of tamattu' and qiran. It was objected that the name "hadyan" may refer to something else, as when one says: if I do such and such, then this garment of mine is a hadi, so let the matter in dispute be likewise. It was answered that the discussion concerns unrestricted "hadi", and what was mentioned is not like that, because the indication

I have translated the passage as given, including the Arabic discussions, transliterated technical terms, and the Qur'anic quotations in quotation marks.

Shaykh Abu al-Fadl Shihab al-Din Mahmud al-Alusi said: "...into the garment you have bound it." According to Mahmud [al-Alusi was referring to the view of Mahmud, meaning the Hanafi scholar Mahmud, in the phrase "Mahmud" as recorded in the text], small livestock is sufficient, because the Companions, as has been mentioned, required a 'anaq (a young female goat) and a jafra (a female kid), and this indicates the permissibility of that in the category of the hady (sacrificial offering). And from Abu Yusuf there are two narrations: one like the saying of the Imam (Abu Hanifa), and another like the saying of Muhammad (al-Shaybani), which is the one found in al-Mabsut, al-Asrar and other works. And according to Abu Hanifa, small animals are permitted by way of feeding (the poor). It is possible that the ruling of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, was based on this consideration, so their mere action at that time does not contradict what the Imam held, and therefore it does not stand as proof against him.

And when he chooses the hady and it reaches the size of what is sacrificed, he must not slaughter it except in the Haram. This is what is meant by the words of the Exalted: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾. However, the mention of the Ka'bah is for honoring it. If he slaughters it outside the Haram, it does not suffice for the hady but only for the feeding (of the poor). Therefore it is required that he give each poor person the value of half a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of other foodstuffs. It is permissible that he give the sheep that is the hady to one poor person, as in the hady of tamattu'. He must not give any of the jaza' (compensation) to someone whose testimony is not accepted in his favor. It is permissible to give it to the People of the Covenant (dhimmis), but a Muslim is more preferred. If he eats from the jaza', he must compensate the value of what he ate. Feeding does not require that it be done within the Haram.

They transmitted from al-Shafi'i that this is required, reasoning by analogy with the hady, and by the common factor of extending benefit to the residents of the Haram. We say: the hady is an act of worship whose reason is not known, so it is restricted to a place or time. But charity is an act of worship whose reason is known, at every time and place, like fasting, which is permitted outside the Haram by consensus. So if he slaughters in Kufa, for example, it suffices in place of the food when he gives away the meat. This is fulfilled, equal in value to the food, because the spilling of blood substitutes for it. If this slaughtered animal is stolen or lost before he gives it in charity, the obligation remains upon him as it was. This differs from the case where the slaughter took place in the Haram, where he is discharged from the obligation even if the slaughtered animal is stolen or lost before he gives it in charity.

When the choice falls upon food, the destroyed animal is valued in money, then food is bought with that value and given in charity as we indicated earlier. In al-Hidayah it says: the destroyed animal is valued by food according to us, because that is what is owed, so its value is considered.

Hamid al-Din al-Darir transmitted from Muhammad that the equivalent (nazir) is valued, because it is the thing obligated in specific form when the slain animal has an equivalent. You know that even if we grant that the equivalent is the thing obligated in specific form when choosing the hady, it does not follow that it must be given precedence when choosing another category. How then, when that is disputed?

If he chooses fasting, then according to what is in al-Hidayah, the slain animal is valued as food, then he fasts one day for the food of each poor person, as already explained, because it is not possible to assign fasting to the slain animal, since fasting has no value. So we estimate it by food. This manner of estimation is well known in the Shari'ah, as in the fidyah. The full discussion of the branches, the expiation, and the food in the verse, according to what the words of some exegetes suggest, is taken in the verbal-noun sense. And if both were kept on their apparent meaning, this would be valid. What we have mentioned about the coordination of "kaffarah" is on the reading "jaza'" in the nominative. On the rest of the readings, it is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the clause is coordinated with the clause "min al-na'am."

Al-Shihab mentioned that on the reading "jaza'an" in the accusative, "kaffarah" may be the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: what is obligatory upon him is an expiation. It may also be that there is a verb understood there, meaning: he must give as compensation, so "aw kaffarah" is coordinated with "an yujzi'a", and it is a subject placed before its predicate. It was read "aw kaffaratu ta'ami masakin" with the genitive construction, to specify the type of expiation, on the basis that it means that by which expiation is made. It is general, including food and other things, and likewise food may be an expiation and other than that, so between the two terms there is a partial overlap in both directions, like an iron ring. Abu Hayyan said: food is not a genus of expiation except by a very remote figurative usage, so the construction is the construction of association. This is not correct.

Al-A'raj read "aw kaffaratu ta'ami miskin" on the basis that the specification is achieved by the singular which indicates the genus. It was also read "aw 'adl" with a kasra on the 'ayn.

The difference between them: "'adl al-shay'" (with fatha), as al-Farra' said, is what equals it from a different kind, like fasting and feeding, while "'idl" (with kasra) is what is equated with it in quantity. It is as if the fatha form is a verbal noun, and the kasra form is in the sense of the passive participle. The Basrans said: "al-'adl" and "al-'idl" both mean "the like", whether of the same kind or of a different kind. Al-Raghib said: "al-'adl" and "al-'idl" are close in meaning, but the fatha form is used for what is perceived by insight, like judgments, and the kasra form for what is perceived by the senses, like "'adil" (with fatha) which is equal distribution. On this basis it is narrated: "By justice the heavens and earth stand," indicating that if any one of the four elements in the world were greater than another or less than it, contrary to the requirement of wisdom, the world would not be ordered.

"That he may taste the evil of his deed" is connected to the settled (istiqrar) that the understood element is connected to. It was said: it is connected to "jaza'", and it was said: to "siyam" or "ta'am". It was said: to a deleted verb, which is "juziya" or "shara'na dhalika" or similar. "Al-wabal" originally means heaviness, and from it come "al-wabil" for heavy rain, "al-wabil" for heavy food that is slow to digest, and "al-mar'a al-wakhim" (unwholesome pasture), and the "wakhshab" (club) of the fullers. The pronoun in "amrih" refers either to God the Exalted, or to the one who killed the game, meaning: that he may taste the heaviness of his act and the evil consequence of violating the sanctity of what he is in, or the severe heaviness of opposing the mighty command of God the Exalted. On this latter reading, a genitive must be understood, as we indicated, because the command of God the Exalted has no evil in it; the evil lies only in opposing it.

﴿God has pardoned what is past﴾ of the game you took while in the state of ihram, so He did not make it a sin for you nor required compensation for you; or He did not hold you accountable for what you did of that in the Jahiliyyah, even though it is also a great sin, since you were then upon the law of Isma'il, peace be upon him, and the hunting of game was forbidden in it. The report that it was forbidden in the Jahiliyyah has already been mentioned, as has the punishment for killing game by a painful blow. ﴿And whoever returns﴾ to the like of that, killing game intentionally while in ihram, ﴿then Allah will take retribution from him﴾, meaning he will be subject to Allah the Exalted's retribution, because when the conditional response is a present affirmative verb, it is not preceded by "fa" due to the resemblance of the subject to the condition, and that "fa" is superfluous, and the clause after it is the predicate, and there is then no need to supply a subject. The retribution here means punishment in the Hereafter. As for expiation, according to Ata', Ibrahim, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and the majority, it is obligatory upon the one who returns, so the compensation is repeated with each repetition of the killing.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Shurayh, that if he returns, he is not judged for expiation, to the extent that they used to ask the one seeking a fatwa: "Did you kill any game before this?" If he said "yes", they did not judge him; if he said "no", there was a judgment against him. This is by clinging to the apparent wording of the verse.

You know that the threat against the one who returns does not contradict the obligation of compensation upon him, and it was not stated explicitly because it was known from what came before. It was said: the meaning of the verse is "and whoever returns" after the prohibition to what he was doing before, and this is not far-fetched. As for taking the retribution to mean retribution in this world through expiation, though it is possible, it is contrary to the apparent meaning; likewise the meaning that he is retributed against if he does not expiate.

They differed concerning the case where a muhrim is compelled to eat carrion or game. Zufar said: he eats the carrion, not the game, because the grounds of prohibition are multiple. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: he takes the game and pays the compensation, because the prohibition of carrion is more severe. Do you not see that the prohibition of game is lifted by exiting the state of ihram? It is thus temporary, unlike the prohibition of carrion. So he should aim at the lighter of the two prohibitions rather than the more severe. Though game is forbidden in ihram, in a case of necessity the prohibition is lifted, so he kills it, eats from it, and pays the compensation, as in al-Mabsut.

In al-Khaniyyah: if a muhrim is compelled to eat carrion or game, then carrion is preferable according to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad. Abu Yusuf and al-Hasan said: he slaughters the game. If the game is already slaughtered, then the game is preferable according to all. If he finds the flesh of game and the flesh of a human, the flesh of game is preferable. If he finds game and a dog, the dog is preferable, because eating the game involves committing two prohibited acts. It is narrated from Muhammad that game is preferable to pork. End of quote. This contradicts what was mentioned in al-Mabsut.

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, the Victorious who cannot be overcome, ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾, severe, so He takes retribution against those who transgress His limits, oppose His commands, and persist in His disobedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 96 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Lawful for you﴾, O those in ihram, is the game of the sea, that is, what is hunted in water, whether sea, river, or pond. It is that whose breeding and dwelling is in water, whether edible or otherwise, as in al-Bada'i'. In Kirmani's Manasik, the one permitted to the muhrim from the game of the sea is fish specifically, and as for its like of birds, there is no concession for it. The first view is the more sound. ﴿And its food﴾, that is, what is fed from its game, and it is conjoined to ﴿game﴾ by way of conjoining the specific to the general. The meaning is: it is lawful for you to pursue all that is hunted in the waters, to benefit from it, and to eat what is eaten from it, which is fish according to us. According to Ibn Abi Layla, "game" and "food" are on their verbal (masdar) meanings, and he supposed an elided noun in "game of the sea," and made the pronoun of "its food" refer to it (the game) and not to the sea. That is: it is lawful for you to hunt the animals of the sea and to feed them and eat them; thus, in his view, eating all the animals of the sea is lawful, insofar as they are its animals. It was also said: the intended meaning of "game of the sea" is what is hunted and then dies, and of "its food" what the sea casts up dead. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Ibn 'Umar, and Qatadah.
It was said: the intended meaning of the first is the fresh, and of the second the salted, and it was called "food" because it is stored to be eaten, so it became like the staple foods of sustenance. This was narrated from Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jarir, and Mujahid, and it is one of the two narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. In it there is remoteness, and more remote than it is that the intended meaning of "its food" is what grows by its water of crops and fruits. And it was read (wa-tu'muhu). ﴿As a provision for you﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for "it is made lawful" (li-uhilla), that is, as enjoyment. Al-Zamakhshari, in the Kashshaf, restricted it to the food, just as ﴿nafilah﴾ in the matter of the circumstantial (hal) from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as a gift (nafilah)﴾ is restricted to Jacob, peace be upon him. What led him to this, as al-Shihab said, is his school, which is the school of our great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, that the game of the sea is divided into what is eaten and what is not eaten, and that its food is what is eaten from it. However, it was objected to him that it leads to the single verb attributed to two conjoined agents having the object of purpose mentioned after them belong to one of them and not the other; like "Zayd and 'Amr stood up out of honor for you," where the honor is restricted to the standing of one of them, and this is ambiguous. As for the circumstantial in the mentioned verse, it is not comparable to this, because in it there is a clear rational indication, since the nafilah is a grandson, so it has no connection to Isaac, for he is the son of Abraham's loins, peace be upon them both. And according to other than the Imam's school, the object of purpose has no restriction to either one of them, and this is evident and clear.
It was said: it is in the accusative as an absolute infinitive (masdar mu'akkad) for an elided verb, that is, "He enjoyed you with it as enjoyment." It was also said: it is emphatic of the meaning of "is made lawful," for it is in the force of "He enjoyed you with it with enjoyment," like His statement: ﴿The Book of Allah upon you﴾. It was also said, and it is not worthwhile: it is a circumstance supposed from "food," that is, enjoyed by it for those of you who are resident, who eat it fresh, and for those of you who are travelling, who take it as provision dried, and it is the feminine of "sayyar" with regard to the group, as al-Raghib said.
﴿And the game of the land is forbidden to you﴾, and it is what breeds and dwells on land, of what is refractory due to its wildness that exists in original creation. Thus the tame gazelle enters, and the wild camel and sheep exit, due to the attribute that occurs to them. The fact that the slaughter of the tame gazelle is by cutting the throat, and of the domestic animal gone wild by wounding, contradicts this, because slaughter by cutting and wounding revolve with possibility and its absence, not with being game and not being game.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ excepted five. In the two Sahihs, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Five of the creatures there is no sin upon the muhrim in killing: the scorpion, the mouse, the rabid dog, the crow, and the kite." What is in a narration of Muslim has been mentioned before, and their being named "fawasiq" (wicked ones) has come. In Fath al-Qadir: some of the land game is excepted, like the wolf, the crow, and the kite. As for the rest of the wicked ones, they are not game. As for the rest of the predatory beasts, the explicit ruling in the apparent narration is that there is no exception, and that killing them necessitates a penalty, which does not exceed a sheep if the muhrim initiated it; and if it initiated against him, there is nothing upon him. This is like the lion, the leopard, the panther, the falcon, and the hawk. As for the author of al-Bada'i', he divides the land animal into the edible and other than it, and the second into what generally initiates harm, like the lion, the wolf, and the panther, and what is not so, like the hyena, the leopard, and the fox. So killing the first and the last is not lawful unless it attacks, and killing the second is lawful and there is nothing upon it even if it does not attack. He considered the text's coming in the case of the wicked ones to be a coming that carries indication, and he did not report a disagreement. However, in al-Khaniyyah, and from Abu Yusuf: the lion is in the position of the wolf. In the apparent narration, all predatory beasts are game except the dog and the wolf. Perhaps the exception of the wolf is because it is mentioned among the excepted ones, as recorded by Abu Shaybah, al-Daraqutni, and al-Tahawi.
It was said: because it is the intended meaning of the "rabid dog" in the preceding report. It was also said: because it is of its meaning, so it is attached to its meaning by indication. As for the dog, its exception has come in the hadith, except that it was described in it with rabidity; perhaps the Imam only considers the genus.
It was examined: this leads to nullifying the stated attribute. It was answered: it is not for the qualification but to show the kind of its harm, for that is its nature. Sa'di Jalabi said: even if this examination were sound, it would necessitate taking account of the concept of the attribute, indeed of all concepts, and this is contrary to our principles. As for the claim that all predatory beasts are game except what is excepted, there is also a disagreement of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. For him they are included among the excepted wicked ones by analogy, or are attached to them by indication, or because the rabid dog encompasses them linguistically.
Some of the companions answered that analogy to the wicked ones is of what attacks us, due to its nearness to us, while the beast of prey is not like that, due to its distance from us, so it is not in the meaning of the wicked ones to be attached to them. And the name "dog," even if it encompasses it linguistically, does not encompass it by custom, and custom is stronger and weightier in this matter, as in oaths, because it is built on caution. And in this there is a lengthy discussion; so consider.
Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (harrama 'alaykum sayd) with the verb "harrama" in the active voice and "sayd" in the accusative, that is, "Allah has forbidden you the game of the land." ﴿As long as you are in ihram﴾, that is, ones in ihram.
It was read (dimtum) with a kasra on the dal, like (khiftum) from dama yadamu, and that is a dialect of it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (haraman) with two fathas, that is, possessors of sacred state (haram), in the sense of ihram, or in hyperbole. The apparent meaning of the verse necessitates the prohibition of what a non-muhrim hunts for the muhrim even if he had no part in it. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, and it is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and a group of the earlier generation. It was also argued for by what Muslim recorded from al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah al-Laythi, that "he gave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a wild donkey, and in another narration a wild ass, and in another from the flesh of a wild ass, and in another from the leg of a wild ass, and in another the hindquarter of a wild ass dripping blood, and in another the side of a wild ass, and in another a part of the flesh of game, and he, peace be upon him, was at al-Abwa' or Waddan, so he returned it to him, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. He said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw what was in my face, he said: 'We did not return it to you except that we are in ihram.'"
And from Abu Hurayrah, 'Ata', Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr, and al-Tahawi narrated from 'Umar, Talhah, and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them all, that it is lawful for him to eat what a non-muhrim hunts even if it was hunted for his sake, provided he did not direct him to it, did not point to it, and did not order him to hunt it.
