And likewise what he slaughtered before his ihram. This is the school of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, according to what al-Tahawi chose, because the address is to the muhrims, so it is as if it were said: "And forbidden to you is what you hunt on land," so the game of others is excluded from it; or it is said that the intended meaning is their game in reality or in legal effect, and the form of indication or command is from the second part. And from Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Dawud, may Allah have mercy on them all, what is hunted for him is permitted, because of what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The flesh of game is lawful for you while you are muhrims, so long as you do not hunt it or it is not hunted for you.'" It was answered: Muhammad narrated from Abu Hanifah, from Ibn al-Munkadir, from Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah, may Allah be pleased with him, that "We discussed the flesh of game that the muhrim eats while the Prophet ﷺ was sleeping, and our voices rose, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ awoke and said: 'About what are you disputing?' We said: 'About the flesh of game that the muhrim eats.' So he ordered us to eat it." Al-Hafiz Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn narrated from Abu Hanifah, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from his grandfather al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, who said: "We used to carry the flesh of game dried, and we used to take it as provision, and we used to eat it while we were muhrims with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."
Muslim recorded from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Qatadah, from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out for hajj and we set out with him, and he sent away a group of his companions, among them Abu Qatadah, and said: 'Take the seashore until you meet me.' He said: So they took the seashore, and when they departed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went ahead, and they had all entered ihram except Abu Qatadah, for he had not entered ihram. While they were journeying, they saw wild asses, so Abu Qatadah charged at them and wounded a female one from them. They dismounted and ate of its flesh. He said: Then they said: 'We ate flesh while we are in ihram.' He said: So they carried what remained of the flesh of the she-ass. When they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we had entered ihram, and Abu Qatadah had not entered ihram, and we saw wild asses, so Abu Qatadah charged at them and wounded a female one from them, and we dismounted and ate of its flesh, and we said: We eat the flesh of game while we are in ihram, so we carried what remained of its flesh.' So he, peace be upon him, said: 'Is there anyone with you who ordered him or pointed to it with something?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Then eat what remains of its flesh.'"
And in a narration of Muslim: "He ﷺ said: 'Do you have any of it with you?' They said: 'We have its leg with us.' So he took it, peace be upon him, and ate it." The hadith of Jabir is interpreted in two ways. The first: the lam is for ownership, and the meaning is that it be hunted and made to be his, so its implication is the conveying of the ownership of the game itself to the muhrim, which is impossible, for he could not own it and then eat from its flesh. The second: the carrying of it to mean that it is hunted by his command. This is because the general case of a person's action for another is that it is by his request, and holding to an interpretation to remove contradiction is as several have said. Ibn al-Humam said: It may be said that the principles require that a contradiction be judged between the hadith of Jabir and the first two of these three reports, because Talhah's saying "so he ordered us to eat it" is restricted, in our view, to when the muhrim did not point to it, according to the sound view, unlike Abu 'Abd Allah al-Jurjani, and not when he did not order him to kill it, as the hadith of Abu Qatadah indicates; so it is necessary to restrict it to when it was not hunted for the muhrim, by the other hadith.
The hadith of al-Zubayr's gist is the narration of events of reports, and events have no generality, so it is possible that what they used to carry of the flesh of game was for provision, provided it was not hunted for the sake of the muhrims; indeed this is the apparent case, for they took provision from the settled area, and the ihram was after departing to the miqat. So it is better to argue for the original claim by the hadith of Abu Qatadah mentioned, by way of contradiction, for it conveys that
the Prophet, peace be upon him, did not give permission for them to eat until he asked them about the impediments to lawfulness, whether they were present or not; so if it were among the impediments that it be hunted for them, he would have included it among what he asked about in the search for impediments, to answer with permissibility upon its absence.

This meaning is almost explicit in negating that hunting is a prohibition, so it contradicts the hadith of Jabir and takes precedence over it, because the hadith of Ibn Abbas (the one stating the opposite) is authentically established: it is in the two Sahihs and the other canonical books, unlike the hadith of Jabir. Indeed, it has been said that the hadith of Jabir is discontinuous (munqati') because al-Mutallib's narration from Jabir was not heard from Jabir according to more than one scholar, and that there are narrators in its chain who are weak (lin). Once what we have adopted is established by what we have mentioned, there is evidence for the interpretation mentioned. End of quotation. You know that the hadith of Jabir also has some difficulty from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, but perhaps the matter there is easy.

There remains the question that the hadith of Sa'b, on its surface, contradicts the evidence used by the people of the last two schools. Some Hanafis answered by saying that it contains irregularity (idtirab), which the hadith of Qatadah does not have, to the point that Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri narrated from his father that Sa'b "presented to the Messenger of God ﷺ the hindquarter of a wild ass at al-Juhfa, and he ate from it, peace and blessings be upon him, and the people ate." So the hadith of Qatadah is preferable. What occurred in it (the irregularity) occurred in the Hajj, as the narration we have cited relates. It is known that the Messenger of God ﷺ did not perform Hajj after the Hijrah except the Farewell Pilgrimage.

al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, answered: It is possible that the Prophet ﷺ knew that it had been hunted for him, so he returned it to him, and therefore it does not contradict the hadith of Jabir. His ﷺ reason for returning it, that he was in ihram, does not preclude that it was hunted for him, because hunted game is only forbidden to a person when it was hunted for him under the condition that he is in ihram. So he ﷺ made clear the condition by which it becomes forbidden. It has also been said that Jabir only gave a wild ass, and the Prophet ﷺ returned it because it is impermissible for one in ihram to own game.

It is not hidden that the narrations indicating partiality (al-ba'diyyah, that he gave part of an animal) are more numerous, and there is no contradiction between them. So the narration that he gave a wild ass is to be interpreted as an instance of using the name of the whole for a part (ithlaq al-kull 'ala al-ba'd). The reverse is impossible here, because using "man" (al-rajul), for example, for the whole animal is not customary. They have stated explicitly that it is not permissible to apply to Zayd "isba'" (finger) or the like, because the condition for applying the name of a part to the whole is mutual necessity (al-talazum), like "neck" (raqabah) and "head" (ra's) for a human, since there is no human without them. This is unlike "man" (rajul) and "nail" (zufr). As for applying "eye" ('ayn) to "sight" (ru'yah), this is not from the standpoint of being a human, but from the standpoint of being a watcher (raqib), and from this standpoint it is realized without an eye. Or it is one of the meanings of a homonym (al-mushtarak al-lafzi), as many of them have counted it. So be alert.

**"And fear God"** regarding what He has forbidden you of hunting, or in respect of all sins, of which this is one, **"to whom you will be gathered."**
69
Not to anyone else, so that one might imagine escape from His taking you to hold on to that other.

* * *

Furthermore, from the allusive (ishari) interpretation (al-ishara, the mystical reading of the verses): **"O you who have believed"** with knowledge-based faith, **"do not forbid"** by your shortcoming in the spiritual journey **"the good things God has made lawful for you"** from the unveilings of states and the manifestations of attributes. **"And do not transgress"** by the appearance of the self with its qualities. **"And eat of what God has provided for you"**, that is, make what God, exalted is He, has bestowed upon you of the knowledge of manifestations and the gifts of states and stations the nourishment of your hearts, **"lawful and good. And fear God"** regarding the attainment of that for you, by returning it from Him and to Him.

Many have considered this an address to the arrivers (al-wasilin) among the masters of the spiritual path, when they wished to return to the people of the beginnings (al-bidayat) through striving (al-mujahadat). So they were forbidden from that and commanded to eat the lawful and good. They interpreted "lawful" as what reaches the gnostics from the treasuries of the unseen without hardship, and "good" as what strengthens the heart in longing for God, exalted is He, and remembrance of His majesty. It has also been said: the lawful and good is what one eats while witnessing (shuhud), and otherwise while remembering (dhikr), for eating in heedlessness is forbidden in the law of the path. Others said: the lawful and good is what the gnostic sees in the treasury of destiny (qadar) and then takes from it with the attribute of contentment and submission. The forbidden is what was decreed for another, and he strives to seek it for himself.

**"God will not hold you accountable for the inadvertence in your oaths"**, which is swearing out of weariness of the self, exhaustion of the faculties, and the dominance of the authority of desire. They counted among the inadvertence in oaths the swearing by God, exalted is He, by His beauty and majesty, when longing overcomes them and the sensing of rapture, that He should grant them some of His turning toward them (iqbal) and His union (wisal), exalted and mighty is He. For that is **"inadvertence"** in the law of contentment and the doctrine of submission. What requires this is what is pointed to in the words: "I desire His union, and He desires my separation, so I abandon what I desire for what He desires." However, God will not hold the swearer accountable for it, because He knows the weakness of his state.

They also counted among this what passes on the tongues of the wayfarers in the overwhelming of ecstasy (wajd): renewing the covenant and confirming the pact, like the saying of one of them: "By your right, I have not looked at anyone other than you with the eye of love until I see you." For that contradicts monotheism (tawhid). And: "Is there in the abode any abode?" No, rather He is God, the One, the Subduer.

But He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have made firmly, and that is when you resolve upon separation and expose yourselves to abandonment from the depths of the heart. **"Its expiation is feeding ten needy persons"**, and it is, according to some, the five outward senses and the five inward senses. **"From the average of what you feed your families"**, and they are the heart, the secret (sirr), and the hidden spirit (ruh khafi). Their food is longing (shawq), love (mahabbah), sincerity (sidq), sincerity of intention (ikhlas), surrender (tafwid), submission (taslim), contentment (rida), intimacy (uns), awe (haybah), witnessing (shuhud), and unveilings (kushuf). The average is remembrance (dhikr), reflection (fikr), longing (shawq), reliance (tawakkul), devotion (ta'abbud), fear (khawf), and hope (raja'), and feeding the senses with that means occupying them with it. **"Or clothing them"** with the garment of piety (taqwa). **"Or freeing a slave"**, which is the slave of the self, so that one frees it from the bondage of greed and desire. **"And whoever does not find"** and is not able, **"then fasting three days"**: so he refrains on the first day from what he resolved upon, on the second day from what does not concern him, and on the third day from returning to it.

It has also been said that God, exalted is He, alluded by fasting three days to repentance and steadfastness in it for as long as the world lasts. For it has been said: the world is three days: a day that has passed, a day you are in, and a day you do not know what God, exalted is He, will decree in it.

**"And obey God"** by annihilation (fana') in Him, **"and obey the Messenger"** by subsistence (baqa') after annihilation. **"And beware"** of the appearance of that by looking at your selves. **"But if you turn away, know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear delivery"**, and he did not fall short in it, so the shortcoming is from you. **"There is no blame upon those who have believed"** by imitation (taqlid), **"and done righteous deeds"**, the bodily legal acts, **"for what they have eaten"** of permissible things, **"when they fear God"** from the polytheism of egoism (shirk al-ananiyyah), **"and believe"** in selfhood (huwiyyah), **"then fear God"** from this polytheism, which is annihilation, **"and do good"** by subsisting through Him, exalted is His majesty. This is what al-Naysaburi said.

Another said: there is no blame upon those who have believed with the faith of the essence (al-iman al-'aini) through the oneness of actions (tawhid al-af'al), and acted in accordance with the requirement of their faith with deeds that bring them out of the veils of actions and make them fit to see the actions of the Real. There is blame and constriction for what they have enjoyed of kinds of portions (huzuz) when they avoid the remnants of their actions and take God, exalted is He, as a shield (wiqayah) in the origination of actions from them. And they believe in the oneness of attributes and do what brings them out of its veils and makes them fit for witnessing the divine attributes by effacement (mahw) in them. Then they fear the remnants of their attributes and take God, exalted is He, as a shield against the manifestation of His attributes over them. And they believe in the oneness of the essence, then they fear the remainder of their essences, and take God, exalted is He, as a shield in their existence through pure annihilation (fana' mahd) and dissolution (istihlak) in the very essence. And they do good by witnessing detail within the very unity, and steadfastness in subsistence after annihilation. **"And God loves the good-doers"**, those who remain in their annihilation, or those who witness the oneness within multiplicity, observing the rights of details within the very unity, through the true existence (wujud haqqani).

**"O you who have believed"** in the unseen, **"He will surely test you"** along the way and in the state of ihram, for visiting the Ka'bah of arrival, **"with something of the game"**, that is, of portions and psychic aims, **"which your hands and spears can reach"**, meaning what is made easy for you and what prepares the means by which it is attained.

It has also been said: what the hands reach is bodily pleasures, and what the spears reach is imaginative pleasures. **"That God may know"** with the knowledge upon which the reward is based **"who fears Him in the unseen"**, that is, in a state of absence. This is not possible except for those who believe in the unseen, because it relates to punishment, which belongs to the category of acts. As for in presence (hudur), there is awe and dread rather than fear. The first is through the manifestation of the attributes of lordship and greatness, and the second through the manifestation of the essence. So fear, as has been said, is from the attributes of the self, dread is from the attributes of the heart, and awe is from the attributes of the spirit. **"And whoever transgresses after that"** by taking some of the portions, **"for him is painful punishment"**, which is the punishment of veiling.

**"O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in ihram"**, that is, in the state of true ihram. **"And whoever of you kills it intentionally"**, by committing some of the carnal portions deliberately, **"then the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed"**, by overcoming that power with which he committed it, from the bestial powers of the self, with something that equals that portion. **"Judged by it are two just men among you"**, and they are the theoretical and the practical faculties. **"As an offering reaching the Ka'bah"** of the reality, and that is by annihilating them in God, mighty and exalted is He. **"Or an expiation: feeding needy persons, or the equivalent of that in fasting"**, that is, or by concealing that faculty through charity or fasting. **"Lawful for you is the game of the sea"**, which is what is in the spiritual world of gnostic knowledge, **"and its food"**, which is beneficial knowledge of dealings and ethics, **"as provision"**, that is, as enjoyment, **"for you"**, O travelers on the path of the Truth, **"and for the traveling caravan"**, those journeying the journey of the Hereafter. **"But forbidden to you is the game of the land"**, which in the corporeal world is the sensible things and carnal portions. **"And fear God"** in your journey. **"And know that you will be gathered to Him"** through annihilation. So strive in the spiritual journey and do not stop at the obstacles. He, God, exalted is He, is the Facilitator of guidance, and to Him is the return and the final destination.

[Page 36]

﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah﴾, i.e., He made it. It was named Ka'bah, as is narrated from Ikrimah and Mujahid, because it is square. Al-taksib (cubing, squaring) means making something square, and the word is used in the language for any square house. It is also said that al-taksib means elevation, and it is said that for this reason the Ka'bah was named Ka'bah because it is elevated. From the same root comes ka'b (ankle) of a person, because it protrudes, and ka'abat al-mar'ah (the woman's breast became prominent), when her breast swelled. It is also said that it was named Ka'bah because it stands apart from other buildings. Al-Kirmani rejected this and returned it to the previous explanation, since whatever stands apart from buildings rises above the ground. His Exalted words ﴿the Sacred House﴾ are an explanatory apposition (ataf bayan) in the sense of praise, because it was known among them for its glorification, so it came to have the meaning of something glorified. Or, because it is described as "sacred," which indicates its sanctity and greatness. The mention of "house" serves as a preparation for it, so the objection by rigidity is rigidity without clarification. It is also said that it was mentioned for clarification, because the Khath'am tribe had a house that they called the Yemeni Ka'bah.

It is permitted that it be a substitute (badal), and that it be a second object (maf'ul thani) of ja'ala (made). His, glory be to Him, words ﴿as a means of support for mankind﴾ are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). This is refuted by the coordination of what follows it to the first object, as you will learn shortly, God willing. Rather, this is the second object.

It is also said that ja'ala here means khalaqa (created), so it takes one object, and this is a state (hal). The meaning of it being a support for them is that it is the means of setting right their affairs and mending them, in religion and in worldly life, since it was a place of security and refuge for them and a gathering place for their trade. They come to it from every deep mountain pass. For this reason Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Whoever comes to this House seeking something of this world and the Hereafter, he will attain it." From this some scholars derived that trade during the Hajj is not disliked. This is narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "All the people had kings who repelled some of them from others, but there were no such kings among the Arabs. So Allah, exalted is He, made the Sacred House a support for them, by which He repelled some of them from others. So if a man met the killer of his father or his son at it, he would not kill him." According to this, the intended "people" are the Arabs specifically. It is also said that the meaning of it being a support for mankind is that it is a security for them from destruction. As long as the House is visited by people, they will not perish. If it is demolished and the Hajj is abandoned, they will perish. This is narrated from 'Ata'.

Ibn 'Amir read qiyaman (with a yā'), as a verbal noun (masdar) like shiyaʿ. The analogy would have been that its waw is not changed to yā', but since it was changed to alif in its verb form, the verbal noun followed it in the modification of its middle radical.

﴿And the Sacred Month﴾, i.e., the month in which the Hajj is performed, which is Dhu al-Hijjah. The definite article is for a specific reference, by the context of its companions. But more than one scholar preferred that it refers to the category (jins), which is the original usage, and the known context does not specify a particular reference. The intended meaning is the Sacred Months, which are four: one single (fard), which is Rajab, and three consecutive (sard), which are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram. The single is Rajab and the consecutive are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram. It is coordinated with the Ka'bah, so the second object is omitted, relying on what has passed, meaning: and He made the Sacred Month, the offering (hady), and the garlands also a support for them. By "garlands" is meant the animals adorned with garlands, which are camels. They are singled out for mention because the reward in them is greater and the Hajj is more evident through them. It is also said that the statement is on its apparent meaning. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Mijlaz that among the people of the Jahiliyyah, a man who entered the state of ihram would wear a garland of hair, and no one would confront him. When he had performed Hajj and completed it, he would wear a garland of idhkhir (a fragrant grass). It is also said: a man would hang on his camel or on himself a garland of the bark of the trees of the Sacred Precinct, so he would fear no one and no one would harm him. They used to change (the rules) in the Sacred Months, and they would sheathe the spear-points in them, and people would go out in them to their livelihoods, fearing no one. They inherited this, as it is said, from the religion of Isma'il, peace be upon him.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the aforementioned appointment alone, or together with what was mentioned of the command to observe the sanctity of the state of ihram and other things. The place of the demonstrative is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, which the context indicates, and the lam that follows is connected to it. It is also said that its place is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the ruling we have established is that. Or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: that ruling is the truth. The first ruling is the nearer one. The estimate is: He legislated that, ﴿so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾. The legislation of these laws, which entail repelling religious and worldly harms before they occur, and bringing about primary and otherworldly benefits, is among the clearest proofs of the wisdom of the Lawgiver and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, glory be to Him. ﴿And that Allah is, of everything﴾, whether necessary, impossible, or possible, ﴿Knowing﴾.

79

Perfect in knowledge. This is a generalization after a specification, and the particular is placed first because it serves as evidence for what follows.

It is permitted that what is in the heavens and the earth means the existing entities within them, and "everything" means the matters related to those existing things, such as accidents and states, which belong to the category of meanings. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is for the reason that has passed more than once.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 98:

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. This is a warning to whoever violates His sacred prohibitions or persists in doing so. Punishment (ʿiqab), as it has been said, is the harm that is accompanied by contempt and humiliation. It is called ʿiqab because it is deserved right after the sin (ʿuqayb al-dhanb). ﴿And that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

89

It is a promise to whoever safeguards the observance of His sacred prohibitions and refrains from violating them. The reason for placing the warning first is clear.

"The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message)" [5:99]. He did not spare any effort in conveying to you what you were commanded, so there is no excuse left for you after this. This is an emphatic statement of the obligation to carry out what He, glorified is He, has commanded.

Al-Balagh (conveyance) is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun (masdar), as has been pointed out, [in the verse] "And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal" [5:99].

99

– So that He may deal with you according to what you deserve in that matter.

Say, O Muhammad: "The corrupt (al-khabith) and the good (al-tayyib) are not equal," i.e., the bad (al-radi') and the good (al-jayyid) of everything. This is a general ruling affirming that there is no equality before God between the two kinds, and a warning against the bad of them. Although the occasion of revelation was that the Muslims wanted to take advantage of the pilgrims of Yamama, who had with them great merchandise, and so they were forbidden from that as has already been mentioned. It was also said: it was revealed concerning "a man who asked the Messenger of God ﷺ, saying: O Messenger of God, wine was my trade, and I have gathered wealth from selling it. Will that benefit me if I spend it in obedience to God Most High?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "If you spend it on the Hajj or on jihad, it will not equal the wing of a gnat. God Most High accepts only the good."

And from al-Hasan, and al-Jubba'i chose it: al-khabith is the unlawful (al-haram) and al-tayyib is the lawful (al-halal). Ibn Jarir and others related from al-Suddi, who said: "The corrupt are the polytheists, and the good are the believers." The mention of al-khabith first is to indicate from the outset that the deficiency that the non-equality reveals lies in it, not in its opposite; and the indication of its verification has already been given earlier. ﴿And even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you﴾, i.e., even if it pleases you, O observer with the eye of reflection, ﴿the abundance of the corrupt﴾.

It was also said: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and what is meant is his community, and the "waw" is for conjoining the conditional clause to a similar one that is implied. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause, i.e., "whether it does not impress you or it does impress you," and both are in the position of a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿is not equal﴾, i.e., they are equal in every supposed state. The first has been omitted in this type of construction because the second clearly indicates it, for when a thing is realized along with an obstacle, it is all the more realized without it. The answer to "law" (even if) is omitted in both clauses because what precedes it indicates it. ﴿So fear God, O people of understanding﴾, in seeking out the corrupt even if it is abundant, and prefer the good even if it is scarce, for the criterion of evaluation is goodness and badness, not abundance and scarcity. In the majority of cases, the best of everything is its least. How well said is the one who said:

"People are a thousand, of them one is like a unit, and one is like a thousand if he is commanded for us."

And in the verse, as has been said, there is an indication of the dominance of the people of Islam even if they are few. ﴿That you may succeed﴾.

1

- Hoping that you will attain success (al-falah) and triumph (al-fawz) with the great reward and lasting bliss.

**"O you who have believed, do not ask about things..."** (5:101). The apparent wording, as Ibn Ya'ish said, requires that *ashya'* be the plural of *shay'*, because *fa'l* with a weak middle radical takes the paucity plural (*jam' al-qilla*) on the pattern *af'āl*, as in *bayt* and *abyāt*, *shaykh* and *ashyākh*. However, they saw that it is not declined when indefinite, as here, so the opinions of the scholars diverged on it.

Sibawayh and al-Khalil held that the *hamza* is the feminine marker, that the word is a singular noun used to mean a plural, like *al-hulafā'* and *al-tur afā'*. Thus *ashyā'* was originally *shay'ā'*, with two *hamzas* separated by an *alif*. The first *hamza*, which is the third radical of the word, was moved before the *fā'* (*shī'*) to avoid the heaviness of two *hamzas* separated by an *alif* and preceded by a weak letter, the *yā'*. The second *hamza* is an added feminine marker, which is why the word is not declined. Its pattern is *la'fā'*. The most that this view involves is metathesis (*qalb*, transposition of sounds), which is frequent in their speech. They accepted it despite the lack of heaviness, as in *aynuq* and *qisan* and similar words, so accepting it when there is heaviness is more appropriate. The objection that it contradicts the basic form does no harm.

Al-Farra' held that it is the plural of *shay'* with a doubled *yā'* and a *hamza*, on the pattern of *hayyin* and *layyin*. They lightened it, saying *shay'* as in *mayt* becoming *mayt*. After lightening, they pluralised it as *ashyā'*, with two *hamzas* separated by an *alif* after a *yā'*, on the pattern *af'alā'*. Two *hamzas* came together, one being the third radical and the other the feminine marker. They lightened this by changing the first *hamza* into a *yā'*, then deleted the first *yā'*, which is the middle radical. Its pattern thus became *af'alā'*. It was also said, in the morphology of this view, that they deleted the *hamza* which is the third radical, because the heaviness came from it, so its pattern is *af'ā'*. The non-declension is due to the feminine *hamza*. This view was considered good if the original form of *shay'*, when lightened, were *shayyi'* with doubling, as evidence.

Al-Akhfash held that it is the plural of *shay'* on the pattern *fals*, and that its original form was *ashyi'ā'* with two *hamzas* separated by an *alif* after a *yā'*. Then the same processes already mentioned were applied to it. Al-Zajjaj rejected this, saying that *fa'l* is pluralised as *af'ilā'*. Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini debated al-Akhfash on this question, as Abu 'Ali said in *al-Takmila*. He said: "How do you diminutive *ashyā'*?" He said: "I say *ushayyā'*." Al-Mazini said: "Why not return it to the singular and say *shuyay'āt*, because *af'alā'* is diminutized?" He did not come up with a convincing answer, end quote. He meant that *af'ilā'* is among the patterns of abundance (*jam' al-kathra*), and plurals of abundance are not diminutized in their own forms but are diminutized in their singular units, then the singular is pluralised with *alif* and *tā'*, as when you say in the diminutive of *dirham*: *durayhimāt*.

Abu 'Ali's answer, as he said, is that *af'ilā'* here may be diminutized in its own form because it has become a substitute for *af'āl*, as shown by their permitting the numeral to be attached to it, just as it is attached to *af'āl*. What shows it is also a substitute is their masculine form of the numeral attached to it, as in *thalāthat ashyā'*. Just as it has come to have the status of *af'āl* in this position, by the indication mentioned, so it may be diminutized from the point of view that *af'āl* may be diminutized. The diminutive in its own form is not prohibited, because the meaning that prevents this pattern from being diminutized elsewhere is lifted from *ashyā'*, namely that it has become like *af'āl*. If this is so, then the word does not combine two things that contradict each other, namely the intention of paucity and abundance in one word, end quote.

His meaning, as Ibn al-Shajari said, is that *fa'lā'* in this position has become a substitute for *af'āl*: the regular analogy for the plural of *shay'* would have been *ashyā'an* declined, as when you say, for the plural of *fay'*, *afyā'*, with that *hamza* of the plural being the *hamza* of the singular. But they placed *ashyā'*, whose *hamza* is feminine, in the position of *ashyā'* whose pattern is *af'āl*. As for his argument for permitting the diminutive of *ashyā'* in its own form, namely that they have become a substitute for *af'āl* by the indication that they attached the numeral to them and added the *tā'* to it, saying *thalāthat ashyā'*, this is not a valid indication, because the paucity and abundance patterns share this feature. Do you not see that they attach the numeral to patterns of abundance when the pattern of paucity is absent, saying *thalāthat shusūʻ* and *khamsat darāhim*? As for attaching the *tā'* in our saying *thalāthat ashyā'*, although *ashyā'* is feminine, because the singular is masculine: do you not see that you say *thalāthat anbiyā'*, *khamsat asdiqā'* and *sab'at shu'arā'*, attaching the *tā'*, even though the plural form is feminine? That is because the singular is *nabī*, *ṣadīq* and *shā'ir*, just as the singular of *ashyā'* is *shay'*. So what indication is there in his statement "and it indicates that they are a substitute, their making the numeral masculine when attached to them," etc.? Then he said: What may be used as evidence for al-Akhfash's view is that the pattern *af'alā'* was diminutized in its own form, although it is one of the patterns of abundance, because its pattern was reduced by deleting its last radical, so it became *af'ā'*. They therefore likened it to *af'āl* and diminutized it.

Al-Kisa'i held that it is the plural of *shay'* like *day/ḍayf* and *adyāf* (plural of *ḍayf*, guest). Against this was raised the objection of non-declension without a reason, and it would require declining *abnā'* and *asmā'*. Al-Kisa'i was aware of this objection and pointed to its answer: that it is on the pattern *af'āl*, but it became frequent in speech so that it resembled *fa'lā'*, and so it was not declined, just as *ḥamrā'* is not declined. They pluralised it as *ashāwā* like *ʻadhrā'* and *ʻadhārā*, and as *ashyāwāt* like *ḥamrā'* and *ḥamrāwāt*. So they treated *ashyā'*, although it is on *af'āl*, as they treat *ḥamrā'* and *ʻadhrā'* in both the broken and sound plurals. This was rejected on the grounds that abundance requires lightening it and declining it. One of the scholars supported it by saying that the Arabs took into account, in the chapter of diptotes, verbal resemblance, as it is said of *sarāwīl* that it is not declined because of its resemblance to *maṣābīḥ*. They also treated the *alif* of extension (*alif al-ilḥāq*) as the *alif* of the shortened feminine, but with the operation of the word intact, so they took into account the mere form. Let this be of that kind.

It was also said that it is the plural of *shay'*, and its pattern is *af'alā'*, the plural of *fa'īl*, like *naṣīb* and *anṣibā'*, and *ṣadīq* and *aṣdiqā'*. The first *hamza*, which is the third radical, was deleted, and the *yā'* was given a *fatḥa* so that the *alif* would be preserved, so *ashyā'* became on the pattern *af'ā'*. And Makki made its morphology like the view of al-Akhfash, when the *hamza* is changed into a *yā'* and then one of the two *yā's* is deleted. Deleting it from the plural was good, as he deleted it from the singular, because of frequency of use and the non-declension due to the feminine extended *hamza*. This is good, except that objections arise against it as they did against al-Akhfash, together with other objections. Other views were also stated. And for al-Shihab, may God have mercy on him:

*Ashyā'* is *la'fā'* in pattern, and they transposed a letter, and before transposition it was *shay'ā'*. It was also said *af'āl*, not declined without a reason on their part. This is an allusion to the reply. Or *ashyā'*, with deletion of the *lām* due to heaviness. *Shay'* is the root of *shay'*, and they are opinions. And the root of *asmā'* is *ism*. Like *kasā*, decline it definitively, and do not let *asmā'* deceive you. Memorise, and say to the one who forgets high things in foolishness: "You have remembered a thing, and *ashyā'* have escaped you."

The apparent course of his treatment, like others, points to preferring the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Several scholars said it is the most apparent, because of their saying in its plural *ashāwī*, so they pluralised it as they pluralised *ṣaḥrā'* as *ṣaḥārī*. Its origin, as Ibn al-Shajari said, is *ashāyā* with *yā'*, because the *yā'* appears in *ashyā'*, but they changed it into *wāw* contrary to analogy, as they changed it into *wāw* in their saying *jaba'tu al-kharāj jibāwa*. Also, what indicates that it is singular is their diminutive of it as *ushayyi'ā'*, like *ṣuḥayrā'*. If it were a plural they would say *shay'āt*, as the indication has preceded. The full discussion is in the *Amālī* of Ibn al-Shajari.

**"If they are shown to you, it will distress you"** (5:101): an adjective of *ashyā'*, serving as a reason to refrain from asking about them. He then joined to it His saying, glorified is He: **"And if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be shown to you"** (5:101), meaning, by revelation, as the restriction of the question to the time of the revelation of the Qur'an indicates. This is because the distress in the first conditional clause is linked to the manifestation of those things, not to the asking about them. So He, may His majesty be exalted, followed it with what clearly implies that asking about them leads to their manifestation, which entails the feared harm. Thus the pronoun in "about them" (*ʻanhā*) refers to those things. It is not in the sense of "I have a dirham and half of it," as was wrongly thought. What is meant by them is what has no benefit for them, such as difficult obligations, which they might be able to bear, and hidden secrets by which they might be exposed. Just as asking about events that have occurred entails their manifestation, so asking about those obligations entails their being imposed upon them as a strictness, because they have wronged courtesy and abandoned what is better for them: submission to God's command without inquiry into it, and without examining its manner or quantity.

Thus in the *Sahih* of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ addressed us and said: "O people, God has prescribed for you the pilgrimage, so make the pilgrimage." A man said, and he is, as Ibn al-Humam said, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and Ahmad, al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim stated it explicitly in a sound hadith which they transmitted on the condition of the two Shaykhs: "Every year, O Messenger of God?" The Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, remained silent until he asked three times. Then he ﷺ said: "If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it. Then he ﷺ said: 'Leave me as I leave you, for those before you perished through their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. So when I order you to do something, do of it what you can, and when I forbid you from something, leave it.'" It is mentioned, as Ibn Hibban said, that the verse was revealed for this reason.

Muslim and others also transmitted that "they asked the Messenger of God ﷺ until they pressed him in questioning. One day he went up onto the pulpit and said: 'Do not ask me about anything but I will make it clear to you.' When they heard that, they fell silent and feared that something was about to happen." Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I began looking to the right and left, and every man had covered his head with his garment, weeping. Then a man who used to be disputed with was called by other than his father, and he said: 'O Messenger of God, who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafa.' Then 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, began and said: 'We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as Prophet. We seek refuge in Allah from trials.' Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'I have never seen good and evil like this day. Paradise and Hellfire were displayed to me until I saw them beyond the wall.'" Ibn Shihab mentioned that the mother of Ibn Hudhafa, whose name was Abd Allah, said to him when he came back to her: "I never heard anything more undutiful than you. Are you not afraid that your mother committed some of what the people of ignorance committed, and you would expose her before people's eyes?" Ibn Hudhafa said: "Even if he had attached me to a black slave, I would have been attached to him." Many transmitted from Qatada that this verse was revealed on that day.

As for its connection with what precedes it, according to the first report, it is very clear, since the discussion concerns matters related to the pilgrimage.

Al-Tabrisi mentioned three aspects of this. The first is that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: **"So that you may prosper"** (5:100), because among prosperity is abandoning questions about what has no good in it. The second is that it is connected to His saying, glorified is He: **"The Messenger's duty is only to convey"** (5:99), meaning that he has conveyed what contains benefit, so do not ask him about what does not concern you. The third is that it is connected to His saying, may His majesty be exalted: **"And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal"** (5:99), meaning: do not ask about those things, lest your secrets be made apparent. **"God has pardoned that"** (5:101), meaning: He has pardoned the question indicated by "do not ask."

The clause is a resumptive statement (istinaf) brought in to show that their prohibition of these matters was not merely to spare them from being troubled, but because they are in themselves a disobedience that brings accountability, and He, glory be to Him, has pardoned them. It also contains, in what it urges them toward, an exhortation to earnestly refrain from them, which is not hidden. That is, God the Exalted pardoned your previous question, in that He did not impose the pilgrimage (ḥajj) upon you every year as a recompense for your question. Or the meaning is that He overlooked your otherworldly punishment because of that, so do not return to the like of it. The pardon may also be taken in a sense that includes overlooking both worldly and otherworldly punishment, and some verifying scholars (muḥaqqiqūn) chose this view.

Another scholar permitted that the clause be a further description of "things" (ashyā'), with the pronoun in the genitive referring back to them, and it is the connecting pronoun (al-rābiṭ), meaning: do not ask about things which God the Exalted has not obligated you to. It was objected that this implies that the pilgrimage had been prescribed first and then abrogated (naskh, i.e. annulment of a ruling by a later one) by way of pardon, and that this would have been known to the addressees, since the attribute must necessarily be known to hold of the thing described before the addressee is told it, and both of these are necessarily absent with certainty. Furthermore, it would require that the prohibition be restricted to the matter of the pilgrimage and the like, whereas the noble wording is clearly intended to forbid asking about things which would distress them if disclosed, whether they are of the kind of rulings and obligations which, by being established and imposed through the question, would distress them as a punishment and an intensification, like the matter of the pilgrimage were it not for God's pardon of it; or of the kind of matters which occurred before the question and which, by being disclosed, cause distress, as in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) reported by Ibn Jarīr and others on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out angry, his face reddened, until he sat upon the pulpit. A man stood up to him and said: 'Where is my father?' He said: 'In the Fire.'" Some have interpreted the pardon as refraining from explaining these matters and from touching upon their affairs, and in that case this objection almost does not arise at all. The first interpretation is indicated by the statement of Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both: Mujāhid reported from him that whenever he was asked about something on which no report had come, he would say: "It is from the pardon," and then recite this verse. What Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, held is the resumptive reading alone, for the reason you know, and some eminent scholars' dismissal of it is not in its place. Then he said: If you say that those things do not at all cause distress, but rather are liable to cause pleasure as well, because their existence is a cause of the first (distress) and, from the standpoint of their non-existence, a cause of the other (pleasure) with certainty, and neither aspect is established in the mind of the questioner, and his purpose in asking is only to make clear whichever aspect it is, in whatever form, indeed the clarification of it under the aspect of causing pleasure, then he did not express it under the aspect of causing distress. I say: this is for the sake of establishing the thing forbidden, as you will come to know, together with what it contains of emphasis and intensification of the prohibition, because that aspect is the one which necessitates desisting, not the second aspect, nor the aspect of hesitation between the two causes. If it is said: the second conditional (clause) states that asking about those things which cause distress necessarily entails their disclosure, so how did it fail to entail disclosure in the matter of the pilgrimage, and it was not prescribed every year? We say: because the question occurred before the prohibition, and what is in the conditional is only the question occurring after it, since that is what necessitates severity and intensification, and there is no failure in that.

If it is said: what has been mentioned applies only where the question concerns matters that are undetermined between occurring and not occurring, as was mentioned regarding burdensome obligations, but where the question concerns matters that occurred before it, this hardly holds, because what the disclosure concerns is what has occurred in reality, and there is no averting it, whether the question came before or after, and what has occurred may be something that causes pleasure, as in the matter of Ibn Ḥudhāfah, so that it would be what the disclosure concerns and nothing else, and failure would then be definitively necessary. We say: there is no possibility of that, let alone its being necessary, for what is forbidden in reality is only asking about things that cause distress, which have occurred in reality before the question, like the question of the one who said: "Where is my father?" and not what encompasses them and other things that have not occurred but are possible to occur in the view of those under obligation, so that failure would have to occur in the case of non-occurrence.

The sum of the matter is that the implication of the noble wording, by way of explicit expression, is only the prohibition of asking about those things whose disclosure necessarily causes distress, either because those things are of the contingent kind that may or may not occur, so that they are disclosed at the question by way of a new ruling as punishment and intensification, as in the case where they belong to the category of burdensome obligations; or because they are things which occurred in reality before the question, so that they are disclosed at it by way of reporting them. Failure is impossible in both cases together. The source of the misconception is the failure to distinguish between what is forbidden and other things, based on not distinguishing, among those things, what actually exists or is contingently existent in reality from what is not so for those under obligation, and their regarding all of them as possibly existing or not. The benefit of this generality is desisting from those things absolutely, for fear of disclosing what is disliked. End. This is an exposition that has not been preceded to.

﴿And God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾

101

That is: He is exceedingly forgiving of sins and overlooks acts of disobedience. For this reason, glory be to Him, He pardoned you and did not punish you for what you had committed. The clause is an explanatory parenthetical (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī) confirming the pardon of God the Exalted mentioned earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 102:

﴿Qad sa'alaha﴾ i.e., the question (al-mas'alah). The pronoun is in the position of the verbal noun (masdar), not the direct object. The meaning is: "a people asked the like of it," in that it was forbidden and entailed calamity. ﴿Qawm﴾ (a people). The failure to state "the like" is for emphasis in warning. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "things" (ashya'), with an elided modifier, so that the pronoun is in the position of the direct object, and this is from the category of elision and conveyance (al-hadhf wal-iisal), the meaning being "asked about them." It has been said: there is no need to make it of that category, because the question here is a request for gifts (isti'ta'), and it transitively takes its object directly, as in your saying: "I asked him for a dirham," meaning "I requested it from him," not an inquiry as in the beginning of the verse.

There is disagreement about identifying the people. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, they are the people of 'Isa, peace be upon him, who asked him to send down the table (al-ma'idah) and then disbelieved in it. It has been said: they are the people of Salih, peace be upon him, who asked him for the she-camel and then hamstrung her and disbelieved in her. It has been said: they are the people of Musa, peace be upon him, who asked him to show them Allah openly, or asked him to explain the cow.

From Muqatil: they are the Children of Israel in general, who used to ask their prophets about things, and when they informed them, they denied them. From al-Suddi: they are the Quraysh, who asked the Prophet ﷺ to turn al-Safa into gold. Al-Jubba'i said: they used to ask him ﷺ about their lineages, and when he informed them, peace be upon him, they did not believe him and would say: "The matter is not so."

Nothing is hidden from you of the sound and the weak among these sayings, and that some of them support taking the question as a challenge (isti'sa'), and some support taking it as an inquiry (istikhbar). Taking it as an inquiry is preferable, and some scholars held that it is definite. ﴿Min qablikum﴾ (from before you) is connected to "sa'alaha." It is permissible that it be connected to an elided element that occurs as a modifier of "qawm," and this has been objected to on the grounds that a time adverbial cannot be a modifier of a solid entity (al-juththah), nor a circumstantial qualifier of it, nor a predicate about it. It was answered that the verified view is that this is conditioned on the absence of benefit; but if benefit is present, it is permissible, as the solid entity resembles meaning in its renewal and its existence at one time rather than another, as in "tonight is the crescent" (al-laylata al-hilal), unlike "Zayd is on Saturday." What we are discussing contains benefit, because it is not known whether the people are of those who passed away or not.

Abu Hayyan said, and it is a wondrous verification which they overlooked: this prohibition applies only to time unaccompanied by a descriptor. But when it includes a descriptor, it is permissible, as with "qabla" and "ba'da," for they are descriptors originally. When you say "Zayd came before 'Amr," the meaning is "he came in a time before the time of his coming," i.e., preceding it. Therefore it occurs as a relative clause for the relative pronoun, even though no descriptor is considered in it. Had it been a bare time adverbial, it would not be permissible for it to occur as a relative clause or a modifier. He, exalted, said: ﴿And those before you (wal-ladhina min qablikum)﴾. It is not permissible to say "wal-ladhina al-yawm" (those today), and what we are discussing is of the included type, not the bare type, which is clear. As for what has been said, that it has nothing to do with the matter in dispute because what functions as a modifier is the prepositional phrase itself and not the adverbial noun alone, this is nothing, for the entry of the preposition upon it, when it is "min" or "fi," does not remove it from being in reality the modifier or something like it. So understand.

﴿Thumma asbahu biha﴾ i.e., because of it (bi-sababiha). It is connected to His saying, exalted be He: ﴿kafirin﴾ (disbelievers).

201

- It was placed before it for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil).

And Ubayy recited: "Qad sa'alaha qawmun bayyanat lahum fa-asbahu biha kafirin" (A people asked it, and it was made clear to them, and then they became disbelievers in it).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 103:

﴿God did not institute any bahira (a she-camel whose ear was split and was let go free)﴾ *bahira* is *fa'ila* in the sense of *maf'ula*, from *al-bahr*, which means splitting. The *ta'* marker either transfers the word into a noun or indicates the omission of the modified noun. Al-Zajjaj said: The people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period), when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring, with the last being a male, would split her ear, abstain from slaughtering or riding her, not drive her away from water, and not prevent her from pasture. She was the *bahira*. Qatada said: When she gave birth to five offspring, the fifth was examined. If it was a male, they slaughtered and ate it. If it was a female, they split her ear and left her to graze, and no one used her for milking, riding, or the like. It was also said: The *bahira* is the female that is the fifth offspring. They made her meat and milk lawful for women, but if she died, men and women shared in eating her. It was reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq and Mujahid that she was the daughter of the *sa'iba*, which will come shortly, God willing. She was also left unattended.

It was said: She is the one who gave birth to five or seven, or it was said ten offspring, and she was left unattended. When she died, her meat became lawful for men only.

It was reported from Ibn al-Musayyib that she is the one whose milk was withheld for the idols (*tawagit*), so she was not milked. It was said: She is the one who gave birth to five females, so they split her ear and left her unattended. Al-Qamus (the lexicon) classified her, according to this view, as applying specifically to sheep. Just as she is called *bahira*, she is also called *ghazira*.

It was said: She is the young camel who, when born, had its ear split, and they said: "O God, if he lives, he is mine, and if he dies, he is slaughtered." When he died, they ate him. It was also said: She is the one left to graze without a herdsman.

﴿Nor sa'iba (a freed animal)﴾ *sa'iba* is *fa'ila* from *sayyabtuhu*, meaning I left him and neglected him, so he is *sa'ib* and she is *sa'iba*, or it is in the sense of *maf'ul*, as in *'Isha radiya* (a pleasing life). Its meaning has been disputed. It was said: She is the she-camel who gives birth to ten female offspring, so she is left neglected, not ridden, her wool not shorn, and no one drinks her milk except a guest. This was attributed to Muhammad ibn Ishaq. It was also said: She is the animal released for the idols, given to the custodians (*sadana*), and none eat of her milk except travelers and the like. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with them. It was also said: She is the camel that sees the offspring of its offspring, so it is left and not ridden. It was said: When a man returned from a long journey, or when his animal was saved from hardship or war, he would say: "She is a sa'iba." Or he would pull out a vertebra or a bone from her back. She was not prevented from water or pasture and was not ridden. It was said: She is what was left to be used for pilgrimage. It was said: She is the slave who is freed on the condition that he has no wala' (patronage claim), no blood money, and no inheritance.

﴿Nor wasila (a connecting one)﴾ *wasila* is *fa'ila* in the sense of *fa'ila* (active), and it was said it is *maf'ula* (passive). The first is more apparent, as the explanation of its meaning indicates. This has been disputed. Al-Farra' said: She is the ewe that gives birth to seven litters, in pairs of twins. If the last of them is a female kid and a male kid, it is said: "She has connected her brother," so only men may drink the mother's milk, not women, and she follows the rule of the *sa'iba*. Al-Zajjaj said: She is the ewe that, if it gives birth to a male, it belongs to their gods, and if it gives birth to a female, it belongs to them. If it gives birth to a male and a female, they say: "She has connected her brother," so they did not slaughter the male for their gods. It was also said: She is the ewe that gives birth to a male and then a female, so it connects her brother, and they do not slaughter her brother for her sake. If it gives birth to a male, they say: "This is an offering to our gods." It was reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that she is the ewe that gives birth to seven litters. If the seventh is female, women do not benefit from her at all, except if she dies, when men and women eat her. Likewise if the seventh is male and female; they say she has connected her brother, so she is left with him, and only men benefit from her, not women. If she dies, they share in her.

Ibn Qutayba said: If the seventh is male, it is slaughtered, and they eat from it, excluding women, saying: "It is exclusively for our males, forbidden to our wives." If it is female, it is left among the sheep. If it is male and female, it is as Ibn Abbas said, may God be pleased with him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: She is the ewe that gives birth to ten consecutive females in five litters, and whatever it gives birth to after that is for males only, not females. When it gives birth to a male and a female together, they say: "She has connected her brother," so they do not slaughter him because of her.

It was said: She is the ewe that gives birth to five or three litters. If it is a male kid, they slaughter it; if it is female, they keep it. If it is male and female, they say: "She has connected her brother."

Some said: The *wasila* is among camels: she is the she-camel who early bears a female, then bears another female, with no male between them, so they leave her for their gods and say: "She has connected female to female with no male between them." It was also said: She is the she-camel who connects between ten litters with no male among them.

﴿Nor ham (a stallion that is protected)﴾ *ham* is the active participle from *al-hima*, in the sense of prohibition. This too has been disputed. Al-Farra' said: He is the stallion, when it has impregnated the offspring of its offspring, so they say: "He has protected his back," and he is left unattended and not driven away from water or pasture. It was reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, and Ibn Mas'ud, and this is the view of Abu Ubayda and al-Zajjaj, that he is the stallion from whose back ten litters are born, so they say: "He has protected his back," so he is not ridden and not prevented from water or pasture. It was reported from al-Shafi'i that he is the stallion that serves in another's property for ten years. It was also said: He is the stallion for which seven consecutive females are produced, so he protects his back.

The previous views regarding all these types were reconciled by the fact that the Arabs' practices differed concerning them. The purpose of this clause is a rejection and nullification of what the people of the Jahiliyya had innovated.

The meaning of ﴿ma ja'ala﴾ (God did not institute) is "did not legislate," and for this reason it has one object, which is ﴿bahira﴾ and what is conjoined to it. The *min* (from) here is an emphatic particle used to strengthen the negation. Some denied that *ja'ala* (to make) came in the sense of *shara'a* (to legislate) from any of the lexicographers, and they took it here to mean "to appoint," with the second object omitted, meaning: God did not make the bahira, nor make it legislated. This is not correct, for al-Raghib transmitted this from the lexicographers, and he is trustworthy and does not fabricate against them.

﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God﴾ by what they do and by saying: "God, glorified and exalted is He, commanded us with this." Their leader was Amr ibn Luhayy, for he is, according to what is well known, the first to do those hideous deeds. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abu Hurayra who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say to Aktham ibn al-Jawn: "O Aktham, the Fire was shown to me, and I saw in it Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'a ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire. I have not seen a man more like a man than you are like him, nor him more like you." Aktham said: "I fear that his resemblance will harm me, O Messenger of God." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No, for you are a believer and he is a disbeliever." 

He was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and split the bahira, free the sa'iba, and protect the ham. Another report from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, adds: "and he connected the wasila."

Abd al-Razzaq and others narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I know the first who released the sawa'ib and erected the nusub (idols), and the first who changed the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him." They said: "Who is he, O Messenger of God?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Amr ibn Luhayy, brother of the Banu Ka'b. I have indeed seen him dragging his intestines in the Fire, harming the people of the Fire with the stench of his intestines. I know the first who split the baha'ir." He said: "Who is he, O Messenger of God?" He, peace be upon him, said: "A man from the Banu Mudlij who had two she-camels. He slit their ears, forbade their milk and their backs, and said: 'These belong to God.' Then he was in need of them, so he drank their milk and rode on their backs. I indeed saw him in the Fire, and the two she-camels were biting him with their mouths and trampling him with their hooves."

The verse is cited as evidence for the prohibition of these matters, which is evident. It is also deduced from it that all forms of rendering benefits idle are forbidden. Ibn al-Majishun used it as evidence to prohibit a man from saying to his slave: "You are sa'iba," and he said: "He is freed thereby."

Some scholars counted among the forms of *sa'iba* the release of birds and the like. Some of our scholars explicitly stated that there is no reward in this. Perhaps the one who makes it does not suffice with this measure and claims sin in it, while people are heedless of this and most of them do not understand.

That is a false fabrication. What was previously mentioned was the action of the leaders, and this is the situation of the followers, and they are the intended meaning of "most" (*akthar*), as narrated from Qatada and al-Sha'bi. The apparent context of the noble text is that they are the imitators of their ancestors who fabricated, among the contemporaries of the Messenger of God ﷺ. This is an explanation of the deficiency of their intellects in being guided by themselves.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 104:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, meaning those whom He referred to by most of them, by way of guidance and direction towards the truth: ﴿Come to what Allah has sent down﴾ from the Clear Book, which makes lawful and unlawful clear, and belief in it, ﴿and to the Messenger﴾ to whom that was revealed, so that you may come to know the reality of the matter and distinguish the unlawful from the lawful. And ﴿they say: "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon"﴾ in this matter, so we will not turn to anything else. This is a statement of their obstinacy and their refusal to be guided by the one who leads to the truth, and their submission to the one who calls to misguidance. ((Ma)) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsulah), and it is permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). Al-wijdan (finding) means encountering, and ʿalayhi is attached to it, or it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of its object. It is also permitted that it means "knowing" (ʿilm), in which case ʿalayhi is in the position of the second object.

﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾

Some have held that the waw is for coordination (ʿatf). Many have stated that it is based on another conditional clause implied before it, and the hamza is for astonishment (taʿajjub). It enters upon something implied in reality, meaning: Would that suffice for them even if their fathers were not ignorant and misguided? And even if they were such? Both clauses are in the position of a ḥāl, meaning: Would what they found their fathers upon suffice them, existing in every hypothetical state? On this view, it is not necessary that the interrogative, performative clause be a ḥāl, so this interpretation does not require a fine analysis. The first clause is omitted because it is clearly indicated, and this kind of omission is common in this type of construction, as in your saying: "Show kindness to Zayd, even if he mistreats you," for when a thing is established in the case of the one who prevents it, it is all the more established in the case of its absence.

The response of law (jawab law), as Abu al-Baqa said, is omitted because its negation is evident from what precedes it, and he estimated it as "they would follow them." It is also permissible to estimate it as "that would be sufficient for them" or "they would say." What is in law of the sense of impossibility and improbability is only with regard to their claim, not in reality. The benefit of this is intensification of the denial and astonishment. It has also been said: the waw is for the ḥāl, and the hamza is for denying the action in this state. The intended meaning is the negation of the validity of following an ignorant, misguided person, and the ḥāl is what is understood from the clause, meaning: existing in this hypothetical state. As for what some said, that they made the waw for ḥāl, and that what the waw entered upon is not a ḥāl in meaning, but rather what law entered upon, meaning: even if the state were that their fathers did not know, so they would do what their knowledge requires, and would not be guided by one who has knowledge arising from little reflection, this is strange regarding the state of that speaker, and even stranger is what has been said: that the meaning is whether what their fathers were upon would suffice for them, even if their fathers were ignorant and misguided, meaning: would the ignorance and misguidance their fathers had be sufficient for them? This is close to being ignorance and misguidance in what befits the revelation.

The verse has been cited as evidence that following someone is valid only when he is known to be a knowledgeable, guided person, and that this cannot be known except through proof. Therefore, mere imitation (taqlid) without knowing that the one imitated has a sound proof for what he is imitated in is not sufficient. Hence they said: the imitator has a general (ijmali) proof, which is the proof of the one he imitates. So reflect.
