**"O you who have believed, take care of yourselves"** (ﷻ). That is, keep to your own souls and guard them from involvement in sins and from persisting in wrongdoing. Here ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (ʿalaykum) is a verb-noun (ism fiʿl) in the imperative sense, and the whole phrase, the preposition together with its object, has been transferred to that meaning, not the preposition alone, as some have said. It is transitive to the object that follows it, though it may also be intransitive. The meaning intended is a command to hold fast, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hold fast to the one who has religion" ("عَلَيْكَ بِذاتِ الدِّينِ"). Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that the *kaf* and *mim* (the suffixes -kum) are in the genitive position, because the verb-noun is the whole compound, and ʿalā by itself has not been used as a verb-noun. This differs from ruwaydakum (take your time), where the *kaf* and *mim* serve only as second-person address and have no grammatical position, because ruwayda has been used as a verb-noun for addressing a person without the second-person *kaf*. Sibawayh held this view, and it is the correct one. Al-Tabarsi reported that the use of ʿalā with a pronoun as a verb-noun is specific to cases where the pronoun refers to the addressee. So if you said ʿalayhi Zaydan, it would not be permitted. There is a difference of opinion on this.

Nafi' read, as a non-canonical reading (shādh), **"your own souls"** (anfusukum) in the nominative. In that case the sentence is a nominal sentence with subject and predicate: "your own souls are incumbent upon you," or "the guarding of your souls is incumbent upon you," with an elided noun (muḍāf) understood in the subject.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"No harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided"﴾ may be read in the indicative (rafʿ), as a new independent sentence placed as a reason for what precedes it. This is supported by the reading of Abu Haywa (lā yuḍīrukum). It may also be read in the jussive (jazm) as a response to the imperative, meaning: if you hold fast to your own souls, no harm will come to you. The *rāʾ* was given a *ḍamma* in imitation of the *ḍamma* of the *ḍād* to which it was transferred from the assimilated *rāʾ*. The original form was lā yaḍrurukum. It may also be a prohibition emphasizing the earlier command, and the sentence would then be like "Let me not see you here." The reading that supports the jussive is that of the one who read (yaḍurrakum) with a *fatḥa*, and lā yiḍḍurrakum with a *kasra* or *ḍamma* on the *ḍād*, from ḍāra yaḍīruhu and yaḍūruhu, meaning "harmed him," like "blamed him" and "censured him."

It was supposed from the apparent meaning of the verse that it grants a dispensation to abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil. This has been answered in several ways.

The first: guidance is not complete except through enjoining good and forbidding evil, for abandoning that while able to do it is misguidance. Ibn Jarir reported from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, who said: "Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) ascended the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), praised Allah, the Exalted, and extolled Him, then said: 'O people, you recite a verse from the Book of Allah, the Glorified, and you consider it a dispensation. By Allah, Allah, the Exalted, has not revealed in His Book anything more severe than it: ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves﴾ to the end of the verse. By Allah, you must enjoin good and forbid evil, or Allah, the Exalted, will surely visit you with punishment.'" In another narration: "O people, you recite this verse and you place it in other than its proper context. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'When people see evil and do not change it, Allah, the Exalted, is about to surround them all with punishment.'"

In a narration of Ibn Marduwayh from Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad, who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq addressed the people, and in his sermon he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O people, do not rely on this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves﴾ and so on. Indeed, when a corrupter is in the tribe and they do not prevent him, Allah, the Exalted, will surround them all with punishment.'"

Some people interpreted guidance here as enjoining good and forbidding evil. This was reported from Hudhayfah and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: the verse is a consolation for one who enjoins good and forbids evil but is not heeded when wickedness prevails and after the era of revelation has passed. Abd al-Razzaq, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani and others reported from al-Hasan that a man asked Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) about this verse, and he said: "O people, it is not its time. But a time is about to come when you enjoin good and it is done to you such and such, or he said: and it will not be accepted from you. Then at that time, ﴿take care of yourselves; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided﴾."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that it was said to him: "If you sat in these days and did not command or forbid, for Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾." He said: "It does not apply to me or to my companions, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Let the one present convey to the one absent.' We were the present ones and you are the absent ones. But this verse is for peoples who will come after us; if they say it, it will not be accepted from them."

Ibn Marduwayh reported from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided﴾." The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: "O Mu'adh, command good and forbid evil. When you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, and every person pleased with his own opinion, then take care of yourselves; the misguidance of others will not harm you. Behind you are days of patience in which the one who holds to his religion is like one grasping a live coal. The one who acts among them on that day will have the reward of fifty men like you." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, fifty of them?" He said: "No, fifty of you."

The third: it is to prevent self-destruction out of grief and sorrow over the misguidance in which unbelievers and wrongdoers are. The believers used to grieve over the unbelievers and wish for their faith, so this was revealed.

The fourth: it is a dispensation to abandon commanding and forbidding when there is corruption in doing them.

The fifth: it is a command to remain steadfast in faith without caring about the accusation of foolishness made against fathers. It has been said: when a man embraced Islam, they would say to him, "You have called your father a fool," and so this was revealed. It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: "O you who have believed, hold fast to the people of your religion, guard them, and support them; no harm will come to you from those among the unbelievers who have gone astray if you do that." The expression of the people of the religion as "souls" is in the manner of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿do not kill yourselves﴾ and similar verses. The expression of that action as "guidance" is to encourage it. What is in this is not hidden.

﴿To Allah﴾ alone, not to anyone else, ﴿is your return﴾, your return on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿all of you﴾, such that none of the guided or others will be absent from it. ﴿Then He will inform you﴾ with reward and punishment ﴿of what you used to do﴾.

[501]

- in this world, of the deeds of guidance and misguidance. So the statement is a promise and a warning to both groups. It also indicates, as has been said, that no one is held accountable for the deeds of another. Likewise it indicates that one is rewarded for such (deeds of others), and the verification of that will come, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 106 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes), brought to explain the rulings concerning their worldly affairs after the explanation of the matters concerning their religious affairs. It contains, as is evident, a demonstration of the complete concern for its content. ﴿The testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest, is two [witnesses]﴾. The word shahadah (testimony) has several meanings: presence (ihdar), judgment (qada'), decision (hukm), oath (halif), knowledge ('ilm), and bequeathing (iña'). The intended meaning here is the last, as a group of exegetes have stated explicitly, and its verification will come, God willing. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it in the nominative (bi-al-raf'), taking it as a subject (mubtada') with ﴿two﴾ as its predicate (khabar), and the sentence is then elliptical of a genitive term (mudaf mahdhuf), so that the meaning is either: [it is] the testimony of two [witnesses] among you (taking the first as the implied term), or: the testimony between you is the testimony of two (taking the second). This elision was made necessary so that the subject and predicate would correspond. It has also been said: shahadah is in the sense of shuhud (witnesses), like "a just man" ('adl), so there is no need to posit an elision. It has also been said: the predicate is elided, and ﴿two﴾ is in the nominative by virtue of the verbal noun which is shahadah, and the meaning is: in what has been prescribed for you, let two [persons] testify. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The word shahadah here is in its familiar sense, not in the sense of causing to testify (ishhad). The statement of some [commentators] seems to imply that, but in reality it is an explanation of the resultant meaning of the sentence.

Some have claimed that it means ishhad, the verbal noun of the passive, and ﴿two﴾ stands in place of its agent. In response: to use a verbal noun of a passive verb with a deputy agent, which is an apparent noun, is not sound, although the Basrans permitted it, as in the commentary on al-Tashil by al-Muradi. The Kufans, however, prohibited it and said that this is the correct view, because the omission of the agent of a verbal noun is permissible and common, so it does not need anything to take the place of its agent, as the agent of an explicit verb does not.

﴿When﴾ (idha) is an adverb of time (zarf) governed by ﴿testimony﴾, meaning: let them testify at the time of the approach of death for the deceased. What is meant is his imminence and the appearance of its signs. ﴿At the time of bequest﴾ is either an apposition (badal) to ﴿when﴾, which indicates that bequest is one of the established important matters which a Muslim should not neglect or forget.

It is also permitted that it be connected to death itself, meaning the occurrence of death, that is, its causes, at the time of bequest, or to [the verb] ﴿approaches﴾. It is also permitted that ﴿testimony﴾ be the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿when approaches﴾, meaning: the occurrence of the testimony at the time of the approach of death, with ﴿at the time of bequest﴾ according to the earlier possibilities. It is not permitted that it be an adverb governed by ﴿testimony﴾, lest one give the relative [clause's] referent before its relative clause or predicate is complete, ﴿at the time of bequest﴾. ﴿When﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿testimony﴾, and it is not permitted for it to be governed by ﴿bequest﴾, even though the meaning would be that, because the complement of a verbal noun does not precede it according to the sound view, together with what would entail the precedence of the complement of the genitive over the genitive, which is not permitted except with ghayr (other than), because it is like la (no).

According to these two possibilities, ﴿two﴾ is either the agent of an implied ﴿let testify﴾ or the predicate of ﴿two witnesses﴾ in the same manner.

It is reported from al-Farra' that ﴿testimony﴾ is the subject and ﴿two﴾ is its agent which stands in place of the predicate, and he took the verbal noun in the sense of an imperative, i.e., ﴿let testify﴾. In this there is the substitution of a verbal noun for an imperative verb, which is weak according to others, because the sufficiency of the agent is specific to a descriptive modifier that is relied upon. ﴿When﴾ and ﴿at the time of﴾, according to this view, are both in the accusative as adverbs of time, as already mentioned. The genitive construction of ﴿testimony﴾ with the adverb is by way of expansion (tawassu'), because it is variable in its syntactic function, and for this reason one reading has ﴿your bond was cut off﴾ (taqatta'a baynukum) in the nominative. It has been said that the original is ma baynakum (what is between you), which is a metonymy for mutual enmity and dispute. The omission of ma is permissible, as in ﴿and when you saw there﴾ meaning ma thamma (what is there). This was objected to: the relative ma cannot be omitted, but some have permitted it.

Al-Sha'bi read ﴿testimony between you﴾ with the nominative and tanwin, so that ﴿between you﴾ is then in the accusative as an adverb of place. al-Hasan read ﴿testimony﴾ with the accusative and tanwin. Ibn Jinni explained this as governed by an implied verb with ﴿two﴾ as its agent, meaning: let two [persons] establish the testimony between you.

This was objected to: the grammarians did not permit omitting the verb and retaining its agent unless something indicating it had preceded, as in God's words ﴿He is glorified therein at morning and evening﴾ in the reading of one who reads (yusabbaha) in the passive, and the poet's line:

*"Let Yazid the petitioner weep for a dispute"*

or unless a negation or interrogation preceded it. That is obvious, and this verse is none of these three.

It was answered: the condition mentioned is not accepted; it is rather a condition of the majority of cases. In al-Bahr he preferred two possible explanations. The first is that ﴿testimony﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun standing in place of the imperative verb, and ﴿two﴾ is raised by it, the meaning being: let two [persons] testify between you. This would be like "striking, Zayd" (darban zaydan), except that the agent in "striking" is attributed to the pronoun of the addressee because its meaning is "strike!", whereas here it is attributed to the explicit noun, because its meaning is "what you know". The second is that it is a verbal noun, not in the sense of an imperative, but a predicate standing in place of the verb in the predicate, though this is rare, as in the poet's line:

*"Standing by them, my companions, upon their mounts"*

Here ﴿my companions﴾ is raised and ﴿their mounts﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿standing﴾, since it is a substitute (badal) for the verbal form in the predicate. The implied meaning is: "Let my companions stand upon their mounts." The meaning in the verse is: ﴿let two testify when death approaches one of you﴾, [the witnesses being] ﴿two just persons from among you﴾, i.e., from among the Muslims, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Baqir, and Ibn al-Musayyab, may God be pleased with them, or ﴿from outside your number﴾, i.e., from your relatives and tribe, as reported from al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah, and this is what the words of al-Zuhri imply. These two [descriptions] are adjectives of ﴿two﴾.

﴿Or two others﴾ is coordinated with ﴿two﴾ in all its possible readings.

God's words ﴿from other than you﴾ are an adjective of it, meaning: being from other than you. ''Other than you'' refers, according to the earlier scholars, to non-Muslims from among the People of the Book, and according to the later scholars, to non-relatives, i.e., strangers. A group of later scholars chose the first view, to the extent that al-Jassas said: the second interpretation has no basis, because the address was first directed to the people of faith, so distinction is to be considered in it, and no mention of kinship has occurred. The occasion of revelation also supports this, and it will come shortly, God willing.

﴿If you travel in the land﴾, i.e., you journey. ﴿You﴾ is in the nominative governed by an implied verb which is explained by what follows, the meaning being: if you travel. Since the verb has been omitted, the pronoun must be detached so that it can stand on its own. This is the view of the majority of the Basrans. al-Akhfash and the Kufans held that it is a subject (mubtada'), on the basis of the permissibility of a subject occurring after the conditional particle in, just as it may occur after idha. Accordingly, the clause ﴿you traveled﴾ has no place in grammar on the first view, being an explanation, and its place is the nominative on the second, as a declarative predicate.

God's words ﴿then a calamity of death befalls you﴾ mean: you approach the end of your term. It is coordinated with the condition, and its response is omitted. If the condition is a restriction on the very act of testimony, the meaning is: if you travel in the land, etc., then let two [witnesses] testify, from among you or from outside you. If the condition is a restriction on the switch to others, in the sense reported from the earlier scholars, then the meaning is: then call others from outside your number, or: then the two witnesses are others from outside your number. In that case the verse indicates that one may turn to non-Muslims for testimony only on condition of travel in the land. This was reported from Shurayh, may God be pleased with him.

God's words ﴿you shall detain them﴾ mean: you shall hold them back and make them wait for the oath. It is a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "How shall we act if we doubt the two witnesses?" And so God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿you shall detain them after the prayer﴾, i.e., the afternoon prayer, as reported from Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, and others. The specification of this time is because it is the time when people gather and crowd together, and because all the people of the religions venerate it and avoid false oaths at it, and because it is the time when the angels of night and day meet and converge. In this there is an increase in witnesses from among them to the truthfulness or falsehood of the swearer, so that it is more fearful. Some have counted this among the stipulations of aggravation imposed upon the one required to swear by means of time. In our school, however, aggravation by time is not required, nor by place; rather, it is permissible for the judge to do so.

It is reported from al-Hasan that the meaning is the afternoon prayer or the noon prayer, because the people of the Hijaz used to sit for judgment after these two. It is also permitted that the definite article be generic, i.e., after whichever prayer. The specification by the prayer is an apposition, because prayer calls one to speak the truth and forbids uttering falsehood, false testimony, and committing indecency and wrongdoing. al-Hasan took the specification by that [prayer] as evidence for his earlier interpretation. It is also permitted that the clause be another adjective of ''others'', and the conditional clause be a parenthetical insertion, so the interposition by it does no harm. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. It was objected to this that it implies that the detention applies only to the others, though it also applies to the first two, if they are assumed to have the same characteristic. The context of the command to call the two as witnesses prevents this, because its ultimate sense would be: "then others whose characteristic is detention and oath." Although it is possible to complete the approximation by considering the qualifier of doubt concerning them, as the subsequent objection suggests, its problems are not hidden.

The address is to the testators, and it has been said it is to the heirs, and it has been said it is to the judges and magistrates.

God's words ﴿so they both swear by God﴾ are coordinated with ''you shall detain them''. ﴿If you doubt﴾, i.e., you suspect their truthfulness and that they have not appropriated any part of the estate. The clause is conditional, its response omitted because the preceding detention and oaths indicate it. The condition together with its omitted response is a parenthetical insertion between the oath and its response, namely God's words ﴿we will not sell it for a price﴾. It has been introduced from His side, may He be glorified and exalted, to call attention to the restriction of the detention and the oath to the state of doubt. This is not among the cases in which an oath and a condition are combined, so that the response of the earlier is used for the response of the later, as is usually the case, because that happens when the response of the earlier takes the place of the response of the later, due to the unity of their content, as in your saying: "By God, if you come to me, I will surely honor you." There is no doubt that this is impossible here, because the oath and its response are the words of the two witnesses, while the conditional clause, as you know, comes from Him, glory be to Him and exalted. Nor should it be supposed that ''in'' here is conjunctive (wasliyya), because even though the wa' is obligatory with it, the meaning does not rest on it, as is evident. Some have claimed that it is permissible for it to be conditional, with ''we will not sell'' as the indicator of the response, the meaning being: "if you doubt, then that should not be the case," or "then you have erred, because we are not among those who sell it for a small price." This is very far-fetched, and the verse is then devoid, apparently, of the condition of the oath and of a pronoun ''by it'' referring back to God, Most High. The meaning would be: we do not take for ourselves in exchange for God, glory be to Him, i.e., from His sanctity, any worldly goods, by causing them to vanish through a false oath. Its sum is: we do not swear by God Most High a false oath for the sake of wealth. It has also been said that it refers back to the oath, on the assumption of an elided genitive term, meaning: we exchange the validity of the oath by God Most High for a worldly commodity, by stripping it of the attribute of truth and describing it as false. It has also been said that it refers back to the testimony, on the basis that it is a statement, and an elided genitive term must also be assumed, and a genitive term is elided before ''price'' as well, meaning: something of price, which nothing calls us to except slight reflection. ﴿Even if it were﴾ the one for whom they swear, implied by the context, ﴿a near relative﴾, i.e., close to us. This is an emphasis on their disavowal of false swearing and an exaggeration in keeping away from it, as if they had said: "We will not take in exchange for that any wealth, even if the side of our relatives were added to it, so how much more so when it is not like that." The preservation of themselves, although it is more important than maintaining the rights of relatives, is, as Shaykh al-Islam said, not an addition of wealth, but rather returns to it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the one for whom testimony is given, in the sense: we do not favor anyone by our testimony, even if he were close to us. The response of ''even if'' is omitted, relying on what preceded it, i.e., "we will not sell it for a price," and the clause is coordinated with another clause omitted, meaning: "even if he were not a near relative, and even if he were." al-Samin made the waw indicate a circumstantial clause, and what benefits you here has already been given to you.

Some scholars allowed the pronoun to refer to the witness, and they supplied a different response for (law) than the one we have supposed: that is, "and if the witness were a relative, the two would swear." They held that the purpose of this is to remove the suspicion that oaths are restricted to outsiders. But the weakness of the construction in this case is not hidden, a weakness that should not appear even in the speech of some people, let alone in the speech of the Lord of all. And we bear witness by Allah, glorified and exalted be He, that interpreting His speech, mighty and majestic, in such a way is unfitting: ﴿And we do not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, meaning the testimony which He, glorified and exalted be He, commanded us to establish and obligated us to render.

So the idafah (genitive construction) is for specification or for the slightest connection. The clause is conjoined to (we do not sell it for a price) and falls together with it within the scope of the oath. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he paused at (shahadah) with the ha' and then began (ʾallāh) with a long vowel and a genitive case, by omitting the particle of oath and compensating with the interrogative particle in its place. This is not the omission of a preposition with its governance retained, which is rare, like the line of poetry: "Kulayb pointed with the fingers of the palms."

Because that occurs where there is no compensation, whereas in the noble name of God there is compensation by the hamzah of interrogation for the omitted element. Whether the genitive is governed by the particle itself or by the compensation is a matter of two opinions. It is also narrated from him, and likewise from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, Yahya ibn Umar, Ibn Jarir and others, (Allāh) without a long vowel. Regarding this there are two possibilities.

The first is that the omission is without compensation, and so it is contrary to analogy. The second is that the hamzah mentioned is the hamzah of interrogation, which is a hamzah of qat' (cutting), and it has compensated for the particle, but it was not lengthened. This is preferable to claiming irregularity, and for this reason al-Samin in Al-Durr al-Masun preferred it. It was also read with tanwin on (shahadah), with the hamzah connected, and with the name of Allah, exalted be He, in the accusative without a long vowel. Abu al-Baqa' explained it as being in the accusative by a verb of oath, omitted: ﴿Indeed, we would then be among the sinners.﴾

- That is, if we did that and concealed. The shift from (ʾāthimūn) to what has been mentioned is for emphasis. It was also read (lamilāthimīn), with the hamzah omitted and its vowel placed upon the lam, and the nun assimilated into it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 107 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Then if it becomes known﴾, that is, it is discovered. It is said: "'athara al-rajul 'ala al-shay' 'usuran" (a man came upon a thing) when he discovers it.

Al-Ghawri said: "You say 'athartu' when I discovered what had been hidden." This is a figurative usage (majaz) according to its original meaning, from their saying "'athara" when he stumbled. The one who stumbles looks at the place of his stumbling, recognizes it, and comes to know it. Al-Layth said: the verbal noun of 'athara in the sense of "discovered" is al-'usur, and in the sense of "stumbled" is al-'ithar. In that case, the claim of figurative usage is not hidden, because the difference in the verbal nouns rules it out. That claim can only stand on what al-Raghib said, namely the unity of the two verbal nouns. In the Qamus: 'athara, like daraba, nasara, 'alima and karuma, 'athran or 'athiran or 'itharan, meaning "stumbled." Al-'usur means "discovery," like al-'athr. The apparent meaning of this is that there is no figurative usage. It is also understood from this that the verbal nouns are one in some cases, so understand.

The meaning is: if it is discovered after the oath, ﴿that those two﴾, that is, the two witnesses who swore, ﴿deserved sin﴾, that is, committed what requires it, such as distortion and concealment, in that something of the estate appeared in their hands and they claimed a right to it on some ground. Al-Jubba'i said: the statement contains an elision of a modifier, that is, "they deserved the punishment of sin." ﴿Then two others﴾, that is, two other men, and this is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿will stand in their place﴾. The fa' is a conditional particle, and it is one of the things that permit beginning with an indefinite noun. There is no objection to separating the predicate from the subject and its qualifier, which is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿from among those upon whom the claim has been established, the two nearest﴾. It is also said: it is the predicate of an elided subject, that is, "so the two witnesses are two others," and the clause "will stand" is its qualifier, and the prepositional phrase is another qualifier. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "will stand." It is also said: it is the agent of an elided verb, that is, "let two others testify," and what follows it is its qualifier. It is also said: it is a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase, and the verbal clause is its qualifier. The pronoun in "in their place" in all these aspects refers back to "those who deserved." What is meant by "in their place" is not the place of giving the testimony which they undertook and did not give as it is, but rather the place of detention and oath-taking.

"Istahagga" is in the active voice according to the reading of 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs from him, and 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them, recited it so. Its agent is "the two nearest." What is meant by the relative clause is the people of the deceased, and by "the two nearest" are the two nearest to him, the heirs who have the better right to testify because of their nearness and their knowledge. In reality, they are the other two who stand in place of the two who deserved sin, except that the apparent noun was put in place of their pronoun to draw attention to their being described by this description.

The object of "istahagga" is elided, and they differed about its estimation. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: that they should cause them to stand up to give testimony, so that by them they might expose the lie of the liars. Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as: their bequest. Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as: what belonged to them and their estate.

Al-Imam said: what is meant by "the two nearest" are the two executors (wasiyyan) whose betrayal became apparent. The reason for their being nearest is that the deceased designated them for the bequest. So the meaning of "the claim has been established against them, the two nearest" is: he betrayed their property, and the two executors on whom the discovery of their betrayal was made committed a crime against them. On this view, there is no need to say the object is elided. The majority read "the claim has been established against them, the two nearest" with the verb in the passive voice.

They differed about the referent of its pronoun. Most say it is the sin, and what is meant by the relative clause is the heirs, because the establishment of sin upon them is a metaphor for the wrong done to them, and there is no doubt that those who were wronged and against whom the sin was committed are the heirs. It is also said: it is the bequest (al-i'sa'), and it is also said: the bequest (al-wasiyya), by interpreting it as what was mentioned. It is also said: the wealth. It is also said: the act is attributed to the prepositional phrase.

Likewise they differed about the parsing of the nominative "the two nearest." It is said: it is a subject whose predicate is "two others," that is, the two nearest by the command of the deceased are two others. It is said: the reverse. This was objected to on the ground that it involves informing about an indefinite noun by a definite one, which is something agreed to be prohibited in such a case. It is said: it is the predicate of an elided subject, that is, "they are the two others," by way of explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani). It is said: it is a substitute (badal) for "two others." It is said: it is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to it, and this entails that the explicative and the explained do not agree in definiteness and indefiniteness, although they stipulated agreement in it, to the point that its indefiniteness was permitted. Yes, it is reported from a rare source that the stipulation is not required. It is also said: it is a substitute for the subject of "will stand."

That the replaced element is in the position of being discarded is not true in every respect, so as to entail that the clause which occurs as a predicate or qualifier is devoid of a pronoun referring to it. Moreover, if it were discarded and this noun stood in its place, that would be placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, so it would serve as a linking element. It is also said: it is a qualifier of "two others," and in this there is describing an indefinite noun by a definite one. Al-Akhfash permitted this here, because the indefinite noun described by a qualifier comes close to the definite. It is said: this is the reverse of the following:

*And indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me*

for there the definite is interpreted as indefinite, while here the indefinite was interpreted as definite, or it was treated as having the status of the definite by being qualified. It is possible, as some researchers said, that it is of this type, by making "the two nearest" like an indefinite noun because they are not specified.

It is reported from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that it is the deputy agent of "istahagga," and the meaning according to this is: "the claim was established upon them" as the designation of the two nearest from them for the testimony, as al-Zamakhshari said, or the sin of the two nearest, as it was said. It is the dual of al-'awwala, its alif having been changed to ya' before it.

Regarding "upon them" in "'alayhim," there are several views. The first is that "'ala" retains its basic meaning. The second is that it means "fi" (in). The third is that both mean "min" (from). "Istahagga" was interpreted as "seeking a right," and as "with a right," and as "prevailed."

Ya'qub, Khalaf, Hamza and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him recited "istuhigga 'alayhi al-awwalin," with the verb in the passive voice, and "al-awwalin" is the plural of "awwal," the opposite of "akhar." It is in the genitive case as an adjective of "alladhina," or a substitute for it, or for the pronoun in "'alayhim," or in the accusative by way of praise. The meaning of "priority" is precedence over outsiders in testimony. It is also said: precedence in mention, because they are included in "O you who have believed."

Al-Hasan recited "al-awlan" with the nominative, which is, as we have mentioned, in the case of "al-awlayan." It was also read "al-awwalayn" in the dual and accusative. Ibn Sirin read "al-awlayayn" with two ya's, the dual of "awla" in the accusative. It was read "al-awlayn" with the waw sukun and the lam fathah, the plural of "awla," like "a'layn." The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of these is clear.

﴿So they swear by Allah﴾ is conjoined to "will stand," and the causal relation is evident. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ is the answer of the oath. By "testimony" is meant, according to most, including Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, the oath, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah﴾. The oath was called testimony, according to what al-Tabarsi said, because the oath is like testimony about what is sworn to, that it is so. That is, our oath that they are lying in what they claimed of the right to possess, while our oath is true and sincere in itself, is more worthy of acceptance than their oath, which is false in itself, because it has become apparent to the people that they deserve sin, and our oath is free of doubt and suspicion.

The form of comparison is used only because it is possible in general for their oath to be accepted, in view of their truthfulness in claiming ownership of what appeared in their hands. It is also said: testimony is in its familiar sense when unqualified, and what some researchers said about something other than that will come, God willing.

His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾ is conjoined to the answer, that is, we have not exceeded the truth in our testimony, and we have not transgressed against them by invalidating their right. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed we, then, would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is a resumptive statement confirming what precedes it: that is, if we transgressed in what was mentioned, we would be among those who wrong themselves by exposing themselves to the wrath of Allah and His punishment, or among those who place the truth in other than its place.

The meaning of the two verses according to many exegetes is this: when a dying person wishes to make a bequest, he should call two just men from among the people of his religion or lineage as witnesses. If he does not find them, such as when he is on a journey, then two others from outside them. Then, if doubt arises about their truthfulness, they swear to the truth of what they say, with an aggravated oath at the time of prayer. If the truth of their lying becomes known through some sign, two others from the family of the deceased swear. It is claimed that the ruling is abrogated (mansukh) if the two are witnesses, since the witness swears and his oath is not opposed by the oath of an heir. It is also said: the oath-taking was not abrogated, but it is conditioned on suspicion.

It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he used to make a witness or a narrator swear if he suspected them. In some books of the Hanafis it is stated that if the witness does not find anyone to vouch for him, it is permissible to make him swear as a precaution. This is contrary to the fatwa, as explained in its place. Likewise some claimed abrogation on the assumption that the witnesses in the journey are non-Muslims, since the testimony of a disbeliever against a Muslim is not accepted in any case. Ibn Jarir reported the hadith of abrogation from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Some said: there is no abrogation, and they permitted the testimony of a dhimmi (non-Muslim protected subject) against a Muslim in this case.

It is reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that when he was governor of Kufa he ruled, in the presence of the Companions, by the testimony of two dhimmis after making them swear, concerning the bequest of a Muslim on a journey. Ahmad ibn Hanbal went to this view. Others said: the two are executors, and the ruling on making them swear when the heirs have doubts is not abrogated. What the verse conveys of returning the oath to the heirs is not because they are claimants, since the betrayal of the two executors has become apparent, so the oath was returned to them, contrary to al-Shafi'i. Rather, it is because they became the ones against whom the claim is made, since the claim was reversed: the executor who was first the defendant became a claimant to ownership, while the heirs deny that. This is supported by what al-Bukhari reported in his History, al-Tirmidhi reported and graded as hasan, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and many others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A man from the Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada' (some say Nada', with the nun). The Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. When they brought his estate, they lost a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made them swear by Allah that they had not concealed or taken anything. Then the cup was found in Mecca, and it was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and 'Adi.' Then two men from the Sahmi's heirs stood up and swore by Allah, glorified is He: 'Indeed our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and indeed the cup belongs to our companion.' And he took the cup, and concerning them was revealed: 'O you who have believed...' etc."

This is the end of the report. Some researchers claimed that the word "testimony" here cannot in any way bear its familiar sense, nor can it be conceived as such. Their testimony is either about the deceased, and there is no sense in that after his death and the transfer of the right to the heirs and their presence, or about the heir who is the opponent, and how can an adversary testify against his adversary? So interpretation is necessary. It was mentioned that the apparent meaning is to take the phrase in His saying, glorified is He: "the testimony between you" as referring to presence or bringing into presence. That is: when death approaches the traveler, let there be present someone to whom he entrusts his property for delivery to his heir, a Muslim, and if he does not find one, then a non-Muslim. The precaution is that they should be two. If they come with what they have, and suspicion arises that some of it has been concealed, then let them swear, because they are trustees, believed by their oath. If what they betrayed is found, and they claim that they had acquired it from him...

[Page 53]

on a sale or the like, and there is no evidence for either of them regarding that. The defendant swears on his lack of knowledge of what the two claim of ownership, and that it belonged to their ancestor, that we do not know its transfer from his ownership. The second testimony (shahadah) means direct, witnessed knowledge, or what is in its position, because direct observation (al-mu'ayanah) is the testimony; so using it for true knowledge (al-'ilm al-sahih) is close. The third testimony is either in this sense or in the sense of oath. According to this, and it is something Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon me by the blessing of His speech, glorified is He, there is no abrogation (naskh) in the verse and no difficulty. Everything they have mentioned is an artificial strain (takalluf) that has not been cleared of turbidity for the palate of any taster. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) and the action of the Messenger (ﷺ) clarify what has been mentioned. End.

Perhaps the specification of the two who swear to the validity of their testimony, according to what has been said, is due to the particularity of the event; otherwise, if the heir is one, he swears, and if they are many, the plural swears, as explained in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). And what has been mentioned, that the occasion of revelation etc. clarifies what he established in it, has some obscurity, since the report does not say that the two heirs swore on lack of knowledge; and in other reports there is something explicit about swearing to certainty. It has been narrated in a report longer than what preceded it that "'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah al-Sahmiyyayn stood up and swore by Allah, glorified is He, after the afternoon prayer, that they, i.e. Tamim and 'Adi, had lied and betrayed. Yes." Al-Tirmidhi in al-Jami', after narrating that report, said: it is a gharib hadith, and its isnad is not sahih. Also, in taking the testimony to mean something of what he mentioned in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And we do not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, there is obscurity; and he himself claimed that taking the testimony to mean an oath is far-fetched, because when it is used without qualification it is the familiar meaning, so consider this. Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an. Al-Wahidi said: it was narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: this verse is the most intractable of the rulings in this surah. Al-Imam said: the exegetes agreed that this verse is in the utmost difficulty in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), composition (nazm) and ruling (hukm). Al-Muhaqqiq al-Taftazani said: they agreed that this verse is the most difficult in the Qur'an in ruling, i'rab and composition. Al-Shihab said: know that they said: there is nothing in the Qur'an greater in difficulty, ruling, i'rab and tafsir than this verse and the one after it, meaning (O you who believe) etc., and His saying, exalted is He: (then if it is discovered) etc., to the extent that they composed separate works on them. They said: despite that, no one has been freed from its responsibility. Al-Tabarsi mentioned that the two verses are among the most intricate verses of the Qur'an in ruling, meaning and i'rab, and he prided himself on what was given in them, and did not bring anything beyond that of their sayings. Glory be to the All-Knowing of realities.

﴿Dhalika﴾ is a resumed (new) statement, brought to explain that what has been mentioned leads to benefits and accords with the requirements of wisdom. It refers to the previously mentioned ruling whose details are explained earlier. It is also said that it refers to the oath taken by the two witnesses, and it is said that it refers to detaining them after the prayer. ﴿Adna an ya'tu bil-shahada ʿala wajhiha﴾ means: it is closer to the witnesses giving testimony in its true form, without altering it, out of fear of the punishment of the Hereafter. This is the wisdom of the oath mentioned first. The first preposition phrase (bi) is connected to (ya'tu), and the second is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial phrase (hal) describing (al-shahada). The words ﴿aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun﴾ mean: or they fear that oaths will be returned to the heirs, so that they swear after their oaths that they had sworn. This is a conjunction (ʿataf) on an implied element indicated by the context, as if it were said: "That is closer to them giving testimony in its verified form, and to them fearing the punishment of the Hereafter because of a false oath, which is forbidden in all religions; or they fear that the oaths will be returned to the heirs, so they swear and take what is in their hands, and then they are shamed before the assembled witnesses, and so they refrain from betrayal." This explains the legal wisdom of the appointment of the other two. Whichever of these two fears occurs, the purpose is achieved, which is giving testimony in its proper form.

It is also said that it is conjoined to (ya'tu), meaning: that ruling which we mentioned is closer to them giving testimony in its proper form than what you used to do, and closer to fear of disgrace. Al-Shihab made this conjunction on the pattern of his statement:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

Al-Samin permitted that (aw) here means (wa, "and"), just as he permitted that it be used to indicate one of two things, which is its basic meaning. So think carefully. The pronoun in (ya'tu) and (yakhafu) is plural, as it is said, because the intended meaning includes the two witnesses mentioned and others from the rest of people. The adverbial phrase (ba'da) is connected to (turadda), as is apparent. Al-Samin permitted, though this is weak, that it be connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of (aymanun).

﴿Wattaqu Allah﴾ means: in opposing His rulings, among which is what has been mentioned. The clause, as it is said, is conjoined to an implied element, meaning: "Preserve the rulings of God, the Glorified, and fear Him, and listen with the listening of acceptance and submission to all that you are commanded." ﴿Wallahu la yahdi al-qawm al-fasiqin﴾.

This is an appended conclusion to what came before. The intended meaning is: if you do not fear Him and do not listen, you are sinners, departing from obedience, and God, the Exalted, does not guide the people who depart from His obedience to what benefits them, or to the path of Paradise.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾. It has been said that it is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) governed by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿will not guide﴾. Al-Halabi examined this, on the grounds that He, glorified is He, would then not guide them absolutely, neither on that day nor in this world. This is a possibility mentioned by al-Zamakhshari and also transmitted from al-Maghribi. It is apparent if the intended meaning is that He will not guide them to the path of Paradise. In this there is an accommodation to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, who hold that negating guidance absolutely cannot be attributed to Allah, exalted is He. For this reason, the one guided (al-mahdiyy) was restricted to "to Him."

It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the object of ﴿and fear Allah﴾. In that case it is an object (maf'ul), not an adverbial.

Abu Hayyan objected that this is remote because of the long separation caused by the two clauses. Al-Halabi said: "It is not remote, for these two clauses complete the meaning of the first clause, and according to those who hold the substitution view it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal)." Al-Iraqi, the scholar, objected to this: "Fairness requires that substitution of inclusion is impossible here, because it necessarily requires that the substitute include the substituted element or vice versa, and here that is impossible." For this reason al-Halabi said: "In this view it is necessary to assume an omitted modifier for it to be correct, and the meaning is: fear the punishment of Allah on the day..." Then the accusative of "the day" as an adverbial becomes valid.

Al-Muhaqqiq al-Taftazani said: The basis for substitution of inclusion is the connection between them, which is neither whole-to-part nor part-to-whole, in the manner of the substituted element including the substitute, not like the adverbial including what is in it. Rather, the meaning is that the mind moves toward it in general and it is implied in a general way. For example, when it is said "Fear Allah," the mind immediately goes to whether, among His affairs and among the days of His acts, fear is obligatory on the day when He gathers the Messengers or on other occasions. It was objected that it is a condition in that view that it not be an adverbial, and this is an adverb of time; if it were substituted, it would give that impression.

It has also been said that it is governed by an implied verb coordinated with "fear" (ittaqu), i.e., "and beware" or "and remember the day," etc., for reminding of that tremendous day compels one toward fear of Allah, exalted is He, and receiving His command with a listening that responds.

It has also been said that it is governed by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and listen﴾, with an omitted modifier, i.e., "and listen to the news of that day."

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb placed later that has been omitted, to indicate that expression is too narrow to explain it and clarify it, because of the extreme horror of what happens in it, as if it were said: "On the day when Allah gathers the Messengers..." there will be among the states and terrors what the scope of speech cannot contain.

The specification of the Messengers by mention, although that is a day on which all people are gathered, is to show their nobility and rank, and to signal that there is no need to state the gathering of others, based on the evident fact that they are followers of them. It has been said, and its subtlety is not hidden from some of the following possibilities regarding the verse: because the context is that of mentioning the witnesses, and the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, are the witnesses over nations, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We will draw forth from every nation a witness﴾. So in explaining their state and what happens to them on the Day of Resurrection, and they are the ones who admonished the witnesses who are the subject of inquiry, there is what is not hidden. By this the verse connects most perfectly with what precedes it. The manifestation of the august Name in place of a pronoun is to cultivate awe and intensify the terror. ﴿Then He will say﴾ to them: ﴿What was your response?﴾ That is, in the world, when you conveyed the message and discharged your duty, as the turning away from opening the address with "Did you convey?" indicates. And in turning away from "What did your nations respond?" there is what is not hidden of informing about the complete contempt for their status and the severity of anger and wrath against them. The question is also for rebuking those (the nations), otherwise He, glorified is He, knows the unseen.

"Mā dhā" is connected to "ujibtum" as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) of it, meaning: "What kind of response were you answered with by your nations, a response of acceptance or a response of rejection?" It has been said that the estimate is: "With what were you answered?" meaning: "With what thing were you answered?" so that the question is about the answer, not the act of answering; the preposition is omitted and the noun it governed becomes accusative. This was judged weak, because omitting the preposition and making its object accusative is not permitted except in poetic necessity, as in the saying: "You pass by the abodes and you have not turned aside." The same applies to assuming it in the genitive.

Al-Awfi said: "mā" is an interrogative noun in the nominative (mubtada'), "dhā" is in the sense of "alladhi" (which) as its predicate, and "ujibtum" is its relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "What is it that you were answered with?" It was objected that it is not permitted to omit a returning pronoun in the genitive unless the relative noun is governed by the same preposition and both governed elements are the same; the response to this is that the omission occurred gradually, and that is, as you see, [weak]. They said it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) founded on a question arising from the flow of speech, as if it were said: "Then what will the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, say at that time?" So it is answered: "They will say: ﴿We have no knowledge﴾." The past tense is used to indicate that it is established and certain, like the blowing into the Trumpet and other things. The negation of knowledge from themselves, while they know what they were answered with, as is indicated by their testimony, upon them be blessings and peace, over their nations at that time, as some verses have stated, is not literal; rather it is a metaphor for showing complaint and seeking refuge with Allah, exalted is He, by entrusting the whole matter to Him, mighty is His affair.

Ibn al-Anbari said: It is literal, but it is not a negation of knowledge of what they were answered with at the time of delivering the message and during their lifetimes, upon them be blessings and peace, but rather of what was in the final outcome and its end, which is the basis for consideration. It was objected that they see the effects of the bad ending upon them, so it is also not valid to negate knowledge of their state and of what came from them after they separated from them. It was answered that this only indicates a bad ending and the manifestation of wretchedness in the outcome, not the reality of the response after the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace; perhaps they responded with acceptance and then wretchedness overcame them. It was objected that it is well known that the meaning of "What were you answered?" is not the very words they would say, nor the response that would occur from them, but rather what they were upon in matters of the Law, of compliance and submission, or the reverse of that. In a report from al-Hasan, the meaning of "We have no knowledge" is "like Your knowledge," because You know their inner states and we do not know that, and upon this depends the sphere of recompense. It has also been said that the purpose of that negation is to establish the disgrace of their nations: that is, You know their state better than we do, and there is no need for our testimony.

Al-Khatib, in his History, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning of negating knowledge is in view of the particular time, which is the beginning of the matter, when Hell roars and the creatures fall on their knees, tears flow, hearts rise to the throats, minds are bewildered, and intellects are stunned. Then, in the second state, after the terror subsides and the senses are gathered, they will respond, and that is at the time of their testimony over the nations. With this, may Allah be pleased with him, he answered Nafi' ibn al-Azraq when he asked him about the contradiction between this verse and what Allah established for them of testimony over their nations in another verse. It was also related from al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and Mujahid, and it is the view chosen by al-Farra'. Al-Jubba'i rejected it and said: "How is it permissible to say they are stunned by the horror of the Day of Resurrection, when He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾, and when He, mighty and majestic is He, says: ﴿No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾?" Al-Tabarsi transmitted this from him and then said: It can be answered that the greatest terror is entering the Fire, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿No fear will be upon them﴾ is only like good news of deliverance from the horrors of that day, just as one says to the sick: "No harm and no fear upon you."

It has also been said that this bewilderment was not due to fear or grief, but is of the kind of floating in the seas of awe because of the manifestation of the signs of the manifestation of majesty. Shaykh al-Islam objected to what was previously stated, saying: His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ is in the position of a reason, and it does not agree with what was mentioned. "'Allām" is an intensive form, and what is meant is the one perfect in knowledge. "Al-ghuyūb" is the plural of "ghayb," and a plural even if it is a verbal noun, according to what al-Samin said, because its kinds differ; and if what is meant by it is "the absent thing," or we say that it is a lightened form of "ghayb," then the matter is clear. "'Allāmu" was also read in the accusative, on the basis that the speech is complete at "Indeed You, You are," and the attribute is put in the accusative for praise, or for address, or as a substitute for the subject of "inna." The meaning of "Inna-ka anta" is "Indeed You are the one described by Your well-known attributes," and the speech is in the manner of the saying:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

Abu Bakr and Hamzah read "al-ghuyūbi" with a kasra on the ghayn wherever it occurs. It has been heard in every plural of the pattern fu'ul, like buyūt, where its first letter is given a kasra so that two damma and a waw do not follow one another consecutively.

﴿When Allah said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾. It is in the accusative by an implied verb, "Remember" (udhkur). It was said that it is in the nominative position, meaning "that [event] when," but this is not correct. The past-tense form is used because of what has been mentioned just before, namely the indication that the occurrence is certain. The purpose is to explain what took place between Allah, exalted is He, and one individual among the gathered Messengers in detail, after explaining in summary what took place between Him, mighty and majestic is He, and all of them. This serves as a model for the detailed states of the rest. The specific mention of Jesus, upon him be peace, is because his situation is connected to both groups of the People of the Book, those who went to extremes and those who fell short, whose wrongdoings this noble surah describes. Thus, detailing his case is greater against them and more productive of their regret. The mention of the Glorious Name is for the reason already given.

"Isa" (Jesus) is indeclinable according to al-Farra' and his followers, either on an implied damma or on an implied fatha, treating it like "ya Zayd ibn 'Amr" in the permissibility of the vocative being either raised or fathah, according to the majority. This applies when "ibn" is taken as an attribute (sifah) of Isa. If "ibn" is taken as an apposition (badal) or a clarifying term (bayan), then it is not permissible to assume a fathah, by consensus (ijma'), as explained in the books of grammar (nahw).

The "ʿalā" in His saying, ﴿Remember My favour upon you and upon your mother﴾, is connected to "ni'mati" (My favour), if this is taken as a verbal noun, meaning "remember My bestowal." Or it is connected to an implied element that serves as a circumstantial state (hal) qualifying "ni'mah," if it is taken as a noun, meaning "remember My favour being upon you," and so on. On both readings, "favour" refers to what is included within the multiplicity. It does not mean, as Shaykh al-Islam said, that on that day he was commanded to mention the favour included in the enumeration, nor that he was obligated to thank for it and fulfil its requirements. This is not a time for obligation, especially since he, upon him be peace, had already been freed from the duty of thanks at its proper time. Rather, it means making manifest his status, upon him be peace, by enumerating those favours as Allah has explained them, taking pride in them, and delighting in mentioning them before the heads of witnesses. The narration of this, as the noble composition indicates, is a rebuke to the disbelievers of both groups, who differ regarding his status, upon him be peace, through excess and deficiency, and an invalidation of both of their claims.

﴿When I strengthened you﴾ is a temporal adverbial clause (zarf) for "favour," meaning "remember My favour upon you both at the time of My strengthening you." Or it is a circumstantial state of it, meaning "remember it as existing at the time of that." It was also said that it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it, and in meaning it is an explanation of it.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a direct object (maf'ul bihi) by way of expansion (al-si'ah). It was read "ayyadtuka" with a long vowel (madd). Its form, according to al-Zamakhshari, is af'altuka, and according to Ibn 'Atiyyah it is fa'altuka. Abu Hayyan said: it requires transmitting its imperfect from the speech of the Arabs. If it is "yu'ayyidu," then it is fa'ala; if it is "yu'ayyidu" with the doubled letter, then it is af'ala. Its meaning and the meaning of "ayyada" are one. It was said that with the long vowel its meaning is strength (quwwah), and with the doubled letter its meaning is victory (nasr). These two are, as it has been said, close in meaning, because victory is a form of strength.

﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾ means Jibril, upon him be peace, or the speech by which he gives life to religion, and which becomes a cause of purification from the defilements of sins. Or it means that by it the dead are revived, or souls are given eternal life. Or it means the very spirit of his, upon him be peace, since Allah, exalted is He, made it manifest as a spirit that is holy, pure, radiant, luminous, and sublime. That this strengthening was a favour upon him, upon him be peace, is beyond dispute. As for it being a favour upon his mother, it is because of what followed from it of her acquittal from what was attributed to her, far be it from her, and other things.

﴿You speak to the people in the cradle﴾ means as a small child. What is in the noble composition is more eloquent than explicitly stating childhood, and more suitable, because a young child is called a child (tifl) until he reaches puberty (hulm). For this reason it was phrased differently. The adverbial phrase is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of "tukallim" (you speak).

It is permitted that it be an adverbial phrase of the verb. The clause is either a resumptive explanatory statement (istinaf mubayyin) clarifying his strengthening, upon him be peace, or it is in the position of a circumstantial state from the pronoun in the accusative in "ayyadtuka," as Abu al-Baqa' said. "Al-mahd" (the cradle) is well known. It is reported from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is the lap of his mother, upon them both be peace. The Christians denied that he, upon him be peace, spoke in the cradle, and they said that he, upon him be peace, only spoke at the time when children speak. This has already been mentioned along with its answer.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and as an adult (kahl)﴾ is, as has been said, to indicate that there was no difference in his speech, upon him be peace, between childhood and adulthood. It is not because each of them is a sign, for speaking in adulthood is known from everyone. The Imam said: the second (speaking as an adult) is also an independent miracle, because the meaning is "you speak to the people in childhood and in adulthood, when you descend from heaven," since he, upon him be peace, when he was raised up, was not an adult. This is based on explaining "kahl" as one whose hair has turned white and who has the dignity of appearance, or one who has passed thirty-four years up to fifty-one. Jesus, upon him be peace, was raised when he was thirty-three years old, it is said, and three months and three days. It is also said he was raised when he was thirty-four. It is not established that he, upon him be peace, had white hair. If "kahl" is explained as one who has passed thirty, then this view cannot be upheld, as is clear.

Some said: it is better to take "wa kahlan" as a complete metaphor (tashbih baligh), meaning "you speak to them being in the cradle and being like an adult." You know that deriving a simile from the conjunction has no basis, and estimating a kaf (like) is an artificial strain.

﴿And when I taught you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿when I strengthened you﴾, meaning "remember My favour upon you both at the time when I taught you," without any teacher, ﴿the Book and the Wisdom﴾, meaning their kind. It was said: "the Book" is writing, and "the Wisdom" is speech that is sound and correct. ﴿The Torah and the Gospel﴾ are singled out for mention to show their nobility over the first.

﴿And when you shape﴾, that is, form from clay, namely its kind, into the likeness of a bird, that is, a shape like its shape, ﴿by My permission, then you breathe into it﴾, that is, into that shaped form, ﴿and it becomes﴾ after your breathing without delay a bird, ﴿by My permission﴾, that is, a living creature that flies like other birds. Nafi' and Ya'qub read "ta'iran" (a bird) in the singular, and it is either a singular noun or a collective noun like "ba'ir" and "samir."

﴿And you heal the blind and the leper by My permission﴾ is conjoined to "takhluqu" (you shape). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and when you bring forth the dead by My permission﴾ is conjoined to "idh takhluqu" (when you shape). The word "idh" is repeated in it, as has been said, because the bringing forth of the dead from their graves, especially after they have become dust, is a manifest miracle that deserves an explicit mention of its time. What is in the noble composition is more eloquent than "when you revive the dead," which is why it was phrased differently. The discussion of who he revived, upon him be peace, has already been given, along with what benefits you in this verse, in Surah Al 'Imran.

"By My permission" is mentioned here four times and there twice. It was said: because here it is for enumerating favours, and there it is for informing. So this repetition fits here.

﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾, meaning the Jews, when they intended to kill him and were not able to do so.

﴿When you came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the manifest miracles, both those mentioned and those not mentioned. This is a temporal adverbial clause of "I restrained," together with considering His saying: ﴿Those of them who disbelieved said, "This is nothing but evident magic."﴾

[11]
This indicates that they intended to assassinate him, upon him be peace, which required the restraint. That is, "I restrained them from you when they said that upon your coming to them with clear proofs." The relative pronoun was placed in the position of their pronoun in order to disparage them by what is in its clause. So "min" (of them) is explanatory. "This" refers to what he brought. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "illa sahirun" (except a magician). Then the reference is to Jesus, upon him be peace. Making the reference to him on the first reading, and interpreting "magic" as "magician" so that the two readings agree, is not necessary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 111:

﴿وإذْ أوْحَيْتُ إلى الحَوارِيِّينَ﴾ That is, I commanded them in the Gospel through your tongue, or they were commanded through the tongues of My messengers. The use of *wahy* (revelation, inspiration) to mean *amr* (command) occurs in Arabic speech, as al-Zajjaj said, and he cited [a line of poetry]: "Praise be to God, by whose leave the heavens stood firm, and were made still. He inspired them to settle, so they settled." That is, He commanded them to remain fixed, and they complied. It was also said that what is meant by the inspiration to them is God's inspiring them (*ilham*), as in His words: ﴿وأوْحى رَبُّكَ إلى النَّحْلِ﴾ and ﴿وأوْحَيْنا إلى أُمِّ مُوسى﴾. This was narrated from al-Suddi and Qatada. The *wahy* was not kept to its literal sense because it is specific to the prophets, upon them be peace, and the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were not such. The meaning of "al-Hawariyyun" has already been explained.

As for His words ﴿أنْ آمِنُوا بِي وبِرَسُولِي﴾, the *an* is explanatory (*mufassirah*), clarifying what the inspiration contains of the sense of speech. It was also said that it is verbal-noun-forming (*masdariyyah*), meaning "that they believe," etc. The discussion of its entry upon the imperative has already been given. The mention of the title of messenger serves to draw attention to the manner of believing in him, upon him be peace, and it hints at not raising him or lowering him beyond his proper limit. ﴿قالُوا آمَنّا﴾ in accordance with what we were commanded. ﴿واشْهَدْ بِأنَّنا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾

- Sincere in our faith, or submitting to what we were commanded.

﴿When the disciples said: "O Jesus, son of Mary..."﴾ is in the accusative, governed by (اذْكُرْ, *udhkur*, "mention"). It begins a new statement, explaining what took place between him, peace be upon him, and his people, and it is disconnected from what precedes it, as the use of the noun in place of the pronoun indicates.

It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of (لَقالُوا, *laqalū*, "they said"). According to what has been said, there is in this a warning that their claim of sincerity, together with their saying: ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?﴾, did not arise from certainty or from knowledge of God Most High and His power, for had they been certain and knowledgeable, they would not have said that, since such a statement does not befit one who believes in God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Halabi criticized this view, saying that it contradicts the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I know of no disagreement that they were believers." This is supported by God's saying: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this...﴾, and by the fact that describing them as disciples (*hawāriyyūn*) is incompatible with their being upon falsehood. It is also supported by God's command to the believers to imitate them and follow their example, in His saying: ﴿Be helpers of God...﴾ and so on. And by the fact that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) praised al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him), saying: "Every prophet has a disciple, and my disciple is al-Zubayr." Moreover, one would have to hold that the disciples were of two groups: believers, who were Jesus's pure companions and those commanded to imitate them, and disbelievers, who were the people of the table. The request of Jesus, peace be upon him, that the table be sent down, and its sending down in order to establish the proof against them, would require a transmitted report, and none has been found.

Because of this, the verse has been answered in several ways. It has been said: the meaning of ﴿Can [your Lord] do it?﴾ is "Will he do it?", just as one says to someone capable of standing: "Can you stand?", as an intensified way of pressing the matter. This view is reported from al-Hasan.

Expressing the act by "ability" (*istita'a*) is an instance of expressing the effect by its cause, since ability is among the causes of bringing something into existence. The reverse is the expression of the will to do an act by the act itself, calling the cause, which is the will, by the name of the effect, which is the act, as in God's saying: ﴿When you rise to prayer...﴾ and so on.

It has also been said: the meaning is ﴿Can your Lord...﴾, with (فَيَسْتَطِيعُ, *fayastaṭī'u*, "so he is able") meaning (يُطِيعُ, *yuṭī'u*, "obeys"), and "obeys" meaning "responds", figuratively. This is reported from al-Suddi. Abu Shama mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) visited Abu Talib during an illness, and said to him: "O my nephew, ask your Lord to heal me." He said: "O God, cure my uncle." So he rose as if he had been released from a shackle. Then he said: "O my nephew, indeed your Lord whom you worship obeys you." He said: "O my uncle, if you obeyed Him, He would obey you." That is, He would respond to you concerning what you seek. The Prophet's (ﷺ) use of this expression is fine because of the figure of speech of correspondence (*mushākala*).

It has also been said: this ability is in accordance with what wisdom and will require, so it is as if they said: "Has the will and decree of God Most High been directed to this or not?", since nothing comes to be without its being connected to His will.

It has been objected that His saying that follows: ﴿Be mindful of God, if you are believers﴾ does not fit this, because asking about such a matter is among the matters of the unseen, which involves no deficiency. It has been said that their request was for reassurance and confirmation, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾. The meaning of ﴿if you are believers﴾ is: "if you are perfect in faith and sincerity." The meaning of (نَعْلَمَ أنْ قَدْ صَدَقْتَنا, *na'lama an qad ṣadaqtanā*, "that we may know that you have spoken truly to us") is: "that we may know by the knowledge of direct witnessing and observation, after we had known it by the knowledge of faith and certainty." From this it is known what removes the objection.

Al-Kisa'i, 'Ali (may God ennoble his face), 'A'isha, Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'adh, and a group of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) read: (هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ, *hal tastaṭī'u rabbaka*), with a *ta'* (addressing Jesus), and (رَبَّكَ, *rabbaka*, "your Lord") in the accusative as the object.

Most scholars hold that there is an omitted noun, meaning "the request of your Lord", that is, "Will you ask Him this without any hindrance?" It is reported from al-Farisi that there is no need for an assumed word, and the meaning is: "Can you ask your Lord to send down by your supplication?" But you know that the wording does not convey that, so the assumed word is necessary.

The table (*māʾida*), in the common usage, is the spread on which the food is placed, from (مادَ يَمِيدُ, *māda yamīdu*, "to sway, to move"), when it moves. Or it is from (مادَهُ, *mādahu*, "to give"), meaning "he gave him". Then it is an active participle (*fā'ila*) in the sense of a passive (*maf'ūla*), as in ﴿a pleasing life﴾. Al-Zahri preferred this in *Tahdhib al-Lugha*. Or it is an active form because it gives what is on it, as if it were itself giving, like the expression used of a fruitful tree: "feeding" (*muṭʿima*).

Some have allowed that it be called (مَيْدَةٌ, *maydah*), and they cited as evidence the verse of the rajaz poet:

"A *maydah* with many kinds, prepared for neighbours and brothers."

Al-Manawi preferred that the table is whatever sways and is spread out, and that what is meant by it is the *sufra* (traveller's cloth). Its origin is food that a traveller prepares, and then the round leather on which it is usually carried was named by it, just as the water-skin was called *rāwiya*. It is also permitted that the leather in question was called a *sufra* because it has fastenings which, when undone, open it out and reveal what is inside.

This differs from the *khiwān* (a raised table), pronounced with *kh* either vowelled with a *ḍamma* or a *kasra*, the latter being more eloquent. It is also called *ikhwān*, with a kasra on the hamza, because it is the name of a raised object prepared for eating food upon. Eating upon it is an innovation (*bid'a*), but it is permissible if free from the intention of arrogance. The word *māʾida* is also applied to the food itself, as some scholars have explicitly stated.

(مِنَ السَّماءِ, *min al-samā'*, "from heaven") may be connected to the verb before it, or it may be connected to an omitted word that serves as a qualifier of (مائِدَةً, *mā'ida*), meaning "a table coming from heaven".

﴿He said﴾, that is, Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them when they said that: ﴿Be mindful of God﴾, from such requests and from demanding signs, as al-Zajjaj said. It is reported from al-Farisi that it is a command to them to be mindful of God in general. Perhaps this is so that it may become a means to attaining what is hoped for, since He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Whoever is mindful of God, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾, and the Most High said: ﴿O you who believe, be mindful of God and seek the means to Him﴾. ﴿If you are believers﴾

— with the perfection of His power, may He be exalted, and with the soundness of my prophethood; or: if you are perfect in faith and sincerity; or: if you are truthful in your claim of faith and submission.
