﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it"﴾: that is, to eat for blessing (ta'arruk). It was also said: to eat for enjoyment and need. The "wish" (irada) is either in its apparent meaning or in the sense of "love" (mahabba), that is, "we love that." The statement, as has been said, is either a preamble or an excuse, and an explanation of what prompted them to ask. That is, "We do not want by the request to remove doubt about His power, glory be to Him, to send it down, or about the truth of your prophethood, such that this would harm our faith and piety. Rather, we want, etc." Or: "Our aim is not to propose signs, but our aim is what has been mentioned."

﴿and that our hearts may be reassured﴾ by an increase in certainty, as 'Ata' said, and ﴿that we may know﴾ with the knowledge of direct witnessing and seeing, as we have already explained. ﴿that you have indeed spoken truly to us﴾: that is, that you have indeed spoken truly in claiming prophethood. It was also said: in that God, exalted is He, answers our supplication. It was also said: in what you have claimed, absolutely.

﴿and that we may be among the witnesses to it﴾

311

To those among the Children of Israel who were not present, so that the believers among them may increase in reassurance and certainty through our testimony, and their disbelievers may believe because of it; or "among the witnesses" means witnesses by sight, not merely hearers of the report. It was also said: witnesses to God, exalted is He, for His oneness, and to you for prophethood.

"ʿAlayhā" (عَلَيْها) is connected to "al-shāhidīn" (الشّاهِدِينَ) if the lam is taken as the definite article, or to a verb understood that is explained by "min al-shāhidīn" (مِنَ الشّاهِدِينَ) if the lam is taken as a relative pronoun. We permit explaining what would not itself govern (the explanation of an element that does not itself operate). It was also said that it is connected to "al-shāhidīn" itself, and in that case it would involve fronting what lies within the relative clause and the prepositional phrase, and both are prohibited.

It is reported from some grammarians that fronting is permitted with an adverbial (dharf), and from some of them that it is permitted absolutely. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "kāna" (كانَ), that is, "devoted to it" (ʿākifīn ʿalayhā). It is read as "yuʿlama" (يُعْلَمَ) in the passive, and "wa-taʿlama" (وتَعْلَمَ) with a ta' prefix, the pronoun referring to the hearts.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 5, verse 114:

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said﴾ because he saw that they had a sound purpose in this. Al-Tirmidhi, in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and others related from Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he (peace be upon him) saw that they refused except that he should supplicate for them with it, he stood up, removed the wool from himself, and put on black hair. Then he performed ablution (*wudu'*) and ritual bathing (*ghusl*), entered his place of prayer, and prayed as much as Allah willed. When he had finished his prayer, he stood facing the qibla, set his feet together until they were level, joined heel to heel, aligned toe with toe, placed his right hand over his left above his chest, lowered his gaze, and bowed his head in humility. Then he let his eyes weep, and his tears kept flowing down his cheeks and dripping from the edges of his beard until the ground in front of his face was soaked. When he saw this, he called upon Allah, the Exalted, and said: ﴿O Allah, our Lord﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, is addressed twice, according to what has been said: once by the attribute of divinity (*uluhiyyah*), which comprises all perfections, and once by the attribute of lordship (*rububiyyah*), which indicates nurturing, to show the utmost humility and to intensify the plea.

He did not make it one vocative (*nida'*) by making ﴿Lord﴾ an apposition (*badal*) or a descriptive adjunct (*sifah*), because they said that the word *Allahumma* is not followed by a modifier. There is a difference of opinion on this among some grammarians (*nuhat*).

The vocative particle was omitted in the first instance and the letter *mim* was added in its place, and likewise in the second, except that compensation (*ta'wid*) is one of the distinctive features of the Glorious Name. That is: O Allah, O our Lord.

﴿Send down upon us a table﴾, that is, a spread with food upon it, or a food-cloth of that kind. The placing of the adverbial phrase before the direct object is, as has been mentioned many times, for the sake of emphasis on the preposed element and to create anticipation for what follows. His saying, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿from heaven﴾,

Page 61

is connected either to *send down* or to a omitted element that serves as a descriptive modifier of *table*, meaning: coming from heaven. By "heaven" is meant either the well-known place, which is what is immediately understood from the word, or the direction of height. The first is supported by what Ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ammar ibn Yasir, that the table which was sent down had upon it fruit from Paradise. Similarly, it is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second is supported by what is related from Salman al-Farisi in a lengthy report, that when the table was sent down, Shim'un, the chief of the disciples (*al-hawariyyun*), said to Jesus, peace be upon him: "O Spirit of Allah and His Word, is this food of this world or food of Paradise?" Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "Has not the time come for you to take heed from the signs you see, and to desist from probing into questions? How I fear for you that you will be punished because of this sign!" Shim'un said: "No, by the God of Israel, I did not intend any harm by it. O son of the truthful woman!" Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "Nothing of what you see upon it is from the food of Paradise or from the food of this world. It is only something that Allah, the Exalted, brought into being in the air by overwhelming and irresistible power. He said to it, 'Be,' and it was, in less than the blink of an eye. So eat of what you have asked for, in the name of Allah, and praise Him for it, your Lord will provide you with more from it and increase it for you, for He is the Originator, the Able, the Thankful."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿will be a festival for us﴾: *takunu* is an attribute of *ma'idah* (table), *lana* is the predicate of *kana* (was/would be), and *'idan* (festival) is a circumstantial element (*hal*) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase or in *takunu*, according to the view of those who permit its operation on the circumstantial element. It is also permissible for *'idan* to be the predicate and *lana* then to be a circumstantial element, either from the pronoun in *takunu* or a circumstantial element from *'idan*, since it is a modifier of it that has been placed before it.

*Al-'id* (festival) is derived from *al-'awd* (return). It is applied to a known time because it returns every year with joy and happiness. In that case, a governed noun must be assumed, and the meaning is: its descent will be a festival for us. It is also applied to the joy itself that returns, and in that case no assumption is needed. There is a subtlety in the expression that is not hidden.

Many have stated that *'id* is used for anything that returns to you at a time. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Ah, my liver, from the passion of love and desire,
when my heart has become accustomed, from Umaymah, to its festival.*

It is a *waw*-root word, as its derivation indicates. However, they said its plural is *a'yad*, whereas the analogical form would be *a'wad*, because plurals return things to their roots to avoid confusion, as Ibn Hisham said, with the plural of *'ud* (wood). Al-Hariri compared this with their saying: *huwa alyatu bi-qalbi minka*, meaning: he is more firmly attached to my heart than you, that is, more closely bound in love to it, since its root is *waw*, but they said it so as to distinguish it from their saying: *huwa alwatu min fulan*. It is not hidden that this contradicts what the verifying scholars of the lexicon have mentioned. From al-Kisa'i: it is said *laata al-shay'u bi-qalbi yalutu wa yaliitu*, and he is *alwatu* and *aliyatu*.

Furthermore, they did not reverse the matter in the plurals of *'ud* and *'id*, so that they would say for the plural of the first *a'yad* and for the plural of the second *a'wad*, even though this would also achieve the distinction. This is on the basis of what has been said: the lighter form is preferred in most usage, while observing the apparent form of the singular.

ʿAbd Allah read *takun* in the jussive, as an answer to the imperative. ﴿For the first of us and the last of us﴾, that is, for the people of our time and those who come after us. It is related that it was sent down on a Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, the meaning is: the first of people and the last of them will eat from it.

The prepositional phrase, according to some, is a substitute (*badal*) for the prepositional phrase *lana*. Abu al-Baqa' said: if *lana* is made a predicate or a circumstantial element, it is a modifier of *'idan*. If it is made a modifier of it, then it is a substitute for the genitive pronoun with the preposition repeated. Its apparent sense is that the pronoun is the thing being substituted, but the preposition has been repeated because a substitute is in effect a repetition of the governing element. This is arbitrary, because the apparent sense, as indicated, is the substitution of a plural by a plural. Furthermore, the pronoun of the absent person may be substituted, whereas for the pronoun of the present person, some permit it absolutely, others permit it in the same way, and some groups distinguish: if it conveys emphasis, comprehensiveness, and inclusiveness, it is permitted; otherwise it is not.

Some have preferred, against the view of the scholar (*al-habr*), that *lana* be the predicate, meaning: a sustenance, or beneficial for us. Zayd, Ibn Muhaysin,

Page 62

and al-Jahdari read *li-'ulana wa-'ukhrana*, with the feminine form of *al-awwal* and *al-akhir*, considering the community and the group. That the intended meaning of *al-'ula* and *al-ukhra* is the first abode and the last abode, that is, this world and the hereafter, is hardly valid.

﴿And a sign﴾ is coordinated with *'idan*. His saying, glorified and exalted, ﴿from You﴾ is connected to an omitted element that serves as its modifier, meaning: a sign coming from You, indicating the perfection of Your power and the soundness of my prophethood. ﴿And provide for us﴾, that is, the gratitude for it, according to what al-Jubba'i related, or the table, according to what has been reported from more than one source. In that case, what is meant by it, as has been said, is the food on the spread, or the more general sense that includes that and this, and perhaps this is the better view. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾.

411

This is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) functioning as a justification: that is, You are the best of those who provide, because He is the Creator of provision and its Giver without seeking any return.

[511]

﴿Allah said: "Indeed I am sending it down to you."﴾ He said "munazziluha" (sending it down) with the intensive form (ṣīghat al-taf'īl, the form that indicates repetition or intensity), as this indicates that it was sent down many times. The fact that Allah the Exalted responded to the request in this manner, even though the supplication came from him (ﷺ) in the form of verbs, shows the completeness of His kindness and grace. This also takes into account the wording used by the petitioners. Opening the sentence with the particle of affirmation (kalimat al-taḥqīq, "indeed") and making its predicate a noun (ism) confirms the promise, indicates that Allah, glorified and exalted, will undoubtedly fulfil it, and signals continuity. This reading belongs to the people of Madinah, al-Sham, and ʿĀṣim.

The rest read "munziluha" (without the intensive form), as al-Ṭabarsī said, and treated *al-inzāl* (sending down) and *al-tanzīl* (sending down, gradually) as having one meaning.

﴿So whoever disbelieves after that among you﴾, i.e., after its sending down, while he is among you, ﴿then I will punish him﴾ for that disbelief of his ﴿with a punishment﴾. The word *ʿadhāban* (punishment) is an ism al-maṣdar (a verbal noun used in place of the full masdar), meaning "punishing," like *matāʿ* meaning "providing enjoyment." It was also said that it is a masdar with its extra letters removed. Its being in the accusative is as a masdar under both views. It was also said that it is in the accusative by way of extension (tawassuʿ), likening it to the direct object, for emphasis, just as the adverbial of time or place is put in the accusative, and the complement of the attributive adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha) is likewise. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that its accusative be by omission of the preposition and making the verb reach its object (ḥadhf wa-l-īṣāl). In that case, *ʿadhāban* means the name of that with which one is punished. It is not hidden that omitting the preposition is not regular except with *anna* and *an* when there is no ambiguity. The tanwīn (nunation) is for magnification, i.e., a great punishment.

His words, glorified and exalted: ﴿I will not punish him﴾ are in the place of the accusative as an attribute of *ʿadhāban*. The pronoun (*hāʾ*) is in the place of the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq), as in *ẓanantuhu Zaydan qāʾiman* (I thought him Zayd standing). It stands in place of the returning pronoun to the modified noun, as has been said. It was argued that in this case it returns to the masdar understood from the verb, so it has the sense of an indefinite noun after negation, in terms of generality, and thus includes the previously mentioned punishment, and the connection is achieved through generality. It was objected that the connection through generality was mentioned by the grammarians only for a sentence functioning as a predicate, so the attribute cannot be analogized to it. It was also permitted that it is of the type: *ḍarabtuhu ḍarba Zaydin* (I struck him a strike like Zayd's), meaning: a punishment that I do not inflict as a punishment like it. In this case the pronoun returns to the earlier-mentioned punishment, so the connection is through it.

It was also said: the pronoun returns to *man* (whoever), with two omitted elements of construction, meaning: I will not punish anyone with a punishment like his punishment ﴿anyone among the worlds﴾.

– i.e., among the worlds of their time, or among the worlds absolutely. This punishment is either in this world, and those among them who disbelieved were punished by being transformed into apes and swine, as is narrated from Qatādah; or it is in the Hereafter, and to this points what Abū al-Shaykh and others narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Indeed the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection are those who disbelieved among the companions of the table (al-māʾida), the hypocrites, and the family of Pharaoh." This indicates that the table was sent down and some of them disbelieved afterward.

Ibn Jarīr and others narrated from al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid that when it was said to the people, "Whoever disbelieves…" and so on, they said: "We have no need for it," so it was not sent down. But the majority hold the first view, and it is upon this that reliance is placed. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, both as a statement of his own (mawqūf) and as a prophetic report (marfūʿ), and the mawqūf version is more authentic, that he said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat, and they were commanded not to betray and not to store up for the next day, but they betrayed and stored, so they were transformed into apes and swine." The bread was of rice, according to what is narrated from ʿIkrimah.

It is narrated that when his people asked Jesus, peace be upon him, for this, he supplicated, and Allah the Exalted sent down upon them a red tray (sufra) between two clouds, one cloud above it and one cloud beneath it, while they were looking at it in the air, descending swiftly from heaven, coming down toward them, while Jesus, peace be upon him, wept out of fear of the condition that had been imposed upon them concerning it. He kept supplicating until the tray settled before him, and the disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn) were around him, smelling a pleasant fragrance they had never smelled the like of. Jesus, peace be upon him, and the disciples fell down in prostration in gratitude to Allah the Exalted. The Jews came looking at them and saw what distressed them, then they went away. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, and those with him came to look at it, and found it covered with a napkin. He, peace be upon him, said: "Who among us is the most daring to uncover it, the most trusting of himself, and the best in trial before his Lord, so that we may see it, praise our Lord, glorified and exalted, and eat from His provision which He has provided for us?" They said: "O Spirit of Allah and His Word, you are most deserving of that." So he stood, renewed his ablution, entered his place of prayer, prayed several cycles, then wept for a long time, and supplicated Allah the Exalted to permit him to uncover it, and to make for him and his people in it blessing and provision. Then he turned away, sat around the tray, took the napkin, and said: "In the name of Allah, the best of providers," and uncovered it. Behold, upon it was a large roasted fish, having no scales, and having no bones in its inside, from which fat dripped. Around it were arranged herbs of every kind except leeks, and at its head was vinegar, at its tail was salt, and around the herbs were five loaves of bread: on one of them was olives, on another dates, on another five pomegranates. In another narration: on one of them was olives, on the second honey, on the third ghee, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat. Shamʿūn asked him about these, and he answered him with what was previously narrated.

Then they said to him, peace be upon him: "We only wish that you show us a sign from these signs." He, peace be upon him, said: "Glory be to Allah the Exalted! Are you not content?" Then he said: "O fish, return by the permission of Allah, alive as you were," and Allah the Exalted revived it by His power. It thrashed, returned alive and fresh, licking its lips as a lion licks, its eyes turning, and having a glint. Its scales returned to it. The people were frightened by it and fled. Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them: "What is the matter with you? You ask for a sign, and when your Lord shows it to you, you dislike it! How I fear for you because of what you do! O fish, return by the permission of Allah, the Exalted, as you were, roasted." Then he invited them to eat. They said: "O Spirit of Allah, it is you who should begin with it." He said: "God forbid! He should not begin with the request for it." When they saw the abstention of their prophet, peace be upon him, they feared that its descent was a sign of wrath, and that eating from it would be likewise, so they refrained. Then he, peace be upon him, supplicated over it for the poor and the chronically ill, and said: "Eat from the provision of your Lord and the supplication of your Prophet, and praise Allah the Exalted who sent it down to you, so that its congratulations are for you and its punishment is for others. Begin all of you with the name of Allah and end with the praise of Allah." They did so, and there ate from it one thousand three hundred people, men and women, and they departed from it, each one of them full, belching. Jesus and the disciples looked at what was upon it, and behold, what was upon it was in the same state as when it descended from heaven, nothing having been diminished from it. Then it was raised back to heaven while they watched. Every poor person who ate from it became rich, and every chronically ill person who ate from it was healed, and they remained wealthy and healthy until they left the world. The disciples and their companions who refused to eat from it regretted it with a regret that caused their eyelids to flow, and its sorrow remained in their hearts.

Whenever the table descended after that, the Children of Israel came to it from every place, running, so some of them crowded others: the rich and the poor, women and children, the old and the young, the healthy and the sick, some of them mounting others. When Jesus, peace be upon him, saw that, he made it arrive in turns among them, so it descended one day and did not descend another day. They remained in this for forty days, descending upon them alternately at the rise of the forenoon, and it was constantly set out, and they ate from it, until when they said that it was lifted from them by the permission of Allah the Exalted to the atmosphere of heaven while they looked, and they watched its shadow on the earth until it disappeared from them. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to Jesus, peace be upon him: "Make My provision for the orphans, the needy, and the chronically ill, not the rich among the people." When Allah the Exalted did that, the rich doubted it and despised that, until they doubted it in themselves, and cast doubt upon it among the people, and spread ugly and reprehensible talk about its matter. Satan achieved his aim among them and cast his whisperings into the hearts of the doubters. When Jesus, peace be upon him, knew that from them, he said: "You have perished, by the God of the Messiah! You asked your prophet to seek the table for you from your Lord, and when he did and sent it down upon you as mercy and provision, and showed you in it the signs and lessons, you denied it and doubted it. So rejoice in the punishment, for it is descending upon you unless Allah, the Exalted, has mercy upon you."

Allah the Exalted revealed to Jesus, peace be upon him: "Indeed, I seize the deniers according to My condition, and indeed I will punish among them whoever disbelieved in the table after its descent with a punishment ﴿that I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾." When the doubters evening came and took their beds, in the best form, with their wives, secure, and at the last part of the night, Allah the Exalted transformed them into swine, and in the morning they were chasing filth in the refuse heaps.

Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to the Children of Israel: "Would you like to fast thirty days and then ask Him, and He will give you what you ask, for indeed the wage of the worker is upon the one for whom he works?" So they did. Then they said: "O teacher of good, you told us that the wage of the worker is upon the one for whom he works, and you commanded us to fast thirty days, and we did, and we never worked for anyone for thirty days without his feeding us. So can your Lord send down upon us a table from heaven?" …up to His words, the Exalted: ﴿anyone among the worlds﴾. Then the angels came flying with a table from heaven upon which were seven fish and seven loaves, until they placed it before them. The last of the people ate from it just as the first of them ate. It is also reported that the table would descend upon them wherever they were, and from Wahb ibn Munabbih that four thousand people would sit around the table, and whenever they ate something, Allah the Exalted replaced it with its like. They remained in this state for as long as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 116 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary,"﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿when the disciples said﴾, and is in the accusative (manṣūb) by the verb that governs it, which is implied, or by an independent implied verb conjoined to that. The past form is used for what is past, and the meaning is that He will say to him, peace be upon him, ﴿"Did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, as a rebuke to the disbelievers and a reproach to them, through his acknowledgment, peace be upon him, before all witnesses, of servanthood and through his command to them to worship Him, Mighty and Majestic.

It has been said: He, glorified is He, will say this to him, peace be upon him, in this world. This was after sunset, so he, peace be upon him, prayed the maghrib (sunset) prayer as three rak'ahs out of gratitude to Allah, Exalted, when He addressed him with this. The first rak'ah was to deny divinity of himself, the second to deny it of his mother, and the third to affirm it for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus he, peace be upon him, was the first to pray maghrib. It is not hidden that what will come, if Allah Exalted wills, in the verses rejects this, and no report that contains it is sound. Furthermore, according to some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn), the basis of the statement is not that the saying is certain while the interrogation is to specify the speaker, as is apparent from placing the hamza (interrogative particle) before the subject in the common usage, and upon this is His saying, Exalted, ﴿"Did you do this to our gods?"﴾ and similar. Rather, the certain matter is the taking (of the gods). The interrogation is to specify whether this was by his command, peace be upon him, or a matter from their own selves, as in His saying, Exalted, ﴿"Did you lead My servants astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾

Some have said: since the saying had come from their leaders in error, it was established like the taking, so the interrogation is to specify
[Page 65]
who issued it, and for this reason the predicate subject (musnad ilayhi) was placed first. It has also been said: the fronting is to strengthen the attribution, because it is far from acceptance, such that the listener's soul does not turn to the notion that its apparent meaning is intended, so as to answer in accordance with it. Therefore it needed strengthening, so that the questioner's attention would be directed to it. In this there is the full rebuke of the disbelievers by attributing this saying to him. In His saying, Exalted, ﴿"Take me and my mother"﴾ rather than "and take me" and Mary, there is a rebuke upon a rebuke, as if it were said: "Did you say what you said, while you are one who was born, and your mother one who gave birth, and God does not beget nor is He begotten?"

You know that in his being called in this manner, peace be upon him, there is an indication of the nullification of that taking. The lām in ﴿lil-nās (to the people)﴾ is for conveying (the message). The verb "taking" is either transitive to two objects, so the ya' (me) is its first object and ﴿ilahayn (two gods)﴾ its second; or it is transitive to one object, so ﴿ilahayn﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of the object, and ﴿min dūn Allāh (besides Allah)﴾ is a ḥāl of the subject of the taking, meaning "exceeding Allah, Exalted", or it is an adjective of ﴿ilahayn﴾, meaning "existing besides Allah, Exalted", i.e., other than Him, joined to Him, glorified is He. So Allah, Exalted, is a god, and they, according to the claim of the disbelievers, are two gods. The intended meaning is taking them by way of associating them with Him, Mighty and Majestic. This is as in His saying, Exalted, ﴿"And they worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them"﴾ and they say, ﴿"These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿"Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate."﴾ This is supported by the fact that rebuke and reproach come only with this.

Al-Raghib said: the apparent meaning of that saying is that they are independently gods, peace be upon them both, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, did not take any god alongside them. There must be an interpretation of that, because the people made a trinity, and we seek refuge in Allah, Exalted. Either it is said that whoever associates with Allah, glorified is He, another, has in effect denied Him, since He, majestic is His name, is alone without partner, and his affirmation of Allah, Exalted, becomes as though it were no affirmation at all. In that case ﴿min dūn Allāh (besides Allah)﴾ is a metaphor for ﴿maʿa Allāh (along with Allah)﴾, Exalted. Or it is said: the intended meaning of ﴿min dūn Allāh (besides Allah)﴾ is an intermediary between them and Him, majestic is His glory, so the word "dūn (besides)" indicates that their rank falls short of His rank, majestic is His majesty, because they said: He, majestic is His name, is like the sun, and they are like its rays.

Some claimed that the intended meaning is the taking of them by way of independence, and its basis is that the Christians believe that the miracles that appeared at the hands of Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, were not created by Allah, Exalted, but rather they created them. So it is correct that they took them as two independent gods with respect to some matters, and did not take Him as a god with respect to that part. The first is almost decisive, and the 'Allāmah (al-Alusi's reference) alludes to it, and Shaykh al-Islam explicitly chose it.

The verse has been questioned on the ground that it is not known that any of the Christians took Mary, peace be upon her, as a god. It has been answered in several ways. The first: since they made Jesus, peace be upon him, a god, it necessarily follows that they would make his mother likewise, because the offspring is of the same kind as the one who bore it. So mention of "two gods" is by way of imposing an obligation upon them. The second: since they exalted her with the exaltation of a god, the name "god" was applied to her, just as the name "lord" was applied to the rabbis and monks in His saying, Exalted, ﴿"They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah"﴾, because they exalted them with the exaltation of a lord. The dual then is according to the principle of "the pen is one of the two tongues." The third: it is possible that among them there were some who said this. What supports this view is what Abu Jaʿfar al-Imami related from some Christians: that in the past there was a people called the Maryamiyya, who believed Mary to be a god. This is like the Jews, among whom there were people who believed ʿUzayr to be the son of Allah, majestic is His name. This, in my view, is the most likely of the opinions. And what the claimant established, that the Christians believe etc., is not accepted regarding the Christians of our time, and no one trustworthy has transmitted it from them at all. The manifest naming of the Glorious Name is because it falls within the scope of the saying attributed to Jesus, peace be upon him.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), answering a question arising from the opening of the discourse, and that is evident. In some reports, when the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, says to him what He says, he, peace be upon him,
[Page 66]
trembles in his joints, and from the root of every hair on his body a spring of blood bursts forth out of fear of his Lord, majestic is His greatness. In some reports, he, peace be upon him, trembles in fear, and the door of answer is not opened to him for five hundred years; then Allah, Exalted, inspires him with the answer afterwards, and he says: ﴿"Glory be to You"﴾, meaning, exaltation of You from my saying that, or it is said concerning You, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya estimated. Some estimated it as: from there being for You a partner, let alone that two gods be taken besides You; and others as: from Your sending a messenger who claims divinity other than You, calls to it, and disbelieves in Your blessing. The first is more fitting to the context of the noble wording. And ﴿Subḥān (Glory be)﴾ under all the estimations, according to one of the opinions concerning it, which has already been mentioned, is a proper noun for glorification, and its accusative status is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its verb is rarely mentioned. In it is intensification of transcendence, from the standpoint of derivation from sabḥ, which is going far away in the land and departing, and from the standpoint of transfer to the form of taf'īl (intensive form), and the shift from the verbal noun to the noun specifically coined for it, which indicates the reality present in the mind, and its placement in the position of the verbal noun together with the verb, which is not hidden.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"It is not for me to say what I have no right to say"﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming the transcendence and specifying what is transcended. The second ﴿mā (what)﴾, whether it is a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun described by a relative clause, is the object of ﴿aqūla (I say)﴾, and what is meant by it on both estimations is the aforementioned saying, or what includes it and other things, and it enters the aforementioned saying as a primary inclusion. The governing of "saying" over single words, such as "sentence," "speech," or "poem," is undoubtedly sound, just as it governs explicit sentences, so there is no need to interpret ﴿aqūlu (I say)﴾ as ﴿adhkuru (I mention)﴾ as is imagined. The subject of ﴿laysa (is not)﴾ is a pronoun referring to ﴿mā (what)﴾, and ﴿biḥaqqin (with right)﴾ is its predicate; the preposition and its object between them are for specification, so it is connected to an omitted element, as in ﴿saqyan laka (watering to you)﴾. The choice of ﴿laysa (is not)﴾ over the negated verb ("does not befit me") is due to its clear indication of the continuance of the negation of rightfulness, and to conveying emphasis through the ba' in its predicate, whose extra use in the predicate of ﴿laysa (is not)﴾ is common.

The meaning of ﴿mā yakūnu lī (it is not for me)﴾ is: it is not fitting, nor suitable, and it is more eloquent than "I did not say it," for which reason it was chosen. The intended meaning is: it is not fitting that I say a saying that it is not right for me to say at all, at any time. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that ﴿lī (for me)﴾ could be the predicate of ﴿laysa (is not)﴾ with ﴿biḥaqqin (with right)﴾ in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in the preposition-phrase, and the governing element in it being the sense of stability that it contains. It could also be connected to an omitted verb as a causal object (mafʿūl lahu), with the ba' indicating cause, meaning: what is not established for me by cause of right. It could also be that the predicate of ﴿laysa (is not)﴾ is ﴿lī (for me)﴾, the attribute of ﴿ḥaqq (right)﴾ fronted over it, so it became a ḥāl. This is based on the view of one who permits fronting the ḥāl of a prepositional phrase over it. It has also been said: ﴿lī (for me)﴾ is connected to ﴿biḥaqqin (with right)﴾, which is the predicate, and this too is based on the view of some grammarians who permit fronting the complement of a prepositional phrase over the preposition, while the majority disallow it, and there is no difference in their prohibition between the preposition being extra or otherwise.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"If I had said it, You would already know it"﴾ is evidence for his innocence of having uttered the aforementioned saying, for its being uttered by him necessarily entails His knowledge of it, Exalted, with certainty; and knowledge of it is negated, so the utterance is negated by necessity, since the negation of the consequent entails the negation of the antecedent. This sentence has been questioned on the ground that the meaning here is past, whereas the particle ("if") turns the past into the future. Al-Mubarrad answered that ﴿kāna (was)﴾ is strongly indicative of the past, to the point that it is said it is coined for the past alone, not for the event, and they made this a reason for its being defective, so ﴿in (if)﴾ cannot convert it to the future.

Ibn al-Sarraj answered that the estimation is: "if I say, I was saying it," etc., and the same applies to similar cases. Ibn Yaʿish transmitted this, but Ibn Hisham weakened it in his Tadhkira. The majority hold that the meaning is: if my saying and claim of that is valid, then your knowledge of it has been made manifest. ﴿You know what is in my self﴾ is a resumptive sentence functioning as a justification for what precedes it. Therefore His saying, majestic is His glory: ﴿"and I do not know what is in Your self"﴾ is an explanation and a manifestation of his, peace be upon him, deficiency.

"Self (nafs)" has various uses in their speech: it is used for the essence and reality of a thing, for the spirit, for the heart, for blood, for will. It has been said that it is also used for the evil eye that strikes, for the unseen, and for punishment. It is understood from some statements that it is literal in the first usage and figurative in the rest. More than one interpreter explained "self" here as "heart," and the intended meaning is: You know what I have concealed in my heart, so how much more what I make public; and I do not know what You have concealed. He followed in this the path of mushakala (matching of terms), as in the verse: "They said: propose something and we will cook it for you. He said: cook for me a robe and a shirt." However, in the verse both terms occur in the speech of one person, whereas in the line of poetry this is not so.

In al-Durr al-Masun it is stated that this interpretation is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he related it also in Majmaʿ al-Bayan. Some explained it as the essence, and claimed that attributing it in this sense to Allah, Exalted, does not need to be considered a matter of mushakala. Among such usages is His saying, Exalted: ﴿"Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy"﴾, ﴿"and I have chosen you for Myself"﴾, and ﴿"and Allah warns you of Himself"﴾; and his saying, ﴿ﷺ﴾: "My Lord swore by Himself that no servant who drinks wine and does not repent to Allah from it will be given to drink of the sweat of the wretched"; and his saying, peace be upon him: "No one loves praise more than Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and for this reason He praised Himself"; and his saying ﴿ﷺ﴾: "Glory be to Allah as many as His creation, and as much as the pleasure of His self," and other reports besides these.

The muhaqqiq al-Sharif (al-Sharif al-Jurjani) said in his commentary on the Miftah and elsewhere: The word *nafs* (self) is not applied to Allah, the Exalted, except by way of *mushakala* (rhetorical correspondence, where a word is used because of its association with another word in the same context), even if it is meant to denote the essence. This is not correct, because of what you know of the verses and hadiths. The claim that what occurs in them is a *mushakala taqdiriyya* (a presumed correspondence), as has been said about His saying, ﴿The baptism of Allah! And who is better than Allah at baptism?﴾, is clearly from "the fallen goods" (*saqat al-mata'*, an idiom for what is worthless or rejected). Rather, the sound and reliable view is that it is permissible to apply it to Allah, the Exalted, in the sense of the essence, without any *mushakala*. However, it has been said that the word *nafs* in this verse, even though it means the essence, must still be accompanied by consideration of *mushakala*, because "You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self" is not a satisfactory statement. It therefore needs to be interpreted entirely as *mushakala*, so that the meaning is: "You know what I know, and I do not know what You know." It was expressed as "I do not know what is in Your self" because the expression "You know what I know" was used in place of "You know what is in my self."

Al-'Allamah al-Thani (al-'Allamah al-Thani, a later scholar) interpreted the words of the author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) in this way, and what is in it is not hidden. The truth is that the verse does contain *mushakala*, but not in the use of the word *nafs*. Rather, it lies in the particle *fi* (in). Its meaning, considered with respect to what is in the self of 'Isa (peace be upon him), is imprinting and engraving, and this is not possible when considered with respect to Allah, the Exalted. Some of the scholars' statements point to this, and from it one can see the confusion found in the books of usul (principles of jurisprudence) on this matter.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: It is possible that the intent is to negate *nafs* from Him, the Exalted, so that it is as if He said: "You know what is in my self," and "You have no self, so I know what is in it," like the words of the poet:

*And you do not see the dabb (lizard) burrowing therein.*

This is, despite its remoteness, something that does not need to be relied upon. Similar to it is what some of the learned have mentioned: that the second *nafs* is also the self of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and that He attributed it to the pronoun of Allah, the Exalted, only in view of it being created by Him, glory be to Him, as if he said: "You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in it." ﴿Indeed You are the Knower of the unseen.﴾

611

- It is a confirmation of the content of the two clauses, both explicitly and implicitly, because of the restriction (*hasr*) it contains, whose indication is affirmation. So it confirms ﴿You know what is in my self﴾, because what selves conceal is among the unseen matters, and the negation follows from it. So it confirms "I do not know what is in Your self," because that is also unseen. The implication of the negation is that no one other than Him, exalted is His majesty, knows the unseen.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 117:

His saying, ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), as Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said, placed to explain what came from him (peace be upon him). It includes, in the most emphatic and forceful manner, the non-occurrence of the said statement from him, since it rules out the occurrence of all statements other than what he was commanded to say. Thus the non-occurrence of the statement, as explicitly mentioned, is included in it by primary inclusion. According to some, the meaning is: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me," except that it was said, "I did not say to them," out of regard for good manners, lest he make his Lord and himself jointly commanders, and in observance of what occurs in the interrogation. This is indicated by the insertion of (an) (the explanatory "an") in His saying, ﴿an-i'budu Allaha rabbi wa rabbakum﴾ ("that worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord").

It is not objected that the verb "amara" (to command) takes its object directly only rarely, as in the line:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded with."

Likewise, what is interpreted in this way (i.e., the object is taken as a command) is not objectionable, because, as Ibn Hisham said, it does not follow that when one thing is interpreted as another, it must take the same transitivity, as they have stated explicitly, since transitivity is judged by the wording. Yes, it has been said regarding taking "an" as explanatory of the verb of command mentioned with its complement, like "amartuka bihadha an qum" (I commanded you with this: stand up), that it was examined either by way of analogy, because each of them dispenses with the other, or by way of usage, because it has not been found. What was mentioned by way of analogy was examined, because the first does not dispense with the second and the second does not dispense with the first; and explanation after ambiguity has evident importance. Ibn al-Munir claimed that interpreting this statement as a command is a burden with no benefit behind it, but there is room for discussion in this.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the statement be taken in its literal sense, and that (an u'budu) is either a predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "it is: an u'budu," or is in the accusative governed by an implied "a'ni" (I mean). It was also said that it is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to the pronoun in (bihi). This was objected to on the ground that in al-Mughni he explicitly stated that explicative apposition in nouns (jawamid) is equivalent to the adjective in derived nouns (mushtaqqat); just as the pronoun is not described by an adjective, it is not followed by an explicative apposition. It was answered that this is among matters in dispute, and many grammarians permitted it, and what is in al-Mughni his commentators have indicated its refutation. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, a substitute of the whole from the whole. Al-Zamakhshari rejected this in al-Kashshaf on the ground that the replaced noun is in the status of being set aside and dropped, so the relative clause would be left without a returning pronoun once it is dropped. It was answered that the preferred position is that the replaced noun is not in the status of being dropped absolutely; rather its dropping may be considered in some rulings, as when it occurs as a subject, where the predicate goes to the substitute, as in: "Zayd, his eye is beautiful," and one does not say "beautiful" (masculine singular in agreement with Zayd). It may also be said that not every replaced noun is like this; rather, that is specific to when the substitute is a substitute of error (badal ghalat). Some answered that although the dropping would leave the relative clause without a returning pronoun, there is no harm in it, because the apparent noun stands in its place, as in the line:

"And you are the one in Allah's mercy I hope for."

It is not hidden that there is dispute over the validity of the apparent noun standing in place of the pronoun here. It was also permitted that it be a substitute for "ma amartani bihi" (what You commanded me with).

It was objected that "ma" is the object of the verb of saying, and it must be either a quoted sentence, or something that conveys its meaning, or something whose wording is intended; and since the worship is a substitute, it is the object of the saying, though it is not one of these matters. Thus one does not say, "I said to them only the worship." In al-Intisaf it is stated that although worship is not said, the command to it is said, and the relative clause with "an" plus the command verb has the command implied with it; so here one says: "I said to them only the command to worship," and there is no doubt about its validity, because the command is something said, indeed a saying. Moreover, making worship a thing said is not far-fetched, in the manner of His saying: ﴿then they return to what they said﴾, i.e., the matter they said, a saying related to it, and His saying: ﴿and We shall inherit what he says﴾, and similar examples. In al-Fawa'id it is stated that the meaning is: "I said to them only His worship," i.e., adhere to His worship; so this is what is meant by ﴿what You commanded me with﴾. It is valid that this sentence be a substitute for ﴿what You commanded me with﴾ in that it has the status of the intended meaning, since it is something said, while ﴿what You commanded me with﴾ is singular in wording but a sentence in meaning. This is not free from strain.

It was permitted to keep the saying in its meaning, with (an) being explanatory either of the verb of saying or of the verb of command. It was objected that the verb of saying is not explained but rather what follows it of sentences and the like is related by it; and that the verb of command is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, and it is not valid to explain it with ﴿worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾, but rather with "worship Me" or "worship Allah," and similar. This was answered that it is possible that it is a narration in meaning, as if he (peace be upon him) related the meaning of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in other words; and as if Allah, the Exalted, said to him (peace be upon him): "Command them to worship Me," or He said to them through the tongue of Jesus (peace be upon him): "Worship Allah, the Lord of Jesus and your Lord." When Jesus (peace be upon him) related it, he said: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord," and he referred to the apparent name by its pronoun, as Allah, the Exalted, said in narrating from Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿He said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾ and ﴿He who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth with it pairs of various plants.﴾ For Moses (peace be upon him) does not say "We brought forth," but rather "Allah brought forth." Yet when Allah related it from him (peace be upon him), He returned the speech to Him, glorified is His dignity, and attributed the bringing forth to His own Essence, the Mighty and Majestic, in the manner of the speaker and not of the narrator, even though the beginning of the speech is narration. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿They will surely say: "The Mighty, the Knowing created them"﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and We revived with it a dead land﴾, and other examples.

Abu Hayyan said: It is possible that the explained part is ﴿worship Allah﴾, and ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾ is from the speech of Jesus (peace be upon him) by an implied supposition, meaning, not as an attribute of Allah, His name being exalted. Ibn al-Sa'igh relied on this and made it parallel to His saying: ﴿We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah﴾ according to one opinion. In the Amali of Ibn al-Hajib: when a narrator relates a speech, he may describe the one reported about with what is not in the speech of the one it is reported from. Al-Halabi and al-Safaqusi found this improbable, while it is what fairness requires.

It was said regarding the first (view): some permitted the occurrence of (an, explanatory) after the word of saying without restricting it to what has the meaning of saying, so it would then serve as an explanation of it. But you know that there should be no disagreement that the quoted speech is connected with the explanatory particle, because what is said is in the accusative place as object, while the explanatory sentence has no place in the i'rab. So perhaps the intent of some is merely the occurrence, and committing that the quoted matter is omitted, namely the reported matter, and this is an explanation of it: i.e., "I said to them nothing but what was said," so reflect. The words of the scholars have spread widely here.

﴿And I was a witness over them﴾, i.e., a watcher, who observes their conditions and urges them to act according to the content of Your command without intermediary, and a witness to their conditions, of belief and disbelief. (Over them) as Abu al-Baqa' said is connected with "witness." Perhaps the fronting is for the reason already mentioned many times. ﴿As long as I remained among them﴾, i.e., the period of my continuance among them. ﴿But when You took me up﴾, i.e., You took me by raising me to the sky, as one says "I took the money" when one has received it. This was narrated from al-Hasan, and the majority hold it.

According to al-Jubba'i, the meaning is "You caused me to die," and he claimed that his raising (peace be upon him) to the sky was after his death; and the Christians adopted this view. The discussion of this has already passed. ﴿You were the watcher over them﴾, i.e., the guardian who observes, so You prevented whom You willed to preserve from opposition by guiding to the proofs and alerting them to them through sending the Messenger and sending down the signs, and You abandoned whom You abandoned among the astray, so they said what they said. It was also said: the watcher means the one who oversees and witnesses. The meaning of the two sentences: as long as I remained among them I was witnessing their conditions, so I could explain them; but when You took me up, You were the one witnessing that, not anyone else, so I do not know their condition and cannot explain it. It is not hidden that the first is more fitting to the context. Some verifiers have stated that the watcher and the witness here have one meaning, namely what the witness was first explained as, but the expression was varied to distinguish between the witnesses and the watchers, because his being a watcher (peace be upon him) is not like the watcher who prevents and compels, but rather like the witness over the one witnessed against, and his prevention is by mere speech; whereas He, exalted is His dignity, is the one who prevents with compulsion through proofs and clear evidence. (You) is a pronoun of separation or emphasis, and (the watcher) is the predicate of "kana" (was). It is also read "al-raqibu" (nominative), on the basis that it is the predicate of "anta," and the clause is the predicate of "kana." (Over them) in both readings is connected with "the watcher."

His glorified saying: ﴿And You are over all things a witness.﴾

It is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it, and it contains, according to what is said, an announcement that He, glorified is He, was the true Witness over all while he (peace be upon him) was among them. (Over) is connected with "witness," and the fronting is for the sake of the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 118:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾. The meaning is: if You punish them, no objection can be raised against You for punishing them, because You are their absolute Owner, and there is no objection to the absolute Owner regarding what He does with His possession. It has also been said that the meaning is: if You punish them, none of them is able to repel that from himself, because they are Your servants, the slaves held in the captivity of Your dominion, and what can the power of a slave amount to beside the power of his owner? It has also been said that the meaning is: if You punish them, then they deserve that, because they are Your servants who have worshipped other than You, opposed Your command, and said what they said. This has been attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, but it is far from the composition of the verse. Yet it is not far-fetched that the verse contains an allusion to it.

﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾.

That is: if You forgive them for what they did, You will not be subject to any incapacity or any disgrace in that. Indeed You are the Powerful, the Capable over all possibilities, of which reward and punishment are among the parts. (The Wise) is the One who does not will or do anything except what contains wisdom. Forgiveness of the disbeliever does not lack a sound rationale of wisdom, because forgiveness is good in rational terms for every criminal. Indeed, the greater the criminal's offence, the better it is to pardon him, since that falls under generosity; although punishment is better in the judgment of the Sharia from other aspects. The non-forgiveness of the disbeliever is by the ruling of the explicit text (nass) and the consensus (ijma') (the agreement of the scholars), not because of an inherent impossibility in it, such that the conditional structure with (in) (if) and its dependence would be impossible.

The Imam has reported that the forgiveness of shirk (associating partners with Allah) is permissible according to us. The majority of the Basrans among the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: because punishment is the right of Allah, Exalted is He, over the sinner, and there is no harm to Allah, glory be to Him, in dropping it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi that the meaning of the verse is: if You punish them, by causing them to die in their Christianity, then the punishment is due for them, for they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, by bringing them out of Christianity and guiding them to Islam, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise. This is the statement of 'Isa, peace be upon him, in this world. End.

It is not hidden that this is contrary to what the context (sibaq) and the flow of the discourse (siyaq) require. It has been said that the division (tardid) is in relation to two groups, and the meaning is: if You punish them, that is, those of them who disbelieved, then they are Your servants; and if You forgive them and pardon those of them who believed, then indeed You etc. This is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning of what they stated is that in His saying, Glory be to Him, ﴿and if You forgive them etc.﴾, there is no implicit request for forgiveness; rather, it is for showing His power and wisdom, glory be to Him. That is why He, Glory be to Him, said (the Mighty, the Wise) rather than (the Forgiving, the Merciful), although the apparent context would call for both.

As for what has come in the reports, which Ahmad in al-Musannaf, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed one night and recited the verse until morning, bowing with it and prostrating with it: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ etc. When he reached morning, I said: O Messenger of Allah, you did not stop reciting this verse until morning. He said: I asked my Lord, Glory be to Him, for intercession, and He granted it to me, and it will be attained, if Allah the Exalted wills, by whoever does not associate anything with Allah the Exalted." And what Muslim reported, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Husn al-Zann, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and others reported from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the saying of Allah, Glory be to Him, concerning Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, they have indeed led many people astray; so whoever follows me, he is of me﴾ (until the end of the verse), and the saying of Him, Mighty and Majestic, concerning 'Isa son of Maryam: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants, and if You forgive them﴾ etc. Then he raised his hands and said: O Allah, my ummah, my ummah! And he wept. So Allah, may His mercy be glorified, said: O Jibril, go to Muhammad (ﷺ) and say to him: Indeed We will gladden you concerning your ummah, and We will not grieve you." And what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said to the Prophet (ﷺ): May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah, you stood last night with a verse from the Qur'an, meaning this verse, and with you was a Qur'an that, if some of us had done this, we would have been blamed for it. He said: I supplicated Allah, Glory be to Him, for my ummah. He said: And what were you answered? He said: I was answered with what, if many of them had known of it, they would have abandoned prayer. I said: Shall I not give good news to the people? He said: Yes. Then 'Umar said: O Messenger of Allah, if you send this to the people, they will rely on it and abandon worship. So he called out to him: Return! And he returned." These do not constitute proof that the verse contains an implicit request for the forgiveness of the disbeliever, since it is not far-fetched from him (ﷺ) to supplicate for his ummah and to seek intercession for them in this composition, but in the manner which 'Isa, peace be upon him, intended by it. It is possible that he (ﷺ) borrowed that from the Qur'an, conveying through it the purpose he intended; and this was not his first borrowing, upon him be blessings and peace, for some scholars have stated explicitly that the supplication of opening the prayer (du'a' al-tawajjuh) according to the Shafi'is is of this kind, and prayer does not preclude supplication. What Muslim and those with him reported does not contain more than that these mentioned reports are traces of the extent of his (ﷺ) compassion for his ummah, so he supplicated for them with what he supplicated; and that does not depend on the verse containing an implicit request for the forgiveness of the disbeliever.

Then, the scholars have a lengthy discussion concerning the secret of mentioning these two noble names in the verse, since the relation of their fit to the context of what we have linked them with was unclear. So much so that it is related of some reciters that he changed them due to the weakness of his intellect, so he would recite: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, until he was imprisoned and beaten seven hundred lashes (durar). And it occurred to some of the heretical critics of the Qur'an (al-mala'ida) that the fitting reading is what occurred in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, as Ibn al-Anbari related; and you have come to know one of their justifications for that.

It has been said: the mention of these two (names) is by way of precaution (ihtiras), because leaving off the punishment of the offender may be due to incapacity in power, or to negligence that contradicts wisdom; so their mention averts the suspicion of that. In the Amali of al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam, it is stated that (the Mighty) here means the One who has no equal. The meaning is: and if You forgive them, indeed You are the One who has no equal in Your forgiveness and the vastness of Your mercy; and You are most worthy of mercy and most deserving of forgiveness and concealment; (the Wise) who does nothing except in its proper place, and they deserve that because of Your bounty and their weakness. This clearly indicates that there is an implicit request for forgiveness in the verse, and I do not think you would say so. Some have claimed that the two names are connected to both conditions, not to the second alone; in that case, the fit of the two names has no cover, since whoever has the power to act and to refrain is Mighty and Wise. It has been mentioned that this is more suitable, more precise and more fitting for the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 119:

﴿Allah said﴾ This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) with which He concludes the narration of what He related of what will occur on the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, and it indicates its outcome and final destination. The use of the past tense (sighat al-madi) is because it is certain. The meaning of Allah's saying, immediately after the answer of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, is that it points to his truthfulness within an explanation of the state of the truthful ones among whom he is counted. By this, his fear of the form of that question is also removed from him, peace be upon him, not that its removal is the intended purpose of the statement, as has been said.

﴿This﴾ i.e., the present day, ﴿is a Day on which the truthful will benefit﴾ i.e., those who persist in truthfulness in the matters required of them, the greatest of which is the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) that we are concerned with, and the laws and rulings related to it, from the Messengers who speak the truth and sincerity and who call to that. Through this the testimony to the truthfulness of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, is attained, and also of the nations who affirmed those noble ones, upon them be blessings and peace, and who followed them in belief and action. Through this is achieved the encouragement of the listeners, which is the aim of the narration, to believe in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Their truthfulness, i.e., regarding what was mentioned, is in this world, since it is what entails benefit and recompense on that day. It has been said: in the Hereafter.

By "the truthful" is meant the nations, and by their truthfulness is meant their truthfulness in testifying for their prophets regarding the delivery of the message, and this benefits them because they fulfilled in it the right of Allah, the Exalted. But this is as you see. It has been said: what is meant is their continuous truthfulness throughout their life in this world until their end, so that what was mentioned may be a testimony to the truthfulness of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, in what he said in answer to the question, according to what the context requires, and the benefit is considered in terms of its realization in this world.
Page 72
And the correspondence with what the context requires is considered in terms of its establishment and the occurrence of some of its particulars in the Hereafter. The continuous quality is the universal matter, which is the attribute of truthfulness. This does not entail the problematic implication that the otherworldly truthfulness is a factor in the recompense, nor is it necessary to make otherworldly truthfulness a condition for the benefit of worldly truthfulness and for being rewarded for it. Perhaps what preceded suffices without this, as is not hidden from the attentive reader. It has been said: by "the truthful" are meant the prophets, and by their truthfulness is meant their truthfulness in this world through delivering the message, and the context of the verse would be a testimony to the truthfulness of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, in his saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me﴾. You know that this purpose is achieved even under the assumption of generalization and more.

It has been said: the intended truthfulness is truthfulness in this world, except that by "the truthful" are meant the nations, and the statement is directed to refute the request of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, for forgiveness from Him, glorified and exalted be He, as if it were said: "This is a Day on which only the truthfulness of the truthful benefits them, and nothing else; so there is no forgiveness for these." It is not hidden that the generalization does not contradict the statement being directed toward what was mentioned, on the assumption of accepting that.

The demonstrative ﴿This﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿Day﴾ in the nominative is its predicate; this is the reading of the majority. Nafiʿ alone read "Yawma" in the accusative, on the basis that it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of ﴿qāla﴾ (said), and ﴿This﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "the speech of ʿIsa, upon him be peace," or "truth," or the like; or it is a stable adverbial phrase that functions as the predicate. The meaning: "This, which has passed, namely the answer of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, or the question and answer, takes place on the Day when it benefits." It has been permitted that ﴿This﴾ be the subject and ﴿Day﴾ its predicate, and it is built on the fatha, on the basis that the adverbial noun is indeclinable when it is annexed to a verbal clause, even if it is otherwise declinable. This is the view of the Kufans, and Ibn Malik and others chose it, while the Basrans do not permit indeclinability except when the clause annexed to it begins with a past verb, as in the poet's saying: "In a time when I reproached gray hair for youth."

They also attached to this a negated verb, and they explain this reading according to one of the aforementioned possibilities.

Al-Aʿmash read ﴿Yawmun﴾ with nominative and tanwin, as the predicate of ﴿This﴾, and the clause after it is its attribute, with the returning pronoun elided. He read ﴿ṣidqahum﴾ in the accusative, so that the subject of ﴿yanfaʿu﴾ is the pronoun of Allah, the Exalted; and ﴿ṣidqahum﴾, as Abu al-Baqaʾ said, is either an object of purpose (maful lahu), i.e., "for their truthfulness"; or an accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "by their truthfulness"; or an absolute infinitive (masdar muʾakkad); or a direct object in the sense of "they speak the truth," like your saying "I said to him the battle," and the meaning is "they realize the truthfulness."

﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ This is an explanation of the benefit, and for this reason it is not conjoined to it by a conjunction; as if it were said: "What is their benefit?" and it was answered: "For them is everlasting bliss and eternal reward." His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ is an explanation that He, exalted be He, has bestowed upon them other than what was mentioned, namely His good pleasure, glorified and mighty be He, beyond which there is no end, as His saying, glorified be He, indicates: ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾, for there is nothing more honorable than Him to which the necks of hopes are stretched. ﴿That﴾ is an indication of attaining His good pleasure, exalted be His majesty, as some of the verifiers have chosen; or it refers to all that preceded, as chosen in al-Bahr; and to this points what was related from al-Hasan. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾

- which no description can encompass, and which cannot be reached by any sought-after object that approaches it at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 5, verse 120:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them.﴾ This establishes the truth and alerts to what it contains of placing the adverbial phrase, which conveys exclusivity, before the predicate, against the lie of the Christians and the corruption of what they claimed concerning the Messiah and his mother, peace be upon them both.

It was also said: it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) based on a question arising from the preceding discourse, as if it had been said: "Who possesses that, so that He may grant it to them?" Then it was answered: "To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens, etc." So He is the Owner and the One Able to grant. Its remoteness is not hidden. In choosing *ma* (what) over *min* (who), which is specific to rational beings, if *ma* is taken to include everything, there is consideration, as it has been said, of the original usage, and an indication of the equality of the two groups in the impossibility of lordship, just as they are equal in the reality of being lordly servants. And if *ma* is taken to be specific to non-rational beings, as the report of Ibn al-Za'bari, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates, then it is an alert to the utter deficiency of their rank from divinity. In giving precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones, contrary to what is known, there is what is not hidden of degrading their worth. ﴿And He is Able over everything﴾ among things, ﴿Competent.﴾

- That is, Exceedingly capable in power. Al-Ghazali (Imam al-Ghazali) explained it as the meaning by which a thing exists as empowered, through the determination of will and knowledge, occurring in accordance with them. He explained the one described by it absolutely as the One who originates every existent with an origination that is singular and by which He is independent of the help of others, and there is none such but Allah, the One, the Subduer. The adverbial phrase is connected to an implied verb, and the fronting is for the sake of the rhyme (fasila). What is in the mention, at the end of this surah, of Allah's greatness, might, subjugation, and exaltedness is not hidden, as an excellent conclusion.

Abu 'Ubayd related from Abu al-Zahrawiyya that 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote at the end of al-Ma'ida: "To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing."
